A webhook is the other system calling me when something changes, so it is fast and cheap. Polling is me asking on a schedule. I prefer webhooks, but they can be missed, duplicated or arrive out of order, so I verify the signature, answer quickly and often keep a slower poll as a catch-up check.
What does idempotent mean, and why does it matter in an integration?
Your grasp of the idea that makes retries safe.
Running the same request twice has the same effect as once; it lets you retry without creating duplicates, often through an idempotency key.

An idempotent operation gives the same result whether it runs once or five times. In HTTP, PUT and DELETE are meant to be idempotent and POST is not. Since networks fail and I retry, I send a unique key with each create request, or check for an existing record first, so a retry never makes a second invoice.
How do you store and handle the credentials your integrations use?
Whether you treat API keys and tokens as the security risk they are.
A secrets manager, not code or spreadsheets; a service account with only the access needed; rotation; tokens never written to logs.

Keys go in a secrets manager or the platform's encrypted store, never in the code repo. I use a dedicated service account, not my own login, so nothing breaks when someone leaves. I ask only for the scopes the job needs, plan for rotation, and make sure logs mask tokens and headers.
Walk me through mapping customer records from a CRM into a billing system.
How you approach data mapping beyond matching field names.
A written field-by-field map, agreed with both owners, covering types, formats, required fields, picklist values, IDs and what happens to bad data.

I list every target field and find its source, with the owner of each system. Then I check types and formats: dates, currencies, phone numbers, state codes. Picklists need a value-by-value table. I decide which system owns the ID and store the other system's ID on each record, and I agree what to do when a required field is empty.
The API you call starts returning HTTP 429. What do you do?
Whether you know rate limiting and how to back off politely.
429 means too many requests: honor Retry-After if sent, back off with growing waits plus jitter, and reduce the call rate by batching or caching.

429 means I am over the rate limit. First I honor the Retry-After header if the API sends one. Otherwise I retry with exponential backoff and a little random jitter so jobs do not all retry at once. Then I fix the cause: use bulk endpoints, cache lookups, and spread the load under the published limit.
A team asks you to automate a manual process. How do you decide if it is worth it?
Your judgement on what to automate and when not to.
Watching the work first; weighing frequency, time saved and cost of errors against build and upkeep; a stable process and a plan for exceptions.

I sit with the person who does it and watch a full run, exceptions included. Then I estimate hours saved per month, the cost of their mistakes, and what building and maintaining it costs me. If the process changes every week or half the cases are exceptions, I fix the process first or automate only the clean part.
What would you monitor on an integration that runs every 15 minutes?
Whether your monitoring catches silent failures, not just errors.
Run heartbeat, error rate, record volume against normal, lag or data age, and regular reconciliation of counts between systems.

Errors alone are not enough; the worst failure is a job that stops running and logs nothing. I alert if no successful run has happened in, say, 45 minutes, if volume drops far below normal, or if the newest synced record is too old. A daily count comparison between both systems catches what slips through.
A nightly sync uses "updated since last run" and some records never arrive. What could be wrong?
How you debug incremental sync logic, a classic source of quiet data loss.
Suspects like time zone mismatch, clock skew, records changed during the run, and pagination issues; fixes like an overlap window with dedupe.

First I compare a missing record's timestamp with the cursor. Common causes: one side stores UTC and the other local time, a record was updated while the job ran, or pagination skipped items when sorting changed between pages. I usually save the cursor from the source's own clock and re-read a small overlap window, then dedupe by ID.
One record keeps failing and blocks the whole queue. How do you handle it?
Whether you can isolate bad data without stopping good data.
Retry a few times, then move it aside to a dead-letter queue with the error, alert, keep processing the rest, and replay after the fix.

After a few retries I move it to a dead-letter queue or error table with the payload and the error message, and the rest of the queue keeps flowing. Someone gets an alert with enough detail to act. Once the data or code is fixed, I replay it. I also check whether it is one bad record or the first sign of a format change.
An order is created in system A, but the call to system B fails. How do you keep them consistent?
How you handle partial failure across two systems with no shared transaction.
No pretending it is atomic: durable record of the step, safe retries, compensation or manual review if it never succeeds, and reconciliation.

There is no transaction across two APIs, so I plan for this. I record that the order needs to reach B, often in an outbox table saved with the order, and a worker retries with an idempotency key. If B still refuses, I either reverse the step in A or flag it for review, depending on the business rule. A daily reconciliation catches anything left over.

automotive-engineer.heading: Automotive engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between understeer and oversteer?
Whether you know the basics of vehicle dynamics.
Front versus rear tires reaching the grip limit first, and why production cars are tuned toward mild understeer.

Understeer is when the front tires reach their grip limit first, so the car turns less than the driver asks and pushes wide. Oversteer is when the rear tires let go first and the back steps out. Most production cars are tuned for mild understeer at the limit, because a normal driver handles it by easing off, while oversteer can lead to a spin.
When do you use a worst-case tolerance stack and when do you use RSS?
Your grasp of tolerance stack-up and its assumptions.
Knows what each method assumes and picks worst case for critical fits, RSS for long stacks with capable processes.

Worst case adds every tolerance at its limit, so parts always fit but tolerances get tight and costly. RSS, root sum of squares, assumes independent, centered, normal dimensions and predicts a smaller spread. I use worst case for safety-critical fits or short stacks, and RSS for long stacks where the supplier processes are proven capable.
How does a new vehicle show it meets the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards?
Whether you understand how US safety compliance works.
Self-certification by the manufacturer before sale, with NHTSA testing afterward, so engineering records are the evidence.

The standards are minimum performance rules issued by NHTSA, covering things like braking, occupant protection and lighting. NHTSA does not approve vehicles in advance. The manufacturer certifies each vehicle complies before sale, and NHTSA later buys and tests vehicles to check. So our test data and records are what we stand on if a compliance test fails.
What is a design FMEA, and when in a program do you start it?
How you use FMEA as a design tool, not as paperwork.
Starts early enough to change the design; knows severity, occurrence, detection and that AIAG-VDA uses action priority.

A design FMEA lists each function, how it can fail, the effect, the cause and the controls. I start it once the concept is set, before drawings freeze, so it can still change the design. We rate severity, occurrence and detection. Under the AIAG-VDA method, action priority replaced RPN, so a high severity item gets action even when occurrence is low.
How is an ASIL assigned under ISO 26262?
Your knowledge of functional safety for vehicle electronics.
Hazard analysis rating severity, exposure and controllability, giving ASIL A to D or QM.

ISO 26262 is the functional safety standard for electrical and electronic systems in road vehicles. In the hazard analysis we rate each hazardous event for severity, exposure and controllability. Together they give a level from ASIL A, the lowest, to ASIL D, the highest, or QM when normal quality processes are enough. Higher levels demand more rigor in design and verification.
A prototype loses CAN messages now and then. What do you check first on the bus?
Whether you can troubleshoot vehicle networks in a methodical way.
Termination resistance check with power off, then scope and error frames, then the harness and connectors.

With power off, I measure resistance between CAN high and CAN low. Two 120 ohm terminators in parallel should read about 60 ohms. About 120 means one is missing; near 40 suggests an extra one. Then I scope both lines for signal shape, log error frames with a bus tool, and flex the harness at connectors while watching for drops.
Drivers report a boom in the cabin around 1800 rpm on a four-cylinder car. How do you approach it?
Your NVH knowledge and ability to link engine orders to frequencies.
Identifies second engine order at 60 Hz, measures with order analysis and looks for a body or driveline resonance near it.

A four-cylinder four-stroke fires twice per crank revolution, so second order dominates. At 1800 rpm the crank turns 30 times a second, so second order is 60 Hz. I would record with microphones and accelerometers on a run-up, run an order analysis, then look for what resonates near 60 Hz, like an exhaust hanger, a mount or a body panel mode.
A suspension bracket cracks on the durability rig at 60% of its target life. What do you do?
How you find the root cause instead of adding material.
Studies the fracture and the loads before redesigning, and matches the fix to the cause.

I would not just make it thicker. First I find where the crack started and look at the fracture surface; beach marks point to fatigue. Then I compare design loads with loads measured on the rig, check material certificates and weld quality, and rerun the FEA at that spot. The fix follows the cause: a bigger radius, a weld change or a new load path.
Your FEA predicts a stress 30% lower than the strain gauges measure. How do you handle it?
How you correlate simulation with test honestly.
Questions both test and model, fixes errors with a physical reason and never tunes numbers just to match.

I treat both as suspects. On the test side I check gauge location, calibration and fixture stiffness. On the model side I check boundary conditions, mesh at the hot spot, material data, and joints like welds and bolts, which are often simplified. I correct what is wrong for a physical reason, not adjust inputs until they match, and I document the correlation.
A supplier part passes the spec, but your own tests show it is marginal, and launch is in six weeks. What do you do?
Your judgement when schedule pressure meets technical risk.
Gets the data, quantifies the risk and brings options to the program; the decision is made and recorded, not ignored.

Passing the spec on paper does not end it. I would compare our test with the spec to see why ours is harder, and ask the supplier for capability data. If the risk is real, I take it to the program with options: containment, extra inspection, a limited deviation or a short delay. The decision gets written down; I would not stay quiet to protect the date.

avionics.heading: Avionics engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between DO-178C and DO-254?
Whether you know the two main design assurance guidelines and where each one applies.
DO-178C covers airborne software; DO-254 covers complex airborne electronic hardware such as FPGAs and ASICs.

DO-178C is the guidance the FAA accepts for airborne software: plans, requirements, code, verification and traceability, scaled by level. DO-254 does the same job for electronic hardware, mostly complex parts like FPGAs and ASICs. An FPGA design written in VHDL falls under DO-254, not DO-178C, even though it looks like code.
When would you choose ARINC 429 over MIL-STD-1553, or the other way round?
Your working knowledge of the data buses common in aircraft.
429 is a simple one-way bus with a single transmitter; 1553 is a faster, two-way, command-response bus with a bus controller and dual redundancy.

ARINC 429 is one transmitter talking to up to 20 receivers over a twisted pair, at 12.5 or 100 kilobits per second. It is simple and common in airliners, but a two-way link needs a second bus. MIL-STD-1553 runs at 1 megabit, with a bus controller polling up to 31 remote terminals on a dual redundant bus, so it suits military and space systems with many boxes.
How is the Design Assurance Level of a function decided?
Whether you understand that the assurance level comes from the safety assessment, not from preference.
From the failure condition: the safety assessment classifies the worst effect of the function failing, and that sets the level from A to E.

It starts with the functional hazard assessment. We ask what happens to the aircraft and the people on board if the function fails or misbehaves. Catastrophic points to level A, hazardous to B, major to C, minor to D, no safety effect to E. Architecture can change it: with truly independent channels, some items can be developed at a lower level under the ARP4754 rules.
What is MC/DC coverage, and why is it required for Level A software?
Your grasp of structural coverage, a core part of verifying critical software.
Each condition in a decision is shown to change the outcome on its own; this finds untested logic that statement and branch coverage miss.

Modified condition/decision coverage means every condition in a decision has been shown to change the result on its own, with the others held fixed. For 'if A and B', I need tests where flipping only A, and flipping only B, each flips the outcome. Branch coverage can pass with fewer tests and miss a condition that never mattered. In a catastrophic function, that hidden logic is the risk.
How do you lay out the wiring for two redundant channels of a flight-critical system?
Whether you design so that one event cannot take out both channels.
Physical separation of the harnesses, separate connectors and power sources, so a single fire, chafe or cut cannot disable both channels.

Redundancy only works if one event cannot reach both channels. I route channel A and channel B in separate bundles, ideally down opposite sides of the airframe, through separate connectors, fed from separate power buses. I keep them away from high-power wiring and check the routes against zone hazards like fluid leaks. Then I review it on the real harness, not only on the drawing.
A cheaper commercial part would save weeks, but it is only rated to 70 °C. Would you use it?
Your judgement on part selection, temperature ratings and derating.
Not without evidence: compare the rating with the real worst-case temperature, the derating rules and obsolescence, and treat any up-screening as a documented risk.

Not on its face. I would check the worst-case temperature inside the box, including a hot day on the ground with cooling off, and apply our derating rules. If it truly stays well under the limit with margin, it may work. If not, up-screening a commercial part is costly and still a risk. I would also check its production life, since an obsolete part forces a redesign and requalification.
Your unit fails the radiated emissions test a week before qualification. What do you do?
How you troubleshoot an EMI failure under schedule pressure without hiding it.
Find the source by frequency, fix the root cause, document it and rerun; no quiet test-setup tweaks to scrape a pass.

First I look at the frequencies: a peak at a clock harmonic points to the processor, a broad hump to a switching power supply. With a near-field probe on the bench I find which board or cable radiates. Often it is a cable shield grounded through a pigtail instead of all around at the connector. I fix that, record the change, tell the program the date risk, and rerun the full test.
How would you protect a launch vehicle flight computer from single event upsets?
Whether you know how radiation affects electronics and the standard defenses against it.
Error-correcting memory with scrubbing, a watchdog, voting for critical logic, and parts chosen with radiation test data.

A charged particle can flip a bit in memory or a flip-flop. I would use memory with error detection and correction, plus a scrubber that rereads and rewrites it so single errors do not build up. In the FPGA, triple modular redundancy for critical logic, and configuration scrubbing if it is SRAM-based. An independent watchdog resets a hung processor, and I pick parts with heavy-ion test data.
Two airspeed channels disagree in flight. How should the system decide which one to trust?
Your understanding of monitoring and voting in redundant sensor systems.
With two sources you can detect a split but not always tell which is wrong; you need a third source, reasonableness checks, or a clear flag to the crew.

With only two, a miscompare tells me something is wrong, not which one. So the design needs more information: a third sensor to vote, or a check against independent data like groundspeed, attitude and engine power. If the logic still cannot decide, it should not guess. It flags the disagreement to the crew and hands the functions that depend on airspeed back to the pilot.
Two months before certification, the systems team asks for a new function in a Level A FPGA. How do you respond?
How you handle a late change to a critical design without breaking the certification evidence.
A change impact analysis first: what requirements, verification and safety analyses it touches, the reverification cost, and an honest schedule answer.

I do not say yes or no on the spot. I do a change impact analysis: which requirements change, what logic and timing are affected, which tests must be rerun, and whether the safety assessment changes. At Level A that can mean redoing a large part of verification. I give the team the cost and date in writing, and suggest a later release if the aircraft can certify without it.

backend-engineer.heading: Backend engineer questions
qs: When should an API return 401 and when 403?
Whether you know the basic HTTP status codes that every client of your API depends on.
401 means the caller is not authenticated; 403 means the caller is known but not allowed. Bonus: sometimes 404 is safer than 403.

I return 401 when the request has no valid credentials, like a missing or expired token, so the client knows to log in again. I return 403 when I know who the user is but they lack permission. If even admitting the resource exists leaks information, I return 404 instead.
Which HTTP methods are idempotent, and why does it matter to you as the server author?
Your grasp of HTTP semantics and what clients and proxies are allowed to assume about retries.
GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not, and PATCH is not guaranteed to be. Clients may retry idempotent calls, so the server must honor that.

GET, HEAD, PUT and DELETE are idempotent: doing them twice leaves the same state as once. POST is not, and PATCH only is if I design it that way. It matters because clients and gateways may retry those calls on a timeout, so a PUT that appends a row instead of replacing it breaks the contract.
How do you store dates and times in a backend system?
Whether you avoid the time zone bugs that corrupt data quietly.
Instants stored in UTC with a time-zone-aware type, converted only at display. Future local events also keep the user's named time zone.

For moments that already happened, like when an order was placed, I store an instant in UTC, for example timestamptz in Postgres, and convert to local time only in the display layer. For a future event like a 9 a.m. weekly meeting, I also store the zone name such as America/Chicago, because daylight saving can shift the UTC offset.
How should a service store user passwords?
Your basic security practice for the most sensitive data a backend holds.
Never plain text or reversible encryption: a slow, salted password hash like Argon2id, bcrypt or scrypt, through a trusted library.

I never store the password itself or encrypt it in a way we could reverse. I hash it with a slow algorithm built for passwords, like Argon2id or bcrypt, with a unique salt per user, using a well-known library. Fast hashes like SHA-256 alone are wrong here because attackers can try billions of guesses quickly.
Offset pagination or cursor pagination: which do you pick for a large list, and why?
Whether you understand how pagination behaves on big, changing tables.
Offset gets slower on deep pages and skips or repeats rows when data changes; a cursor on an indexed, unique sort key stays fast and stable.

For a large or busy list I use a cursor. With OFFSET 100000 the database still reads and throws away those rows, and new inserts shift pages so users see duplicates. With a cursor I return the last created_at and id, then query rows after that pair, ordered the same way and backed by an index. Offset is fine for small admin tables.
What is the difference between a liveness check and a readiness check, and what should each one test?
How you make a service behave well under an orchestrator and a load balancer.
Liveness failing means restart the process; readiness failing means stop sending traffic. Liveness should not depend on the database or other services.

A failed liveness check tells the platform to restart the container, so I keep it simple: is the process responding at all. A failed readiness check only takes the instance out of the load balancer, so that is where I check that it can serve, like a warm connection pool. If liveness checked the database, one database blip would restart every instance at once.
Two requests withdraw from the same account balance at the same moment. How do you keep the balance correct?
Whether you can spot and prevent a lost update between concurrent requests.
Not read-then-write in app code: an atomic conditional UPDATE, a row lock with SELECT FOR UPDATE, or optimistic locking with a version column.

If both requests read 100, subtract, and write back, one withdrawal is lost. The simplest fix is one atomic statement: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 30 WHERE id = 7 AND balance >= 30, then check rows affected. If the logic is more complex, I lock the row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside a transaction, or use a version column and retry on conflict.
Your queue consumer sometimes gets the same message twice, and one bad message keeps crashing it. How do you handle both?
Your experience with real message queues and their delivery guarantees.
Assume at-least-once delivery and make processing idempotent; cap retries and move poison messages to a dead-letter queue with an alert.

Most queues deliver at least once, so I make the handler idempotent: I record the message ID in the same transaction as the work and skip IDs I have seen. For the bad message, I limit retries, then send it to a dead-letter queue so the rest of the queue keeps moving. An alert on that queue means a person looks at it the same day.
Requests start timing out, and the logs say the service cannot get a database connection from its pool. What do you do?
How you diagnose connection pool exhaustion instead of guessing.
Find what holds connections (leaks, slow queries, long transactions) before resizing; keep pool size times instances under the database limit.

First I look at what the connections are doing: in Postgres, pg_stat_activity shows long-running queries and sessions idle in transaction. Often it is a code path that does not return the connection, or a slow call made while a transaction is open. Raising the pool size is a last step, because pool size times the number of instances must stay below the database connection limit.
You are on call. At 3 a.m. the error rate jumps, and a deploy went out an hour ago. Walk me through what you do.
Your judgement on call: restoring service first, then finding the cause.
Confirm impact, roll back the suspect deploy quickly instead of debugging live, tell people, then investigate and write it up.

I check the dashboards to confirm real users are affected and that errors line up with the deploy. If they do, I roll back right away rather than debug at 3 a.m.; a working old version beats a clever fix. I post in the incident channel what I did and when. Once errors drop, I gather logs for the morning and we write a blameless review.

barista.heading: Barista questions
qs: What is the difference between a latte, a cappuccino and a flat white?
Whether you know the core espresso drinks well enough to make them and explain them to a guest.
Clear differences in milk volume and foam, and how that changes the taste, said simply enough for a customer.

All three are espresso with steamed milk. A latte has the most milk and a thin layer of foam, so it tastes mild. A cappuccino traditionally has much more foam and less milk. A flat white is smaller with a thin, velvety microfoam, so the coffee tastes stronger. I follow our shop's recipe for exact sizes.
Walk me through how you steam milk for a latte.
Your hands-on technique at the steam wand.
Purging, adding air early, rolling the milk, stopping at the right temperature, and cleaning the wand right away.

I pour cold milk into a clean pitcher and purge the wand. I start with the tip just under the surface to add a little air, then sink it slightly so the milk spins and the bubbles get fine. I stop around 140 to 150°F, check with a thermometer if unsure, then wipe and purge the wand at once.
How should coffee beans be stored so they stay fresh?
Whether you understand what makes coffee go stale.
Air, light, heat and moisture are the enemies: airtight, cool, dark storage, small batches, and grinding just before brewing.

I keep beans in a sealed, opaque container away from the machine's heat and out of sunlight. I don't put the working stock in the fridge, because moisture gets in. I only fill the hopper with what we'll use soon, rotate older bags first, and grind to order, since ground coffee goes stale fast.
How do you handle milk during a shift so it stays safe?
Your food safety habits with dairy and milk alternatives.
Keeping milk cold, pouring fresh for each drink, never topping off old milk, and checking dates and fridge temperature.

Milk stays in the fridge at 41°F or below until I need it, and it goes back right after I pour. I don't re-steam leftover milk or top off an old pitcher; I rinse and start fresh. I check dates and rotate first in, first out, and if the fridge reads warm I tell the lead so we can check the milk.
A ticket has a latte, a cold brew and a pour-over. In what order do you make them?
How you plan your workflow so every drink is ready at about the same time.
Starting the slowest drink first, overlapping tasks, and finishing the quick cold drink last so nothing sits.

The pour-over takes longest, so I start it first: grind, rinse the filter, and start the bloom. While it drips, I pull the shots and steam milk for the latte. Cold brew is just ice and a pour, so I do it last. All three go out together, and nothing sits melting or cooling on the counter.
Your espresso shot runs much faster than usual and tastes sour. What do you do?
Whether you can diagnose and fix a shot that is off.
Knowing fast and sour means under-extracted, checking dose and tamp first, then grinding finer, one change at a time.

Fast and sour usually means the water rushed through and didn't pull enough out of the coffee. First I check that my dose is right and my tamp is level. If those are fine, I grind a bit finer and pull another shot, changing only one thing at a time. I taste each shot until it's back to balanced.
A regular says her latte tastes burnt today. What do you do?
How you handle a quality complaint and look for the cause.
Remaking it without argument, then checking likely causes: overheated milk, bitter shots, or a dirty wand or machine.

I thank her and remake it right away. Then I look for the cause. Burnt taste often means milk steamed too hot, so I check my temperature. I also taste a shot, because a bitter, over-extracted shot can taste burnt, and check that the wand and group heads are clean. If the batch of beans is off, I tell the lead.
A customer says he has a severe nut allergy and asks what is safe. How do you answer?
Whether you take allergies seriously and are honest about cross-contact.
No promises the bar can't keep: name the risk of shared equipment, offer what reduces it, and let the customer decide.

I tell him honestly that we use nut milks and nut syrups on the same bar, so I can't promise anything is nut-free. I can check ingredient labels with him, use a freshly washed pitcher, and purge and wipe the steam wand first. Then he decides. I don't guess about ingredients; if I'm unsure, I say so.
You hand out a drink and then realize you used dairy milk instead of the oat milk ordered. What do you do?
How you own a mistake that could affect someone's health.
Stopping the customer right away, being honest, remaking it in clean equipment, and fixing the step that caused the error.

I go to the customer right away, before they drink more, and tell them plainly I used the wrong milk. Some people order oat milk because of an allergy or intolerance, so I don't wait. I remake it with a clean pitcher and a purged wand. Then I check how it happened, like an unclear label, and fix that.
Walk me through cleaning the espresso machine at close.
Whether you know the daily cleaning that keeps the machine working and the coffee tasting right.
Backflushing with cleaner then rinsing, soaking baskets and portafilters, scrubbing gaskets, cleaning the wand, following the maker's steps.

Following the maker's steps for our machine, I put a blind basket in each group, backflush with espresso machine cleaner, then backflush with plain water until it runs clear. I soak portafilters and baskets, scrub the group gaskets with a brush, soak and purge the steam wand, and wipe down the drip tray and grinder.

battery-engineer.heading: Battery engineer questions
qs: What does a C-rate mean, and why does it matter when you pick a cell?
Whether you know the basic unit used to talk about charge and discharge current.
A correct definition with a worked number, and the link between high rates, heat and usable capacity.

1C is the current that would charge or discharge the rated capacity in one hour, so 5 A for a 5 Ah cell, and 2C is 10 A. At higher rates the cell heats more and gives less usable capacity. Power cells use thinner electrodes to handle high rates. Energy cells use thicker ones to store more.
When would you choose LFP cells over NMC cells?
Your grasp of the trade-offs between the two main lithium-ion chemistries.
Names energy density, cycle life, thermal stability and cost, plus the flat LFP voltage curve that makes state of charge harder to read.

I pick LFP when cycle life, safety margin and cost matter more than weight, like grid storage or standard-range cars. It is more thermally stable and uses no nickel or cobalt. NMC stores more energy per kilogram. LFP has a very flat voltage curve, so the battery management system needs a better state of charge estimate.
What are the main ways a lithium-ion cell loses capacity over its life?
Whether you understand degradation mechanisms, not just the symptom.
Names SEI growth, lithium plating and loss of active material, and the conditions that speed them up.

The SEI, a thin film on the anode, keeps growing and uses up lithium. Charging fast or in the cold can plate metallic lithium on the anode. Electrode particles crack and lose contact. High temperature and long storage at high state of charge speed most of this up, so I watch both in the usage profile.
Explain passive and active cell balancing, and what balancing cannot fix.
How you understand cell matching in a pack and the limits of the BMS.
Passive burns off excess charge as heat; active moves it between cells. Balancing corrects charge mismatch, not a weak or faulty cell.

Passive balancing bleeds the highest cells through resistors, so the energy turns into heat. It is simple and cheap. Active balancing moves charge between cells with inductors, capacitors or transformers, which wastes less but costs more. Neither fixes a cell with lower capacity or a leak. It only hides it for a while.
How does a BMS estimate state of charge, and where does that estimate go wrong?
Your knowledge of SOC methods and their error sources.
Coulomb counting corrected by open-circuit voltage or a model-based filter, with sensor drift and flat voltage curves named as error sources.

Most systems count the current in and out, which drifts because of small current sensor offsets. They correct it with the open-circuit voltage after a rest, or with a model such as a Kalman filter. On LFP the voltage barely changes in the middle range, so corrections mostly happen near full or empty. Cell aging also shifts the model.
After a week at rest, one parallel group in a pack reads 40 mV lower than the others. What do you do?
How you investigate a possible internal short instead of hiding it.
Rules out measurement errors first, then treats unusual self-discharge as a possible safety risk and does not just keep balancing it.

First I check the measurement: sense wire, connector and the BMS channel against a calibrated meter. If the drop is real, I look at the logs to see how fast it falls. Faster self-discharge can mean a small internal short. I flag the pack, keep it out of service and test that group alone rather than letting balancing cover it up.
Your cycle test shows a sudden capacity drop on every channel on the same day. How do you handle it?
Whether you suspect the test setup before you report a result.
Recognizes that real aging is gradual and differs by cell, and checks chamber, calibration, fixtures and software before trusting the data.

Cells do not all fade on the same day, so I suspect the rig. I check the chamber temperature log, since a colder chamber lowers measured capacity. Then I check calibration records, fixture contact resistance and any software update. If I find the cause, I mark the affected cycles in the data and note it in the report.
A customer wants faster charging at freezing temperatures. How do you respond?
Your judgement on lithium plating risk against a customer request.
Explains plating risk in the cold and offers safe options: preheating, current limits by temperature and SOC, and testing to prove it.

In the cold the anode takes lithium in slowly, and high current can plate metal lithium, which costs capacity and can cause shorts. I would offer to heat the pack before charging and to set a current limit that depends on temperature and charge level. Then we prove it with cycle tests and teardowns before we promise faster charging.
Walk me through how you design a pack so one cell in thermal runaway does not spread to the rest.
How you design and test for propagation, the main safety risk in large packs.
Covers spacing and thermal barriers, a vent path for hot gas, electrical protection and a test where one cell is forced into runaway.

I put heat barriers like mica or aerogel between cells and leave enough spacing. Hot gas needs a planned vent path away from other cells and from people. Fuses and cooling help limit the damage. Then we prove it: we force one cell into runaway with a heater and check that neighbors stay below their runaway temperature.
What does a new lithium-ion pack need before it can ship, and how do you plan for it?
Your knowledge of transport testing and how design changes affect it.
Names UN 38.3 as required for shipping under DOT rules, its main test types, and that design changes may require retesting.

US DOT rules require lithium cells and batteries to pass the UN 38.3 tests before shipping. They cover altitude, thermal cycling, vibration, shock, external short circuit and overcharge. I build the samples and test time into the schedule early. If we change the cells or the design in a meaningful way, I check whether we must test again.

bi-developer.heading: BI developer questions
qs: What is a star schema, and why do BI tools work well with it?
Whether you know the data model most dashboards are built on.
Facts hold the numbers at one level of detail and dimensions hold the descriptions. Simple joins make filters predictable and queries fast.

A star schema has one fact table in the middle, like sales lines with amounts and quantities, and dimension tables around it for date, product, store and customer. Each dimension joins to the fact on one key. Filters flow from dimension to fact, so totals behave predictably and the tool can query it fast.
What does the grain of a fact table mean, and why do you decide it first?
Whether you design tables so sums come out right.
Grain is what one row represents. Fixing it first prevents double counting and sets which questions the table can answer.

The grain is what a single row stands for, for example one product on one order line. I settle it before adding columns, because mixing grains, like putting order-level shipping cost on every line, makes sums wrong. I can always roll line-level data up to daily store totals, but I can never drill below the grain I chose.
In Power BI, when do you use a measure and when a calculated column?
Your grasp of how the model calculates, beyond dragging fields onto a page.
Columns are computed at refresh and stored per row; measures are computed at query time under the current filters. Totals and ratios belong in measures.

A calculated column is worked out row by row when the data refreshes and is stored in the model, so I use it for things I slice or filter by, like an age band. A measure is calculated when a visual asks for it, under the filters on the page, so sales, margin % and growth are measures. Too many columns also bloat the model.
Why build a separate date table instead of using the dates in the fact table?
Whether you know what time comparisons need to work.
A full, continuous calendar makes period comparisons work, holds fiscal periods and holidays, and lets several fact tables share one date filter.

Year-to-date and same-period-last-year calculations need a continuous calendar, and the fact table skips days with no sales. In a date table I add fiscal year, week numbers and a holiday flag once. In Power BI I mark it as the date table, and both sales and budget join to it, so one slicer filters both.
Import or DirectQuery, extract or live connection: how do you choose?
How you weigh speed against data freshness.
A trade-off of speed, freshness, data size and load on the source, decided per report rather than by habit.

Import copies the data into the model, so visuals are fast and all features work, but data is only as fresh as the last refresh. DirectQuery asks the source each time, so it is current, but slower and it loads the database. For a daily sales review I import. For an operations screen showing the last few minutes, I use DirectQuery on a well-tuned source.
The total row of your table shows a margin of 240%, while every row is around 30%. What went wrong?
Whether you spot a ratio being added up instead of recalculated.
Ratios cannot be summed or simply averaged across rows. The total must be total profit divided by total revenue.

The margin percentages are being added up, not recalculated. A ratio cannot be summed, and a plain average of ratios is also wrong. I would write the measure as total profit divided by total revenue, so each row and the total compute it from their own sums. The total then shows a weighted figure near 30%, matching the finance number.
How would you set up one report so each regional manager sees only their own region?
Your knowledge of row-level security.
Row-level security driven by the user's login and a mapping table, tested as real users, rather than separate copies of the report.

I use row-level security. A small table maps each manager's login email to the regions they may see, and a role filters the region dimension by the signed-in user, so every visual is limited. Managers get viewer access, since in Power BI workspace editors are not restricted by these roles. I test by viewing as a few users before release.
A sales rep moves from the East region to the West in June. How should last year's sales report show their history?
Whether you know how to keep history in a dimension that changes.
Knows slowly changing dimensions: Type 1 overwrites, Type 2 adds a new row with dates. The choice follows what the business wants to see.

It depends on what the business wants. If old sales should stay with East, I use a Type 2 dimension: the rep gets a new row with a new key and valid-from and valid-to dates, and new sales point to the new row. If all history should follow the rep to West, Type 1 simply overwrites the region. I confirm which before building.
The overnight refresh failed and the executive meeting starts at 9. What do you do?
How you handle a failure when people are about to rely on the numbers.
Warns users first, finds the cause in the refresh log, fixes or reruns, and shows what date the data covers. Then prevents a repeat.

First I tell the meeting owner the dashboard shows yesterday's data, so nobody presents stale numbers as current. Then I read the refresh error; often it is an expired password or a source that timed out. If I can fix and rerun in time, I do and check key totals. Afterward I add a failure alert and a last-refreshed date on the page.
Finance and Sales define revenue differently, and both want the dashboard to match their number. How do you handle it?
Your judgement on metric definitions that people disagree about.
Does not pick a side alone: shows both definitions, gets the metric owner to decide, and names and documents each metric clearly.

I put both definitions side by side: Finance counts revenue when it is recognized, Sales when the deal is booked. I show where they differ on a real month. Then I ask the metric owner, often the finance lead, to decide what the dashboard calls revenue. If both are needed, they get distinct names, like booked sales and recognized revenue, defined in one place.

billing-specialist.heading: Billing specialist questions
qs: What is the difference between a credit memo and a debit memo?
Whether you know the two basic tools for correcting a customer's balance.
A credit memo lowers what the customer owes and a debit memo raises it, and both tie back to the original invoice.

A credit memo reduces the customer's balance, for example when we overbilled or they returned goods. A debit memo increases it, for example when we underbilled a shipping charge. Either way I reference the original invoice number so anyone can follow the change later.
What do you check before an invoice goes out?
Your habits for catching errors before the customer sees them.
Checks against the contract or order: rates, quantities, dates, PO number, tax status and the right billing contact.

I compare the invoice to the contract or order: rate, quantity, service dates and any agreed discount. I confirm the PO number if the customer requires one, whether they are tax exempt with a certificate on file, and that it goes to the right billing contact. A missing PO alone can hold up payment for weeks.
A customer upgrades from a $300 monthly plan to a $450 plan with 10 days left in a 30-day cycle. How do you bill the change?
Whether you can calculate a prorated charge and explain it.
The price difference times the share of the cycle left, shown clearly on the invoice so the customer can check it.

The difference is $150 a month. With 10 of 30 days left, that is $150 times 10/30, so $50 for the rest of this cycle. The next invoice is the full $450. I put the proration on its own line with the dates, so the customer sees why the amount is not a round number.
Why should you not simply edit or delete an invoice that has already been sent?
Whether you understand the audit trail behind billing records.
Sent invoices stay on record; you correct them with a credit memo and a new invoice so the history is complete.

Once the customer has it, it is part of both companies' records. If I edit it, their copy and ours no longer match, and an auditor sees a changed or missing number. I issue a credit memo against the wrong invoice and send a corrected one that references it, so anyone can see what happened.
How do you read an accounts receivable aging report, and what do you do with it?
How you use the aging report to decide where to spend your time.
Balances grouped by days past due; you work the oldest and largest first and look for disputes behind them.

It groups open balances by how long they are past due: current, 1 to 30, 31 to 60, 61 to 90 and over 90 days. I start with the oldest and largest. Often an old balance is not a slow payer but a billing problem, like a wrong rate or missing PO, so I check that before it goes to collections.
A customer says they were billed twice. Walk me through how you handle it.
How you investigate a common complaint before acting.
Find out whether it is two invoices, two payments or a misread statement, fix it the right way, then find the cause.

First I find out what doubled: two invoices for the same service, or one invoice paid twice. A duplicate invoice I credit. A double payment I refund or keep as a credit, whichever the customer chooses. Then I look for the cause, like a contract entered twice, so it does not happen again.
A payment arrives with no remittance information. What do you do?
Whether you apply cash carefully instead of guessing.
Hold it as unapplied cash, match it by amount and payer, confirm with the customer, never force it onto an invoice.

I record it as unapplied cash so it is on the books but not on the wrong invoice. Then I match it by payer name and amount against open invoices. If one invoice matches exactly, I still confirm with the customer's AP team. Guessing wrong makes one invoice look paid and another look late.
A customer emails you their full credit card number to fix a failed payment. What do you do?
Whether you protect card data even when a customer sends it to you.
Do not use or store the number from email, follow the company's card data procedure, and send the customer to a secure channel.

I do not process it from the email. I follow our card data procedure, which usually means deleting the email and reporting it to whoever owns security. Then I reply without quoting the number, and ask the customer to update the card through our secure portal or by phone. Card rules do not allow full card numbers sent by plain email.
A customer disputes an invoice because a sales rep promised them a discount that is not in the contract. How do you handle it?
Your judgement when the contract and a promise do not match.
No credit on your own authority; verify with the rep, get documented approval, then correct and update the contract.

I tell the customer I am looking into it and give a date. I ask the rep what was promised and in writing. If a manager approves the discount, I issue a credit memo with the approval noted and make sure the contract or order gets updated. If not, I explain the contract terms to the customer clearly.
You find a setup error that has underbilled a customer for six months. What do you do?
How you handle your company's own mistake that will upset a customer.
Fix the setup, size the gap, escalate before contacting the customer, and let management decide on back-billing with the contract in mind.

I correct the setup so this month bills right, then work out the exact shortfall, say $4,200. I take it to my manager with the contract terms before telling the customer. If we back-bill, the customer hears it from a person first, with an explanation and maybe a payment plan, not as a surprise invoice.

biologist.heading: Biologist questions
qs: Why does an experiment need both a positive and a negative control?
Whether you understand what makes a result interpretable.
The negative control shows background and false signal; the positive control proves the assay can detect a real effect that day.

The negative control tells me what 'nothing happening' looks like, so I can spot background signal or contamination. The positive control proves the assay worked that day. If my sample shows no signal and the positive control also failed, I learned nothing about my sample. I only learned the run failed.
What is the difference between a biological and a technical replicate, and which one is your n?
Whether you know what your statistics actually count.
Biological replicates are independent samples; technical ones repeat a measurement. Only biological replicates count as n, which avoids pseudoreplication.

A biological replicate is an independent sample: a different mouse, or a separate culture grown and treated on its own. A technical replicate is the same sample measured again, like three wells of one cDNA in qPCR. Technical replicates show how precise my measurement is. Only biological replicates go into n; otherwise I overstate my confidence.
Your cells look fine under the microscope. Why would you still test them for mycoplasma?
Your cell culture habits and awareness of hidden contamination.
Mycoplasma does not cloud the medium and cannot be seen by routine microscopy, yet it changes cell behavior. Regular testing, for example by PCR, catches it.

Mycoplasma are tiny bacteria with no cell wall, so they don't make the medium cloudy and I can't see them at normal magnification. They still change growth and gene expression, which can quietly ruin data. I test new lines on arrival and then on a schedule, usually by PCR, and keep new lines separate until they test clean.
In qPCR, how do you choose and check a reference gene?
Your grasp of normalization in gene expression work.
The reference gene must be stable across your conditions, checked in your own samples, ideally using more than one. Primer efficiency matters for the delta-delta Ct method.

I don't assume a common housekeeping gene is stable; some shift with treatment. I test a few candidates in my own samples and keep the ones whose Ct, the cycle where signal crosses the threshold, barely moves across conditions. I also run a standard curve per primer pair, because delta-delta Ct assumes efficiencies near 100% and close to each other.
You want to start work with a new organism or viral vector. How do you decide what containment it needs?
Whether you follow biosafety review before starting new work.
A written risk assessment guided by the CDC/NIH biosafety manual (BMBL), and approval from the institutional biosafety committee before work begins.

I start with a risk assessment: what the agent is, how it spreads, and what procedures I plan, especially anything that makes aerosols. I check the CDC and NIH biosafety manual for the recommended level, then submit it to our institutional biosafety committee. I wait for their approval and get trained on the specific practices before I start.
Your western blot shows a band at a different size than the protein's predicted weight. How do you work out what it is?
How you troubleshoot an unexpected result instead of guessing.
Considers modifications, splice variants, cleavage and antibody cross-reactivity, then tests with knockout or knockdown lysate.

Predicted weight is only a guide. Glycosylation can make a protein run higher, and cleavage or a splice variant can make it run lower. To check the band is really my protein, I run lysate from knockout or knockdown cells: if the band disappears, it's mine. I'd also try a second antibody that binds a different part of the protein.
Halfway through an animal study, you realize a different dose or procedure would work better. What do you do?
Whether you respect the rules of an approved animal protocol.
Submits an amendment to the IACUC and waits for approval before changing anything; never works outside the approved protocol.

I don't change it on my own, even if it seems minor. Any change to doses, procedures or animal numbers needs an amendment approved by the IACUC, the animal care and use committee, before I do it. I'd write up the reason, talk with the veterinarian if welfare is affected, and keep to the approved protocol until the amendment is approved.
An experiment that worked last month now fails every time. Walk me through how you find the cause.
How you troubleshoot systematically.
Compares records to list what changed, then tests one variable at a time side by side, with controls.

I go back to my notebook and list what changed: reagent lots, a new antibody vial, cell passage number, a serviced instrument. Then I test one thing at a time, running old and new reagent side by side with a positive control. When this happened to me, a new batch of serum was the cause, and the side-by-side test found it in a week.
You knock down a gene with siRNA and see a strong effect. How do you show the effect really comes from losing that gene?
Your standard for proving specificity, not just getting a result.
Confirms knockdown at the protein level against a non-targeting control, uses two or more independent siRNAs, and ideally a rescue experiment.

First I confirm the knockdown worked, ideally at the protein level, against a non-targeting siRNA control. siRNAs can hit other genes by accident, so I repeat with at least two siRNAs of different sequence. The strongest proof is rescue: I add back a version of the gene the siRNA can't target and check that the effect goes away.
Your PI asks you to drop an outlier and clean up a blot image before a paper is submitted. How do you respond?
Your judgement on data integrity under pressure.
Excludes data only for a documented reason or a rule set in advance. Image changes apply to the whole image, splices are marked, and raw files are kept.

I'd ask the reason. If that sample has a documented problem, like a failed control, I exclude it and say so in the methods. I won't drop it just because it weakens the result. For the image, I can adjust brightness or contrast across the whole image, never one band, and spliced lanes get marked. I keep the raw files to show anyone who asks.

blockchain-engineer.heading: Blockchain engineer questions
qs: What is an account nonce on Ethereum, and how do you fix a transaction that has been stuck for an hour?
Whether you understand transaction ordering at the account level.
The nonce orders an account's transactions, so one stuck transaction blocks the rest. The fix is a replacement with the same nonce and a higher fee.

The nonce counts the transactions an account has sent. Each new one must use the next number in order. A low-fee transaction holds up every later one. I send a replacement with the same nonce and a clearly higher fee, either the same call or a zero-value transfer to myself to cancel it.
What does finality mean, and how is it different in proof of work and in Ethereum's proof of stake?
Your grasp of when a block can be treated as permanent.
Proof of work finality is only probabilistic. Proof of stake finality is economic: reverting a finalized checkpoint would cost at least a third of all stake.

In proof of work, each new block on top makes a reversal less likely but never impossible. Ethereum's proof of stake adds checkpoints. Once two-thirds of the stake votes for one, it is finalized, usually after about two epochs. Reverting it would mean at least a third of all staked ETH gets slashed, so it is final in practice.
You are building the deposit service for an exchange. When do you credit a user's deposit?
How you protect a backend from chain reorganizations.
Credit only after finality or a confirmation depth matched to the amount, and handle the case where a block disappears.

A reorg can replace recent blocks, so a deposit seen at the chain head may vanish. I show it as pending at once and credit it only after its block is finalized. I store the transaction hash and block hash. If the block at that height changes, I re-check the deposit before anything is credited.
Your Ethereum node keeps falling behind the head of the chain. Walk me through how you find the cause.
Your practical skill in running and troubleshooting nodes.
A method: check peers, disk speed, CPU and memory, both clients and the link between them, clock sync, and the logs.

I read the logs of both the execution client and the consensus client first. Then I check the peer count, because few peers means slow sync. Next is disk: a slow drive is the usual cause, so I watch I/O wait. I confirm the two clients connect over the Engine API with the right shared secret, and that the clock is synced by NTP.
You are moving a validator to a new server. What mistake gets operators slashed, and how do you avoid it?
Whether you know the main slashing risk in validator operations.
Running the same keys on two machines leads to conflicting signatures. Stop the old one, confirm it is off, wait, and carry over the slashing protection data.

The classic mistake is the same keys running on two machines, which sign two conflicting messages. I stop the old validator and make sure it cannot restart. I wait a couple of epochs, export the slashing protection history in the standard interchange format, import it on the new server, and only then start it.
Why does a classic Byzantine fault tolerant protocol need at least 3f + 1 nodes to survive f bad ones?
Your understanding of the math behind consensus safety.
Quorums of 2f + 1 out of 3f + 1 always overlap in f + 1 nodes, so at least one honest node is in both and blocks conflicting decisions.

Up to f nodes may be silent, so a node can only wait for n minus f replies. Some of those replies can be lies. With 3f + 1 nodes and quorums of 2f + 1, any two quorums share at least f + 1 nodes. At least one of those is honest, and it will not vote for two conflicting blocks.
A contract lets users act through signed messages that a relayer submits. What do you check in the signature logic?
Whether you can spot signature replay and related flaws in a review.
A nonce, an expiry, and a domain that includes chain ID and contract address, plus a library that rejects malleable signatures.

Without a nonce, the same signature can be submitted twice. Without the chain ID and contract address, it can be replayed on another chain or another deployment. So I look for an EIP-712 domain with both, a per-user nonce, and an expiry. I also want a well-tested recovery library that rejects malleable signatures.
What can go wrong when you upgrade a contract behind a proxy?
Your knowledge of how upgradeable contracts store data.
Storage layout collisions and initializer mistakes, since logic runs in the proxy's storage through delegatecall.

The proxy uses delegatecall, so the new code reads and writes the proxy's storage. If I reorder or remove a variable, data lands in the wrong slot. I only add new variables at the end. Constructors do not run in the proxy, so setup goes in an initializer, and I lock the initializer on the logic contract so no one else can call it.
In a security review, a lending protocol reads its collateral price from one DEX pool. What is the risk, and what do you recommend?
Whether you can recognize oracle manipulation.
A flash loan can move a spot price within one transaction. Recommend a time-averaged or decentralized price source, with staleness and sanity checks.

An attacker can take a flash loan, push the pool price up, borrow against inflated collateral, and repay all in one transaction. I would flag it as critical. I recommend a decentralized oracle feed or a time-weighted average price, plus checks that reject stale prices or sudden jumps outside a set range.
You find an exploitable bug in a live contract that holds user funds. What do you do in the first hour?
How you handle a live security incident with judgement.
Confirm quietly, keep the circle small, use pause or other controls if they exist, and avoid publishing details before the funds are safe.

I confirm it on a local fork, not on the live chain. Then I tell a small trusted group: the lead, the security contact and the key holders. If the contract can be paused, we pause it. We prepare the fix and have it reviewed. Nothing about the bug goes public until funds are safe. Afterward we publish a clear post-mortem.

brand-ambassador.heading: Brand ambassador questions
qs: Walk me through a sampling shift, from the moment you arrive to the moment you leave.
Whether you know the full job, not just the part where you talk to shoppers.
Check-in with the store, setup to the brand's standards, steady engagement, tracked counts, a clean breakdown and a recap sent on time.

I arrive 15 minutes early, check in with the store manager and find my spot. I set up the table the way the brand's photo guide shows, prep samples and take a setup photo. During the shift I keep a tally of samples and sales. At the end I clean the area, pack up, check out with the manager and send my recap the same day.
How do you get someone who is walking past to stop at your table?
Your skill at starting a conversation with a stranger in a few seconds.
A friendly, specific opener from beside the table, not behind it, and reading who has time to stop.

I stand beside the table, not behind it, and make eye contact. Instead of asking “Would you like a sample?”, which gets a quick no, I say something like “Have you tried the new mango flavor yet?” and hold out the cup. If someone is rushing, I smile and let them go. I focus on the people who slow down.
How do you learn a product well before your first event for it?
Whether you prepare ahead and stick to what the brand has approved.
Studying the brand's training and talking points, trying the product, and preparing answers to common questions.

I read the brand's training packet and talking points twice, and I try the product myself so I can describe it honestly. I write down three key points, the price, and questions shoppers are likely to ask, like ingredients and where to buy it. If something isn't in the material, I ask my event manager before the shift, not during it.
A shopper asks if your sample contains peanuts, and you are not sure. What do you do?
Whether you put a shopper's safety ahead of handing out one more sample.
Never guessing. Showing the label, and if it is still unclear, suggesting they skip the sample.

I never guess about allergens. I hand them the package so they can read the ingredient list and allergen statement themselves. If the label is unclear or they still feel unsure, I tell them it's better to skip it today and offer a coupon so they can check later. A missed sample is better than an allergic reaction.
A shopper says a competing brand is cheaper and tastes better. How do you respond?
Whether you can stand behind your product without criticizing another brand.
Agreeing where it is fair, never bad-mouthing the competitor, and naming one honest reason to try yours.

I don't argue or knock the other brand. I'd say, “That one's popular, and price matters.” Then I give one honest difference, like less sugar or more product for the price, and ask them to taste it and decide. If they still prefer the other one, I thank them and move on, so they leave with a good impression of us.
You arrive for a demo and the store manager says nobody told them and you cannot set up. What do you do?
How you handle a booking problem calmly without arguing with the store.
Staying polite, showing the confirmation, calling your agency right away, and accepting the manager's final decision.

I stay polite, since it's their store. I show the event confirmation on my phone and call my event manager while I'm still there. If the manager still says no, I leave without arguing and note the time and the manager's name, so the agency can sort it out with the store and reschedule the event.
A shopper asks if the energy drink you are sampling is safe with her blood pressure medicine. What do you say?
Whether you stay inside approved claims and avoid giving health advice.
No medical advice. Pointing her to her doctor or pharmacist, showing the label, and not pushing a sample.

I tell her I can't give medical advice and that her doctor or pharmacist is the right person to ask, especially with medicine involved. I show her the label with the caffeine content and the warnings so she has the facts to take to them. I don't push a sample on her, even if it costs me a count.
If you post about the brand on your own social media, what do you have to include?
Your knowledge of the FTC rule on disclosing a paid or gifted connection to a brand.
A clear disclosure of the connection, placed where people will see it, and only honest claims.

The FTC expects me to disclose my connection to the brand, whether I'm paid or got free product. I use clear words like “#ad” or “#sponsored” near the start, not buried among hashtags at the end. I also turn on the platform's paid partnership label but don't rely on it alone, and I only say things I believe.
Your goal was 300 samples, but traffic was slow and you gave out 140. What goes in your recap report?
Your honesty in reporting and whether you give the client useful information.
The real numbers, never padded, with the reasons, shopper feedback and a concrete idea for next time.

I report 140, the true number. Padded counts hide the real problem and lead the brand to bad decisions. I'd note the slow traffic, the hours, where my table was, shelf sales if the store shares them, and what shoppers said. Then I'd suggest something specific, like a Saturday slot or a spot near the entrance.
At a wine tasting, one person in a group looks underage and another seems to have had too much. What do you do?
Whether you follow alcohol service rules even when it makes the moment awkward.
Checking ID under state rules and store policy, refusing politely, watching for pass-offs, and not serving anyone who seems intoxicated.

I check ID following state rules and the store's policy, and when in doubt I card. If someone can't show valid ID, I politely say I can't serve them and watch that nobody in the group hands them a cup. I don't serve the person who seems intoxicated and I let the store manager know. The store's license, and often my own permit, is on the line.

brand-designer.heading: Brand designer questions
qs: What is the difference between a logo, a visual identity and a brand?
Whether you know the job is wider than drawing a logo.
The logo is one mark, the identity is the full system of visual assets and rules, and the brand is the reputation people hold.

The logo is the mark itself. The visual identity is the whole system around it: colors, typefaces, imagery style, layouts and the rules for using them. The brand is what people think and feel about the company. The identity supports that, but it cannot create it alone. Most of my work is the identity, built to serve the brand.
What do you put in a brand guidelines document?
Whether you can turn an identity into rules other people can follow.
Logo use, color values for every medium, type, imagery and templates, with clear do and don't examples, kept short enough to be used.

Logo versions and when to use each, clear space, minimum size and examples of misuse. Color values for print and screen: spot, CMYK, RGB and hex. Typefaces with fallbacks, a type scale, imagery and icon style, and real templates. I keep it short and show good and bad examples, because people skim it under deadline.
How do you make sure a logo works from a billboard down to a browser tab?
Your practical testing of a mark across sizes and backgrounds.
A set of logo versions tested at real sizes and in one color, with detail removed as the size drops and a minimum size set.

I test early at 16 pixels for a favicon, in one color, reversed out of a dark background and on a busy photo. I usually end up with a full lockup, a stacked version and a simple symbol for small spaces. I set a minimum size in the guidelines so thin parts never fill in on print or blur on screen.
A client says their brand blue looks different on the website, the brochure and the van. Why, and what do you do?
Whether you understand color across screen, print and other materials.
Screens use RGB light, print uses CMYK or spot ink, other materials differ again; each needs its own specified value, checked on physical proofs.

Screens mix light in RGB, presses mix ink in CMYK, and vinyl on a van is another material again. Some spot colors cannot be matched in CMYK at all. I set one reference color, choose the closest match for each medium, approve physical proofs, and write every value into the guidelines so vendors stop guessing.
What do you check before choosing a typeface for a brand?
Whether you think past looks to licensing, coverage and real use.
Licensing for each use such as desktop, web and app, language and weight coverage, readability at small sizes, and a fallback font.

First the license: a desktop license usually does not cover embedding the font on a website or in an app, so I check each use and the cost as the client grows. Then the character set, in case they need other languages, enough weights, and how it reads small on a phone. I also name a system fallback for email and office documents.
Before you hand over a new logo, what do you do to lower the risk of a trademark conflict?
Whether you know where design work meets legal risk.
Early searches for similar marks in the same field, then a clear handoff to a trademark attorney for a full clearance search.

Early on I run a reverse image search and check competitors and the USPTO trademark database for similar marks in the same industry. If a concept is too close, I drop it. I tell the client this is only a first screen: a trademark attorney should run a full clearance search before they pay for signs and packaging.
You find regional teams using a stretched logo, old colors and their own fonts. How do you handle it?
How you keep a brand consistent without becoming the brand police.
Finds out why the rules were broken, makes the right assets easy to get, then follows up, instead of only sending a reminder.

I ask why first. Usually the right files were hard to find or the templates did not fit their needs. I put approved logos, fonts and editable templates in one shared library, run a short training session and offer a quick review channel. Then I check back after a month. Most misuse stops when the correct way is also the easiest way.
A new CEO wants a complete rebrand. How do you decide between a refresh and starting over?
Your judgement on brand equity versus change.
Weighs what customers already recognize against real business problems, using evidence, and keeps assets that still work.

I start with what the brand already owns in people's minds: a color, a shape, a name. If the problem is dated execution, a refresh keeps that recognition and costs less to roll out. If the company now does something different or the identity hurts trust, a bigger change makes sense. I decide with research and customer feedback, not just taste.
A sign maker printed your logo blurry and in the wrong color. What went wrong, and how do you stop it happening again?
How you own production problems and fix the handoff.
Owns the file package: vector files, outlined type, color values per medium, clear file notes, and a proof check before production.

In my case the vendor had pulled a JPG off the website, and raster files blur when enlarged. I now hand over a package: vector files (SVG, EPS, PDF) with text converted to outlines, PNGs with transparency for screens, a short note on which file goes where, and color values for each medium. I also approve a proof before anything large is produced.
A company buys two smaller brands. How do you decide how they should look next to the parent brand?
Your grasp of brand architecture and the business reasons behind it.
Knows the range from branded house to house of brands, with endorsed brands between, and ties the choice to recognition and strategy.

It depends on brand architecture. In a branded house everything carries the parent name and look. In a house of brands each brand stands alone. In between, an endorsed brand keeps its own identity with a line like “part of” the parent. I ask whether customers value the acquired names, whether they might be sold later, and whether the parent adds trust.

brand-marketing.heading: Brand marketing manager questions
qs: What goes into a brand positioning statement?
Whether you know the basic tool that the rest of brand work is built on.
Target, need, category, point of difference and reason to believe, with an example that makes a sharp choice.

Who we are for, the need we meet, the category we compete in, what makes us different, and why people should believe it. For a meal kit I worked on: for busy parents who want to cook real dinners, it is the kit with 15-minute recipes, because every step comes prepped. If the difference could also describe a competitor, it is not done.
What is the difference between aided and unaided awareness, and why track both?
Your grasp of the basic measures of brand health.
Unaided means naming the brand with no prompt; aided means recognizing it from a list. Unaided shows top-of-mind presence, which matters more when people choose.

Unaided is when I ask which running shoe brands you can name and you say ours without help. Aided is when I show a list and you say you have heard of us. Aided usually grows first and tells me we are known. Unaided is harder to move and tells me we come to mind when someone is about to buy, which is closer to sales.
Walk me through how you write a creative brief for an agency.
How you turn strategy into direction a creative team can actually use.
One clear objective, a real audience, a single message, proof, must-haves and how success is judged, kept to a page or two.

I keep it to one or two pages. What we want people to think, feel or do, and the business problem behind it. Who the audience is, described as people, not a demographic box. One message, not four. The proof that makes it believable, must-haves like logo and legal lines, budget and timing, and how we will judge the work. Then I brief in person and take questions.
You find a regional team using an old logo and its own tagline. What do you do?
How you protect brand consistency without becoming the brand police.
Ask why first, fix it with easy tools and a date, and treat the cause, such as assets that are hard to find or a real local need.

I call the regional lead and ask why before I ask for changes. Often the new files were hard to find or the tagline did not work locally. I send the current assets, agree a date to swap them out, and if their local need is real, we write an approved local line together. Then I fix the asset library so the next team does not make the same mistake.
How do you pick a partner for a co-branded campaign?
Your judgement on fit, value to both sides and risk in brand partnerships.
A shared or wanted audience, values that fit, a clear gain for both sides, and checks on reputation plus contract terms for approvals and exit.

I look for an audience we want but do not yet reach well, and values that sit naturally next to ours. Both sides need a clear gain, or the effort dies after launch. I check their recent press and social history, and the contract covers who approves creative, how each logo is used, and how either side can exit if something goes wrong.
We are paying an influencer to post about our product. What rules apply?
Whether you know the FTC rules for disclosing paid endorsements.
Any material connection, even free product, must be disclosed clearly and conspicuously; claims must be honest and backed up; the brand shares responsibility.

The FTC expects the creator to disclose the relationship clearly in the post itself, where people will see it, like #ad near the start, not lost among hashtags. That applies to free product too, not only cash. The creator must give an honest opinion and cannot make claims we could not back up ourselves. I put this in the contract and check the posts, because the brand is responsible too.
How do you tell whether a dip in your brand tracking survey is real?
Whether you read research data with care instead of reacting to noise.
Check sample size and margin of error, look at the trend over several waves, and ask whether the sample or questions changed before acting.

First I check the margin of error. A two-point drop on a sample of 400 people is usually inside it. Then I look at the trend over several waves, not one. I ask the research team whether the sample mix or question order changed. If the drop holds and lines up with something real, like a competitor launch or fewer searches for our name, I act on it.
The CEO wants to change the logo because it looks dated. How do you respond?
How you weigh years of brand recognition against the wish for something new.
Take it seriously, ask what problem it solves, separate a refresh from a rebrand, and test which cues people recognize before touching them.

I would not say yes or no in the meeting. I would ask what problem we want to solve. Then I would test which of our assets, like the color, the shape or the name, people actually recognize. Usually the answer is a refresh: modernize the type and details, keep the recognized cues. A full rebrand costs a lot and throws away years of memory, so it needs a bigger reason than taste.
Walk me through your first 24 hours after a post from our brand account sparks an angry backlash.
How you handle a brand crisis with speed and sound judgement.
Pause scheduled content, get the facts, bring in legal and leadership, own it plainly if the brand was wrong, then track sentiment and fix the process.

First I pause all scheduled posts and ads so we do not look tone-deaf. I find out who posted it, why, and how far it has spread. I pull in communications, legal and the executive on call. If we were wrong, we say so plainly, say what we are doing about it, and do not argue in the replies. Then I track sentiment daily and change our approval process.
We want to launch a lower-priced product line. Should it carry our main brand name?
Your understanding of brand architecture and the risk of stretching a brand too far.
Borrowed trust weighed against dilution, the options named (master brand, endorsed sub-brand, separate brand), and a decision backed by research.

It depends on what the main name stands for. If we are known for premium quality, a cheap line under the same name can pull down how people see the whole brand. An endorsed sub-brand, a new name “by” us, lends some trust while keeping distance. I would test the options with current and target customers, and weigh the high cost of building a separate brand.

browser-engineer.heading: Browser engineer questions
qs: What is the same-origin policy, and what exactly counts as an origin?
Whether you know the basic security boundary of the web precisely.
Origin is scheme, host and port together; cross-origin reads are blocked unless CORS allows them. Site is a looser idea than origin.
