An origin is the scheme, host and port together. So https://a.example and http://a.example are different origins, and so is the same host on port 8443. A script can send a request to another origin but cannot read the response unless that server allows it with CORS headers. A site is looser: scheme plus registrable domain, so sub.a.example and a.example are same-site.
Walk me through how a browser turns the DOM and CSS into pixels on the screen.
Your grasp of the rendering pipeline, stage by stage.
Style, layout, paint, raster and compositing in order, and the point that a change can restart the pipeline at different stages.

The parser builds the DOM and the style sheets are parsed into rules. Style resolution computes the final style of each element. Layout works out sizes and positions. Paint records drawing commands, the page is split into layers, the layers are rasterized into pixels, often on the GPU, and the compositor assembles the frame. A change can restart the work at style, layout, paint or just compositing.
How does the event loop treat tasks and microtasks, and how can microtasks freeze a page?
Whether you understand when script runs relative to rendering.
One task runs to completion, then the whole microtask queue is drained before rendering; a microtask chain that keeps queueing starves painting.

The loop takes one task, like a click handler or a timer callback, and runs it to the end. When the stack is empty it drains the whole microtask queue, promise callbacks and queueMicrotask work, including microtasks added during the drain. Only after that can the browser render. So a promise chain that keeps adding work blocks painting just like a long loop would.
What is a forced synchronous layout, and how do you avoid it?
Whether you can spot layout thrashing in code and fix it.
Reading geometry after writing styles forces layout immediately; batching reads before writes, or deferring writes to requestAnimationFrame, avoids it.

If code changes a style and then reads offsetHeight or getBoundingClientRect, the browser must run layout right away to give a correct answer. In a loop that writes and reads in turn, that happens on every pass, which is called layout thrashing. I batch all reads first, then all writes, or move the writes into requestAnimationFrame. Profiler traces flag these as forced reflows.
Why does animating transform usually stay smooth while animating width or top stutters?
Your understanding of the main thread versus the compositor.
Geometry changes need layout and paint each frame on the main thread; transform and opacity can often run on the compositor. Extra layers cost memory.

Animating width or top changes geometry, so every frame needs layout and paint on the main thread, and any long script makes it stutter. Transform and opacity can usually be handled by the compositor on its own thread, moving an already painted layer. So I animate transform instead of left, and use will-change sparingly, because every extra layer costs GPU memory.
An extension's content script cannot see a JavaScript variable the page defines. Why, and what would you do?
Whether you know how extension code is separated from page code.
Content scripts run in an isolated world: shared DOM, separate JavaScript globals. Reaching the page means a main-world script and treating its data as untrusted.

Content scripts run in an isolated world. They share the page's DOM but have their own JavaScript globals, so page variables are invisible, and the page cannot tamper with the extension's code either. If I truly need page data, I inject a small script into the main world, for example with scripting.executeScript and world set to MAIN, pass results back with postMessage, and treat them as untrusted.
A tab's memory keeps growing every time a user opens and closes a dialog. How do you find the leak?
How you track down memory leaks in a long-lived page.
Compare heap snapshots around a repeated action, look for detached DOM nodes, and follow the retainer chain to the reference that keeps them alive.

I take a heap snapshot, open and close the dialog a few times, take another, and compare. Growth in detached DOM nodes is the usual sign: removed elements still referenced by a listener, a cache or a closure. The retainers view shows what keeps them alive. Last time it was a resize listener on window that each dialog added and never removed.
Why do browsers put different sites in different processes, and what did Spectre change?
Your understanding of process isolation as a security boundary.
Spectre lets code read memory in its own process via CPU side channels, so the process is the real boundary. Links site isolation to COOP and COEP.

Spectre showed that script can read memory in its own process through CPU side channels, whatever the language checks say. So the only firm boundary is the process. With site isolation each site gets its own renderer process, and cross-site data is kept from reaching it. That is also why SharedArrayBuffer needs cross-origin isolation through COOP and COEP headers, since it enables precise timers.
A fuzzer reports a use-after-free in the renderer. Walk me through what you do.
How you handle a memory-safety security bug from report to fix.
Reproduce and reduce, read the sanitizer stacks, keep the bug restricted, fix the ownership problem rather than the symptom, add a test, consider a backport.

I reproduce it on an AddressSanitizer build and reduce the test case. The report gives three stacks: where the object was allocated, freed and used again. I keep it as a restricted security bug, find who owns the object's lifetime and fix that, not just add a null check. Then I add the reduced case as a regression test and flag whether the fix should go to the stable release.
Your engine follows the spec, but a major site breaks because other browsers behave differently. What do you do?
Your judgement on standards versus web compatibility.
Verify against the spec and shared tests, measure real usage, raise a spec issue when engines and sites agree otherwise, and avoid permanent site hacks.

First I confirm the spec says what we think and check web-platform-tests. Then I measure how many pages hit this path with a usage counter. If the other engines agree with each other and real sites depend on it, I open a spec issue; often the spec changes to match the web. Meanwhile I contact the site, and any site-specific fix gets a plan to remove it.

business-analyst.heading: Business analyst questions
qs: What makes a user story ready for the team to build?
Whether you can write requirements that developers and testers can actually use.
A clear user, need and reason, acceptance criteria that can be tested, and no open questions left on the team's side.

It names who, what and why: as a billing clerk, I want to filter invoices by status so I can chase late ones first. It has acceptance criteria a tester can check, often written as given, when, then. It fits in one sprint, and nobody on the team still has a question about it.
How do you map a current process you have never seen before?
Your method for capturing how the work really runs today.
Talks to and watches the people who do the work, draws it by role, and checks the draft with them, exceptions included.

I start with the trigger and the end point, then interview and shadow the people at each step. I draw it in swimlanes, one lane per role, with decisions and hand-offs marked. Then I walk the draft back with them. That is when I hear 'except on Fridays' or 'when the form is missing', and those exceptions are often where the time goes.
A sales director tells you, 'I need a new report.' What do you ask next?
Whether you dig for the need behind a request.
Asks what decision the report supports, who uses it, how often and what happens today, before talking about columns.

I ask what decision the report will help her make and how she makes it today. Then who reads it, how often, and what action follows. Once a director asked for a 40-column export; the real need was a weekly list of deals stuck over 30 days, and an alert solved it better than a report.
How do you prioritize requirements with stakeholders? Have you used MoSCoW?
How you get people to rank their needs instead of calling everything critical.
Knows MoSCoW (Must, Should, Could, Won't have this time) and ties every Must to a business reason or a hard constraint.

MoSCoW sorts items into Must have, Should have, Could have and Won't have this time. I agree a rule first: a Must is something the release fails without, like a legal need or a blocked process. When everything lands in Must, I ask what happens on day one if this item is missing. That question usually moves half of them down.
Two department heads want opposite things from the same system. How do you handle it?
How you resolve conflicting requirements without quietly taking sides.
Finds the reason behind each request, lays out options with cost and impact, and lets the right decision owner decide, in writing.

I meet each one to understand why they want it, then bring them together with facts. Once, finance wanted approval on every purchase and operations wanted none under a set amount. I showed the volume and delay each option would create. They agreed on a threshold, and the sponsor signed it off in writing.
What is a requirements traceability matrix, and why keep one?
Whether you can prove every requirement was built and tested.
A table linking each requirement to its source, design and tests, so nothing gets lost and the impact of a change is visible.

It is a table where each requirement has an ID and links back to where it came from, like a stakeholder or a regulation, and forward to the design item and the test cases. Before sign-off I check that every row has a passing test. When someone wants a change, the matrix shows me what else it touches.
Halfway through a project, a stakeholder adds a 'small' new requirement. What do you do?
How you handle scope creep without saying no by reflex.
Writes it down, finds the impact on time, cost and other items, and takes it through the agreed change process for a decision.

I write it up and ask why it matters now. Then I check with the team what it costs in time and what it touches. I take that to the product owner: add it and move the date, swap it for something of similar size, or plan it for the next release. Small changes added quietly are how projects slip.
A process has too many errors and nobody agrees why. Walk me through finding the root cause.
Your method for getting from symptoms to causes.
Counts where errors happen first, then uses tools like the five whys or a fishbone diagram, and checks the cause explains the data.

First I count: which step, which team, which type of error. I take the biggest group and keep asking why with the people who do the work, often four or five times. A fishbone diagram helps sort causes into groups like people, methods, tools and data. In one case most errors came from one free-text field; a drop-down cut them by more than half.
During user acceptance testing, users find a requirement you missed. What do you do?
How you own a mistake and fix the habit that caused it.
Owns it, writes and sizes the gap fast, lets the decision owner choose now or later, and changes how requirements are gathered next time.

I say plainly that I missed it, then write the requirement and get an estimate the same day. The product owner decides whether it blocks go-live or waits for the next release. Then I look at why. Last time it was a user group I never interviewed, the night shift. Now I check my stakeholder list against the org chart before I start.

business-development.heading: Business development and partnerships questions
qs: What is the difference between a reseller, a referral partner and an integration partner?
Whether you know the main partnership models and how each one makes money.
Clear lines on who owns the customer, who bills, and how the partner earns, plus when each model fits.

A reseller buys our product and sells it under its own contract, so it owns the billing and earns a margin. A referral partner sends us leads and gets a fee; we close and bill. An integration partner connects its product to ours so joint customers get more value. Money may not change hands at all; the payoff is better retention and new leads.
How do you decide which companies are worth approaching as partners?
How you pick partners through research instead of chasing big logos.
A clear profile: shared customers, a product that complements ours, a partner with real reasons to care, and the size of the chance checked before outreach.

I start from our best customers: what other tools they use and who they buy from. A good partner sells to the same buyers, does not compete with us, and gains something real, like fewer lost deals or a new service to offer. I rank a list by customer overlap and sales reach, then test the top five with short calls before I build a full pitch.
What is a BATNA, and how do you use it in a partner negotiation?
Your grasp of the basic preparation behind any negotiation.
Best alternative to a negotiated agreement. You know yours, estimate theirs before talks, and use it to set a walk-away point.

BATNA means best alternative to a negotiated agreement: what I do if this deal fails. Before talks I write ours down, for example signing a different reseller in that region, and I estimate theirs. That sets my walk-away point. If our alternative is strong I can hold firm on margin. If it is weak, I work to improve it before the meeting, not during it.
Which terms in a reseller agreement do you read most carefully?
Whether you know the contract terms that decide if a channel deal works.
The business terms: margin, territory and exclusivity, minimums, term and exit, support duties, and who keeps the customers when it ends.

Margin and how it is paid, territory, and any exclusivity come first. Then minimum commitments, the length of the term, and how either side can exit. I check who handles first-line support and what happens to the customers if we part ways, since that is where fights start. Our lawyers review liability and indemnity; I make sure the business terms match what we agreed.
How do you get a partner's sales team to actually sell your product?
Whether you know that a signed deal is only the start of a partnership.
Enablement and reasons to care: short training, ready materials, a clear incentive, early joint wins and steady contact with the reps.

Their reps carry many products, so I make ours the easiest to sell. I run a short training on the two use cases that close fastest, give them a one-page pitch and pricing they can quote, and join their first few calls. I make the incentive clear, like a small bonus per deal. When one rep closes, I share that story with the rest of their team.
How do you measure whether a partnership is working?
Your ability to tie partnerships to numbers the business cares about.
Separates sourced from influenced revenue, tracks early signs like activations or registered deals, and compares the return to the cost.

I agree on the measures with the partner before launch. For a reseller, I track partner-sourced revenue, meaning deals they brought us, and influenced revenue, deals they helped close. For an integration, I watch how many joint customers turn it on and how those customers renew. Each quarter I weigh that against what the partnership costs us in time, discounts and support.
A large reseller asks for exclusive rights in its region. How do you respond?
How you trade a big concession for something of equal value.
No flat yes or no: exclusivity tied to targets, limited in time and scope, with a way out if they miss.

I would not refuse outright, but exclusivity has to be earned. I would offer it for one segment or region for twelve months, tied to a new-customer target we set together. If they miss it, the deal turns non-exclusive. I would also keep our right to serve accounts we already work with, so we do not lock ourselves out of our own pipeline.
Two of your resellers claim the same customer. How do you settle it?
How you handle conflict between partners fairly and by the rules.
Applies a clear rule, often deal registration, the same way to both partners, and fixes the gap that caused the clash.

Partners register opportunities with us to claim them, so I check the registration log first: who registered first, and is the claim still active and backed by real work, like a demo. That partner gets the deal. I call the other one myself to explain. If the rules were unclear, I fix them. Splitting the deal to please both only teaches them the rules do not matter.
Six months after launch, almost no one uses your new integration with a partner. What do you do?
How you diagnose a partnership that signed well but is not delivering.
Finds the cause with data and customer calls before blaming the partner, then agrees on a fix plan or an honest wind-down.

I would look at the funnel first: how many joint customers know it exists, how many try it, and where they stop. Then I would call five customers who tried it and five who did not. Often the cause is plain: it is buried in settings, or neither sales team mentions it. I would bring this to the partner with a 90-day plan, and if neither side will invest, scale it back.
You agreed on terms with a partner's business lead, then their legal team sends back changes that cut your revenue share. What do you do?
How you protect an agreed deal without damaging the relationship.
Stays calm, goes back to the person who agreed, separates legal concerns from business terms, and trades rather than gives in.

I would not argue with their lawyer over email. I would call the business lead, point out the change and ask if it was intended. Often legal changed it without knowing what was agreed, which is why I send a written summary after every key call. If they now want a lower share, I treat it as a new request and ask for something back, like a longer term or a volume commitment.

business-operations.heading: Strategy and business operations questions
qs: How would you size the market for a new product line, say scheduling software for dental offices?
Whether you can build a market estimate from logic, not from a number you found quoted somewhere.
A bottom-up count of buyers times a realistic price, checked against a top-down figure, with each assumption stated.

I'd go bottom-up first: estimate the number of dental practices in the US, the share that fit our product, and a realistic yearly price per practice. Then I'd check it top-down against what practices spend on software overall. If the two numbers are far apart, I look for the wrong assumption before I show either one.
What makes a financial model driver-based, and why do planners prefer it?
Whether you build models that others can follow, question and change.
Outputs come from a few business drivers, so changing one assumption flows through the model and leaders can test it.

Instead of typing revenue as last year plus a flat percent, I build it from drivers: leads, conversion rate, average order value, churn. Costs tie to drivers too, like support staff per thousand customers. When sales says conversion will slip, I change one input, the whole plan updates, and everyone can see why the number moved.
How do you write OKRs so they don't turn into a task list?
How you set goals that measure outcomes rather than activity.
The objective states the change wanted; key results are a few measurable outcomes, not activities.

The objective says what we want to change, like 'make onboarding painless for small customers.' Key results measure the result, such as cutting time to first order from ten days to five, not 'launch new onboarding emails.' Tasks belong in the project plan. I keep it to about three key results per objective so teams can focus.
Walk me through how you would run the annual planning cycle for a company of a few hundred people.
Whether you can run a process that spans finance, the leadership team and every department.
Top-down targets meet bottom-up plans, with a published calendar, one template and a set meeting where trade-offs get decided.

Leadership sets top-down targets and priorities, agreed with finance. Each team then submits a bottom-up plan on one template: goals, headcount, spend. I compare the total to the target, and the gap goes to a decision meeting with clear options. I publish the calendar up front, and after approval I set up quarterly check-ins against the plan.
The CEO wants a model for entering a new region by Friday. How do you handle the uncertainty in it?
How you show risk in a model instead of hiding it behind one number.
Base, downside and upside cases, a sensitivity test on the few drivers that matter most, and the break-even conditions stated plainly.

I'd build a simple driver model and run three cases: base, downside and upside. Then I'd flex the two or three inputs that move the result most, like price and time to ramp up, to show which ones really matter. I'd tell the CEO what has to be true for the entry to break even and by when, since that is easier to judge than one confident number.
Revenue came in 8% below plan last quarter. How do you break down the miss?
Your method for variance analysis against a plan.
Split the gap into volume, price and mix, then by segment, and separate a bad forecast from bad execution.

I split the gap into parts: fewer units sold, which is volume; lower prices or more discounts, which is price; and selling more of the cheaper products, which is mix. Then I cut it by region and channel to see where it sits. Last, I ask whether the plan assumption was unrealistic or the business underdelivered, because those need different fixes.
Sales and product both want the same engineers next quarter, and you manage neither team. What do you do?
How you drive a decision when you have no formal authority.
Put both cases in the same terms, show the trade-off with numbers, and bring a recommendation to the person who owns the decision.

I'd meet each leader and get their case in writing: expected impact, cost of waiting, how confident they are. I'd put both on one page in the same units, like revenue at stake, and add options such as splitting the team or doing one after the other. Then I'd take it to the executive who owns the call, with my recommendation, and make sure the decision is written down.
After a forecast goes to the leadership team, you find a formula error that changes the answer. What do you do?
Your honesty and how you handle your own mistakes.
Tell your manager fast, send the corrected figure and what it changes, then add checks so the same error cannot recur.

I'd tell my manager right away and send a correction the same day: the old figure, the new one, and whether it changes the recommendation. I wouldn't wait for someone else to find it. Then I'd fix the cause, for example a range that missed new rows, add a check that totals tie back to the source data, and have a second person review models before they go out.
A project has spent $2 million, it is behind schedule, and its sponsor wants six more months. How do you advise?
Whether you judge an investment on what lies ahead, not on money already spent.
Set the sunk cost aside; compare the remaining cost and value with other uses of the same people, and agree stop criteria up front.

The $2 million is spent whatever we decide, so it shouldn't drive the choice. I'd ask: from today, what does finishing cost, what is it likely to return, and what else could the same team do? If it still wins, I'd back the extension with milestones agreed now and a point where we stop if they're missed. I'd talk it through with the sponsor privately first.

business-systems.heading: Business systems questions
qs: What is the difference between configuring a system and customizing it?
Whether you know the long-term cost of each kind of change.
Configuration uses the vendor's built-in settings; customization adds code. Code costs more to test, maintain and carry through upgrades.

Configuration means using what the vendor built: fields, page layouts, approval rules, settings. Customization means writing code or scripts on top. I start with configuration, because custom code has to be tested again at every vendor release, and someone has to own it after I leave.
Walk me through a procure-to-pay process and where the system controls it.
Your grasp of a core business process that these systems run.
The steps in order, with the controls: approvals by amount, and a three-way match of order, receipt and invoice before payment.

Someone raises a requisition, it is approved based on the amount, and it becomes a purchase order to the vendor. When goods arrive, the warehouse records a receipt. The invoice comes in and the system matches it against the order and the receipt. If quantities and prices agree within tolerance, it goes to payment; if not, it is held for review.
A team says they want the new system to work just like the old one. How do you gather their requirements?
How you get to the real need behind a request.
You ask about outcomes and pain points, watch the work being done, and separate true requirements from old habits.

I sit with them while they do the work and ask why at each step. Often a step exists only because the old system could not do something. I write each need as an outcome, like “the approver sees the budget left before approving,” and agree on priorities with the process owner, not just the loudest user.
How do you move a change from the sandbox to production?
Your release discipline in a live business system.
Built and tested in a sandbox, signed off by the business owner, released in a planned window, with a rollback plan and a note to users.

I build in a sandbox that is a recent copy of production and test the change plus the processes around it. A key user signs off in user acceptance testing. It goes through change approval, deploys in a quiet window, and I check it live right after. I keep a rollback plan ready and tell users what changed.
How do you set up system access for a new accounts payable team?
Whether you apply least privilege and segregation of duties.
Roles built from job duties, only the access needed, and no single person who can both create a vendor and approve paying it.

I build roles from what each job actually does, not by copying a coworker's access. Clerks can enter invoices; a separate approver releases payments. The same person should not be able to add a vendor and pay it, since that opens the door to fraud. I document the roles and review access with the manager on a set schedule.
A sales VP asks you for full admin rights so he can fix his own reports quickly. What do you do?
How you say no to a senior person while still solving the problem.
You decline admin rights, explain the risk briefly, and give him what he needs another way, such as permission to build reports.

I would not give admin rights. One wrong click could change data or security for the whole company, and auditors would flag it. I would ask what reports he needs, give him permission to build and edit reports in his own folder, and offer a short session to show him how. Usually that is what he wanted all along.
Walk me through how you plan a data migration from an old system.
Your method for moving data without losing or corrupting it.
Decide what to move, clean and remove duplicates first, map fields, run test loads, and reconcile counts and totals before and after.

First I agree with the data owners what to bring: often open records and a few years of history, not everything. We clean the source and remove duplicates, then map each old field to a new one. I run at least two test loads in a sandbox and reconcile record counts and money totals, like open receivables, so finance signs off before the final load.
Two months after go-live, half the sales team still tracks deals in spreadsheets. What do you do?
How you handle poor user adoption after a launch.
You find out why before pushing, fix real friction, train by role, and get managers to run their meetings from the system.

I ask a few reps why. Often entering a deal takes too many clicks or a field they need is missing. I fix what I can quickly, like trimming required fields, and run short sessions for each role. Then I ask the sales manager to run the weekly pipeline review from the system's dashboard only. Once the meeting depends on it, the spreadsheets fade.
Orders entered in the CRM have stopped showing up in the ERP, and nobody got an error. How do you find the problem?
How you troubleshoot an integration between two systems.
You check the integration logs, find when it broke and what changed, fix the cause, resend the missed records, and add an alert.

I find the last order that synced and check the integration logs from that time. Common causes are an expired password or access token, a new required field in the ERP, or a value like a new product code with no mapping. Once fixed, I reprocess the failed records, check for duplicates, and set up an alert so a failed sync emails us next time.
An automation you released updated 4,000 customer records with the wrong value. What do you do?
How you own and recover from your own mistake in a live system.
Stop the automation first, size the damage, restore from field history or a backup, tell those affected, and close the gap in the process.

First I turn the automation off so the damage stops spreading. Then I use field history or a backup export to see which records changed and their old values, and restore them with a controlled update tested on a few records first. I tell my manager and the affected teams right away, then add a test case and a peer review step so it cannot slip through again.

buyer.heading: Buyer and purchasing agent questions
qs: A supplier offers terms of 2/10 net 30. What does that mean, and would you take the discount?
Your grasp of payment terms and what they cost.
The correct meaning, plus the point that skipping the discount is expensive borrowing, so it is usually worth taking if cash allows.

It means we can take 2% off if we pay within 10 days. Otherwise the full amount is due in 30. Giving up 2% to keep the cash 20 more days works out to roughly 37% a year, so I would take it whenever our cash position allows and make sure accounts payable knows the invoice is time-sensitive.
Explain the three-way match and why it matters.
Whether you understand the control that protects payments.
PO, receiving record and invoice must agree on item, quantity and price before payment. Differences get resolved, not paid.

Before we pay, three documents have to agree: the purchase order, the receiving record that shows what actually arrived, and the supplier's invoice. If we ordered 500, received 480 and were billed for 500, the match fails and the invoice is held. It stops us paying for goods we never got or at a price we never agreed.
What is the difference between FOB shipping point and FOB destination?
Whether you know who owns the goods and carries the risk in transit.
Title and risk pass when goods go to the carrier for shipping point, and at delivery for destination. Who pays freight is a separate term.

With FOB shipping point, title and risk pass to us when the supplier hands the goods to the carrier, so if they are damaged on the way, we file the claim. With FOB destination, the supplier owns the goods until they arrive at our dock. Who pays the freight is set separately, for example freight prepaid or collect, so I spell out both on the PO.
Walk me through how you prepare for a price negotiation with a supplier.
How you plan a negotiation instead of improvising it.
Data first: spend history, market prices, competing quotes, a target and a walk-away point, plus levers other than price.

I pull our 12-month spend with the supplier, their on-time and quality record, and at least two competing quotes. I check market trends for the main raw material. Then I set a target price and a walk-away point, and list other levers: payment terms, volume commitments, lead time, freight. I go in knowing what I can give and what I need back.
You have three quotes, and the cheapest is 8% lower than the others. How do you decide?
Whether you buy on total cost rather than unit price.
Makes the quotes comparable, weighs landed cost, quality, lead time and supplier risk, and finds out why the low bid is low before awarding.

First I make sure the quotes are comparable: same spec, quantity, freight terms and payment terms. Then I look at total cost: freight, duties, minimum order, reject rate, lead time. I ask why the low bid is low; sometimes it leaves out tooling or packaging. If it holds up and the supplier qualifies, I might start with a trial order before moving the full volume.
An invoice arrives with a unit price higher than the price on the PO. What do you do?
How you handle a price discrepancy without damaging the relationship.
Holds the difference, checks the record, contacts the supplier, and gets a corrected invoice or a documented, approved change.

I check the PO and any change orders to confirm what we agreed. If the PO is right, I call the supplier's rep, point to the agreed price, and ask for a corrected invoice or a credit memo. Nothing over the PO price gets paid until that is settled. If the price really changed, it needs a revised PO with approval, not a quiet payment.
A key supplier announces a 12% price increase, citing raw material costs. How do you respond?
How you push back on a price increase with facts.
Asks for the cost breakdown, checks it against market data, negotiates size or timing, and gets alternate quotes as leverage.

I ask what share of the part's cost is that material and how much it moved. If steel is 40% of the cost and rose 10%, that supports about 4%, not 12%. I compare with a public price index, ask for a delay or a phased increase, and get quotes from other suppliers. For the next contract I would propose a price tied to the index, both up and down.
You notice you ordered 200 cases when the requester needed 200 units, and the order ships tomorrow. What do you do?
How you own and fix a costly mistake fast.
Acts at once, calls the supplier, tells the manager, and fixes the cause, such as the unit of measure on the item record.

I call the supplier right away, not email, and ask them to hold the shipment and change the quantity. If it has already shipped, I ask about return terms and restocking fees. I tell my manager what happened and the likely cost. Then I fix the cause: if the item record showed case instead of each, I correct it so the next order is right.
A supplier's sales rep offers you game tickets while their bid is still being evaluated. What do you do?
Your ethics and how you protect a fair bidding process.
Declines politely, follows the company gift policy, tells the manager, and decides the award on the bid alone.

I thank them and decline, and I say plainly that it is because the bid is open. I follow our gift policy and tell my manager, so there is a record. Even if the tickets would not change my decision, the other bidders and my own company need to trust that the award was fair. Then I score their bid exactly like the others.

cad-designer.heading: Drafter and CAD designer questions
qs: Which projection do US drawings use, and how does a reader know?
Whether you know the basic drawing convention used in the US.
Third-angle projection, shown by the truncated cone symbol in the title block, and how the views are placed.

Most US drawings use third-angle projection. The top view sits above the front view, and the right side view sits to its right. The title block carries the truncated cone symbol so the reader knows. Many European drawings use first-angle, where the views are placed on the opposite side, so I always check the symbol before I read one.
Why do you dimension from datums instead of chaining dimensions one after another?
Whether you understand how tolerances add up on the shop floor.
Chained tolerances add up, while baseline dimensions from a datum keep each feature's error separate. Each feature is dimensioned once.

If I chain five dimensions at plus or minus 0.005 inch, the last hole can be off by 0.025 from the edge. Dimensioning each feature from the same datum keeps every error to its own tolerance. I also make sure each feature is dimensioned only once. Any extra dimension I show as a reference dimension in parentheses.
What does design intent mean when you build a parametric model?
How you build models that update correctly when the design changes.
Fully defined sketches, references to stable planes and faces, and features ordered so a change behaves the way the engineer expects.

It means the model changes the way the real part should. If a hole must stay centered, I constrain it to the midplane, not with a number measured from an edge. I fully define sketches, reference datum planes rather than fillet edges that may disappear, and name key features. Then when the width changes, the hole moves with it and nothing fails.
An engineer puts plus or minus 0.0005 inch on every dimension of a simple bracket. What do you do?
Whether you think about cost and manufacturing, not only about copying input.
You ask which features are functional, propose the title block tolerance for the rest, and leave the decision to the engineer.

Tight tolerances everywhere can push a part into slower machining and more inspection, which raises its cost a lot. I would ask which features actually mate with something. Those keep the tight values. The rest can fall under the general tolerance in the title block. I would show the engineer a marked-up print and let them sign off.
Walk me through changing a drawing that has already been released to production.
Your discipline with revision control.
A change order, a new revision letter, a revision block entry, a where-used check, and no overwriting of the released file.

I never edit a released file quietly. The change starts with an engineering change order that says what changes and why. I check where the part is used, update the model and drawing, raise the revision letter and describe the change in the revision block. After checking and approval it is released, and the old revision is kept and marked superseded.
What does maximum material condition mean, and when would you use it in a callout?
Your grasp of a core GD&T modifier.
Smallest hole or largest pin, bonus tolerance as the feature departs from MMC, used for clearance fits rather than by default.

MMC is the size where the part has the most material: the smallest hole or the largest pin. If a position tolerance applies at MMC, the hole gets bonus tolerance as it is made bigger, because a bigger hole still clears the bolt. I use it for clearance holes. Under ASME Y14.5, if no modifier is shown, the tolerance applies regardless of feature size.
Why would you use a position tolerance on a bolt hole pattern instead of plus-minus coordinates?
Whether you can explain GD&T in terms of fit and cost.
A round zone matches how a bolt fits, gives about 57% more area than the square zone, and ties the holes to clear datums.

Plus-minus coordinates give a square tolerance zone, but a bolt does not care which direction the hole moves, only how far. A position tolerance gives a round zone. If the circle passes through the corners of the square, the shop gets about 57% more usable area for the same fit. It also names the datums, so the machinist and the inspector measure the same way.
How do you make sure a sheet metal flat pattern comes out right?
Your knowledge of how bent parts are actually made.
Bend radius and K-factor or the shop's bend table, matched to their tooling, with features kept clear of the bends.

The flat length depends on the bend radius and where the neutral axis sits, which the K-factor describes. I set material, thickness and inside radius to match the shop's tooling, and use their bend table if they have one. I keep holes far enough from bends that they do not stretch, add bend reliefs, and check the flat against the first part made.
Walk me through a worst-case tolerance stack-up for several parts stacked on a shaft.
Whether you can prove that parts will fit before they are made.
A loop of dimensions across the gap, signs for direction, min and max gap from all tolerances, and root-sum-square named as the statistical option.

I pick the gap I care about, say the end play between a retaining ring and the last part. I go around a loop of dimensions from one side of the gap to the other, with a sign for each direction. Nominals give the nominal gap. Adding all tolerances gives the worst minimum and maximum. If the minimum is below zero, I tighten key dimensions or discuss a root-sum-square check.
The shop says a part you drew will not assemble, and their parts measure to print. How do you find the problem?
How you track down a design error without blaming others.
Check the revision used, the mating parts, the datum scheme and the stack-up, then own the error and fix it through a change.

First I confirm they built to the current revision and that the mating parts are right too. Then I run an interference check on the CAD assembly and redo the stack-up with the real tolerances. Once, a hole pattern was dimensioned from a different datum than its mating part. I fixed the datums through a change order and told the shop exactly what changed.

call-center.heading: Call center representative questions
qs: What is the difference between average handle time and first call resolution?
Whether you know the two numbers most call centers run on and how they pull against each other.
Correct definitions, plus the point that rushing a call to cut handle time often causes a callback and hurts resolution.

Average handle time is talk time plus hold time plus after-call work, averaged over calls. First call resolution is the share of problems solved on the first contact, with no need to call back. If I rush to cut handle time, the customer often calls again, so I watch both.
How do you put a caller on hold the right way?
Your basic call handling habits.
Ask first, give the reason and a time, come back when promised, and thank them for waiting.

I ask if they mind a short hold and say why: I need to check their order history. I give a time, like two minutes. If it takes longer, I come back at the two minutes and update them rather than leaving them in silence. When I return, I thank them and pick up exactly where we stopped.
Walk me through how you verify a caller's identity before you discuss an account.
Whether you protect account data before you try to help.
Follows the set verification steps every time, lets the caller supply the details, and never hints at the right answer.

Before I share anything, I ask for the details our process requires, for example name, the address on file and a security answer or code. I let them say the details; I never read them out and ask for a yes. If they fail, I explain politely that I cannot discuss the account and tell them how the account holder can reach us.
A caller says, “I'm her husband, just tell me the balance.” He is not on the account. What do you do?
How you hold a privacy rule with someone who sounds reasonable.
No account details, a calm explanation, and a real path forward, such as the holder calling or adding him as an authorized user.

I tell him I understand, but I can only discuss the account with the account holder or someone she has authorized. I do not confirm or deny anything about the account. Then I give him options: she can call with him, or she can add him as an authorized user, and I explain how. Most people accept it once they hear it protects them too.
What is schedule adherence, and why does a call center care about it so much?
Whether you understand how staffing works on the phones.
Being available when the schedule says, breaks included, because staffing is planned to the interval around call forecasts.

It means being logged in and taking calls when my schedule says, and taking breaks and lunch at the planned times. Staffing is planned in short intervals to match forecast call volume. If I take a break fifteen minutes late, someone else's plan breaks and the queue grows. If I need to change something, I ask first.
The call drops in the middle of fixing a customer's problem. What do you do?
Whether you take ownership when a call ends before the problem is solved.
Calls back promptly if policy allows, uses the number on file, and leaves notes so any agent can continue.

I check the number on the account and call back within a minute or two, if our policy allows outbound calls. If I reach voicemail, I leave a short message with no private details and say how to reach us. Then I write clear notes on what we had done and what is left, so whoever picks up the next call does not start from zero.
A caller starts reading out their full card number while you are typing notes. What do you do?
Whether you know the basic rules for handling card data on calls.
Never writes card data in notes, follows the secure payment process, and reports it if the number reached a recording or note.

I stop them politely and say I will take payment the secure way. Depending on our setup, that means sending them to the automated payment line or pausing the recording first. I never type the card number into notes or chat. If the number already got into a note or recording, I tell my supervisor right away so it can be removed under our procedure.
A caller is swearing at you personally and will not stop. Where is the line, and what do you do?
How you protect yourself and the call within policy.
Separates anger at the problem from abuse, gives one clear warning, then ends the call per policy and documents it.

Frustration about the problem I can take; that is part of the job. When it becomes personal abuse, I say calmly that I want to help but I will end the call if the language continues. If it does, I end it as our policy allows, note the account with exact facts, and tell my supervisor. Then I take a short breath before the next call.
Your handle time is two minutes above the team average. How do you bring it down without hurting customers?
How you improve a number without cutting corners.
Finds where the time actually goes, fixes that part, and does not rush calls or transfer to save minutes.

First I look at where the time goes: talk, hold or after-call work. Last time, mine was after-call work: I wrote notes from scratch. I built short templates and typed notes during the call, and dropped about ninety seconds. I also asked a top agent to let me listen to a few calls to learn faster ways to find things in the system.
During a call, a customer says something that makes you worried they may hurt themselves. What do you do?
Whether you stay calm and follow procedure in a rare, serious call.
Stays on the line, alerts a supervisor at once, and follows the company's emergency procedure, including 988 or 911 where it calls for it.

I do not hang up or rush back to the account issue. I listen, speak calmly, and signal my supervisor through chat right away. I follow our emergency procedure, which may mean giving the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline or, if there is immediate danger, getting emergency services involved. I do not promise to keep it secret. Afterward, I document it and take a moment.

care-coordinator.heading: Care coordinator and case manager questions
qs: What is the difference between Medicare and Medicaid?
Whether you know the two programs many of your patients rely on.
Medicare is federal and based mainly on age or disability. Medicaid is federal and state, based on income, with rules that differ by state.

Medicare is a federal program for people 65 and older and some younger people with disabilities or kidney failure. Medicaid is run by each state with federal money and covers people with low income, so benefits vary from state to state. Some patients qualify for both, and then I check which one pays first.
What is the teach-back method, and when do you use it?
Whether you make sure patients understand their plan, not just hear it.
The patient explains the plan in their own words. If they miss something, you re-explain differently. It tests your explanation, not the patient.

I ask the patient to tell me in their own words what they will do, like 'Tell me how you will take this new pill.' If part of it is wrong, I explain again a different way and ask again. It checks how well I explained, not the patient. I use it for every new medicine, appointment and warning sign.
A patient keeps missing appointments. How do you find out why?
How you look for the real barrier instead of labeling a patient as noncompliant.
You ask without blame, consider rides, work, childcare, cost and understanding, then fix the actual barrier.

I call and ask plainly what got in the way, without blame. Often it is a ride, a work shift, childcare, cost or not seeing why the visit matters. Then I fix the real problem: set up transportation, which Medicaid often covers, move the visit to a time that works, or explain the reason for it and check with teach-back.
Walk me through what you do in the first week after a high-risk patient leaves the hospital.
How you prevent problems and readmissions after a hospital stay.
A call within days, medicines checked against the discharge list, a follow-up visit booked with a ride, services confirmed and clear warning signs.

I call within two business days. I go through every medicine against the discharge list and ask what is in the cabinet at home, since old pills cause many errors. I confirm the follow-up visit is booked and they have a ride, check that home services and equipment arrived, and review which symptoms mean they call the doctor that day.
You referred a patient to a cardiologist a month ago. How do you know the referral actually happened?
Whether you close the loop on referrals instead of assuming they went through.
The referral is tracked until the visit happens and the notes reach the primary doctor, with follow-up calls when it stalls.

I do not count a referral as done when I send it. I track it until the visit happens and the notes come back. If the specialist office has not scheduled within a week, I call them, then the patient. When the notes arrive, I make sure the primary doctor sees them and that any new orders are acted on.
A patient going home needs help bathing and dressing. Will Medicare home health pay for an aide to do that?
Your knowledge of what Medicare home health does and does not cover.
Not on its own. The patient must be homebound and need skilled care; personal care alone or round-the-clock care is not covered.

Not by itself. Medicare home health needs the patient to be homebound and to need skilled care, like nursing or therapy, ordered by a doctor. If that is in place, a part-time aide for bathing can be added. Help with daily tasks alone, or care around the clock, is not covered, so I look at Medicaid programs, family help or private-pay options.
A prior authorization for a patient's MRI was denied. What do you do?
How you work a denial through to a decision instead of stopping at the first no.
Read the exact reason, fix what is missing, use a peer-to-peer review, appeal before the deadline and keep the patient informed.

First I read the denial to see the exact reason: missing notes, a wrong code, or the plan wants another treatment tried first. Often the fix is sending the missing records. If not, I ask the doctor about a peer-to-peer review with the plan's reviewer, and if that fails we file an appeal before the deadline in the letter. I keep the patient informed at each step.
A family says their father was in the hospital four days, so Medicare will pay for rehab in a nursing facility. What do you check?
Whether you know the rule that most often surprises families about skilled nursing coverage.
Original Medicare needs a qualifying inpatient stay of three days; observation days do not count. Medicare Advantage plans set their own rules.

I check whether he was formally admitted as an inpatient for at least three days in a row, not counting the day of discharge. Days under observation are outpatient and do not count, even in a hospital bed. If he has a Medicare Advantage plan, I check that plan's rules, since some waive the three days but need prior approval. I tell the family early so the cost is not a surprise.
The team recommends a skilled nursing facility, but the patient insists on going home alone. What do you do?
How you balance patient choice with safety.
Respect for the choice if the patient has capacity, the safest possible plan built around it, risks explained and documented.

It is her choice if she has the capacity to make it, so I check that the team has assessed that. Then I ask what matters to her about going home and build the safest plan around it: home health, a medical alert device, meals, a family check-in schedule. I explain the risks plainly, document that she understood them and set follow-up calls for the first days.
On a home visit you find a frail patient alone, unwashed and with little food, and the daughter who cares for him seems overwhelmed. What do you do?
How you handle possible neglect while keeping the patient safe and the family on your side.
Immediate safety first, reporting as policy and state law require, and real support for the caregiver rather than blame.

First I make sure he is safe today: food, medicines, any urgent medical need. I tell my supervisor and report to Adult Protective Services as our policy and state law require; I do not decide alone whether it is neglect. Then I talk with the daughter without blame and line up help: respite care, an aide, meal delivery and a caregiver support group.

cfo.heading: Chief financial officer (CFO) questions
qs: Why can a profitable company run out of cash?
Whether you separate profit from cash, the first thing a CFO watches.
Names the real drivers: slow collections, inventory, capital spending and debt repayments that do not show up as expenses.

Profit is recorded when revenue is earned, not when cash comes in. A growing company can book sales while customers take 60 days to pay, inventory piles up, and equipment and loan principal are paid in cash but barely touch the income statement. That is why I watch the cash flow statement and the forecast as closely as earnings.
Walk me through how you build a 13-week cash flow forecast.
Whether you can manage liquidity week by week, not just month by month.
Direct method from actual receipts and payments, an owner for each line, and a weekly comparison of actual to forecast to sharpen it.

I build it on the direct method: cash in and cash out by week, starting from today's bank balance. Collections come from the receivables aging and customer habits, payments from payroll dates, rent, debt service and the payables run. Every week I compare actual to forecast, explain the gaps and roll a new week on. Within two months it is reliable enough to steer by.
How do you decide between raising debt and raising equity?
How you weigh cost, risk and control in a funding decision.
Ties the choice to the stability of cash flow: debt needs predictable cash to repay, equity has no repayment but costs ownership.

Debt is usually cheaper and does not dilute owners, but it must be repaid and often comes with covenants, so it suits a business with steady cash flow. Equity has no repayment and fits an early or volatile company, but it costs ownership and is usually the most expensive capital. I model both against a bad year and ask what happens to us then.
How do you prepare the finance section of a board meeting?
Whether you give directors what they need to govern, not a pile of data.
A short narrative first, results against plan, key risks and decisions needed, materials sent early, no surprises in the room.

I start with a one-page summary: results against plan, what changed in the forecast and why, cash runway, and the decisions we need from the board. Detailed statements go in the appendix. I send it several days ahead and brief the audit committee chair on anything sensitive, so no director hears bad news for the first time in the meeting.
Your top sales leader wants to book a big deal on the last day of the quarter, with a side letter letting the customer return the product. What do you do?
Whether you hold the line on revenue recognition under pressure.
Knows ASC 606: the side letter is part of the contract, the return right affects the transaction price, and revenue follows the real terms.

Under ASC 606, the revenue standard, the side letter is part of the contract, so the return right changes how much revenue I can recognize this quarter, possibly none. I would read the full terms, book only what the standard allows and explain why. Then I would require finance approval for any side letter, because hidden terms are how revenue problems start.
Your forecast shows you will breach a loan covenant in two quarters. What do you do now?
How you handle a lender problem before it becomes a default.
Checks the math against the loan agreement, tells the board, and goes to the lender early with a plan to get a waiver or amendment.

First I recheck the calculation using the credit agreement's own definitions, since its adjusted EBITDA often differs from ours. If the breach is real, I tell the CEO and board, then call the lender early with a recovery plan. Asking for an amendment two quarters out is a negotiation; asking after a breach is a default. I also check cross-default clauses in our other agreements.
Your CEO wants to give investors a revenue target you think the business cannot hit. How do you handle it?
Your independence and judgement when the CEO and the numbers disagree.
Pushes back privately with the data, offers a range both can defend, and will not stand behind a number they cannot support.

I would take it to the CEO privately with the pipeline, conversion rates and the downside case, and show what it would take to hit that number. Usually we agree on a range we both believe. Missing guidance costs more trust than a modest target. If we still disagreed, I would not present a number I cannot defend, and the board would need to know.
After year-end you discover an error in financial statements you already issued. Walk me through what happens.
Whether you know how to assess and correct an error in issued statements.
Judges materiality by amount and nature, brings in auditors and the audit committee early, and chooses a restatement or a correction to match.

I size the error and judge materiality by amount and by nature, such as whether it flips a loss to a profit. I tell the auditors and audit committee at once. If it is material to prior periods, we restate them, and a public company discloses they can no longer be relied on. If not, we correct the prior figures in the next filing. Then I fix the control that missed it.
Your controller notices payments to a new vendor whose address matches an employee's home. What do you do?
How you handle suspected fraud without tipping anyone off or spoiling the evidence.
Evidence preserved quietly, legal counsel and the audit committee involved early, no solo confrontation, and the control gap closed afterward.

I would not confront the employee. I would quietly hold further payments to that vendor, preserve the records and system access logs, and bring in legal counsel and the audit committee chair. Counsel decides whether to hire forensic accountants. Once the facts are clear we act, then close the gap that allowed it, such as setting up vendors without independent checks.

change-management.heading: Change and transformation manager questions
qs: How is change management different from project management?
Whether you know where your work starts and the project plan stops.
Project management delivers the solution on time and on budget. Change management gets people to use it, so the benefits actually arrive.

The project manager makes sure the new system is built, tested and live on the date. I make sure the people who must use it understand why, can use it, and keep using it. A project can finish on time and still fail if nobody adopts it. We share one plan, but I own the people side.
Walk me through how you do a change impact assessment.
Your method for finding out who is affected and how much.
Group by group: what changes in process, tools, roles, skills and reporting lines, rated by degree. The ratings then drive training and communication.

I list every group the change touches. For each one I note what is different: process, tools, job roles, skills, who they report to, how they are measured. I rate each impact high, medium or low with the team leads, not on my own. High-impact groups get earlier contact, hands-on training and more support at go-live.
How do you decide which stakeholders need the most of your time?
How you map stakeholders and spend your effort where it counts.
A map by influence, by how much the change affects them and by whether they support it. A plan for each group, revisited as positions shift.

I map people by how much influence they have over the change and how much it affects them, and I note whether they support it. High influence and skeptical gets my time first, usually one to one. Heavily affected groups with little influence get strong two-way channels. I update the map every few weeks because people move.
What should an executive sponsor do, and what do you do if yours goes quiet?
Whether you know why sponsorship matters and how you manage upward.
The sponsor visibly explains why, rallies peer leaders and holds managers to it. You bring short, specific asks rather than complaints.

The sponsor should explain why we are changing, in person, stay visible after kickoff, and get other leaders to back it. If mine goes quiet, I book 20 minutes, show where adoption is lagging and give three specific asks: say this at the town hall, send this note to your directs, ask about it in your staff meeting. Sponsors respond to clear, small asks.
How do you set up and use a network of change champions?
Your use of local influence to spread a change.
Respected peers from each affected team, trained early and given time by their managers. They help colleagues and feed problems back to the project.

I ask managers for the people their teams already go to for help, not just volunteers with free time. I get their managers to free up a few hours a week, train them before everyone else and give them a direct line to the project. They answer questions on the floor and tell me what is really happening. A short weekly call with them is my best early warning.
Training is done, but people are still not using the new process. How do you find out why?
Whether you diagnose the real cause instead of just adding more training.
Finding the actual gap: awareness, desire, knowledge, ability or reinforcement. Each needs a different fix, and more training only fixes knowledge.

I use the ADKAR model to find where people are stuck: awareness of why, desire to take part, knowledge of how, ability to do it on the job, or reinforcement to keep it. I talk to a few users and their managers. If they know how but their manager still asks for the old report, that is a reinforcement problem, and another class will not help.
A respected team lead keeps telling his team the new system will not work for them. What do you do?
How you handle resistance from someone with real influence.
Meet privately, listen for a genuine issue, fix what is valid and involve him. Escalate through his manager only if the undermining continues.

I meet him alone and ask what exactly will not work. Often there is a real gap, like a step his team does that the design missed. If so, I take it to the project and tell him what we changed. I may ask him to test the fix. If he still undermines it after being heard, I raise it with his manager, because managers own their team's adoption.
How do you measure whether a change has actually been adopted?
Whether you measure real use rather than activity like logins or attendance.
How fast, how widely and how well people use the new way, tied to the business result. Not training completions or emails sent.

Training attendance and emails sent tell me what we did, not what people do. I track how many people use the new way, how quickly they got there, and how well: error rates, rework, time per task. Then I check the outcome the change was for, like a faster month-end close. I set the baseline before go-live so we can compare.
Three weeks after go-live, logins look fine, but teams still keep their old spreadsheets on the side. What do you do?
How you spot and deal with workarounds after go-live.
Workarounds treated as information: find out why, fix real gaps or coach, then retire the old tool on a date agreed with leaders.

First I find out why. I sit with two or three teams and see what the spreadsheet gives them that the system does not. Sometimes it is a missing report, sometimes habit or distrust of the data. Real gaps go to the project as fixes. Then, with the sponsor, we set a date to retire the old files, and managers stop accepting them.
Leadership wants to launch three changes to the same team in one quarter. How do you advise them?
Your judgement on change saturation and on sequencing.
Showing the combined load on that team, naming the risk of fatigue and weak adoption, and offering sequencing options with clear trade-offs.

I build a simple view of every change landing on that team, week by week, with the training hours and the dip in output each one brings. Then I show leaders where it peaks, often at month-end. I offer options: stagger them, combine the training, or delay the lowest-value one. They decide, but they decide knowing the cost to adoption.

channel-sales.heading: Channel sales manager questions
qs: How does deal registration work, and why do partners care about it?
Your grasp of the main tool that protects a partner's work on a deal.
The partner who finds a deal registers it and, once approved, gets protection and usually better pricing for a set time. Fast, fair approvals keep trust.

A partner logs an opportunity it found. If we approve it, that partner gets protection on the deal for a fixed period, say 90 days, and usually an extra discount. It rewards finding new business instead of racing other partners on price. I approve within a day or two, give a reason when I reject, and let stale registrations expire.
How do you decide which partners to recruit?
How you pick partners who will actually sell, not just sign an agreement.
A written ideal partner profile: customers that match yours, skills to deliver, a reason to care, and a committed owner on their side.

I start from our best customers and ask who already serves them. Then I check fit: same segment, the technical skills to deploy us, and products that pair with ours rather than compete. Last, I want a named executive sponsor and a sales lead who will commit to a joint plan. A partner without an internal champion signs and then goes quiet.
Walk me through your first 90 days with a newly signed partner.
Whether you can turn a signed agreement into a first deal.
A joint plan with targets, training for sellers and technical staff, a few target accounts, and a first deal worked together early.

In the first two weeks we agree on a short business plan: target accounts, revenue goal, who does what. Then I train their sellers on how to spot a fit and their engineers on delivery. By day 45 I want two or three live opportunities we work jointly. By day 90 I want a closed deal or a clear reason why not, because early wins keep a partner engaged.
What is the difference between partner-sourced and partner-influenced revenue, and why does it matter?
Your understanding of how channel results are measured and credited.
Sourced means the partner found the deal; influenced means it helped one already in motion. Mixing them hides which partners create new business.

Partner-sourced is a deal the partner brought to us, usually proven by an approved registration. Partner-influenced is a deal our team or another source found where the partner helped, for example with a reference or the implementation. Both count, but I report them separately. If I blend them, a partner who only joins late looks as valuable as one who fills the pipeline.
You have 40 partners, but five bring in most of the revenue. How do you split your time?
How you prioritize a partner base where results are uneven.
Most time on the top partners and a few promising risers, with a scalable, low-touch program for the rest instead of ignoring them.

I would put about half my time into the top five: joint planning, pipeline reviews and help on big deals. Another chunk goes to three or four partners showing real growth, since they are my next top tier. The rest get a scaled program: online training, a monthly webinar and fast deal registration. I review the list each quarter so it is based on results, not habit.
A direct sales rep and a partner both claim the same customer deal. How do you handle it?
How you resolve channel conflict without losing the partner's trust.
Use written rules of engagement and registration records, decide fast with facts, and fix the rule if it caused the clash.

I pull the facts first: who registered the deal, when, and what each side has done with the customer. Then I apply our rules of engagement, which should already say what happens here. If the partner registered first and is working the deal, it is theirs and the rep may still earn credit. I tell both sides the decision the same day. If the rules were unclear, I get them rewritten.
A partner asks for marketing development funds for a big event. How do you decide?
Your judgement in spending partner marketing money on results, not on goodwill.
MDF tied to a plan with measurable outcomes, like meetings and pipeline, plus proof of spend and a follow-up review.

Marketing development funds are money we give partners to generate demand for our product. I ask for a short plan: who will attend, how many meetings they expect, and what pipeline they will register within 60 days. I check past results from that partner. If I approve, payment depends on proof of spend and a lead list, and we review the numbers together after the event.
You learn your top partner has started pushing a competitor's product. What do you do?
How you respond when a key partner's loyalty shifts.
Calm fact-finding about why, then making it easier and more profitable to sell you, not threats or panic.

I would ask their sales leader directly, without blame, what changed. Often it is margin, an easier deal process, or better support from the other vendor. Once I know, I fix what I can: faster quotes, a sales engineer on their deals, a clearer incentive. Many partners carry more than one vendor, so my goal is to stay their first choice, not to demand exclusivity.
A partner has held your top tier for two years but has closed nothing in three quarters. What do you do?
How you handle a hard conversation with a long-standing partner.
Find the cause, agree on a recovery plan with a deadline, and apply tier rules fairly if results do not come back.

First I find out why. Maybe their lead seller left or they shifted focus. I meet their executive sponsor, show the numbers, and propose a 90-day plan with clear targets and extra support from us. I also say plainly that tier benefits depend on results. If nothing moves by the deadline, I lower the tier as the program rules say. Being fair keeps the program credible for every other partner.

chat-support.heading: Chat and email support agent questions
qs: How is writing a chat reply different from writing an email reply?
Whether you adapt your writing to the channel.
Chat is short, quick turns while the customer waits; email is complete and structured and answers everything in one go.

In chat the customer is waiting, so I send short messages, one step at a time, and say when I need a minute to check something. In email they may not read again until tomorrow, so I answer every question in one message, use numbered steps and say exactly what happens next.
How do you use saved replies, or macros, without sounding like a robot?
How you balance speed with a personal tone.
Macros as a starting point only: edited to fit the customer's words and situation, and checked that they answer what was asked.

I use a macro for the parts that never change, like the steps to reset a password. Then I add a first line that answers what the customer actually wrote, and I delete anything that does not apply. Before sending, I read it once as the customer would. If a macro is often wrong, I ask to have it fixed.
What do you do to solve a problem in one reply instead of three?
Whether you anticipate the customer's next question.
Reads the whole message and history, answers every point, and covers the likely next step or what to do if the fix does not work.

I read the full message and check the account and past tickets before I write. I answer every question, not just the first one. Then I think about what they will ask next: if I send reset steps, I also say what to do if the email does not arrive, like checking spam. One complete reply saves the customer a day of waiting.
What goes in an internal note on a ticket?
Whether you leave a ticket the next agent can pick up without starting over.
Facts, not opinions: what was checked, what was tried, what was promised and by when, and what is still open.

I write what the customer reported, what I checked, what I tried and what I told them, especially any promise with a date. If it is waiting on another team, I note which team and the reference. I keep it factual and polite, because notes can be read later. The next agent should never need to ask the customer the same thing twice.
The customer stops answering in the middle of a chat. What do you do?
Your routine for a customer who goes silent.
One check-in, a wait that follows team rules, a polite closing that leaves the next step and a way back, and a note on the ticket.

I send one check-in, like: Are you still there? Take your time. If there is no answer after the time our team uses, I close with a summary of where we got to, the next step they can take on their own, and how to reach us again without starting over. I note the ticket so whoever picks it up has the context.
Someone in chat asks you to change the email on an account but cannot pass verification. What do you do?
Whether you protect accounts from people pretending to be the owner.
Follows the verification process with no exceptions, stays polite, and points to the official path the real owner can use.

I do not change it. Changing the email is a common way to take over an account, and urgency or a sad story is a common tactic. I kindly explain that I can only make that change after verification and describe the other route our process allows. If it looks like an attack, I flag the account as our process says.
A customer pastes their full card number into the chat. What do you do?
Whether you handle sensitive data safely.
Does not repeat or use the number, has it masked or removed as tools and policy allow, and tells the customer kindly not to send it.

I do not repeat the number or copy it anywhere. I use our tool to redact it from the transcript, or report it to whoever handles that, as the policy says. Then I tell the customer, without blaming them, that we never need the full card number in chat and that the last four digits are enough for me to find the payment.
A customer complains about us in a public post on social media. How do you reply?
How you handle a complaint that other people can read.
A short, calm public reply that acknowledges the issue, no personal details in public, and a move to a private channel to solve it.

I answer publicly first, briefly, so others see we responded: I'm sorry about the late delivery, please send us a direct message with your order number and we'll sort it out. I never ask for or post personal details in public. Once it is solved in private, I may add a short public follow-up if the customer is happy with that.
Here is a reply a new agent wrote: “As per our policy, refunds are not possible after 30 days. Ticket closed.” Rewrite it.
How well you write a firm answer that still helps the customer.
Keeps the no, drops the cold wording, gives the reason in plain words and offers whatever the company does allow instead.

I'd write: “Thanks for writing to us. I checked your order, and it was placed 45 days ago, which is past our 30-day refund window, so I can't refund it. If the item is faulty, it may still be covered by its warranty, and I'm glad to start that for you now.” I'd also leave the ticket open until they answer.
An email thread has passed between three agents over two weeks, and the customer now writes “Is anyone actually reading this?” You pick it up. What do you do?
How you take ownership of a case that has already gone wrong.
Reads the whole thread first, admits the delay plainly, gives one clear status with a date, and stays the owner until it is closed.

I read the whole thread and notes before replying, so I don't ask for anything they already sent. Then I write that I'm sorry they had to repeat themselves, that I'm handling it personally now, what the real status is, and when they'll hear from me next. I keep the ticket assigned to me and write on that date even if there is no news yet.

chief-of-staff.heading: Chief of staff questions
qs: How is a chief of staff different from an executive assistant?
Whether you understand the scope of the role.
A clear split: the assistant manages the executive's time and logistics; the chief of staff manages priorities, follow-through and special projects.

An executive assistant runs the calendar, travel and correspondence, and that work is essential. I work on what the time is spent on: the priorities, the operating rhythm of the leadership team, and projects that cross departments. The best setups have us working closely, because my plans fail if they never reach the calendar.
How do you learn how a new executive likes to work?
How you build the working relationship in the first weeks.
Asks directly and observes: how they want information, what they decide alone, what to escalate. Then confirms it in writing.

In week one I ask for an hour on their goals for the year, how they want updates, written or spoken, and what they want to hear about at once versus weekly. Then I watch a few weeks of meetings and email. I write a short page of working agreements and ask them to correct it. We revisit it after 90 days.
The weekly leadership meeting runs two hours and decides nothing. Walk me through how you would fix it.
Your skill in designing meetings that lead to decisions.
Starts with the purpose, separates updates from decisions, uses pre-reads, owners and time limits, then checks whether it worked.

First I ask the executive what the meeting is for. Then I move status updates into a written note sent the day before, so room time goes to two or three decisions, each with an owner and a clear question. I set a time for each item, close by reading back decisions and actions, and after a month I ask attendees whether it is better.
What goes into the brief you prepare before your executive's big meeting?
Whether you can prepare an executive in minutes, not hours.
