One page: purpose, who is in the room and what they want, the decision or ask, key facts, risks and a recommended position.

One page, read in five minutes. Why the meeting exists and what we want to leave with. Who attends, what each person wants and any history between us. The three facts that matter, the likely pushback, and my recommended position. Background goes in an appendix they can skip. I send it the evening before, not in the hallway.
How do you make sure the decisions made in a meeting actually happen?
How you run follow-through across the leadership team.
One log of decisions and actions, each with a single owner and a date, sent quickly and reviewed at the next meeting.

Before people leave I read back each decision and action, with one owner and a due date. Within a few hours I send that list and add it to a shared tracker. The next meeting opens with overdue items. If something slips twice, I talk to the owner privately first, so the meeting does not become a public scolding.
How would you check whether your executive's time matches their priorities?
Whether you can run a calendar audit and act on it.
Tags past weeks of the calendar by priority, shows the gap with numbers, and proposes concrete cuts or delegations.

I take the last four to six weeks of the calendar and tag each meeting against the executive's stated priorities, plus a bucket for everything else. Last time the top priority got about 10% of the hours. I showed that on one page and proposed dropping three recurring meetings and sending a delegate to two others. We freed six hours a week.
When do you make a call on behalf of your executive, and when do you take it to them?
Your judgement about decision rights and the limits of your role.
Rules agreed in advance: decides on reversible matters where the executive's view is known; escalates new direction, people decisions and anything hard to undo.

We agree the lines early. I decide on things that are reversible, low cost, and where I already know the executive's position, like meeting changes or which team leads a small project. I escalate anything new in direction, anything about people's jobs or pay, and anything hard to undo. When unsure I ask, and I report calls I made in their name.
A vice president asks you privately whether the rumored reorganization is real. You know it is. What do you say?
How you protect confidential information without lying.
Neither confirms nor lies; says it cannot be discussed, and tells the executive the rumor is spreading.

I would say: I can't talk about organization plans, and I would not rely on hallway talk either way. I would not deny it, because a lie would cost me their trust later. Then I would tell the executive that the rumor has reached the VP level, so they can decide whether to move up the announcement.
A direct report of your executive tells you that you are blocking their access to the boss. How do you respond?
Whether you see yourself as a bridge, not a gatekeeper.
Listens without defending, checks the facts, fixes the process, and never stands between direct reports and their manager.

I would thank them and ask for examples. Direct reports should always be able to reach their own manager; my job is to make that time well used, not to ration it. If my process slowed them down, say by asking for pre-reads on urgent items, I would change it and tell the executive about the complaint myself, so they hear it from me first.
You sent a note to the company in your executive's name, and it promised more than they had agreed to. What do you do?
How you own a mistake made with someone else's authority.
Tells the executive at once, brings a correction, fixes it quickly and openly, and changes the approval step.

I would go to the executive right away, explain what went out and what it promised, and bring a draft correction. A short, plain follow-up the same day is better than letting people plan around a wrong promise. Then I would fix the cause: from then on, any message in their name gets their sign-off on the final text, not an earlier draft.

civil-engineer.heading: Civil engineer questions
qs: What does a Proctor test tell you, and how is it used in the field?
Whether you understand the basis of soil compaction control.
Lab maximum dry density and optimum moisture, a spec stated as a percentage of that, and field density compared against it.

A Proctor test compacts a soil sample at several moisture contents to find its maximum dry density and optimum moisture. The spec then asks for a percentage of that, often 95% under pavement. In the field the tester measures density, usually with a nuclear gauge, and compares it with the lab value for that same soil.
What slopes do you design to for an accessible route across a parking lot?
Your working knowledge of ADA site design limits.
Running slope up to 1:20 before it is a ramp, cross slope up to 1:48, ramps up to 1:12, and a margin for construction tolerance.

Under the 2010 ADA Standards, a route can run up to 1:20 before it counts as a ramp, and the cross slope can be no more than 1:48. A ramp can be up to 1:12, with landings, and handrails once the rise is over 6 inches. I design below the limits, like 1.5% instead of 2.08%, because concrete never lands exactly on grade.
When would you use the rational method, and what are its limits?
Whether you know the basic runoff method and where it stops working.
Q = CiA explained, peak flow only, intensity tied to time of concentration, and use limited to small areas per the local manual.

Q equals C times i times A: a runoff coefficient, the rainfall intensity for a storm as long as the time of concentration, and the area in acres, giving cubic feet per second. It gives a peak flow only and assumes even rain over the area, so I use it for small areas like inlets and parking lots, within the size limit the local drainage manual sets.
Why do you check the hydraulic grade line in a storm sewer, and not just pipe capacity?
How well you understand storm sewer hydraulics beyond pipe sizing.
Tailwater and structure losses can flood a pipe that has capacity; you work upstream from the outfall and keep the HGL below rims with freeboard.

A pipe can have room on paper and still flood if water backs up from downstream. The hydraulic grade line shows how high water rises in each structure, counting tailwater, friction and losses at junctions. I start at the outfall and work upstream, and check the line stays below every rim and inlet with the freeboard the local manual requires.
On a site visit after a storm, you see muddy water running past the silt fence into a creek. What do you do?
How you handle an erosion control failure under a stormwater permit.
Immediate notice and repair, finding why it failed, documenting it under the SWPPP, and updating the plan if the control was wrong.

I take photos, note the time, and tell the superintendent right away so the fence is repaired and sediment cleaned up. Then I look at why it failed: often the fence runs downhill or drains too big an area. The SWPPP inspection log must record it, the plan may need a sediment trap instead, and if the permit requires reporting the discharge, the operator reports it.
A compaction test under the pavement fails, and the contractor wants to pave tomorrow anyway. What do you say?
Your judgement when schedule pressure meets a failed test.
No paving over a valid failure; confirm the test is right, have the area reworked and retested, and keep the delay short and in writing.

I would not let them pave over a failed test. Once asphalt is down, a soft spot becomes a pothole and a fight over who pays. I check the test first: right Proctor value for that soil, moisture in range. If it holds, they rework the area, adjust moisture, recompact and retest. I put the decision in writing and line up a quick retest.
Your 28-day concrete cylinder breaks come back below the specified strength. Walk me through what you do.
Whether you know the acceptance rules and the steps before talking about removal.
Applies the ACI 318 acceptance criteria, checks testing and curing, then cores reviewed by the engineer of record before any tear-out.

First I check if it is truly a failure: under ACI 318, the average of three consecutive tests must reach f'c, and no single test may fall more than 500 psi below it when f'c is 5,000 psi or less. Next I check curing and handling at the lab. If doubt remains, we take cores and the engineer of record judges them before anyone talks about tearing out.
The geotechnical report says the building sits on expansive clay. How does that change your site and foundation design?
How you turn a geotechnical finding into design decisions.
Explains swell and shrink, follows the geotech's options for soil and foundation, and controls water around the building.

Expansive clay swells when wet and shrinks when dry, so it can lift and crack a slab. I follow the geotechnical engineer's recommendations, which might be replacing the top few feet with non-expansive fill, moisture conditioning, or a post-tensioned slab or piers. I also grade so water drains away and keep downspouts and irrigation off the foundation.
The contractor finds your new sanitary sewer would cross just above an existing water main. How do you handle it?
How you resolve a utility conflict while protecting drinking water.
Verifies actual locations, checks the state separation rule, adjusts grade or uses an approved alternative, and gets regulator approval.

I have the real depths surveyed first; record drawings are often off. Then I check the state separation rule, which in many states wants the water line 18 inches above the sewer at a crossing. If I cannot lower the sewer enough, I use an approved alternative such as pressure-rated pipe or encasement at the crossing, and get the regulator's approval.
After the curbs are poured, you find your grading plan sends parking lot water toward the building entrance. What do you do?
Whether you own a design mistake and fix it fast.
Tells the client and manager quickly with a fix ready, picks the cheapest fix that works, and changes the review process.

I tell my manager and the client the same day, with the cause and a proposed fix, not just the problem. Then I find the cheapest fix that works, maybe a trench drain at the low spot or regrading pavement not yet placed. I document the change, and afterward I add a check of flow arrows against finished floor elevations to my review list.

client-services.heading: Client services manager questions
qs: How is managing client accounts different from working a support queue?
Whether you understand the account side of the role, not only ticket work.
Ownership of the whole relationship over time: goals, renewals, several contacts, and problems spotted before the client raises them.

In a queue I solve the ticket in front of me and move on. With accounts I own the same clients for months. I know their goals, who signs the contract, and what went wrong last quarter. A lot of the job is spotting problems before they call, and making sure the service still fits what they need at renewal.
You inherit twenty accounts from a manager who left. What do you do in your first weeks?
How you take over relationships without dropping anything.
Reading the history, ranking accounts by risk and renewal date, and meeting each key contact early instead of waiting for problems.

First I read each account's notes, open issues, contract terms and renewal date. I rank them: anything with an open complaint or a renewal in the next few months goes first. Then I call each main contact, introduce myself, and ask what is working and what is not. I write down every promise the last manager made so nothing gets lost in the handover.
What is an SLA, and what do you do when your team is about to miss one?
Your grasp of service commitments and how you act before a breach.
A service level agreement is a written promise, such as response or fix times. Telling the client before the deadline passes, with a new time and the reason, beats silence.

An SLA, or service level agreement, is the part of the contract that sets measurable promises, like how fast we respond or fix an issue. If we are about to miss one, I tell the client before the deadline, not after. I say what is late, why, and when they will have it. Then I check whether the contract gives them a credit and make sure it is applied without them having to ask.
A client asks your team for extra work that is not in their contract. How do you handle it?
Whether you can protect the scope of the contract without hurting the relationship.
Acknowledging the need, checking the contract, and turning the request into a priced change order or a clear decision, not quietly absorbing it.

I first check the contract to be sure it really is out of scope. Then I tell the client it is a fair request and explain it falls outside what we agreed. I get an estimate from the team and send a short change order with cost and timing. If it is tiny and good for the account, my manager and I might do it once, but we say so openly so it does not become the new normal.
Walk me through how you would run a quarterly business review with a client.
Your ability to run a structured review that shows value and sets next steps.
Prepared numbers tied to the client's goals, honesty about problems, a focus on their next quarter, and an ending with owners and dates.

Before the meeting I ask the client what they want to cover and pull the numbers that match their goals, like volume, response times and open issues. In the meeting I start with their goals, show results against them, and name anything we missed and what we changed. Then we plan the next quarter. I send a summary the same day with each action, its owner and its date.
What early signs tell you a client might not renew?
Whether you can spot the risk of losing a client before the renewal talk.
Concrete signals such as falling usage, a quiet or departed main contact, new decision makers, late payments, or questions about exporting data.

Usage dropping is the clearest one. Others: my main contact stops answering, a new executive arrives, invoices start being paid late, or they ask how to export their data. Complaints are actually a better sign than silence, because they still care. When I see two or three signals together I flag the account and set up a call to ask directly how things are going.
Your main contact at a big client leaves their company. What do you do?
How you protect an account that depended on one person.
Quickly meeting the new owner, recapping the value delivered, and having more than one contact at every account so it does not happen again.

If I can, I ask the departing contact who takes over and get an introduction. I meet the new person soon, with a short recap of what we do for them, the results so far and open items. I treat it like a new sale, because they did not choose us. Afterward I make sure I know at least two or three people there, including someone senior.
A client's executive emails your CEO to complain and skips you. How do you respond?
How you handle an escalation over your head without getting defensive.
Owning it quickly, briefing your leaders with facts, reaching the executive with a plan, and finding out why they felt they could not come to you.

I would not take it personally; it means the problem felt big to them. I give my CEO a short brief the same day: what happened, what we have done, and what I propose. Then I call the executive, with my leader if that helps, and give a plan with dates. Later I ask my usual contact what made them go higher, so I can fix the gap.
Our system sent a client a report with wrong numbers, and they have already used it. How do you tell them?
How you communicate an error your own company made.
Telling them fast and plainly: what is wrong, the impact and what you are doing, then a follow-up with the cause and the fix, without excuses.

I call before they find it, then confirm in writing. I say plainly which report was wrong, which numbers, and since when. I send the corrected figures or a time when they will have them, and offer to help explain it to anyone who used the report. Once we know the cause, I send a short note on what happened and what we changed so it does not repeat.
Your company is raising prices, and your largest client will be upset. How do you deliver the news?
How you handle a hard commercial message while keeping the client.
Notice as the contract requires or earlier, a personal call before the letter, the reason tied to value, and knowing in advance what flexibility you have.

I check the contract for the notice it requires and tell them well before that, by phone, before any formal letter. I explain the reason and remind them of the results we delivered this year. Before the call I agree with my manager what we can offer, like a phased increase or a longer term at a fixed rate, so I am not inventing deals on the spot. Then I follow up in writing.

clinical-research.heading: Clinical research and medical affairs questions
qs: What does ALCOA mean for source documents?
Whether you know the basic standard for trial data.
Each letter explained with what it looks like at a site, plus awareness that ALCOA+ adds more qualities.

Attributable, Legible, Contemporaneous, Original and Accurate. At a site I can see who wrote each entry and when, it was recorded at the time, corrections are a single line with initials, date and reason, and the chart matches the case report form. ALCOA+ adds complete, consistent, enduring and available.
What is the difference between an adverse event and a serious adverse event?
Your grasp of safety definitions that drive reporting.
Seriousness is defined by outcome, not intensity, and the candidate can name the criteria.

An adverse event is any unfavorable medical occurrence in a participant, related to the study drug or not. It is serious if it causes death, is life-threatening, requires or prolongs a hospital stay, causes lasting disability, is a birth defect, or is an important medical event. Serious is about outcome, not intensity: a severe headache can be non-serious.
What is the Form FDA 1572, and who signs it?
Whether you know the investigator's commitments in an FDA drug study.
It is the Statement of Investigator under an IND, signed by the principal investigator, and kept up to date.

It is the Statement of Investigator for a drug or biologic study under an IND. The principal investigator signs it and commits to follow the protocol, personally supervise the study, use IRB review and informed consent, and report as required. It lists sub-investigators, sites and labs, so I update it when those change. Device studies use an investigator agreement instead.
During a monitoring visit you find a participant signed an older version of the consent form. What do you do?
How you handle a consent problem without losing sight of the participant.
Re-consent on the current approved version, document and report the deviation, and check every other participant.

I confirm which version the IRB had approved on that date. If the participant signed a superseded form, the site re-consents them on the current version at the next visit, or sooner if the change affects safety. I note it in my report, the site logs it as a deviation and reports it per IRB rules, and we check every other consent that day.
The study drug fridge log shows the temperature went out of range over the weekend. What happens next?
Your handling of investigational product when storage fails.
Quarantine, document, let the sponsor decide on use, dose no one meanwhile, and find the cause.

The site quarantines the affected kits, labels them do not use, and keeps them at the right temperature. We record the highest or lowest reading and how long it lasted, then send that to the sponsor, who decides if the drug is usable. No patient gets those kits until then. I also look at why: the alarm, the power, who checks the log.
You discover a participant who did not meet one inclusion criterion was enrolled and has already been dosed. How do you handle it?
How you balance participant safety, data integrity and honest reporting.
Safety first, the sponsor's medical monitor decides on continuation, the deviation is reported, and the cause is fixed.

First I tell the investigator, who checks the participant is safe. The sponsor's medical monitor then decides whether they stay on drug and how their data are handled; the site does not decide alone. It is reported as an important deviation to the sponsor and to the IRB if its rules require. Then we fix the cause, for example a second person checking eligibility before randomization.
A physician asks you, as a medical science liaison, about using your product for an unapproved indication. How do you respond?
Whether you know the line between scientific exchange and off-label promotion.
Answer only an unsolicited request, stay balanced and narrow, document it, and keep sales out of it.

If the question came unprompted, I can answer it. I give a balanced scientific answer limited to what was asked, say clearly the use is not approved, and share the data, including weak or negative results. I log the request through medical information. I never raise the topic myself and never pass it to sales to follow up.
An investigator calls at night wanting to unblind a participant who is in the emergency room. What do you advise?
Your judgement on emergency unblinding in a blinded trial.
Unblind when knowing the treatment changes care, use the proper system, limit it to one participant, and document it.

Safety comes first. If knowing the treatment would change how the patient is treated, the investigator can unblind; a quick call to the medical monitor helps, but they need no permission. If care is the same either way, stopping the drug may be enough. They use the randomization system, unblind only that participant, keep others blinded, and document why and when.
How do you decide what to check when you cannot verify every data point at a site?
Whether you can apply risk-based monitoring sensibly.
Focus on data critical to safety and the main result, and use central data trends to target visits.

I start with what protects participants and the main result: consent, eligibility, serious adverse events, study drug, and the primary endpoint. Those get full checks. For the rest I follow the monitoring plan and central data: sites with unusual query rates, late entry or odd patterns get more on-site time. ICH E6 supports this risk-based approach.
A site enrolls twice as fast as the others and its data look almost perfect. What concerns you, and what do you do?
How you spot possible misconduct and escalate it properly.
Knows real data are messy, looks for concrete evidence, and escalates to quality assurance instead of accusing.

It might just be a great site, but real data are messy. I would look for identical vital signs, visits on days the clinic is closed, or lab dates that do not match. I compare source to outside records like pharmacy or lab reports. If it does not add up, I take the evidence to my manager and quality assurance rather than accusing the site myself.

cloud-engineer.heading: Cloud engineer questions
qs: What makes a subnet public or private in a cloud network?
Whether you know how traffic really enters and leaves a cloud network.
The route table decides it: a public subnet routes to an internet gateway, a private one does not.

It is the route table, not the name. A public subnet has a route that sends internet traffic to an internet gateway, so servers with public IPs can be reached. A private subnet has no such route. Its servers go out through a NAT gateway that sits in a public subnet, and nobody on the internet can start a connection to them.
How are security groups different from network ACLs?
Your grasp of the two firewall layers and when each one matters.
Security groups are stateful and attach to instances. Network ACLs are stateless, work per subnet and can deny.

A security group attaches to an instance's network interface, has only allow rules, and is stateful: if traffic is let in, the reply goes out automatically. A network ACL sits on the subnet, has allow and deny rules checked in number order, and is stateless, so I must also allow return traffic on the high ephemeral ports. I do most work in security groups.
Your team will connect a new VPC to the office network later. How do you choose its IP range?
Whether you plan address space before it becomes a problem.
A range that does not overlap with other networks, with room to grow, recorded in one shared plan.

First I check the ranges already used by the office, the VPN and our other VPCs, because overlapping ranges cannot be peered or routed cleanly. I pick a free private range, size it bigger than today's need, say a /16 split into /20 subnets per zone, and write it into our shared IP plan so the next team does not collide with it.
What is the state file in an infrastructure-as-code tool, and how do you keep it safe on a team?
Whether you have run infrastructure as code with more than one person.
State maps the code to real resources. It lives in a remote, locked, encrypted store and is never edited by hand.

The state file records which real resource each block of code created, so the tool knows what to change. On a team I keep it in a remote backend with locking, so two people cannot apply at once, plus encryption and tight access, because it can hold secrets in plain text. Nobody edits it by hand; if it must change, we use the tool's own state commands.
A server in a private subnet cannot download updates. Walk me through how you find the cause.
How you trace a network path step by step instead of guessing.
Following the packet: DNS, security group, ACL, route table, NAT gateway, and the NAT's own route out.

I follow the packet. Does DNS resolve? Does the security group allow outbound on 443? Does the subnet's ACL allow that port out and the return traffic on ephemeral ports? Does the route table send 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway? Is that NAT in a public subnet whose route goes to the internet gateway? Flow logs then show me where packets get rejected.
Someone changed a setting by hand in the console, and now your plan wants to undo it. What do you do?
How you handle drift between the code and what is really running.
Not applying blindly: finding out why it changed, then putting the fix into code or reverting it on purpose.

I do not just apply. I find who changed it and why; often it was a fix made during an incident. If the change is right, I put it into the code so the plan comes back clean. If it was wrong, I agree with the owner when to revert it. Then I raise how to stop it recurring, such as read-only console access in production.
When would you buy committed-use discounts, and when would you use spot instances?
Whether you match pricing models to how a workload behaves.
Commitments for the steady baseline, spot for work that can be interrupted, on-demand for the rest.

I look at usage over a few months. The floor that never goes away, like core databases and always-on services, gets a one- or three-year commitment. Spot capacity is much cheaper, but the provider can take it back with short warning, so I use it only for batch jobs, build runners or stateless workers that can restart. Spiky, unknown load stays on demand.
A developer asks for full admin rights to get unblocked today. How do you respond?
How you hold the line on access without blocking people's work.
Solving the real need with a narrow role and short-lived credentials, never a standing admin grant.

I ask what exactly they are trying to do. Usually it is one service, so I give a role scoped to that service and that environment, used through temporary credentials rather than long-lived access keys. If it is urgent I add a time limit and review it afterwards. Admin in production stays with a small group, with every action logged.
The monthly bill jumped 40% and nobody launched anything new. How do you find out why?
How you investigate cost the way you would investigate an outage.
Breaking the bill down by service, account, tag and usage type, then checking the common hidden drivers.

I open the cost report and split the increase by service, then by account and tag, then by usage type. Hidden growth is often data transfer, traffic through a NAT gateway, log volume or old snapshots. Last time a config change made a nightly job copy data across regions. After the fix I added a budget alert and anomaly detection so we hear in days, not at month end.
Your plan shows it will destroy and recreate the production database. What do you do?
Whether you stop and understand a dangerous change before applying it.
Stopping the apply, finding the field that forces replacement, protecting the data, and changing the approach.

I stop and do not apply. The plan marks which attribute forces replacement; often it is a renamed resource, a changed subnet group or an engine setting. A rename I fix by moving the state address, not by recreating. For a real change I take a snapshot, plan a migration with the data owner, and make sure deletion protection is on so one bad apply cannot drop the database.

cloud-security.heading: Cloud security engineer questions
qs: What does the shared responsibility model mean for a team running virtual machines versus a managed database?
Whether you know where the provider's job ends and your team's job begins.
The provider secures the cloud itself; the customer secures what it puts in the cloud, and the line moves with the type of service.

The provider always owns the data centers, the hardware and the hypervisor. On virtual machines we own the operating system, patching, firewall rules and access. On a managed database the provider patches the engine, but we still own who can connect, encryption settings, backup retention and the data itself. Bad access settings are always on us.
In AWS, how is a security group different from a network ACL?
Your grasp of the basic network controls in a cloud account.
Security groups are stateful, attach to instances and have allow rules only; network ACLs are stateless, apply to subnets and have both allow and deny rules.

A security group sits on the network interface, has only allow rules, and is stateful: if inbound traffic is allowed, the reply goes back out on its own. A network ACL covers a whole subnet, has numbered allow and deny rules checked in order, and is stateless, so I must allow the return traffic myself, usually the ephemeral port range.
Why do you push teams to use roles instead of long-lived access keys?
Whether you understand why temporary credentials are safer than stored secrets.
Roles hand out short-lived credentials that expire on their own; static keys get copied into code and logs and stay valid until someone rotates them.

A role gives temporary credentials that expire after a set time, by default one hour when a role is assumed, and nothing has to be stored in code. Static keys end up on laptops, in build logs and in repos, and they work until someone rotates them. For workloads I use instance roles or workload identity; for people, single sign-on into roles.
How do you lock down the root user of a new AWS account?
Your habits for protecting the most powerful identity in an account.
Strong MFA, no access keys, a controlled process to use it, an alert on every sign-in, and daily work done through other identities.

I put a hardware MFA key on it, delete any access keys, and keep the credentials in a vault that needs two people to open. Daily work goes through single sign-on and roles. I set an alert on every root sign-in, so the team knows within minutes. Root is only for the few tasks that require it, like closing the account.
An engineer asks you to open SSH to 0.0.0.0/0 on a production server to debug an outage. How do you respond?
How you balance urgent business needs against exposing a server to the internet.
You help fix the outage fast but through a logged, narrow access path, and you make sure any temporary rule gets removed.

I would not open port 22 to the whole internet, but I would not block the fix either. I would get them in through Session Manager, which needs no open inbound port and logs the session, or allow only their IP for a set time with a ticket to remove it. After the outage, we make the logged path the default.
A scanner flags an S3 bucket that is open to the public. What do you do in the first hour?
How you contain an exposure while keeping the evidence you need.
Confirm it is not public on purpose, close access, save the old policy, check what was exposed and who read it, then fix the cause.

First I make sure it is not a public website bucket by design. If not, I turn on Block Public Access and save the old policy as evidence. Then I check what data it holds and search access logs or CloudTrail data events for outside reads. I tell the owner and the incident lead, then find how the setting got there so it stays fixed.
A developer pushed an AWS access key to a public code repository an hour ago. What now?
Whether you treat a leaked secret as already used and act in the right order.
Disable the key at once, give the app a new one, search the audit logs for what the key did, and only then clean up the code history.

Bots scan public repos within minutes, so I assume the key was used. I deactivate it right away and issue a new one to the app. Then I search CloudTrail for that access key ID: new users, new roles, servers started in odd regions. Removing the commit comes last, because the key has already been copied.
What logging do you set up in a new cloud environment, and how do you stop an attacker from erasing it?
Whether you can build an audit trail that survives a compromised account.
Audit logs for every account and region, sent to a separate locked account with write-once storage, plus an alert if logging is changed.

I turn on an organization-wide CloudTrail trail for all regions, plus VPC flow logs and DNS logs where they help. The logs go to a separate log-archive account that workload admins cannot touch, into a bucket with Object Lock, so nobody can delete them during the retention period. I also alert if anyone stops or edits the trail.
Why does it matter whether EC2 instances use IMDSv2?
Your knowledge of a common path from a web bug to stolen cloud credentials.
IMDSv2 needs a session token from a PUT request, which blocks most server-side request forgery attempts to read the instance role's credentials.

The metadata service hands out the instance role's credentials. With version 1, a server-side request forgery bug can trick the app into fetching them with a plain GET. Version 2 first needs a PUT request that returns a token, sent back in a header, which most such bugs cannot do. I require it in launch templates and flag any instance still allowing v1.
How do you stop a risky setting across 200 AWS accounts instead of fixing it one by one?
Whether you can secure an organization with guardrails rather than manual cleanup.
Preventive controls at the organization level, such as service control policies, plus detective checks and code review for what gets past them.

I use service control policies in AWS Organizations to deny actions outright, like turning off CloudTrail or using unapproved regions. An SCP never grants access; it only caps what any role in the account can do. Then I add AWS Config rules to flag drift, and check infrastructure-as-code templates before they deploy.

commercial-counsel.heading: Commercial and product counsel questions
qs: Which carve-outs from a limitation of liability clause do you usually accept, and why?
Your working knowledge of the clause that most often decides how much a deal can cost the company.
A short standard list with a reason for each, and a sense of where a separate higher cap works better than unlimited liability.

I usually accept carve-outs for fraud, gross negligence or willful misconduct, breach of confidentiality, and our indemnity for third-party IP claims. A party controls those risks, or a normal cap would make the promise empty. When a customer wants all data breaches uncapped, I offer a separate, higher cap instead.
What is the difference between a warranty and an indemnity?
Whether you can separate two promises that business teams often treat as the same thing.
A warranty is a promise about a fact or quality; an indemnity is a promise to defend and cover losses from set events, usually third-party claims.

A warranty is a promise that something is true, for example that the software will perform as the documentation says. If it fails, the remedy is often repair, replace or refund. An indemnity is a promise to defend and pay if a set event happens, usually a third-party claim, such as someone suing the customer for patent infringement over our product.
We signed our master agreement with a customer, and now their purchase order arrives with their own preprinted terms on the back. What do you do?
How you handle the battle of the forms in day-to-day contracting.
Relying on an order of precedence clause in the master agreement, not on whoever sent the last form, and fixing the process so it does not repeat.

First I check that our master agreement says its terms control over any purchase order terms, and that preprinted PO terms have no effect. For sales of goods, UCC 2-207 can let a form with different terms still form a contract, so I do not count on having the last word. If the clause is missing, I send a short written note and fix the template.
Engineering wants to use an AGPL-licensed library in our hosted SaaS product. What do you check?
Your understanding of open source license obligations as they apply to a real product.
Knowing that the AGPL can reach network use, and asking whether the code is modified and how it connects to the product before deciding.

The AGPL differs from the GPL because it reaches network use: if we modify the library and users interact with it over the network, we must offer them the source of our modified version. So I ask whether we will change it, how tightly it links to our code, and whether a permissively licensed option exists. Many companies simply keep AGPL code out of the product.
Marketing wants the launch page to say we are “the most secure platform on the market.” How do you review it?
Whether you know the rules on advertising claims before a launch.
Treating it as an objective comparative claim that needs proof in hand before it runs, and offering wording the team can support.

The FTC expects a company to have a reasonable basis for an objective claim before it runs, not after. “Most secure on the market” reads as a comparison buyers can rely on, so I ask what testing compares us to competitors. Usually there is none, so I suggest a claim we can prove, like naming the specific certifications we hold.
We are launching a monthly subscription that renews automatically. What do you build into the sign-up and billing flow?
Your knowledge of federal and state automatic renewal rules.
Clear terms before payment, express consent to the renewal, and an easy way to cancel, with a check of the strictest states where customers live.

Before we take card details, the page must clearly show the price, that it renews, how often and how to cancel. The customer must agree to those terms, not just to a buried link, and gets a confirmation that repeats them. Cancelling must be simple; if they signed up online, they should be able to cancel online. I design to the strictest state law, like California's.
A customer sends back our template with 80 redlines two days before quarter end. Walk me through how you handle it.
How you triage a negotiation under time pressure without giving away what matters.
Sorting changes into accept, trade and hold, using an approved playbook, and telling sales early which points need a business decision.

I go through all 80 once and sort them. Wording and clarity edits I accept. Points with a fallback in our playbook, like payment terms, I trade. The few that touch liability, IP ownership or data I hold, and I tell the sales lead the same day which ones need a business call. Then I ask for a call with their counsel to clear the big items live.
A large customer insists on unlimited liability for any data breach. How do you respond?
Your judgement on a high-stakes ask that can block a big deal.
Understanding the customer's real worry, sizing our exposure and insurance, and offering a structured answer such as a higher separate cap.

I ask what they fear most: regulator fines, notification costs or their own customers suing. Then I check our cyber insurance limits with finance. Usually I offer a separate data breach cap, a multiple of annual fees, plus clear coverage of notification costs. That answers their worry without betting the company on one account.
After a deal closes, you find a sales email promising the customer a custom service credit that is not in the contract. What do you do?
How you handle a side promise that can create legal and accounting problems.
Not hiding behind the entire agreement clause: bringing in sales and finance and then either papering or withdrawing the promise.

The entire agreement clause helps, but I would not rely on it alone; the customer may have signed because of that email. I speak with the rep, then tell finance, since a side promise can affect revenue. We decide together: document it in an amendment, or have the account owner clearly walk it back. Then I add side letters to sales training.
The product team wants to train an AI model on data our customers have already given us. What do you check before saying yes?
Whether you can trace data rights through contracts, privacy notices and regulator expectations.
Checking contract use rights and privacy promises, and knowing that a material retroactive change to data use needs affirmative consent.

I check three things. First, what our customer contracts allow us to do with their data; many limit use to providing the service. Second, what our privacy notice told users. Third, whether we would be changing terms after the fact: the FTC has long said a material retroactive change in how collected data is used needs affirmative consent. If the rights are not there, we use opt-in or new data.

communications.heading: Communications and PR questions
qs: What is the difference between on the record, on background and off the record?
Whether you know the ground rules for talking to reporters.
Clear definitions, plus the point that terms must be agreed before speaking, since outlets read them differently.

On the record, the reporter can quote me by name. On background, they can use what I say but credit it to something like “a company spokesperson.” Off the record usually means they cannot use it at all. Outlets read these terms differently, so I agree on them before I say anything, never after.
What is a press embargo, and how do you use one?
Your grasp of a common tool for timing news coverage.
An agreement not to publish before a set time. It rests on trust, not law, so it goes only to reporters who have agreed to it.

It is an agreement that a reporter gets the news early but does not publish before a set date and time. It gives them time to write a better story. It is a courtesy, not a contract, so I ask first, get a yes before sending, state the time with the time zone, and keep the release ready in case it breaks early.
Walk me through how you build a press release for a product launch.
Whether you can write the core document of the job.
Inverted pyramid: the news in the headline and first paragraph, a quote that adds something, the facts, the boilerplate and a media contact.

The headline states the news, not an adjective. The first paragraph answers who, what, when, where and why, so a reporter can stop there. Then the details and one quote that gives a view or a reason, not “we are thrilled.” I close with the boilerplate, the standard paragraph about the company, and a named media contact with a phone number.
How do you prepare an executive for a tough media interview?
How you get a spokesperson ready to speak for the company.
Research on the reporter, two or three key messages with proof, a mock interview with the hardest questions, and clear ground rules.

I write a one-page brief: who the reporter is, what they have written lately, the likely angle. We agree on three messages and the proof for each. Then I run a mock interview with the questions they hope will not come up. I remind them nothing is off the record unless agreed first, and that “I don't know, I'll find out” is a fine answer.
How do you show that a PR campaign worked?
Whether you measure outcomes, not just the number of articles.
Measures tied to a goal set at the start, such as message pickup, coverage quality, site traffic or inquiries, and not advertising value equivalency.

I set the goal before the campaign and measure against it. Article counts are a start, but I check whether coverage hit the right outlets and carried our key message, and whether it moved something: site visits, demo requests, sign-ups. I don't use advertising value equivalency, the ad cost of the space. The industry's own measurement principles reject it.
You find a wrong figure in a press release that went out an hour ago. What do you do?
How you own and fix a public error.
A fast correction: tell your manager, issue a corrected release that says what changed, contact reporters who used it, then fix the cause.

First I tell my manager and confirm the right number with its owner. Then we send a corrected version through the same channel, marked as a correction, with the change noted. I contact each reporter who already used it and update our website. Afterward I add a step so the owner of every number signs off before release.
Your company is announcing layoffs. In what order do people hear the news?
Your judgement on the timing of internal and external messages.
Affected staff first, privately and from their managers, then all employees, then the public close behind, with HR and legal involved early.

People losing their jobs hear first, in person or by call from their manager, with HR present. Then the rest of the staff, from the CEO, before it can reach the news. The public statement follows within the hour. I bring in HR and legal early, since rules like the federal WARN Act can require advance notice for large layoffs.
Walk me through the first hour after a crisis breaks, such as a data breach.
How you act when facts are incomplete and pressure is high.
Gather facts, convene the crisis team, issue a short holding statement, brief staff, and set the next update time, with no guessing.

I get the crisis team on a call: leaders, legal, IT security, HR. We list what we know and what we don't. Within the hour a holding statement goes out: we are aware, we are investigating, here is what customers should do now, next update at a set time. Staff get the same message. I don't guess at numbers or causes.
The CEO wants to post a personal view on a divisive public issue from the company account. How do you advise?
Your judgement and your nerve when advising leaders.
You weigh the link to the business, staff and customers, and whether actions back the words, give a clear recommendation, and let the leader decide.

I ask a few questions. Does the issue touch our business, our people or our customers directly? Do our actions back up the words? Who will be upset, and will we still stand behind it a week later? If it passes, I help write it. If not, I say plainly that I recommend against it and why, and offer a better route, like a note to staff.

community-manager.heading: Community manager questions
qs: What are the most common scams in a crypto Discord, and how do you set up a server to resist them?
Whether you know how members actually lose funds in community spaces.
Names fake support DMs, impersonators and fake links, and pairs each with a concrete server setting or rule.

The big ones are fake support DMs, admins impersonated by copied names, and fake mint or airdrop links. I pin a rule that staff never DM first and never ask for a seed phrase, use a verification gate, block links in busy channels, and give staff a distinct role colour so fakes stand out.
A member asks in general chat when the token will be listed and whether the price will go up. How do you answer?
How you handle price talk without making promises the team cannot back.
No predictions, no hints about listings, and a pointer to official announcements. The tone stays friendly, not robotic.

I would say I can't talk about price or unannounced listings, and that anything official will come through the announcements channel first. Then I steer to something I can help with, like what the team shipped this month. I never hint or wink, because a hint from staff gets read as a promise.
How do you set up roles and permissions for a moderation team?
Your grasp of access control as a security issue, not just an organisation issue.
Least privilege, two-factor required for moderator actions, few admins, tight control of bots, webhooks and mass mentions.

Each role gets only what it needs. Mods can time out, delete and ban, but not edit roles or webhooks. Only two or three people hold admin. I turn on the setting that requires two-factor for moderator actions, limit who can ping everyone, and review bot permissions, since a hacked bot or webhook is a common way servers get drained.
Walk me through how you run an AMA with the founders.
How you plan a live event so it is useful and does not create risk.
Questions gathered ahead, a mix of popular and hard ones, a review of sensitive topics, a moderator on chat, and a written recap.

A week before, I collect questions in a thread and let members upvote them. I pick a mix, including two critical ones, and flag anything on price or legal matters for the team to decide on. During the AMA a second mod watches chat for scammers. Within a day I post a written recap and list the questions we owe answers to.
Member count went from 20,000 to 60,000 in a month. How do you tell whether the community actually grew?
Whether you measure engagement rather than headline numbers that bots inflate.
Looks at active and returning members, message quality, support resolution, and checks where the joins came from.

I would look at how many people post weekly, how many come back the next month, and whether questions get answered. Then I check the source of the joins. A jump right after a quest campaign with almost no new posters usually means farmers or bots. If active members rose 10% while joins tripled, that 10% is the real growth.
Your quest programme is being flooded by airdrop farmers using many wallets. What do you change?
How you design member programmes that reward real people, not sybil accounts.
Rewards tied to effort that is hard to fake, sybil checks before payout, and no promised rewards that invite gaming.

I would stop rewarding cheap actions like follows and reposts, and reward things that take real effort: good bug reports, guides, helping newcomers. Before any payout I'd check for wallets funded from the same source or acting in lockstep. I'd also stop announcing exact reward amounts in advance, since a fixed price per action is what draws the farms.
How do you turn a month of Discord chatter into a feedback report the product team will act on?
Your ability to turn noise into clear, ranked input for builders.
Groups issues by theme, counts them, adds real quotes and links, separates bugs from wishes, and suggests priority.

I tag feedback as it comes in, then group it by theme. The report opens with the top five issues, each with a count, two short member quotes and links to the threads. Bugs go separately with steps to reproduce. For example: 43 reports that a bridge transfer looked stuck, mostly mobile users. I close by noting what we fixed since last month.
A moderator banned a long-time member who had been loudly criticising the team. What do you do?
Your judgement on criticism versus rule-breaking, and how you hold moderators to the rules.
Checks what rule was broken. Criticism alone is not grounds for a ban; reverses it if needed and talks to the moderator privately.

I read the messages and the rules first. If he was harsh but not abusive or spamming, the ban was wrong and I lift it, with a short note to him. Then I talk to the mod in private, not in public. Banning critics tells everyone their voice doesn't count, and they'll take the complaint to places we can't answer it.
A moderator's account gets hacked and posts a fake mint link to the whole server. Walk me through your first hour.
How you respond to a compromise fast and in the right order.
Removes access first, deletes the posts, warns members clearly, tells victims how to revoke approvals, then finds the cause.

First I strip the account's roles and lock posting in public channels. Then I delete the messages and check webhooks and bots for anything new. Next I post a warning: do not click, and if you connected a wallet, revoke the approvals you gave that site and move funds if you signed anything. After that I find how the account was taken and write it up.
At 2 a.m. members report that funds are draining from the protocol, and the team has not confirmed anything. What do you post?
How you communicate in a crisis without speculating or spreading false advice.
Acknowledges quickly, states only what is known, gives no unverified instructions, escalates to the team, and sets a time for the next update.

I wake the on-call engineer first. Within minutes I post: we're aware of reports and investigating; updates will come only in the announcements channel. I don't guess at causes or tell people what to do until the team confirms it. I turn on slow mode, delete fake help links, and post an update every 30 minutes, even if it's only to say we're still looking.

compensation-benefits.heading: Compensation and benefits questions
qs: What is a compa-ratio, and how is it different from range penetration?
Your command of the basic measures used to read where someone sits in a pay range.
Correct formulas: salary over midpoint, and position between minimum and maximum, with a sense of when each is more useful.

Compa-ratio is salary divided by the range midpoint. At 1.0 the person is paid at midpoint; at 0.85 they are well below it. Range penetration shows where pay falls between minimum and maximum, so 25% means the lower quarter. I use both, because the same compa-ratio means different things in a narrow range and a wide one.
Walk me through how you benchmark a job using salary survey data.
Whether you can turn survey data into a market rate you can defend.
Matching on job content, not title, using several sound surveys, aging data to one date, and reading percentiles against the pay philosophy.

I match on duties, not title: I read the survey job description and only accept the match if most of the work fits. I use two or three surveys with similar company size and industry, age the data forward to a common date, and look at the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles. Then I check the result against our pay philosophy, such as paying at median for most roles.
A manager wants a new role slotted one level higher than you think it belongs. How do you decide the level?
How you level jobs on objective criteria and hold the line with a manager.
Leveling the role, not the person, against a framework and peer roles, and asking what the role owns that the lower level does not.

I level the role, not the person. I compare the job against our leveling guide on scope, complexity, independence and impact, then against roles already at each level. I ask the manager what decisions this role owns that the lower level does not. If there is a real answer, I move it up. If not, I explain why, and that title follows level, not the reverse.
What decides whether a job is exempt or non-exempt under the Fair Labor Standards Act?
Your knowledge of federal overtime classification rules.
The salary basis, salary level and duties tests, overtime for non-exempt staff over 40 hours, and that titles and state law matter.

Non-exempt employees get overtime at one and a half times their regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek. To be exempt, a role usually must pass three tests: paid on a salary basis, paid at least the minimum salary level, and doing exempt duties such as executive, administrative or professional work. Job title never decides it, and some states set stricter rules.
A hiring manager wants to offer a candidate 15% above the top of the range. What do you do?
Your judgement when one offer could break the pay structure.
Asking whether the range or the case is the problem, using other tools first, and checking the effect on current team pay.

First I ask why. If the market data shows our range is out of date, I fix the range for everyone in the job. If it is one exceptional candidate, I look at a sign-on bonus or a higher level if the scope supports it. Before any offer, I check what the current team earns, so we do not create a fairness problem on day one.
Tell me about a time you found pay compression and how you fixed it.
How you spot and correct new-hire pay catching up with tenured staff.
Data to size the problem, a costed fix phased within budget, and a change to ranges so it does not come back.

New engineers were being hired at almost what five-year staff earned. I pulled pay, compa-ratios and tenure for the team and found 14 people paid below recent hires in the same level. I proposed targeted raises costing about 3% of team payroll, phased over two cycles, and updated the ranges so offers and existing pay move together.
How are RSUs, nonqualified stock options and incentive stock options taxed for the employee?
Whether you understand equity well enough to explain it to employees correctly.
RSUs taxed at vesting, NSO spread taxed at exercise, ISOs with possible AMT at exercise and the holding periods for capital gain treatment.

RSUs are taxed as ordinary income on the share value when they vest and are delivered. With NSOs, the gap between exercise price and market value is ordinary income at exercise. ISOs have no regular income tax at exercise, but the gain can trigger alternative minimum tax. Holding the shares two years from grant and one from exercise makes the gain long-term capital gain.
Our medical plan renewal comes in 12% higher. What would you look at and propose?
How you manage benefit costs without simply shifting them onto employees.
Understanding the cause, modeling several levers, showing the cost to employees at different pay levels, and checking ACA rules.

I would ask the broker what drives it: overall trend, a few large claims or our demographics. Then I would model options: market the plan to other carriers, change deductibles or copays, add a high-deductible plan with an HSA, or change contributions. For each, I would show cost to the company and to employees at several pay levels, and confirm we still pass ACA affordability.
You discover a role paid as exempt does not meet the duties test. What do you do?
How you handle a classification mistake that carries legal and money risk.
Counsel involved early, reclassifying going forward, paying back overtime owed, telling the employee clearly, and checking similar roles.

I bring in legal counsel first. We reclassify the role as non-exempt going forward and start tracking hours. With counsel, we estimate the overtime owed for past workweeks and pay it. I tell the employee plainly that this is a classification fix, not a demotion, and explain how hours and overtime work now. Then I review similar roles for the same issue.
Walk me through how you would run a pay equity analysis.
Your method for finding and fixing pay gaps that legitimate factors do not explain.
Regression on valid factors, review of small groups by hand, work done with counsel, adjustments for unexplained gaps, and fixing the root cause.

I run a regression of pay on legitimate factors such as level, job family, location, tenure and performance, then see if gender or race still explains a gap. Groups too small for statistics I review one by one. We usually do this with counsel so it is privileged. Unexplained gaps get adjusted, and I look for the cause, often starting pay, so it does not return.

compliance.heading: Compliance questions
qs: Why is a US crypto exchange treated as a money services business, and what does that require?
Whether you know the legal base of crypto AML in the US.
Names the Bank Secrecy Act, FinCEN registration, a written AML program, reports and records, plus state licenses.

Under FinCEN guidance, a business that accepts and transmits convertible virtual currency for others is a money transmitter under the Bank Secrecy Act. So we register with FinCEN, run a written AML program, file SARs and keep records. Most states also require a money transmitter license, and New York has its own virtual currency license.
How do you set a risk rating for a new customer?
How you apply a risk-based approach at onboarding.
Several factors weighed together, a clear rule for what each rating triggers, and a fresh review when the facts change.

I look at who they are, where they are, what they say they will do, and how they fund the account. A US retail user buying small amounts is low risk. A business with a complex ownership chain, or someone planning large transfers to other platforms, is higher. Each rating sets the checks: high risk means source of funds, closer monitoring and a periodic review.
A customer deposits $15,000 worth of bitcoin in one go. Do you file a Currency Transaction Report?
Whether you know which reports apply to crypto and which do not.
No: a CTR is for physical cash. The deposit can still need review, and a SAR if something about it is suspicious.

No. A CTR covers physical currency, coins and paper money, above the reporting threshold, so a crypto deposit does not trigger one. That does not end it. I check whether the size fits the customer's profile and where the coins came from. If it looks off, it goes to investigation and possibly a SAR. A bitcoin ATM taking cash is a different story.
Our blockchain analytics tool flags a deposit with indirect exposure to a darknet market, three hops back. What do you do?
How you read analytics alerts with judgement rather than by reflex.
Weighs how much value came from the source, how the funds moved and the customer's history, then documents the decision either way.

Three hops back can be noise, since busy wallets touch many things. I check what share of the deposit traces to the market, whether the hops look like a peel chain, small amounts split off wallet after wallet to hide the source, and whether the customer has done this before. A small share in a normal pattern I close with a written reason. A large share or a repeat goes to investigation.
A deposit arrives from an address on OFAC's sanctions list. Walk me through your next steps.
Whether you know how sanctions blocking works, not just screening.
Block and hold the funds, do not send them back, report to OFAC on time, and review the customer and linked accounts.

I make sure the funds are frozen and held, not returned, because sending them back would itself be a prohibited dealing in blocked property. We file a blocking report with OFAC within ten business days. Then I review the customer, their other activity and linked accounts, and check whether our screening worked as it should. If there is more to the story, we consider a SAR.
A retired customer wants to send most of her savings to an investment site a new online friend recommended. What do you do?
How you protect a likely scam victim while staying within your role.
Spots the scam pattern, contacts the customer, uses holds the terms allow, escalates, and considers a SAR.

This fits a common scam pattern: a new online friend, an unknown platform, a large first transfer. I would hold the withdrawal for review where our terms allow and have someone call her with open questions, not accusations. I would check the receiving address against scam reports, escalate, and file a SAR if the facts support it. It is her money, but she deserves a clear warning.
The business wants to launch a new product next quarter. How do you write the AML policy and procedures for it?
How you turn a new product's risks into rules people can follow.
Starts with a risk assessment, separates policy from procedure, works with the product team, and gets approval, training and testing before launch.

I start with a risk assessment: who will use it, how money moves, and how it could be abused. The policy states what we require and who owns it; the procedures say step by step what analysts do. I draft with the product and engineering teams so the controls are actually built in. Then senior management approves it, staff are trained, and we test it before launch.
You find out a transaction monitoring rule was switched off by mistake six months ago. What do you do?
How you handle a compliance failure honestly and fix it.
Restores the control, tells leadership at once, runs a lookback, files any SARs found, fixes the root cause, and documents it all.

First I turn the rule back on and check that it fires. I tell the BSA officer, who runs our AML program, and management that day. Then we run a lookback: apply the rule to the six missed months, review every alert, and file SARs where warranted. Last, I find how it was switched off, require sign-off for rule changes, and keep a full record for auditors and examiners.

compliance-officer.heading: Compliance officer questions
qs: What does an effective compliance program need to have?
Whether you know the framework that regulators and prosecutors use to judge a program.
The seven elements from the federal sentencing guidelines, plus risk assessment, and the point that a program must work in practice, not only exist on paper.

The federal sentencing guidelines list seven elements: written standards, oversight by senior leaders, care about who gets authority, training, monitoring with a way to report concerns anonymously, consistent discipline and incentives, and fixing problems once found. I add a regular risk assessment, because it tells you where to point all the rest.
How is the compliance function different from legal and from internal audit?
Your grasp of where compliance sits among the company's lines of defense.
Legal advises on what the law means. Compliance builds and monitors controls as a second line. Internal audit independently tests both as a third line.

Legal tells us what a law requires and defends the company. Compliance turns that into policies, training and monitoring, and challenges the business, which owns the risk day to day. Internal audit is the third line: it reports to the audit committee and tests whether we all do our jobs. I want audit to find my gaps before a regulator does.
Walk me through how you would run a compliance risk assessment for a business you just joined.
How you decide where to spend limited time and budget.
A clear method: list the rules that apply, rate likelihood and impact, look at existing controls, and rank the remaining risk with the business owners.

First I map which laws apply, by product, country and activity. Then I sit with each business owner and rate each risk for how likely it is and how bad it would be. I check which controls exist and how well they work, which gives the remaining risk. The top items get a plan, an owner and a date. I redo it yearly or when the business changes.
How would you show the board that the program works in practice and not just on paper?
Whether you measure results rather than activity.
Evidence beyond completion rates: control testing, hotline data, how fast cases close, repeat findings, and what employees actually know.

A 98% training completion rate says little. I test samples of transactions against the policy, track hotline volume and how quickly cases close, and watch for repeat findings. Short surveys show whether staff know how to raise a concern and trust that they can. If a region has no hotline reports at all, I treat that as a warning, not good news.
An anonymous hotline report says a manager is splitting purchases to stay under his approval limit. What do you do first?
How you triage a report and start an investigation without harming it.
Log it, protect the reporter, quietly preserve records, decide who investigates, and keep the manager out of the loop until the facts are gathered.

I log the report and reply through the hotline so the reporter can answer follow-up questions. Before anyone talks to the manager, I pull the purchase records and approvals and ask IT to preserve his email. I check for links to the vendors involved. Then I agree with legal on who investigates, and I make sure nobody tries to identify the reporter.
Your top salesperson broke the gifts policy, and the sales VP wants it handled quietly. How do you respond?
Whether you hold to consistent discipline under pressure.
Same rules for stars as for everyone, because regulators check whether discipline is consistent, and staff notice when it is not.

I tell the VP the outcome has to match what we did for others with the same breach, or the policy stops meaning anything. Prosecutors ask directly whether high performers get a pass. I bring the facts and past cases to HR so the result is fair, not harsher because of who he is. If the VP keeps pushing, I raise it through my reporting line, up to the board.
We want to hire a sales agent in a country with high corruption risk. What due diligence do you do, and what red flags stop the deal?
Your practical knowledge of third-party bribery risk under the FCPA.
Knows the company can be liable for an agent's bribes, checks ownership and ties to officials, and names real red flags such as odd payment requests.

Under the FCPA we can be liable for bribes an agent pays on our behalf, and looking away from obvious signs is no defense. I check ownership, links to officials, reputation and the business reason for the hire. Red flags: a commission well above market, requests for cash or payment to a third country, a referral from an official, or refusal to sign anti-bribery terms.
You are sitting in on an internal investigation interview with company counsel. What has to be said at the start, and why?
Whether you know how to run a fair interview that protects privilege.
The Upjohn warning: counsel represents the company, not the employee, and the company may choose to share what is said. Plus a reminder that retaliation is banned.

Counsel gives what is called an Upjohn warning: the lawyer represents the company, not the employee. The talk is privileged, but the privilege belongs to the company, which may decide to share it, even with the government. We ask the employee to keep it confidential and remind them retaliation is not allowed. Someone takes careful notes.
You learn that routine email deletion kept running for two weeks after the company received a subpoena. How do you handle it?
How you respond to a preservation failure honestly and fast.
Stop deletion now, try to recover data, document what was lost and why, and let counsel decide how to disclose it. No hiding it.

First I have IT suspend deletion for the people and systems covered and confirm in writing that it stopped. Then we check backups and devices to recover what we can. I document what ran, when, and what may be lost, and give that to counsel, who decides how to disclose it. Then I fix the gap: legal holds now go straight to IT with a named owner and a confirmation step.
Our review finds a violation that no regulator knows about. How do you decide whether to recommend self-disclosure?
Your judgement on one of the hardest calls in the job.
Weighs it with counsel: any legal duty to report, the credit given for disclosure and fixes, the chance of discovery. Stops and fixes the conduct either way.

Some rules require reporting, so I first ask counsel whether we have a legal duty. If not, we weigh it: DOJ and many regulators give real credit for voluntary disclosure, cooperation and fixing the cause, and that credit is lost if a whistleblower gets there first. We stop the conduct and remediate regardless. I give the board my recommendation in writing.

computer-vision.heading: Computer vision engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between semantic, instance and panoptic segmentation?
Whether you know the basic output types of vision models.
Clear definitions, and a sense of which task needs which: counting separate objects needs instances.

Semantic segmentation gives each pixel a class, so three touching cars become one car blob. Instance segmentation separates each object, so you get car 1, car 2 and car 3. Panoptic does both: every pixel gets a class, countable objects also get their own ID, and regions like road or sky stay as one area.
What is IoU, and how is it used to score an object detector?
Your grasp of how detection results are measured.
IoU as overlap divided by union, a threshold that makes a box a hit, and mAP averaged over classes and sometimes thresholds.

IoU, intersection over union, is the area where the predicted box and the true box overlap, divided by the area they cover together. A prediction counts as a hit if IoU passes a threshold, often 0.5. Average precision is computed per class from the precision-recall curve, then averaged into mAP. Some benchmarks also average over thresholds from 0.5 to 0.95.
Your detector puts five boxes on the same pedestrian. What is happening, and how do you fix it?
Whether you understand non-maximum suppression and its limits.
Explains non-maximum suppression step by step and knows the threshold trade-off in crowded scenes.

Detectors predict many overlapping candidates, and non-maximum suppression should clean them up. It keeps the highest-scoring box, drops same-class boxes that overlap it above an IoU threshold, and repeats. If duplicates survive, the threshold may be too high. Set it too low and it deletes real people standing close, so I test on crowded images.
Which data augmentations would you avoid, and why?
Whether you choose augmentations that keep the label true.
Augmentations must not change what the image means, with examples like flips on text, road signs or left-right anatomy.

I avoid any change that makes the label wrong. A horizontal flip turns a left-turn arrow into a right-turn arrow and mirrors text. On chest X-rays it puts the heart on the wrong side. Strong color shifts are a bad idea when color is the signal, like ripe versus unripe fruit. I always look at a batch of augmented images before training.
You have 200 hours of video from 40 cameras. How do you split it into training and test sets?
Whether you can spot data leakage in image and video data.
Split by camera, site or recording, never by random frames, so the test set shows truly new scenes.

Not by random frames: neighboring frames are almost identical, so the test score would mostly measure memory. I split by camera, holding out, say, 8 whole cameras for test and a few for validation. I check that night, rain and each site type appear in every set. For medical scans the same rule applies per patient.
Two annotators label the same images and disagree on 15% of the boxes. What do you do?
How you manage label quality, the base of every vision model.
Finds where and why they disagree, fixes the guideline with examples, measures agreement again, and routes hard cases to review.

First I sort the disagreements by type: missed objects, loose boxes, or class confusion. Usually the guideline is unclear, for example whether to label a half-hidden bike. I add rules with picture examples, retrain the annotators and re-measure agreement on a shared sample. Truly ambiguous cases go to an expert reviewer or get an ignore label.
You can pay to label 5,000 more images out of 500,000 unlabeled ones. How do you choose them?
Your judgement on spending a labeling budget where it helps most.
Targeted selection from known failures, model uncertainty and diversity, plus a small random slice, not a random draw only.

I start from error analysis: if the model fails at night or on bikes, I pull those images first. Then I add images where the model is unsure, and use image embeddings to avoid picking hundreds of near-duplicates. I keep a small random slice so I still see normal data. After labeling I retrain and check that those failures improved.
A model that scored well in testing drops sharply on a customer's new camera. Walk me through how you find the cause.
How you debug a model that fails after deployment.
Checks the pipeline first (color channel order, resizing, normalization), then compares the images themselves before retraining.

First I rule out bugs: I run one image through the training code and the production code and compare the inputs. Common culprits are BGR versus RGB channel order, a different resize or crop, or missing normalization. If those match, I compare the images: resolution, lens distortion, compression, lighting. Then I label a small set from the new camera and fine-tune if needed.
Your detector misses small objects, like distant people in drone footage. What can you try?
Your toolbox for a common detection weakness.
Resolution and architecture fixes such as larger input, tiling, multi-scale features and fitting anchor sizes, with the speed cost of each.

Small objects often shrink to a few pixels when the image is resized down. I would try a larger input size, or cut the frame into overlapping tiles and merge the results. I check that the model uses fine, multi-scale feature maps and that anchor sizes fit small boxes. Each step costs speed, so I measure recall on small objects separately.
The model must run at 30 frames per second on a small device, and it runs at 8. How do you get there without losing much accuracy?
How you optimize a model for real hardware.
Profiles first, then uses levers like input size, quantization with calibration, pruning or distillation, checking accuracy after each step.

I profile first to see whether time goes to the model, preprocessing or copying data. Then the cheap wins: a smaller input size and the chip vendor's optimized runtime. Next, 8-bit quantization calibrated on a few hundred real images, or quantization-aware training if accuracy drops. If still slow, a smaller model trained by distillation from the big one.

construction.heading: Civil engineering and construction questions
qs: Walk me through how a submittal moves from a subcontractor to approval.
Your grasp of the paperwork that controls what gets built and installed.
The sub prepares it, the contractor checks it against the specs, the design team reviews it, and a log ties every due date to the schedule.

The sub sends shop drawings or product data. I check them against the specs and drawings before they go to the architect or engineer, so we do not waste their review time. They return it approved, approved as noted, or revise and resubmit. I keep a log with due dates tied to the schedule, because a late steel submittal delays fabrication, not just paper.
Before we grade a 12-acre site, which environmental permit do you check for, and what does it require on site?
Your knowledge of the stormwater permit that comes with almost every large site.
