NPDES construction stormwater coverage for disturbing one acre or more, a written plan, controls installed before grading, and regular inspections.

Disturbing an acre or more needs coverage under the NPDES construction stormwater permit, issued by EPA or, in most states, the state agency. That means a written stormwater pollution prevention plan, silt fence, inlet protection and a stabilized construction entrance in place before mass grading, inspections on the permit schedule, and records kept on site.
A crew wants to dig a 6-foot trench for a duct bank and get in quickly before the rain. What has to be in place first?
Whether you know the excavation rules that prevent cave-ins.
A protective system at 5 feet or deeper unless it is stable rock, a competent person inspecting, safe access and spoil set back. Rain calls for more care.

At 5 feet or deeper OSHA requires a protective system: sloping, shoring or a trench box, unless it is all stable rock. A competent person inspects before work and after rain. Spoil stays at least 2 feet back from the edge, and a ladder must be within 25 feet of each worker since it is over 4 feet deep. Rain weakens the walls, so I would not rush it.
Halfway through the schedule you have spent 55% of the budget. Is the job over budget?
Whether you measure cost against work done, not against time or spending alone.
You cannot tell without earned value: compare the budgeted value of the work actually done with actual cost and with planned value.

Not necessarily. I need the earned value, the budget for the work actually in place. If 60% of the work is done, we are under budget and ahead. If only 45% is done, the cost performance index is 45 over 55, about 0.82: we spend a dollar for 82 cents of work, and I dig into which cost codes are driving it.
A subcontractor bills 80% complete on its electrical work, and your walk says it is closer to 60%. What do you do?
How you control cost without damaging the working relationship.
Verify in the field against the schedule of values, pay for what is in place, document it, and keep retainage and lien waivers in order.

I walk the work with their foreman, line by line against the schedule of values: conduit, wire pulled, gear set, terminations. We agree a number and I approve that, with notes on why. I hold retainage per the contract and collect conditional lien waivers with the payment. Overpaying early leaves no leverage if they walk off the job.
On a data center, how do you deal with switchgear, generators and transformers that take many months to arrive?
Whether you plan procurement as part of the schedule, not after it.
Long-lead items are named early, released ahead of final design if needed, tracked through fabrication, and tied to the schedule.

I list long-lead equipment at the start and put procurement in the schedule: submittal, approval, release, fabrication, shipping. Often the owner orders gear early on approved specs before drawings are final. I ask for factory progress reports and witness test dates, and plan a fallback, like temporary power, if a unit slips.
Excavation hits soil that smells of fuel and is not in the geotechnical report. What do you do?
Whether you protect people and the contract when the ground is not what was expected.
Stop in that area, protect workers, notify the owner in writing promptly per the contract, bring in an environmental consultant, and track cost.

I stop digging there, move the crew back and keep that spoil separate and covered. I notify the owner in writing the same day, because differing site condition clauses have notice deadlines. An environmental consultant tests it and sets handling and disposal. Meanwhile I photograph everything, track time and equipment on a separate cost code, and move crews to other work.
The 28-day cylinder breaks for a foundation come back below the specified strength. What happens next?
How you handle a quality failure in work that is already built.
No panic and no hiding: check the tests, compare with the acceptance rules, tell the engineer of record, and take cores if needed.

First I check the test itself: how the cylinders were made, cured and handled, since poor field curing lowers breaks. Then I compare results with the spec's acceptance rules, which usually follow ACI 318. I tell the engineer of record right away. If more data is needed we take cores from the structure, and the engineer decides if it is fine, needs strengthening or must be replaced.
How would you plan commissioning for a data center so it is ready for the owner's load on day one?
Whether you see commissioning as a planned phase, not a final checklist.
Levels from factory tests to an integrated systems test, planned into the schedule early, with load and failure scenarios proven before handover.

I plan it from the start with the commissioning agent, in levels: factory witness tests, delivery inspection, startup, functional tests of each system, then an integrated systems test. That last one uses load banks to simulate IT load and cuts utility power to prove generators and cooling take over. I leave real float before handover, because problems show up there.

construction-manager.heading: Construction project manager questions
qs: What is the difference between an RFI, a submittal and a change order?
Your grasp of the basic paperwork that controls scope, cost and time.
An RFI asks for clarification. A submittal shows what will be installed, for review. A change order changes the contract's scope, price or time.

An RFI is a written question to the design team when the documents are unclear. A submittal is shop drawings, product data or samples sent for review before we buy or build. A change order is a signed change to the contract's scope, price or time. An RFI answer that adds work is not a change order by itself. I still have to price it and get it signed.
Walk me through how you review a subcontractor's monthly pay application.
How you protect the owner and the job before money goes out.
Checks billing against work actually in place, approved changes, stored materials, retainage and lien waivers before approving.

I compare each line of the schedule of values to what I see in the field, not to what the sub says. I check that change orders are approved before they are billed, that stored materials are documented, and that retainage is held per the contract. I also need a conditional lien waiver for this payment and an unconditional one for the last payment before I sign off.
The framing inspection fails the day before drywall is set to start. What do you do?
How you react to a failed inspection without losing control of the schedule.
Gets the correction list, fixes the items fast, rebooks the inspection, and moves crews instead of covering anything up.

First, nobody hangs a board in the failed areas. Covering work before it passes means tearing it out later. I get the inspector's correction list, assign each item to the right sub with a deadline, and book the reinspection right away. If only part of the building failed, I ask whether the areas that passed can proceed and move the drywall crew there.
The owner asks your superintendent in the field to move a wall. How do you handle it?
Whether you control scope changes and protect the contract.
No work on verbal direction alone: the request in writing, priced with its schedule impact, and a signed change order or directive before work starts.

I get the request in writing and route it through the architect so the drawings and code review are updated. I price it with the subs, including the schedule impact, and submit a change order. If it cannot wait, I ask for a signed construction change directive so work can go ahead while we settle the price. My supers know not to act on verbal changes.
A subcontractor on the critical path is two weeks behind. What steps do you take?
How you recover a schedule and use the contract without burning the relationship.
Finds the cause, gets a recovery plan with crew numbers, documents everything, and follows the subcontract's notice steps if nothing improves.

I sit down with the sub's owner, not just the foreman, and find out why: manpower, material or money. I ask for a written recovery plan with crew sizes and dates and track it daily. I look at resequencing to help. If they still miss, I send the written notice the subcontract requires, because any later right to supplement their crew depends on that paper trail.
Your excavator hits old concrete footings that are not on any drawing. What happens next?
Whether you know how to handle a differing site condition.
Stops work in that area, documents it, gives written notice promptly and before the condition is disturbed, then waits for direction.

I stop digging in that spot, take photos and measurements, and note the time and location in the daily log. Then I send written notice to the owner and architect right away, because most contracts require prompt notice before the condition is disturbed. I get a price for removal and the schedule impact, and we proceed once there is written direction.
What has to happen between substantial completion and final payment?
Your knowledge of closeout and handover.
Punch list, final inspections and the certificate of occupancy, closeout documents, owner training, and final waivers before retainage is released.

We walk the punch list with the architect and close every item. We finish final inspections so the building department can issue the certificate of occupancy. I collect warranties, operation and maintenance manuals and as-built drawings, and set up training for the owner's staff. Final lien waivers from every sub come in before final payment and release of retainage.
Halfway through the job, your forecast shows the project finishing over budget. What do you do?
How you manage cost and deliver bad news early.
Finds where the overrun comes from, separates owner changes from own losses, looks for real savings, and tells the owner early with numbers.

I break the forecast down by cost code to see where it is: a subcontract that came in high, extra labor, or unpriced changes. Owner-driven changes get priced and submitted. For our own losses I look at contingency and savings ideas the owner must approve. Then I tell my executive and the owner now, with a number and a plan, not at the last pay app.
Tell me about a scope gap you missed in buyout and how you dealt with it.
Whether you own mistakes and fix the process, not just the problem.
Admits the miss, gets the work done without fighting the subs, takes the cost honestly, and changes how scopes are written.

On a medical office job, neither the drywall sub nor the carpentry sub had wall blocking for cabinets in their contract. I caught it at framing, got a price from the carpenter, and covered it from our savings instead of forcing it on either sub. Now I use a checklist across trades when I award subcontracts, so blocking and firestopping always have a named owner.

content-designer.heading: Content designer and UX writer questions
qs: What is the difference between voice and tone in product writing?
Whether you know the basic tools of a content style guide.
Voice stays the same across the product; tone shifts with the user's situation and mood, especially when something goes wrong.

Voice is who the product is, and it stays the same everywhere: say, plain, warm and direct. Tone is how that voice adjusts to the moment. On a success screen we can be a little lighter. On a failed payment or a locked account we drop the jokes and get straight to what happened and what to do next.
A user types a date in the wrong format and sees "Invalid input." How would you rewrite that message?
How you write an error message that helps someone fix the problem.
Says what went wrong and how to fix it, in plain words, next to the field, without blame. Bonus for asking whether the error can be avoided.

I'd say how to fix it, right under the field: "Enter the date as MM/DD/YYYY, for example 03/14/2025." No "invalid," no blame, no error code unless support needs it. Then I'd ask the designer whether the field can accept several formats or use a date picker, so the error rarely shows at all.
Why shouldn't placeholder text inside a form field be used as the field's label?
Your grasp of accessible, usable form copy.
Placeholders vanish when typing starts, are often low contrast, and are not a dependable label for assistive tech. Use a visible label and helper text.

Placeholder text disappears as soon as someone starts typing, so people lose the hint while they still need it. It's usually light gray and hard to read, and it isn't a dependable label for screen readers. I put a visible label above the field and move format hints into helper text below it.
A designer hands you a finished mockup full of lorem ipsum and needs the words by tomorrow. What do you do?
How you work with design when content comes in last.
Delivers on time but asks about the goal, the user and real data, and flags where real words may change the layout.

I'd ask three things fast: what the user is trying to do here, what we want them to do next, and what real data shows up, like long names. Then I'd write real copy by tomorrow and flag spots where it won't fit the layout. Next time I'd ask to join earlier, at the wireframe stage, so the words shape the design.
On a confirmation dialog for deleting a project, what goes on the buttons, and why?
Whether you write clear labels for destructive actions.
Specific verbs instead of Yes/No or OK, a title naming the action, and a plain note on whether it can be undone.

Not "Yes" and "No." The title says what will happen: "Delete Q3 Budget project?" The body says what gets lost and whether it can be undone. The buttons read "Delete project" and "Cancel," with the delete button styled as dangerous. Someone who reads only the buttons still knows what they're agreeing to.
How would you test whether new onboarding copy works before it launches?
Your methods for checking words with real users.
Task-based usability testing with a few real users, think-aloud, no leading questions, plus a simple method like a highlighter test.

I'd run a short usability test with five or six people who match our users. I give a task, like "set up your first invoice," and ask them to think aloud, without reading the copy to them or hinting. I'd also try a highlighter test: green for what's clear, red for what's confusing. Where people hesitate or misread, I rewrite and test again.
When would you use a card sort, and when a tree test, to work on a product's navigation?
Your knowledge of information architecture research.
Card sorting helps build a structure from users' mental models; tree testing checks whether people can find things in a proposed structure.

A card sort helps me build the structure: people group topics and, in an open sort, name the groups, so I learn how they think. A tree test checks a structure: people see only the text menu, no visual design, and try to find where they'd go for a task. I'd sort first, draft the menu, then tree test it and fix labels where people got lost.
Legal asks you to put three paragraphs of terms directly on the sign-up screen. How do you handle it?
How you balance legal requirements with a usable flow.
Respects legal's goal, asks what must be shown versus linked, proposes a clear alternative, and gets sign-off rather than overriding them.

I'd ask what the actual requirement is: what must appear on screen, what can be linked, and whether we need active consent. Often a checkbox with a one-line plain summary and a link to the full terms meets it. I keep their exact wording wherever it's required, show them the two versions side by side, and get their sign-off before it ships.
The product is launching in German and Japanese. What changes in how you write the strings?
Whether you write content that survives translation.
No string concatenation, full sentences with placeholders, notes for translators, room for longer text, no idioms or text in images.

I stop building sentences from fragments, because word order changes between languages; I write full strings with placeholders like {name}. I add notes so translators know where a string appears and how much space it has. I leave room, since German often runs longer. I cut idioms and puns, let the code handle plurals, and keep text out of images.
You renamed a menu item, and the next week support tickets about finding that feature went up. What do you do?
How you own a content mistake and fix it with evidence.
Checks the data before assuming, says it openly, looks at what words users search, and fixes or rolls back fast, then tests the label.

First I'd confirm it's the label: did anything else ship that week, and what do the tickets actually say? If people are searching for the old name, that's my answer. I'd tell the team, roll back or add the old term as a search keyword right away, then run a quick tree test on two or three label options so the next change is based on users, not taste.

content-writer.heading: Content writer and editor questions
qs: What is search intent, and how does it change the article you write?
Whether you understand what search optimisation is really for.
Intent is the need behind the query. The format and depth of the piece follow from it, not from the keyword alone.

Search intent is what the person typing the query actually wants: to learn, to compare, to buy or to find a page. Someone searching “how to descale a kettle” wants steps, fast, so I lead with a numbered list. Someone searching “best electric kettles” wants a comparison, so I build a table and explain how we chose. I check the top results to see what format readers expect.
Walk me through how you edit a colleague's 2,000-word draft.
How you organize an edit instead of fixing commas at random.
Separate passes from big to small: structure, then sentences, then facts and style. Notes explain the changes.

I read it once without touching anything, to see if the argument holds and the order works. Then I fix structure: moving sections and flagging gaps. Next comes the line edit for clarity and length, then a copy edit for style, names, numbers and links. I use tracked changes and leave short comments saying why, so the writer learns and can push back.
How do you prepare for an interview with a source, and what do you do during it?
Your interviewing method, from research to recording.
Research first, open questions, permission to record, and checking spellings and titles before the call ends.

I read what the person has already said publicly so I don't waste time on basics. I write five or six open questions, ranked, and expect to drop half. I ask permission to record, since some states require everyone's consent. I ask follow-ups like “Can you give me an example?” and end by confirming name spelling, title and how they want to be described.
How do you write the title tag and meta description for an article?
Whether you know how a page appears in search results.
Main topic first, short enough not to be cut off, a promise the page keeps, and knowing search engines may rewrite both.

The title tag is the clickable headline in search results, so I put the main topic near the front and keep it short enough that it isn't cut off. The meta description is the snippet below. It doesn't directly affect ranking, but it affects clicks, so I say plainly what the reader gets. Search engines sometimes rewrite both, so the page itself has to match the promise.
A client wants the keyword used 15 times in an 800-word post. How do you respond?
How you handle a request that would hurt both the piece and the client.
Explaining that keyword stuffing reads badly and is treated as spam, then offering a better plan for placement and related terms.

I'd explain that repeating a phrase that often makes the text read like spam, and search engines' spam policies name keyword stuffing directly. I'd offer a plan instead: the keyword in the title, the first paragraph and one subheading, then natural variations and related questions readers ask. I'd show them a sample paragraph written both ways so they can judge.
You find a striking statistic on a blog. What do you do before you use it?
Your fact-checking habits.
Tracing the number to the original study, checking date, sample and what it measures, and linking the primary source.

I follow the trail back to the original source, often a survey or a government dataset, because blogs copy each other and numbers drift. I check the year, who was surveyed and what the number actually measures. Once a “70% of shoppers” figure turned out to be 70% of 300 people in one survey. If I can't find the original, I don't use it.
A source asks to approve the article before it goes live. What do you say?
Your judgement on accuracy versus editorial control.
Knowing the publication's policy, offering to check quotes and facts for accuracy, and keeping the editorial decisions.

First I check our policy, because a brand blog and a news site differ. Usually I offer to read back their quotes and technical facts so nothing is wrong, but I explain that the angle and the edit stay with us. If they want to change what they said, not just fix an error, I talk to my editor before agreeing to anything.
Our article recommends products and we earn a commission on sales. What does the piece need?
Whether you know the FTC disclosure rules for affiliate content.
A clear, conspicuous disclosure in plain words near the recommendations, not hidden in a footer or behind a link.

The FTC expects a material connection, like a commission, to be disclosed clearly and conspicuously. So I put a plain sentence near the top, before the first link: “We earn a commission if you buy through links on this page.” Not only in the footer, and not behind a vague word like “partners.” The commission also can't change what we honestly say about the products.
A reader emails to say a fact in your published article is wrong. What do you do?
How you handle a mistake that is already public.
Verify fast, fix it, add a dated correction note instead of erasing it quietly, thank the reader and tell the editor.

I check the claim against the source that same day. If the reader is right, I fix the text and add a short note at the bottom with the date and what changed, rather than silently editing. I tell my editor, reply to the reader with thanks, and look at how it slipped through. Once it was a misread table, so now I check every number against the original twice.
Traffic to an older guide has dropped by half. How do you decide what to do with it?
How you diagnose and refresh existing content.
Data first: lost queries, what now ranks, outdated facts, overlapping pages. Then update, merge with a redirect, or retire.

I start with our search data: which queries it lost and what now ranks for them. Often the guide is out of date, or a newer page on our own site competes with it. If it's outdated, I update facts and screenshots and add what readers now ask. If two pages overlap, I merge them and set a 301 redirect from the weaker one. If nobody searches for it anymore, I retire it.

contract-manager.heading: Contract manager questions
qs: What is the difference between a master agreement and a statement of work, and why does the order of precedence clause matter?
Whether you understand how a set of contract documents fits together.
The MSA holds the general legal terms and the SOW the specific work. The precedence clause says which document wins when they conflict.

The master agreement sets the terms for every deal: liability, IP, payment, termination. Each SOW describes one project: scope, deliverables, price, dates. The precedence clause decides which wins in a conflict. Usually the MSA wins unless the SOW expressly overrides a named section. Without that clause, a loose SOW can quietly rewrite the MSA.
How is an indemnity different from a limitation of liability?
Your grasp of the two clauses that move the most risk.
An indemnity shifts specific losses, often third-party claims, to one party. A limitation caps or excludes damages. How the two interact matters most.

An indemnity is a promise to cover certain losses, often claims a third party brings, like an IP infringement suit, including defense costs. A limitation of liability caps what one side can recover from the other and often excludes indirect damages. I always check whether the indemnities sit inside the cap or are carved out of it.
Once a contract is signed, how do you make sure nothing is missed?
How you manage obligations and dates after signature.
A central record with key terms, a named owner for each duty, and alerts set before notice deadlines, not just before the end date.

Every signed contract goes into our repository with the key data pulled out: term, renewal type, notice period, price increases, reporting duties, insurance certificates. Each item gets an owner. Alerts fire before the notice deadline, not the end date, usually 90 and 30 days ahead. Each month I send owners a short list of what is coming due.
The other side sends back a clean version and says they only changed two clauses. What do you do?
Whether you verify a counterparty's changes yourself.
You run a compare against your last version every time and raise any unmarked change openly and calmly.

I never rely on a summary. I run a document compare of their version against the last one we sent, so every change shows, marked or not. Once that caught a payment term moved from 30 to 60 days that nobody mentioned. I raised it politely as a likely oversight, put it back, and from then on asked for tracked changes only.
A customer sends a purchase order with its own preprinted terms that conflict with our signed agreement. How do you handle it?
Whether you know which document governs and how to protect it.
Check what the master agreement says about PO terms, confirm in writing, and bring in counsel when there is no master agreement.

First I check whether our master agreement says preprinted PO terms do not apply; well-drafted ones do. If so, I reply in writing that we accept the PO under the master agreement only. If there is no master agreement, it is a battle of the forms, which UCC 2-207 governs for goods, and I bring in legal rather than assume the last form sent wins.
A supplier tells you it cannot perform because of force majeure. What do you check in the contract?
How you read a clause under pressure instead of assuming it applies.
The exact wording decides it: covered events, notice, which duties are excused, mitigation, and the right to exit a long delay.

In the US, force majeure mostly turns on the contract wording, so I read the clause closely. Is the event listed or caught by the general words? Did they give notice on time and in the required form? Does it excuse only delay or also payment? Must they mitigate? Can we terminate if it lasts past a set period? Meanwhile I line up a backup source.
Sales needs a deal signed today, and the customer refuses any cap on our liability. What do you do?
Your judgement on risk when the business is pushing hard.
Neither blocking nor caving: offer workable options, explain the exposure, and get the decision from someone with authority, in writing.

I would not just say no. I offer options: a cap tied to fees paid, a higher cap for data breaches, or no cap only for the risks they fear most. If they still refuse, I send the deal owner and approver a short note: what is exposed, rough size, what insurance covers. Signing uncapped is their documented call, not something I approve quietly to hit a date.
After signing, you find an email in which our sales rep promised the customer a free extra year of support. How do you handle it?
How you deal with promises made outside the signed contract.
Find out whether it could bind the company, involve the rep's manager and legal, settle it openly with the customer, and prevent repeats.

I check the entire agreement clause and the rep's authority, and ask legal whether that email could still bind us. Then I talk to the rep and their manager. If we honor it, it goes into a signed amendment. If not, the account owner tells the customer directly and soon. Then I remind sales that only signed paper commits the company.
You missed a notice deadline, and a software contract renewed for a year at a higher price. What now?
How you own and repair a costly mistake.
Telling your manager quickly, looking for options in the contract and the law, negotiating with the vendor, and fixing the tracking gap.

I tell my manager the same day, with the cost. Then I reread the contract: any right to reduce seats, a cap on price increases, termination for convenience. Some states have auto-renewal notice laws, so I ask legal whether one applies. Then I call the vendor; many will trade a better price for a longer commitment. Last, I find out why the alert failed and fix it.
A key supplier is being bought by one of our competitors. Walk me through what you check.
How you find your rights and risks when a counterparty changes hands.
Assignment and change of control clauses, termination rights, confidentiality and data terms, and a realistic exit plan.

I pull every contract with that supplier. I check assignment and change of control: do they need our consent, or can we terminate? Then confidentiality and data use, because our pricing and forecasts must not reach a competitor. I check termination notice, transition help and how long a switch takes. Then I brief the business with options and dates.

controller.heading: Financial controller questions
qs: Walk me through how you run the month-end close.
Whether you run the close as a planned process, not a scramble.
A dated checklist with owners, a clear order (subledgers, accruals, reconciliations, review), and a review of big changes before results go out.

I keep a close calendar with each task, its owner and its due day. Subledgers close first: payables, receivables, payroll, fixed assets. Then accruals and reclasses, then balance sheet reconciliations. Before I sign off, I review the reconciliations and a flux analysis that explains large changes from last month. Only then does the package go to leadership.
What is the difference between an accrued expense and a prepaid expense?
Your grasp of accrual accounting and matching costs to the right period.
Accrual: cost incurred but not yet billed, booked as a liability. Prepaid: paid before use, held as an asset and expensed over the period it covers.

An accrued expense is something we used but have not been billed for yet, like contractor hours in the last week of the month. I book the expense and a liability, then reverse it when the invoice arrives. A prepaid is paid in advance, like a year of insurance. It sits as an asset and I expense one twelfth each month.
What does a good balance sheet reconciliation look like?
Whether you know a reconciliation must prove a balance, not just make two numbers match.
Ties the ledger to independent support, explains every reconciling item with its age, has a separate preparer and reviewer, and clears old items.

It ties the general ledger balance to something outside the ledger: a bank statement, a subledger, a loan schedule. Every reconciling item is listed with a date and a reason, and anything older than 60 days gets chased. One person prepares it, another reviews and signs with a date. A plug to make it tie is not a reconciliation.
Explain the five steps of revenue recognition under ASC 606.
Your knowledge of the US revenue standard.
The five steps in the right order, with a sense of where the judgement sits, such as finding the separate promises in a contract.

First, identify the contract with the customer. Second, identify the performance obligations, the distinct promises in it. Third, determine the transaction price, including variable consideration. Fourth, allocate it to the obligations based on standalone selling prices. Fifth, recognize revenue when or as each one is satisfied. Step two is where most hard calls are.
Your accounting team is three people. How do you handle segregation of duties?
How you build controls when you cannot fully separate duties.
Separate the riskiest pairs, such as vendor setup and payment release, and add compensating controls like independent review where overlap can't be avoided.

No one can both create a vendor and release a payment to it, and the person who records cash does not reconcile the bank. Where overlap is unavoidable, I add a compensating control: each month I review the bank reconciliation, a report of vendor master changes and the payment runs, and the owner approves payments above a set amount.
Accounts payable gets an email from a long-time vendor asking to change the bank account for its payments. What do you do?
Whether you recognize a common payment fraud and stop it.
Treat it as possible fraud: confirm by calling the vendor at a number already on file, not one in the email, and require a second approval for the change.

Nothing changes based on an email. Someone calls the vendor at the phone number we already have on file, not the one in the message, and confirms with a known contact. The change needs a second person to approve it, and I watch the first payment to the new account. Business email compromise often looks exactly like this request.
Two days before quarter end, the CEO asks you to book revenue on a large order that will ship next week. How do you respond?
Your independence when leadership pushes on the numbers.
A clear, respectful no grounded in the rule that control has not passed to the customer, an offer of what can be shown honestly, and escalation if pressed.

I would explain that for a product sale, revenue is recognized when control passes to the customer, usually at shipment or delivery under the contract terms. Booking it now would misstate the quarter, and the auditors would find it. I can show the order as backlog in the board report. If the pressure continued, I would raise it with the audit committee.
Your auditors propose an adjustment you believe is wrong. How do you handle it?
How you work with auditors when you disagree with them.
Learn their reasoning, answer in writing with the standard and the evidence, escalate properly, and accept the adjustment if they turn out to be right.

I ask them to walk me through their reasoning and the guidance they rely on. Then I write a short memo with our position, the specific standard and the documents that support it. Often a missing fact is the issue, and the evidence settles it. If we still disagree, I take it to the CFO and, if needed, the audit committee. If I am wrong, we book it and move on.
Your close takes 12 business days and the CFO wants it in 5. Walk me through how you would get there.
Whether you can redesign a process instead of just pushing people to work faster.
Map the close to find the bottleneck, move work before month end, use thresholds for estimates, automate repeat entries, and shorten in stages.

I would map every task with its work time and wait time to find the critical path. Then I move work earlier: reconcile steady accounts during the month, accrue from estimates above a set threshold instead of waiting for invoices, and agree cutoff dates with other departments in advance. I automate recurring entries and drop low value steps. I would aim for 8 days first, then 5.

controls-engineer.heading: Controls and PLC engineer questions
qs: What happens during one PLC scan?
Whether you understand how the controller actually runs your logic.
Read inputs, solve logic in order, write outputs, handle communications, and know what that means for fast signals.

Each scan, the PLC reads all inputs into an input image, runs the logic top to bottom using that snapshot, then writes the output image to the real outputs and handles communications. An input that changes mid-scan is seen next scan, and a very short pulse can be missed unless I use a fast input or an interrupt.
Why is a stop button usually wired normally closed, and how does that look in the ladder logic?
Whether you design so that a wiring failure stops the machine.
A broken wire drops the input and stops the machine. The candidate knows the ladder contact type differs from the field contact type.

Wired normally closed, the input is on while all is well. If a wire breaks or a terminal comes loose, the input drops and the machine stops, so the failure is safe. In the ladder I use a normally open contact, examine if closed, in series with the run rung, so the rung is true only while the button is not pressed.
A PNP sensor is wired to an input card and the input never turns on. What do you check?
Your grasp of sinking and sourcing I/O.
A PNP sensor sources current and needs a sinking input; NPN is the reverse. Mismatch means no current flows.

A PNP sensor is sourcing: when it switches, it supplies +24 V to the input. That needs a sinking input card, which takes the current and returns it to the 0 V common. If the card is a sourcing type, meant for NPN sensors, nothing flows. I check both data sheets, the common wiring, and measure the voltage at the terminal before swapping parts.
A pressure transmitter sends 4 to 20 mA for 0 to 150 psi. The input reads 12 mA. What pressure is that, and what would 2 mA tell you?
Your skill with analog scaling and live-zero signals.
75 psi, from linear scaling over a 16 mA span. A reading below 4 mA points to a fault, not a real pressure.

4 mA is zero and the span is 16 mA. 12 mA is 8 mA above zero, half the span, so 75 psi. A reading of 2 mA is below the live zero, so it most likely means a broken wire, lost loop power or a failed transmitter. I raise it as a signal fault instead of showing a negative pressure or letting the logic act on it.
You find the same output coil written on two different rungs. Why is that a problem?
Whether you know how duplicate outputs behave and mislead troubleshooting.
The last rung to write the coil in the scan wins. The fix is to drive each output from one place.

Outputs are written at the end of the scan, so the last rung that writes the coil wins and the earlier one has no effect. A technician sees the first rung true and the motor off and loses an hour. I would build intermediate bits for each condition and drive the output from a single rung, with a comment saying why.
A heated zone overshoots its setpoint by 15 degrees on every startup. How do you tune it?
How you approach PID tuning methodically.
Check the basics first, change one term at a time, test with setpoint steps and record results. Reduce integral before anything else.

First I confirm the thermocouple reads right, the output scaling is correct and the heater responds. Overshoot on a slow thermal zone often means too much integral action, so I reduce it, make a setpoint step and watch the trend. I change one term at a time and log each try. I add derivative only if needed, with filtering, because sensor noise makes it jumpy.
Walk me through an I/O checkout on a new machine during commissioning.
Your commissioning discipline before anything moves.
Point by point, with the real field device, a checklist, a clear area and every wiring fix marked on the drawings.

I check the panel against the drawings and verify power first. For each input I actuate the real device, like blocking the photo eye, and confirm the right tag changes. For outputs, with the area clear and the mechanical crew told, I turn on one at a time and confirm the right device moves. Each point gets ticked on a checklist, and every wiring fix goes on the redlines.
A customer wants the emergency stop to be just an input to the standard PLC program. What do you tell them?
Whether you know safety functions do not belong in ordinary PLC logic.
E-stop works through safety-rated hardware sized by a risk assessment; the standard PLC only monitors. Reset must not restart the machine.

I would advise against it. A hung program, a forced bit or a welded output could leave the machine running. The E-stop should remove power through a safety relay or a safety-rated controller, chosen from the risk assessment. The standard PLC reads its status to show the alarm and stop the sequence. Resetting the E-stop must not restart the machine by itself.
Production asks you to fix a nuisance stop with an online edit while the line is running. How do you decide?
Your judgement on changing live logic.
Weighs what the change touches, backs up first, informs operators, tests before accepting, and waits for downtime if unsure.

I look at what the rung affects. Changing an alarm timer preset is low risk; anything touching motion or an interlock waits for a planned stop. Before editing I save a copy of the running program, tell the operators and the shift lead, and test the edit before I accept it. If I cannot fully predict the effect, it waits for downtime.
You download your program and the line behaves differently than yesterday. The PLC had online changes your file did not. What do you do?
How you recover from a version control mistake and stop it happening again.
Makes the line safe, restores the known good version, merges the lost edits with their owners, then fixes the process.

First I stop the line safely and restore the upload I took before downloading, so production runs as before. Then I compare that upload with my file, find the missing edits, and merge them with whoever made each one. I test the merged version at a planned stop. Afterward I push for one master copy under version control and a rule: upload and compare before every download.

corporate-trainer.heading: Corporate trainer questions
qs: What makes teaching adults at work different from teaching in a school?
Whether you know how adults learn on the job.
Adults want relevance to their real tasks, bring experience you can build on, and need to practice, not just listen.

Adults walk in asking how this helps them on Monday morning. So I open with a real task they struggle with, draw on their experience in discussion, and keep lecture short. They have work waiting, so every activity has to earn its time. Many also have bad memories of school, so I keep practice low-stakes and never put anyone on the spot.
How do you write a learning objective?
Your grasp of the basics of instructional design.
An action you can observe, the conditions and a standard. Not vague verbs like “understand” or “know”.

I start with what the learner will do, using a verb I can see, like “process a return” instead of “understand returns.” Then I add conditions and a standard: “Using the point-of-sale system, process a customer return with no errors in under three minutes.” If I can't watch someone do it, it isn't an objective yet.
Walk me through how you would build a course from scratch.
Whether you follow a structured design process.
A clear sequence such as ADDIE: analysis, design, development, a pilot, delivery and evaluation, with stakeholder sign-off along the way.

I use a version of ADDIE: analyze, design, develop, implement, evaluate. I confirm the business goal and the audience, write objectives, then outline activities and assessments and get sign-off before I build materials. I pilot with a small group, fix what confused them, then roll out. After launch I check results against the goal I started with.
How do you keep people engaged in a live virtual session?
How you run live online training, not just slides on a video call.
An interaction every few minutes (polls, chat, breakouts), shorter sessions, and a co-host for tech so the trainer can keep teaching.

I plan an interaction every few minutes: a poll, a chat question, a quick breakout. I call on people by name, kindly, so they expect to take part. I split a long course into 90-minute sessions with practice in between. And I ask for a co-host to handle tech problems and the chat so I can stay focused on teaching.
When would you choose e-learning instead of a live class, and when not?
Your judgement in picking the right delivery format.
E-learning for consistent knowledge across large or spread-out groups; live sessions for skills that need practice and feedback; often a blend.

E-learning fits knowledge that is the same for everyone and rarely changes, like a policy update for 2,000 people in five time zones. It is consistent and easy to track. For skills that need practice and feedback, like coaching conversations or handling a tough customer, I want a live session with role plays. Often I blend them: short e-learning for facts, live time for practice.
A subject matter expert gives you a 120-slide deck and wants all of it covered in two hours. How do you handle it?
How you work with experts and cut content down to what learners need.
Respect for the expert, steering by the objectives, need-to-know versus nice-to-know, and reference material moved into job aids.

I thank them, because their knowledge is the raw material. Then we sort the slides together against the objectives: what people must do on the job versus what they can look up. Usually the must-know fits in about 30 slides plus practice. The rest becomes a reference guide. I keep the expert involved by asking them to review the practice scenarios.
A manager asks you for customer service training because complaints are up. What do you do first?
Whether you check that training is the right fix before you build anything.
A needs analysis first: find the performance gap and its cause. If the cause is a process, tool or incentive, training will not fix it.

I ask for the complaint data and talk to a few reps before designing anything. Once a request like this turned out to be a refund policy reps couldn't apply without a supervisor, so customers waited. The fix was a policy change and a one-page job aid, not a full-day course. If skills really are the gap, I build the training around those specific calls.
How do you make sure people actually use what they learned once they are back at their desks?
Whether you plan for the transfer of learning to the job.
Managers involved before and after, practice on real tasks, job aids, and reinforcement spread over the following weeks.

Before the course I brief managers so they know what their people will learn and can set a goal with them. In class we practice on real cases from their work. Afterward they get a one-page job aid and short refreshers at one, two and four weeks. Managers get a few coaching questions for one-on-ones, because what the manager reinforces is what sticks.
A senior leader sits in on your workshop and keeps taking over the discussion. What do you do?
How you manage power in the room without embarrassing anyone.
Acknowledge the input, use structure to bring others in, and talk privately at a break, framed as helping the team speak up.

I thank them for the point and then use structure: “Let's hear from people who haven't spoken yet,” or small-group work so they can't steer every table. At the break I tell them privately that the team tends to go quiet when they speak first, and ask if they would share their view at the end. Most leaders take that well because they want honest input too.
Halfway through a rollout, you realize you taught one step of the new process wrong. What do you do?
How you own and correct a mistake that has already spread.
Tell the process owner and your manager at once, fix the materials, reach everyone already trained, and check for work done the wrong way.

I'd confirm the correct step with the process owner and tell my manager the same day. I'd fix the slides and job aid before the next session. For people already trained, I'd send a short correction with a screenshot and ask team leads to mention it in huddles. I'd also ask whether anyone already processed work the wrong way, so it can be checked and fixed.

cpp-developer.heading: C++ developer questions
qs: What is RAII, and why does it matter in C++?
Whether you understand the idea that C++ resource handling is built on.
A resource is tied to an object's lifetime and released in its destructor, so cleanup happens on every exit path, including exceptions.

RAII means a resource is acquired in a constructor and released in the destructor. A std::lock_guard locks a mutex and unlocks it when it goes out of scope, even if an exception is thrown. So I don't write cleanup code by hand on every return path, and leaks of memory, files or locks become much rarer.
When do you use unique_ptr and when do you use shared_ptr?
How you think about who owns an object.
unique_ptr by default. shared_ptr only when ownership is truly shared, knowing it costs a control block and atomic reference counts.

unique_ptr is my default: one owner, no overhead beyond a raw pointer in the usual case, and it can be moved. I reach for shared_ptr only when several parts really share the lifetime, like a cache entry used by many threads. It has a control block and atomic reference counting, so it costs more, and cycles need weak_ptr to avoid leaks.
What does std::move actually do?
Whether you understand move semantics beyond the name.
It moves nothing. It is a cast to an rvalue that lets a move constructor or move assignment be chosen. The moved-from object stays valid but unspecified.

std::move is just a cast. It turns its argument into an rvalue so overload resolution can pick the move constructor or move assignment, which may take over the buffer instead of copying it. If the type has no move operations, you get a copy. After a move, a standard library object is valid but unspecified, so I don't read its value until I assign a new one.
What is undefined behavior, and why should a C++ developer care?
Your grasp of the rule that makes C++ both fast and dangerous.
The standard places no requirements on it. The optimizer may assume it never happens, so the bug can show up anywhere, often only in optimized builds.

Undefined behavior is code the standard gives no meaning to, like signed integer overflow, reading past an array, or using a pointer after delete. The compiler is allowed to assume it never happens, so it may remove a check I wrote or reorder code. The program can seem fine in testing and break with a new compiler or flag. I use sanitizers in CI to catch it early.
A class hierarchy has a base class without a virtual destructor. What can go wrong?
Whether you know a classic object lifetime trap.
Deleting a derived object through a base pointer is undefined behavior. The fix is a public virtual destructor or a protected non-virtual one.

If code deletes a Derived through a Base pointer and Base's destructor is not virtual, the behavior is undefined. In practice the derived destructor usually never runs, so its members leak. If the base is meant for polymorphic delete, I make the destructor public and virtual. If it is not, I make it protected and non-virtual so that delete through the base won't compile.
A loop over a std::vector crashes now and then after a teammate added a push_back inside it. Why?
How you spot iterator invalidation.
push_back can reallocate, which invalidates all iterators, pointers and references. Fix by looping by index or collecting changes and appending after the loop.

When push_back exceeds capacity, the vector moves its elements to a new buffer, so every iterator, pointer and reference into the old one dangles. It crashes only sometimes because that happens only when capacity runs out. I would loop by index, or collect new items in a second vector and append them after the loop.
We insert into the middle of a list of a few thousand items often. Would you use std::list or std::vector?
Whether you reason about real hardware, not only big-O.
Usually vector: contiguous memory is cache-friendly and often beats a linked list despite slower inserts on paper. Then measure with a benchmark on real data.

My first choice would be std::vector. A list insert is O(1) once you have the position, but finding it means walking nodes scattered in memory, with a cache miss at almost every step. A vector shifts elements, but a few thousand contiguous items move fast. I would still write a small benchmark with realistic sizes and decide on numbers, not on theory.
Two threads increment a shared int counter and the total comes out wrong. What is happening, and how do you fix it?
Your understanding of data races and the basics of the C++ memory model.
++ is a read-modify-write, and unsynchronized writes are a data race, which is undefined behavior. Fix with std::atomic or a mutex, then check with ThreadSanitizer.

Increment is read, add, write. Two threads can read the same value and both write back the same result, so counts are lost. In C++ this is a data race, which is undefined behavior, not just a wrong number. For a plain counter I'd use std::atomic<int> with fetch_add. If it guards more state, a mutex. Then I run ThreadSanitizer to check for other races.
Two threads each update their own counter, yet the code runs much slower with two threads than with one. What would you suspect?
Whether you know performance problems that come from the CPU cache.
False sharing: separate variables on one cache line bounce between cores. Fix by giving each its own line or counting locally, and confirm with a profiler.

I'd suspect false sharing. If the two counters sit next to each other, they likely share one cache line, often 64 bytes. Each write forces the other core to reload that line, so the cores keep fighting over it. I'd align each counter to its own line with alignas, or have each thread count locally and combine at the end, then confirm the gain with a profiler.
A bug crashes the optimized release build but never the debug build. How do you track it down?
How you hunt bugs that hide behind compiler optimizations.
Suspects undefined behavior, uninitialized data or timing. Builds optimized with debug symbols and runs sanitizers instead of guessing.

That pattern usually points to undefined behavior, an uninitialized variable or a race that debug timing hides. I build with optimization plus debug symbols so the crash still happens with a readable stack. Then I run AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, plus ThreadSanitizer if threads are involved. Full compiler warnings often point at the line too.

creative-director.heading: Creative and design director questions
qs: What goes into a good creative brief, and what do you do when a brief arrives incomplete?
Whether you know the document the whole job starts from.
Names the core parts: objective, audience, single message, deliverables, budget, deadline, approver. Pushes back before work starts, not after.

A good brief says what we want people to think or do, who they are, the one thing we must say, what we deliver, the budget, the deadline and who approves. If the objective or the approver is missing, I go back to the requester before anyone designs. A vague brief always turns into extra rounds later.
How do you give feedback in a design critique without redesigning the work yourself?
How you guide designers while leaving them ownership of their work.
Feedback tied to the brief, framed as problems to solve rather than fixes to copy, with a clear priority order.

I start with what works, then name the problems against the brief: the headline gets lost, the hierarchy is unclear on mobile. I say what has to change and why, not how to draw it. I rank the notes so the designer knows what matters most, and I only sketch myself if we are stuck on the same point twice.
A client looks at your concept and says, "Make it pop." What do you do?
How you turn vague client feedback into something the team can act on.
Asks questions to find the real concern, ties it back to the goal, and confirms the change before redoing work.

I ask what they want people to notice first and what feels flat to them. Usually it is the product or the offer getting lost. I might show two quick options, one with stronger contrast and one with a bigger hero image, and agree which direction we take before the team spends a day on it.
How do you keep a brand consistent when many designers, freelancers and agencies are producing work?
Your ability to build systems that keep quality up without you checking every file.
Clear guidelines, shared templates and asset libraries, a defined review point, and examples of what is and is not on brand.

I keep one source of truth: brand guidelines with logo, color, type and tone rules, plus templates and a shared asset library. Each guide shows good and bad examples. New partners get an onboarding call, and work goes through a set review step. When the same mistake shows up twice, I fix the guideline, not just the file.
How do you make sure your team's work is accessible?
Whether you know accessibility standards and build them into the work.
Knows WCAG basics such as contrast ratios, not relying on color alone, alt text and captions, and checks them during review, not after launch.

I build it into the design system so nobody has to remember it. Body text meets the WCAG AA contrast ratio of 4.5 to 1, large text 3 to 1. We never use color alone to carry meaning. Images get alt text and video gets captions. I check contrast with a tool during review, not after launch.
You find out a designer used an image from a web search in a final ad. What do you do?
Your grasp of image rights and how you prevent the problem from coming back.
Knows images online are copyrighted by default, stops the asset, licenses or replaces it, and adds a process step.

I pull it before it goes anywhere. An image found online is copyrighted by default, even with no notice on it, so we need a license or permission. I find the source and license it properly or replace it. Then I add a step: every asset in a final file has its source and license logged before I approve it.
You hire a freelance illustrator for a campaign. What do you need in writing before work starts?
Whether you understand who owns commissioned creative work under US law.
Knows the freelancer owns copyright unless there is a written assignment or a qualifying work-for-hire agreement, and covers scope, fee and usage.

Under US copyright law, the freelancer owns what they create unless we agree otherwise in writing. So I want a signed contract that assigns the rights we need, or a work-made-for-hire clause where the category qualifies. It also covers scope, usage, fee, rounds of changes, deadlines, and confirms any stock or fonts they use are licensed for us.
The CEO wants a change at the last minute that you believe weakens the work. How do you handle it?
How you defend the work while respecting who has the business decision.
Argues from the goal and evidence, offers an alternative, then commits fully once the decision is made.

I ask what is behind the request; often it is a real concern said as a design fix. I explain the risk in business terms, like the offer getting buried, and show a version that solves their concern without that cost. If they still want their change, it is their call. I make it look as good as it can and do not grumble to the team.
A print run of 20,000 brochures comes back with a wrong phone number on it. What do you do?
How you own a mistake and fix the process that let it through.
Stops distribution, tells the client fast with options and costs, takes responsibility, and fixes the proofing step.

I stop distribution first, then call the client the same day with the facts and options: a reprint, a printed correction sticker, or a redirect from the old number if that is possible. I own it, not the junior who typed it. Then I add a rule: phone numbers, prices and dates get checked against the source by a second person at final proof.
A test shows the version you thought was weaker performs better. How do you respond?
How you balance your own taste against evidence about what works.
Respects the data, checks the test was sound, looks for why it won, and uses that to make better work rather than defending taste.

First I check the test was fair: enough traffic, same audience, one clear difference. If it holds up, the weaker-looking version won and we use it. Then I ask why. Maybe the plain layout made the price clearer. My job is work that looks good and works, so I take that lesson and design the next version to keep both.

credit-analyst.heading: Credit analyst questions
qs: How do you calculate debt service coverage, and what does a ratio of 0.9 tell you?
Your grasp of the core repayment ratio.
Cash flow available for debt service divided by scheduled principal plus interest; below 1.0 the cash does not cover the payments.

I take cash flow available for debt service, usually EBITDA less taxes, unfinanced capital spending and distributions, and divide it by the year's scheduled principal and interest. At 0.9 the business earned 90 cents for every dollar owed to lenders. The gap was covered somehow, by new debt, owner cash or a shrinking cash balance, and I need to know which.
What is the difference between a primary and a secondary source of repayment?
Whether you know what a loan should be repaid from.
Primary is ongoing cash flow; secondary is collateral or a guarantor. A deal that only works on the secondary source is a weak deal.

The primary source is the borrower's own cash flow from running the business. Secondary sources are the fallback if that fails: selling collateral or calling on a guarantor. I want the primary source to work on its own. If I only get comfortable by counting on selling equipment, I am lending against assets, and that is a riskier loan.
Why is EBITDA not the same as cash available to repay debt?
How you look past an earnings figure to real cash.
Lists what EBITDA ignores: taxes, capital spending, working capital needs and owner distributions.

EBITDA leaves out cash that really goes out the door. Taxes get paid. A trucking company has to replace trucks, so capital spending is not optional. Growth ties up cash in receivables and inventory. Owners of pass-through companies often take distributions to pay their personal taxes. I subtract those before I decide what is left for the lender.
A borrower's sales grew 30% last year but its cash fell. Where do you look?
Whether you can read working capital and spot growth that eats cash.
Checks receivable and inventory days, payables, and whether the credit line is funding growth or hiding a problem.

Fast growth often eats cash, so I start with working capital. I compare days sales outstanding and inventory days to the prior year. If receivables grew faster than sales, customers are paying slower or some invoices may not be collectible. I pull the aging report and look for one large slow payer. Then I check whether payables were stretched to cover the gap.
The company's statements show $900,000 of net income, but its tax return shows $300,000. What do you do?
How you handle conflicting numbers from the same borrower.
No assumption either way: reconciles the two line by line, asks the borrower or CPA, and escalates if the gap stays unexplained.

Some difference is normal; tax depreciation, for example, is often faster than book depreciation. So I reconcile line by line: depreciation, revenue timing, other book and tax differences. If most of the $600,000 gap is bonus depreciation, fine. If not, I ask the borrower's CPA, and if I still can't tie it out, I tell my manager. I don't lend on numbers I can't trust.
What covenants would you put on a five-year equipment loan to a mid-sized manufacturer, and why?
Whether you can structure protection that fits the risk.
Financial covenants tied to the real risks, like minimum coverage and maximum leverage, plus reporting and limits on new debt or distributions.

I'd set a minimum debt service coverage ratio tested annually, and a maximum total debt to EBITDA so they can't pile on borrowing. I'd require yearly reviewed or audited statements and tax returns, and limit distributions and new debt without our consent. I set levels with room below their projections, so a covenant warns early instead of tripping on one normal bad quarter.
A relationship manager wants a deal approved by Friday and says the client will walk otherwise. You have concerns. What do you do?
How you keep independent judgement under sales pressure.
Names the specific risks, offers structures that could fix them, and writes the view honestly rather than softening it.

I'd tell the relationship manager exactly what bothers me, for example thin coverage and one customer at 40% of sales. Then I'd offer fixes: a shorter term, more equity, a personal guarantee, or a covenant on that concentration. If none work, my memo says so plainly. Losing a client is a cost; a loan that goes bad is a bigger one.
A borrower you've had for eight years misses its coverage covenant for the first time. Walk me through what you do.
How you handle an early warning on an existing loan.
Finds the cause, judges if it is temporary, updates the risk rating and collateral, then picks a waiver, amendment or tighter terms for a stated reason.

First I find out why: one bad quarter from a lost contract is different from margins slowly sliding. I get current numbers and aging reports and talk to the owner. I update the risk rating and collateral values. If it's temporary, a waiver with a fee or extra reporting may fit. If it's a trend, I tighten terms or add collateral while the business can still give it.

custody-wallets.heading: Crypto custody and wallet specialist questions
qs: How do you decide what share of client assets sits in hot, warm and cold wallets?
How you balance speed of withdrawals against exposure to theft.
Hot holds only what normal withdrawals need, sized from real flow data. Cold holds the rest, with a planned refill path through warm storage.

I size the hot wallet from withdrawal history: enough for a normal day plus a buffer, with a hard cap. Warm storage refills hot within hours, under approvals. Everything else sits cold, offline. If hot drops below its floor, a refill request goes to signers. If it goes above the cap, the excess is swept down.
What is a seed phrase, and what does a derivation path do?
Whether you know how one backup can recover many keys and addresses.
The mnemonic encodes the seed. A path picks which key in the tree is used. A wrong path or passphrase makes the wallet look empty, not lost.

A seed phrase, usually 12 or 24 words under the BIP-39 standard, encodes the random value the whole wallet grows from. BIP-32 builds a tree of keys from that seed, and the derivation path, such as m/44'/60'/0'/0/0, says which branch to use. If a restore shows zero balance, I check the path and any optional passphrase before anyone panics.
Multisig or MPC: how do they differ, and when would you choose each?
Your grasp of the two main ways to require several parties to approve a transaction.
Multisig is enforced on-chain with separate keys. MPC splits one key into shares that sign together into one normal signature. Trade-offs named for each.

With multisig, say 2-of-3, the chain itself checks that enough separate keys signed, and the setup is visible on-chain. It depends on each chain supporting it. With MPC, multi-party computation, the key is never whole; shares on different machines produce one ordinary signature, so it works on almost any chain, but I rely on the MPC code being correct.
What does a hardware security module add to a signing setup?
Whether you know where keys live and how they are protected.
Keys are generated and used inside tamper-resistant hardware and never leave in plain form. You still need a policy deciding what it is allowed to sign.

An HSM generates the key inside the device and signs there, so the raw key never sits in server memory or on disk. I check which FIPS 140 level it is validated to and whether it supports secp256k1, the curve Bitcoin and Ethereum use. It still signs whatever it is told to, so the approval policy in front of it matters just as much.
A trader asks you to allowlist a new withdrawal address urgently. What happens next?
How you apply withdrawal controls under time pressure.
The normal process holds: verify the address through a second channel, a quorum approves, any cooling-off period applies, and a small test transfer goes first.

I follow the same steps as any other day. I confirm the address with the trader by calling a number we already have, not the chat the request came from. Two approvers sign off in the policy engine, the address waits out our cooling-off period, and we send a small test amount first. Urgency is a common sign of social engineering.
What is address poisoning, and how do you protect operators from it?
Whether you know a common attack on people who copy addresses.
An attacker plants a look-alike address in your history with a tiny transfer. Defense is allowlists and full-address checks, never copying from history.

An attacker creates an address with the same first and last characters as one we pay often, then sends a tiny or zero-value transfer so it shows in our history. An operator who copies from history pays the attacker. We only pay allowlisted addresses, our tool shows the full address, and we hide dust transfers from the view operators use.
Walk me through a key generation ceremony for a cold vault.
Your hands-on knowledge of creating root keys with no single point of trust.
Scripted steps, air-gapped devices, several witnesses, recording and logs, backups split and stored apart, and a test restore before funding.

We use a written script, air-gapped machines checked beforehand, and at least two witnesses plus a recording. Keys or shares are generated on the devices, backups go into numbered tamper-evident bags, and each holder signs for theirs. Before funding, we restore from backup on a separate device and confirm it derives the same addresses. Backups then go to sites in different cities.
An Ethereum withdrawal from the hot wallet is stuck pending, and every later withdrawal is queued behind it. What do you do?
How you handle transaction ordering without paying a customer twice.
Replace the stuck transaction using the same nonce and a higher fee. Never resend the withdrawal with a new nonce, since both could confirm.

Transactions from one address confirm in order of their nonce, a counter, so one low-fee transaction blocks the rest. I rebroadcast it with the same nonce, recipient and amount, and higher fees. I never send a fresh copy with a new nonce, because both may land and the customer gets paid twice. Then I find out why our fee estimate was too low.
You learn that a laptop holding one MPC key share may have been compromised. What are your first steps?
Your incident response when key material may be exposed.
Freeze outbound activity, revoke that device, then refresh shares or move funds to new keys, depending on whether the threshold could have been reached.

I pause withdrawals from that vault and revoke the device from the signing group. Then I check logs for any signing requests from it. If only one share was exposed and the threshold is two of three, a share refresh makes the old share useless. If I cannot rule out a second share, we move funds to a newly generated wallet. Then we write up the root cause.
What does a proof of reserves show, and what can it miss?
Whether you can judge what a reserve attestation really proves.
It shows control of on-chain assets at one moment. It can miss liabilities left out, off-chain debts, and assets borrowed just for the snapshot.

It usually pairs signed messages proving we control certain addresses with a Merkle tree of customer balances, so each customer can check they are included. It is a snapshot. It does not show other debts, and funds could be borrowed for the day of the check. I would add frequent reconciliations of our ledger against the chain and an outside audit of liabilities.

customer-education.heading: Customer education specialist questions
qs: How is customer education different from onboarding and support?
Whether you understand where your work fits in the customer journey.
Education teaches skills to many customers ahead of need; onboarding gets one account live; support fixes one problem. Each feeds the others.

Support solves one customer's problem after it happens. Onboarding gets a new account set up and live. Education teaches many customers at once, before they get stuck, and keeps going after onboarding ends. I read support tickets and onboarding notes to choose what to teach next.
How do you decide whether a topic needs a help article, a short video or a full course?
How you match the format to what the customer is trying to do.
By the task: quick lookups get an article, hard-to-describe steps get a short video, new skills that need practice get a course.

If someone needs one answer in the middle of their work, an article they can scan is best. If the steps are hard to describe in words, a two-minute video helps. If they must build a new skill, like designing reports, that needs a course with practice and feedback. I also ask how often the screen changes, since video costs the most to update.
What are SCORM and xAPI, and when does the difference matter?
Your knowledge of the standards behind learning platforms.
SCORM packages courses for an LMS and tracks completion and scores; xAPI records learning activity anywhere and sends it to a learning record store.

SCORM is an older standard for packaging a course so a compliant LMS can launch it and record completion, time and score. xAPI records statements like “Ana completed lab 3” and sends them to a learning record store, even from outside the LMS, such as a product sandbox. If we want to track hands-on practice in the product, xAPI matters.
Walk me through turning a new feature into a course.
Your process from product spec to finished training.
Starts with who uses the feature and what they must be able to do, then objectives, practice, expert review and a pilot with real users.

I meet the product manager to learn which customers the feature is for and what problem it solves. Then I write two or three objectives as tasks, like “set up an approval rule.” I build short lessons around a hands-on exercise, get the product expert to check accuracy, and pilot it with a few customers before launch day.
How do you keep a webinar for 300 customers from becoming a one-way demo?
How you build interaction into a large live session.
Planned interaction every few minutes, a second person handling chat and questions, and a clear follow-up.

I open with a poll on what attendees want to do, so I can adjust my examples. Every ten minutes or so there is a poll, a chat question or a quick task to try in their own account. A colleague moderates chat and groups questions for me. Afterward everyone gets the recording, the slides and a link to the next step.
The product interface changes every few weeks. How do you stop courses from going out of date?
How you plan content so it can be maintained.
Short modular pieces, a link to the release process, an owner and review date for each asset, and teaching the concept more than the click path.

I build short modules, so one change means re-recording three minutes, not an hour. I join release planning to see changes early and keep a list of which assets show which screens. Each asset has an owner and a review date. Where I can, I teach why and when to use a feature, which lasts longer than which button to press.
Support sees the same setup question again and again. What do you do?
Whether you use tickets to find learning needs, and know when training is not the fix.
Reads the tickets to find the real gap, puts help where users get stuck, and tells product when the design itself is the problem.

I read a sample of the tickets to see exactly where people fail. If it is missing knowledge, I write a short guide and ask to link it inside the product at that step and in support replies. If the screen itself is confusing, I tell product with the ticket count; training should not cover for a design flaw. Then I watch whether tickets drop.
Certified customers renew at a higher rate. Leadership wants to say certification drives renewals. What do you tell them?
Whether you can tell correlation from cause when reporting on education.
Points out that engaged customers are the ones who certify, and proposes a fairer comparison before claiming cause.

I would say the link is real but not proof. Customers who certify are often already committed, so they may have renewed anyway. I would compare certified accounts with similar ones by size, age and usage before certifying, or offer the program to some accounts first. If the gap holds, we can claim more with confidence.
You find out a course has taught a wrong setting for a month. What do you do?
How you handle your own error when customers may already have acted on it.
Fixes the content at once, finds and tells affected learners with the correct step, briefs support, and changes the review process.

I pull or correct the lesson the same day. I ask support and the product team how much harm the wrong setting can do. Then I use the LMS records to email everyone who took that lesson, with the right step and how to check their setup. I give support a note for related tickets, and I add a product expert review before any course goes live.

customer-experience.heading: Customer experience manager questions
qs: What is the difference between NPS, CSAT and customer effort score, and when do you use each?
Whether you know the core CX metrics and what each one actually measures.
Correct NPS math, and each metric matched to its use: loyalty overall, satisfaction with one contact, ease of a task.

NPS asks how likely someone is to recommend us, from 0 to 10. Promoters give 9 or 10, detractors 0 to 6, and the score is percent promoters minus percent detractors. It tracks loyalty. CSAT asks how satisfied someone was with one interaction, so I send it after a support case. Effort score asks how easy a task was, like a return.
How do you write a customer survey that gets honest, useful answers?
Your survey design basics and how you avoid biased questions.
Short, neutral wording, one idea per question, sent soon after the event, with an open question and answers tied to the account.

I keep it to two or three questions: the score first, then one open question, such as what is the main reason for your score. I avoid leading words like how great was, ask one thing per question, and send it soon after the event while memory is fresh. I also link answers to the account so I can follow up and split results by segment.
Walk me through how you build a customer journey map.
How you turn scattered data into a clear picture of the customer's path.
One persona and goal, every stage and touch point, real data plus interviews, pain points marked, and an internal owner for each step.

I pick one customer type and one goal, like a small business owner opening an account. I list every stage, from the first ad to the first bill, using tickets, survey comments, web analytics and a handful of interviews. For each step I note what they do, feel and where they get stuck. Then I name who inside owns each step, so every fix has an owner.
What does closing the loop mean in a voice of the customer program?
Whether you know feedback must lead to action for the person and for the business.
Both loops: a quick personal follow-up with the customer, and fixing the root cause with the owning team, then telling customers what changed.

The inner loop is following up with the person, especially a detractor, within a few days, by someone who can actually help.
