The outer loop is fixing the cause: grouping feedback into themes, taking the top ones to the team that owns them, and telling customers what changed. Without both, people stop answering surveys.
Our NPS went from 32 to 28 this quarter. What do you do first?
How you react to a score change without panic or guessing.
First check whether the drop is real given sample size and normal noise, then segment it, then read the comments before naming a cause.

First I check whether it is real: how many responses we got, and whether a 4-point move is within the normal swing for that sample. Then I split it by segment, channel and product to find where it came from, and read the detractor comments for the period. Last time I did this, the whole drop sat in one region after a delivery partner changed.
Survey response rate fell from 18% to 6%, and most comments are now angry. How do you treat the results?
Whether you understand non-response bias and how it distorts a score.
Does not report the score as-is; finds what changed, compares responders to the customer base, and checks behavior data that does not depend on who answers.

I would not report the score as if nothing changed. I check what changed: send time, channel, email delivery, survey length. I compare who answered with the full customer base by segment and tenure, and flag or weight the result if they differ. I also look at behavior like repeat orders and cancellations, which does not depend on who chooses to answer.
You have thirty known pain points and room to fix three this quarter. How do you choose?
Your judgement in ranking problems by impact, not by who complains loudest.
Sizes each by reach, harm (contacts, drop-off, churn) and cost to fix, weighs high-value segments, and makes the ranking visible to owners.

I size each one by how many customers hit it, how much it hurts, such as extra contacts, drop-off or churn among those who hit it, and what a fix costs. A clumsy password reset that 40,000 people hit a month beats a rare billing glitch, unless that glitch is losing big accounts. I share the ranking openly so the choice is clear, not political.
The support director wants to cut average handle time, and you think it will hurt the experience. How do you settle it?
How you handle a conflict between efficiency targets and customer outcomes.
Brings data, not opinion: handle time next to repeat contacts and CSAT, and proposes a test judged on cost per resolved issue.

I would bring data. I would put handle time next to repeat contacts and CSAT for the same cases. If shorter calls mean customers call back, the saving is not real. Then I would propose a four-week pilot: one team aims at lower handle time, one at solving it on the first contact, and we compare cost per resolved issue and satisfaction.
You redesigned onboarding, CSAT for onboarding went up, but churn did not move. What might have gone wrong?
Whether you can question your own success metric and find the real driver.
Sees that the metric may not sit on the path to churn, considers who answered, and goes to churned customers for the real reasons.

Maybe we measured the wrong thing. The survey rated the new onboarding screens, but people may leave later over price or a missing feature. Maybe the happier responders were customers who would have stayed anyway. I would read exit reasons, interview a few churned accounts, and check whether onboarding is even linked to churn before spending more there.
How do you convince a finance leader that a customer experience project is worth the money?
How you link experience to revenue and cost in a way finance trusts.
Uses the company's own data to tie experience to retention and cost to serve, gives a range with stated assumptions, and agrees on a measure upfront.

I tie it to money with our own data. For example, I compare renewal rates of customers who had a bad support case with those who did not, and show what that gap means in revenue. Then I add savings, like fewer calls once a confusing bill is fixed. I give a range, state my assumptions, and agree before launch on the number we will check after.

customer-success-manager.heading: Customer success manager questions
qs: What is the difference between customer success and customer support?
Whether you understand what the role is for.
Support reacts to problems; success works ahead of them to get the customer to their goals and to renewal.

Support fixes what is broken when the customer asks, ticket by ticket. Success is proactive. I learn what the customer bought the product to achieve, track whether they are getting there, and step in before a problem shows up at renewal. I work closely with support, but I own the account's outcome, not a single ticket.
Walk me through how you run onboarding for a new account.
How you get a new customer to first value quickly.
A kickoff that confirms goals and owners, a dated plan with an early first win, and a clean handoff from sales.

Before kickoff I read the sales notes so the customer does not repeat themselves. At kickoff we agree on two or three goals, who owns each task on their side, and dates. I aim for one visible win in the first few weeks, like the first team going live. I send a short recap after every call and flag slipping dates early.
What would you put into a customer health score, and where can it mislead you?
Whether you can read account risk beyond a single number.
A mix of usage, engagement, support and sentiment signals, plus awareness that a green score can hide a lost sponsor.

I would combine usage against what they bought, active users, escalated tickets, whether we still have an engaged sponsor, and survey answers. I check the weights against accounts that actually churned. It misleads when usage looks fine but the buyer has left or a budget cut is coming, so I treat it as a prompt to look closer, not a verdict.
You own 60 accounts. How do you decide where your time goes?
How you manage a book of business with limited hours.
Segmenting by value and risk, scaled one-to-many touches for smaller accounts, and a weekly look at what changed.

I group accounts by revenue and by risk. Large or at-risk accounts get regular calls. Healthy smaller ones get scaled touches: webinars, emails triggered by usage, open office hours. Each week I check health changes and renewals due in the next 90 to 120 days, and those move to the top. Time follows risk and value.
How do you prepare a business review that the customer's executive will find worth the time?
Whether you can show value in the customer's terms, not yours.
Results tied to the goals they set, honesty about gaps, and a forward plan they agree to; not a feature tour.

I start from the goals we agreed at onboarding and show progress in their terms, like hours saved, not logins. I name what is behind and what we are doing about it. Then I propose next quarter's priorities and ask what has changed on their side. I send the deck to my contact a few days early, so nothing surprises the executive.
When do you raise an upsell with a customer, and when do you hold off?
Your judgement on expansion without damaging trust.
Expansion follows proven value and a real need; you hold off while the customer is unhappy or not using what they have.

I raise it when the customer has hit their goals and a need shows up that the extra product solves, like a new team asking for seats. I hold off if they use a fraction of what they bought, have an open escalation, or are unhappy, because pushing then puts the renewal at risk. When it fits, I bring in the account executive if they own the commercial side.
At kickoff you learn sales promised a feature the product does not have. What do you do?
How you handle a broken expectation without blaming a colleague.
Clarify quickly and honestly, offer a workaround or path, loop in sales and product, and fix the handoff for next time.

I would not let it ride, because it surfaces at renewal anyway. I confirm with the sales rep what was said, then tell the customer plainly what the product does today, show the closest workaround, and bring in product if it is on the roadmap. I keep it about the customer, not whose fault it was. Afterward I ask sales to add a check to the handoff notes.
Usage at an account fell 40% over two months and renewal is in 90 days. What do you do?
Whether you dig for the cause before you react.
Finding out why first, from data and from people, then a dated recovery plan shared with the sponsor.

First I check the data: which teams or features dropped, and when. A sudden drop often means a reorg, a lost admin or a broken integration. Then I call my contact and ask what changed, without pitching. Once I know the cause, we agree a dated recovery plan with the sponsor. I flag the renewal risk to my manager now, not in the final weeks.
Your main champion at a key account just left the company. What do you do?
How you protect a relationship that rested on one person.
Moving fast to find and win the new owner, proving value again, and seeing that relying on one contact was the real risk.

I ask the departing champion, if I can, who takes over and for an introduction. I meet the new owner quickly, learn their goals, and show what the account has achieved, since they did not choose us. I mark the account at risk and build contacts with other users and an executive. The real lesson: every key account needs several relationships, not one.

customer-success-specialist.heading: Customer success specialist questions
qs: What is the difference between customer support and customer success?
Whether you understand what this role is for.
Support reacts to problems as they come in. Success works ahead of them so customers reach their goals and renew.

Support answers when a customer asks for help: fix the problem, close the ticket. Success starts before the customer asks. I look at how each account uses the product, find who is stuck or drifting, and reach out with the next step. The goal is that they get value and renew, not just that their tickets are closed.
What does time to value mean, and how would you shorten it for a new small customer?
Your grasp of onboarding as the stage that often decides whether a customer stays.
A clear definition, one first outcome to aim for, and steps that remove setup friction early.

It is the time from signing up to the first real result the customer cares about. For a small account I pick one early win, like their first report sent, and build the first emails around it: a short checklist, a two-minute video, and an offer of a 15-minute call if they have not finished setup by day five.
Which signs tell you a low-touch account might churn before they say anything?
Whether you can read usage data and spot risk early.
Several signals, not one: falling logins, unused key features, fewer active users, billing trouble, repeated tickets, unanswered emails.

Logins dropping week over week, fewer active seats, and the core feature going unused are the big ones. I also watch for a failed payment, a run of support tickets on the same problem, and emails that stop getting answers. One sign alone can be noise, like a holiday. Two or three together means I reach out now.
You own 400 accounts and have time for about 15 calls this week. How do you choose them?
How you spend scarce one-to-one time across a large book of accounts.
A clear rule based on risk, revenue and timing, with everyone else covered by email or webinars.

I sort by risk and timing first: accounts with renewals in the next 60 to 90 days and a falling health score. Then I weigh revenue and a clear chance to help, like a team that is stuck mid-setup. The rest get a targeted email or an invite to the next webinar. I note why I chose each call so I can check later whether the rule worked.
Walk me through how you would plan a webinar for customers who are not using a key feature.
Whether you can run one-to-many sessions that change what customers do.
A narrow goal, the right audience picked from usage data, a live demo of a real task, a follow-up, and a check of usage afterward.

I would pull the list of accounts that have not used the feature in 30 days and invite only them. The session is 30 minutes: why it matters in one slide, then a live demo of one real task, then questions. Everyone gets the recording and a one-step guide. Two weeks later I compare how many attendees started using it with those who did not attend.
You sent an email about a new feature. Open rates were good, but almost nobody used the feature. What do you look at?
How you diagnose a campaign that got attention but no action.
Checking clicks, the call to action, the steps after the click and whether the audience fit, then testing one change.

Opens only tell me the subject line worked. I would check clicks next: if few clicked, the message or the button was weak. If many clicked but did not use it, the problem is after the click, like a confusing setup or the wrong audience. I would call two customers, fix the biggest gap, and send a revised version to a small test group.
Your main contact at a small account leaves the company. What do you do?
Whether you know how to handle a champion leaving, one of the top churn risks.
Act fast: find the new owner, re-onboard them, check that admin access moved, and spread contacts across more people.

I treat it as a risk right away. I look in the account for other active users and write to the most active one to ask who owns the tool now. I offer that person a short call to show what the team uses it for and what results they have had. I make sure admin access moved over, and from then on I keep at least two contacts per account.
The health score says an account is green, but a user tells you they are looking at a competitor. What do you do?
Your judgement when the data and what a customer says disagree.
Trust the customer, ask why, act on the reason, and flag the gap so the health score can be improved.

The customer's words win over the score. I would ask what is pushing them to look: price, a missing feature, or a bad experience. Then I would act on that reason, maybe a workflow they have not found or a talk with my manager about pricing. I would also tell whoever owns the score, since it missed a real risk and may lean too much on logins.
What is the difference between gross revenue retention and net revenue retention?
Your understanding of the main numbers a success team is judged on.
Both track the same customers' revenue. Gross counts only losses and cannot exceed 100%; net also adds expansion and can.

Both take the recurring revenue from a group of customers at the start of a period and compare it with what those same customers pay at the end. Gross retention counts only losses from churn and downgrades, so it tops out at 100%. Net retention also adds upgrades and added seats, so it can go above 100% when growth beats losses.
Before renewal, you see a customer pays for 20 seats but only 8 are used. What do you do?
Whether you put the customer's long-term value ahead of short-term revenue.
Raise it honestly and early: try to grow adoption first, and if the seats will not be used, support a right-sized plan instead of risking a surprise churn.

I raise it well before the renewal date, not after. First I ask about the other 12: are they people who never got invited, or seats no one needs? If it is an adoption gap, I help them onboard those users. If they truly need eight, I tell my manager and support a smaller plan. A customer who feels overcharged often leaves entirely; one who gets an honest fit usually stays.

customer-support.heading: Customer support questions
qs: How do you use a saved reply without sounding like a robot?
How you use macros, the saved replies most help desks have, and still answer the actual person.
The macro is a base: you add the customer's details, cut what does not apply, and check that it answers their exact question.

I treat the macro as a first draft. I open with a line that shows I read their message, like naming the order they mentioned, and I delete steps that don't fit their case. Before sending, I reread their question once more and check that my reply answers it. If I edit the same macro every time, I suggest a fix to whoever owns it.
Why does it matter how you tag or categorize a ticket?
Whether you see that ticket data is used beyond the single ticket.
Tags feed reports, routing and bug counts. Careless tags hide trends and send work to the wrong people.

Tags are how the team sees patterns. If twenty people write about a login error and half are tagged billing, the product team never sees how big the problem is. Tags can also route tickets to the right queue. So I pick the most specific tag that fits, and if none fits, I ask my lead instead of guessing.
On a call, you need two minutes to look something up. Walk me through what you say and do.
Your phone habits around hold time and silence.
Ask before placing someone on hold, give a time, check back if it runs long, and thank them when you return.

I say what I'm checking and ask, “Is it okay if I place you on a short hold, about two minutes?” I wait for a yes. If it runs longer, I come back on the line, tell them where I am and ask if they can hold a bit more. When I return, I thank them for waiting and give the answer first.
Walk me through how you structure an email reply to a customer.
How you organize a written answer so the customer can act on it.
The answer up front, steps numbered, all needed questions asked at once, and a clear next step: what you will do and what they need to do.

First line: a short acknowledgment and the answer, or what I'm doing about it. Then the steps, numbered, one action each. If I need information, I ask for all of it in one place, so we don't go back and forth. I end with what happens next and when. Then I reread it as the customer would, on a phone screen, and cut anything they don't need.
A customer pastes their full credit card number into the chat. What do you do?
Whether you protect payment data when the customer does not.
Do not repeat or copy the number, redact it or flag it as your policy says, and tell the customer kindly not to share it.

I don't copy it, repeat it or use it. If our tool lets me redact the message, I do that right away; if not, I flag it to whoever handles that, following our policy. I tell the customer, without blaming them, that we never need the full card number in chat and that I've removed it. Then I help with their actual question.
A caller wants to change the email on an account but cannot pass verification. They are upset. What do you do?
Whether you hold the security line under pressure.
No change without verification, however convincing the story. Explain why, and offer the official path to prove ownership.

I don't make the change. Someone trying to take over an account can sound just as upset and convincing as the real owner. I explain that the check protects them, and I walk them through the other ways our process allows, such as a reset link sent to the email on file. If they still can't verify, I note the attempt and pass it to the team that handles account recovery.
A customer says, “Let me speak to your manager.” What do you do?
How you handle an escalation demand without getting defensive.
Find out what they need, try once to solve it, and if they still want a supervisor, follow the process without arguing or promising outcomes.

I don't take it personally. I say, “I can do that. Can you tell me what you'd like to happen, so they have the full picture?” Sometimes I can solve it right there. If not, or if they still want a manager, I follow our escalation process and write a short summary so they don't have to repeat themselves. I don't promise what the manager will decide.
You posted an internal note as a public reply, and the customer saw it. What do you do?
How you handle a ticketing mistake that the customer can see.
Tell the lead at once, check what was exposed, follow up with the customer honestly, and change your habit so it does not happen again.

I tell my lead right away, because the note might hold something sensitive, like another customer's details or a blunt comment. If the tool allows, we hide or delete it. Then I write to the customer: a short apology, a plain explanation that it was a note meant for my team, and the real answer. Since then I check whether the reply box says public or internal before every send.
In one hour, fifteen customers report the same error. What do you do?
Whether you spot a wider incident and act on it, not just ticket by ticket.
Alert the lead or engineering early with examples, link the tickets, use one agreed message, and never promise a fix time you were not given.

After the third or fourth one, I tell my lead or post in the incident channel with ticket numbers, times and screenshots, so engineering can check quickly. I tag and link the tickets so we can update everyone at once later. I reply with the agreed message: we know, we're working on it, we'll update you. I don't give a fix time unless engineering has given one.
A customer replies “still not working” for the third time. What do you change?
How you break a loop when your usual steps are not working.
Stop repeating steps, reread the thread from the start, switch to a call or screen share if available, and escalate with what was tried.

Three rounds means my approach isn't working, not just the fix. I reread the whole thread for something I missed, like the device or the exact error text. Then I change how we talk: I offer a call or screen share if we have one, so I can see what they see. If I still can't solve it, I escalate with a list of everything tried and tell the customer who has it now.

customs-trade.heading: Customs and trade compliance specialist questions
qs: Walk me through how you classify a product you have never seen before.
Whether you follow the legal method for tariff classification.
Facts about the product first, then the General Rules of Interpretation in order, starting with heading text and notes, and a ruling when in doubt.

First I get the facts: what it is made of, how it works, what it is used for, plus a spec sheet or photo. Then I apply the General Rules of Interpretation in order. Under GRI 1, the heading text and the section and chapter notes decide first. I check past CBP rulings in the CROSS database. If it is still unclear and the duty matters, I ask CBP for a binding ruling.
We use a customs broker. Who is responsible if an entry is wrong?
Whether you know the importer's legal duty of reasonable care.
The importer of record stays responsible. A broker files for you but does not take over the duty to classify, value and declare correctly.

The importer of record. The law puts the duty of reasonable care on us, even when a licensed broker prepares and files the entry. So I give the broker accurate product data, review their classifications and values, and keep a classification database so the same part is entered the same way every time.
What goes into the customs value of an import besides the invoice price?
Your grasp of transaction value, the main US valuation method.
Knows the additions, like assists, royalties, packing and selling commissions, and that international freight and insurance are not part of US value.

Transaction value starts with the price actually paid or payable. Then I add packing costs, selling commissions, assists, certain royalties and license fees, and resale proceeds that go back to the seller. An assist is something we give the supplier free or cheap, like a mold. International freight and insurance are left out, because the US values goods on a foreign-port basis.
What does substantial transformation mean when you decide country of origin?
Whether you understand how origin is decided, not just where goods ship from.
Processing that makes a new article with a new name, character or use. Shipping from a country or simple repacking does not change origin.

Origin is where the goods were made or last substantially transformed, not where they shipped from. Substantial transformation means processing that turns the inputs into a new and different article with a new name, character or use. Repacking or labeling does not count. Trade agreement preference is a separate question with its own rules, so I check both and document how we decided.
Before we ship a product abroad, how do you decide whether we need an export license?
Your method for export control classification under US rules.
Jurisdiction first, then ECCN or EAR99, then destination, end user and end use. Never assumes an ordinary item is always license free.

First I check jurisdiction: a defense article on the US Munitions List falls under ITAR. Otherwise it is under the EAR, and I find its ECCN on the Commerce Control List or confirm it is EAR99. Then I check the country chart for that ECCN and screen the end user and end use. Even EAR99 items can need a license for embargoed places or banned parties.
Screening flags a new customer as a possible match on a restricted party list. What do you do?
How you handle a screening hit without guessing.
Holds the order, compares full details to the list entry, documents the decision, and escalates a true or unclear match instead of shipping.

I put the order on hold first. Then I compare the full name, address, country and other identifiers with the list entry, using the Consolidated Screening List and OFAC's list. If it is clearly a different party, I write down why and release it. If it matches or I cannot rule it out, it goes to our compliance lead. Nothing ships while it is open.
You find a part has been classified wrong for two years and we underpaid duty. What do you do?
Whether you correct errors properly with CBP.
Fixes new entries at once, corrects entries still open with Post Summary Corrections, considers a prior disclosure for older ones, and pays what is owed.

First I fix the classification so new entries are right. For entries still open for correction, I file Post Summary Corrections. For older ones I gather the numbers and recommend a prior disclosure to CBP, made before CBP opens an investigation, with the extra duty paid. That greatly reduces penalties. Then I find out why the error happened so it does not repeat.
A foreign national engineer joins our team next week. Is there an export issue?
Whether you know about deemed exports.
Knows that releasing controlled technology to a foreign person in the US counts as an export to their country and may need a license first.

Possibly. Under the EAR, releasing controlled technology or source code to a foreign person inside the US is a deemed export to that person's country. So I check what technical data the job needs, its ECCN, and the person's citizenship. If a license is needed, access waits until we have it, and IT limits access in the meantime.
CBP detains a shipment under the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act. How do you respond?
How you handle a forced labor detention and the proof it demands.
Knows goods tied to Xinjiang or listed entities are presumed made with forced labor, and that release takes full supply chain records back to raw materials.

Under that law, goods made wholly or partly in Xinjiang, or by listed entities, are presumed made with forced labor. I pull records back to raw materials: purchase orders, invoices, production and shipping records for every tier. If we can show the goods have no such tie, we submit that to CBP. If we cannot, the goods may be excluded, and we must rethink that supplier.
Sales wants to ship today, but the buyer will not say what the product will be used for. What do you do?
Your judgement when business pressure meets an export red flag.
Treats evasive end-use answers as a red flag, holds the shipment until it is resolved, and explains the risk to sales plainly.

A buyer who dodges end-use questions is a classic red flag in export rules. I hold the shipment, ask for an end-use statement, and check whether the order fits the buyer's business. I tell sales plainly: a late order costs a day, but shipping to a banned end use can bring fines, loss of export privileges and even criminal charges. No answers, no shipment.

cybersecurity.heading: Cybersecurity questions
qs: How should an application store user passwords, and why not just encrypt them?
Whether you know the difference between hashing and encryption.
A slow, salted, one-way password hash such as Argon2 or bcrypt; encryption can be reversed by anyone who gets the key.

Passwords should go through a slow hashing function built for passwords, like Argon2 or bcrypt, with a unique random salt per user. Hashing is one-way, so at login we only compare hashes. Encryption is reversible: steal the database and the key, and you have every password. The salt stops cracking many accounts at once with precomputed tables.
How does SQL injection work, and what actually stops it?
Your grasp of a common web attack and its real fix.
User input gets read as part of the query; parameterized queries are the fix, not filtering characters.

It happens when an app builds a query by pasting user input into the SQL text, so input like a quote followed by OR 1=1 changes what the query does. The real fix is parameterized queries, where the database treats input only as data. Input checks and a low-privilege database account limit damage, but hand-escaping characters is not a fix I trust.
Walk me through threat modelling a new feature that lets customers upload files.
How you think like an attacker before the code ships.
A structured method: map the data flow, list what can go wrong at each step, for example with STRIDE, and tie each threat to a control.

I draw where the file goes: browser, upload service, storage, and whatever opens it later. Then I ask what can go wrong at each step. Someone uploads malware or a script disguised as an image, a huge file fills the disk, or a crafted filename writes outside the folder. My controls: check type by content, cap size, rename files, store them outside the web root and scan them.
You get an alert: one user signed in from Ohio and from overseas 40 minutes apart. What do you do?
How you triage an alert without overreacting or ignoring it.
Rule out benign causes such as a VPN fast, then treat signs of takeover seriously: revoke sessions, reset credentials, review what the account did.

First I check if it is real: does the overseas address belong to our VPN or a cloud provider, and did MFA succeed or get pushed again and again? If it looks like a takeover, I revoke active sessions, reset the password and confirm with the user by phone, not email. Then I review what the account touched: mailbox rules, file downloads, new MFA devices.
A scanner flags a critical flaw on a Linux server, but the admin says the package is already patched. How do you settle it?
Whether you verify findings instead of trusting the scanner or the admin blindly.
Checking evidence: distributions often backport fixes without changing the version number, so you read the advisory and compare package releases.

Scanners often go by version number, and Linux distributions often backport security fixes into an older version. So I look up the distribution's advisory for that CVE, see which package release fixes it, and compare it to what is installed. If it is fixed, I mark a false positive with that proof attached. If not, it goes back in the queue.
Why might you not want to wipe or shut down a compromised machine right away?
Whether you protect evidence while containing an incident.
Shutting down loses memory evidence; isolate the host from the network first and capture volatile data, unless damage is ongoing and cannot be stopped otherwise.

Memory holds things that vanish on shutdown: running processes, network connections, sometimes keys or injected code. Wiping also destroys the disk evidence that shows how they got in. So I usually cut the host off the network, capture memory and a disk image, then rebuild. If it is actively encrypting files and isolation fails, stopping the damage comes first.
Tell me about a time a security change you made broke something. What did you do?
How you own a mistake and fix the process behind it.
A quick rollback, honest communication, and a change to how such changes are tested or rolled out.

I pushed a firewall rule to block an old protocol and it cut off a payroll export that still used it. Within about 20 minutes I rolled it back and told the payroll lead what happened. Then we found every system using that protocol, moved them, and re-applied the block. Since then I run new blocking rules in log-only mode for a week first.
An actively exploited flaw hits an internet-facing system, and the business wants to wait two weeks for a launch. What do you do?
Your judgement when security and business goals collide.
No flat no and no silent yes: offer compensating controls, put the risk in writing, and have the system owner formally accept it.

I explain in plain terms what an attack would mean for them, not just the severity score. Then I offer options: patch in a short window this week, or add controls now, like a web application firewall rule blocking the exploit and extra monitoring. If they still wait, the system owner signs off on the risk with an end date. Their call, but on record.
After an intrusion, how do you know the attacker is really out of the network?
How deep your incident response goes beyond the obvious cleanup.
Scoping and hunting for persistence before eviction, removing all footholds at once, resetting credentials broadly, then watching closely.

Before evicting them, I scope every host and account they touched and hunt for persistence: scheduled tasks, new services, new admin accounts, web shells. Then we remove them all at once, reset exposed credentials, and in Active Directory reset the KRBTGT password, the key behind all Kerberos tickets, twice. Then we watch closely for weeks.

data-analyst.heading: Data analyst questions
qs: Walk me through how you check your numbers before a report goes out.
Whether you have a routine for catching your own errors before others do.
Concrete checks: totals against a trusted source, row counts through joins, filters and dates, and a sense check of whether the number is plausible.

I compare the total against a source I trust, like the finance system or last month's report. I check row counts before and after each join, look for nulls and duplicates in the keys, and confirm the date range and filters match the request. Then I ask if the number makes sense. If revenue doubled overnight, I assume a bug before a miracle.
Sales are up 30% in December compared with November. Is that good news?
Whether you account for seasonality before calling a change good or bad.
Not on its own: compare with the same period last year and check calendar effects and promotions before judging.

Not on its own. December is a peak month for many businesses, so I compare it with last December, year over year, and check that the number of weekend days and promotions line up. If December was up 40% over November last year, a 30% jump actually points to a weaker season.
A colleague reports the overall conversion rate as the average of the regional conversion rates. What is wrong with that?
Whether you know how to combine ratios correctly.
A simple average of rates ignores group size; the overall rate is total conversions divided by total visits, or a weighted average.

It gives a tiny region the same weight as a big one. If a region with 200 visits converts at 10% and one with 20,000 visits converts at 2%, the simple average says 6%. The true overall rate is 420 conversions out of 20,200 visits, about 2.1%. I divide totals by totals instead.
Two teams report different numbers of monthly active users. How do you settle it?
How you reconcile metric definitions across teams.
Finds the definition differences first, tests both on the same data, and ends with one written, agreed definition and an owner.

Usually the definitions differ, not the math. I write down each team's rule: what counts as active, which time zone, whether test accounts and bots are removed, and whether a person on two devices counts once. I run both rules on the same data, explain the gap, and get the owners to agree on one written definition for the dashboard.
After you join orders to another table, total revenue is suddenly twice what finance reports. What happened?
Whether you recognize a join that multiplies rows.
Spots a one-to-many join counting each order more than once, proves it with row counts and key checks, and fixes it by aggregating first.

Most likely the join fanned out. One order matched several rows on the other side, say one row per shipment, so its revenue was counted more than once. I compare row counts before and after the join and check that the key is unique where I expected. The fix is to sum the many side up to one row per order first, or join on the full key.
Marketing surveyed current customers and found 90% love the product. What would you warn them about?
Whether you can spot selection bias in how data was collected.
Only customers who stayed were asked, so unhappy ones who left are missing; the result describes current customers, not everyone.

Only people who stayed got the survey. Customers who left, maybe over price or a bug, are not in the sample, so the picture looks better than reality. I would label the result as what current customers think, and add an exit survey or look at what churned customers did before leaving to see the other side.
What is Simpson's paradox? Give an example of how it could fool a business.
Your grasp of how combining groups can reverse a trend.
A trend that holds in every group reverses when the groups are combined, usually because the group mix differs; the fix is to look at segments and the mix.

It is when a pattern holds inside every group but flips when you combine them. Say a new checkout converts better on both mobile and desktop, yet worse overall. That can happen if far more of its traffic came from mobile, which converts lower. The mix changed, not the checkout. I always break results down by the main segments before I trust a total.
Three days into a two-week A/B test, the result is significant and the product manager wants to stop and ship. What do you say?
Whether you understand the risk of stopping a test early when it looks good.
Explains that peeking and stopping at the first significant result inflates false positives; keeps the planned length or uses a sequential method set up in advance.

If we stop the first time the p-value dips under 0.05, our real false positive rate is much higher than 5%, because results swing a lot early on. I would run the test to the planned sample size and full weeks, to cover weekday patterns. If the team needs early reads next time, we can plan a sequential testing method before the test starts.
You split test results into 20 customer segments, and one shows a significant effect. How do you report it?
Whether you know the multiple comparisons problem.
With many tests, some will be significant by chance; treat it as a lead, adjust the threshold, and confirm with a new test.

With 20 tests at a 5% threshold, I would expect about one significant result by luck alone. So I report it as a lead, not a finding. I check whether that segment was named before the test, apply a correction like Bonferroni, which here means a threshold of 0.0025, and if it still looks real, I retest that segment on its own.
A director asks you to leave an unfavorable number out of a board presentation. How do you handle it?
Your integrity and how you push back on pressure to shade results.
Refuses to hide a number that changes the conclusion, offers a fair way to frame it, and escalates calmly if needed.

I would say I am glad to lead with the good news, but I cannot drop a number that changes the conclusion. If someone finds it later, we lose the decision and our credibility. I would offer to frame it well: the problem, its likely cause and the plan to fix it. If the director still insists, I would raise it with my own manager.

data-center.heading: Data center operations questions
qs: What is a hot aisle and cold aisle layout, and why do blanking panels matter?
Whether you understand how air moves through a data hall.
Racks face each other so server intakes share cool air, and panels stop hot exhaust from looping back to the front.

Rows of racks face front to front, so servers pull cool air from the cold aisle and blow hot air into the hot aisle behind. An empty slot is a hole: hot exhaust gets pulled back to the front and raises intake temperatures. A blanking panel closes that gap, so I put one in every time I remove a server.
How do you protect parts from static when you work inside a server?
Whether ESD protection is a habit for you.
A tested, grounded wrist strap, parts kept in anti-static bags, and handling by the edges.

I wear a wrist strap clipped to a ground point or the ESD mat, and I test the strap at the start of my shift. Parts stay in their anti-static bags until I install them, and I hold memory and cards by the edges. A failed part goes back into a bag, never loose on a floor tile.
A 70-pound server has to go near the top of a half-full rack. How do you do it?
How you handle heavy equipment without hurting yourself or tipping a rack.
Question the position first, check the rack's rating and anti-tip feet, mount rails first, and never lift it alone.

First I ask if it can go lower, since heavy gear belongs near the bottom. If the top is required, I check the rack's weight rating, put the stabilizer feet down and make sure no other server is pulled out on its rails. Rails go in first, then two of us lift it, or we use the server lift. I never lift that weight above my shoulders alone.
What do you do before you plug in a fiber patch cable?
Your fiber handling and eye safety.
Match the fiber type to the optic, inspect and clean both ends, and never look into a fiber end.

I check that the cable matches the optic: single-mode or multimode, and the right connector, usually LC. Then I inspect both ends with a fiber scope, clean them with a click cleaner or a lint-free wipe, and inspect again. Dirt is the most common cause of a bad link. I never look into a fiber end, because the laser light can be invisible.
A ticket says to replace a failed drive in a RAID 5 array. Walk me through it.
Whether you verify before you pull and understand what is at risk during a rebuild.
Confirm the array is degraded, not failed, and identify the exact drive by bay, serial and locator LED before pulling.

First I check the RAID controller: one drive failed, the array is degraded but still online. I match the bay and serial number to the ticket and turn on the locator LED. If it is hot-swap, I pull only that drive, insert the new one and watch the rebuild start. In RAID 5 a second failure before the rebuild finishes loses data, so pulling the wrong drive is the real danger.
A server will not boot after a memory upgrade. How do you find the cause?
Your hardware diagnostic method.
Start from what changed, read the management controller's log, check slot population rules, then isolate step by step.

I start with what changed: the memory. I read the event log in the management controller, the small built-in computer that monitors the server; it often names the failing slot. I confirm the modules are a supported type and sit in the slots the vendor's guide gives. I reseat them, and if it still fails I boot on the old memory and add new modules back a few at a time.
A server has two power supplies. How do you plug it in, and what do you check on the circuits?
Whether you understand redundant power and how a failover can overload a circuit.
One supply on the A feed and one on B, with total load small enough that one feed can carry it all if the other fails.

One power supply goes to the A-side PDU and the other to the B-side, which come from separate power paths. Then I check the load. If A drops, B suddenly carries everything, so the combined load of both sides must fit on one circuit within its continuous limit, normally 80% of the breaker rating. Adding one more server can quietly break that.
A customer asks you to power-cycle the server in rack 12, slot 20, but the label there shows a different hostname. What do you do?
Your judgement when the instructions and the hardware disagree.
Stop, touch nothing, verify with the customer by serial or locator light, and record the mismatch.

I stop and do not touch it. I take a photo of the label and the slot, contact the customer and ask them to confirm by serial number or by turning on the locator light remotely. A power cycle on the wrong box can take down someone's database. I also note the label mismatch in the ticket so the records get fixed.
You pulled a cable and then realize it was the wrong one. What do you do in the next few minutes?
How honestly and quickly you handle your own mistake.
Put it back if you are sure where it goes, tell the operations center at once, and write it up honestly.

If I am sure where it came from, I plug it back in right away. Then I call the network operations center, the team that watches the systems, and give them the port and the exact time so they can check what went down. I do not wait to see if anyone notices. Afterward I write it up and look at why the labels let me make that mistake.
A vendor wants a failed drive back for a warranty credit, but the drive held customer data. What do you do?
Whether you put data security and chain of custody ahead of convenience.
Follow the data-handling policy: the drive stays in custody and is wiped or destroyed by the approved method.

The drive stays with us unless policy says it may leave. Many sites buy a keep-your-drive option from the vendor for this reason. I log the serial number, lock the drive in the secure bin and track it until it is wiped or shredded by the approved method, with a certificate. A small warranty credit is not worth a data breach.

data-engineer.heading: Data engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between ETL and ELT, and when would you pick each?
Whether you know the two basic ways to move data into a warehouse.
The order of the steps explained clearly, plus a real reason to choose each one, such as masking data before it lands.

In ETL I transform the data before loading it into the warehouse. In ELT I load the raw data first and transform it inside the warehouse with SQL. I usually pick ELT because cloud warehouses scale well and keeping raw data lets me rebuild models. I pick ETL when data must be cleaned or masked before it lands, like personal data that should never be stored raw.
What is a star schema, and what goes in a fact table versus a dimension table?
Your grasp of the most common way to model data for analysts.
Facts are measured events at a stated grain, dimensions describe them, and the grain is decided first.

A fact table holds events or measurements, for example one row per order line, with numbers like quantity and price and keys to the dimensions. Dimension tables describe the who, what, where and when: customer, product, store, date. Analysts filter and group by dimension columns and sum the facts. I always write down the grain of the fact table before anything else.
Why store large analytics tables in a columnar file format instead of CSV?
Whether you understand how storage choices affect query speed and cost.
Queries read only the needed columns, compression is better, and the schema and types travel with the file.

Analytics queries usually read a few columns across many rows. A columnar format stores each column together, so the engine reads only the columns it needs and compresses them well because similar values sit side by side. It also keeps the schema and data types, which CSV does not. CSV is fine for a small file sent to a person, not for a big table queried every day.
A customer moves to a new city. How do you keep their address history so old orders still show the old address?
Whether you can model data that changes over time.
A Type 2 slowly changing dimension: close the old row, add a new one with dates and a surrogate key, never overwrite.

That is a Type 2 slowly changing dimension. I do not overwrite the row. I close the old row by setting its end date and setting its current flag to false, then insert a new row with a new surrogate key, a start date and the current flag true. Facts store the surrogate key that was valid at the time, so old orders keep the old address.
What does it mean for a pipeline to be idempotent, and how do you build one?
Whether your pipelines survive retries and reruns without corrupting data.
Running a job twice gives the same result; loads replace a partition or merge on a key, and the run date is a parameter.

It means running the same job twice for the same period gives the same result, not double the rows. Jobs fail and get retried, and backfills rerun old dates, so this matters all the time. I make loads replace a date partition or merge on a business key instead of appending, and I pass the run date in as a parameter instead of reading the current time.
How do you load a large source table incrementally, and how do you handle records that arrive late?
How you move only new data without losing or duplicating rows.
A watermark on a change timestamp, a lookback window for late rows, a merge on the key, and a plan for deletes.

I keep a watermark, the highest updated_at value I loaded, and on the next run I pull rows changed since then. Because records can arrive late, I go back a safety window, say three days, and merge on the primary key so rows already loaded are updated, not duplicated. Deletes need care: I ask the source for a deleted flag or read its change data capture log.
Which data quality checks do you put on a pipeline, and what happens when one fails?
Whether you catch bad data before analysts do.
Concrete checks on freshness, volume, keys and values, and a clear split between checks that block a load and checks that only alert.

Freshness: did data arrive on time. Volume: is the row count in a normal range. Keys: no nulls or duplicates in the primary key, and foreign keys find a match. Values: amounts not negative, dates not in the future. A failed key check stops the load before analysts see bad data; an odd volume alerts the owner but lets the data through.
The source team renamed a column without telling you, and the nightly job failed. Walk me through what you do.
How you handle a broken pipeline and prevent the same break next time.
Users told first, a fix that shields downstream tables, a rerun with checks, then an agreement and an early schema check.

First I tell the users of the table that today's data is late and when I expect it. Then I confirm the rename in the source and map the new name in our staging layer, so downstream tables keep the old name. I rerun the failed date and check row counts. Afterwards I agree with the source team on notice before schema changes and add a check that fails early with a clear message.
You discover the revenue table has held duplicate orders for the past week. What do you do?
Your judgement when bad data has already reached the business.
Warn the affected users at once, find the root cause, fix and backfill, reconcile with the source, and add a test.

I tell finance and the dashboard owners right away which dates and reports are affected, so nobody shares wrong revenue. Then I find the cause, for example a retried job that appended instead of replacing. I fix the job, dedupe on order ID, rebuild the week and compare totals with the source system. Last, I add a uniqueness test on order ID so it cannot happen silently again.
Your streaming system delivers events at least once. How do you keep counts and totals correct?
Whether you understand delivery guarantees in streaming and how to design around them.
Duplicates are expected after failures; a unique event ID plus an idempotent write or a dedupe step keeps results exact.

At-least-once means that after a failure some events are delivered again, so a plain count can come out too high. I make sure every event carries a unique ID set by the producer, and I make the sink idempotent: an upsert on that ID, or a dedupe on it within a time window before aggregating. Then a replay overwrites the same rows instead of adding new ones.

data-governance.heading: Data governance and quality questions
qs: What is the difference between a data owner and a data steward?
Whether you know the basic roles a governance program runs on.
The owner is accountable and decides; the steward does the daily care. A strong answer also places IT as the custodian.

The data owner is a business leader accountable for a domain, like customer data. They approve access and set the quality bar. The steward works day to day: keeps definitions current, reviews quality reports and routes issues. IT is the custodian that runs the systems where the data lives.
How do a business glossary, a data dictionary and a data catalog differ?
Whether you can separate the core tools of the trade.
Glossary defines business terms, dictionary describes technical fields, catalog is the searchable inventory that links the two.

The glossary says what a business term means, like what counts as a customer. The dictionary describes fields in a system: name, type, allowed values. The catalog is the searchable inventory of data assets that links each column to its glossary term, owner and lineage.
What are the main dimensions of data quality, and how would you measure one of them?
Your grasp of data quality as something you can measure, not a feeling.
Names the common dimensions and turns one into a metric with a threshold agreed with the owner.

The usual ones are completeness, accuracy, validity, consistency, timeliness and uniqueness. For completeness, I would count the share of customer rows with a required field filled, like email. I track it daily and alert when it drops below a threshold the owner agreed to, say 98%.
What should a catalog entry for a table contain so that people actually use it?
Whether you build a catalog for its users, not just to fill it.
Plain description, owner and contact, definitions, sensitivity, freshness, quality status and how to get access.

A plain sentence on what the table holds and what it is good for. The owner and steward to contact. Column definitions linked to the glossary. A sensitivity label, refresh schedule, quality score and lineage. And a clear button or link for requesting access, or people go back to asking in chat.
Why does data lineage matter? Give an example of using it.
How you use lineage for impact analysis and root cause.
Lineage shows where data comes from and where it goes, so you can predict what a change breaks and trace errors back.

Lineage maps data from source through each transformation to reports. Once an engineer wanted to rename a revenue column. Lineage showed 12 dashboards and a finance extract depended on it. We warned the owners, planned the switch together and nothing broke on the release day.
How do you decide who gets access to a dataset with personal information?
Whether you apply least privilege and protect personal data in practice.
Minimum access by role and purpose, owner approval, masking where identity is not needed, and regular reviews.

I start from least privilege: people get only what their role needs. Requests name a purpose and the data owner approves. If analysts do not need identities, they get a view with names and emails masked. Access is reviewed on a schedule, and people who leave or change roles lose it.
Two departments report different numbers for active customers. How do you resolve it?
How you settle a conflicting business definition.
Find both definitions, show why they differ, get owners to agree on one certified term, name any variant clearly.

I collect both definitions and trace each number. Often one counts 30 days of activity and the other 90, or one includes trials. I bring both owners together with the facts. We agree on one certified definition in the glossary, and any other version gets its own clear name.
Six months after you launch a data quality program, nobody looks at the dashboards. What went wrong, and what do you do?
How you own a governance failure and make the work useful to the business.
Admits the program measured what was easy, not what mattered, and ties fixes to business pain and named owners.

Likely we tracked hundreds of rules nobody cared about, with no owner for each. I would ask owners which errors cost them money or time, cut the dashboard to those, and assign each rule a person. Alerts would go to that owner directly, and I would report fixes in business terms.

data-leader.heading: Head of data and analytics questions
qs: Would you run the data team centrally or embed analysts in the business units?
How you think about team structure and its trade-offs.
Knows both sides and often picks a hybrid: shared standards and platform at the center, analysts close to the teams they serve.

A central team keeps standards and definitions consistent, but it can feel far from the business. Embedded analysts know their area well but drift into their own versions of the truth. I usually run a hub and spoke: analysts sit with product or sales day to day, but report to data, share one platform and go through the same code review.
When would you buy a data tool instead of having your team build it?
How you weigh build versus buy for the data stack.
Buys common pieces like data ingestion, builds where the company has an edge, and counts upkeep and staff time, not only the license price.

If the work is the same at every company, like copying data from common apps into the warehouse, I buy; my engineers' time costs more than the license, and upkeep never ends. I build where our logic is unique, like our pricing models. Before deciding I compare total cost over three years, including who maintains it when the builder leaves.
The CFO and the head of sales bring two different revenue numbers to the same meeting. What do you do?
How you settle conflicting metric definitions.
Finds the difference in definitions, gets one owner to sign off on the official one, and builds it once in a shared, governed place.

First I find out why they differ; it is usually definitions, like booked versus recognized revenue, or how refunds are timed. Often both numbers are right for their purpose. I write each definition down, have the CFO own the official one, give the other a different name, and build both once in the shared model so every dashboard pulls from there.
An analyst asks for full access to customer tables, including names and emails, to speed up their work. How do you respond?
Your judgement on privacy and access to personal data.
Least privilege: give what the task needs, mask identifiers, log access, and know that privacy laws and contracts limit use.

Most analysis does not need names or emails, so I would give access to a version where those are masked or replaced with an ID. If a task truly needs them, access is approved for that purpose, time-limited and logged. State privacy laws and our customer contracts limit how we use personal data, and the fewer people who see it, the smaller any breach.
A product team checks its A/B test every day and wants to stop it the first day it looks significant. What do you tell them?
Whether you understand experiment discipline well enough to set rules for other teams.
Stopping at the first significant look raises the false positive rate; fix sample size and run time up front, or use a method built for monitoring.

Each extra look is another chance for noise to cross the line, so stopping on the first good day makes false wins far more likely than the error rate they planned for. I ask them to set the sample size and run time before launch, usually whole weeks to cover weekday patterns. If they truly need to watch daily, we use a sequential test designed for that.
Your cloud data warehouse bill has doubled in three months. Walk me through what you do.
How you manage platform cost without slowing the business.
Finds what drives cost by job, user and dashboard, fixes the worst offenders, and sets budgets and alerts so the next jump is seen early.

I pull usage by job, user and dashboard; usually a handful cause most of the spend. Common culprits are a dashboard refreshing every five minutes that nobody opens, full table rebuilds that could be incremental, and oversized compute left running. We fix those first, then set budgets and alerts per team so the next jump shows up in a week, not a quarter.
A dashboard your team built showed the board a wrong number last quarter. How do you handle it?
How you own a data error and stop it from happening again.
Tells leaders quickly with the corrected figure, finds the root cause, and adds a test or sign-off that would have caught it.

I would tell the CEO and CFO the same day, with the right number and what it changes. Then we trace the cause; in one case I had, a source system started sending duplicate orders after an update. We fixed the model, added a uniqueness test and a row-count alert, and I put a sign-off step on any figure that goes to the board.
The CEO wants an AI project this year. How do you decide what, if anything, to build?
Whether you tie machine learning and AI work to business value and data readiness.
Starts from a business problem with a measurable outcome, checks the data and a simple baseline first, and pilots small before committing.

I ask which decision or task we want to improve and how we would measure success, like fewer hours spent on support tickets. Then I check whether we have the data, and what a simple rule or existing tool already achieves. If a pilot beats that baseline on a small slice, we scale it. If not, I would rather say so than ship a demo nobody uses.
You join and find 400 dashboards, low trust in the numbers and a long request backlog. What do you do in your first 90 days?
How you diagnose a data function and set a plan for your first quarter.
Listens first, restores trust in a few core metrics, cuts unused work, and shows an early win before any big rebuild.

The first month I talk with leaders about the decisions they make and check usage logs; often most dashboards are barely opened. I pick the five to ten metrics leadership runs on and make them correct, tested and documented. We retire unused dashboards and set up an intake process. By day 90 I want one trusted weekly report and a roadmap agreed with the exec team.

data-product-manager.heading: Data product manager questions
qs: What makes a dataset a product rather than just a table someone built?
Whether you understand what data product management adds to plain data work.
Named users, an owner, documentation, quality and freshness promises, and a way to get support and hear about changes.

A table is output. A product has users it was built for and an owner who answers for it. It has documentation, a stated refresh time, quality checks, a support channel and a change policy. If nobody would notice it broke, or nobody would fix it, it is not a product yet.
What goes into a data contract between the team that produces data and the teams that use it?
Your grasp of how data teams agree on what they deliver to each other.
Schema, field meanings, freshness and quality expectations, ownership, and how changes are announced. All written down, and ideally checked automatically.

The schema with field types and meanings, which fields can be empty, the refresh schedule and how late is too late, quality rules like unique IDs, the owner, and how much notice users get before a breaking change. I like the schema part enforced in the pipeline, so a breaking change fails a check instead of a dashboard.
An internal data platform earns no revenue. How do you show it is working?
How you pick success measures for a product whose users are your colleagues.
Adoption, reliability and trust measures tied to time or decisions saved, not row counts or the number of tables.

I track active users and queries by team, how often data lands on time, incidents and time to fix, and how long a new analyst takes to answer a first question. Then I tie a few to outcomes, like a report that took two days now refreshing on its own. Number of tables is not a measure; more tables can mean more mess.
A sales leader asks for real-time data in their dashboard. How do you respond?
Whether you weigh the cost of fresher data against the decision it supports.
Asks what decision changes with fresher data, matches the refresh speed to that, and explains the extra cost and complexity of streaming.

I ask what they would do differently if the number were minutes old instead of a day old. Often the answer is a morning review, so hourly or daily is enough. Streaming costs more to build, run and test. If a decision truly needs minutes, like stopping fraud, I make the case for it. Otherwise I offer the cheapest refresh that fits.
An upstream team renamed a column overnight and your customer-facing feed broke. Walk me through your morning.
How you run a data incident and keep it from happening again.
Contain, tell affected users early, fix or roll back, refill the missed data, then fix the process: contract, schema checks, change notice.

First I confirm the scope: which feeds, which customers, since when. I post a status note to affected users before I have a fix. With engineering we map the new name or roll back, rerun the missed loads and check the counts. Then the follow-up: a schema check that blocks publishing, and the upstream team added to our contract and change process.
Two dashboards show different numbers for active customers. How do you settle it?
Your approach to metric definitions and a single source of truth.
Traces both definitions and sources, gets the business owner to choose one, documents it in one shared place and retires the other version.

I trace both: source tables, filters, time windows and what counts as active. Usually one uses 30 days and one counts any login. I bring the difference to the metric's business owner to pick one, document it in our shared metric definitions, and point both dashboards there. The old version is removed, so it does not come back.
A team wants customer email addresses and exact locations added to a shared dataset. What do you check first?
Whether you handle personal data with care, not as just another column.
Purpose and real need, whether less identifying data would do, privacy or legal review, access limits, masking and how long it is kept.

I ask what they are trying to do, because often a hashed ID or a city works instead of an email and exact location. If they truly need it, I check with privacy or legal that our notice and terms allow that use, since several state laws give people rights over their data. Then access only for named roles, masking for others, and a retention limit.
You want to retire an old dataset that 40 scheduled jobs still query. How do you do it?
How you shut down a data product without breaking the people who depend on it.
Finds every user through query logs and lineage, offers a replacement and migration help, announces dates, then removes access in stages.

I use query logs and lineage to list every job and its owner. I make sure the replacement covers their needs, with a field-by-field mapping. Then I announce a date, contact owners directly and track who has moved. Near the end I mark it deprecated, then revoke access for a week before deleting, so anything we missed fails loudly and can be restored.
Your data warehouse bill doubled this quarter. What do you do?
Whether you manage the cost of a data product as part of the product.
Breaks cost down by team, job and table, finds the few heavy drivers, cuts waste and agrees on budgets or cost visibility with users.

I break the bill down by team, job and query; usually a few things drive most of it. I look for queries scanning whole tables that could read one date range, dashboards refreshing every few minutes that nobody opens, and duplicate pipelines. Then I show each team its own cost, so new heavy usage starts with a conversation, not a surprise.
A paying customer of your data feed finds wrong values that already went into their own reports. How do you handle it?
How you own a quality failure with outside customers who rely on your data.
Fast, honest notice of what was wrong and for which dates, corrected data with a clear note, a check of contract terms, and a lasting fix.

I confirm it, then tell every affected customer, not only the one who found it: which fields, which dates, and when corrected data arrives. We redeliver the corrected history with a clear note on what changed. I check the contract for any credits owed. Then we add the test that would have caught it, such as a range or row-count check before delivery.

data-scientist.heading: Data scientist questions
qs: What is the difference between L1 and L2 regularization?
Whether you know how models are kept simple, not just that they can be.
L1 can set weights to exactly zero, so it selects features. L2 shrinks all weights smoothly. Features should be scaled first.

Both add a penalty for large weights to the loss. L1, used in lasso, penalizes the absolute values and pushes some weights to exactly zero, so it drops features. L2, used in ridge, penalizes the squared values and shrinks weights without zeroing them, which helps when features are correlated. Either way I scale the features first, or the penalty hits them unevenly.
What is data leakage? Give an example you have seen or caught.
Whether you can spot a model that looks good only because it saw the answer.
A clear definition and a real case, such as a feature known only after the outcome, or preprocessing fit on all the data before the split.

Leakage is when the model trains on information it will not have at prediction time. In a churn model I once saw 98% accuracy. The cause was a cancellation reason field filled in only after a customer left. I removed it and accuracy fell to a believable 81%. I also fit scalers and imputers on the training set only, never on all the data.
Only 1% of transactions are fraud. How do you build and judge a model for that?
How you handle rare events, where accuracy says almost nothing.
Precision, recall or PR AUC instead of accuracy, class weights or resampling on training data only, and a threshold set by the cost of each error.

A model that calls everything legitimate is 99% accurate and useless, so I look at precision, recall and the area under the precision-recall curve. I try class weights first, and if I resample, I do it inside the training folds only. Then I pick the threshold with the fraud team, based on what a missed fraud costs versus a wrongly blocked customer.
Why is random k-fold cross-validation risky for a sales forecast, and what do you use instead?
Whether you validate models the way they will actually be used.
Random folds let the model learn from the future. Time-based splits train on the past and test on a later period.

Random folds mix dates, so the model trains on next month to predict last month, and lag features leak too. The score looks better than reality. I use a rolling or expanding window: train on data up to a date, test on the weeks after it, then move the cutoff forward. Each test period is one the model has never seen, just like in production.
Your model says a customer has an 80% chance to buy. How do you check whether that number means anything?
Whether you know the difference between ranking well and giving honest probabilities.
Calibration: among cases scored near 0.8, about 80% should buy. Check with a reliability curve; fix with Platt scaling or isotonic regression.

That is a question of calibration. I group held-out cases by predicted score and compare each group's average score with the share that actually bought; near 0.8, about 80% should buy. A reliability plot or the Brier score shows it. Some models are poorly calibrated out of the box, so I recalibrate with Platt scaling or isotonic regression fit on a separate validation set.
A product manager checks the A/B test every morning and wants to stop the day it hits p < 0.05. What is the problem?
Whether you understand how peeking at results inflates false positives.
Repeated looks at a fixed-horizon test push the false positive rate well above 5%. Fix the sample size in advance or use a sequential method.

Each look is another chance for noise to cross the line, so with daily checks the real false positive rate ends up far above 5%. I would agree on the sample size before launch and decide only then. If the team truly needs early answers, I would set up a sequential design, such as alpha spending, where the threshold is adjusted for each planned look.
You tested 20 metrics and one came out significant at 0.05. How do you report it?
How you handle multiple comparisons without fooling yourself or others.
With 20 tests, about one false positive is expected by chance. Correct for it, and lead with the primary metric picked before the test.

If nothing really changed, 20 tests at 5% would still give about one win by chance, so I would not call it a result. I report the primary metric we chose before the test first. For the others I apply a correction such as Benjamini-Hochberg and label any survivor as a lead to test again, not a finding.
Overall conversion went up after a change, but it went down in every region. How can that be?
Whether you recognize Simpson's paradox and know to check the mix.
The mix shifted toward segments with higher base rates. Compare within segments or reweight to a fixed mix before drawing a conclusion.

That is Simpson's paradox. Say traffic shifted toward a region that always converts better: each region dropped a little, but more visitors now sit in the strong one, so the total rises. I would show the change within each region and a total reweighted to the old mix. Then I would ask why the mix moved, since that may be the real story.
Your 50/50 test shows 50,000 users in control and 48,500 in treatment. What do you do?
Whether you catch a broken experiment before reading its results.
Test for sample ratio mismatch with a chi-square test. If it fails, do not trust the results; look for bugs in assignment or logging.

A gap of 1,500 on nearly 100,000 users is far too big for chance; a chi-square test gives a tiny p-value. That is a sample ratio mismatch, so I would not read the metrics yet. I would look for causes such as a redirect that drops some treatment users, a logging bug, or bot filtering that hits one group more. Once it is fixed, I rerun the test.
Marketing launched a campaign in some states only, with no experiment. How would you estimate its effect?
Whether you can estimate a causal effect from observational data and name the assumptions.
A method like difference-in-differences or synthetic control, with its key assumption stated and checked, such as parallel trends before launch.

I would use difference-in-differences: compare the change in sales in launch states with the change in similar states without the campaign, over the same weeks. It rests on parallel trends, so I would check that both groups moved together for months before launch. If no single comparison group fits, I would build a synthetic control from a weighted mix of states.

database-administrator.heading: Database administrator questions
qs: What is the difference between RPO and RTO?
Whether you know the two targets that every backup and recovery plan is built around.
RPO is how much data loss is acceptable, RTO is how long downtime is acceptable, and each one drives a different part of the plan.

RPO, the recovery point objective, is how much data we can afford to lose, measured in time. RTO, the recovery time objective, is how long we can be down. An RPO of 15 minutes means changes must be backed up or replicated at least that often. The RTO sets how fast the restore or failover must be, so I time real restores against it.
Explain full, differential and transaction log backups, and how you would combine them.
Your grasp of backup types and the order a restore must follow.
Correct definitions, a realistic schedule, and the right restore sequence: full, latest differential, then logs in order.

In SQL Server terms, a full backup copies the whole database. A differential copies what changed since the last full. A log backup holds every transaction since the last log backup. A common plan is a weekly full, a nightly differential and logs every 15 minutes. To restore, I apply the full, the latest differential, then the logs in order up to the moment I need.
What is the trade-off between synchronous and asynchronous replication?
Whether you understand the balance between data safety and write speed in replication.
Synchronous protects committed data but slows every write; asynchronous is faster but can lose recent changes on failover.

With synchronous replication, the primary waits for the replica to confirm before a commit returns, so a failover loses no committed data, but every write pays the network round trip. Asynchronous commits at once and ships changes after, so it is faster, but a failover can lose the last few seconds. I often use synchronous nearby and asynchronous to a distant region.
What is a deadlock, and how do you reduce them?
Your knowledge of locking and how you work with developers to prevent conflicts.
A clear definition, knowing the database kills one victim, and practical fixes in both the code and the schema.

A deadlock is two transactions each holding a lock the other needs. Neither can move, so the database picks one as the victim and rolls it back. To reduce them, I have code touch tables in the same order, keep transactions short, and add indexes so updates lock fewer rows. The app should also retry the victim, since some deadlocks will still happen.
How do you know your backups will actually restore?
Whether you test recovery or only trust that the backup job ran.
Scheduled test restores, integrity checks, restore times measured against the RTO, alerts on failed jobs, and a protected off-site copy.

A backup is only proven by a restore. I restore the latest backups to a separate server on a schedule, run an integrity check like DBCC CHECKDB, and compare row counts on key tables. I time each restore against our RTO. I also alert on any failed or skipped backup job and keep one copy off site that production accounts cannot delete.
An execution plan shows an estimate of 10 rows, but the actual count is 2 million. What does that tell you?
How well you understand the query optimizer and the statistics it depends on.
Knowing the plan was built on a bad row estimate, and naming likely causes: stale statistics, parameter sniffing, correlated columns.

The optimizer built its plan for 10 rows, so it likely chose a nested loop or an index seek that is terrible for 2 million. First I check whether statistics on those columns are stale and update them. If they are fresh, I look at parameter sniffing, where the plan was built for a rare value, and at correlated columns, which the optimizer treats as independent.
A read replica is 30 minutes behind the primary, and users see old data. What do you check?
How you trace replication lag to a cause while limiting the harm to users.
Splitting the lag into shipping versus applying, checking load on both sides, and routing fresh reads to the primary in the meantime.
