First I check whether the lag is in shipping or applying: are changes reaching the replica, or arriving and waiting? Then I look for a big write on the primary, like a bulk update, and for slow disk on the replica. On PostgreSQL, a long report query on the replica can hold back replay. Meanwhile I tell the app team so reads needing fresh data go to the primary.
Someone ran a DELETE without a WHERE clause on a production table 20 minutes ago. What do you do?
How you recover lost data without destroying the good work done since.
No restore over production; a point-in-time restore to a separate copy, then copying the missing rows back and checking them.

I stop anything that could make it worse, like jobs that sync that table. I do not restore over production, because that would wipe 20 minutes of good work. I restore the last backup plus logs to a separate database, stopping just before the delete, which I find by its time in the log. Then I copy the missing rows back and check counts with the data owners.
How would you add an index to a 500-million-row table in production without downtime?
Whether you can change a large live database without blocking the business.
Testing on a copy first, using an online or concurrent build, knowing its limits, and watching locks and replica lag.

I test the change on a restored copy first to see the time and locks. On PostgreSQL I use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, which avoids blocking writes, but it cannot run inside a transaction and can leave an invalid index if it fails, so I check afterward. I run it off peak and watch locks and replica lag. Any data backfill goes in small batches.
The primary database is down, and automatic failover did not trigger. Walk me through what you do.
Your judgement in a manual failover, especially avoiding two primaries taking writes.
Confirming the outage, fencing the old primary, stating possible data loss to the business, then promoting and rebuilding the old one.

First I confirm the primary is really down, not just cut off from monitoring. Then I fence it so it cannot take writes if it comes back, because two primaries means split data. I check how far behind the replica was, tell the business what data could be lost, promote it and repoint the apps. The old primary rejoins only after it is rebuilt as a replica.

defense.heading: Defense and national security questions
qs: What is the difference between holding a clearance and having access to classified information?
Whether you understand how cleared work is actually controlled.
A clearance is eligibility. Access also needs a need-to-know for that specific information and a signed nondisclosure agreement.

The clearance means the government has found me eligible at a given level, like Secret. It does not let me see everything at that level. I also need a need-to-know for that specific program, and I sign a nondisclosure agreement before I'm read on. If a cleared coworker asks about my program and isn't on it, the answer is no.
What is CUI, and how do you handle it day to day?
Your habits with information that is unclassified but still protected.
CUI is unclassified information the government requires to be safeguarded. It stays on approved company systems and goes only to people with a lawful business need.

Controlled Unclassified Information isn't classified, but a law or government policy says it must be protected, like export-controlled drawings. I keep it on approved company systems, never on a personal phone or personal email. I check the marking before I share a file, and I send it only to people with a lawful business need for it.
Why does it matter which charge number you put your hours on?
Whether you understand the rules for billing work to government contracts.
Hours go to the contract you actually worked on, recorded daily. Moving hours to a contract with budget left is mischarging and can be fraud.

On government contracts the hours I record become costs the government pays for, and auditors check them. So I record time every day, on the charge number for the work I actually did. If my program is out of budget and someone suggests charging another contract, I refuse and tell my manager or the ethics office. That is mischarging, and it can be treated as fraud.
A coworker here on a work visa asks to see the drawings for an ITAR-controlled part. What do you do?
Whether you know that sharing technical data with a foreign person counts as an export.
Under ITAR, releasing controlled technical data to a foreign person, even inside the US, is an export and needs authorization first.

I don't share it yet. Under ITAR, releasing technical data to a foreign person is an export, even if we sit in the same US office. I'd ask our export compliance team whether we hold a license or agreement that covers this person. If not, I tell my coworker kindly that I can't, and that it isn't about trust.
Someone on a networking site offers you a consulting fee to answer questions about your program. What do you do?
Your counterintelligence awareness and whether you report suspicious contacts.
You don't answer or engage further, you keep the messages, and you report the contact to your security officer.

I don't reply with any details, even harmless ones, because small facts add up. I keep the messages, screenshot the profile, and report it to our facility security officer the same day. Fake recruiter profiles are a known way that foreign intelligence services target cleared people. Security decides what happens next, not me.
A buyer found an obsolete chip we need from a broker at half price. What do you say?
Whether you know the risk of counterfeit parts and how to source them safely.
Buy from the original maker or its authorized distributors first. Any other source needs vetting, traceability, testing and approval, because counterfeits fail in the field.

I'd slow down. Brokers outside the authorized channel are the main risk for counterfeit electronics: used or relabeled chips sold as new. First I'd look for stock from the manufacturer or an authorized distributor. If there is none, we use a vetted supplier, get traceability paperwork, test the parts before use, and tell the customer if the contract requires it.
Production wants to move a hole 2 mm because assembly would be easier. Can they just do it?
Whether you respect configuration control on an approved design.
No. The change goes through the engineering change process, the drawing is updated first, and changes to form, fit or function may need customer approval.

Not on the floor. Even a small move can change how the part fits the next assembly or a spare already in the field. I'd write an engineering change request, check what else that hole interfaces with, and update the drawing before anyone cuts metal. If it affects form, fit or function, the customer usually has to approve it, because they control the approved design.
You notice a file with classified markings on an unclassified network share. What do you do?
How you handle a possible classified spill without making it worse.
You don't reopen, copy, forward or delete it. You note where it is and tell the security officer at once, in person or by phone, not by email.

I stop. I don't open it again, forward it, print it or delete it, because each of those can spread it or destroy evidence. I write down the file path and the time, and I call or go see our security officer right away. I don't describe the content in an email. Then I follow their instructions, which may include leaving my computer alone.
A unit fails a vibration test the day before the government witness arrives. How do you handle it?
Your honesty with test results under schedule pressure.
Record the failure, tell the customer, and find the root cause. Never quietly retest until it passes or hide the first result.

I record the failure exactly as it happened and tell my lead and the program office the same day. Then we find out why: the fixture, the setup, or the unit itself. If it's the unit, the witness test moves, and we say so plainly. Rerunning until it passes and showing only the good run would be falsifying a test record, and these units go to people in the field.
The customer's engineer asks you to add a feature that is not in the contract, since you are in there anyway. What do you do?
Whether you know who can change a government contract and how to say no politely.
Only the contracting officer can change the contract. You thank the engineer, log the request and send it to your program manager or contracts team.

I'd say it's a good idea and I'll pass it on, but I can't start it yet. Only the government contracting officer can change what the contract covers; an engineer, even a senior one, can't authorize it. If we did it anyway, we might not get paid and it could cause a dispute later. I write down the request and send it to our program manager and contracts team the same day.

defi.heading: DeFi and protocol specialist questions
qs: In a constant-product pool, how is the price of a swap set?
Whether you understand the basic pricing math behind automated market makers.
Price comes from the ratio of the reserves, the product of the reserves stays constant, and bigger trades move the price more.

The pool holds two tokens and keeps their quantities multiplied together at a constant: x times y equals k. The price is the ratio of the two reserves. When I buy token A, I add B and remove A, so A gets scarcer and pricier with every unit. That is price impact: a trade that is large next to the pool pays far more than the quoted price. A small fee goes to the pool on top.
What is impermanent loss, and when does it become permanent?
Whether you can explain the main risk of providing liquidity.
LP value falls behind simply holding when prices diverge. It is locked in if you withdraw while prices are apart, and fees may or may not cover it.

If I deposit two tokens and one doubles in price against the other, arbitrage traders rebalance the pool and I end up holding less of the winner. My position is then worth about 5.7% less than if I had just held both. It is called impermanent because it shrinks if prices return, but if I withdraw at the new price it is real. The question is whether trading fees cover it.
On a lending protocol, what is a health factor, and what happens when it drops below 1?
Your grasp of overcollateralized lending and how liquidations work.
Collateral weighted by its liquidation threshold, divided by debt. Below 1, liquidators repay part of the debt and take collateral at a discount.

Borrowing is overcollateralized: I lock more value than I borrow. The health factor is my collateral value times its liquidation threshold, divided by my debt. If prices move and it falls below 1, anyone can repay part of my loan and take some of my collateral plus a bonus. I tell users to keep a wide buffer and to watch the collateral price, not just the debt.
Why do borrowing rates on a lending pool jump sharply when most of the deposits are borrowed?
Whether you understand utilization-based interest rate models.
Rates follow utilization, with a steep slope above a target point so lenders can still withdraw and borrowers are pushed to repay.

Utilization is the share of deposits that is lent out. Most pools raise rates gently up to a target, often called the kink, then steeply above it. If the pool hit 100%, lenders could not withdraw because the cash is out on loan. The steep rate draws in new deposits and makes borrowers repay, which puts liquidity back. I watch that point on any pool I add funds to.
A user's large swap filled at a much worse price than quoted. What likely happened, and how do you prevent it next time?
Whether you know how sandwich attacks and slippage settings affect real users.
Names price impact and sandwiching by bots reading the public mempool, and gives fixes: tighter slippage, private submission, smaller orders.

Two things are likely. The trade was large next to the pool depth, so price impact was high, and a bot saw it in the public mempool, bought just before and sold just after, taking the gap up to the slippage limit. I would check the block for that pattern. Next time: a tight slippage tolerance, a private transaction route, and splitting the order.
A user asks why their wallet wants an unlimited token approval before a swap. What do you tell them?
How you explain approval risk, one of the most common ways users lose funds.
An approval lets a contract move your tokens later and stays open, so approve only what is needed, check the spender and revoke old approvals.

An approval lets the contract move that token from your wallet, not just now but until you change it. Unlimited saves fees on future trades, but if the contract is hacked or the site is fake, the attacker can take the whole balance. I suggest approving only the amount needed, checking the spender address, and revoking old approvals by setting them back to zero.
How can a flash loan be used to attack a protocol that reads prices from one DEX pool?
Whether you understand oracle manipulation and how to defend against it.
Borrow big with no collateral in one transaction, skew a thin pool's spot price, exploit the target, repay. Fix with time-weighted or aggregated oracles.

A flash loan is borrowed and repaid in one transaction, or the whole transaction reverts. The attacker borrows a large sum, swaps it into a thin pool to skew the price, uses that fake price to borrow too much from the target, then repays in the same transaction. The fix: never trust one pool's spot price. Use a time-weighted average or an oracle that aggregates many sources.
A protocol's contracts are upgradeable by an admin key. How do you judge that risk?
How you weigh upgradeability and admin control when assessing a protocol.
Who holds the key, single wallet or multisig, whether a timelock gives users time to exit, and what the admin can change alone.

Upgradeable means a proxy points to logic the admin can swap, so the code reviewed today may not be the code tomorrow. I check who holds the key: one wallet is a red flag, a multisig with known signers is better. I want a timelock so users see changes and can exit first, and I check what the admin can do alone, such as pause, change fees or move funds.
A governance proposal wants to raise the loan-to-value on a volatile, thinly traded token. How do you evaluate it?
Your judgement on collateral risk settings for a lending market.
Looks at liquidity for liquidations, volatility, oracle quality and holder concentration, and offers caps or a smaller step, not just yes or no.

The key question is whether liquidators could sell that collateral in a crash without the price collapsing. I would check how much can be sold on-chain within a few percent of price impact, recent drawdowns, how robust the oracle is, and whether a few wallets hold most of the supply. If it is borderline, I would propose a supply cap and a small step up instead.
You see funds draining from a pool you help run, in what looks like a live exploit. What do you do in the first hour?
How you handle an incident under pressure without making it worse.
Confirms fast, follows the runbook, uses pause powers if they exist, saves evidence, and warns users without exposing the bug.

I confirm it is real from the transactions, then alert the team in our private incident channel and follow the runbook. If we have a pause role, the signers use it to stop further loss. I save transaction hashes and attacker addresses. We tell users to stop depositing, without describing the bug, since copycats read posts too. Root cause comes after the bleeding stops.

delivery-driver.heading: Delivery driver and courier questions
qs: What do you check on the vehicle before you start a route?
Whether you inspect the vehicle as a habit, not only when something feels wrong.
A quick, ordered walk-around: tires, lights, mirrors, brakes, fluids and damage, with problems reported before leaving the lot.

I walk around the van: tires for pressure and cuts, all lights and signals, mirrors, wipers and any new dents, which I photograph. Inside I check brakes, horn, fuel or charge and warning lights. If something is unsafe, like a brake light out, I report it and don't take the van out until it's fixed or swapped.
How do you load your vehicle so the route runs smoothly?
How you organize the cargo area to save time and avoid damage.
Loading in stop order or by zones, heavy items low, fragile items on top, and the load secured so nothing shifts.

I load so the first stops are nearest the door and the last ones deep in the back, grouped by street. Heavy boxes go low and against the walls, fragile ones on top. I strap or brace the load so it doesn't slide on turns. At each stop I can grab the right package in seconds instead of digging.
What makes a good proof-of-delivery photo?
Your care in protecting the package, and yourself, from “not received” claims.
The package clearly visible with the door or house number in the frame, placed out of sight from the street and out of the weather.

The photo shows the package and enough of the door, mat or house number to prove the address. I put the package somewhere hidden from the street and dry, like behind a planter or inside a porch, and follow any delivery note. A blurry photo of a box on concrete proves nothing if the customer calls.
A package needs a signature and nobody answers the door. What do you do?
Whether you follow delivery rules instead of taking shortcuts.
Never signing for the customer or leaving it anyway; leaving a notice and following the company process for a reattempt or pickup.

I knock, ring and wait a reasonable moment, and call or text if the app allows it. If no one comes, I don't leave it and I never sign for them. I scan it as an attempt, leave a notice saying what happens next, like a reattempt or a pickup location, and bring the package back with me.
You pull up to a house and there's a loose dog in the yard. What do you do?
How you handle a common hazard without taking risks.
Staying in the vehicle, not entering a yard with a loose dog, contacting the customer or following policy, and flagging the address.

I stay in the van and honk or call the customer to see if they can secure the dog. If not, I don't go in. I mark the stop as unsafe to attempt with a note about the dog, and add an alert for the address so the next driver knows. If a dog comes at me, I keep the package between us and back away slowly. I never run.
How do you keep a food order safe and in good shape from the restaurant to the door?
Your handling of hot and cold food and of the customer's trust.
Insulated bags, hot and cold kept apart, drinks upright, sealed bags never opened, and going straight to the customer.

I use insulated bags, one for hot and one for cold, and a drink carrier so cups stay upright. I check the order number and that the bag is sealed, and I never open it. I go straight to the customer unless the app has batched orders. Food that spilled or sat too long gets reported, not handed over as if nothing happened.
How do you back up a van safely in a tight spot?
Whether you know the habits that prevent the most common delivery vehicle crashes.
Avoiding backing when possible, getting out to look first, using mirrors and camera, going slowly, and using a spotter when one is available.

First I try not to back at all: I plan to pull through, or back in when I arrive so I can pull forward when I leave. If I must back, I get out and walk around to check for kids, poles and low branches. Then I back slowly using both mirrors and the camera, and stop and look again if I'm unsure.
You're running an hour behind and dispatch is pushing you to finish. How do you handle it?
Whether you keep safety above speed under pressure.
No speeding or phone use while driving; telling dispatch early with a realistic estimate so they can reassign stops or warn customers.

I don't speed, run yellows or text at the wheel to catch up. At my next stop I tell dispatch where I am, how many stops are left and a real finish time. They can move some stops to another driver or tell customers. Then I tighten what I safely can: quicker scans, parking closer, fewer trips back to the van.
Two stops later, you realize you left a package at the wrong address. What do you do?
How you own and fix a mistake.
Going back to retrieve it if possible, delivering it correctly, and reporting honestly to dispatch rather than hiding it.

I tell dispatch right away and go back if it's close. I knock, explain politely, get the package back, then deliver it to the right house and update the scan. If no one is home at the wrong address, I report it with the address and photo so the company can follow up. Hiding it only turns a small error into a lost package claim.
You hit a parked car while making deliveries. It's minor. Walk me through what you do.
Whether you know your legal and company duties after a crash.
Stopping, checking for injuries, finding the owner or leaving contact details, calling police when required, documenting, and reporting to the company at once.

I stop, put on hazards and make sure nobody is hurt. I try to find the owner; if I can't, I leave a note with my name, contact details and what happened where it can be seen, and call police if local rules require it. I photograph both vehicles and the scene, then report it to my supervisor right away. I never just drive off, even for a scratch.

demand-generation.heading: Demand generation manager questions
qs: What is the difference between an MQL and an SQL?
Whether you know the basic stages of the lead funnel.
An MQL meets marketing's fit and interest bar; an SQL has been accepted by sales as worth working, using criteria both teams agreed on.

An MQL is a lead marketing judges ready for sales, based on fit, like company size and role, and on behavior, like a demo request or several content visits. It becomes an SQL when sales reviews it and agrees it is worth working. The handoff rules should be written down and agreed by both teams, or the numbers mean nothing.
How do you set up tracking so you know which campaign a lead came from?
Whether you can build the data that every later report depends on.
Consistent UTM tags, hidden form fields that pass them to the CRM, and campaign records set up and tested before launch, not after.

Before launch I write a naming rule for UTM tags, the labels added to links for source, medium and campaign, and I tag every link. Forms carry hidden fields that capture those values and pass them to a campaign record in the CRM. Then I test it: I submit a form myself from each link and check the record shows the right campaign.
When do you gate a piece of content behind a form, and when do you leave it open?
Your judgement on trading lead volume against reach.
Gate high-value, late-stage assets where the contact data is worth the friction; keep early education open to build reach and search traffic.

I gate things a buyer close to a decision would trade an email for: a benchmark report, an ROI calculator, a pricing guide. Blog posts and short guides stay open, because they build search traffic and trust. If I gate everything, I collect names of students and competitors, and sales stops trusting the leads. I also track how many gated leads ever become opportunities.
Walk me through how you would build a lead scoring model.
How you turn fit and behavior data into a rule sales will trust.
Starts from closed-won data, scores fit and engagement separately, adds decay and negative points, then checks the threshold against real conversion.

I start with the last year of closed deals and ask what they had in common: industry, size, job title, and actions like pricing page visits. I score fit and engagement separately, let activity points fade over time, and subtract for students or competitors. Then I back-test: do leads above the threshold convert better than those below? I review it with sales every quarter.
Your webinar had 400 sign-ups and 90 people showed up. What do you do next?
How you get value from a webinar after it ends.
Separate follow-up for attendees and no-shows, a recording sent fast, hot signals passed to sales, and a look at why the show rate was low.

Within a day, attendees get the recording, the slides and one clear next step; anyone who asked a question or stayed to the end goes to sales. The 310 no-shows get the recording too, since many sign up just for that. Then I compare the show rate with past webinars and look at reminder timing, the time slot and how far ahead people registered.
Walk me through working out how many leads you need for $2 million of new pipeline next quarter.
Whether you can plan backward from a revenue goal using funnel rates.
Works back from pipeline to opportunities to SQLs to MQLs using the company's own conversion rates, then checks timing and channel capacity.

I divide by average deal size. At $40,000 that is 50 opportunities. If half of SQLs become opportunities, I need 100 SQLs; if a quarter of MQLs become SQLs, 400 MQLs. I use our own rates, not industry averages, and check timing: leads from late in the quarter may not become pipeline in time. Then I split the 400 across channels by past cost and yield.
Last-touch attribution says paid search drives most deals, and the CEO wants to cut events. How do you respond?
How you read attribution models without being fooled by them.
Explains that last-touch credits only the final click, shows the earlier touches on won deals, and proposes a measured cut instead of a blind one.

Last-touch gives all the credit to the final step, and buyers often search our name right before a demo request because they met us somewhere else first. I would pull won deals and show every touch: how many met us at an event before they searched. I would not defend events blindly either. I would cut the weakest events first and watch branded search and pipeline.
Leads are up 40% this quarter, but pipeline is flat. Where do you look?
How you diagnose a gap between volume and real results.
Checks lead quality by source, conversion at each stage, follow-up speed and routing, before calling the quarter a success.

First I break the leads down by source. Often one channel, like a giveaway or a paid content deal, added cheap names that never convert. Then I check each stage: did MQL to SQL drop, or did sales not follow up? I look at routing and time to first contact too. I would report pipeline, not lead count, and move spend away from the source that inflated the number.
Someone wants to buy a contact list and email it next week. What do you say?
Whether you know the email rules and the risk to deliverability.
Knows CAN-SPAM basics: honest headers, a postal address, a working opt-out. Warns that bought lists hurt sender reputation and may bring in other privacy laws.

In the US, CAN-SPAM does not ban emailing a bought list, but each email needs honest sender and subject lines, our postal address and an unsubscribe we honor within 10 business days. The bigger risk is deliverability: bad addresses and spam traps can get our domain blocked for every email we send. If it has EU contacts, GDPR applies. I would put that money into ways people opt in.
How would you prove that a paid channel brings in pipeline we would not have gotten anyway?
Whether you can measure the real added impact of a channel, not just a correlation.
Proposes a holdout or regional test with a control group, agreed in advance, and judges it on pipeline rather than clicks.

I would run a holdout test. I pick matched regions or a random set of target accounts, turn the channel off for one group and keep it on for the other, long enough to cover our sales cycle. Then I compare pipeline per account between the groups. Any lift is what the channel really adds. I agree the success measure with finance before the test, so nobody argues about it after.

design-systems.heading: Design systems designer questions
qs: What is a design token, and why not just use hex values in components?
Whether you know the basic building block of a modern design system.
A named value stored once and shared by design and code, so one change reaches every product.

A token is a named design decision, like color-text-primary or space-4, stored in one place and exported to design files and code. Components point at the name, not the raw value. If the brand blue changes, we update one token instead of hunting through hundreds of screens, and design and code stay in sync.
How would you structure the color tokens for a product that serves two brands?
How you build token tiers so the system can grow without a rewrite.
Primitive tokens hold raw values, semantic tokens name the purpose and point to primitives, and each brand swaps the mapping, not the components.

I use two or three tiers. Primitives are the raw palette, like blue-600. Semantic tokens name the job, like color-action-primary, and point to a primitive. Components only use semantic tokens. For a second brand I keep the same semantic names and map them to that brand's palette, so every component works for both without changes.
Which states do you design for a button before you call it done?
Your eye for the details that make a component usable in real products.
Every interactive state, including keyboard focus, disabled and loading, plus long labels and icon-only use.

Default, hover, pressed, keyboard focus, disabled and loading, for each variant and size. Focus needs a visible ring that looks different from hover. I also test a very long label, a translated label that runs longer, and icon-only use, which needs an accessible name in code. Most bugs I see come from the states nobody drew.
A product team asks you to add a new component to the system. How do you decide?
Your judgement on what belongs in a shared library and what stays local.
A check against existing components, evidence of the same need in several teams, and the willingness to say not yet.

First I check whether an existing component or a new variant already solves it. Then I look for the same need in other products. If only one team needs it, it stays in their code for now. If two or three teams are building it separately, that is my signal to design it once, with their input, so we do not ship three versions.
What goes into the documentation page for a component?
Whether you write docs that prevent misuse, not just show pictures.
When to use it and when not to, anatomy, states, content rules, accessibility behavior and the matching code props.

I start with when to use it and when to use something else, because that prevents most misuse. Then anatomy, variants, states and spacing, do and don't examples from real screens, content rules like label length, keyboard and screen reader behavior, and the code props named the same as in the design file.
How do you release a change that will break existing screens?
How you manage change for the teams that depend on your work.
Treat it as a major version, announce early, deprecate before removing and give teams a clear migration guide.

We use semantic versioning: patch for fixes, minor for additions that break nothing, major for breaking changes. For a breaking change I announce it early, mark the old version deprecated but still working for a set period, write a migration guide with before and after examples, and hold office hours. Nobody should find out from a broken build.
We want to add dark mode. How would you add it to the existing system?
Whether you think in themes and tokens rather than repainting screens.
A second set of values for the same semantic tokens, surfaces designed for dark, and every contrast pair checked again.

If components use semantic tokens, dark mode is mostly a second set of values for the same names. I do not just invert colors: pure white on pure black is harsh and shadows barely show, so raised layers get lighter surfaces. Then I check every text and background pair again, at least 4.5 to 1 for normal text.
You find a team has detached your card component and rebuilt it. What do you do?
How you handle teams that work around the system.
Curiosity before policing: find the gap that made them detach, then fix the system or agree on an exception.

I ask them why before anything else. A detach usually means the component failed them: a missing variant, a rigid layout, a bug. Last time it was a card that could not hold an image on the left. We added that option in the next minor release, they switched back, and I added the case to our docs.
How do you tell whether a design system is actually working?
Whether you measure the system's value, not just its size.
Adoption and detach rates in design files and code, time saved for teams, less visual drift and regular feedback.

I track how many screens and code files use system components, and how often components get detached or overridden. I ask teams how long common tasks take with and without the system. I run a short survey each quarter and audit a few live flows for drift. A big library nobody uses is not working; a small one used everywhere is.
A spacing change you shipped broke layouts in three products. Walk me through what you do.
How you own a mistake and limit the damage for other teams.
Roll back or patch fast, tell the affected teams plainly, then find the gap in testing and close it.

First I stop the damage: revert or ship a patch that restores the old value, and tell the three teams what broke and when the fix lands. Then I find why it got through; often a layout change was labeled minor. I would add visual regression tests, which compare screenshots before and after, on key screens.

design-verification.heading: Design verification engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between code coverage and functional coverage?
Whether you know what each kind of coverage can and cannot prove.
Code coverage shows what RTL was exercised. Functional coverage shows whether the planned features and scenarios were hit. Neither proves the design is correct.

Code coverage is collected by the simulator: lines, branches, toggles and FSM states the RTL actually exercised. Functional coverage is what I write from the verification plan, covergroups and cover properties for the scenarios that matter. High code coverage with a hole in functional coverage means we ran the code but never tried a case the spec cares about.
Walk me through the main parts of a UVM testbench for one interface.
Your grasp of the standard testbench structure and why it is split up.
Sequencer, driver and monitor grouped in an agent, with scoreboard and coverage fed by the monitor, and a reason for each split.

A sequence produces transactions, the sequencer hands them to the driver, and the driver drives the pins through a virtual interface. The monitor only watches the pins and rebuilds transactions, which it sends through an analysis port to the scoreboard and coverage. Those three sit in an agent, which I can set to passive when real RTL drives that interface at a higher level.
Why use constrained random stimulus instead of only directed tests?
Whether you know when random stimulus finds bugs and when a directed test is the better tool.
Random reaches combinations nobody planned, coverage shows what it really hit, and directed tests still have a place for bring-up and rare corners.

Directed tests only check what I already imagined. Constrained random lets the solver pick legal values and orders I would not write by hand, like back-to-back writes to one address during a reset. Coverage then tells me what was really hit. I still write directed tests for first bring-up and for corners random rarely reaches.
What is the difference between blocking and nonblocking assignments, and why does it matter for verification?
Your understanding of simulation scheduling and race conditions.
Nonblocking for clocked logic so all flops update together, and awareness that mixing them causes races that depend on simulator order.

A blocking assignment updates the variable at once, so the next line sees the new value. A nonblocking assignment schedules the update for later in the same time step, so every flop samples the old values first. In RTL I use nonblocking for clocked logic. In the testbench I drive through clocking blocks so the design and testbench never race on the same edge.
Write an assertion, in words or in code, that a request must be granted within four cycles.
Whether you can turn a sentence from the spec into a property a tool can check.
A correct implication and delay range, reset handled, and a question back about the spec, such as whether a same-cycle grant counts.

I would write: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) req |-> ##[1:4] gnt); The implication checks only when req is high, the range allows the grant one to four clocks later, and disable iff turns the check off during reset. I would ask whether a same-cycle grant counts; if so the range becomes ##[0:4].
A test fails in the nightly regression but passes when you rerun it. What do you do?
How you debug a failure that looks random.
Reruns with the same seed and build, since a new seed is a new test, then separates testbench bugs from design bugs before filing.

First I rerun with the exact seed and the same build from the log, because a random test with a new seed is a different test. If it reproduces, I dump waves around the first error and trace back to the root cause. If the same seed does not reproduce, I look outside the seed: a testbench race, uninitialized memory or a build change.
What is a clock domain crossing problem, and why might simulation miss it?
Whether you know the limits of RTL simulation.
Plain RTL simulation does not model metastability, so you need synchronizers, structural CDC checks and safe schemes for multi-bit signals.

When a signal moves between unrelated clocks, the receiving flop can sample it mid-change and go metastable. Plain RTL simulation does not model that, so a missing synchronizer can pass every test. I rely on a static CDC check for structure, and I check that multi-bit buses use a handshake, gray-coded counters or an async FIFO, not a flop pair per bit.
When would you use formal verification instead of simulation?
Whether you can pick the right method for a given block.
Formal for small, control-heavy logic where exhaustive proof pays off; simulation for large datapaths and full systems where formal runs out of capacity.

Formal tools search every legal input sequence, so a full proof covers every case, not just the seeds I ran. That fits small control logic like arbiters, FIFO full and empty flags and deadlock checks. Big datapaths and full chips blow up the state space, so simulation stays the main tool there. I also run formal early on a new block, before the testbench exists.
Coverage is at 100% and the scoreboard is clean, but you are not sure the block is ready. What would worry you?
Your judgement about sign-off beyond the numbers.
Knows coverage only measures what was modeled: checkers can be weak, the plan can have holes, and the reference model can copy the designer's misreading.

Coverage only says we hit what we chose to measure. I would review the coverage model against the spec with the designer, look for weak checkers, like a scoreboard that ignores some fields, and confirm the reference model came from the spec, not the RTL. I would also plant a known bug in the design and make sure some test fails.
You find a bug the week before tape-out and the designer says it is a spec ambiguity, not a bug. How do you handle it?
How you handle disagreement and risk late in a project.
Brings evidence, gets the spec owner to decide, weighs fix options against schedule, and records the decision.

I would not settle it in a hallway. I write a short note with the waveform, the spec text and what software would see, and bring in the architect who owns the spec. If it is a bug, we weigh an RTL fix, a small late netlist change or a software workaround against the schedule. Either way the decision goes into the bug tracker and the spec gets clarified.

detection-engineer.heading: Detection engineer questions
qs: Why is a detection built on behavior usually worth more than one built on a file hash?
Whether you know which signals attackers can change cheaply.
Hashes and IP addresses are trivial for an attacker to change. Behavior costs them more to change, so behavior rules last longer.

A hash breaks the moment the attacker recompiles or changes one byte. An IP address changes when they rent a new server. What they do, like dumping credentials or creating a scheduled task to survive a reboot, is much harder to change. I use indicators for quick wins, but I put most of my effort into behavior rules.
How do you use MITRE ATT&CK when planning detections?
Whether you use the framework as a map, not a scorecard.
Maps rules to techniques to find gaps. Prioritizes the threats relevant to the company. Does not treat coverage counts as the goal.

I tag every rule with the techniques it covers. Then I compare that with the techniques used by groups that target our industry, which shows the real gaps. I'm careful with the heat map, though: one weak rule can make a technique look covered. I'd rather cover twenty techniques that matter well than two hundred badly.
Before you write a rule, how do you check that the logs you need actually exist?
Whether you start from the data, not from the idea.
Confirms the source is collected and parsed and has the needed fields. Checks it arrives from all relevant hosts and is kept long enough.

I find a real example of the event in our log platform. I check that the fields I need are parsed, not stuck in a raw text blob. Then I check coverage: is it coming from all servers or only half? A rule that needs command-line logging is useless on hosts where that setting is off, so I fix the collection first.
A new rule fires 400 times a day and almost all of it is benign. What do you do?
How you tune noise without blinding the rule.
Finds what the benign hits share and excludes narrowly, on fields attackers can't easily copy. Documents each exclusion and measures again. Does not just switch the rule off.

I'd pull a week of hits and group them. Usually a few sources make most of the noise, like a backup tool or a patching script. I exclude those narrowly, on the full path plus the parent process, not on a broad name an attacker could copy. Each exclusion gets a comment and a ticket. Then I watch the volume for a week.
How do you test that a detection really works?
Whether you prove a rule fires, and keep proving it.
Safely emulates the technique in a test environment and confirms the alert. Adds the case to automated regression tests.

I run the technique myself on a lab machine with a safe emulation script. I confirm the event arrives and the alert fires with useful details. I also run a few normal admin actions to check it stays quiet. Then I save the sample logs as a test case, so every change to the rule or the parser is checked automatically.
Walk me through how you would detect credential theft from LSASS memory on Windows.
Your hands-on knowledge of a common, high-value attack technique.
Watches for unusual processes opening lsass.exe with memory-read rights, for LSASS dump files, and for known tricks like rundll32 calling comsvcs.dll MiniDump.

LSASS holds login credentials in memory, so attackers try to read or dump it. I'd alert when a process opens lsass.exe with memory-read access and isn't on a short list of expected ones, like our security agent. I'd add rules for rundll32 calling comsvcs.dll with MiniDump, and for LSASS dump files being written. I'd also check that LSASS runs as a protected process.
An attacker renames a tool to get past your rule. How do you write rules that survive that?
Whether your rules rely on things an attacker cannot easily change.
Matches on the original file name stored inside the binary, the signer, command-line patterns and behavior, not on the file name on disk.

If my rule says the process name equals a tool name, a rename beats it. Windows binaries carry an original file name in their version info, and many endpoint logs record it, so I match on that. I also match on distinctive command-line arguments and on what the tool does, like the memory or network access it needs.
How would you notice that a log source has gone silent?
Whether you watch the health of your data, not only the attacks in it.
Tracks volume per source and per host against a normal baseline and alerts on drops. A silent source can look exactly like a safe network.

No alerts can mean no attacks or no data, and the two look the same. I track event counts per source and per host and alert when one drops far below normal or stops. I also watch for parsing failures after vendor updates. Attackers clear or stop logging too, so some silences deserve a security alert, not just an IT ticket.
The SOC asks for an alert on every admin login outside business hours. How do you respond?
Your judgement about what deserves an analyst's attention.
Weighs volume and accuracy first. Offers better options, such as extra context, risk scoring or a hunting query, instead of a noisy alert.

First I'd check the volume over the past month. If on-call admins log in at night all the time, a raw alert just trains people to ignore it. I'd combine it with other signals, like a new location or a first login to that server. The plain event could feed a risk score or a weekly hunt. I'd agree the plan with the SOC lead, not decide alone.
Tell me about a detection that missed something or broke. What did you change?
How you own a failure and fix the process, not just the rule.
Gives an honest account and the root cause. Fixes the rule and the process, so the same kind of gap gets caught next time.

A rule for suspicious scheduled tasks stopped firing after a parser update renamed a field. A red team exercise found the gap, not us. I fixed the field name, then added test cases with sample logs that run whenever parsers or rules change. I also added a check that warns us when a rule that usually fires weekly goes quiet for a month.

developer-advocate.heading: Developer relations and experience questions
qs: What makes a good getting-started guide?
Whether you know what a new developer needs in the first few minutes with a product.
A fast path to one real success, exact steps, expected output shown, and testing it on someone new.

I aim for one clear success in a few minutes: install, authenticate, make one call, see a real result. I list prerequisites up front, give exact commands that can be copied, and show the expected output after each step so readers know they are on track. Then I watch someone new follow it without my help and fix every place they stall.
What is the difference between a tutorial, a how-to guide, reference docs and an explanation?
Your grasp of the main types of documentation and why they should not be mixed.
Each type serves a different reader need: learning, doing a task, looking something up, understanding why.

A tutorial teaches a beginner by doing, with one path that is sure to work. A how-to guide solves a specific task for someone who knows the basics. Reference lists every parameter and error, plainly and completely. An explanation covers the why, like design choices. The common mistake is mixing them: a tutorial full of options loses the beginner.
Walk me through how you write sample code that developers will copy and paste.
Whether you treat sample code as code that will end up in production.
No hardcoded secrets, real error handling, pinned versions, short and readable, and tested automatically.

I assume it will be pasted into production. Keys come from environment variables, never hardcoded, and placeholders are obvious. I handle errors the way I would want them handled, pin dependency versions, keep it short enough to read on one screen, and run it in CI so it keeps working. A comment marks anything simplified for the demo.
How do you prepare a live coding demo for a conference talk?
How you plan for what goes wrong on stage.
Rehearsal on the real setup, an offline fallback, a recorded backup, readable fonts, and a calm switch if it breaks.

I script it and rehearse on the same laptop I will present from. I pre-install dependencies, keep a local version in case the Wi-Fi fails, and make the font big enough for the back row. I have a recording of the demo ready and git checkpoints so I can jump ahead if a step breaks. If it fails, I say so calmly and switch.
A developer posts angrily in a public forum that our SDK is broken. What do you do?
How you handle public criticism and turn it into a fix.
A fast, non-defensive public reply, reproducing the problem, owning it, a tracked fix, and closing the loop.

I reply publicly and quickly without defending: thank them, ask for the version, code and error. I try to reproduce it. If it is our bug, I say so, file it with the repro, link the issue and post a workaround. When it is fixed I come back to the same thread. If a doc gap caused it, I fix the doc too, since others hit it silently.
How would you find out where new developers get stuck with our product?
Whether you know practical methods to find friction in the developer experience.
Doing the journey as a new user and logging every snag, plus data and support tickets, then prioritizing fixes.

I go through onboarding as a new user on a clean machine, with a timer, and keep a friction log: every confusion, error and search, with what I expected and what happened. I add support tickets and drop-off data, sort issues by severity and walk the owning teams through the top few. Last time, a hidden API key screen caused most of the delay.
Your tutorials and samples keep breaking as the API changes. How do you stop them going stale?
How you keep content accurate over time rather than fixing it after complaints.
Treat docs as code: tested samples in CI, code in docs pulled from tested files, versions shown, docs part of release.

I treat docs and samples as code. Samples live in a repo and run in CI against the current API, and code in the docs is pulled from those tested files, not pasted. Dependency updates open pull requests automatically. I show the version each tutorial uses. And updating docs is part of the definition of done for any release that changes behavior.
The product team plans a breaking API change. How do you speak up for developers?
Your judgement on protecting users while still letting the product move forward.
Know who is affected, push for a non-breaking option, and if not, a deprecation period, migration guide and early notice.

First I find out who it breaks, using usage data. Then I ask whether a versioned or additive change would work. If the break is needed, I push for a deprecation period announced early, warnings in the SDK, a migration guide with before-and-after code, and a changelog entry. I also contact the most affected users directly before they discover it.
Marketing wants you to publish a comparison with a competitor that you think is misleading. What do you do?
Whether you protect your credibility with developers when there is pressure to oversell.
Refuse to publish unsupported claims, explain why, offer an honest alternative, and escalate if needed.

I would not publish a claim I cannot back up; developers test claims, and trust is the whole job. I would show marketing where the comparison is unfair and offer an honest version: a benchmark with the method published so anyone can rerun it, or a post on our strengths without the dig. If they insist, I take it to my manager.
How do you show that developer relations work is paying off?
Whether you can link your work to outcomes the business cares about, not just attention.
Outcome metrics like activation and time to first call, views treated as signals only, plus product feedback that shipped.

I tie it to developer outcomes: share of sign-ups that make a first successful API call, time to that call, and fewer support tickets on topics we covered. Views and stars are signals, not goals. I also track feedback I brought to product and which items shipped. I agree the targets with my manager at the start of each quarter.

devops-engineer.heading: DevOps engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between a blue-green and a canary deployment?
Whether you know the main ways to release without downtime.
Blue-green switches all traffic between two full environments; canary sends a small share first and grows it while watching metrics.

Blue-green runs two full copies of production. I deploy to the idle one, test it, then switch all traffic over, and switching back is fast. A canary sends the new version a small slice of traffic, say 5%, and I compare its error rate and latency with the old version before I raise the share. Canary needs less spare hardware but takes longer.
What is the difference between a liveness probe and a readiness probe?
Your grasp of how an orchestrator decides a container is healthy.
A failed liveness check restarts the container; a failed readiness check only stops traffic to it. Liveness should not depend on outside services.

Readiness answers "can you take traffic now?" If it fails, the pod is taken out of the load balancer but keeps running. Liveness answers "are you stuck?" If it fails, the container is restarted. I keep liveness simple and never make it check the database, or one database blip restarts every pod at once.
Why would you not deploy an image tagged "latest" to production?
Whether you understand reproducible, traceable releases.
Tags can move, so "latest" does not say what is running. Pin a version or the image digest so a rollback is exact.

A tag is just a pointer, and "latest" moves with every build. Two nodes can pull different code under the same name, and I cannot roll back to a known good version. I tag each image with the commit it was built from, and for production I pin the digest, a hash of the image content, which can never point to anything else.
What is the Terraform state file, and how do you handle it on a team?
Your understanding of how infrastructure-as-code tools track real resources.
State maps code to real resources. It belongs in a shared remote backend with locking and access control, never in Git, since it can hold secrets.

The state file records which real resource each block of code manages, with its IDs and settings. Without it the tool would try to create everything again. On a team I keep it in a remote backend with locking, so two applies cannot run at once. It is encrypted with tight access, because state can hold passwords in plain text, and it never goes into Git.
A pod is stuck in CrashLoopBackOff after a deploy. Walk me through what you check.
How you troubleshoot a failing container step by step.
Events and exit reason first, then logs from the crashed run, then config, memory limits and probes; roll back first if users are affected.

First I describe the pod to see its events and the last exit reason. OOMKilled means the memory limit is too low. Then I read logs from the previous, crashed container, not the new one. Common causes are a missing secret or environment variable, a wrong start command, or a liveness probe that fires before the app is ready. If users are affected, I roll back first and debug after.
Our pipeline takes 40 minutes and developers are unhappy. How would you speed it up?
How you find and remove the slow parts of a build.
Measure each stage before changing anything, then cache, parallelize and skip work that has not changed, without dropping the tests that matter.

I would first time each stage over a week of runs to see where the minutes go. Usual wins: cache dependencies, copy the dependency file before the source code in the Dockerfile so that layer is reused, split tests across parallel runners, and skip jobs a change does not touch. I would not drop tests to save time; slow end-to-end tests can move after merge if that is safe.
A few flaky tests keep failing the build and people just click retry. What do you do?
Your judgement on keeping a pipeline trustworthy.
Flakes are tracked and fixed, not ignored: quarantine with an owner and a deadline, and find the root cause, since blind retries hide real bugs.

Retrying teaches everyone to ignore red builds, and then a real failure slips through. I track which tests both fail and pass on the same commit, move the worst to a quarantine job that does not block merges, and open a ticket with an owner for each. Causes are usually timing, shared test data or test order. A test that stays in quarantine gets fixed or deleted.
During an incident someone changed a firewall rule by hand in the cloud console. What do you do afterwards?
How you handle drift between code and real infrastructure.
No blame: run a plan to see the drift, decide whether the change should stay, then put it in code or revert it so code is the source of truth again.

Hand fixes during an incident are fine; leaving them is not. I run a plan to see exactly what differs from the code. If the change was right, I add it to the code through a normal review, so the next apply does not undo it. If it was a guess, I revert it. Then I set up a scheduled plan that alerts on drift, so we hear about the next one quickly.
Our service has an SLO of 99.9% and the error budget for the month is used up. What changes?
Whether you can use reliability targets to make release decisions.
Knows a 99.9% target leaves 0.1% for failure, about 43 minutes of downtime in 30 days, and that a spent budget shifts work to reliability.

99.9% over 30 days leaves about 43 minutes of failure. Once that is spent, the policy we agreed with product kicks in: we pause risky releases, ship only fixes and reliability work, and look at what burned the budget. If one bad deploy did it, I would push for better canaries or faster rollback. The rule was set in advance, so it is not a fight each time.
Your plan output says it will destroy and recreate the production database. What do you do?
How you react to a dangerous infrastructure change before it happens.
Stop, find the rename or setting forcing replacement, and fix the code or state so nothing is destroyed; then add guards like deletion protection.

I do not apply. I find the line in the plan that forces replacement. Usually it is a renamed resource or a setting that cannot change in place, such as the instance name. For a rename I add a moved block so the tool knows it is the same database. For a setting, I revert it or plan a real migration. Then I add prevent_destroy and turn on deletion protection.

digital-marketing.heading: Digital marketing specialist questions
qs: What is the difference between SEO and paid search, and when do you lean on each?
Whether you understand the two sides of search and their trade-offs.
Paid is fast and controllable but stops when spend stops. SEO is slow to build but keeps working. Using both together is normal.

Paid search buys a spot in the ads above the results. Traffic starts the day you launch and stops the day you pause. SEO earns the unpaid listings through content, site health and links, which takes months but keeps paying off. For a launch I lean on paid. For steady demand I build SEO and use paid to test which keywords convert.
How do you tag links so you know which campaign sent the traffic?
Whether you set up tracking before launch, not after.
UTM parameters on every link you control, with one naming convention the whole team follows.

I add UTM parameters, the tags at the end of a URL, to every link we control: source, medium and campaign, plus content when I test two versions. A shared sheet holds the naming rules, all lower case, so "Email" and "email" don't split into two rows. I never tag links within our own site, because that overwrites the visitor's original source.
What does a commercial email need to comply with US law?
Your knowledge of the CAN-SPAM rules for marketing email.
Honest sender and subject lines, a valid postal address, and a clear opt-out that works and is honored within 10 business days.

Under CAN-SPAM, the from line and subject can't mislead, the message must be identifiable as an ad, and it needs a valid physical postal address. Every email needs a clear way to opt out, and opt-outs must be honored within 10 business days. The rules still apply to us when an agency sends on our behalf.
In search ads, what is Quality Score and how would you raise it?
Whether you know that ad auctions reward relevance, not just higher bids.
Expected click-through rate, ad relevance and landing page experience. Tighter ad groups and matching landing pages improve it.

It is a 1 to 10 rating per keyword, based on expected click-through rate, how well the ad matches the search, and the landing page experience. The same factors feed the auction, so improving them usually lowers my cost per click. I split broad ad groups into tight themes, write ads that echo the search terms, and send clicks to a fast page that answers that exact search.
Open rates on your newsletter dropped by half in two weeks. How do you find out why?
How you diagnose email deliverability before blaming the content.
Checks inbox placement first: authentication, bounces, complaints and results by mailbox provider. Only then looks at list or content changes.

A drop that sharp usually means we are landing in spam, not that readers got bored. I check bounce and complaint rates, and whether SPF, DKIM and DMARC, the records that prove our mail is really from us, still pass after any domain or tool change. If opens collapsed at one mailbox provider, that is the clue. Then I look at subject lines or a recent import of old contacts.
Your manager wants to buy a list of 50,000 email addresses to grow fast. What do you say?
Your judgement when a shortcut puts the company's sender reputation at risk.
Explains the deliverability and legal risks plainly and offers a faster honest route to real subscribers.

I would push back. People on a bought list never asked to hear from us, so complaints and bounces climb. These lists often contain spam traps, addresses that exist to catch senders, which can get our domain blocked. Most email platforms ban purchased lists. I would propose a free guide promoted with paid social, and show the cost per real subscriber.
A campaign reports a return on ad spend of 4. Is that good?
Whether you connect ad metrics to profit, not just revenue.
It depends on margin. ROAS counts revenue, so a low-margin product can lose money at 4. Targets are set against break-even.

It depends on margin. ROAS of 4 means $4 of revenue for every $1 of ads. If gross margin is 20%, that $4 leaves 80 cents of profit, so we lose 20 cents per ad dollar. Break-even ROAS is 1 divided by the margin, here 5. I set targets above that, and accept lower only if repeat purchases make a new customer worth more over time.
Organic search traffic fell 30% overnight. Walk me through what you check.
How you work through an SEO drop in a sensible order.
Rules out a tracking error first, then technical causes on the site, then lost rankings by page and any search algorithm update.

First I check it is real: did our analytics tag break, or do search console clicks show the same drop? If clicks fell too, I look at recent releases: a noindex tag telling search engines to skip pages, a robots.txt block, or changed URLs without redirects. Then I compare pages and queries before and after, and check whether an algorithm update was announced.
The ad platforms together report 900 sales last month, but the store recorded 600. How do you explain that?
Your understanding of attribution and why platforms over-count.
Each platform claims any sale it touched, by its own rules, sometimes after a view only. Reporting starts from the store's real total.

Each platform counts a sale if its ad was in the path, using its own time windows, sometimes after just a view. A buyer who saw a social ad and then clicked a search ad gets counted by both. I report 600 as the truth, split credit with one analytics tool and one model, and run holdout tests, where a group sees no ads, to learn what a channel really adds.
You find that a tracking change double-counted conversions for the last three weeks. What do you do?
How you own and fix a data error that already shaped decisions.
Fixes the tag, tells stakeholders quickly with corrected figures, and reviews the budget and automated bidding decisions made on bad data.

I fix the tag and confirm with a test order that one purchase fires one conversion. Then I tell my manager that day, with corrected numbers from the order system. Automated bidding learned from inflated results, so I check what it changed and exclude that period's data where the platform allows. Finally I add a weekly check of ad conversions against real orders.

distributed-systems-engineer.heading: Distributed systems engineer questions
qs: What does the CAP theorem actually say?
Whether you know the theorem beyond the slogan.
It applies during a network partition: you choose between consistent answers and answering every request. Without a partition, the main tradeoff is latency.

When the network splits a cluster, a node that cannot reach the others has two options. It can refuse or wait, which keeps data consistent. Or it can answer with what it has, which keeps it available but maybe stale. You cannot have both during the split. "Pick two of three" is misleading, because partitions are not optional.
Why are five-node clusters common, and what does a fourth node add to a three-node cluster?
Your grasp of quorums in consensus systems.
A majority must agree. Three nodes tolerate one failure, five tolerate two, and four still tolerate only one while needing more votes.

Consensus systems like Raft need a majority to elect a leader and commit writes. With three nodes the majority is two, so one can fail. With four the majority is three, so still only one can fail, and there are more machines that can break. Five needs three votes and survives two failures, which covers one planned upgrade plus one surprise.
Two servers log events with timestamps. Why can't you use those timestamps to say which happened first?
Whether you know the limits of time across machines.
Clocks drift and can jump even with NTP, so ordering needs causality: logical clocks, version numbers, or a single sequencer.

Each machine has its own clock. NTP keeps them close, but they can still be off by milliseconds or more and can jump backwards after a correction. So an event stamped later may have happened first. If order matters, I use a logical clock like a Lamport counter, version numbers on the data, or one writer that assigns sequence numbers.
A queue promises at-least-once delivery. What does that mean for the code that consumes it?
How you handle duplicate messages and the myth of free exactly-once.
Expect the same message more than once and make processing safe to repeat, for example by recording the message ID in the same transaction as the change.

It means a message can arrive twice, for example if my consumer crashes after doing the work but before acknowledging it. So I make the handler safe to repeat. Each message carries a unique ID, and I store that ID in the same database transaction as the change. A repeat finds the ID and is skipped.
A user saves a change, refreshes the page and sees the old value. What is likely going on, and how do you fix it?
Whether you recognise replication lag and the read-your-writes problem.
The read hit a replica that is behind the primary. Fixes: read from the primary just after a write, or wait for a replica that has caught up to that write.

The write went to the primary, but the read went to a replica that has not received it yet. Replication is often asynchronous, so a lag of a second or more is normal under load. I would send that user's reads to the primary for a short window after a write, or keep the write's log position in the session and read only from a replica that has reached it.
A downstream service comes back after an outage and falls over again within a minute. What do you suspect?
How you spot retry storms and load that multiplies during recovery.
Retries and queued requests all arrive at once. Exponential backoff with jitter, retry limits and load shedding let the service recover.

Every client has been retrying and queues have built up, so the moment it is back it gets several times its normal traffic. I would check that clients use exponential backoff with random jitter so they do not retry in step, cap retries with a budget, and have the service reject work it cannot handle quickly instead of letting every request time out.
Why would you use consistent hashing instead of hash modulo the number of servers?
Your knowledge of spreading data across nodes.
With modulo, changing the node count moves almost every key. Consistent hashing moves only about one share in N, and virtual nodes even out the load.

With hash mod N, going from 10 to 11 servers changes the home of most keys, so a cache goes cold or a store has to move nearly all its data. With consistent hashing, servers and keys sit on a ring and a new server takes only the keys next to it, roughly one share in N. I give each server many points on the ring so the load spreads evenly.
Why is a node that is slow harder to deal with than one that has crashed?
Whether you understand partial failures and failure detection.
A timeout cannot tell slow from dead. Slow nodes pass simple health checks while hurting latency, so detection must use real latency and accept some false alarms.

A crashed node stops answering and health checks remove it. A slow node, say with a failing disk, still passes a simple ping but makes every request it touches slow. I check health with real work, watch latency per node, and send a backup request to another node when one is slow, accepting that we will sometimes remove a healthy node.
A node holding a lock pauses 30 seconds for garbage collection, its lease expires, and another node takes the lock. What goes wrong, and how do you prevent it?
How you reason about leases, process pauses and two nodes acting as owner.
The old holder wakes up, still believes it owns the lock and writes. Fencing tokens fix it: a rising number that storage checks, rejecting older ones.

The first node wakes up unaware that time passed and writes as if it still holds the lock, so two writers corrupt the data. Checking the lease before writing does not help, since the pause can come right after the check. I have the lock service hand out a number that rises with each grant, send it with every write, and have storage reject any lower number.
An order service must save an order and publish an "order created" event. How do you make sure one never happens without the other?
Your approach to consistency between a database and a message broker.
No dual write. A transactional outbox stores the event in the same database transaction, and a separate process publishes it at least once.

If I save and then publish, a crash in between loses the event; publish first and I may announce an order that never saved. So I write the order and an event row into an outbox table in one transaction. A separate process reads the outbox, publishes, and marks rows as sent. It can publish twice, so consumers skip event IDs they have seen.

driver-chauffeur.heading: Driver and chauffeur questions
qs: Walk me through your pre-trip inspection.
Whether you inspect the vehicle as a fixed routine, not a quick glance.
A set order covering tires, lights, brakes, fluids, mirrors and safety gear, with defects written up and not driven on.

I walk around the vehicle the same way every time: tires and lug nuts, lights and signals, mirrors, wipers, leaks underneath. Inside I check the horn, brakes, gauges, seat belts and the emergency kit. Anything wrong goes on the inspection report, and if it affects safety the vehicle stays parked until it is fixed.
How much following distance do you keep, and when do you change it?
Your grasp of space cushions and how conditions change them.
A time-based rule of at least three seconds, more for rain, night, heavy loads or larger vehicles.

I use time, not car lengths. I pick a sign, and when the car ahead passes it I count; I want at least three seconds before I reach it. In rain, fog, at night or in a heavier vehicle I add more, because it takes longer to stop. If someone cuts in, I drop back and rebuild the gap.
You are picking up an executive at the airport and the flight shows a delay. What do you do?
How you plan a pickup and keep the passenger and dispatch informed.
Tracks the flight, adjusts arrival time, agrees on a meeting point, and tells dispatch and the client of changes.

I track the flight number, not the scheduled time, so I arrive ahead of the new landing time. I text the passenger my name, car and where I will meet them. I tell dispatch about the delay so later rides can be moved. If the passenger does not appear, I call, follow our wait policy and log every attempt.
A passenger is late for a meeting and asks you to speed. How do you handle it?
Whether you keep control of safety while staying polite with a client.
A calm, respectful no, plus something useful: a better route, an updated arrival time, or calling ahead.

I would say kindly that I will get them there as fast as I safely and legally can. Then I offer what I can do: check traffic for a faster route, give an honest arrival time and suggest they message the meeting. Most passengers relax once they know the plan. Speeding risks them, me and the license I need to do the job.
You are driving a bus with passengers and come to a railroad crossing. What do you do?
Your knowledge of the federal rule for passenger vehicles at rail crossings.
Stops between 15 and 50 feet from the tracks, looks and listens both ways, then crosses without shifting gears.

I stop no closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet from the nearest rail. I turn off the radio and fans, open the window or door to listen, and look both ways. When it is clear and there is room on the far side for the whole bus, I cross in a gear that will not need changing until I am over the tracks.
Your GPS sends your high-roof van toward an underpass with no posted height you can see. What do you do?
Whether you know your vehicle's height and refuse to guess on clearance.
Knows the vehicle height, uses routing set for it, stops short when unsure, and reroutes instead of trying.

I know my van's height, it is on a label on the dash. If I cannot confirm the clearance, I do not go under. I stop somewhere safe, check the route on a map or with dispatch and take another way. Next time I set the GPS to the vehicle's size so it avoids low bridges. A detour costs minutes; a roof strike can hurt people.
Your vehicle starts to hydroplane on a wet highway. What do you do?
Your reaction to a loss of traction, which must be learned before it happens.
Eases off the gas, keeps the wheel steady, avoids hard braking or sharp turns, then slows for conditions.

I take my foot off the gas and hold the wheel straight, steering gently only where I want to go. I do not slam the brakes or jerk the wheel. If I must brake and the vehicle has ABS, I press firmly and steadily and let it work. To prevent it, I slow down in rain, keep cruise control off and watch my tires' tread.
You took a cold medicine that says it may cause drowsiness, and your shift starts in an hour. What do you do?
Whether you treat your own fitness to drive as part of the job.
Does not drive impaired, tells the supervisor early, and knows legal medicine can still make driving unsafe.

I would call my supervisor right away and say I cannot drive safely today. Legal medicine can slow reactions just like being tired, and many employers' rules forbid driving on it. Calling early gives them time to cover my route. Next time I would ask a pharmacist for something that does not cause drowsiness before a work day.
Tell me about a near miss or mistake behind the wheel and what you changed afterward.
Whether you own errors and turn them into a lasting habit.
A real example, told without excuses, and a specific habit that came out of it.

Backing a shuttle at a hotel, I relied on mirrors and tapped a low post I could not see. No one was hurt, and I reported it the same hour. Since then I get out and look before every backing move in a tight spot, and I ask for a spotter when there is one. I also park where I can pull forward to leave when I can.
You have a minor collision in traffic with a client in the back seat. Walk me through the next 30 minutes.
How you handle an incident: safety, the law, the passenger and the report.
Stops, protects the scene, checks for injuries, calls 911 if needed, swaps info, documents, informs dispatch.

I stop, turn on hazards and check that my passenger and the other driver are okay. If anyone is hurt or the road is blocked, I call 911. If it is safe and allowed, I move out of traffic. I exchange license and insurance details, take photos and do not argue about fault. I call dispatch to send another car for my client, then write my report the same day.

ecommerce.heading: E-commerce and merchandising questions
qs: How do you calculate conversion rate, and what can that number hide?
Whether you know the core metric of the shop and its limits.
A clear formula with a stated base, plus awareness that a blended average can mislead when the traffic mix changes.

Orders divided by sessions, times 100, for the same period. I always say whether the base is sessions or users, because they give different numbers. A blended rate can hide a lot: if mobile traffic grows and mobile converts lower, the total drops even when nothing broke. So I split it by device, channel, and new versus returning visitors.
What is the difference between margin and markup?
Your grasp of the basic math behind every pricing decision.
Margin divides profit by price, markup divides it by cost, with a worked example and the cost of confusing them.

Both start from price minus cost. Margin divides that by the price; markup divides it by the cost. An item that costs us $40 and sells for $100 has a 60% margin and a 150% markup. Mixing them up is expensive: if someone asks for a 50% margin and you add 50% to cost, you end up at about a 33% margin.
What is sell-through rate, and how do you use it?
Whether you can read inventory performance and act on it in time.
Units sold over units received for a period, compared to plan, used early to drive placement or markdown decisions.

It is units sold divided by units received over a period, usually tracked weekly. If we took in 500 units and sold 200 in four weeks, that is 40%. I compare it to the plan for the season. Slow sell-through early tells me to give the item better placement, fix its page, or plan a markdown before the season ends, not after.
A product page gets plenty of traffic but very few sales. Walk me through what you check.
How you diagnose a product page that attracts visitors but does not sell.
An orderly check: stock and sizes, price, shipping cost, images, reviews, then whether the traffic source matches the product.

First the basics: is it in stock in the common sizes, is the price in line with similar items, and is the shipping cost shown early. Then the images: do they show scale and detail. Then reviews and answers to common questions. Last, where the traffic comes from; an ad promising something the page does not deliver looks like a page problem.
What do you do with the report of site searches that returned zero results?
