Whether you treat onsite search data as a source of demand and fixes.
Sorts by volume, fixes wording and tagging gaps, and passes real unmet demand to buying with numbers.

It is a list of what customers want and cannot find. I sort it by volume. Some are wording gaps, like shoppers typing sweatshirt when we call it a crewneck, and I fix those with synonyms. Some are products we carry but tagged poorly. The rest are items we do not sell, and I send those to buying with the search counts as evidence of demand.
Your bestseller will sell out in about ten days and the restock is five weeks away. What do you do?
How you protect customers and spend when a key item runs short.
Confirms the date, stops paying for traffic to an empty page, adjusts placement, captures demand and offers alternatives.

I confirm the restock date with the buyer first. Then I cut paid ads pointing to the item so we do not pay for clicks on an empty page, and move it out of the top homepage spots. When it sells out, I keep the page live with a back-in-stock signup and show the closest alternatives. I would not run any promotion that speeds up the sellout.
How would you set a free shipping threshold?
How you set a pricing lever while keeping an eye on profit.
Starts from how order values are spread and the real shipping cost, tests the change, and judges it on profit, not order value alone.

I look at how orders are spread by value, not just the average, and at our real shipping cost per order. A threshold a little above where many orders cluster nudges people to add one item. I test it against the current setting and judge it on gross profit per visitor, because order value can rise while margin falls if we pay shipping on too many orders.
On a marketplace, another seller lists the same product 15% below your price. Do you match?
Your judgement on price competition when margins and brand rules are at stake.
No automatic match: checks the offer is real, margin after fees, brand price policies, and other ways to compete.

First I check whether the offer is real: in stock, same condition, a seller with a solid rating. Then I work out my margin after marketplace fees and shipping at the lower price. If the brand has a minimum advertised price policy, I follow it. Sometimes I match for a short time; sometimes I hold price, compete on delivery speed, and accept fewer sales on that item.
Conversion rate dropped 30% overnight. What do you do first?
How you work through a sudden drop without guessing.
Rules out tracking first, then site breakage by segment, then traffic mix, and raises the alarm fast if checkout is broken.

First I check the data: did a tracking tag change with last night's release, and do orders in the back end show the same drop. If orders really fell, I split by device, browser and payment method; a checkout broken on one phone type shows up fast. I place a test order myself. If the site works, I look at traffic mix, like a new campaign sending visitors who were never going to buy.
A $99 item has been live at $9.90 for three hours and orders keep coming in. What do you do?
How you contain a costly error and treat customers fairly.
Stops the error everywhere first, sizes the damage, brings options to a manager, tells customers fast, and fixes the process.

I fix the price at once and check that it has reached every channel, including marketplace feeds. Then I count the orders and the cost and bring my manager options: honor all, honor some, or cancel under our terms of sale. If we cancel, customers get a quick apology and a full refund. Afterward I add a rule that flags any price change above a set percentage.

education.heading: Teaching and education questions
qs: What makes a learning objective well written?
Whether you can write objectives that can actually be assessed.
It names what the learner will do, with an observable verb, under what conditions and to what standard. It avoids “understand” or “know”.

It says what the learner will be able to do, in a verb I can observe. “Understand fractions” is vague. “Add two fractions with unlike denominators and simplify the result” is not. If I cannot picture the task that would prove it, the objective is not done yet, and the assessment will drift.
What do you look for in a good multiple-choice question?
Your skill at writing test items that measure the skill, not test-taking tricks.
One clear stem, one correct answer, and plausible wrong options built from real mistakes. No clues such as a longer correct option.

The stem should pose the whole problem, so a learner could answer before seeing the options. Wrong options should come from real mistakes I have seen, like dropping a minus sign. I keep options similar in length, avoid “all of the above” and double negatives, and check that only one answer can be defended.
How do you build a rubric for a written assignment?
How you make grading consistent and useful to the learner.
Criteria tied to the objectives, level descriptions that are observable, and a test run on sample work before release.

I start from the objectives, usually three to five criteria, like argument, use of evidence and clarity. For each level I describe what the work looks like, not just “good” or “poor”. Then a colleague and I score a few real samples. Where we disagree, the wording is unclear, and I fix it before students see it.
How do you make an online course accessible to learners with disabilities?
Whether you build accessibility in from the start instead of patching it later.
Knows the WCAG guidelines and the basics: captions, transcripts, alt text, contrast, real headings, keyboard use, and testing with a screen reader.

I work to the WCAG guidelines, usually level AA. Videos get accurate captions, not raw auto-captions, plus a transcript. Images get alt text that says what matters, documents use real headings, and I never rely on color alone. Before launch I go through the course using only a keyboard, and again with a screen reader.
A subject matter expert hands you 80 slides and wants a 20-minute module. What do you do?
How you cut content down to what learners need to do.
Starts from what the learner must do after the module, separates need-to-know from nice-to-know, and keeps the expert on side.

I ask the expert what people should do differently after the module and which mistakes cost the most today. Then I sort the slides into need-to-know and nice-to-know. The core becomes practice and examples. The rest goes into a reference guide, so the expert sees nothing was thrown away. I review the draft with them before building.
The course data shows most learners stop in module 3. How do you find out why?
How you use learning platform data to diagnose a problem.
Finds exactly where in the module people stop, checks the item itself, and talks to learners before changing anything.

First I find the exact item where they leave: a long video, a hard quiz, a broken link. I check time on page and quiz attempts for that spot, and test it myself on a phone. Then I ask five or six learners who stopped. Once it was a 25-minute video. Split into short parts with a check after each, completion went up.
You find out a quiz went live with a wrong answer key and 200 learners have taken it. What do you do?
How you handle your own mistake when grades are at stake.
Fix the key, regrade everyone, check what the grade affected, tell learners plainly and quickly, and prevent a repeat.

I fix the key and regrade every attempt, then confirm the gradebook updated, since regrading is not always automatic. I check whether anyone was blocked from the next module or a certificate. Then I send learners a short note on what happened and that grades are fixed. Last, I add a second review of every answer key to our checklist.
How do you design online assessments when learners can look things up or use AI tools?
Whether you can protect assessment integrity without relying only on surveillance.
Tasks that need the learner's own reasoning or context, large question banks for recall, evidence of process, and clear rules on which tools are allowed.

I accept that recall questions are easy to look up, so I keep them low stakes and draw them from a large bank. For graded work I use tasks tied to the learner's own situation, ask for drafts or a short recorded explanation, and say clearly which tools are allowed. If someone can explain their work live, I trust that more than any detector.
A sales team wants to use one district's real student data in a demo for another district. What do you say?
Whether you know student privacy rules bind the people who build education products.
Knows FERPA protects student education records and that a vendor may use them only for the purpose the school authorized. Offers invented data instead.

I say no and offer an alternative. Under FERPA, records a district shares with us are for the service it contracted, not for showing to other customers. Many states add their own student privacy laws on top. I would build a demo account with invented names and realistic scores, so the demo looks just as good and no real student's records are exposed.
Learners rate a course highly, but most fail the final assessment. What do you check?
Your grasp of alignment between objectives, practice and assessment.
Checks that objectives, practice and the final test ask for the same skill at the same level, and that the test items are sound, before blaming learners.

High ratings mean they liked it, not that they learned it. I line up each objective with the activities and the exam items. Often the lessons ask learners to recognize an answer and the exam asks them to produce one. I also run an item analysis: if strong learners miss a question as often as weak ones, the item is the problem. Then I fix the practice, the test, or both.

ehs.heading: Environment, health and safety questions
qs: What is the hierarchy of controls, and how do you use it?
Whether you know the basic order for reducing a hazard.
The five levels in the right order, with PPE as the last line of defense, and a real example of going higher.

From most to least effective: eliminate the hazard, substitute something safer, engineer it out, use administrative controls like procedures and job rotation, then PPE. On a noisy grinding line I would look at a quieter process or an enclosure before handing out earplugs, because PPE only works if it is worn right every time.
How do you tell a first aid case from a recordable injury on the OSHA 300 log?
Your working knowledge of OSHA recordkeeping rules.
Knows first aid is a defined list, names what makes a case recordable, and the seven-day deadline to enter it.

First aid is on OSHA's list: bandages, cleaning a wound, cold packs, over-the-counter medicine at normal strength, flushing an eye. Stitches, a prescription, days away or restricted duty make it recordable. If a worker gets four stitches, it goes on the 300 log within seven calendar days, even if he is back at work that afternoon.
A new degreaser arrives at the plant without a safety data sheet. What do you do?
How you apply hazard communication rules in daily work.
No use until the SDS is in hand, then a check of hazards, labels and storage, and training for the users.

It stays sealed and out of use until I have the SDS from the supplier. Then I read the hazard, PPE and storage sections, check the label matches, add it to our chemical inventory and brief the people who will use it. If it is more hazardous than what it replaces, I ask whether we need it at all.
Walk me through locking out a machine for a maintenance job.
Whether you know the lockout/tagout steps well enough to audit them.
Notify, shut down, isolate all energy, personal locks, release stored energy, and verify zero energy before work.

I tell the operators, shut the machine down normally, then isolate every energy source in the written procedure: electrical, air, hydraulic, gravity. Each worker puts on a personal lock and tag. We bleed stored pressure and block parts that could drop. Then we try the start button to verify zero energy and return it to off before work begins.
Before entry into a permit-required confined space, in what order do you test the air, and why?
Your knowledge of confined space entry, where mistakes are often fatal.
Oxygen, then flammables, then toxics, with the reason, testing at several levels, and no rescue entry by the attendant.

Oxygen first, because many combustible gas sensors need enough oxygen to read correctly. Then flammable gases, then toxics like hydrogen sulfide or carbon monoxide. I test at the top, middle and bottom since gases layer, and keep monitoring during the job. The attendant stays outside and never goes in to attempt a rescue.
An investigation of a hand injury comes back with "employee was not careful" as the root cause. What do you do with it?
How you dig past blame to the real cause of an incident.
Rejects carelessness as a root cause and asks why the unsafe act made sense, then fixes the system.

I send it back. Carelessness is where the questions start. Why was his hand near the blade? Was the guard hard to use, was the job behind, had anyone shown him the push stick? In one case like this, operators cleared a jammed infeed by hand every shift. We fixed the jam and the hand injuries on that line stopped.
A production manager wants to run a machine with its guard removed to make a shipment. How do you handle it?
Whether you hold a safety line under pressure while staying useful to operations.
A firm no to running unguarded, an offer to solve the real problem, and calm escalation if needed.

I say no to running unguarded, calmly, and offer help instead. I ask what the guard is slowing down, get maintenance to look at a better guard design, and help find time elsewhere in the schedule. If he still insists, we go to the plant manager together. I would rather explain a late shipment than an amputation.
An employee is admitted to the hospital after a fall at work. What do you owe OSHA, and by when?
Your knowledge of severe injury reporting deadlines.
Inpatient hospitalization within 24 hours, death within 8, the observation-only exception, and recording it too.

If he is admitted as an inpatient for treatment, I report it to OSHA within 24 hours of learning about it; a death is 8 hours, and amputations or loss of an eye are 24 hours. A stay only for observation or tests does not count. I also check our state plan's rules, record it on the 300 log and start the investigation.
A forklift punctures a drum of hydraulic oil near a storm drain. What happens in the first hour?
How you handle an environmental release, not only a safety event.
People safe, source stopped, drain protected first, proper cleanup and disposal, and reporting per the spill plan.

People safe first, then stop the source: upright or plug the drum. Next I cover the drain or berm around it before cleaning the floor, then absorb and bag the oil for proper disposal. If any oil reached the drain or a waterway, I follow our spill plan, which includes calling the National Response Center and the state agency. Then I document everything.
An OSHA compliance officer arrives unannounced at the front gate. Walk me through the visit.
Whether you can manage an inspection professionally and protect the company's record.
Checks credentials, joins the opening conference, escorts throughout, documents the same things, and follows up.

I check credentials, call the plant manager and ask the reason for the visit in the opening conference. I walk with the inspector the whole time, take the same photos and notes, and provide the documents asked for. Employees may speak privately. If we fix a hazard on the spot, I note it. Afterward I track every closing conference item to closure.

electrical-engineer.heading: Electrical engineer questions
qs: Why does a decoupling capacitor need to sit close to the chip's power pin?
Whether you understand the physics behind a basic layout rule.
Names trace inductance and fast current bursts, and says the goal is a small current loop.

The chip pulls current in fast bursts, and the trace to the capacitor has inductance that resists fast changes in current. A long path means the rail dips right at the pin. I put a small ceramic cap at the power pin with short vias to the ground plane, so the loop is tiny and the cap feeds each burst locally.
How do you choose between a linear regulator and a switching regulator?
Your grasp of the basic power tradeoff: efficiency against noise.
Knows a linear part turns the voltage drop into heat, does the math, and weighs ripple against efficiency.

A linear regulator turns the drop into heat: roughly input minus output voltage, times the load current. Going from 12 V to 3.3 V at half an amp wastes over 4 W, too much for a small part. A buck converter is far more efficient but adds ripple. For small drops or a quiet analog rail I use an LDO; for big drops, a buck, sometimes with an LDO after it.
How do you size a PCB trace that carries several amps?
Whether you size copper from a method, not by habit.
Starts from current and allowed temperature rise, uses IPC-2152 data, and also checks voltage drop and vias.

I start from the current and the temperature rise I can accept, then use the IPC-2152 charts or a calculator built on them. Copper weight matters, and inner and outer layers are treated differently. On high-current paths I also check voltage drop and use pours and several vias, because one small via can become the hot spot.
You probe a switching node and see large ringing spikes. How do you know they are real?
How you separate a real signal problem from a measurement artifact.
Suspects the long ground lead first, shortens the probe loop, and compares the result.

The long ground clip makes a loop with inductance. On a fast edge it rings with the probe capacitance and picks up magnetic field, so I can see spikes that are not on the board. I swap the clip for the short spring tip and measure right across the node and its local ground. If the ringing shrinks a lot, it was the probe.
Why is it dangerous to clip a standard oscilloscope ground to a circuit powered straight from the wall?
Whether you know a common lab hazard and the safe way around it.
Explains the scope ground is earthed, names differential probes or an isolation transformer, and never defeats the safety ground.

The scope's ground clip is tied to earth through its power cord. If I clip it to a mains-referenced node, I short that node to earth, which can destroy the board or the probe and can hurt someone. I use a high-voltage differential probe, or power the unit through an isolation transformer. I never lift the scope's safety ground to make it float.
Walk me through powering up a brand-new prototype board for the first time.
Your bring-up discipline and how you protect the first boards.
Checks for shorts and orientation before power, limits current, and brings rails up one at a time.

Before power I meter each rail to ground for shorts and check the orientation of diodes, polarized caps and ICs. Then I use a bench supply with a low current limit and watch the current as I raise the voltage. If it hits the limit, I find the hot part with a thermal camera. I confirm each rail before enabling the next stage.
For the switch in a buck converter, how do you trade on-resistance against gate charge?
Your understanding of where losses come from in power electronics.
Splits conduction and switching loss, links gate charge to switching speed and frequency, and checks voltage margin.

Conduction loss is the current squared times on-resistance, scaled by the share of time the switch is on. Switching loss grows with frequency and with how long each transition takes, which depends on gate charge. Lower on-resistance usually means more gate charge. At high frequency, a part with a bit more resistance but less gate charge can run cooler overall.
Your product works on the bench but fails a radiated emissions pre-scan at one frequency. What do you do?
How you trace and fix an emissions failure step by step.
Identifies the frequency source, locates it with a near-field probe, changes one thing at a time and rescans.

First I work out what the frequency is: often a harmonic of a clock or the switching frequency. Then I use a near-field probe to find where it comes from and check whether a cable is acting as the antenna. Fixes go from cheap to costly: a ferrite or slower edges, then a broken return path, then a board change. I rescan after each change.
After a production run, you find two pins swapped on a regulator footprint you created. What do you do?
How you own a costly mistake and stop it from happening again.
Reports fast with facts, offers a rework path, fixes the root cause in the process, not just the part.

I would tell my lead the same day with the facts: which part, how many boards, and whether rework is possible. In a similar case we mounted the part on a small adapter board for the first lot and fixed the footprint in the next revision. I also added a pin-by-pin check against the datasheet to our library review.
A resistor divider scales a 24 V signal into a 3.3 V ADC input. How do you do the worst-case analysis?
Whether you design for every tolerance, not just the typical value.
Lists all error sources, uses true worst case for limits and protection, and checks the highest input against the pin rating.

I list every error: resistor tolerance, drift over temperature, the ADC reference tolerance, and the ADC offset and gain error. I push each to the extreme that hurts most and check two things: accuracy stays in spec, and the highest possible input never drives the pin past its rating. Root-sum-square is fine for typical accuracy, not for the limits.

electrical-technician.heading: Electrical and electronics technician questions
qs: How do you measure voltage and current with a multimeter, and what is the common mistake?
Whether you know basic meter use and the risk of leaving a lead in the amps jack.
Voltage in parallel, current in series with the lead in the amps jack, and moving the lead back afterward.

Voltage is measured across the part, in parallel, with the red lead in the volts jack. For current the meter must be in the path, so I open the circuit and put it in series with the lead in the amps jack. Then I move the lead back right away. Touching a voltage source with the lead still in the amps jack is a short through the meter and can blow its fuse.
What does a good solder joint look like, and what makes you reject one?
Your eye for joint quality on the bench.
Good wetting and a smooth concave fillet, knowing lead-free can look duller, and naming the common defects.

The solder wets both the pad and the lead and flows into a smooth, concave fillet, so I can still see the shape of the lead. Tin-lead joints are bright; lead-free joints can look duller and a bit grainy, which is normal. I reject cold or lumpy joints, solder balled on the pad, bridges, holes, and too little or too much solder.
How do you protect parts from static when you work at the bench?
Whether ESD control is a habit for you.
Grounded strap and mat, a strap check each shift, shielding bags, and knowing static damage can be invisible.

I wear a wrist strap connected to the bench ground point and test it at the start of each shift. Parts stay in shielding bags until they go on the grounded mat. I keep plastic cups and foam off the bench and hold boards by the edges. A discharge I cannot even feel can weaken a part that then fails later in the field.
Which parts on a board must go in a certain direction, and how do you check them?
Your knowledge of polarity markings, including the ones that catch people out.
Names the polarized parts, reads their markings correctly, and knows the tantalum band is the positive side.

Electrolytic and tantalum capacitors, diodes, LEDs, ICs and many connectors. On an aluminum electrolytic the stripe marks negative, but on a tantalum the band marks positive. A diode band is the cathode. ICs have a dot or notch for pin 1 that I match to the silkscreen. A reversed electrolytic can bulge or vent, so I check every polarized part before I solder.
How do you know a crimped terminal is good?
Whether you make crimps that hold, not just crimps that look done.
Right tool and die for the terminal and wire size, correct strip length, visual checks and a pull test.

I use the tool and die the terminal maker lists for that wire size and strip to the length on the spec. After crimping, the conductor shows just past the barrel, no strands stick out, and the insulation grip holds the insulation, not bare wire. I pull test samples, and I do not add solder to a crimp unless the drawing asks for it.
The build calls for 18 AWG wire and the bin only has 20 AWG. Can you use it?
Whether you understand wire gauge and stay away from unapproved substitutions.
Knows a higher AWG number is a thinner wire with less current capacity, and gets a written change instead of swapping.

No, not on my own. A higher AWG number is a thinner wire, so 20 AWG carries less current, drops more voltage over the same run, and can run hot. I would stop that harness, tell my lead, and wait for the right wire or a written change from engineering. Even a thicker wire needs approval, since it may not fit the terminal.
You must replace a part on a lead-free board and your station only has tin-lead solder. What do you do?
How you handle solder alloys and rework rules.
Does not mix alloys, gets the right solder, and adjusts heat, flux and tip for lead-free work.

I get lead-free solder before I start. Mixing alloys gives a joint nobody has qualified, and a board built to be lead-free, for example to meet RoHS rules for export, would no longer comply. Lead-free solder melts hotter, so I set the iron for it, use fresh flux, and keep a separate tip for lead-free work.
A new board pulls far more current than it should on first power-up. Walk me through what you do.
Your method for finding a short without destroying the board.
Current-limited supply, power-off checks first, then locating the hot spot safely; names the usual causes.

I cut power and switch to a bench supply with the current limit set low. With power off I look for solder bridges, reversed parts and wrong values, then measure resistance between the rails. If it is a hard short, I power it at the limit and find the part that heats up with a thermal camera or freeze spray. Often it is a reversed capacitor or a bridge under an IC.
You learn a part went in backwards on 20 boards you built, and some are already in test. What do you do?
How you own a mistake and contain it before it spreads.
Stops, reports at once, holds every affected board, reworks and retests, and fixes the cause.

I stop building and tell my lead right away, with the serial numbers. All 20 boards are tagged and held, including the ones in test, so nobody powers them again. I rework each one per the rework instruction and retest it fully, since the reversed part may have damaged others. Then I find the cause, such as an unclear marking, and fix it.
Why is the ground clip on a scope probe dangerous on a mains-powered circuit, and how do you measure safely?
Whether you know the hidden earth path in a bench scope.
The clip is tied to earth; clipping it to a non-earth point is a short. Uses a differential probe or isolation transformer.

On a normal bench scope the probe ground clip is connected to earth through the power cord. If I clip it to a point that is not at earth, like the primary side of an offline supply, I make a short that can destroy the probe and the board. I use a differential probe, or power the unit through an isolation transformer. I never defeat the scope's ground pin.

electrician.heading: Electrician questions
qs: What is the difference between the grounded conductor and the grounding conductor?
Whether you know the basic code terms and the job each wire does.
The neutral carries current in normal use. The equipment grounding conductor carries current only during a fault, so the breaker can trip.

The grounded conductor is the neutral, usually white or gray, and it carries current whenever the load runs. The grounding conductor is the bare or green wire. It should carry no current in normal use. It bonds the metal parts and gives fault current a low-resistance path back, so the breaker trips fast.
What does a GFCI protect against, and what does an AFCI protect against?
Your understanding of what each protective device actually detects.
A GFCI compares hot and neutral current to protect people from shock. An AFCI looks for arcing to prevent fires. Some locations need both.

A GFCI measures the current going out on the hot and coming back on the neutral. If a few milliamps go missing, likely through a person, it trips. An AFCI watches for the pattern of an arc, like a loose connection or a nail through a cable, which can start a fire. They protect against different things, so I use a dual-function device where the code calls for both.
Walk me through how you verify a circuit is dead before you touch it.
Whether you test for absence of voltage properly instead of trusting a breaker label.
Lockout and tag, then a live-dead-live test with a properly rated meter, checking every combination of conductors.

I find the right disconnect, turn it off, and put my own lock and tag on it. Then I prove my meter on a known live source, test between every phase and from each phase to neutral and ground, then prove the meter again. Panel labels are often wrong, so I never trust them alone. A non-contact tester is only a first check.
You connect a new three-phase motor and it spins the wrong way. What do you do?
Your hands-on knowledge of three-phase motors.
Lock out, then swap any two of the three supply leads. Ideally check rotation before the motor is coupled to its load.

I shut it off and lock it out, then swap any two of the three supply leads at the motor or the starter, and note it on the drawing. That reverses the phase sequence. On equipment that reverse rotation can damage, like some pumps, I check with a phase rotation meter or bump the motor uncoupled before the first real start.
You need to pull nine current-carrying conductors through one conduit. What changes?
Whether you know that bundled conductors lose ampacity and how that affects wire size.
Mentions the ampacity adjustment for more than three current-carrying conductors, plus conduit fill and ambient temperature correction.

Once a raceway has more than three current-carrying conductors, I have to reduce their ampacity using the adjustment factors in the code, because they can't shed heat as well. With nine, the reduction is large enough that I may need a bigger wire size or a second conduit. I also check conduit fill and the ambient temperature correction before I order wire.
A customer wants a 20-amp circuit run to a shop 200 feet from the panel. What do you think about?
Whether you account for voltage drop on long runs, not only ampacity.
Calculates voltage drop from load, length and wire size, upsizes conductors as needed, and knows the ground wire must be upsized in proportion.

On a run that long, voltage drop matters more than ampacity. I calculate it from the load, the length and the wire resistance. The code's informational notes suggest about 3 percent on a branch circuit, so I'd likely go up a size or two. If I upsize the hot and neutral, the code also requires upsizing the ground wire in proportion.
A homeowner asks you to swap a 20-amp breaker for a 30 because it keeps tripping. The circuit is 12-gauge copper. What do you say?
Whether you hold to the code when a customer pushes for a quick fix.
Refuses, explains that the breaker protects the wire, and offers to find out why it trips: overload, a fault, or a bad breaker.

I tell them no, and why: the breaker is there to protect the wire, and 12-gauge copper on a 30-amp breaker can overheat inside the wall before anything trips. Then I find the cause. I measure the load, look for a short or ground fault, and check the breaker itself. Often the real fix is a dedicated circuit for a heater or an appliance.
On a remodel you find the neutral and ground bonded together in a subpanel. Why is that a problem, and what do you fix?
Whether you know where neutral and ground may be joined and what goes wrong otherwise.
Bonding belongs at the service disconnect only. In a subpanel it puts neutral current on grounds and metal parts. Separate the bars and remove the bonding screw or strap.

Neutral and ground should be joined only at the service equipment. Bonded in a subpanel, normal neutral current splits onto the ground wires, conduit and metal boxes, so parts people touch carry current. I move the grounds to a ground bar bonded to the enclosure, keep the neutrals on an isolated bar, and remove the bonding screw or strap.
An inspector fails your rough-in for something you believe meets code. How do you handle it?
How you work with the inspector when you disagree.
Stays professional, asks for the exact code section, checks the adopted edition and local amendments, then fixes it or uses the proper appeal process.

I ask politely which code section they're citing and write it down. Then I check it myself, including the edition and any local amendments, since the inspector enforces what the local jurisdiction adopted. If I was wrong, I fix it and learn from it. If I still disagree, I bring the code text back calmly, and use the formal appeal process if needed.
A customer says lights get very bright in one room and dim in another when big appliances run, and a TV just died. What do you suspect?
Whether you can recognize an open neutral and treat it as urgent.
Recognizes a loose or open neutral, tests each leg to neutral under load, and treats it as urgent, calling the utility if the fault is on their side.

That points to a loose or open neutral, at the service or on a shared circuit. Without a solid neutral, 120-volt loads on the two legs end up in series across 240 volts, so one side runs high and the other low. I measure each leg to neutral under load and check the neutral lugs in the panel. If the fault is at the meter or service drop, I call the utility. It's a fire risk.

embedded-engineer.heading: Embedded engineer questions
qs: What should and should not happen inside an interrupt service routine?
Whether you keep interrupt handlers short and safe.
Do the minimum and hand the rest to a task. No blocking, printing or heap use, and only interrupt-safe RTOS calls.

As little as possible. I read the hardware, clear the flag, put the data in a buffer or queue and signal a task, then return. No blocking calls, no printf, no malloc, no long loops. With an RTOS, I only call its interrupt-safe functions. A long ISR delays every other interrupt and makes timing bugs very hard to find.
How do you choose between polling, interrupts and DMA to move data from a peripheral?
How you match the method to the data rate and the CPU time you can spare.
A clear rule based on how often data arrives and how much of it, with an example for each method.

It depends on the rate and the CPU budget. A button checked every 10 ms can be polled in the main loop. A UART receiving a few bytes now and then suits one interrupt per byte. For a fast ADC stream or an SPI display, I use DMA into a double buffer, so the CPU only wakes up when half the buffer is full and can process one half while the other fills.
Why do many firmware teams avoid malloc and free?
Your grasp of memory limits on devices that run for months without a restart.
Fragmentation and unpredictable timing, plus a real alternative such as static buffers or fixed-size pools.

The heap can fragment over weeks of uptime, so an allocation that worked on day one fails on day forty. Allocation time is also not predictable, which hurts real-time tasks. I size buffers statically or use fixed-size pools set up at startup, so running out of memory shows up at build or boot, not in the field. Coding rules like MISRA C ban the heap for these reasons.
How do you use a watchdog timer so it actually catches a hang?
Whether you know the common watchdog mistakes.
The watchdog is fed only when the whole system is proven healthy, never from a timer interrupt, and watchdog resets are logged.

I never feed it from a timer interrupt, because that interrupt keeps firing even when the main code is stuck. In an RTOS, each important task sets a check-in bit, and one monitor feeds the watchdog only when all of them have checked in. At boot I read the reset cause register and log watchdog resets, so a hidden hang shows up in the data.
Your I2C sensor stops responding after a few hours. Walk me through how you find out why.
How you debug a bus problem with real tools, not guesses.
Capture the bus when it fails, know the stuck-SDA case and its recovery, and check pull-ups and error handling.

I put a logic analyzer on the bus and let it run until it fails. Often SDA is held low because the sensor was cut off mid-byte by a reset or noise. My driver detects that and toggles SCL up to nine times until SDA is released, then sends a STOP. I also check the pull-up values and rise times with a scope, and I log every bus error.
How do you tell whether a bug is in the hardware or in the firmware?
Your judgement when the fault could be on either side of the pin.
Experiments that separate the two: other boards, older firmware, and measuring the real signal instead of trusting the debugger.

I look for a test that splits them. If the same firmware fails on one board and not on others, I suspect that board: solder, a part, the power supply. I measure the signal at the pin with a scope instead of trusting what the code thinks it wrote. I also flash the last firmware that worked. If it fails too, something in the hardware or environment changed.
Your code works in the debug build but fails once optimization is turned on. What do you suspect?
Whether you look for your own bug before blaming the compiler.
Missing volatile, uninitialized variables, undefined behavior, or a race exposed by faster code, and the tools to find them.

Usually it is my bug, not the compiler's. I suspect a missing volatile on a flag shared with an interrupt, a variable read before it is set, or undefined behavior such as signed overflow or casting a byte buffer to a struct pointer. I turn on all warnings and run the logic on a host build with sanitizers. Faster code can also expose a race that was always there.
How would you design a firmware update so a power cut in the middle cannot brick the device?
How you design for failure in devices nobody can reach to fix by hand.
Two image slots, verification before switching, a boot confirmation with automatic rollback, and a bootloader that stays fixed.

I keep two image slots. The new image downloads into the inactive slot while the old one keeps running. The bootloader checks its signature and CRC before switching. The new image must confirm that it booted and connected; if it resets before that, the bootloader goes back to the old slot. I keep the bootloader small and avoid updating it in the field.

employee-experience.heading: Employee experience manager questions
qs: What is the employee journey, and which moments in it matter most?
Whether you see employee experience as a whole path, not a list of separate perks.
Names the stages from offer to exit and picks the moments that shape how people feel and whether they stay.

It is the path from accepting the offer to leaving: preboarding, the first day, the first 90 days, growth, life events, and exit. The moments I watch most are the first week, the first manager change, a promotion or a missed one, and coming back from leave. People judge the company by how those moments go.
How is eNPS calculated, and what does it not tell you?
Your grasp of a common engagement measure and its limits.
The correct formula, plus the point that one score says how people feel but not why.

People rate from 0 to 10 how likely they are to recommend us as a place to work. Nine and ten are promoters, zero to six are detractors. eNPS is the percent of promoters minus the percent of detractors, so it runs from -100 to +100. It tells me the mood, not the cause, so I pair it with open comments and a few driver questions.
Walk me through how you would design the first 90 days for a new hire.
How you build onboarding that gets people productive and connected, not just processed.
Covers preboarding, a clear first week, manager check-ins and a buddy, with a way to check that it works.

Before day one, the laptop, accounts and a welcome note from the manager are ready. Week one has a written plan, a buddy, and one real task. The manager holds check-ins at 30, 60 and 90 days with clear goals. I send a short survey at 30 and 90 days and compare the answers with early turnover to see where the plan breaks.
How do you protect people's anonymity in an engagement survey?
Whether you know the safeguards that make people answer honestly.
A minimum group size for reports, care with comments and demographic cuts, and honest wording about anonymous versus confidential.

Results only show for groups above a minimum size, often five, and small teams roll up a level. I limit demographic filters so no one can narrow a group down to one person, and I check comments for identifying details. I also say plainly whether the survey is anonymous, meaning no one can link answers, or confidential, meaning only the vendor can.
Survey participation fell from 78% to 52% this year. What do you look into?
How you diagnose a trust or fatigue problem behind a falling response rate.
Checks where the drop happened and whether people saw action on the last survey, before pushing reminders.

First I see if the drop is everywhere or in a few teams. A local drop often points to a manager or a recent change. A broad one usually means survey fatigue or that people saw nothing change last time. I would ask a few people directly, show what we did with last year's results, and cut extra pulse surveys before adding reminders.
One team's scores dropped sharply, and their manager is upset and defensive. What do you do?
How you turn bad results into action without blaming or exposing anyone.
Calms the manager, frames the data as a starting point, and helps them hold a safe team conversation and pick a few actions.

I meet the manager alone first and let them react. Then we look at which questions moved and what changed this year, like a reorg or lost headcount. I help them share the results with the team, ask what is behind the numbers, and pick two actions with dates. I make clear we will never try to find out who said what.
An anonymous survey comment says a named manager harasses people on the team. What do you do?
Whether you know when feedback becomes a matter that must be escalated and handled properly.
Treats it as a possible complaint, escalates it under policy, does not try to unmask the writer, and points people to safe channels.

I treat it as a possible complaint, not just feedback. The company now knows about it and should look into it, so I pass the comment to HR or employee relations under our policy the same day. I do not use the survey tool to find out who wrote it. In the next update I remind everyone of the confidential reporting channels and that retaliation is not allowed.
How do you plan a company event so that everyone can take part?
Your practical sense for inclusion in events and culture programs.
Thinks about timing, place, food, alcohol, access and remote staff, and asks people instead of guessing.

I avoid major religious holidays and late evenings that rule out parents. The venue has to be accessible, and the RSVP form asks about dietary and access needs. Drinking is never the main activity, and good alcohol-free drinks are always there. Remote staff get their own version, not a camera pointed at a room. Afterward I ask who did not come and why.
Leadership cuts your budget in half. How do you decide what to keep?
Your judgement on priorities and on what truly drives the employee experience.
Protects programs tied to retention and core moments, drops low-impact extras, and explains the choices openly.

I rank each program by reach, cost per person and its link to outcomes like early turnover or survey scores. Onboarding and manager support usually stay because they touch every employee. Big parties and swag usually go first. I would tell staff what changed and why, and keep a few low-cost things, like peer recognition, so the cut does not feel like we stopped caring.
Tell me about a program you ran that did not work. What did you learn?
Whether you measure your own programs honestly and change course.
A real failure with numbers, a clear reason found, and a change made, without blaming others.

I launched a mentoring program with 120 pairs. By month three, only about 30 still met. Exit comments showed the matches were random and nobody had a goal. I stopped it, then relaunched with people choosing mentors from short profiles and a six-month end date. About two thirds of pairs finished. I learned to pilot small and check in at week four, not month three.

employment-counsel.heading: Employment lawyer questions
qs: What does at-will employment mean, and where does it stop?
Whether you know the default rule of US employment and its main exceptions.
Either side may end the job for any lawful reason; limits are bias and retaliation laws, contracts, public policy, and Montana's good-cause rule.

It means the employer or the employee can end the job at any time, for any reason or none, as long as the reason is not illegal. The limits are discrimination and retaliation laws, written contracts or handbook promises that act as a contract, and public policy, like firing someone for serving on a jury. Montana is different: after a probation period, it requires good cause.
How do you decide whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor?
Your grasp of misclassification risk under the different legal tests.
Knowing that the IRS, federal wage law and the states use different tests, and that the label in the contract does not decide.

I look at the real relationship, not the contract title. The IRS asks about control, money and the relationship. Federal wage law asks whether the worker is really in business for themselves. Some states, like California, use the stricter ABC test, where the work must be outside the usual course of the hiring business. One worker can pass one test and fail another.
A client says its staff are exempt from overtime because they are salaried. Is that enough?
Whether you know how overtime exemptions actually work.
No: a salary alone exempts no one; the role must also meet a salary level and a duties test, and state rules can be stricter.

No. Under federal wage law, most white-collar exemptions need three things: pay on a salary basis, at or above a minimum salary level, and duties that fit an exemption, such as executive, administrative or professional. Job titles do not decide it. I also check state law, because states like California and New York set higher salary levels.
An employee with a disability asks to work from home. Her manager says the job requires being in the office. How do you advise?
How you handle the interactive process under the ADA.
Starting a good-faith dialogue, testing which duties are truly essential, and documenting each step, rather than a quick yes or no.

I tell the manager not to refuse yet. Under the ADA we must talk with her about her limits and what would help. Then I ask which duties truly need her in the office, and why. If remote work would cause undue hardship, we can offer another effective option, like a changed schedule. She does not get to pick, but it must work. I make sure each step is written down.
A manager wants to fire an employee two weeks after she filed a harassment complaint. What do you advise?
Whether you spot retaliation risk and know how to test the decision.
Seeing that close timing can support a retaliation claim, and checking whether the reason was documented before the complaint and applied to others.

I ask him to pause. Retaliation is the most common basis alleged in EEOC charges, and close timing is strong evidence of it. I want the performance record from before the complaint, who decided and when, and how others with the same issues were treated. If the reason is solid and documented, we can go ahead with care. If it showed up only after the complaint, we wait.
A client in Texas wants new hires in California to sign the same non-compete as everyone else. What do you say?
Your knowledge of how state law limits restrictive covenants.
California voids most employee non-competes, even ones signed elsewhere, and other states set their own limits, so one form does not fit all.

I tell them not to use it for California staff. California law makes most employee non-competes void, and since 2024 employers may not use or try to enforce them, even if signed in another state. Other states vary: some ban them below an income level or limit their length. For California I would rely on a confidentiality agreement and trade secret law instead.
A client plans to cut 80 jobs at one site next month. What do you check first?
Whether you know the notice rules and the bias risk in a layoff.
Federal WARN and state mini-WARN notice rules, plus a review of who was selected for any pattern by age, race or sex.

First, notice. The federal WARN Act can require 60 days' notice from employers with 100 or more workers, and 80 layoffs at one site can count if they are at least a third of the staff there. Some states, like New York, are stricter. A month may be too short. Then I review how people were chosen and check the numbers by age, race and sex before names are final.
The company will rely on its harassment investigation as a defense. Should its own lawyer run it?
How you weigh privilege against using an investigation as evidence.
Seeing that relying on the investigation can waive privilege and turn the investigator into a witness, so a separate investigator is often wiser.

Usually not. If we plan to show we responded promptly and properly, the investigation itself becomes evidence, and privilege over it may be waived. The lawyer who ran it could become a witness and be unable to try the case. I would use a separate trained investigator and keep our legal advice in its own privileged channel.
A US client wants to dismiss an employee in Germany the way it would in Texas. What do you tell them?
Whether you know that at-will employment rarely exists outside the US.
Most countries require a valid reason, a set procedure and notice; the client needs local counsel before acting, not after.

That it cannot. Germany has no at-will rule. After six months, in a business with more than ten staff, a dismissal needs a valid reason linked to conduct, capability or business needs. Notice must be in writing with a handwritten signature. If there is a works council, it must be heard first, or the dismissal is void. I would bring in local counsel before anyone talks to the employee.
You find that a severance agreement signed by 30 laid-off staff left out the required age disclosures. What do you do?
How you handle a defective release and own a mistake.
Knowing the age-claim waiver likely fails for workers 40 and over, that keeping the money does not cure it, and fixing it openly.

I tell the client right away. In a group layoff, a valid waiver of age claims for workers 40 and over needs the ages and job titles of who was and was not selected, plus 45 days to review. Without them, that waiver likely fails, and the Supreme Court has held that keeping the payment does not fix it. I would offer a new, compliant agreement with something extra.

endpoint-engineer.heading: Endpoint and device management engineer questions
qs: What is zero-touch enrollment, and what has to be in place before it works?
Whether you understand how a new device reaches a user already set up.
The device is tied to the company before it ships, assigned to the management server, and enrolls itself on first boot with no IT hands.

The device is registered to our company account with the OS vendor, usually by the reseller at purchase, and assigned to our device management server. When the user turns it on and joins Wi-Fi, it checks in, enrolls, and pulls apps and settings. The user signs in with a work account, and the enrollment cannot be skipped or removed.
How do you manage a company-owned phone differently from an employee's own phone?
Your grasp of ownership, privacy and how much control is fair.
Full control on company devices; on personal ones, only a separate work space, with no view of personal data and wipe of work data only.

On a company phone I can enforce settings, push any app and wipe the whole device. On a personal phone I only manage a separate work profile or work apps. I cannot see photos or personal apps, and when someone leaves I remove just the work data. I explain this to staff up front so they trust enrolling.
Where do the disk encryption recovery keys for your laptops live, and how do you know they are there?
Whether you treat encryption as something you can prove, not assume.
Keys escrowed to the management system, access limited and logged, a report of devices with no key, and rotation after a key is used.

Every laptop must turn on full-disk encryption at enrollment and send its recovery key to our management server. Only a few admins can view keys, and each view is logged. I run a weekly report of encrypted devices with no stored key and fix those first. After a key is given to a user, the policy rotates it.
How do you roll out operating system updates to a few thousand devices?
How you balance security speed against the risk of breaking people's work.
Rings: IT first, then a pilot group, then everyone, with set deadlines, watching for problems at each step.

I use rings. IT devices get the update on day one, a pilot group of about 5% from different teams a few days later, then everyone else. Users get a grace period and then a forced install with warnings. Between rings I check crash reports and help desk tickets. For an actively exploited flaw I shorten the whole schedule.
A user calls: they cannot open email on their laptop, and the system says the device is not compliant. Explain what is happening.
Your understanding of how device health controls access to company apps.
Compliance rules mark the device, the sign-in system checks that status, and the fix is on the device, not the account.

Our management tool checks each device against rules such as encryption on, OS up to date and a screen lock set. If one fails, the device is marked not compliant and the sign-in service blocks company apps. I look at which rule failed, often a pending update, walk the user through fixing it, and access returns once the device checks in again.
A senior developer asks for permanent local admin rights on their laptop. What do you do?
Your judgement between security rules and getting people's work done.
Find the real need, offer time-limited, logged elevation or self-service installs, and avoid permanent admin by default.

I ask what they need admin for. Usually it is installing tools, so I add those to our self-service catalog. For the rest we offer admin rights that last a short time after a request, and every elevation is logged. Permanent admin means malware also runs as admin, so I only grant it with a manager's and security's sign-off.
An employee reports their laptop was stolen from a car an hour ago. Walk me through your response.
How you act fast and in the right order when a device is lost.
Cut access first, then lock or wipe, confirm encryption, and record everything for security and any report.

First I revoke the user's sessions and reset their password, since that works even if the laptop never goes online. Then I send a lock and a wipe; they queue until the device connects. I confirm the disk was encrypted, which protects data meanwhile. I log the serial number, tell security, and help the user file a police report.
What has to happen to a laptop when its user leaves the company?
Whether you close every loose end so the device is safe and reusable.
Access removed, data kept if needed, device wiped, any personal account lock cleared, and it stays in company enrollment for the next user.

Accounts are disabled on the last day. Before wiping, I check whether legal or the manager needs files kept. Once the laptop is back, I wipe it from the console and make sure no personal account lock remains; on company devices our tool can bypass it. The device stays registered to us, so it re-enrolls itself for the next hire.
You pushed a new Wi-Fi profile with a wrong certificate, and 300 laptops dropped off the network. What now?
How you recover from your own change when the broken devices cannot hear you.
Stop the rollout, find another path to reach devices, fix and test on a few, tell users plainly, and add a pilot step.

I pause the assignment so no more devices get it. The broken laptops cannot download a fix over Wi-Fi, so I tell users to connect by cable, a guest network or a phone hotspot, which lets the device check in and receive the corrected profile. I test the fix on five laptops first. Afterward, every network change goes to a pilot group first.
How would you move 2,000 devices from one device management system to another?
Your planning for a large change that touches every user.
Re-enrollment planned for, since a device has one manager at a time; settings rebuilt and tested, waves with a pilot, clear user guidance.

A device can be enrolled in only one system, so most devices must leave the old one and enroll in the new. Leaving removes managed apps and settings, so I rebuild and test every policy in the new system first. I point the vendor accounts to the new server for new devices, then move existing ones in waves of 100, pilot first, with a short guide for users.

engagement-manager.heading: Engagement manager questions
qs: What is the difference between a master services agreement and a statement of work?
Whether you know the contracts your engagement runs on.
The MSA sets the legal terms for the whole relationship. The SOW defines one project's scope, deliverables, fees and timeline.

The MSA is the umbrella contract. It covers payment terms, confidentiality, liability limits and who owns the work product. Each SOW sits under it and describes one project: scope, deliverables, timeline, fees and acceptance. If the two seem to conflict, I check the order-of-precedence clause rather than guess.
How does running a fixed-fee engagement differ from running a time-and-materials one?
Your understanding of who carries the risk under each pricing model.
On fixed fee the firm absorbs overruns, so you guard margin and scope. On T&M the client pays for hours, so you watch their budget burn.

On fixed fee, the client pays a set price, so every extra hour comes out of our margin. I guard scope tightly and track effort weekly against the plan. On time and materials, the client pays for hours used, so I watch their budget burn and warn them well before it runs out. In both, scope changes go through a written change request.
Walk me through the first two weeks of a new engagement.
How you set up a project so it starts on solid ground.
Confirming scope and sign-off early, setting a reporting rhythm, and chasing access and dependencies before they become delays.

Before kickoff I read the SOW line by line and list anything vague. In week one I hold the kickoff with the sponsor to confirm goals, success measures and who signs off. I set the meeting rhythm and start access and data requests, since those always lag. In week two I share a detailed plan, a risk and issue log, and a first status report.
A client asks for one small extra report that is not in the SOW. What do you do?
How you handle scope creep without damaging the relationship.
Neither a flat no nor a silent yes: size it, check it against the SOW, and agree in writing whether it is a change request or a favor.

I thank them and say I will check what it involves. If it is truly an hour, I may do it, but I say it is outside scope so it is a visible favor, not a new baseline. If it is real work, I estimate it and send a short change request with the cost and timeline impact. Small unlogged extras are how a project quietly loses its margin.
Which numbers do you look at each week to know whether an engagement is healthy?
Your grip on the financial side of an engagement.
Cost burned against plan, estimate at completion, projected margin and real progress on deliverables, read together rather than alone.

I compare hours and cost to date with the plan. Then I work out the estimate at completion: actual cost so far plus an honest estimate of what is left. I set that against the fee to see projected margin. I also check deliverable progress, because spending half the budget means little if we are only a third done.
Halfway through a fixed-fee project, your estimate at completion shows a 20% overrun. What do you do?
How you respond when a fixed-fee project is heading over budget.
Find the cause first. Tell your own leadership early, fix what you control, and raise a change request if client-side changes caused it.

First I find out why. If the client added work or delayed data, I document it and raise a change request with the sponsor. If we underestimated, that is on us: I tell my practice lead right away, review the staffing mix and what can be simplified without hurting quality, and agree a revised plan. What I never do is hide it until the last month.
The client sponsor asks you to take one of your consultants off the project. How do you handle it?
How you balance the client's request with fairness to your own team member.
Take it seriously, ask for specifics, act quickly for the client, and treat the consultant with respect and in private.

I ask the sponsor for specific examples and whether it is a skill gap or a fit issue. If they want the person off, I usually agree, because forcing it hurts the project. I tell the consultant privately and honestly, with the feedback framed fairly. Then I work with staffing on a replacement and a handover plan so the client loses no time.
You find out the sales team promised the client something your team cannot deliver by the agreed date. What do you do?
Whether you reset expectations honestly instead of carrying an impossible promise.
Align internally with the seller first, then reset with the client early, bringing options instead of only a problem.

I first talk with the account lead to learn exactly what was promised and why, so we speak to the client with one voice. Then I go to the sponsor early, ideally before work starts, with options: trim scope to fit the date, add a second phase, or move the date. Telling them in week one costs some goodwill. Telling them in month three can cost the account.
Your day-to-day contact is happy, but you sense the executive sponsor is not. What do you do?
Whether you manage the relationship above your daily contact.
Ask for direct time with the sponsor, learn how they measure success, and change reporting or priorities to match.

On one project our daily contact cared about tasks getting done, but the sponsor cared about whether costs would drop. I asked her for a 30-minute check-in and asked what success meant for her board. She had never seen a savings figure from us. We added a one-page monthly summary tied to her goal, and her tone changed within a few weeks.
Your team delivered an analysis with an error, and the client has already shown it to their leadership. How do you handle it?
How you own a mistake once it has reached the client.
Tell the client fast and directly, with the corrected figure, what it changes and how you will prevent it, before they find it themselves.

I confirm the error and its size within hours, not days. Then I call the sponsor rather than email, explain what was wrong, give the corrected number and say whether the conclusion changes. I offer to help brief their leadership. Afterward I add a second-person review for any figures that leave the team. Clients forgive errors far more easily than silence.

engineering-intern.heading: Engineering intern questions
qs: What is a factor of safety, and why do engineers use one?
Whether you understand why designs carry extra margin.
The ratio of what a part can take to what it is expected to carry, used to cover unknowns in loads, materials and models.

It is the ratio of the load or stress a part can withstand to the load it is expected to see. A factor of 2 means it should take twice the design load before it fails. We use it because loads, material strength, manufacturing and our own models all carry uncertainty. The right factor depends on the field's codes and on the cost of a failure.
What does a tolerance on a drawing tell you, and why not make every tolerance tight?
Whether you connect design choices to how parts are made and what they cost.
A tolerance is the allowed variation of a dimension; tight ones cost more, so they go only where fit or function needs them.

A tolerance is the range a dimension may vary and still work, like 10.00 mm plus or minus 0.05. No part is made exactly to size. Tighter tolerances need slower machining, better tools and more inspection, so they cost more. I hold tight tolerances only where a fit or a function depends on them and loosen the rest.
Pick one design decision from a school or team project and tell me what you traded off.
Whether you can explain the reasoning behind a choice, not just the result.
A clear choice, the options compared, what was given up, and when the other option would have won.

On our student rover I chose aluminum tubing over carbon fiber for the frame. Carbon was lighter, but aluminum cost about a third as much, we could cut and drill it in the school shop, and we could repair it at competition. We gave up roughly 400 grams. If weight had been our hard limit, I would have chosen carbon.
Your mentor describes your project in one sentence. How do you turn that into requirements you can test?
How you turn a vague goal into something you can design and check against.
Asks who uses it and how success is judged, writes measurable requirements and constraints, and gets them agreed before designing.

I ask who will use it, what problem it solves and how we will know it works. Then I write each need as something measurable, like "holds 20 kg with no visible bending" instead of "strong." I add limits such as budget, space and deadline, and I send the list to my mentor for review before I design anything, so we agree on what done means.
Your calculation says a small steel bracket will deflect two meters. What do you do next?
Whether you sanity-check your numbers before trusting them.
Treats the result as an error, checks units, inputs and formula, and compares with a rough estimate.

Two meters on a small bracket is not believable, so I assume a mistake first. I check units, since mixing millimeters with meters or MPa with Pa is a common cause. Then I check the formula and inputs like the material stiffness and the section properties, and do a quick rough estimate. If anyone already used the number, I tell my mentor.
Your simulation and your hand calculation disagree by 40 percent. Which one do you trust?
Your judgement when two methods give different answers.
Neither by default: checks supports, loads, mesh and assumptions until the gap is explained, then reviews with a mentor.

Neither yet. A hand calculation simplifies the shape; a simulation depends on how I set loads, supports and mesh. I check the supports first, since they cause big gaps, then refine the mesh near the high-stress area and see if the result settles. If the gap stays, I review both with my mentor before I use either number.
You need to run a test on a lab machine, and the person who trained you is out today. What do you do?
Whether you put safety and training rules ahead of your schedule.
Does not run equipment without being trained and authorized; tells the mentor and finds an approved person or other work.

I do not run it. Watching someone once is not the same as being trained and signed off, and I may not know that machine's lockout steps or emergency stop. I tell my mentor the test is blocked, ask who else is authorized to run it or train me, and use the time for setup or data work. A day late is better than an injury.
You notice what looks like an error on a senior engineer's drawing. How do you raise it?
How you speak up respectfully when you think someone more senior is wrong.
Checks your own reading first, asks privately as a question with evidence, and lets the fix go through the normal change process.

First I make sure I am right: latest revision, notes, units. If it still looks wrong, I go to the engineer privately and show what I found: "This hole seems to clash with the mating part. Am I missing something?" Often there is a reason. If it is an error, they correct it through the usual revision process.
A part you inspected measures just outside tolerance, and the build is tomorrow. What do you do?
Your honesty and judgement when a deadline pushes against a spec.
Records the true value, flags the part right away, and leaves the decision to the people authorized to handle nonconforming parts.

I record the real measurement and do not round it into spec. I tag the part as out of tolerance and tell my mentor and quality right away, so they have time before the build. They may accept it after review, rework it or scrap it, but that is their call through the nonconformance process, not mine. A hidden bad part can fail later in the field.
Two weeks before your internship ends, your project is not finished. Walk me through how you hand it off.
Whether you leave work that someone else can pick up and use.
Raises it early, agrees what can finish, and leaves clear documents, files and a walkthrough for the next person.

I tell my mentor early, not on my last day, and we agree what can realistically finish. Then I focus on leaving it usable: a short report on what works, what does not, the test data and the open issues. I put files and code in the shared system with clear names, and I walk the person taking over through it before I leave.

engineering-manager.heading: Engineering manager questions
qs: What do you use one-on-ones for?
Whether you treat one-on-ones as the engineer's time, not a status meeting.
The agenda belongs to the engineer: growth, blockers, feedback both ways. Status updates go elsewhere, and the meeting is rarely cancelled.

They are the engineer's meeting, not mine. We keep a shared doc, and they add topics first: blockers, career goals, things that frustrate them. I add feedback and context they would not see otherwise. Project status goes in standup or the tracker. If I have to move a one-on-one, I reschedule it the same week rather than drop it.
How much code do you still write, and why?
How you balance staying technical with not becoming a bottleneck.
Stays close to the code through reviews and small tasks, but keeps off the critical path so the team is never waiting on the manager.

With a team of seven, very little production code. I review designs, read pull requests to stay current, and pick up small fixes or tooling work that nobody is waiting on. I stopped owning key features after one slipped because my week filled with interviews. My job is to make the team faster, not to be its slowest engineer.
Walk me through how you run a review after a production outage.
Whether you run a blameless review that leads to real fixes.
A blameless format: timeline, contributing causes, what helped and what hurt, and a few action items with owners and dates that are tracked until done.

Within a few days I bring the people involved together, with a written timeline drafted beforehand. We ask how the system allowed this, not who slipped. We list contributing causes, including how long detection and response took. Then we pick three or four action items, each with one owner and a date, and I check them weekly until they are closed.
How does your team decide whether to hire someone after an interview loop?
Whether your hiring process limits bias and produces a clear, defensible decision.
Criteria agreed before the interviews, written feedback submitted independently before the debrief, and a decision based on evidence rather than the loudest voice.

Before the loop we agree what each interview tests and what a strong answer looks like. Each interviewer writes feedback and a hire or no-hire before seeing anyone else's, so nobody anchors on the first opinion. In the debrief we talk about evidence, not vague feelings about fit. If the evidence is mixed on a must-have skill, the default is no.
Product asks you for a launch date on a project with big unknowns. What do you give them?
How you plan and communicate under uncertainty without overpromising.
A range tied to the named unknowns, a short piece of work to reduce the biggest risk, and a date when the estimate will get firmer.

I would not give a single date yet. I would say six to ten weeks, and explain that the spread comes from a payment integration we have never touched. We spend one week building a small prototype of that piece, then I come back with a tighter range. I also offer scope options: what could ship first if the date is fixed.
How do you decide how much time goes to technical debt versus new features?
Whether you can make the case for maintenance in terms the business understands.
Debt is tied to concrete costs like incidents, slow delivery or on-call load, and gets a regular, agreed share of capacity instead of a fight every sprint.

I avoid a vague debt bucket. I list items with their cost: this flaky deploy fails one time in five and costs us about a day a week. Then I agree with the product manager on a standing share of each cycle, say a fifth, and we adjust it as incidents rise or fall. The items that remove the most pain go first.
An engineer tells you they want to be promoted to senior within a year. What do you do?
How you guide growth with clear expectations instead of vague encouragement.
Compares their work to the written level expectations, names specific gaps, finds real work that closes them, and reviews progress regularly without promising the outcome.

I go through our career ladder with them, item by item, using examples of their own work. Usually the gap is scope, like leading a project end to end or mentoring others. I find a project that gives them that chance, and we check progress every month. I am honest that I cannot promise the promotion, only a fair shot and clear feedback.
Two senior engineers disagree strongly about an architecture choice, and the debate has dragged on for weeks. What do you do?
How you bring a technical disagreement to a decision without damaging the working relationship.
Gets the options and trade-offs written down, sets a deadline and a decision maker, and makes sure both engineers feel heard even if one loses.

I ask them to write one short design doc together, with both options, the trade-offs and what would prove each one wrong. Then we set a date and a decision maker, usually the tech lead, or me if needed. Once decided, we commit and note when we would revisit it. I talk privately with whoever lost, so the debate does not continue in code reviews.
Your on-call engineer gets paged several times a night. How do you fix it?
Whether you protect people from burnout while fixing the system behind the pages.
Short-term relief for the people, then the cause: removing noisy or unactionable alerts and putting the top sources of pages on the plan.

First the person: they take the morning off after a bad night, and I add a backup or cover some shifts myself. Then we review a month of pages. Often most come from a few alerts that need no action, so we tune or remove them. Real problems behind the rest go on the plan with time reserved, and I track pages per week to show it is improving.
Tell me about a hire you got wrong. What did you change afterward?
Whether you own hiring mistakes and fix the process, not just the situation.
Takes responsibility, explains what the process missed, treated the person fairly, and names a concrete change to the interview loop.

I hired an engineer who did brilliantly on algorithm questions but struggled with our old, messy code and rarely asked for help. I set clear goals and supported him, but after three months it still was not working, and we agreed on a respectful exit. Our loop never tested reading unfamiliar code, so we added a session where candidates debug a realistic sample service.

enterprise-account-executive.heading: Enterprise account executive questions
qs: What is the difference between a champion and a coach in a deal?
Whether you know who can actually move a deal inside the account.
A coach gives information. A champion has influence and sells for you when you are not in the room, and you test that rather than assume it.

A coach is friendly and tells me what is going on, but may have no pull. A champion has influence, gains personally if we win, and sells for me in meetings I am not in. I test it. I ask them to set up time with the person who signs, or to walk me through the approval process. If they cannot or will not, they are a coach.
Who is the economic buyer, and how do you get to them?
Whether you can find the person who signs, not just the person who likes you.
The person who can release the budget and say yes when others say no. You reach them through the champion, with a reason that matters to them.

It is the person who can approve the spend even if nobody below them agrees, and often not the one running the evaluation. I ask my champion how a purchase this size got approved last time and who signed. Then I give the champion a reason for the meeting that the buyer cares about, like a short business case, not a demo.
What goes into a mutual action plan?
Whether you can manage a long buying process with the customer, not around them.
Shared dates worked back from the customer's go-live: validation, security, legal, procurement and signature, each with an owner on both sides.

I start from the date the customer needs to be live and why. Then I work backward: technical validation, security review, legal redlines, procurement and signature. Each step has an owner on their side and ours, plus a date. It lives in a shared document we review weekly. When a step slips, we both see it early, and it shows me whether they are really buying.
How do you multithread a deal, and why does it matter?
How you avoid hanging a large deal on one person.
Relationships across levels and functions, each with its own reason to care, so a reorg or a departure does not stall the deal.

One contact is a single point of failure. I map the org: business owner, users, IT, security, finance, procurement. Each one has a contact on our side, our engineer with their architects, our executive with theirs. On one deal our champion went on leave for two months. Because we knew the IT director and the finance team, the deal kept moving.
How do you decide whether a deal goes in your forecast as commit, best case or pipeline?
Your forecasting discipline and honesty with your manager.
Categories based on evidence of what the buyer has done, such as approval from the signer and a mapped paper process, not on how a meeting felt.
