Site conditions: supply voltage and phase rotation, grounding, utilities, ambient conditions, installer wiring and shipping damage.

First what the factory could not test: the site. I measure supply voltage on every phase under load and check phase rotation on three-phase equipment. I check grounding, air and water pressure, heat and dust, the network, and the field wiring done by the installer. Then shipping damage: loose connectors, a bent bracket, a board knocked out of its seat.
The customer reports an intermittent fault, but the machine runs fine while you are there. What do you do?
How you track down a fault you cannot see.
Gets the exact conditions, reads the logs, tries to reproduce it, and sets up monitoring instead of closing the call as no fault found.

I ask exactly when it happens: time of day, which product, after how long running, whether something nearby starts at the same time. I pull the alarm log. I inspect connectors and cable runs that move, vibrate or get hot. If it still won't show, I leave a data logger or set up trending and agree with the operators what they write down the next time it happens.
You arrive for an installation and the site is not ready: no power at the location and the floor is not level. What do you do?
How you handle a site that blocks the job without cutting corners.
Documents the gaps, tells the customer and own office at once, does the work that is possible, and does not improvise around site work.

I don't run a temporary cord or shim the machine past what the manual allows. I photograph the issues, show the site contact and call my office within the hour so the cost of a return trip is clear early. Then I do what I can: unpack, inspect for shipping damage, pre-assemble. My report lists exactly what must be done before I come back.
You replaced a board, the fault cleared, and two days later it is back. How do you handle it?
How you own a repair that did not hold and find the real cause.
Admits the first fix treated a symptom, goes back quickly, and looks for what killed the part instead of swapping another one.

I tell the customer right away that my first fix didn't hold and I'm coming back. Before I fit another board, I look for what could damage it: voltage spikes, a shorted output, a bad ground, heat or moisture in the cabinet. I measure those, fix the cause, then replace the board. The failed board goes back to the factory with a note so they can analyze it.
A production manager asks you to bypass a door interlock so the line can run until the part arrives. What do you say?
Whether you hold firm on safety devices under production pressure.
A clear no with a reason, then real help: a faster part, a spare, or running the rest of the line safely.

I say no, and I say why: that interlock is what stops someone reaching into a moving machine, and with it bypassed an injury is only a matter of time. Then I work on his real problem. I check for a spare switch locally, get the part shipped overnight, and look at whether the rest of the line can run safely without that station.
The damage you find looks like misuse, but the customer insists it is a warranty repair. How do you handle it?
Your judgement between the customer relationship and the company's warranty rules.
Facts recorded without accusing anyone, the decision left to whoever owns warranty, and the customer kept informed.

I don't argue on site and I don't promise anything. I document what I see with photos, readings and the log, for example an overload alarm acknowledged twelve times. I explain calmly what I found and that the warranty team decides. I send it to them the same day, and I offer to repair it now on a quote if they need the machine running.

finance-manager.heading: Finance manager questions
qs: What is the cash conversion cycle, and how would you shorten it?
Whether you understand how working capital ties up cash.
The formula, days sales outstanding plus days of inventory minus days payables outstanding, and a practical lever for each part.

It is how many days cash is tied up between paying suppliers and collecting from customers: days sales outstanding plus days of inventory minus days payables outstanding. I would tighten invoicing and follow-up on overdue accounts, cut slow-moving stock, and negotiate longer supplier terms without ever paying late.
What is the difference between a static budget and a flexible budget?
Whether you can separate a volume effect from a spending problem.
A flexible budget restates costs for actual volume, so the remaining variance shows real overspending or savings per unit.

A static budget stays at the volume we planned. A flexible budget restates costs for the volume we actually ran. If we made 20% more units, the static budget makes materials look overspent. The flexible budget shows whether we spent too much per unit, which is the question a manager can act on.
How do you decide whether a purchase is a capital expenditure or an expense?
Your grasp of capitalization rules and how they move profit.
Long-lived items above the company threshold are capitalized and depreciated; repairs that only maintain are expensed. The policy is applied the same way every time.

If it gives benefit beyond a year and is above our capitalization threshold, I capitalize it and depreciate it over its useful life. A machine upgrade that adds capacity goes on the balance sheet. Fixing a broken part to keep it running is an expense. I follow the written policy so the choice never depends on what we want this quarter's profit to be.
A department head wants to hire an engineer at $120,000. What does that hire really cost?
Whether you know the fully loaded cost of headcount.
Salary plus employer payroll taxes, benefits, equipment, software and recruiting, timed to the real start date.

Salary is only the start. I add the employer share of Social Security and Medicare, federal and state unemployment tax, health and retirement benefits, a laptop and software licenses, and any recruiting fee. In my last plan an engineer at $120,000 came to about $155,000 in the first year. I also cost it from the start date, not from January.
Sales wants to offer a 10% discount to win more volume. How do you assess it?
Your use of contribution margin in a pricing decision.
Shows how much extra volume is needed to break even on the discount, and asks about side effects on other customers and capacity.

I look at contribution margin, not revenue. Say a product sells for $100 and variable cost is $70. A 10% discount cuts the margin from $30 to $20 a unit, so we need 50% more volume just to earn the same contribution. I ask sales how likely that is, whether existing customers will demand the same price, and whether we have the capacity.
How would you evaluate whether we should buy a new production machine?
Whether you judge an investment on cash flows and the time value of money.
Net present value at the cost of capital, using only extra cash flows and taxes, with a sensitivity check on the weakest assumptions.

I list the extra cash flows the machine creates: savings, added margin, maintenance, the tax effect of depreciation and any working capital. I discount them at our cost of capital to get net present value; positive means it beats the hurdle. I add payback because owners ask for it, and I test what happens if savings come in 20% lower.
Some budget owners pad their budgets. How do you deal with it?
How you challenge budget requests without damaging trust.
Driver-based budgets and comparisons to actuals expose padding, and a central contingency removes the reason to hide cushions.

I build budgets from drivers, like units, headcount and rates, so a padded line stands out. I compare each request to the last two years of actuals and ask the owner to explain the gaps. I also make it safe to be honest: a contingency held centrally, so no one needs to hide a cushion in their own lines.
You notice one person in accounts payable can set up new vendors and also release payments. Why does that matter, and what do you do?
Whether you spot a basic internal control gap and fix it.
Names the fraud risk, a fake vendor paid by the same person, and splits the duties or adds a review that actually works.

One person who can create a vendor and release payment could pay a fake company with no one noticing. I would move vendor setup and bank detail changes to someone else. If the team is too small, I would review a vendor change report every week and confirm any new bank details by calling the vendor at a number we already had on file.
The CEO asks you to book a large order as revenue this quarter, but the goods ship next quarter. What do you do?
Your integrity under pressure and your knowledge of revenue recognition.
A clear no, based on the rule that revenue is recognized when control passes to the customer, plus honest options for the quarter.

I would say no and explain why. Under the revenue standard, ASC 606, we record revenue when the customer gets control of the goods, which here is next quarter. Bill-and-hold has strict tests we do not meet. I would offer real options: ship part of the order early if the customer agrees, or show the board the signed backlog.
Your forecast shows the company will break a loan covenant in two quarters. What do you do?
How you handle bad news that carries legal and financial risk.
Checks the loan definitions, tells leadership at once with options, and goes to the lender early with a plan instead of waiting for the breach.

First I check the math against the exact definitions in the loan agreement, since covenant EBITDA often differs from ours. Then I tell the CEO with a model of options: cost cuts, slower capital spending, faster collections. I would rather call the lender months ahead with a plan and ask for a waiver or amendment than surprise them in a compliance certificate.

financial-analyst.heading: Financial analyst (FP&A) questions
qs: What is the difference between a budget, a forecast, and a rolling forecast?
Whether you know the basic planning tools and what each one is for.
The budget is the fixed target set once a year. A forecast is the current best estimate. A rolling forecast always looks the same distance ahead.

The budget is the plan we commit to before the year starts, and we measure against it. A forecast is our best current view of where we will land, updated as facts change. A rolling forecast adds a new period each time one closes, so we always see, say, 12 or 18 months ahead instead of only to December.
What is a flexible budget, and when is it more useful than the static one?
Whether you can separate overruns caused by volume from overruns caused by spending.
A budget restated at actual volume using planned rates, so variable costs are judged against what was really produced or sold.

A flexible budget recalculates the plan at the volume we actually hit, using the budgeted cost per unit for variable costs and the same fixed costs. If the plant made 20% more units, materials will run over the static budget. Comparing to the flexed number shows whether we spent more per unit, which is the part a manager can act on.
What is the difference between zero-based and incremental budgeting?
Whether you know the main budgeting methods and their trade-offs.
Incremental starts from last year and adjusts. Zero-based justifies every cost from nothing; it finds waste but takes far more time.

Incremental budgeting takes last year's spend and adds or trims a percentage. It is fast, but it carries old waste forward. Zero-based budgeting starts each cost line at zero and makes the owner justify every dollar. It finds savings but takes a lot of time, so I would use it on a few large or growing cost areas, not the whole company every year.
How do you set up a financial model so someone else can use and audit it?
Your modelling discipline: structure, clarity and built-in checks.
Separate inputs, calculations and outputs, no hard-coded numbers in formulas, a consistent layout, and check cells that flag errors.

I keep inputs on one tab, color-coded, and every assumption has a source note. Calculations use the same columns on every sheet, and I never type a number into a formula. Outputs pull only from the calculations. I add check cells, like the balance sheet balancing and totals tying, so a broken link shows up at once, not in the board deck.
Revenue came in $2 million over plan. How do you split that into price, volume and mix?
Your command of the standard revenue variance breakdown.
Volume at budget price and mix, mix from shifts between products, price at actual units. The three parts must add back to the total.

Volume is the change in total units times the budgeted average price at planned mix. Mix is the shift between products, valued at budget prices. Price is actual minus budget price, times actual units of each product. I check the three add to $2 million, then say which drove it, since a price gain and a volume gain mean very different things.
The CEO asks what happens to profit if sales drop 15%. How do you answer quickly?
Whether you understand cost behavior and operating leverage.
Lost sales times the contribution margin ratio, with fixed costs held unless cut, and the point that profit falls by more than 15%.

I take the drop in sales times the contribution margin ratio, since fixed costs do not move on their own. If we sell $40 million at a 35% contribution margin, a 15% drop costs about $2.1 million of profit. Because fixed costs stay, profit falls by a bigger percentage than sales. Then I list which fixed costs we could cut, and how fast.
The company shows a profit but is running short of cash. How can that be, and what do you look at?
Whether you can connect profit to cash through working capital.
Profit is not cash: receivables, inventory, capital spending and debt payments absorb it. Looks at receivable, inventory and payable days.

Profit counts sales when earned, not when paid. If customers pay slower, inventory builds up, or we buy equipment, cash goes out while profit looks fine. I would check days sales outstanding, days of inventory and days payable, plus capex and debt repayments. Then I build a 13-week cash forecast from expected receipts and payments to see the low point coming.
A department head sends you a budget you think is padded. How do you handle it?
How you challenge a budget owner without damaging the relationship.
Asks for the drivers behind the numbers, compares with history and run rate, and agrees changes with the owner instead of cutting silently.

I would not just cut it. I ask what drives each big line: headcount plan, unit costs, projects. Then I compare with last year's actuals and the run rate. If travel is up 40% with flat headcount, I ask why. Often we agree a lower number or hold the extra as a contingency released on a trigger. I tell the manager what I will present, so there are no surprises.
You find a formula error in a forecast after it already went to the CFO. What do you do?
How you own a mistake in numbers that leaders rely on.
Tells the CFO quickly with the corrected figure and its impact, fixes the cause, and adds a check so it cannot happen again.

First I size it: which numbers change and by how much. Then I tell the CFO the same day, with the corrected figure and whether any decision used the old one. I do not fix it quietly. Once a sum skipped a new row and overstated operating expenses by $300,000. After that I added a check tying each total to the sum of departments.
Leadership wants the forecast raised to match the target, but your drivers do not support it. What do you do?
Your integrity and judgement when the honest forecast is not the welcome one.
Keeps the forecast as the best estimate, shows the gap and what would close it, and keeps the target separate from the forecast.

A forecast is our best estimate, not a goal, so I would not change it to look better. I would show the gap to target, the drivers behind my number, and what would have to be true to close it, such as a price increase or faster sales hiring. If leaders want a stretch case, I add it as a separate, labeled scenario so the business still plans on the realistic one.

financial-reporting.heading: Technical accounting and financial reporting questions
qs: What are the five steps of revenue recognition under ASC 606?
Whether you know the revenue standard well enough to apply it, not just recite it.
All five steps in order, with a word on where the judgement sits, such as deciding which performance obligations are distinct.

Identify the contract, identify the performance obligations, set the transaction price, allocate it to the obligations based on relative standalone selling prices, and recognize revenue when or as each obligation is satisfied. The hard part is usually step two: deciding whether a setup service is distinct from the software it supports.
A major customer files for bankruptcy two weeks after year end, before the statements are issued. Does that change the year-end numbers?
Whether you can tell a subsequent event that is recognized from one that is only disclosed.
It depends on whether the condition existed at the balance sheet date. A customer's slow decline usually means adjusting the allowance.

Usually yes. If the customer was already in financial trouble at year end, the bankruptcy is evidence of a condition that existed then, so I would adjust the credit loss allowance on that receivable. If a sudden event after year end caused it, like a fire at their plant, I would disclose it but not change the balance sheet.
Legal says a lawsuit loss is probable and likely between $2 million and $5 million, with no amount in that range more likely than another. What do you book?
Your knowledge of the loss contingency rules under ASC 450.
Accrue the low end of the range when no amount in it is a better estimate, and disclose the possible loss above the accrual.

Both tests for accrual are met: the loss is probable and can be reasonably estimated. With no best estimate inside the range, the rule is to accrue the minimum, so $2 million. I would also disclose the nature of the case and that a further loss of up to $3 million is reasonably possible.
How do you decide whether a lease is a finance or an operating lease for the lessee, and why does it matter?
Whether you know the lease classification tests and their effect on the statements.
Names the five criteria and explains that both types go on the balance sheet, but the expense pattern differs.

It is a finance lease if any test is met: title transfers, a purchase option is reasonably certain, the term is a major part of the asset's economic life, the present value of payments is substantially all of its fair value, or the asset is specialized with no other use. Operating leases show one straight-line cost; finance leases show interest plus amortization, which is heavier early.
Our app sells goods from third-party sellers and we keep a 15% fee. Do we report revenue gross or net?
Whether you apply the principal versus agent test by control, not by who handles the cash.
The test is whether the company controls the good before it passes to the customer, supported by indicators like fulfillment duty, inventory risk and pricing.

It turns on control before the transfer. If the sellers own the stock, set the prices and are responsible for the product, we are an agent and report only our 15% fee as revenue. If we bought the goods, held inventory risk and set prices, we would be the principal and report the full sale. Collecting the cash alone does not make us the principal.
We are buying a company whose value is almost all in one office building. Is that a business combination?
Whether you know the screen test for a business and why the answer changes the accounting.
Applies the screen: if substantially all fair value sits in one asset or group of similar assets, it is an asset acquisition, with no goodwill and costs capitalized.

Probably not. I would first run the screen: if substantially all the fair value of the gross assets acquired is in a single asset or group of similar assets, it is not a business. Then it is an asset acquisition: no goodwill, transaction costs are capitalized, and cost is allocated on relative fair values. In a business combination those costs would be expensed.
We are amending a term loan with the same lender. How do you decide whether it is a modification or an extinguishment?
Your grasp of the debt modification rules and the 10 percent cash flow test.
Explains the 10% present value test at the original effective rate, including lender fees, and how fees are treated under each outcome.

I compare the present value of the new cash flows, including fees paid to the lender, with the present value of the remaining old cash flows, both discounted at the original effective rate. If they differ by 10% or more, it is an extinguishment: I write off old costs and book a gain or loss. Under 10%, it is a modification: lender fees adjust the yield and third-party costs are expensed.
While preparing this year's statements, you find an expense that was left out of last year's audited numbers. What do you do?
How you handle a prior-period error, from materiality to restatement.
Assesses materiality with numbers and qualitative factors, picks restatement or revision, and tells management and the auditors early.

I quantify it first, both on last year and on what it does to this year if I just book it now, and look at qualitative factors such as whether it turns a profit into a loss or affects a covenant. I bring it to the controller and auditors quickly. If material to the prior year, we reissue restated statements; if not, but correcting it now would be material, we revise the comparatives.
At quarter end, sales wants to bill a customer for goods still in our warehouse and book the revenue. How do you respond?
Whether you hold the line on revenue cutoff and know the bill-and-hold criteria.
Revenue only if control has passed, with all bill-and-hold criteria met and documented. Otherwise a calm no, with the reason.

I would ask why the goods are staying with us. Revenue is allowed only if the customer has control: there must be a substantive reason for the arrangement, like the customer asking for it, the goods must be set aside as theirs, ready to ship, and we cannot use them or send them to anyone else. If that is not met and documented, the revenue waits, and I explain why to sales.
A business unit signs a deal unlike anything we have done before. Walk me through how you reach and document the accounting answer.
How you work through new accounting questions and leave a record an auditor can follow.
Gets the full contract and facts, finds the right guidance, weighs alternatives, writes a memo with a conclusion, and agrees it with auditors before closing.

I read the whole contract and talk to the people who negotiated it, because side letters and verbal promises change answers. Then I find which standard applies, check our existing policies and firm guides, and write a memo: facts, the question, guidance, alternatives I rejected and why, conclusion and journal entries. I share it with the auditors early, ideally before the quarter closes.

firmware-engineer.heading: Firmware engineer questions
qs: What does the volatile keyword do in C, and when do you need it?
Whether you know how the compiler treats memory that can change outside your code.
It stops the compiler from caching or removing reads and writes. It is needed for hardware registers and ISR-shared flags, and it is not a lock.

It tells the compiler the value can change behind its back, so every read and write must really happen. I use it for memory-mapped registers and for flags an interrupt sets. It does not make an access atomic, so for shared data I still need a critical section.
Walk me through what happens between power-on and the first line of main().
Your knowledge of startup code and how a program sits in memory.
Reset vector, stack pointer, copying .data, zeroing .bss, clock setup, then main, with real detail for one chip family.

On a Cortex-M the core loads the initial stack pointer from the first word of the vector table and jumps to the reset handler in the second. Startup code copies initialized variables from flash to RAM, zeros the .bss section, usually sets up clocks, then calls main. If .bss is not zeroed, globals start with garbage.
What do you keep in an interrupt handler, and what do you move out of it?
How you write interrupt code that stays fast and safe.
Short handlers: clear the source, grab the data, queue it or set a flag. No blocking calls, long loops or printf.

In the handler I clear the interrupt flag, read data that would otherwise be lost, like a UART byte, put it in a ring buffer and set a flag. Parsing and anything slow runs in the main loop or a task. I never block or call printf in an ISR, because it delays every other interrupt.
A push button gives you several presses for one push. How do you fix it?
Whether you know switch bounce and the usual ways to handle it.
Names contact bounce and debounces in hardware or software, for example by requiring a stable state for a set time.

That is contact bounce: the metal contacts chatter for a few milliseconds. I sample the pin from a timer every few milliseconds and accept a new state only after it reads the same several times in a row, about 20 ms stable. On a new board, an RC filter into a Schmitt trigger input also helps.
When would you use polling, an interrupt or DMA to move data from a peripheral?
Your judgement in trading CPU time, latency and complexity.
Matches the method to the data: polling for simple or rare cases, interrupts for events, DMA for steady streams.

Polling is fine at startup or when the CPU has nothing else to do. Interrupts suit events that arrive at unknown times, like a button or a few UART bytes. For fast ADC sampling or a big SPI transfer I use DMA, so the CPU is not interrupted for every byte, and I take an interrupt only at half or full buffer.
On an 8-bit microcontroller, the main loop reads a 32-bit tick counter that a timer interrupt updates. Sometimes the value is wildly wrong. Why?
Whether you spot a non-atomic access shared between an interrupt and main code.
The read takes several instructions, so the ISR can update the value mid-read. Fix it with a short critical section or a read-until-stable loop.

The CPU reads the four bytes one at a time. If the timer interrupt fires between bytes, I get low bytes from the old value and high bytes from the new one, so the result can jump by 256 or more. I disable interrupts just for the copy and restore them, or read the counter twice until both reads match.
How do you use a watchdog timer, and where do you refresh it?
How you use a watchdog to recover from a hang without hiding real faults.
Refresh only when the whole system is healthy, never from a timer ISR alone, and log the reset cause after a watchdog reset.

The watchdog resets the chip if the code does not refresh it in time. I refresh it in one place, or from a monitor task that checks every other task has checked in. I never kick it from a timer interrupt, because interrupts can keep running while the main code is stuck. At boot I read the reset cause and log watchdog resets.
After a reset in the middle of a transfer, your I2C bus is stuck with SDA held low. What do you do?
Whether you know a common I2C failure and how to recover from it.
A slave is mid-byte waiting for clocks: drive SCL as GPIO up to nine times until SDA is released, then send a STOP.

The slave was sending a byte when the master reset, so it still holds SDA low and waits for clocks. In init I set the pins as GPIO, toggle SCL up to nine times until SDA goes high, create a STOP condition, then give the pins back to the I2C peripheral. If it keeps happening, I check the pull-ups and the reset sequence.
Your Cortex-M device hits a HardFault about once a day in testing. How do you find the cause?
How you debug a crash from the state the processor saves at the fault.
Captures the stacked PC and LR plus fault status registers, maps the address to code, and keeps the data across reset when no debugger is attached.

My fault handler saves the stacked PC and LR plus the CFSR and HFSR into RAM that is not cleared at reset, and logs them on the next boot. The PC usually points at the faulting instruction, which I find with the map file or addr2line. The status bits say if it was a bus error, an undefined instruction or a bad memory access.
How would you design firmware updates in the field so a power cut cannot brick the device?
Your judgement in designing a safe update path.
A small protected bootloader, two image slots, an integrity and signature check before switching, and rollback if the new image fails.

I keep a small bootloader that normal updates never overwrite. The new image goes into a second slot while the old one keeps running. The bootloader checks its CRC and signature, then boots it on a trial basis. If the new firmware does not confirm it is healthy, for example after a watchdog reset, the bootloader rolls back to the old slot.

fleet-manager.heading: Fleet manager questions
qs: What goes into the total cost of ownership of a fleet vehicle?
Whether you look past the purchase price.
Purchase or lease cost, financing, fuel, maintenance, insurance, registration, downtime and resale value, compared per mile or per month.

Everything the vehicle costs from buying it to selling it: the purchase price or lease payments, financing, fuel, maintenance and tires, insurance, registration and taxes, and the cost of downtime. Then I subtract the resale value. I divide by miles driven, so I can compare a van and a pickup on the same basis.
How do you set preventive maintenance intervals for a mixed fleet?
How you plan maintenance so vehicles break down less.
Starts from the maker's schedule, adjusts for how each unit is used, triggers service by miles, engine hours or time, and tracks on-time completion.

I start with the manufacturer's schedule for each model, then look at how it is used. A truck that idles all day on a job site gets serviced by engine hours, not miles. Low-mileage units still get a calendar check. The system flags units coming due, and I track how many services we finish on time each month.
What do you keep in a driver qualification file for a CDL driver?
Your working knowledge of federal driver rules.
The main contents named correctly, and knowing that drug and alcohol testing records are kept secure and separate.

The employment application, the driving record checks from each state where the driver held a license in the past three years, the road test certificate or the CDL accepted in its place, the medical examiner's certificate, the inquiry to previous employers, and the annual driving record review. Drug and alcohol records go in a separate, locked file.
How would you spot fuel card misuse?
How you control fuel spending, often the largest running cost.
Sets card limits, then compares purchases with vehicle data: tank size, fuel type, time, location and miles per gallon.

I set limits on each card: fuel only, a daily gallon cap, and a PIN plus odometer entry. Then I look for exceptions: a fill larger than the tank, premium fuel in a unit that runs on regular, a purchase on a day off, or a station miles from where telematics shows the truck. A sudden drop in miles per gallon on one unit is another flag.
How do you decide when a vehicle should be replaced?
Whether you time replacement on cost data and not on habit.
Tracks cost per mile over the vehicle's life and replaces near the point where rising repairs outweigh falling depreciation, also weighing safety and downtime.

I track each unit's cost per mile. Depreciation falls each year while repairs and downtime rise. Where the total starts climbing is the replacement window. I also look at big repairs coming up and resale value. A truck at 140,000 miles that needs a $6,000 transmission is a candidate to sell before the repair, not after.
When would you lease vehicles instead of buying them?
Your judgement on how to finance a fleet.
It depends on cash, cost of money, mileage, how long units are kept and upfits; compare the total cost both ways over the same term.

Leasing makes sense when the company wants to keep cash for the business, replaces vehicles on a short cycle, or wants a fixed monthly cost. Buying often wins when we keep units a long time or drive high miles, since leases can charge for extra miles and wear. I compare total cost both ways over the same term and bring finance in on the tax side.
Telematics shows one driver with three times the harsh braking events of everyone else. What do you do?
How you use driver data fairly to improve safety.
Checks the data and the route first, then coaches in private with a clear goal and a follow-up date; discipline only if nothing changes.

First I check the data: his route, his vehicle, and whether the sensor is set like the others. If it holds up, I sit down with him privately, show the events and ask what is going on. Often it is following too close in city traffic. We agree on a goal, I check again in two weeks, and I say so when the number drops.
A driver calls you right after a crash. Walk me through what happens next.
Whether you know the steps after an accident, in the right order.
People first and 911 called, then photos and facts, no arguing fault, a DOT post-accident test if the criteria are met, then insurer and records.

First I ask if anyone is hurt and make sure 911 is called. Then I ask for photos, the other driver's details, witnesses and the police report number, and tell him not to argue about fault. For a CDL driver I check at once if the crash meets the DOT post-accident testing criteria, since the time window is short. Then I report it to our insurer and log it.
A safety recall comes in for 40 of your vans and operations wants them all kept on the road. What do you do?
Your judgement when safety and operations pull in different directions.
Reads what the defect is, obeys any do-not-drive warning, schedules repairs in waves with spare units, and records each repair by VIN.

I read the notice first. If the maker says park the vehicles, they are parked and I find rentals. If the risk is lower, I check every VIN, book dealer slots in batches of five or six so routes stay covered, and use spare vans to fill the gaps. I record each repair against its VIN so no van is missed.
You learn a driver has been driving for two months on a suspended license. How do you handle it?
How you handle a serious compliance failure and fix the process behind it.
Takes the driver off the road at once, brings in HR and the insurer, then finds why the check missed it and closes the gap.

He stops driving today, and I bring in HR and our insurer. Then I find out how we missed it. Often it is because records were only pulled once a year. I would move all drivers to continuous record monitoring, which alerts us when a state posts a change, and make it a clear rule that drivers report any suspension to us right away.

flight-software.heading: Flight software engineer questions
qs: Why do many flight software teams forbid dynamic memory allocation after startup?
Whether you know why flight code must behave the same way every time.
Fragmentation, allocation failure and unpredictable timing, plus the fix: allocate everything at initialization.

Calling malloc in the middle of a mission can fail when the heap is fragmented, and how long it takes is not predictable. Neither is acceptable in a control loop. I size every buffer and pool at startup, so if memory is short we find out on the ground during initialization, not in orbit.
What does a watchdog timer do, and where in the code do you reset it?
Whether you understand how a system recovers from a hang without a human.
The watchdog resets the processor if not serviced in time; it is serviced only after checking that all critical tasks are alive, not from an interrupt.

It is a hardware counter that resets the processor if the software stops servicing it. I never service it from a timer interrupt, because that keeps running while the main tasks are stuck. A low-priority monitor checks that each critical task has checked in this cycle, and only then resets the watchdog.
In embedded C, what does the volatile keyword do, and what does it not do?
Your grasp of how the compiler treats hardware registers and shared data.
Volatile stops the compiler from caching or removing reads and writes; it does not make an operation atomic or protect data shared between tasks.

It tells the compiler every read and write must really happen, so a status register is read from the hardware each time instead of from a cached copy. It does not make a read-modify-write atomic, and it is not a lock. For data shared between tasks I still need a mutex, disabled interrupts or an atomic operation.
What is priority inversion, and how do you prevent it?
Whether you can reason about real-time scheduling, not just code that works on the bench.
A clear example with three tasks and a shared lock, and a fix: priority inheritance or a priority ceiling, plus short critical sections.

A low-priority task holds a mutex the high-priority task needs. A medium-priority task then preempts the low one, so the high one waits on less important work. I use mutexes with priority inheritance, so the holder is raised to the waiting task's priority, and I keep critical sections short. Then I check worst-case blocking times in the timing analysis.
What is MC/DC coverage, and why is it required for the most critical airborne software?
Your knowledge of the structural coverage asked for at DO-178C Level A.
Each condition in a decision is shown to change the outcome on its own; Level A asks for it because plain branch coverage can miss a condition.

Modified condition/decision coverage means every condition in a decision has been shown to flip the result on its own, with the others held fixed. For 'A and B' that takes three tests: true-true, true-false and false-true. DO-178C asks for it at Level A, where a failure could be catastrophic, because branch coverage alone can leave a condition untested in effect.
How does flight software protect itself against radiation flipping bits in memory?
Whether you know the software side of designing for single event upsets.
Error-correcting memory with scrubbing, checksums on code and tables, redundant copies of critical data, and a way to reload a clean image.

The hardware usually has error-correcting memory, and the software runs a scrubber that reads through it regularly, so a single-bit error gets corrected before a second one lands in the same word. I keep checksums on code and parameter tables, store critical state in more than one copy and compare them, and can reload a clean image from protected storage.
A gyro starts reporting a value outside its physical range in flight. Walk me through what the software should do.
How you design fault detection, isolation and recovery.
No overreaction to one bad sample; a persistence check, isolation of the unit, a switch to a backup or safe mode, and clear telemetry for the ground.

First the reading is rejected, so it never reaches the control law. If it stays bad for a set number of cycles, the fault is declared, the unit is marked failed and the software switches to the redundant gyro or a mode that does not need it. Every step goes into telemetry with a time stamp, so the ground team can see what happened and why.
Code reused from an earlier vehicle converts a 64-bit float to a 16-bit integer and overflows on the new trajectory. What went wrong, and how do you stop it?
Whether you check the assumptions in reused code against the new mission.
Reuse without rechecking ranges is the root cause; the fix is range analysis for the new vehicle, limits before conversion and a defined response.

The code was right for the old flight profile, and nobody rechecked its ranges for the new one. I treat reused code as new for analysis: every input range is traced against the new vehicle's envelope. Before any narrowing conversion I check the range and saturate or flag it, and a fault in a nonessential function must never shut down an essential one.
Two days before launch you find a bug in an error path that only runs if a rare fault occurs. What do you do?
Your judgement about risk when the schedule is tight.
Report it at once with an honest risk assessment; let the review board weigh a late change against a workaround, since every change needs retesting.

I write it up and tell my lead the same day: what triggers it, what happens if it fires and how likely that is. Then I lay out the options: a code change with the regression tests it needs, a procedure the operators can use instead, or flying as is with the risk on record. The board decides; I make sure they decide with the facts.
The vehicle is in orbit and you need to upload a software patch. How do you plan it so a mistake cannot lose the mission?
How you plan an in-flight software change with no chance to touch the hardware.
Testing on a flight-like testbed, a known good image kept untouched, checksum checks before switching, and a fallback if the new image fails to boot.

The patch runs first on our flight-equivalent testbed, including the upload itself and a failed boot. On orbit we write it to a spare memory slot, never over the known good image, and verify the checksum before anything changes. We switch during a ground contact, and if the new image does not come up healthy, the boot logic falls back to the old one.

forward-deployed-engineer.heading: Forward deployed engineer questions
qs: How is the forward deployed engineer role different from a solutions engineer or a consultant?
Whether you understand what the role actually is.
You write and ship production code inside the customer's work, and you carry what you learn back to the product team.

A solutions engineer mostly helps close the sale with demos. A consultant often advises and hands off. I sit with the customer's team, write the code that connects our product to their data and workflow, and own it until people use it. Then I tell our product team what kept breaking, so the next customer needs less custom work.
A customer asks you for a dashboard. How do you find out what they actually need?
Your customer discovery skills.
Asking what decision the dashboard will drive and how they do the work today, before building anything.

I ask what decision they would make differently with it, who makes it and how often. Then I ask them to show me how they do it now, often in a spreadsheet. Once, a dashboard request turned out to be a need for one daily alert about late shipments. We built the alert in two days and skipped the dashboard.
Walk me through your first week on a new customer site.
How you get oriented fast without wasting the customer's time.
Meeting the real users, starting data and system access early, and agreeing on one first problem with a clear way to measure it.

On day one, I make sure access requests are started, since they often take days. Then I sit with the people who do the work, not just the sponsor, and watch how they do it today. By the end of the week I want one narrow problem, a number that shows success, and a rough prototype on real data they can react to.
The data you need sits in an old on-premise database, a vendor API and a few spreadsheets. How do you bring it together?
How you approach data integration in a messy real environment.
Reading without disturbing source systems, matching records across sources, checking totals with the business, and making loads safe to rerun.

I start read-only, ideally from a replica or an export, so I never slow down a system people rely on. I map how records match across sources, like customer IDs formatted differently. I load into a staging area, check row counts and totals with someone who knows the numbers, and make each load safe to rerun without creating duplicates.
The customer wants a tool that answers questions from their internal documents, and you have one week. How do you build the prototype?
Your rapid prototyping with language models on customer data.
Retrieval-augmented generation on a small document set, answers that cite their sources, and a test set of real user questions.

I would use retrieval-augmented generation: split the documents into passages, search for the passages relevant to a question, and give those to the model with the question. Answers show their sources so users can check them. Early on I collect 30 or 40 real questions with known answers, so I can measure whether each change makes it better or worse.
Their security team says no data can leave their network. What are your options?
How you work within a customer's security and compliance limits.
Treating the rule as a requirement, offering options like running inside their environment, and involving security early instead of working around them.

I take it as a design constraint, not an obstacle. Options include deploying our software inside their cloud account or data center, or using models that run in their environment. I would meet the security team early, ask what review they need, and give them a clear diagram of where data goes. I never copy data to my laptop to move faster.
Your prototype impressed the customer, and they want it in production next week. What do you say?
Your judgement about the gap between a demo and a system people depend on.
Being honest about what is missing, like error handling, monitoring and access control, and offering a limited, safe rollout instead of a flat no.

I thank them and say plainly what the demo skips: it runs on a sample, has no login controls, and nobody gets alerted if it fails. I offer a pilot with five users next week while we close those gaps, with a date for wider rollout. That keeps the momentum without putting their operations on something fragile.
A customer asks for a feature only they need. How do you decide whether to build it for them or push for it in the core product?
How you balance one customer's needs against the product as a whole.
Finding the general need behind the request, keeping true one-offs out of shared code, and sending repeated patterns to the product team.

I ask what problem sits under the request, because a one-off ask is often a common need in disguise. If other customers have the same need, I write it up for the product team with examples. If it is really unique, I build it as configuration or a separate extension, not a change to shared code, so it does not make every future upgrade harder.
A week after you ship a report, a finance analyst says your revenue numbers are 8% too high. What do you do?
How you handle your own mistake in front of a customer.
Owning it quickly, warning users, finding the root cause, fixing it, and adding a check so it cannot happen again.

I thank her and tell the report's users right away that the figures are under review. Then I trace it. An overcount like that often comes from a join that duplicates rows, such as orders matched to several address records. I fix it, show her the corrected numbers against her own totals, and add a daily check that compares our totals to the finance system.
The executive who signed the contract wants one thing, and the people who will use the tool want another. How do you handle it?
How you handle conflicting stakeholders inside a customer.
Making the conflict visible with evidence, tying the work to the sponsor's goal, and not quietly choosing a side.

I bring them together with facts. On one project the vice president wanted a forecast, while planners needed cleaner order data, because the forecast would be wrong without it. I showed her forecast errors caused by bad data and proposed two weeks on the data first, then the forecast. She agreed, because it served her goal. I don't quietly build what one side wants.

founders-office.heading: Founder’s office and special projects questions
qs: How is a founder's office role different from being the founder's executive assistant?
Whether you understand what the job is and what it is not.
You own outcomes on priority projects, not the calendar. You work with the founder's context but earn authority through results.

An assistant protects the founder's time. I take whole pieces of work off the founder's plate: a launch, a hiring push, a fundraise. I run it end to end, bring decisions back in short form, and then move to the next priority when the quarter changes.
How do you put together a board meeting pre-read?
Your grasp of how a board is kept informed.
It goes out days ahead and is short. It shows numbers against plan, states bad news honestly, and lists the decisions the board is asked to make.

I send it about a week ahead so directors read it before the meeting. It opens with a one-page summary, then key metrics against plan, cash and runway, and what went wrong. The last page lists the decisions we need, so the meeting is spent on discussion, not on reading slides.
Walk me through setting up a data room for a fundraise.
Whether you know what investors look at in due diligence.
Organized documents are ready before the first meeting: corporate records, cap table, financials, contracts, IP and people records, with access tracked.

I build the folders before outreach starts: incorporation and board documents, the cap table, financials and the model, key contracts, IP assignment agreements, and employee and option records. I work with our lawyers to find gaps early, like a missing IP assignment. I also track who opens what, so we can see which investors are serious.
In plain words, what is the difference between raising on a SAFE and raising a priced round?
Your grasp of basic startup financing terms.
A SAFE puts off setting a price and converts into shares later. A priced round sets a valuation and issues shares now.

A SAFE is a simple agreement for future equity. The investor pays now and gets shares later, usually at the next priced round, often with a valuation cap or a discount. A priced round sets a valuation today and issues preferred shares. It comes with more negotiated terms and more legal work.
The founder hands you a project called 'fix churn' and nothing else. What do you do in the first two weeks?
How you turn a vague mandate into a clear plan.
You define the problem with data and with people, agree on a measurable goal and owners, and bring back a plan before doing big work.

In week one I pull the numbers: who leaves, when, and from which plan. I also call ten customers who cancelled and talk to support and sales. In week two I bring the founder a one-page brief: the two biggest causes, a target we agree on, who owns each fix, and what I need from the founder.
You are asked to run the search for the company's first head of sales. How do you run it?
Whether you can run a senior hire without wasting the founder's time.
A written scorecard is agreed first. The process is structured, every finalist is assessed the same way, and references are checked with care.

First I write a scorecard with the founder: what this person must achieve in year one and which skills prove it. I screen candidates myself and only send the founder people who fit. Every finalist gets the same interviews and a practical exercise. Before any offer, I check references, including people who managed the candidate.
A department head sees you as the founder's spy and will not share data for your project. How do you handle it?
How you get work done through others without formal authority.
You build trust directly, share credit, and are open about your next steps. You go to the founder only as a last resort.

I meet them one on one and ask what worries them. I show them exactly what I need and why, and I offer to share my findings with them before the founder sees anything. Usually that is enough. If it is not, I tell them I will raise it with the founder, so nothing happens behind their back.
The founder makes a call you think is wrong, and the team asks you what is going on. What do you do?
Your judgement about loyalty, candor and the team.
You disagree with the founder in private and give reasons. Once the decision is made, you explain it to the team without undermining it.

I raise my concern with the founder in private, with evidence, before the decision is final if I can. Once it is decided, I explain the reasons to the team as clearly as I can and do not hint that I disagreed. If new facts show it is not working, I bring them back to the founder quickly.
Tell me about a project you kept alive too long. What did you learn?
Whether you can admit a mistake and stop work that is not paying off.
An honest story with the cost named, and a habit you use now, like setting stop criteria at the start.

I ran a partner program for seven months because we had announced it to the whole company. It brought in two small deals. I should have stopped at month three. Now every project I start has a written goal and a review date. If we miss the goal, I bring the founder a stop-or-change decision, not a status update.
Several people tell you a senior leader is losing their team, and that leader is the founder's close friend. What do you do?
How you handle sensitive people issues close to the founder.
You confirm it is a pattern, protect the people who spoke up, tell the founder plainly, and suggest a fair next step, not a verdict.

First I check that it is a pattern, not one bad week: people leaving, missed goals, what I see in meetings. Then I tell the founder in private, with facts, without naming people who asked to stay anonymous. I suggest a fair next step, like structured feedback or a coach. If any complaint could be a legal matter, I bring in HR.

fpga-engineer.heading: FPGA engineer questions
qs: In Verilog, when do you use blocking and when do you use nonblocking assignments?
Whether you know the basic coding rule that keeps simulation and hardware in agreement.
Nonblocking in clocked blocks, blocking in combinational blocks, and an understanding of why mixing them causes simulation races.

In a clocked always block I use nonblocking, <=, so every register updates from the values present at the clock edge, the way real flip-flops behave. In combinational logic I use blocking, =. I never mix both on one signal. That causes races where simulation order changes the result, and the simulation stops matching the hardware.
What makes a synthesis tool infer a latch, and why do you avoid it?
Whether you can spot a common coding mistake in combinational logic.
An output not assigned on every path, the reasons latches are a problem, and a habit that prevents them.

A latch appears when combinational logic does not assign an output on every path. Examples are an if without an else, or a case without a default. The tool must hold the old value, so it builds a latch. Latches are hard to time and are usually a bug. I give every output a default value at the top of the block, and I read the synthesis warnings for inferred latches.
Explain setup and hold time. Which one does a slower clock fix?
Your grasp of the timing basics behind every FPGA design.
Correct definitions, plus the point that a slower clock helps setup but does nothing for hold.

Setup time is how long data must be stable before the clock edge. Hold time is how long it must stay stable after the edge. A setup violation means the path is too slow for the clock period, so a slower clock fixes it. A hold violation means the data changes too soon after the edge. That does not depend on the period, so slowing the clock does not help.
How do you move a signal safely from one clock domain to another?
Whether you handle clock domain crossings for single bits and for buses.
A two-flop synchronizer for one bit, care with short pulses, and a FIFO or handshake for multi-bit data, never per-bit sync.

For one control bit I use a two-flop synchronizer in the receiving domain, which gives a metastable value time to settle. A short pulse from a faster clock can be missed, so I convert it to a toggle first. For a bus I never synchronize each bit separately, because bits can land in different cycles. I use an async FIFO with Gray-coded pointers, or a handshake that holds the data steady.
How do you design the reset, and what does asynchronous assert, synchronous deassert mean?
How you avoid reset problems that only show up on real hardware.
Reset goes active at any time but is released in step with each clock, and only registers that need a reset get one.

The reset can go active at any moment, even with no clock running. Its release is synchronized to each clock domain through a couple of flops. That way no register leaves reset right at a clock edge, which could free some registers a cycle before others. I also reset only what needs it, like state machines and valid flags. Data paths often don't, and that saves routing.
Timing analysis shows negative setup slack on one path at 250 MHz. Walk me through what you do.
How you close timing in a methodical way instead of trying random tool settings.
First check the constraints are right, then find whether logic or routing causes the delay, then fix the design before tuning the tools.

First I confirm the constraints are right: every clock defined, I/O delays correct. Then I see where the delay sits, too many logic levels or long routing. For logic, I add a pipeline register or restructure, like splitting a wide compare. For routing, I look for high fanout and duplicate the driving register. Only then do I try other placement strategies.
Your design passes every simulation but fails on the board. Where do you look?
How you debug the problems simulation cannot show.
Focus on what simulation does not model: constraints, clock crossings, reset and clocks, I/O, then capture real signals on chip.

I start with what simulation doesn't model. I check the timing report for unconstrained paths and undefined clocks. I review clock domain crossings and confirm the logic waits until the clocks are locked before leaving reset. Then I add an on-chip logic analyzer to the failing interface, trigger on the error, and compare the capture with the simulation waveform.
A colleague wants to put a false path on a failing path to close timing before a release. What do you say?
Your judgement on timing exceptions when there is pressure to ship.
A false path only when the path truly never needs to meet timing, documented; otherwise it hides a real failure and the fix belongs in the logic.

I'd ask why the path is false. If it goes through a proper synchronizer, or it's a config register that only changes while the logic is idle, the constraint is right, and we write down why. If it's a normal register-to-register path on one clock, a false path just hides the bug. The build passes and the board fails at random, maybe only when hot. Then we fix the logic or move the date.
For a low-latency trading design, how do you weigh pipeline depth against latency?
Whether you think about latency in real time, not just in clock cycles.
Latency is cycles times clock period, so more stages at a faster clock can win; keep only decision logic on the critical path.

Latency is cycles times the clock period, so I count in nanoseconds, not stages. Each register adds a cycle, but it can let the clock run faster. Ten stages at 400 MHz is 25 ns; eight at 250 MHz is 32 ns. I keep the path from packet in to order out short, run checks in parallel instead of one after another, and move anything not needed for the decision off that path.
Your design will fly on a satellite in an SRAM-based FPGA. How do you deal with radiation?
Whether you know how radiation affects FPGAs and the standard ways to protect a design.
Upsets hit both user logic and configuration memory; scrubbing, triple modular redundancy and ECC, verified with fault injection.

Radiation can flip bits, called single event upsets, in my registers and in the configuration memory that defines the circuit. I use scrubbing, which periodically checks and rewrites the configuration to fix flipped bits. Critical logic gets triple modular redundancy: three copies and a voter. Block RAM gets error-correcting codes, and I test it all by injecting faults on the ground.

fraud-analyst.heading: Fraud analyst questions
qs: What is the difference between first-party and third-party fraud?
Whether you know the basic types of fraud and who the victim is in each.
Third-party fraud is a stranger using someone else's identity or account. First-party fraud is the real customer lying, such as a false dispute.

In third-party fraud a stranger uses someone else's card or identity, so the account holder is a victim too. In first-party fraud the real customer is the fraudster, for example buying something and then claiming the charge was not theirs. They need different handling: the first gets a victim care process, the second does not.
What is synthetic identity fraud, and why is it hard to catch?
Your grasp of a fraud type that looks like a good customer for months.
Real and invented data are mixed into a new person, credit is built slowly, then the accounts are maxed out. No single victim reports it.

A fraudster mixes a real Social Security number, often a child's, with a made-up name and birth date. They pay small accounts on time for months, get higher limits, then max everything out and disappear. No real person notices and complains, so I look for thin credit files and for phones or addresses shared across many applications.
What signs tell you an account has been taken over?
Whether you can read the signs that someone else is inside a real customer's account.
A new device or location, then changes to contact details or password, then money moving out soon after. The sequence matters more than any one signal.

The pattern I watch is a login from a new device or an unusual location, then a password, email or phone change, then a new payee or a large transfer soon after. Any one alone is common. Together, in a short window, they are a strong sign. I would hold the payment and confirm with the customer through the contact details on file before the change.
At 3 a.m. you see hundreds of $1 authorizations on your checkout from different cards, most of them declined. What is happening and what do you do?
How you recognize card testing and respond while it is happening.
Names card testing, slows it fast with limits or challenges, and follows up on the cards that were approved.

That is card testing: someone checking which stolen card numbers still work. I would add velocity limits by IP, device and session, put a challenge such as a CAPTCHA on checkout, and alert the on-call engineer. Then I list the cards that were approved, void those charges and flag the cards, because they will be used for bigger fraud next.
A new-user promotion got 4,000 sign-ups in one day, and you suspect one group made many of them. How do you check?
Whether you can link accounts that pretend to be different people.
Looks for shared devices, cards, addresses and email patterns, and confirms a cluster by hand before acting on it.

I group the sign-ups by what is hard to fake: device fingerprint, payment card, IP range and delivery address, including small variations like 'Apt 2' and 'Unit 2'. Emails like jsmith1 and jsmith2 are another clue. When a cluster looks clear, I check a few accounts by hand, then cancel the promo credit for that cluster rather than banning every loose match.
A customer is about to send $9,000 to a 'bank security team' that told her to move her money to a safe account. What do you do?
How you protect a customer who is being scammed and is authorizing the payment herself.
Holds the payment, names the scam plainly and does not accept a coached answer. The customer is the victim here, not the suspect.

That is a known impersonation scam: no real bank asks you to move money to keep it safe. I would hold the payment, contact her directly, ask if someone is on the other line and explain the script calmly. Scammers coach victims to lie to us, so 'yes, it's me' does not end it. I would note everything and escalate if she still insists.
Walk me through how you test a new fraud rule before you turn it on.
Your method for proving a rule works before it touches real customers.
Backtests on past data with known outcomes, counts fraud caught against good customers hit, then runs it silently before going live.

First I backtest it on past transactions where we know the outcome, and count how much fraud it would catch and how many good customers it would hit. Then I run it in shadow mode for a week or two: it scores live traffic but blocks nothing. If the numbers hold, I turn it on, often as a review or extra check first, and watch decline rates daily.
Your new rule cut fraud losses by a third, but the sales team says good customers are being declined. How do you decide what to do?
How you weigh fraud losses against lost good business.
Puts both sides in dollars, including lost sales and customers who leave, then tunes the rule instead of just defending or dropping it.

I would put both sides in money. Fraud saved is easy to count. Then I estimate the good orders declined, using a sample of declined customers who later proved good, and add the value of those who stop buying. If that cost is higher than the savings, I narrow the rule or send borderline cases to review or extra verification instead of a hard decline.
Tell me about a time a rule or decision of yours caused a problem, and how you handled it.
Whether you own mistakes and fix the process, not just the single case.
Admits it fast, limits the harm to customers, and changes how future changes are checked.

I once shipped a rule with a wrong country code, so it flagged every order from a whole region. Declines jumped within an hour. I rolled it back, told my manager and support, and we contacted the 140 customers affected. After that our team added a second reviewer and a quick decline-rate check for every rule change.
If you work at a bank and a customer asks whether you reported them to the government, what do you say?
Whether you know the confidentiality rule for suspicious activity reports.
Never confirms or denies a report; federal law forbids disclosing one. Stays polite and tells compliance the customer asked.

I would not confirm or deny anything. Federal law forbids telling anyone involved, including the customer, that a suspicious activity report was filed or is being considered. I would say I can't discuss internal reviews, help with what I can in general terms, and let our compliance team know the customer asked.

fraud-risk.heading: Fraud and risk analyst questions
qs: What is the difference between a false positive and a false negative in fraud rules, and what does each one cost?
Whether you weigh both kinds of error, not only fraud caught.
Both errors defined, with a real cost on each side, and the idea that a rule is judged in dollars on both sides.

A false positive is a good customer we block or delay. It costs the sale, support time and sometimes the customer for good. A false negative is fraud we let through. It costs the goods, the chargeback and the fee. I put a dollar figure on both, because a rule that stops $1,000 of fraud but blocks $20,000 of good orders is a bad rule.
What is friendly fraud, and how do you tell it apart from true third-party fraud?
Whether you know the main dispute types and the data that separates them.
The real cardholder disputes a purchase they made; you compare device, address and history with past good orders.

Friendly fraud is when the real cardholder makes the purchase and then disputes it, saying they never ordered it or it never came. I check whether the device, IP address, shipping address and login history match that customer's past good orders, and whether the item was used or downloaded. A match on all of those points to the cardholder, not a thief.
What signs tell you a checkout is being hit by card testing, and what do you do first?
Whether you recognize a common attack pattern and act on it quickly.
Many small attempts, high declines, shared device or IP; a fast response with limits and a check of cards that got through.

A burst of small authorizations, often a dollar or less, with a high decline rate and many card numbers from one device, IP range or BIN, the first digits that identify the card issuer. I add velocity limits per device and IP, put a challenge such as a CAPTCHA on checkout, block the pattern, and then list the cards that were approved so they can be flagged.
Walk me through how a chargeback works from the merchant's side.
Your grasp of the dispute process and where the merchant can act.
Issuer, network and acquirer in the right order, reason codes and deadlines, and representment with evidence.

The cardholder disputes the charge with their issuing bank. The chargeback moves through the card network to our acquirer, and the money is pulled back, usually with a fee. We get a reason code and a deadline. If we fight it, we send representment: proof of delivery, matching address and device data, customer messages. If the issuer still rules against us, it can go to pre-arbitration or arbitration.
What does an account takeover look like in the data?
Whether you read events as a sequence rather than single flags.
New device or location, then quick changes to contact details or address, then a purchase or payout; the order and timing are the signal.

A login from a new device and place, often after failed attempts, then fast changes: password, email, phone, shipping address, followed by a purchase or payout. Each step alone is normal. The sequence in a short window is the signal. I would hold the transaction and confirm with the customer using the contact details that were on file before the change.
How do you test a new fraud rule before you turn it on?
Your method for launching rules without hurting good customers.
Backtesting on labeled history, a shadow period on live traffic, then a careful launch with monitoring.

I backtest it on several months of labeled data: how many known fraud cases it would have caught, how many good orders it would have hit, and the dollars on each side. Then I run it in shadow mode, scoring live traffic without acting, for a week or two. If the numbers hold, I launch it to a review queue before it ever hard-declines anyone.
A sales manager asks you to whitelist a large customer whose orders keep getting flagged. What do you do?
How you balance revenue pressure against risk.
Find the cause, tune narrowly instead of a full bypass, keep key checks on, and document the exception.

First I look at why the orders flag. If it is a known pattern, like big orders to a new warehouse, I can tune the rule for that account with limits, not a blanket whitelist. A full bypass is exactly what fraudsters exploit when they take over trusted accounts, so I keep account-change and velocity checks on, write down the exception and set a review date.
A rule you launched on Friday doubled declines on good orders over the weekend. What do you do on Monday?
How you own a mistake and fix both the damage and the process.
Stop the harm first, find the cause, recover customers where possible, and change the launch process.

First I roll the rule back or switch it to review-only so the damage stops. Then I pull the declined orders, find the condition that caught good customers, maybe a country list or a new payment method, and work with support to reach the ones we can win back. I write up what happened and add decline-rate alerts to every launch. No more Friday launches.
You suspect an employee is issuing refunds to their own card. How do you investigate?
How you handle an internal case with care for evidence and process.
Quiet data review, refunds matched to original sales, secure records, and HR, legal and security involved before any interview.

I quietly pull the refund logs: who issued each refund, to which card, and whether it matched an original sale. Refunds with no matching purchase, or many going to one card, are the core evidence. I keep everything documented and access-limited, I do not confront the employee myself, and I bring in HR, legal and security before anyone is interviewed.
At a bank, you find activity that may call for a Suspicious Activity Report. What can you tell the customer?
Whether you know the confidentiality rule around SARs.
Never reveal a SAR or anything that shows one exists; routine questions are fine; escalate through compliance.

Nothing about the SAR. Federal law bars disclosing a SAR, or anything that would reveal one exists, to the person involved. I can still ask normal questions about the activity as part of due diligence. I document the facts, escalate to the BSA officer, and let compliance decide on filing. Tipping off the customer can be a crime and can ruin the investigation.

freight-forwarding.heading: Freight and forwarding operations questions
qs: When would you book a shipment as LCL instead of a full container load?
Whether you know the basic ocean options and how to choose between them.
Explains that LCL shares a container and is priced by volume, while FCL is a whole box, and weighs cost, transit time and handling risk.

LCL means the cargo shares a container with other shippers and we pay by cubic meter. It suits small volumes, but it adds consolidation time and extra handling. Once the volume gets close to what a 20-foot box would cost, I price both, because FCL is often faster, safer and not much more expensive.
An air shipment is one pallet, 120 by 80 by 100 cm, weighing 90 kg. What weight will the airline charge?
Whether you can work out chargeable weight for air freight.
Knows the airline charges the greater of actual and volumetric weight and uses the standard divisor of 6,000 cubic cm per kg.

Airlines charge the greater of actual weight and volumetric weight. Volume is 120 x 80 x 100, so 960,000 cubic centimeters. Divided by 6,000, that is 160 kg. The actual weight is 90 kg, so we pay for 160 kg. I would tell the customer that a lower, stackable pallet could cut the cost.
What is the difference between a house bill of lading and a master bill of lading?
Your grasp of the core shipping documents and who issues them.
Master bill is issued by the ocean carrier to the forwarder; house bill is issued by the forwarder or NVOCC to its own customer.

The master bill is issued by the ocean carrier, usually with us as the shipper and our agent at destination as the consignee. The house bill is the one we issue as the NVOCC, meaning a carrier that does not run ships, to our customer, showing the real shipper and consignee. The cargo is released against the right bill at each level.
A buyer says they bought on FOB terms. What does that mean for who books and who carries the risk?
Whether you understand Incoterms and how they set your role in the shipment.
FOB is for sea freight: the seller loads the goods on board at the named port; risk passes then, and the buyer books and pays the main ocean freight.

Under FOB the seller clears the goods for export and loads them on board at the named port. Risk passes to the buyer once the goods are on board. The buyer books and pays the ocean freight, so we would take the booking from the buyer. FOB is meant for sea freight; for containers handed over at a terminal, FCA usually fits better.
What is an ISF filing and when must it be done for an ocean import into the US?
Your knowledge of US import security filing rules.
The Importer Security Filing, or 10+2, goes to CBP at least 24 hours before cargo is loaded on the vessel at the foreign port.

The ISF, often called 10+2, is a set of data elements the importer must send to US Customs and Border Protection for ocean cargo. It is due at least 24 hours before the container is loaded at the foreign port, not before arrival. Late or wrong filings can bring penalties and holds, so I chase the supplier details as soon as the booking is made.
Explain demurrage and detention, and how you keep a customer from paying them.
How well you know container charges and how you plan to avoid them.
Demurrage is for a container left at the terminal past free time; detention is for keeping the carrier's container outside too long. Planning pickup and return prevents both.

Demurrage is charged when a loaded container sits at the terminal past its free days. Detention is charged when the container is out of the terminal, at the customer, past its free days. I confirm free time when booking, get customs cleared before arrival, book the trucker early and remind the consignee of the return date.
The carrier rolls your customer's container to the next vessel, a week later. What do you do?
How you handle a service failure and keep the customer informed.
Tells the customer fast with facts, looks for a real alternative, and checks knock-on effects like deadlines and documents.

I tell the customer the same day, with the new vessel and arrival date, before they hear it elsewhere. Then I check other sailings or carriers that could beat that date and what they cost. I also check what the delay hits, such as a store launch or a letter of credit date, and update the documents and the delivery booking.
A customer wants to air ship 'electronics' and you learn they contain lithium batteries. What happens next?
Whether you treat dangerous goods by the rules and refuse shortcuts.
Holds the booking, gets the battery details and UN 38.3 test summary, and has trained staff classify, pack and declare under air rules.

Lithium batteries are regulated dangerous goods by air, so I would not book them as general cargo. I hold the booking and ask for the battery type, watt-hours, how they are packed and the UN 38.3 test summary. Then someone with current dangerous goods training classifies and declares them, or we move the cargo by sea if it cannot fly.
A customer complains the final invoice was much higher than your quote. How do you prevent that?
How you build complete quotes and own a pricing mistake.
An all-in quote listing origin, freight, surcharges and destination charges, with clear validity and exclusions, and honesty when a cost was missed.

I quote door to door in clear lines: pickup, origin charges, freight, fuel and other surcharges, destination charges and delivery. I state what is not included, like duties and storage, and how long the rate is valid. If a charge was missed on our side, I say so, and we discuss absorbing part of it instead of just sending the bill.
Cargo arrives with damaged cartons and the consignee wants the carrier to pay in full. What do you advise?
Whether you know the claim steps and the limits of carrier liability.
Note damage on the delivery receipt, take photos, notify the carrier in writing fast, and explain that carrier liability is limited, so insurance matters.

First, write the damage on the delivery receipt before signing and take photos of the cartons and contents. Keep the packaging. Then we send written notice to the carrier quickly, since the notice deadlines are short. I would be honest that carrier liability is limited by law per package or per kilo, so a full payout usually needs cargo insurance.

frontend-engineer.heading: Frontend engineer questions
qs: When do you use a button element and when do you use a link?
Whether you know that HTML elements carry meaning for keyboard and screen reader users.
Links go somewhere, buttons do something. A clickable div is not a substitute for either.
