A link navigates to a URL, so it belongs in an a tag with an href. A button triggers an action on the page, like opening a menu or submitting a form. Using the right one gives me keyboard support and the correct role for screen readers for free. A div with a click handler gets neither, so I would have to rebuild all of that by hand.
What is layout shift, and what usually causes it?
Your grasp of one of the Core Web Vitals and its everyday causes.
Content that moves after it appears. Usual causes: media without reserved space, late ads or banners, and web fonts swapping in.

It is when visible content moves after the page has drawn it, so someone taps the wrong thing. Google measures it as Cumulative Layout Shift. The usual causes are images without width and height, banners injected above content, and fonts that swap in at a different size. I reserve space with dimensions or aspect-ratio and give late content a fixed slot.
A designer wants light gray body text on a white background, and it fails the contrast check. What do you do?
How you balance a design request against accessibility rules.
Knows the WCAG AA ratio for body text, shows the problem with a tool, and offers a close color that passes instead of just refusing.

WCAG AA asks for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 for normal text and 3 to 1 for large text. I would run the colors through a contrast checker with the designer, then propose the lightest gray that passes so the look stays close. If the product has accessibility commitments I would mention them, but usually the side-by-side comparison settles it.
A teammate added lazy loading to every image, and now the main content of the page shows up later. Why?
Whether you understand how the browser prioritizes the largest image on the page.
The hero image is often the Largest Contentful Paint element, and lazy loading delays it. Load it eagerly, with high priority.

The big hero image is often what Largest Contentful Paint measures. With lazy loading, the browser waits until layout to know the image is in view, so the download starts late. I would remove lazy loading from images above the fold, add fetchpriority high on the hero, and keep lazy loading only for images further down the page.
Walk me through what a modal dialog must do for keyboard and screen reader users.
Your knowledge of focus management in one of the most common components.
Focus moves in and stays in, Escape closes it, focus returns to the trigger, and the background is inert. Knows the native dialog element.

When it opens, focus moves inside, usually to the heading or the first control. Tab stays within the dialog and the page behind cannot be reached. Escape closes it, and focus goes back to the button that opened it. It also needs an accessible name. The native dialog element opened with showModal handles most of this, so I start there before building my own.
After someone clicks Add to cart, the cart count updates but a screen reader user hears nothing. How do you fix it?
Whether you know how to announce changes that happen without a page load.
A polite live region that is already in the page before its text changes, with a short, clear message, tested with a real screen reader.

I would add a live region, for example an element with role status, which screen readers announce politely when its text changes. It has to be in the page from the start; if I insert it together with the message, many screen readers miss it. Then I set its text to something short like 'Added to cart, 3 items' and test it with an actual screen reader.
After a merge, the JavaScript bundle grew by 200 KB. How do you find out why and fix it?
How you investigate and control what your code ships to the browser.
Compares builds with a bundle analyzer, finds the cause, then trims or splits it. Adds a size budget so it cannot happen silently again.

I run a bundle analyzer on the build before and after the merge and compare. Often it is a whole library imported for one function, or a date library pulling in every locale. I import only the piece needed, swap in a lighter option, or load it with a dynamic import on the screen that uses it. Then I add a size check to CI so the next jump fails the build.
Typing in a search box that filters a list of 5,000 rows feels laggy. How do you approach it?
How you diagnose slow interactions, the kind measured by Interaction to Next Paint.
Profiles first, then cuts the work done per keystroke: render only visible rows, avoid needless re-renders, keep the input itself responsive.

I record a profile in the browser dev tools while typing to see whether time goes to filtering or to rendering. Usually it is rendering thousands of rows, so I virtualize the list and draw only what is visible. I keep the input updating at once and let the list follow a moment later, with a debounce or React's useDeferredValue, and check that nothing unrelated re-renders.
In a server-rendered React app you see a hydration mismatch warning. What causes it, and how do you fix it?
Whether you understand why server and client rendering must agree.
The first client render differs from the server HTML, often due to time, random values, locale or browser-only checks. Match first, update after mount.

Hydration attaches React to HTML the server already sent, so the first client render must produce the same markup. Mismatches come from things like the current time, random IDs, locale formatting, or reading window during render. I make the first render match, use useId for IDs, and move browser-only values into an effect that runs after mount.
Your shared component library needs to change the Button props in a way that breaks existing uses. How do you roll it out?
How you manage change in code that many teams depend on.
Old and new side by side when possible, deprecation warnings, a migration guide or codemod, and removal only in a major version with a date.

First I check whether the new API can live next to the old one. If so, the old props keep working with a warning in development, and I document the migration, ideally with a codemod that rewrites call sites. Removal goes in a major version under semantic versioning, announced ahead. Before picking a date, I search the product code to see how many uses each team has.

full-stack-engineer.heading: Full-stack engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between a 401 and a 403 response, and when do you send each?
Whether you use HTTP status codes the way clients expect.
401 means the caller is not authenticated; 403 means they are known but not allowed. Bonus: sometimes 404 hides that a resource exists.

I send 401 when there is no valid login, like a missing or expired token, so the front end knows to send the user to sign in. I send 403 when we know who you are but you lack permission. For private records I may return 404 so a stranger cannot even learn the record exists.
The sign-up form already checks every field in the browser. Why validate again on the server?
Whether you know the browser is not a trusted place.
Anyone can skip the form and call the API directly; client checks are for user comfort, server checks are for correctness and security.

The browser checks are there so people get quick feedback. They protect nothing, because anyone can send a request with a script and skip the form entirely. The server is the only place I control, so it checks types, lengths, formats and permissions on every request, and the database adds constraints as a last line.
How do you stop SQL injection in code that builds queries from user input?
Your grasp of a basic security risk in database code.
Parameterized queries or a query builder that binds values; never glue strings into SQL. Allowlists for things that cannot be parameters, like column names.

I never put user input into the SQL string. I use parameterized queries, so the database gets the query and the values separately and a value can never become code. Column names and sort directions cannot be parameters, so I map them from an allowlist, like sort=price becomes a known column name, and reject anything else.
How should a product store user passwords?
Whether you know safe password storage.
A slow, salted password hash such as Argon2, bcrypt or scrypt. Never plain text, never reversible encryption, never a fast hash like MD5 or plain SHA-256.

I store only a hash made with a slow algorithm built for passwords, like Argon2 or bcrypt, which adds a unique salt per user. At login I hash what was typed and compare. Fast hashes are wrong here because an attacker with a leaked table can try billions of guesses a second. And nobody, including support, should be able to see a password.
The front end calls your API and the browser console shows a CORS error. What is going on and how do you fix it?
Whether you understand how browsers enforce cross-origin rules.
The browser blocks the response because the server did not allow that origin. Fix it on the server with an allowlist, not by turning checks off.

CORS is the browser protecting the user: a page from one origin can only read a response from another origin if that server says so. The same call works from curl, which proves the API is fine. I set Access-Control-Allow-Origin on the server for our real front-end origins, make sure OPTIONS preflight requests are answered, and avoid a wildcard for anything that uses cookies.
A list page is slow and the query filters by customer and sorts by date. How do you decide whether to add an index?
How you reason about indexes and their cost.
Read the query plan first, index for the filter and sort together, and remember every index slows writes and takes space.

First I run EXPLAIN to see if the database scans the whole table. If it does, a composite index on customer_id then created_at lets it find that customer's rows already in date order. Column order matters: the filter column goes first. I check that the table is not write-heavy enough for the extra index to hurt inserts, then compare the plan and timing after.
When would you use cursor pagination instead of page numbers with an offset?
Your understanding of how pagination behaves on large, changing data.
Offset gets slower deep in a list and skips or repeats rows when data changes; a cursor continues from the last row seen using an index.

Offset is fine for small admin tables. But OFFSET 50000 still makes the database walk past 50,000 rows, and if new rows arrive while someone scrolls, they see duplicates. For feeds I return a cursor, like the last created_at and id, and the next query asks for rows before that pair. It stays fast with the right index and never shifts.
Where would you keep a user's login on the web: a token in local storage or a cookie? Why?
Whether you weigh session security choices on the client.
An HttpOnly, Secure cookie with SameSite set keeps the token away from scripts; local storage is readable by any script, so one XSS bug leaks it. Mention CSRF.

I prefer a session cookie marked HttpOnly, so page scripts cannot read it, Secure, so it only travels over HTTPS, and SameSite=Lax, which blocks most cross-site requests. A token in local storage is readable by any script, so one XSS bug hands it to an attacker. Cookies bring CSRF risk, so state-changing requests also need a CSRF token or similar check.
You need to rename a field in an API response, but users have the old front end open in their browsers. How do you ship it?
How you change contracts between front end and back end without breaking live users.
Expand then contract: add the new field alongside the old one, move clients over, watch usage, and remove the old field only when nothing reads it.

I never rename in one step. First the API returns both full_name and the old name. Then I ship the front end that reads full_name. Open tabs and cached apps keep working on the old field. I log or measure who still reads the old one, and after a few weeks with no use, I remove it. Database columns follow the same pattern.
Users type fast in a search box and sometimes see results for an earlier word, not what they typed. What is wrong and how do you fix it?
Whether you spot a race condition between requests and the screen.
Responses arrive out of order and an old one overwrites a newer one. Cancel or ignore stale requests, and debounce to send fewer.

Each keystroke sends a request, and a slow response for "sho" can arrive after the one for "shoes" and overwrite it. I fix it in two ways: wait about 300 milliseconds after typing stops before sending, and cancel the previous request with an AbortController or tag each request with an id and drop any response that is not the latest.

game-artist.heading: Game and concept artist questions
qs: Why does the silhouette of a character matter so much in a game?
Whether you design for how a character reads in play, not only in a close-up painting.
Players often see characters small, fast or in the dark, so the shape alone must say who they are and what they do.

In play, a character is often a few dozen pixels tall and moving. If I fill the shape in solid black, I should still know the class and the threat level. I test that with thumbnails before I add any detail, because detail never saves a weak silhouette.
How do you check that a scene or key art reads clearly before you add color and detail?
Your control of value, the light and dark structure under the color.
Working in a few grouped values first, and checking in grayscale that the focal point has the strongest contrast.

I block the scene in three or four values first: background, middle ground, foreground and the focal point. Then I flip the image to grayscale and mirror it now and then. If the eye doesn't land where the player needs to look, I fix the values before I touch color.
What does a 3D modeler need from your character sheet to build the model without guessing?
Whether your concepts are usable for production, not just nice to look at.
Front, side and back views that line up, scale next to a reference, material callouts and close-ups of tricky parts.

I give an orthographic turnaround, front, side and back, with the proportions lined up across views. I add a height reference, callouts for materials like worn leather or brushed steel, and close-ups of buckles or how armor plates overlap. I also note what is hard surface and what is cloth that will move.
In a PBR workflow, what belongs in the base color map and what should stay out of it?
Your grasp of how physically based materials work in a game engine.
Base color holds the surface color only; lighting, shadows and shine are left out because the engine and other maps handle them.

The base color, or albedo, is the color of the surface without light on it. I keep baked shadows and highlights out, because the engine lights the asset and baked light would look wrong when it moves. Roughness, metalness and ambient occlusion go in their own maps.
What is texel density, and why do you keep it consistent?
Whether you understand a core technical rule of game texturing.
Texture pixels per unit of world space; consistent density keeps assets equally sharp next to each other and spends memory well.

Texel density is how many texture pixels cover one unit of the world, for example per meter. If a crate is sharp and the wall behind it is blurry, the scene looks broken. I set the project's target, check it while I lay out UVs, and only break it on purpose, like giving more to a hero prop the camera gets close to.
The art director needs twenty enemy variations by the end of tomorrow. How do you approach it?
How you produce volume fast without losing quality or consistency.
Quick thumbnails, a clear set of things that vary, an early check-in, then refinement of only the chosen few.

I would not paint twenty finished pieces. I'd agree first on what varies: body shape, weapon, color by rank. Then I do forty fast silhouette thumbnails in an hour or two, show them by midday, and refine the picks. Sharing early keeps me from polishing designs that get cut.
You join a project mid-way and the art bible has a style you would not have chosen. What do you do?
Whether you can serve an established style instead of your own taste.
Studying the art bible and existing assets, matching them closely, and raising concerns with examples through the right channel.

I study the art bible and paint a few studies of existing assets until my work blends in. A game with mixed styles looks worse than one with a style I don't love. If I see a real problem, say characters getting lost against the backgrounds, I bring a side-by-side example to the lead rather than quietly drifting.
Your character looked great in the concept, but in the engine it reads as muddy and noisy. What went wrong and how do you fix it?
How you diagnose the gap between a painting and the real game view.
Checking at the real camera distance and lighting, then simplifying detail and pushing larger shapes and value contrast.

Usually I designed it at close-up size. At the gameplay camera, fine detail turns into noise and similar values merge. I grab screenshots from the real camera in a few lighting setups, then simplify: bigger shape breaks, fewer small details, stronger contrast between main parts. For future concepts I add a small in-game-size view to every sheet.
How do you use photo reference and photobashing without creating legal problems for the studio?
Whether you know the basic rules of using other people's images in commercial work.
Using only own photos, licensed or properly cleared images in final work, and never copying another artist's work.

Reference I only look at can come from anywhere. Anything that ends up in the image itself must be my own photo or come from a source whose license covers commercial use, and I keep a note of the source. I never paint over another artist's work. If I'm unsure about a license, I ask before the piece ships, not after.
Playtesters keep missing the ledges they can climb and the objects they can use. How would you fix that through the art?
How you shape the environment so it guides play, not just looks good.
A consistent visual language for interactive things, kept rare elsewhere, with value and color contrast, then retesting with players.

I'd give interactive things one clear rule, for example worn light-colored edges on every climbable ledge, and keep that look off everything decorative. I'd quiet the background detail around paths so they stand out in value. Then I'd watch new playtests; if people still miss a spot, that spot needs work, not the player.

game-designer.heading: Game designer questions
qs: What is a core loop, and what was the core loop of a game you worked on?
Whether you know the basic unit of game design and can name one from your own work.
A clear definition, then a real loop with an action, a reward and a reason to repeat it.

A core loop is the set of actions the player repeats most, plus the reward that sends them back in. On my last project, a small dungeon game, it was: explore a floor, fight, collect loot, upgrade gear at camp, then go deeper. Every new feature had to feed that loop, or we asked hard questions about it.
How do you teach a new mechanic in a level without a text tutorial?
Your grasp of level design as a teaching tool.
A step-by-step method: safe first contact, practice, a real test, then a twist, with the level itself guiding the player.

I use introduce, practice, test, twist. The player first meets the mechanic where failure is cheap, like a wall jump over a short gap with no pit below. Then a few easy repeats, then a test with real stakes, then a twist that mixes it with something they know. Level shape and lighting point the way, so I rarely need text.
What are sources and sinks in a game economy, and why do they matter?
Whether you understand how in-game currency stays balanced over time.
Sources add currency, sinks remove it; if sources outrun sinks, inflation follows. Bonus for modeling it and watching data after launch.

Sources, or faucets, are where currency enters: quest rewards, drops, daily gifts. Sinks are where it leaves: repairs, upgrades, fees, consumables. If sources outrun sinks, players pile up gold, prices climb and rewards stop meaning anything. I model both per hour of play in a spreadsheet, then watch average balances by player level after launch.
A rare item has a 5% drop chance per kill. How many kills does it take, and how will players feel about it?
Your basic probability and whether you think about how random rewards feel.
The average is 20 kills, but many players need far more. A good answer spots the unlucky tail and offers a fix like a pity timer.

On average it takes 20 kills, but about 36 percent of players will still have nothing after 20, and some will go past 60. That long tail feels unfair. If the item matters, I would add a pity timer that guarantees it after a set number of tries, or raise the odds a little after each miss.
Playtesters find one weapon that beats everything else. What do you do?
How you handle a dominant strategy without breaking what players enjoy.
Finding the cause first, using data not just complaints, small changes tested one at a time, and preferring counters over heavy nerfs.

First I find out why it wins: are the numbers off, or is there no counter to it? I look at pick rate and win rate, not just complaints. If it is numbers, I make small changes one at a time and retest. If it is a design gap, I would rather add a counter than nerf it into the ground, because players chose it for a reason.
Data shows a lot of players quit during level 3. Walk me through how you find out why.
Your method for diagnosing a player problem from data and observation.
Starting from data to find the exact spot, then watching real players, fixing the cause and measuring the result.

I start with data: where exactly they quit, how long they spent, how often they died. Then I watch recordings or run a playtest of that level without helping. Last time, players did not read a door as a door and wandered for ten minutes. We changed the lighting and added a sound cue, and completion went from about 55 to 80 percent.
How do you make a game work for both new players and experts?
How you think about difficulty and challenge for different skill levels.
A fair baseline plus optional depth, lower cost of failure, and testing with both groups, not just the team.

I set a baseline that a new player can finish with some effort, then give experts optional depth: harder side paths, time goals, hidden challenges. Difficulty modes help, but so do things like checkpoints, which make failure cost less without making the game easier. I test with both groups, because the team is always too good at its own game.
The producer wants to cut a feature you designed to save schedule. How do you respond?
Your judgement on scope and whether you can trade off without ego.
Weighing the feature against the core experience, accepting cuts that do not hurt it, and offering a smaller version when it matters.

I ask what the feature costs and what it does for the player. If the core loop works without it, I agree and keep notes so we can add it in an update. If it carries the game, I offer a smaller version. On one project we cut a full crafting tree down to six recipes, which kept the hook and saved about four weeks.
You are asked to add a mechanic that pushes players to spend more money. How do you approach it?
Whether you can design monetization that earns money without tricking players.
Asking about the real goal, offering fair options, and pushing back on manipulative tactics with reasons the business cares about.

I first ask what goal we need to hit, then offer options that earn without tricking players: cosmetics, a fair season pass, prices shown clearly in real money. I push back on fake countdown timers, hidden odds or pay-to-win items. They hurt trust, reviews and long-term revenue, and some bring legal risk. If we sell random items, the odds should be shown.
Tell me about a design change you made that made the game worse. How did you catch it?
How you own a mistake and what process you changed because of it.
A specific change, honest about the cause, a quick fix, and a lasting lesson about testing or data.

On a mobile puzzle game I cut the time limit on later levels by 10 percent because testers said they were too easy. Those testers were veterans. In the soft launch, a small early release, quit rates on those levels doubled. I rolled it back and retested with new players. Now I always ask who the testers are before I trust what they say.

game-developer.heading: Game developer questions
qs: Why do we multiply movement by delta time, and what goes wrong if we forget?
Whether you understand frame-rate independence, the first thing every game loop needs.
Delta time is the time since the last frame. Without it, speed depends on frame rate and the game plays differently on every machine.

Delta time is how many seconds passed since the last frame. If I move a character 5 units every frame, it runs twice as fast at 120 fps as at 60. Moving 5 units per second times delta time gives the same speed on any machine. I forgot it once in a game jam and the game was unplayable on a fast laptop.
What is your frame budget at 60 fps, and how do you split it?
Whether you think about performance in milliseconds, not just frames per second.
About 16.7 ms per frame at 60 fps (33.3 ms at 30), shared by gameplay, physics, animation and rendering, with headroom left for spikes.

At 60 fps one frame is about 16.7 milliseconds; at 30 fps it is 33.3. I agree a rough split with the team, for example a few milliseconds for gameplay and physics and most of the rest for rendering. I keep a margin, because a frame that averages 16 ms will still miss when an explosion spawns. I talk in milliseconds because fps numbers do not add up.
The game runs at 40 fps on the target hardware. How do you find out what is slowing it down?
Your method for profiling before you optimize.
Measure first: compare CPU and GPU frame times in a profiler, find the bottleneck, then drill into the slowest systems instead of guessing.

I profile a build close to release settings, not the editor. I compare CPU and GPU frame times. If the GPU is the long one, I drop the render resolution: if the frame rate jumps, I am pixel bound. If the CPU is long, I open the CPU timeline and look for the biggest blocks, like pathfinding or too many draw calls. I fix the largest one and measure again.
The game holds 60 fps but hitches for a moment every few seconds. What do you suspect?
Whether you can read a spike pattern and know the usual causes of hitches.
Spikes, not average cost: garbage collection, asset loading or shader compilation. Find the spike frame in the profiler, then fix the cause, such as per-frame allocations.

A regular hitch smells like garbage collection. I capture the spike frame in the profiler and look at memory allocated per frame. Often it is bullets created and destroyed, or strings built every update. I pool the bullets, cache the strings, and allocations drop to near zero. If it is not memory, I check for loading or shaders compiling the first time they are used.
Why would you run physics on a fixed timestep when rendering runs at a variable rate?
Your grasp of the game loop and of stable, repeatable simulation.
A fixed step keeps physics stable and repeatable. An accumulator runs as many steps as time allows, and rendering interpolates between the last two states.

Physics behaves badly with a changing step: springs explode and jumps reach different heights. So I add each frame's time to an accumulator and run physics in fixed steps, say 1/60 of a second, while the accumulator has enough. Rendering then blends between the last two physics states, so motion looks smooth even when frame rate and physics rate differ.
A fast projectile sometimes passes straight through a thin wall. How do you fix it?
Whether you recognize tunneling and know the standard fixes.
The object jumps past the wall between two physics steps. Use a raycast or sweep along its path, or continuous collision detection, rather than just thickening walls.

That is tunneling: in one physics step the bullet is in front of the wall, in the next it is behind it, so they never overlap. For a bullet I cast a ray from the old position to the new one each step and hit whatever is in between. For bigger fast objects I turn on continuous collision detection for that body only, because it costs more than the default check.
A designer asks for a grappling hook two weeks before a milestone. How do you respond?
How you weigh a design request against scope and schedule.
Neither yes nor no at once: estimate it, offer a quick prototype or smaller version, and make the trade-off visible to whoever owns the schedule.

I ask what problem the hook solves for the player. Then I give an honest estimate: a rough prototype in two days, a polished version with animation and edge cases in maybe three weeks. I suggest the prototype once the milestone build is safe, we playtest it, and the producer decides what it replaces. Saying yes quietly and slipping the milestone helps no one.
In an online shooter, a player swears they hit an enemy on their screen, but the server said miss. What is going on, and what would you do?
Your understanding of latency, server authority and lag compensation.
Each client sees others slightly in the past. The server stays authoritative, and lag compensation rewinds targets to what the shooter saw, within a limit.

The shooter sees the enemy where it was some milliseconds ago, because of latency and interpolation. The server checks the hit against where the enemy is now, so it misses. I keep the server authoritative to stop cheating and add lag compensation: the server stores recent positions and rewinds targets to the time the shooter saw, with a cap on how far back.
A patch you shipped breaks old save files for some players. Walk me through what you do.
How you handle a live mistake and protect player data.
Stop the damage first, keep the broken saves, fix it with a versioned migration, and add old saves to the tests so it cannot happen again.

First I make sure the game does not overwrite the old files, and we tell players not to delete them. I find which field changed, then write a loader that reads the save's version number and converts old formats step by step. We ship a hotfix, and I add saves from every past version to our automated tests so the next change is checked against them.
In a large open world, objects far from the starting point begin to jitter. Why, and how do you fix it?
Whether you understand floating-point precision limits in big game worlds.
32-bit floats lose precision as numbers grow. Keep the play area near the origin by shifting the world, or use double precision for positions.

Positions are usually 32-bit floats, which hold about seven significant digits. Around 10 kilometers from the origin the smallest step is close to a millimeter, so the camera and animation start to shake. I would move the world origin with the player: when they go far enough, shift everything back toward zero. Some engines also offer 64-bit positions for this.

game-programmer.heading: Game programmer questions
qs: Why do you multiply movement by delta time, and when would you not?
Whether you understand how frame rate affects gameplay code.
Movement must not depend on frame rate. Physics usually runs on a fixed step instead, so its code uses the fixed step, not the render delta.

Delta time is the time since the last frame. If I add speed times delta time each frame, a character covers the same distance per second at 30 or 144 fps. Physics is different: I run it on a fixed timestep, so results stay stable and repeatable whatever the frame rate is.
What is your frame budget at 60 frames per second, and how do you use it?
Your sense of performance as a hard limit, not a nice-to-have.
About 16.7 ms per frame for everything, split between systems and checked in the profiler regularly, not only at the end.

At 60 fps I have about 16.7 milliseconds per frame; at 30 fps about 33.3. Logic, physics, animation, audio and render submission all share it. On our last project each system had a target, physics around 2 ms, and we checked a profile capture on every nightly build, so a regression showed up the day it landed.
Why do engines store rotations as quaternions instead of three angles?
Your grasp of the 3D math behind cameras, animation and movement.
Euler angles can hit gimbal lock and interpolate badly. Quaternions avoid gimbal lock and blend smoothly between two rotations.

With three angles, when two rotation axes line up you lose one degree of freedom. That is gimbal lock, and the camera or bone flips or sticks. Quaternions do not have that problem, they are cheap to combine, and spherical interpolation gives a smooth, even turn between two orientations. I still show angles to designers in the editor because they are easier to read.
A fast projectile sometimes passes straight through a thin wall. What is going on and how do you fix it?
Whether you can spot tunneling and know the standard fixes.
Names tunneling and gives fixes: a sweep or raycast between positions, continuous collision detection, thicker colliders, with their costs.

That is tunneling. In one physics step the bullet is in front of the wall, in the next it is already behind it, so the shapes never overlap. For bullets I cast a ray from the old position to the new one each step. For bigger fast objects I turn on continuous collision detection, but only on those objects, because it costs more.
Players report a short hitch every few seconds, even in an empty room. How do you find the cause?
How you track down a regular stutter with a profiler instead of guessing.
Captures the spike frame, checks for garbage collection or loading, finds per-frame allocations and removes them with reuse or pooling.

A regular hitch that does not depend on what is on screen often means garbage collection. I capture a profile, jump to the spike frame and see what ran. Then I look at memory allocated per frame: string building in an update loop, new lists, temporary arrays. I reuse buffers and pool objects like bullets and effects, then check the allocation counter stays near zero.
The frame rate drops in one area of the level. How do you tell if you are CPU-bound or GPU-bound?
Your method for diagnosing a slow frame before optimizing anything.
Measures first: profiler timings and a quick test like lowering resolution, then targets the side that is actually late.

I first look at the profiler to see whether the CPU is waiting on the GPU or the other way round. A quick test helps: if I drop the render resolution and frame time improves, pixel work on the GPU is the limit. If nothing changes, I look at the CPU side, like too many draw calls, AI or animation updates. I only optimize once I know which side is late.
A designer says the jump feels floaty. What do you change?
Whether you can turn a feel note into concrete code changes and tools for designers.
Knows common game feel techniques and exposes the values as tunables so the designer can iterate without a programmer.

I would ask to play it with them first. Common fixes: stronger gravity on the way down than on the way up, cutting the jump short when the button is released, a few frames of grace to jump after leaving a ledge, and buffering a jump pressed just before landing. I put every value in the editor so the designer can tune it live.
In a large open world, objects far from the start start to jitter. Why, and what do you do?
Your understanding of floating point precision in world coordinates.
Explains that 32-bit floats lose precision as values grow, and fixes it by shifting the world origin or using doubles for positions.

A 32-bit float keeps only about seven significant digits, so the farther from the origin, the bigger the gap between values it can store. Far out, positions snap between those values and things shake. I would move the world origin to stay near the player and shift everything by that offset, or store world positions in doubles and convert to local floats for rendering.
In our online shooter, players complain they got hit after they were already behind cover. Is that a bug, and what do you do?
Your knowledge of network latency handling and the tradeoffs it forces.
Explains server-side lag compensation, why it favors the shooter, and limits it, for example a cap on how far back the server rewinds.

Often it is lag compensation working as designed. The server keeps a short history of hitbox positions, rewinds to what the shooter saw, and checks the hit there. That makes aiming fair, but the target may already be behind cover on his own screen. I would check that the rewind is capped, so very laggy players cannot hit from far in the past, and log real cases to see if anything is off.
The day before a console certification submission, QA finds a rare crash. Do you fix it or ship?
Your judgement on risk when a late fix could cause more harm than the bug.
Weighs how often and how badly it happens against the risk of the fix, decides with QA and production, and plans a patch if it ships.

I would first get a repro rate and a call stack. If it can crash a player during normal play and the fix is small and contained, I make it, have a second programmer review it, and QA retests that area. If the fix touches shared systems, I would raise it with the producer and QA lead, ship with the known issue documented, and put the fix in the first patch.

general-counsel.heading: General counsel questions
qs: As general counsel, who is your client?
Whether you know you represent the company, not the CEO or any one officer.
The organization is the client, acting through its board and officers, with clear lines when a person's interests split from the company's.

The company is my client. I take direction from the CEO and the board because they act for it, but I do not represent them personally. If an officer's interests split from the company's, I say so plainly and tell them they may want their own lawyer. That keeps the advice honest and the privilege with the company.
A manager copies you on every email so it will be privileged. Does that work?
Your grasp of when attorney-client privilege actually covers in-house communications.
Privilege covers confidential communications made to get legal advice. Copying a lawyer on business email does not create it, and overuse weakens real claims.

No. Privilege protects confidential communications made to get or give legal advice. Courts look at the main purpose of the message, and they look harder at in-house lawyers, since we also give business advice. A cc on routine email adds nothing. I would show the manager how to send me a direct question, marked as a request for legal advice, and keep the wider thread clean.
Walk me through putting a litigation hold in place.
Whether you can preserve evidence correctly once a dispute is expected.
Acting when litigation is reasonably anticipated, not only when served, and covering people, systems, auto-deletion and follow-up.

The duty starts when we reasonably expect a lawsuit, so a demand letter can trigger it. I identify the people and systems involved, send a written hold in plain language, and have IT suspend auto-delete for those accounts, chats and phones. Each person confirms in writing. I send reminders, add people as facts emerge, and release the hold only when the matter is over.
You are about to interview an employee in an internal investigation. What do you tell them first?
Whether you know the Upjohn warning and why it matters.
You represent the company, not them; the talk is privileged, but the privilege belongs to the company, which may waive it and share what they say.

I tell them I am a lawyer for the company, not for them. What we discuss is privileged, but the privilege belongs to the company, and the company can decide to waive it and share it, including with the government. I ask them to keep the talk confidential and note in my file that I gave the warning. Skipping it can hurt both the privilege and the employee's trust.
How do you decide what to send to outside counsel, and how do you keep the spend under control?
How you run a legal budget and match work to the right lawyers.
Clear criteria for sending work out, plus budgets, staffing rules and regular review of bills against results.

Routine contracts, employment questions and policy work stay in-house. I send out major litigation, deals outside our expertise, and anything needing a specialist or local counsel. Each matter gets a written budget and staffing plan. I read the bills monthly, push back on padded hours, and use fixed fees where work is predictable. Last year that cut our outside spend by about 18%.
The CEO wants to sign a deal this week that you think carries real legal risk. What do you do?
Your judgement in advising on risk while leaving business calls to the business.
Explains the risk in business terms, offers ways to reduce it, and accepts the business decision unless it is illegal, with the advice documented.

I explain the risk in business terms: what could go wrong, how likely it is, what it could cost. Then I bring options, like an indemnity, a cap on liability or a short delay to finish diligence. If the risk is lawful and the CEO accepts it, that is their call, and I put my advice in writing. If the deal would break the law, I say no and take it to the board if needed.
You find evidence the CFO may be booking revenue early to hit targets. What do you do?
Whether you know your duty to report up the ladder when an officer may be breaking the law.
Preserves evidence, does not tip off the officer, reports to the CEO and audit committee, and pushes for an independent investigation.

I preserve the records first and do not tip off the CFO. The professional rules, and for public companies the SEC's attorney conduct rules, require me to report evidence of a material violation up the ladder. Because the CFO is involved, I go to the CEO and the audit committee chair, and recommend the committee hire independent counsel and forensic accountants.
How do you help the board make a big decision that will hold up if a shareholder sues?
Your understanding of directors' fiduciary duties and the business judgment rule.
A careful, informed process: full information in time, conflicts disclosed, independent advice, and minutes that show real deliberation.

Courts generally defer to directors under the business judgment rule if they acted informed, in good faith and without conflicts. So I build the record: materials sent days ahead, expert advisers present, conflicts disclosed and conflicted directors recused. My minutes show the options weighed, not a script. A good process protects directors more than a good outcome does.
IT tells you on a Friday night that customer data may have been stolen. What do you do in the first 48 hours?
How you lead an incident response with legal duties, privilege and deadlines in mind.
Containment with IT, outside counsel directing forensics, mapping state, contract and regulator notice duties, and one voice to the outside.

I convene the response team while IT contains the attack. Outside breach counsel hires the forensic firm to support privilege, though courts do not always protect those reports. We work out whose data was taken: state notice laws differ and customer contracts may set short deadlines. If we are public, I start the SEC materiality analysis. One channel handles all outside statements.
You find the standard severance agreement bars departing employees from contacting any government agency. What do you do?
Whether you can spot and fix a contract term that breaks whistleblower protection rules.
Knows the SEC rule against impeding whistleblowers and other legal limits, fixes the template, and deals with agreements already signed.

I pull the template right away. The SEC bars any action that impedes someone from reporting possible securities violations to it, and it has fined companies for clauses like this. Other agencies and labor law limit such terms too. I add a clear carve-out for reporting to any government agency, and I consider telling past signers in writing that the clause will not be enforced.

general-manager.heading: General manager questions
qs: What is the difference between gross margin and contribution margin, and when does each matter?
Whether you know the P&L measures you will be judged on.
Gross margin takes out cost of goods sold; contribution margin takes out all variable costs. Contribution is the one for volume and pricing decisions.

Gross margin is revenue minus cost of goods sold, which can include fixed factory costs. Contribution margin is revenue minus only the costs that move with volume, like materials, freight and commissions. When I decide on a price or an extra order, I use contribution, because it shows what each extra sale really adds toward fixed costs and profit.
Your unit made a profit last year but ran short of cash. How can that happen?
Whether you understand that profit and cash are not the same thing.
Names the usual causes: growing receivables, inventory build, capital spending, debt payments. Then says how to fix them.

Profit counts sales when they are earned, not when customers pay. If we grew fast, receivables and inventory soak up cash before it comes back. Capital spending and loan repayments also use cash without hitting profit in full. I would look first at how many days customers take to pay and how many days of stock we hold, then tighten collection and cut slow stock.
Revenue is on plan for the quarter, but operating profit is three points below. Where do you look first?
How you find the cause of a margin gap in the P&L.
A structured walk from plan to actual: price and mix, then volume-driven costs, then fixed costs and one-offs, before acting.

I build a walk from plan to actual, one cause at a time. First price and mix: are we selling more low-margin products or giving bigger discounts? Then variable costs like materials, freight and overtime. Then fixed costs and one-offs. In my last unit the gap was mostly mix: a large low-margin order had replaced smaller profitable ones, so we changed how sales were paid.
A large customer asks for an 8% price cut to renew. How do you decide?
Your judgement on pricing and on what a customer is worth.
Looks at contribution after the cut, the cost of losing the volume, what the customer gives in return, and the effect on other customers' prices.

I check what the cut does to contribution on that account and what happens to our fixed cost coverage if we lose it. I ask what we get back: a longer contract, more volume, faster payment. I also think about precedent, because other customers hear about prices. Often I offer a smaller cut tied to volume levels rather than a flat 8%.
Sales keeps promising delivery dates that operations cannot meet. How do you fix it?
How you settle conflict between your own functional leaders.
Treats it as a process problem: one shared view of capacity, a clear rule for quoting dates and shared goals, not picking a side.

I get both heads in a room with the data: promised dates, actual dates and capacity. Usually sales simply cannot see capacity. We set up a weekly sales and operations meeting, give sales a simple way to check lead times before quoting, and put on-time delivery in both teams' goals. Then neither side wins by blaming the other.
Head office asks you to cut costs by 10% this year, starting now. How do you approach it?
Whether you can cut costs without damaging the business.
Separates waste from spending that drives revenue, protects customer-facing capacity, involves leaders and is honest with staff.

I sort spending into what keeps customers and revenue, what is required, and what is habit. Habit goes first: contractors, travel, unused software, overtime caused by poor planning. I give each leader a target and ask for options ranked by risk. If people must go, I decide once, do it quickly and explain it plainly, rather than cutting in small rounds that wear everyone down.
Your plant manager asks for $2 million for a new production line. How do you evaluate it?
How you judge a capital investment request.
Uses yearly cash flows, payback and net present value at the company's required return, and tests the assumptions behind volume and savings.

I ask for the cash flows year by year: the spend, the savings or extra margin, and running costs. I look at payback and at net present value, which discounts future cash to today at our required return. Then I challenge the inputs, because the math is rarely wrong but the volume forecast often is. I want a downside case and the cost of doing nothing.
At quarter end you learn a sales manager booked revenue on orders the customer had not yet received. What do you do?
Your integrity when the numbers and the rules conflict.
Corrects the books promptly with finance, accepts the miss, and looks at the incentives that caused it, not only the person.

I tell finance the same day and we reverse anything booked before the customer took control of the goods under the contract terms. I would rather miss the quarter and explain it than report wrong numbers. Then I talk to the manager to learn whether pressure from me or the bonus plan drove it, and fix that cause, because a target that invites this is my problem too.
A product line shows a loss once overhead is allocated, but it has a positive contribution margin. Do you drop it?
Whether you understand fixed cost allocation before cutting a product.
Not automatically: dropping it loses its contribution, and the overhead stays unless it truly goes away. Also weighs links to other sales and capacity use.

Not on those numbers alone. If it covers its variable costs, it is helping pay for fixed costs. Drop it and that overhead lands on the other lines, so total profit falls unless the costs actually leave, like a lease we can end or staff we no longer need. I would also check whether customers buy it with other products and whether the capacity could earn more elsewhere.
You take over a unit that has lost money for two years. What do you do in your first 90 days?
How you diagnose a failing unit and start a turnaround.
Secures cash first, finds where money is made and lost by customer and product, assesses the team, and commits to a few clear actions.

First, cash: a 13-week cash forecast so we do not run out while fixing things. Then I split profit by customer, product and site to see where we lose money. I meet key customers and front-line staff, not just managers. By day 60 I know which leaders I keep, and by day 90 I commit to a short plan with three or four actions and monthly numbers to track them.

gis.heading: GIS and mapping specialist questions
qs: When would you store data as vector and when as raster?
Whether you know the two basic GIS data models and can pick the right one.
Vector for discrete features with clear edges, raster for continuous surfaces, with a real example of each.

Vector is points, lines and polygons, so I use it for things with clear edges: roads, parcels, fire hydrants. Raster is a grid of cells, each holding a value, so it suits things that change smoothly, like elevation, temperature or satellite imagery. If I need slope or a cost surface, I want a raster. For a street network, I want vector.
What is the difference between a geographic and a projected coordinate system?
Your grasp of coordinates, the base of every measurement you make.
Geographic uses angles on a model of the earth, projected uses flat x and y in linear units; distance and area need a suitable projection or geodesic math.

A geographic system, like WGS 84, gives positions as latitude and longitude in degrees on a model of the earth. A projected system flattens that onto a plane, with x and y in meters or feet. A degree of longitude shrinks as you move toward the poles, so I never buffer or measure in degrees. I project first, or I use geodesic tools.
A planner wants the total acres of wetland in each county of a state. Which projection do you use?
Whether you know that every projection distorts something and choose one for the task.
An equal-area projection fitted to the region, such as Albers, or geodesic area; never Web Mercator for area.

I use an equal-area projection fitted to the region, such as an Albers equal-area conic, or I calculate geodesic area. I would not compute area in Web Mercator: it keeps local shapes but inflates area away from the equator, which is why Greenland looks as big as Africa on web maps. Then I convert to acres and spot-check one county.
Two layers of the same streets do not line up when you overlay them. What do you check?
How you troubleshoot coordinate system and datum problems.
Uses the size of the offset as a clue, checks each layer's defined coordinate system and datum transformation, and fixes the source, not the symptom.

First I look at the size of the shift. Hundreds of meters, or data landing in the wrong place entirely, usually means a layer has the wrong coordinate system defined or none at all. A shift of about a meter points to a datum issue, like NAD83 against WGS 84 with no transformation applied. I fix the definition at the source rather than nudging the data by hand.
A manager wants a county map of crime counts, shaded dark to light. What would you change?
Whether you avoid the classic choropleth mistakes that make a map mislead.
Maps a rate instead of a raw count, chooses class breaks on purpose, and warns about small-area rates and the effect of the chosen units.

Raw counts mostly show where people live, so I would map a rate, like incidents per 10,000 residents. I pick class breaks on purpose and name the method, since quantiles and natural breaks can tell different stories. I would also flag that small counties give unstable rates, and that the pattern can change with the areas you choose.
You geocode 50,000 customer addresses and only 78% match. What do you do?
How you handle messy address data without hiding bad results.
Studies why records failed, cleans and standardizes, reviews low scores and ties, and reports the match rate instead of forcing matches.

I sample the failures to find the pattern: PO boxes, missing ZIP codes, typos, new subdivisions not yet in the reference data. I standardize abbreviations, fix the common errors and rerun. I would not just lower the match score, because that turns misses into wrong points. What still fails I report with the rate, so nobody thinks the map covers every customer.
You merge parcel layers from two counties and find slivers and overlaps along the border. How do you fix them?
Your approach to topology errors and data cleaning.
Runs topology checks to find every error, snaps within a tolerance tied to source accuracy, reviews larger cases by hand and logs changes.

I run topology checks for gaps and overlaps so I see every error, not just the ones I spot. Then I snap edges within a small tolerance, set from the accuracy of the source data, so I do not move real boundaries. Anything bigger I review by hand with the county, since a GIS parcel map is not a legal survey. I keep a log of each change.
A query that finds every store within 2 km of 5 million delivery points runs for hours. How do you speed it up?
Whether you know how spatial indexes and spatial queries work at scale.
Spatial index on both tables, an index-aware distance test instead of computing every distance, and correct units.

First I make sure both tables have a spatial index, like an R-tree, and fresh statistics. Then I write the test as a within-distance check, not distance less than 2,000, because many spatial databases can use the index for the first and must compute every pair for the second. I also check units: in degrees, 2,000 means nothing, so I use a projected system in meters.
Your routing engine sends trucks from an overpass straight onto the highway below, where there is no ramp. What went wrong?
Whether you understand network connectivity, not just line geometry.
Knows that lines crossing on a map are not a junction, and fixes it with grade separation data and connectivity rules, then tests.

Most likely the network was built so every crossing became an intersection, giving the overpass and the highway a shared node. Two lines crossing on a map does not mean you can turn. I would record grade separation with elevation or z-level fields, connect lines only at real junctions, and check one-way and turn restrictions. Then I rerun test routes through known interchanges.
You have GPS traces from delivery vans and need to know which road each van was on. Downtown the points jump around. How do you approach it?
How you deal with noisy location data and real map matching.
Knows why GPS degrades downtown and uses map matching that weighs road connectivity and travel time, not just the nearest road.

Downtown, signals bounce off tall buildings, so points can land a block away. Snapping each point to the nearest road fails at parallel streets and overpasses. I use map matching that scores candidate roads by distance and by whether the drive between them is plausible in the time elapsed, often with a hidden Markov model. Stretches with low confidence I flag, not guess.

gnc-engineer.heading: Guidance, navigation and control engineer questions
qs: How would you explain the difference between guidance, navigation and control?
Whether you can separate the three jobs in the loop clearly.
Navigation estimates where you are, guidance decides where to go, and control makes the actuators follow that command.

Navigation answers where am I: it fuses sensors into an estimate of position, velocity and attitude. Guidance answers where should I go: it turns the mission and that estimate into a commanded path or acceleration. Control answers how do I get there: it drives the fins, thrusters or motors so the vehicle follows the command.
Why pair an IMU with GPS instead of using either one alone?
Your grasp of sensor strengths and why fusion is needed.
The IMU is fast and self-contained but drifts. GPS has bounded error but is slower and can drop out or be jammed.

An IMU gives high-rate acceleration and rotation with no outside signal, but integrating it lets small biases grow into large position errors over time. GPS has bounded error but updates more slowly and can be blocked or jammed. Together, GPS keeps the IMU drift in check and the IMU carries the solution smoothly through the gaps.
Walk me through how a Kalman filter works, in plain words.
Whether you understand the filter you will tune, not just its equations.
Predict with a model, correct with a measurement, and weight each one by its uncertainty through the process and measurement noise.

It runs two steps. Predict: push the state and its uncertainty forward with a motion model, adding process noise for what the model misses. Update: compare a new measurement with what the filter expected and move the estimate toward it by a gain. If the sensor is precise compared with the state uncertainty, the gain is large and the filter trusts the sensor more.
Why do attitude systems often use quaternions instead of Euler angles?
Your knowledge of attitude representation and its pitfalls.
Euler angles hit gimbal lock. Quaternions avoid that singularity but must be kept unit length, and q and minus q mean the same attitude.

With a yaw-pitch-roll sequence, at plus or minus 90 degrees of pitch two axes line up and you lose a degree of freedom. That is gimbal lock. A quaternion uses four numbers, has no such singularity and is cheap to propagate. The care points: renormalize it so it stays unit length, and remember q and minus q describe the same attitude.
Your rate loop has an integrator and the actuator saturates during a big maneuver. What goes wrong and how do you fix it?
How you handle actuator limits, a common cause of flight problems.
Names integrator windup and the overshoot it causes, and gives an anti-windup method such as clamping or back-calculation.

While the actuator is pinned, the error stays large and the integrator keeps growing. When the vehicle catches up, that stored value drives a big overshoot. I add anti-windup: stop integrating while saturated, or feed back the gap between commanded and actual output to bleed the integrator down. Then I test it in the sim with the real rate and position limits.
Your navigation filter's innovations are consistently larger than the filter predicts. What do you check?
How you debug an estimator using its own health signals.
Data issues first (timing, frames, units, lever arms), then the model and noise tuning, using normalized innovation tests.

First the plumbing: timestamps and latency, sensor frames, units, sign conventions and the lever arm from IMU to antenna. Those cause most of it. Then I normalize the innovations and see if they are biased or just too big. A bias points to a missing state, like a sensor bias. Centered but too big usually means the noise settings are too low.
The vehicle oscillates in its first flight test, though the simulation was stable. How do you approach it?
Whether you know what simulations often leave out.
Pause testing, then use the data: the oscillation frequency points to delay, actuator limits, filter lag or a structural mode.

I pause testing and pull the logs. The oscillation frequency is the first clue. Near a bending mode, the sensor is seeing the structure flex, and a notch filter or a new sensor spot helps. Lower, I look for unmodeled delay, actuator rate limits or filter lag eating phase margin. I add what was missing to the sim and match the flight data before we fly again.
Your Monte Carlo run of 1,000 cases shows 3 failures and the review is Friday. What do you do?
Your judgement on rare failures under schedule pressure.
Treats each failure as real until explained, finds the cause, and reports it honestly instead of calling it 99.7% success.

I don't report 99.7% and move on. I rerun the three seeds, look at which dispersed parameters they share and find the mechanism. If it is a sim bug, I fix it and rerun the full set. If it is a real weakness, like a strong gust with low control authority, I tell the lead what it is, how likely it is and what a fix costs, so the schedule call is made with facts.
Walk me through how you would show that the flight code does what your design model does.
Whether you know the verification steps between a design and flying software.
A stepped chain from model to software, processor and hardware in the loop, with output comparisons and traceable requirements.

I start with model-in-the-loop tests tied to each requirement. Then I run the flight code against the same plant model and inputs, first on a desktop, then on the target processor, comparing outputs to the model within set tolerances. Hardware-in-the-loop adds real sensors, actuators and timing. Any mismatch gets explained, not just covered by a looser tolerance.

go-developer.heading: Go developer questions
qs: How is a goroutine different from an operating system thread?
Whether you understand the basic unit of concurrency in Go.
The Go runtime schedules goroutines onto a smaller set of OS threads. Goroutines start with a small, growable stack, so a program can run very many of them.

The Go runtime schedules a goroutine, not the operating system. It starts with a stack of a few kilobytes that grows as needed, so I can run thousands of them. The runtime spreads goroutines over a smaller set of OS threads. GOMAXPROCS sets how many threads run Go code at the same time, and by default it is based on the available CPUs.
When do you use an unbuffered channel, and when a buffered one?
Whether you know what channels guarantee and how a buffer changes that.
Unbuffered means a handoff that also synchronizes the two sides. A buffer has a clear purpose and a known size, and it is never used to hide a deadlock.

With an unbuffered channel, the sender waits until a receiver takes the value, so the handoff also syncs the two goroutines. With a buffered channel, the sender keeps going until the buffer is full. I start with unbuffered. I add a buffer when I know why I need it, for example a channel of capacity 10 used as a semaphore to cap concurrent calls.
How do you handle and wrap errors in Go?
Your everyday Go error handling style.
Errors are wrapped with %w to add context, and callers check them with errors.Is and errors.As. Each error is handled once, not logged at every layer.

I return errors as values and add context on the way up, with fmt.Errorf("load user %d: %w", id, err). The %w keeps the original error, so a caller can check errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows) or use errors.As to get a specific type. I handle each error once: I either log it or return it, never both, so it does not show up five times in the logs.
You append to one slice and another slice changes too. Explain why.
Whether you know how slices share their underlying arrays.
A slice is a pointer, a length and a capacity. Append writes in place when there is room, and the fix is copy, slices.Clone or a full slice expression.

A slice is a pointer to an array plus a length and a capacity. If a has capacity 5 and I take b := a[:2], then append(b, x) has room, so it writes into the same array and overwrites a[2]. When I need an independent slice, I use slices.Clone or copy into a new one. I can also use a[:2:2], which caps the capacity so the next append has to allocate.
How do you use context.Context in a service?
Whether you use context for cancellation and deadlines the way Go code expects.
ctx is the first parameter and is passed down to all I/O, cancel is always deferred, and context values hold only request-scoped data.

Every function that does I/O takes ctx as its first parameter and passes it down. Then, when a client disconnects or a deadline passes, the database and HTTP calls stop too. After context.WithTimeout I defer cancel right away. I do not store a context in a struct. I use context values only for request data like a trace ID, never for optional parameters.
When do you choose a mutex over a channel?
Your judgement in picking the simplest safe concurrency tool.
Channels for passing work or ownership, a mutex for guarding shared state, atomics for simple counters. Clarity about who owns the data is the deciding factor.

When goroutines hand work or ownership to each other, like a pipeline of jobs, I use channels. When they only share some state, like an in-memory cache, a sync.Mutex is simpler and easier to read. For a plain counter, sync/atomic is enough. I pick whatever makes it obvious who owns the data, not whatever looks more like Go.
Two goroutines write to the same map. What happens, and how do you catch this kind of bug?
Whether you know what a data race does in Go and how to detect it.
Concurrent map writes can crash the program with a fatal error that recover cannot catch. The race detector finds races only on code paths the run actually executes.

The runtime can stop the whole program with a fatal error, "concurrent map writes", and recover cannot catch it. I protect the map with a mutex, or use sync.Map for its intended cases, like keys written once and read often. I run tests with -race. It only reports races that happen during the run, so I write tests that really exercise the concurrent paths.
Your function returns a nil *MyError as an error, and the caller's err != nil check is true. Why?
Whether you understand how interface values work and can spot the typed nil trap.
An interface holds a type and a value, so a nil pointer of a concrete type is still a non-nil interface. The fix is to return a literal nil and declare error as the return type.

An interface value holds two things: a type and a value. When I return a nil *MyError as an error, the interface has the type *MyError and a nil pointer, so it is not equal to nil. The fix is to return a plain nil when there is no error, and to declare the return type as error, not *MyError, so a typed nil never slips through.
Memory in your service grows slowly and the goroutine count keeps climbing. How do you find and fix the leak?
How you diagnose and fix a goroutine leak in a running service.
Uses the pprof goroutine profile to see where goroutines are blocked, then gives each goroutine a way to exit, through context, a timeout or a buffered result channel.

I open the goroutine profile from net/http/pprof and look at where most goroutines are parked. Usually it is a send on a channel nobody reads anymore, or a call with no timeout. The fix is to give every goroutine a way out: select on ctx.Done(), or use a buffer of 1 for a result that may be abandoned. Then I add a goroutine count metric with an alert.

gpu-performance-engineer.heading: GPU and performance engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between a memory-bound and a compute-bound kernel?
Whether you know the first question to ask about any slow kernel.
Uses arithmetic intensity, the work done per byte moved, and compares it with the chip's ratio of peak math speed to memory bandwidth.

A memory-bound kernel spends its time waiting on data. A compute-bound one is limited by the math units. I work out arithmetic intensity, the floating-point operations per byte read or written, and compare it with the chip's peak FLOPs divided by its memory bandwidth. Below that ratio, faster math will not help. I need to move fewer bytes.
What does memory coalescing mean, and how do you get it?
Your grasp of how GPU memory access patterns drive speed.
Neighbouring threads reading neighbouring addresses, and a concrete layout change that makes it happen.

When threads next to each other read addresses next to each other, the hardware combines those reads into a few wide memory transactions. If each thread jumps by a large stride, the same data takes many transactions. I lay out data so the fastest-changing thread index walks the contiguous dimension, for example a structure of arrays instead of an array of structures.
Your kernel has an if-else that depends on each thread's data. Why might that slow it down?
Whether you understand how threads are grouped and executed on a GPU.
Explains that diverging threads in one group run both paths in turn, and offers a fix that is checked against real data.

Threads run in groups called warps, usually 32, that share one instruction stream. If threads in a warp take different branches, the warp runs both paths one after the other with some threads idle. I first check how often threads really disagree. If it is often, I sort or bucket the data so similar items land in the same warp, or rewrite the branch as arithmetic.
A colleague times a GPU function with a CPU timer and reports 0.05 ms. Why might that number be wrong?
Whether you can measure GPU work correctly before trying to speed it up.
Names asynchronous launches, the need to synchronize or use GPU events, warm-up runs, and repeated measurements.

GPU work is launched asynchronously, so the CPU timer may only measure the launch, not the kernel itself. I synchronize the device before stopping the timer, or use GPU events. I also run a few warm-up iterations first, because the first call can include setup and compilation, and I report the median of many runs, not a single one.
Walk me through how you find out why a training step is slower than expected.
How you narrow down a performance problem from the whole system to one kernel.
Starts with a timeline of the whole step to find idle gaps, then profiles only the kernels that take the most total time.

I start with a timeline profile of a few steps after warm-up, not a single kernel. It shows gaps where the GPU sits idle, often waiting on data loading, CPU-side launch overhead or host-to-device copies. If the GPU is busy, I sort kernels by total time and take the top few into a kernel profiler to see if each is limited by memory bandwidth, compute or latency.
Why does fusing several small operations into one kernel often make things faster?
Whether you know where time goes in chains of simple operations.
Fewer trips to GPU memory and fewer launches, with intermediate values kept on chip.

Each separate kernel reads its input from GPU memory and writes its output back, and each launch has overhead. A chain like add bias, then activation, then dropout is mostly memory-bound. Fusing them keeps the intermediate values in registers, so the data crosses memory once instead of three times and there is one launch instead of three.
Is higher occupancy always better? When would you accept lower occupancy?
Your judgement about a common tuning metric that can mislead.
Occupancy helps hide latency but is not the goal; heavy register or shared memory use can win through data reuse. Runtime decides.

Occupancy is how many warps are active on a multiprocessor compared with the maximum. More warps help hide memory latency, but it is a means, not the goal. A matrix-multiply kernel may use many registers and a lot of shared memory per thread block, so fewer blocks fit, yet each thread reuses data more and the kernel runs faster. I judge by measured runtime, not the occupancy number.
When would you train in BF16 instead of FP16, and what changes?
Your understanding of reduced-precision number formats and their risks.
BF16 keeps FP32's exponent range with less precision; FP16 usually needs loss scaling. Master weights and accumulation stay in FP32.

BF16 has the same 8 exponent bits as FP32, so it covers about the same range of values with less precision. FP16 has only 5 exponent bits, so small gradients can underflow to zero and you usually need loss scaling. With BF16 I can often drop loss scaling. In both cases I keep a full-precision copy of the weights and accumulate sums in FP32.
After your optimization, the model's outputs differ from the old version in the fifth decimal place. Is that a bug?
How you tell normal floating-point noise from a real correctness error.
Knows reordering sums changes results, and checks against a higher-precision reference with a sensible tolerance instead of guessing.

Not necessarily. Floating-point addition is not associative, so a new reduction order or atomic adds can change the last bits. I compare against a higher-precision reference, like an FP64 run, using a tolerance that fits the data type, and check that the error does not grow with input size. If it is far outside that tolerance or shows a pattern, I treat it as a bug.
Generating text one token at a time with a large language model leaves the GPU's math units mostly idle. Why, and what would you do?
Whether you can apply performance reasoning to serving AI models.
Each token reads all weights for little math, so it is bandwidth-bound; batching helps until the key-value cache limits memory.

At batch size 1, each new token needs every weight read from memory but does only about two operations per weight, so the step is bound by memory bandwidth. Batching many requests reuses each weight read across them. The limit then becomes the key-value cache, which grows with batch size and sequence length, so I watch cache memory and consider quantized weights to move fewer bytes.

graphic-designer.heading: Graphic and brand designer questions
qs: When do you use vector artwork and when do you use raster?
Whether you know the two basic kinds of image files and what each is for.
Vectors for logos, icons and type that must scale; raster for photos and painterly work, made at the size and resolution of the final use.

A logo is always built as vectors, paths defined by math, so it stays sharp on a business card or a billboard. Photos and textured illustrations are raster, a grid of pixels, so I make or buy them big enough for the final output, around 300 pixels per inch at print size. Enlarging a small raster image only makes it blurry.
What is the difference between kerning, tracking and leading?
Your command of basic typography terms.
Kerning is the space between one pair of letters, tracking is even spacing across a range of text, and leading is the space between lines.

Kerning adjusts the space between two specific letters, like a capital A next to a V, which often sit too far apart. Tracking loosens or tightens a whole word or block evenly; I add a little to all-caps labels. Leading is the distance from one baseline to the next. Body text usually needs more of it than a tight headline.
Walk me through how you prepare a brochure file before it goes to the printer.
Whether you can hand off print work that will not come back with problems.
Gets the printer's specs first, then sets bleed and safe margins, the right color mode, sharp images, embedded fonts, a press-ready PDF and a proof.

First I get the printer's specs. I set bleed, usually an eighth of an inch, and keep text inside a safe margin. I convert colors the way the printer asks, CMYK or spot, check that images are sharp at print size, embed the fonts and export a PDF/X file. Then I proof it on paper myself and approve the printer's proof before the run.
How do you specify a brand color so it looks the same on screen, on paper and on a sign?
How you control color across different media.
Separate values for each use: HEX or RGB for screens, CMYK and a spot ink for print, checked by eye on real proofs, not just converted by software.

One color needs several recipes. I pick a spot ink color and check it in both the coated and uncoated swatch books, since the same ink looks duller on uncoated paper. Then I set a CMYK build, plus RGB and HEX for screens. I compare them side by side on proofs and a few screens and adjust by eye. The guidelines list every value.
Before you show a client a new logo, how do you test it?
Whether you check that a mark works in real use, not just on the presentation slide.
Tests it at tiny sizes, in one color, in black, reversed on dark, and in real mockups like a site icon, a social avatar and a sign.

I shrink it to browser icon size and to a quarter inch in print to see if details fill in. I try it in one flat color, in black, and reversed white on dark, since someday it will be embroidered or stamped. Then I put it on real mockups: a profile picture, an invoice, a storefront sign. If it only works big and in full color, it is not done.
The client keeps asking you to make the logo bigger on every ad. How do you respond?
How you handle a common client request without simply giving in or arguing.
Finds the worry behind it, usually recognition, and solves that with hierarchy, placement or a side-by-side test, not a flat yes or no.

Usually the real worry is that people will not know who the ad is from. I ask about that, then show two versions at actual size: one with a bigger logo, and one where the logo sits in a clear spot with more space around it. Seeing them side by side settles most of it. If they still want it bigger, it is their brand, and I make it work.
A client sends you a photo they found online and asks you to use it in an ad. What do you do?
Whether you understand image rights and protect the client from a claim.
Explains that online images are protected by copyright by default, tries to find the owner, and offers a licensed stock or custom alternative.

I explain that a photo online still belongs to someone, and using it in an ad without permission can bring a legal claim. I try a reverse image search to find the owner and ask about a license. If that fails, I find a similar stock photo with a commercial license or suggest a short shoot. I keep every license on file with the project.
