I'd pull 20 charts to confirm the care happened. If it holds up, I report it with the checks I did; if not, I fix the measure before anyone celebrates.

help-desk.heading: Help desk technician questions
qs: A user calls and says the internet is down. What do you ask first?
Whether you narrow down the scope of a problem before you start fixing it.
Questions that find out who is affected and what exactly fails, so one laptop is not treated like an office outage.

First: is it just you, or are people near you affected too? Then: are you on a cable or Wi-Fi, and does every site fail or only one? Those answers tell me if it is one laptop, one app or the whole office. The whole office is a different call with a different urgency.
A user's IP address starts with 169.254. What does that tell you?
Your basic networking knowledge on the most common connection fault.
Knowing it means no DHCP lease was received, and checking the link before blaming the laptop.

It means the computer did not get an address from the DHCP server, so Windows gave itself one. That address cannot reach the internet. I check the cable or Wi-Fi first, then run ipconfig /release and ipconfig /renew. If other users have the same thing, the DHCP server or the switch is the problem, not the laptop.
How can you tell whether a problem is DNS or the network connection itself?
Whether you can isolate a fault with simple tests instead of guessing.
A clear test: an IP address answers but a name does not. Plus knowing when it is one PC and when it is the network.

I ping a known IP address, like a public DNS server, and then ping a website by name. If the IP answers and the name fails, it is DNS. nslookup shows which DNS server the PC is asking. On one PC I try ipconfig /flushdns; if many users are hit, I send it to the network team.
Walk me through a printer that shows online but prints nothing.
Your method on one of the most frequent help desk tickets.
An order of checks: the queue, the spooler, the port and IP, then the driver, and comparing with other users.

I look at the print queue first; one stuck job can block everything behind it. I clear it, and if it will not clear I restart the Print Spooler service. Then I check that the printer's IP matches the port on the PC, since a printer can get a new address. If only one person fails, I reinstall that user's driver.
A user says their laptop has become very slow. Where do you start?
How you diagnose a vague complaint and protect the user's data.
Asking what changed, looking at real usage data, the usual causes, and backing up data if the drive may be failing.

I ask when it started and what changed. Then I open Task Manager to see what uses CPU, memory and disk, and check how long since the last restart. Low disk space, too many startup apps and a pending update are the usual causes. If the drive looks close to failing, I back up the user's files before anything else.
Someone calls, says they are a senior manager traveling, and needs a password reset right now. What do you do?
Whether you hold to identity checks under pressure from rank and urgency.
Verification every time, a callback on a known number, and a polite refusal plus escalation if identity cannot be confirmed.

I follow the verification process, whatever the title or the hurry. I call back on the number in the company directory, not one they give me, or use the checks our policy sets. Urgency and rank are exactly what attackers use. If I cannot verify, I tell them politely and escalate to my lead.
A user asks for admin rights to install a free tool they found online. How do you answer?
Your judgement on least privilege while still helping the user get their work done.
No admin rights for convenience, a look at the real need, and the approved request path with a time frame.

I would not give admin rights for one tool; anything that runs under that account would have full control of the machine. I ask what they need to do, since an approved app often does it already. If not, I file a software request so security can review it, and we install it if approved. I tell them how long that usually takes.
How do you handle the user's privacy when you connect to their computer remotely?
Whether you treat remote access with respect and transparency.
Asking first, saying what you will do, staying on the problem, and clearly ending the session.

I ask before I connect and tell them what I am going to do. I suggest they close email and personal tabs first. I stay on the problem and do not open files I do not need. When I am done, I say so and disconnect while they watch, so they know I am out of their machine.
Three users report the same Outlook error within ten minutes. What do you do?
Whether you spot a wider incident instead of fixing the same thing one ticket at a time.
Treating it as one likely cause, linking tickets, alerting the team, escalating with facts, and updating users.

Three in ten minutes is likely one cause, not three problems. I check the service status page and ask my lead whether anything changed today. I open one parent ticket, link the others, and tell the team so every new caller hears the same thing. Then I escalate with times, the exact error and who is affected, and keep users updated.
A user tells you they clicked a link in an email and typed in their password. Walk me through what you do next.
How you contain a likely account compromise quickly and in the right order.
Thanking them, resetting and revoking sessions, checking MFA and mailbox rules, and reporting to security with evidence.

I thank them for telling me fast; that matters. I reset the password and sign them out of all sessions, then check that no new MFA method or phone was added. I look for new forwarding or delete rules in the mailbox, which attackers add to hide. I report it to security with the email and the time, and we warn others if it went out widely.

hospitality.heading: Food and hospitality questions
qs: What is the temperature danger zone, and how do you keep food out of it?
Whether you know the core food safety rule behind every kitchen task.
The right range, 41°F to 135°F, plus daily habits: cold food kept cold, hot food kept hot, checked with a thermometer, with little time out.

It is 41°F to 135°F, where bacteria grow fastest. I keep cold food at 41°F or below and hot food at 135°F or above. I probe food on the line every couple of hours and log it. During prep I pull only what I need from the cooler, and I never leave a pan sitting out while I do something else.
How do you organize raw and ready-to-eat food on the shelves of a walk-in cooler?
Whether you prevent cross-contamination in storage.
Ready-to-eat food on top, raw food below in order of required cooking temperature, with poultry on the bottom shelf.

Ready-to-eat food and washed produce go on the top shelves. Below that come raw items in order of the temperature they must be cooked to: seafood and whole cuts of beef and pork, then ground meat, and poultry on the bottom. Anything that drips only lands on food that gets cooked hotter. Everything is covered, labeled and dated.
A delivery arrives during lunch prep. What do you check before you sign for it?
How you protect quality and the stock count at the back door.
Temperatures, signs of thawing or damage, and counts against the order, with problems refused and noted before signing.

I check it right away, not after service. I probe refrigerated items and make sure frozen items are hard frozen, without large ice crystals or stains that show they thawed and refroze. I look for torn packaging, swollen or badly dented cans and pests, and count against the invoice. Anything wrong is refused and noted before I sign. Cold and frozen goods go away first.
How do you work out the menu price for a new dish?
Your grasp of plate costing in menu planning.
Every ingredient costed by the portion, including trim loss, then priced to a target food cost percentage and checked against the market.

I write out the recipe and cost every ingredient by the amount on the plate, using the yield after trimming, not the purchase weight. Sauce and garnish count too. Then I divide plate cost by our target food cost percentage. If the plate costs $4.20 and the target is 30%, the price lands around $14. Last, I check it against what our guests will pay.
A guest tells the server they have a sesame allergy. Walk me through what happens from order to plate.
Whether you can keep an allergic guest safe through the whole kitchen.
Clear communication, checking recipes and labels, preventing cross-contact with clean tools and surfaces, and honesty if it cannot be done safely.

The server flags the allergy on the ticket and tells the lead cook. We check the recipe and labels, since sesame hides in breads, dressings and spice blends. I wash my hands, use a clean board, pan and utensils, and plate it away from the line. The server carries that plate alone. If we cannot be sure it is safe, we tell the guest honestly.
You have a large pot of chili left at close. How do you cool it safely?
Whether you know the cooling rule, a common cause of foodborne illness outbreaks.
Two-stage cooling, 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours and to 41°F within 6 hours total, using shallow pans, ice baths or ice wands.

A big pot will not cool fast enough in the cooler on its own. I split it into shallow pans, stir it in an ice bath or use an ice wand, and store it loosely covered. It must drop from 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours and reach 41°F within 6 hours total. I log the temperatures. If it misses the first stage, I reheat it to 165°F and start over, or throw it out.
A line cook arrives for a shift and says they were vomiting last night. What do you do?
How you apply the sick worker rules when you are short-staffed.
The cook does not work, the manager is told, and the shift is covered; the cook returns only after at least 24 hours without symptoms.

They go home, even if we are short. Vomiting is a symptom that keeps a worker out of the kitchen under the food code, because illnesses like norovirus spread fast through food. I thank them for telling me and inform the manager. They come back after at least 24 hours with no symptoms. Then I call in cover or simplify the menu for the shift.
You open the kitchen and the walk-in cooler reads 48°F. What do you do?
How you handle a food safety problem when money and service are on the line.
Checks actual food temperatures and the log, discards what cannot be shown safe, moves the rest, records losses and calls for repair.

First I probe food in several spots instead of trusting the dial. I check the log to see when it last read 41°F or below. Cold food that sat above 41°F too long, or for a time I cannot prove, gets thrown out, and I record what and how much. Anything still cold moves to reach-ins or ice. Then I call for service, tell the manager and adjust the menu.
Your food cost went from 30% to 35% in a month with no menu change. Where do you look?
How you trace a stock and cost problem to its cause.
A step-by-step check: count accuracy, supplier prices, waste, portion sizes, then missing stock from theft or unrecorded free meals.

First I make sure the inventory count is right, since one bad count can swing the number. Then I compare invoice prices with last month, because one supplier increase on proteins can do it. I read the waste log and watch portions on the line, checking scoops and scales. Last I compare what we sold with what we used, which shows unrecorded free meals or theft.
A strong cook on your team keeps skipping the temperature logs. How do you handle it?
How you lead on food safety standards without losing a good worker.
A private, direct talk about why it matters, a clear expectation, follow-up, and the same rule for everyone.

I talk to them alone, not on the line. I say what I saw, explain that the log is our proof the food was safe if a guest gets sick or an inspector asks, and ask what gets in the way. Often it is timing, so we set a fixed moment in the shift for it. I check the logs over the next weeks. If it continues, it becomes a written warning, like for anyone.

hr-business-partner.heading: HR business partner questions
qs: How is an HR business partner different from an HR generalist?
Whether you see the role as advising leaders, not only running HR tasks.
The partner works from the department's goals and shapes decisions early; routine transactions go to specialists or shared services.

A generalist handles the day-to-day: questions, leave paperwork, onboarding. As a business partner I sit with one leadership team, learn their goals and numbers, and advise on structure, talent and pay before decisions are made. I still take the hard cases, but routine work goes to the HR service team.
You take over a new client group. What do you do in the first 90 days?
How you learn a business and earn the trust of its leaders.
Listening meetings, a look at the people data, one or two early wins, then a plan agreed with the department head.

In the first month I meet every leader one to one and ask what worries them most. I pull turnover, open roles, overtime and survey results by team. By day 60 I fix one or two small pains, like a stuck job posting. By day 90 I bring the department head a short people plan with three priorities, and we agree on it together.
A manager wants to make a role exempt so he no longer has to pay overtime. What do you tell him?
Your grasp of the overtime exemption rules.
Exempt status depends on salary basis, a minimum salary level and the actual duties, never on the title or on what the manager wants.

Under the federal Fair Labor Standards Act a role is exempt only if it passes three tests: a fixed salary, at or above the required level, and real duties that fit an exemption, like executive or administrative. Some states are stricter. I'd review the actual work with him and our pay team. If it doesn't qualify, we budget for overtime.
Walk me through setting up a performance improvement plan.
Whether you build a fair plan with goals the employee can actually meet.
Specific, measurable goals, real support, a set time frame, regular check-ins and written notes, with a genuine aim to help, not just a paper trail.

First I check that the manager has already given clear feedback. Then we write two to four measurable goals, like closing tickets within two days, plus the support offered and a time frame, often 30 to 60 days. The manager meets the employee weekly and notes progress. At the end we decide on the facts: pass, extend or exit.
A manager wants to fire someone tomorrow for poor performance. What do you ask first?
How you spot legal and fairness risk before a termination.
Documentation, prior warnings, consistency with similar cases, and any recent complaint, leave or accommodation request that could look like retaliation.

I ask what is documented and whether the employee was told clearly that the job was at risk. I check how we treated others with similar issues. Then timing: has the person recently complained, asked for leave or an accommodation? If so, a firing tomorrow looks like retaliation, so I'd slow down and bring in employment counsel.
In a performance talk, an employee says a health condition is behind his missed deadlines. What happens next?
Whether you recognize when disability and medical leave duties start.
The company is now on notice: start the ADA interactive process, check leave eligibility, and keep medical details private.

That comment can count as a request for accommodation, even if he never uses the word. I would not push discipline through that day. I'd start the ADA interactive process: what limits he has and what would help, with medical confirmation if the need isn't obvious. I'd also check FMLA eligibility. Medical details go in a separate confidential file.
A director asks for an off-cycle raise for a top performer who has an outside offer. How do you handle it?
How you balance keeping a person against pay fairness and budget.
Look at the pay range, peers in the same role and the cost of replacing her; a counteroffer that breaks internal equity creates new problems.

I check where she sits in her range and how she compares with peers doing the same work. If she is below them with equal results, a raise fixes a real gap. If it would put her far above them, I suggest other options: a retention bonus, more scope, a promotion path. I also ask why she is looking, because money alone rarely keeps people.
In calibration, one manager has rated everyone on his team 'exceeds expectations.' What do you do?
Whether you can challenge a leader with evidence and keep ratings fair across teams.
Ask for evidence person by person, compare with other teams, and coach him before the meeting rather than embarrass him in it.

Before the session I sit with him and go person by person: what did each one deliver beyond their goals? I show how his ratings compare with teams that had similar results. Usually a few ratings hold and the rest move to 'meets.' I explain that inflated ratings hurt his best people, because they get the same raise as everyone else.
Your department head plans to cut 15 roles. Walk me through your part.
How you run a layoff that is fair, legal and humane.
Written business reason, objective selection criteria, adverse impact review with counsel, notice rules like WARN, proper releases for workers 40 and over, and a plan for the day.

First I get the business reason in writing. Selection criteria must fit the future structure, not who is easiest to cut. With counsel I check the list for adverse impact by age, race and sex, check WARN and state notice rules, and make sure releases give workers 40 and over the time the age law requires. Then I prepare managers for the talks and plan support for those who stay.
Tell me about a time you gave a leader advice that turned out to be wrong. What did you do?
Whether you own mistakes and protect the trust of your client group.
A fast correction, an honest explanation, a fix, and a change in how you check advice from then on.

I once told a manager that a leaving employee's unused vacation would be forfeited. Then I checked our policy against state law; in that state, earned vacation had to be paid out. I called the manager the same day, said I had been wrong, and we added it to the final pay. Now I check state rules before I answer any exit pay question.

hr-director.heading: HR director and HR manager questions
qs: What is the difference between an exempt and a non-exempt employee?
Whether you know the wage-and-hour basics behind many costly claims.
Exemption depends on salary basis, salary level and job duties, never the title. Non-exempt staff earn overtime past 40 hours in a workweek.

Under the FLSA, non-exempt employees get overtime at one and a half times their regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek. To be exempt, a role usually must be paid on a salary basis, meet the salary level, and pass a duties test, such as executive or administrative. The title does not decide it. Some states have stricter rules, so I check state law too.
During an audit you find a dozen current employees with no Form I-9 on file. What do you do?
How you fix a compliance gap without making it worse.
Complete the forms now with today's date, never backdate, note why they are late, and fix the onboarding step that failed.

I would have each employee complete a new I-9 right away, dated today. Backdating would turn a paperwork error into a false record. I attach a short signed note explaining the late completion. Then I find out why onboarding skipped the form and fix it so Section 2 is done within three business days of the start date. If the gap is large, I bring in counsel.
A manager tells you an employee asked for a later start time because of a medical condition. How do you handle it?
Whether you recognize an ADA accommodation request and run the process correctly.
Treat it as a request even without legal words, start the interactive process, keep medical details confidential, and document each step.

I treat it as an accommodation request under the ADA, even though the employee never used that term. I meet with the employee, ask for medical documentation only about the limitation if it is not obvious, and check whether a later start works for the role. If not, we look at other options. Medical records go in a separate confidential file, not the personnel file.
How would you build salary ranges for a company that has never had them?
Your grasp of compensation design from job levels to cost.
Job levels first, then market data, a chosen market position, ranges around midpoints, and the cost of moving people who fall outside them.

First I group jobs into families and levels so similar work sits together. I price benchmark jobs with two or three salary surveys and agree with leadership where we want to pay, say at the market median. I set midpoints and wider ranges for senior roles. Then I map every employee, check compa-ratios, and cost out raising anyone below the minimum. Several states also require ranges in job postings.
Turnover on one sales team doubled this year while the rest of the company held steady. How do you find the cause?
How you use data and conversations to diagnose a people problem.
Look at who left, when and why, compare against other teams, talk to people still there, and test whether it is the manager, pay or the work.

I pull the exits: tenure, performance, regretted or not, and timing. If most left within months of a new manager or a commission plan change, that is a lead. I read exit interviews, then hold stay interviews with people still on the team, since they speak more freely. Last time I did this, a quota change had cut real pay by about 15%, and we fixed the plan.
Finance gives you a flat headcount budget, but three department heads each want two new hires. How do you decide?
Your judgement in workforce planning and in working with finance.
Tie each request to business priorities, look at alternatives to hiring, and put clear tradeoffs before leadership instead of splitting evenly.

I ask each leader what the hire would deliver and what fails without it, then rank the requests against company goals. I also look at other options: open backfills we could redirect, internal transfers, contractors for short-term work, or a process fix. I bring the executive team a ranked list with costs and risks. Splitting the budget evenly is easy, but it is rarely right.
Walk me through how you investigate a harassment complaint against a senior leader.
Whether your investigations are fair, prompt and defensible.
Quick interim steps that do not punish the complainant, a neutral investigator, full interviews and documents, a reasoned finding and action.

I act fast. Interim steps protect the complainant without moving or punishing them. Because the accused is senior, I usually bring in an outside investigator so no one questions independence. We interview the complainant, the accused and witnesses, and gather emails and messages. I promise confidentiality only as far as possible. We decide what is more likely than not, act on it, and document everything.
How would you run a pay equity audit, and what do you do with what you find?
Your method for finding and fixing unfair pay gaps.
Compare similar jobs, control for legitimate factors, work under counsel, and fix gaps by raising pay, never by lowering anyone's pay.

I group employees doing similar work, then run a regression that controls for legitimate factors like level, location, tenure and performance. Gaps by gender or race that those factors do not explain need action. I do the audit with counsel so the analysis is privileged. Fixes are raises from a set budget. The Equal Pay Act does not allow lowering anyone's pay to close a gap.
The CEO wants to fire an employee who filed a complaint two weeks ago, and says it is about performance. What do you do?
How you handle retaliation risk when a senior leader pushes.
Name the timing risk plainly, test whether the performance record predates the complaint, and slow the decision until it can stand up.

I tell the CEO directly that firing someone two weeks after a complaint looks like retaliation, whatever the reason. Then I check the facts: was the performance problem written down before the complaint, and were others with similar results treated the same way? If the record is solid, counsel reviews it before we act. If not, we pause and manage performance properly.
The company has to cut 15% of its staff. Walk me through how you plan it.
Whether you can run a layoff that is lawful, fair and humane.
Clear selection criteria, an adverse impact check, WARN and OWBPA rules, a well-run notice day, and care for the people who stay.

First, selection criteria tied to the business, such as roles we no longer need. Before anything is final, I check for adverse impact by age, race and sex. I confirm whether the federal WARN Act or a state version requires 60 days or more of notice. For releases, workers 40 and over in a group layoff get 45 days to consider and 7 to revoke. Managers get scripts, and survivors hear the plan the same day.

hris.heading: HRIS and people analytics specialist questions
qs: What is the difference between headcount and FTE, and when would you report each?
Whether you know the two basic ways of counting a workforce.
Headcount counts people; FTE converts scheduled hours into full-time equivalents. Each answers a different question, such as budget versus benefits.

Headcount is the number of people, so a part-timer counts as one. FTE divides scheduled hours by the full-time standard, so someone working 20 of 40 hours is 0.5. I use FTE for labor budgets and staffing capacity, and headcount for things that follow people, like benefits enrollment or span of control.
How do you calculate the annual turnover rate, and what choices do you have to state with it?
Your grasp of the most requested HR metric and the definitions behind it.
Separations divided by average headcount for the period, with clear rules on who counts, and voluntary split from involuntary.

I divide the separations in the year by the average headcount, usually the average of the monthly counts, and multiply by 100. Then I state the rules: are interns and seasonal staff in, do internal transfers count (they should not). I split voluntary from involuntary, because 15% means something different if most of it is layoffs.
What does an effective date mean in an HR system, and what goes wrong when a change is entered late?
Whether you understand how HR systems keep history over time.
The effective date is when the change applies, not when it was keyed in. Late or retro entries can hit payroll, benefits and reports already sent.

Each record carries the date the change takes effect, separate from the date someone typed it. If a promotion dated March 1 is entered April 10, payroll may need a retro adjustment, and any March report already sent is now wrong. I check what downstream systems pulled in that window and tell payroll and whoever got the report.
Finance says headcount is 1,212 and your report says 1,187. How do you sort it out?
How you reconcile numbers between systems instead of picking a side.
Comparing definitions and the as-of date first, then matching records by ID, and agreeing on one written definition.

I first compare definitions: the as-of date, whether contractors, people on leave or future starters are included, and how each side treats a termination dated the last day. Then I pull both lists by employee ID and look at the 25 that differ. Usually it is a rule, not an error, so we agree on a written definition and label both reports with it.
A manager asks you to give her access to salaries for the whole department, including teams she does not lead. What do you do?
Your judgement on data access and giving people only the access their role needs.
Access follows role and need, approved by the data owner. You find out what she actually needs, which is often an aggregate.

I would ask what decision she is making. Often she needs ranges or averages for a role, which I can give as a report without names. If she truly needs individual pay outside her team, that goes to the HR or comp lead who owns the data for approval. I would not widen her security role on my own, and I would log what we decide.
An executive wants engagement scores broken down by team, and one team has three people. How do you handle it?
Whether you protect confidentiality when you report on small groups.
Applying a minimum group size so no one can be identified, rolling small groups into a larger unit, and watching combined filters.

With three people, anyone can guess who said what, and the survey promised confidentiality. We set a minimum group size before results go out, often five, so I would roll that team into its department. I also check that two filters together, like team and tenure, cannot reveal a small group by subtracting one result from another.
Your HR system vendor pushes a major release twice a year. Walk me through how you prepare for it.
How you manage change in a live system without breaking it.
Reading release notes, testing real scenarios in a sandbox, checking integrations and reports, and telling users what changes.

I read the release notes and flag what touches our setup: features that turn on automatically, changed fields, anything near payroll or benefits. In the sandbox I run test scripts for hire, pay change and termination, and check that integrations and scheduled reports still run. Then I tell users what will look different before it goes live.
You ran a mass upload and later found it changed the cost center on 140 wrong records. What do you do?
How you handle your own error in live employee data.
Stopping the spread, telling payroll and finance fast, correcting with the right dates, and fixing the process that allowed it.

First I check whether payroll or the finance feed has already picked up the change, and I tell both teams right away. I pull the old values from the audit trail and load a correction with the same effective date so history stays clean. Then I tell my manager and add a step: a peer checks sample rows in the sandbox before any mass load.
Leadership asks you to check whether women and men are paid fairly. How would you approach it?
Whether you can run a pay comparison that controls for legitimate factors.
Comparing like with like: control for job, level, location and tenure, study the unexplained gap and outliers, and involve legal early.

A raw average gap mixes in differences in job and level, so I would compare people in similar roles and use a regression with factors like job level, location and time in role. The gap that remains unexplained is what we study, plus individual outliers. I would run it with employment counsel and agree up front how gaps will be fixed.
A VP wants a model that names each employee likely to quit in the next six months. How do you respond?
Your judgement on the ethics and limits of predictive people analytics.
Weighing accuracy, bias and how a list gets used; steering toward drivers and group-level action, and keeping protected traits out.

I would ask what action the list would drive. A named list is often wrong about any one person and can quietly change how a manager treats someone. I would offer a team-level view of risk drivers, like time since last raise. If we model at all, I keep out age, sex and similar traits and check results for bias with HR and legal.

human-resources.heading: Human resources questions
qs: What makes a job exempt from overtime under federal law?
Whether you know the tests behind overtime classification.
Salary level, salary basis and duties must all be met. A job title or being paid a salary is not enough.

Under the FLSA, a role is exempt only if it passes three tests. It pays at least the federal salary level, it is paid on a salary basis, and the actual duties fit an exemption such as executive, administrative or professional. Paying someone a salary or calling them a manager does not make them exempt. I also check state law, which can be stricter.
Employment here is at will. What does that mean, and where does it stop?
Your grasp of the basic rule of US employment and its limits.
Either side can end the job without cause, but not for an illegal reason such as discrimination or retaliation, and not against a contract.

It means either the company or the employee can end the job at any time, with or without a reason. It does not allow an illegal reason, like discrimination or retaliation for a complaint. A contract or union agreement can limit it too, and Montana requires good cause after a probation period. So I still want a documented, legitimate reason for every firing.
A new hire brings a U.S. passport, but the manager wants to see a Social Security card for the I-9. What do you say?
Whether you know the I-9 document rules and the risk of asking for specific papers.
The employee chooses which acceptable documents to show. Asking for specific ones can be illegal document abuse.

I say no. A U.S. passport is a List A document, which proves both identity and work authorization, so the I-9 needs nothing else. The employee picks which acceptable documents to present, and demanding a particular one can count as document abuse. I also make sure Section 2 is finished within three business days of the start date.
A manager hands you a doctor's note and asks you to put it in the employee's file. Where does it go?
Whether you keep medical information confidential and separate.
In a separate medical file with restricted access, never the general personnel file. Managers get only what they need to know.

Not in the personnel file. Under the ADA, medical information must be kept confidential and stored apart from the general file, with access only for people who need it. I put it in a restricted medical file. I tell the manager what they need to plan around, such as dates away or work limits, but not the diagnosis.
An employee asks for six weeks off to care for a parent after surgery. How do you check whether FMLA applies?
Your working knowledge of FMLA eligibility and the steps that follow.
Checks employer coverage, employee eligibility and the qualifying reason, then sends the required notice on time.

FMLA covers private employers with 50 or more employees. The employee needs 12 months of service, 1,250 hours in the last 12 months, and a worksite with 50 employees within 75 miles. Caring for a parent with a serious health condition qualifies. I send the eligibility notice within five business days, can ask for a medical certification, and check state leave law too.
An employee says back pain makes it hard to sit all day and asks for help. What happens next?
Whether you know how to run the interactive process for a disability accommodation.
Treats it as an accommodation request even without legal words, talks it through, and finds an effective option unless it causes undue hardship.

I treat it as an accommodation request, even though the employee never mentioned the ADA. I meet with them, ask about their limits and what would help, and may ask for medical information confirming the need. Then we look at options like a sit-stand desk or short breaks. I document each step and follow up to check that the solution works.
Walk me through how you would set up a performance improvement plan.
How you make a PIP fair, clear and defensible.
Specific gaps with examples, measurable goals, a set time frame, real support, regular check-ins, and a written record.

I start with the manager's evidence: what exactly is not being met, with examples. The plan lists two or three measurable goals, a time frame such as 60 days, and the support offered, like training or weekly check-ins. The employee gets a copy and a chance to respond. We record each check-in, so whatever the outcome, the decision rests on facts.
A manager wants to fire someone two weeks after that person filed a harassment complaint. The manager says it is about attendance. What do you do?
Whether you spot retaliation risk and slow a risky decision down.
Pauses the firing, checks whether the attendance problem was documented before the complaint and treated like others, and brings in counsel if needed.

I ask the manager to pause. That timing looks like retaliation, which is illegal even if the complaint is not proven. I look at the record: was attendance documented before the complaint, and how were others with the same record treated? If the evidence is solid and consistent, we can proceed, often after a check with counsel. If not, the firing does not happen.
You find that a group of hourly workers has not been paid for required setup time before their shifts. How do you fix it?
How you handle a pay compliance mistake you found yourself.
Stops the practice at once, works out and pays back wages with payroll and counsel, and fixes the cause instead of hiding it.

First I stop it: required setup is work time, so from the next shift it is clocked and paid. Then, with payroll and our employment counsel, I estimate how much time was missed and for how long, and we pay back wages, including overtime where it pushed someone past 40 hours in a week. I change the clock-in process and explain to managers why it happened.
Leadership wants to cut 30 roles. What do you check before the list is final?
Whether you can run a layoff that is fair, well designed and legally sound.
Written role-based criteria, a check for impact on protected groups, WARN notice rules, and proper release terms for workers 40 and over.

I get the selection criteria written first, based on roles and business need. Then I check whether the list falls harder on a protected group, such as workers over 40, and ask why. We see if federal or state WARN rules require advance notice. If severance comes with a release, workers 40 and over in a group layoff get 45 days to consider it and 7 days to revoke.

hvac-technician.heading: HVAC technician questions
qs: What are superheat and subcooling, and when do you charge by each?
Whether you understand the basic refrigerant measurements behind every charging decision.
Correct definitions, and knowing that fixed-orifice systems are usually charged by superheat and TXV systems by subcooling.

Superheat is how many degrees the suction vapor is above its boiling point at that pressure. Subcooling is how many degrees the liquid line is below its condensing point. On a piston or other fixed-orifice system I charge by superheat. On a TXV system I charge by subcooling, always to the manufacturer's target.
How do you check whether a system is moving enough air?
Whether you diagnose airflow with measurements instead of guessing.
Uses static pressure and the blower table, plus temperature rise on a furnace, and knows the usual causes of high static.

I measure total external static pressure with a manometer, on the supply and return sides, and read the blower table to estimate the airflow. On a furnace I also compare the temperature rise with the range on the nameplate. High static usually points to a dirty filter, a restrictive coil or undersized ducts.
The indoor fan runs on a no-cooling call but the outdoor unit is silent. Walk me through it.
How you work through an electrical fault in a logical order.
Control voltage first, then line voltage and safeties, then components, with power off and the capacitor discharged before testing.

I confirm the thermostat is calling and that 24 volts reach the contactor coil. If not, I look for an open safety like a float switch or pressure switch. If the contactor pulls in, I check line voltage at the load side. If motors hum but won't start, I kill power, discharge the capacitor and test it against its printed rating.
You find an evaporator coil covered in ice. What do you do?
Whether you avoid the classic mistake of adding refrigerant to a frozen coil.
Thaws the coil before reading the charge, checks airflow first, and only then looks at charge and leaks.

I turn off cooling and let the coil thaw, running the fan to speed it up. Pressures read on an iced coil mislead, so I don't touch the charge yet. I check the filter, blower, closed registers and a dirty coil. Once airflow is right, I check superheat or subcooling, and if it's low I look for the leak.
A customer asks you to just top off the refrigerant again, like every summer. What do you say?
Your judgement and honesty when a quick fix hides the real problem.
Explains that refrigerant is not consumed, so low charge means a leak, and offers to find and repair it.

I tell them refrigerant isn't used up like fuel. If it's low every year, it's leaking. Topping off costs them money each time, releases refrigerant and can shorten the compressor's life. I offer a leak search with an electronic detector and bubbles, then a repair price, or a replacement quote if the coil itself is failing.
Walk me through replacing a compressor, from the refrigerant side.
Whether you know proper recovery, brazing, evacuation and charging practice.
Recovers instead of venting, brazes with nitrogen flowing, replaces the drier, pressure tests, verifies vacuum with a micron gauge and weighs in the charge.

I recover the charge into a rated recovery cylinder and keep it under 80% full. I swap the compressor and filter drier, brazing with nitrogen flowing so no scale forms inside. I pressure test with dry nitrogen, pull a deep vacuum checked with a micron gauge and a hold test, then weigh in the charge the nameplate and line length call for.
What changes for you when you work on a system with an A2L refrigerant like R-454B or R-32?
Whether you are current on the newer, mildly flammable refrigerants.
Knows A2L means mildly flammable and adjusts tools, ignition control, ventilation and brazing prep to match.

A2L refrigerants are mildly flammable, so I treat ignition sources seriously. I use recovery machines, vacuum pumps and leak detectors rated for A2L, and I keep the area ventilated. Before brazing I recover fully and purge the lines with nitrogen. I also follow the manufacturer's rules on leak sensors and how much charge the space allows.
On a Friday night you find a cracked heat exchanger, and the owner wants heat for the weekend. What do you do?
How you hold the line on a life-safety issue under customer pressure.
Shuts the furnace down, explains the carbon monoxide risk plainly, documents it and offers real alternatives.

I shut off the gas and tag the furnace out, following our policy. I show them the crack on camera and explain it can let carbon monoxide into the house. I check that their CO alarms work, suggest electric space heaters for the weekend and set up a replacement quote. I document everything and ask them to sign that they were told.
How is working in a data center different from servicing an office building?
Whether you understand mission-critical sites where cooling failure stops the business.
Puts uptime first: change approval, maintenance windows, confirming redundancy before isolating a unit, and constant communication.

In a data center a lost cooling unit can take down servers in minutes. I work only under an approved change ticket and window. Before I isolate a unit, I confirm the redundant units are carrying the load. I tell the site team before I start and when I finish, and I keep hot and cold aisle containment closed while I work.
Tell me about a mistake you made on a job and how you handled it.
Whether you own errors quickly and change your habits so they don't repeat.
A real mistake, reported right away, fixed fast, and a concrete habit added to prevent it.

I once jumped out a condensate float switch to test a unit and left with the jumper still in. I realized it in the truck an hour later. I called my supervisor, drove back, removed the jumper and cleared the drain. Now I tag every jumper I place and check for tags before I close any panel.

identity-access-management.heading: Identity and access management questions
qs: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
Whether you keep apart the two core ideas of the job.
Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do. A clear example of each.

Authentication answers who you are: a password, a passkey or a second factor proves it. Authorization answers what you may do once you are in, like read-only access to payroll. A user can log in fine and still be denied a page. That is authorization working, not a login problem.
When would you use SAML and when OpenID Connect for single sign-on?
Your working knowledge of the main single sign-on protocols.
SAML for many enterprise web apps; OIDC, built on OAuth 2.0, for modern web and mobile apps. Knows plain OAuth is for authorization, not login.

SAML passes signed XML assertions through the browser and is still the standard for many older enterprise web apps. OpenID Connect adds a login layer on top of OAuth 2.0 and returns an ID token, a signed JSON web token, so it fits mobile apps and APIs better. I never treat a plain OAuth access token as proof of who the user is.
What does current NIST guidance say about password rules, and how would you apply it?
Whether your password policy follows current guidance or old habits.
Length over complexity rules, no forced scheduled resets without signs of compromise, and screening against breached-password lists.

NIST SP 800-63B moved away from forced complexity and scheduled expiry. I set a solid minimum length, allow long passphrases, block passwords found in breach lists and common words, and force a reset only when there is evidence of compromise. Then I push MFA, because a good password alone can still be phished.
Someone moves from finance to marketing. What should happen to their access?
How you handle the mover step, where access quietly piles up.
New role access granted, old role access removed, with a short approved overlap at most. Names privilege creep as the risk.

The HR change should trigger it. Marketing access is granted based on the new role, and the finance access, like the ledger and payment tools, is removed, not kept just in case. If a handover is needed, I allow a short overlap with an end date. Skipping the removal is how people collect years of extra access, which we call privilege creep.
A fired employee was disabled in the directory, but a week later you find they still logged in to one app. What happened and what do you do?
How you handle a deprovisioning gap, both the cleanup and the fix.
Spots a local account or long-lived session outside SSO, cuts it at once, checks what was done, and fixes the process so it cannot repeat.

Most likely the app has its own local login, or sessions and tokens that outlive the directory change. I disable that account and revoke sessions right away, pull the app logs to see what they did, and tell security and the app owner. Then I connect the app to SSO with automatic provisioning, such as SCIM, or add it to a checked offboarding list.
A user reports getting dozens of MFA push prompts in the middle of the night. What does that tell you and what do you change?
Whether you recognize an MFA fatigue attack and know the stronger fixes.
The password is likely stolen. Reset it, revoke sessions, check logs, then add number matching and move toward phishing-resistant MFA.

Someone probably has the password and hopes the user taps approve to make it stop. I reset the password, revoke active sessions and check sign-in logs for where the attempts came from. Longer term I turn on number matching, limit repeated prompts, and move high-risk users to phishing-resistant methods like FIDO2 security keys or passkeys.
How do you manage service accounts that no person logs in to?
Your handling of non-human identities, a common blind spot.
A named owner, minimal rights, no interactive login, secrets in a vault with rotation, and regular review of unused accounts.

Every service account gets a human owner and a stated purpose in the inventory. It gets only the rights the job needs and cannot log in interactively. Its secret lives in a vault and rotates, or better, I use managed identities or certificates so there is no stored password. Accounts with no owner or no recent use get disabled, then deleted.
Users of one app suddenly cannot sign in through SSO, while every other app works. Walk me through how you troubleshoot it.
How you find the failure point in a single-app SSO problem.
Asks what changed, captures the SAML or OIDC exchange, and checks the usual suspects: certificate, clock, URLs and attribute mapping.

First I ask what changed: a certificate rollover on our side or an update on the app's side. Then I capture the exchange with a browser SAML tracer and read the app's error. Common causes are a replaced signing certificate the app does not trust yet, clock skew on the server, a wrong reply URL, or a changed attribute, like the email the app uses to match users.
Your quarterly access review came back with managers approving 99% of access in a few minutes. What do you do?
Your judgement about whether a control actually works.
Treats rubber-stamping as a failed control and makes reviews smaller, clearer and risk-based instead of just running them again.

A review approved in minutes is a signature, not a check. I would cut what managers see: hide access that comes automatically with the role, flag access that is risky or unused for months, and show plain names instead of group codes. High-risk systems also go to the app owner, and I track how many removals each review produces.
How would you set up break-glass accounts so the team is not locked out if SSO or MFA fails?
Whether you plan for your own identity system failing without opening a back door.
A few cloud-only emergency accounts, kept out of policies that could block them, strongly protected, alerted on and tested.

I keep two emergency admin accounts that do not depend on federated login or on any one person's phone. They use long random credentials and hardware security keys stored in separate safes, and are excluded from access rules that might block them. Any sign-in alerts the whole team, and we test them on a schedule so we know they still work.

implementation.heading: Implementation and onboarding questions
qs: What happens in a kickoff call with a new customer, and what do you need to leave with?
Whether you know how an implementation starts and what it depends on.
Named owners on the customer side, an agreed goal and scope, a date, and a clear list of what the customer must deliver.

I confirm who owns what on their side: an executive sponsor, a project lead, an IT contact and a data owner. We agree on what success means in numbers, the go-live date, and what is in and out of scope. I leave with a shared plan, a weekly call booked, and a list of what I need from them by when, like data exports and admin access.
What is the difference between configuration and customization, and why does it matter?
Your grasp of a basic trade-off in setting up a product.
Configuration uses built-in settings and survives upgrades; customization is custom work that costs more to maintain and can break.

Configuration uses settings the product already has: fields, workflows, roles, templates. It survives upgrades and support can help with it. Customization means custom code or scripts built for one customer. It can break when the product changes and few people understand it. So I push for configuration first and treat customization as a cost the customer agrees to.
Walk me through how you move a customer's data from their old system into ours.
Whether you follow a safe, repeatable migration method.
Field mapping signed off by the customer, cleaning in a copy, test loads, customer validation, then a planned final cutover.

First I get a sample export and map every old field to a new one, and the customer signs off on the mapping. I clean and transform a copy, never the source. Then a test load into a sandbox, and the customer checks record counts and spot-checks records they know well. We fix, load again, and only then plan the final cutover with a short freeze on the old system.
The customer's export has duplicates, blank required fields and dates in three formats. What do you do?
How you handle dirty data without making business decisions for the customer.
Report the problems, fix format issues by approved rules, and let the customer's data owner decide on duplicates and blanks.

I don't fix it silently. I send a short report: how many duplicates, which required fields are blank, which date formats appear. Formats I can standardize with a rule they approve. Duplicates and blanks are business decisions, so their data owner decides which record wins or what default to use. I log every rule so the final load repeats it exactly.
How would you plan training for a customer with three admins, ten managers and 200 frontline users?
Whether you can design training around roles and real tasks.
Different sessions per role, admins first, frontline training short and task-based, with materials to keep and timing close to go-live.

I train by role, not one session for all. Admins get deep hands-on training first, because they will support everyone else. Managers learn reports and approvals. Frontline users get short sessions on the few tasks they do daily, using their own data in a sandbox, plus a one-page guide and recordings. I time it close to go-live so they don't forget.
How do you decide a customer is ready to go live?
Your judgement on launch readiness and willingness to call a delay.
Clear criteria agreed in advance, customer sign-off on testing, a rollback and support plan, and a delay if a must-have fails.

I use a checklist we agreed on early: final data checked against counts, integrations tested end to end, users and permissions set, key users trained, and customer sign-off on acceptance testing. There is also a rollback plan and support for the first weeks. If a must-have item fails, I recommend a delay and say so plainly, even if the date was announced.
The customer's IT team still has not set up the single sign-on we need, and launch is in two weeks. What do you do?
How you unblock work that depends on the customer's own people.
Find the real cause, make the task easy to do, then escalate to the sponsor in writing with the risk and clear options.

I find out why first; often the IT contact never got a clear request. I send exactly what we need with a step-by-step guide and offer a 30-minute working session to do it together. If it still stalls, I tell the sponsor in writing what is blocked, since when, and what date it puts at risk, with options: move launch, or start with regular logins and add sign-on later.
On go-live morning, users say a large share of their records are missing. What do you do?
How you handle a migration failure under pressure.
Tell the customer fast, compare counts and logs to find the cause, reload only what is missing, and verify with the customer.

I tell the customer right away that we are on it and when they will hear from me next. Then I compare record counts between the source export and what loaded, and read the load logs. Often it is a filter, a failed batch, or records rejected by a validation rule. I fix the cause, reload only the missing records, and check with the customer before closing it.
The customer wants us to rebuild their old system's workflow exactly as it was. How do you respond?
Whether you can steer a customer toward a better process without dismissing their needs.
Ask why each step exists, keep what protects a real need, drop old workarounds, and document true gaps instead of forcing them.

I ask why each step exists. Some protect something real, like an approval before spending. Others were workarounds for the old tool's limits. I show how our standard process covers the real need, ideally in a quick demo with their data. If a step truly matters and our product can't do it, I record it as a gap and raise it, rather than build something fragile.
How do you know onboarding worked, and how do you hand the customer over when it ends?
Your sense of what success means and how you close a project cleanly.
Success measured by the kickoff goal and real usage, plus a written handoff and a joint call so nothing is lost.

It worked when the customer reaches the goal we set at kickoff and people really use the product: logins, key tasks done, fewer how-to tickets. For handoff I write a summary of setup decisions and why, integrations and their owners, open issues, and contacts. Then I hold a joint call so the customer meets their account manager or support team before I step away.

indirect-tax.heading: Indirect tax and transfer pricing specialist questions
qs: What is the difference between a US sales tax and a VAT?
Whether you understand how the two main consumption taxes work.
Sales tax is charged once, at the final retail sale. VAT is charged at every stage, and businesses reclaim the tax they paid on purchases.

Sales tax is a single-stage tax: the retailer charges it to the final buyer, and sales for resale are exempt with a certificate. VAT is charged at each step of the chain. Each business charges VAT on its sales, deducts the VAT it paid on purchases and pays the difference, so the final consumer bears the full tax.
When does a company owe use tax, and how do you catch it?
Your grasp of the buyer's side of sales tax.
Use tax applies when a taxable item is used in a state and the seller charged no tax. You find it by reviewing purchases, not sales.

If we buy something taxable for our own use and the vendor charges no tax, say an out-of-state supplier with no duty to collect, we owe use tax to the state where we use it. I review payables data each month for untaxed invoices, accrue the tax on the taxable items and report it on the return.
What does the arm's length principle mean in transfer pricing?
Whether you know the rule every intercompany price is tested against.
Related companies must price their dealings as unrelated parties would in similar circumstances. In the US this comes from Section 482.

The price one part of a group charges another should be what independent companies would agree to in comparable circumstances. If it is not, the IRS can reallocate income under Section 482, and most other countries apply the same idea through the OECD guidelines. We support our prices by comparing them with deals or margins of independent companies.
A customer says they are buying for resale and asks you not to charge sales tax. What do you need?
How you protect the seller from tax it failed to collect.
A complete, valid resale certificate the state accepts, checked and kept on file, because without it the seller usually owes the tax on audit.

I ask for a resale certificate the state accepts, with the buyer's name, address, permit number, signature and type of goods. I check it is complete and that the items fit their business. I keep it on file and track renewals, because if an auditor finds no valid certificate, we owe the tax ourselves.
A client sells online into states where it has no office or staff. Does it have to collect sales tax there?
Whether you know how nexus works after the Wayfair decision.
Possibly yes: since 2018 states can require remote sellers to collect once sales pass economic thresholds, which differ by state and must be checked.

Since the Supreme Court's Wayfair decision in 2018, a state can require a seller with no physical presence to collect once its sales there pass a threshold, a dollar amount and in some states a number of transactions. I would pull sales by state, compare them with each state's current rules, and register before the obligation starts.
Sales wants to start selling software as an online subscription instead of a download. What do you check?
How you work out taxability when the product changes.
That states treat software as a service very differently, plus where each sale is sourced and how bundled charges are invoiced.

States differ a lot: some tax software as a service like software, some tax it as a data or information service, and many do not tax it. I map where customers are, check each state's rule and confirm we source by the customer's location. I also check bundles, since a mixed charge can become fully taxable in some states.
How do you choose a transfer pricing method for a distributor that buys from a related manufacturer?
Your judgement in applying the best method rule.
Weighs comparability and data: a comparable uncontrolled price if one exists, otherwise often a method testing the distributor's margin.

US rules ask for the best method: the one giving the most reliable arm's length result for the facts and data we have. If we sell the same product to unrelated distributors on similar terms, that comparable price is strongest. Usually it is missing, so I test the distributor's operating margin against independent distributors.
Why does the timing of transfer pricing documentation matter for US penalties?
Whether you know what protects the company from transfer pricing penalties.
To get penalty protection under Section 6662(e), documentation must exist when the return is filed and be given to the IRS within 30 days of a request.

Penalty protection under Section 6662(e) needs contemporaneous documentation: it must exist by the time the return is filed, and we must provide it within 30 days if the IRS asks. A report written after an audit starts does not count. So I plan the study during the year, update the comparables and have it finished before filing.
You find the company had nexus in a state for two years and never collected sales tax. What do you do?
How you handle a past exposure honestly and limit the cost.
Quantify the exposure, tell management, and consider a voluntary disclosure agreement before the state makes contact.

First I size it: taxable sales into the state by period, plus tax, interest and possible penalties. I brief the tax director in writing. If the state has not contacted us, a voluntary disclosure agreement often limits the lookback period and waives penalties. I also check whether customers already paid use tax, which can cut what we owe.

industry-marketing.heading: Industry and solutions marketing manager questions
qs: How is industry marketing different from core product marketing?
Whether you understand what this role adds beyond product launch work.
Product marketing explains what the product does. Industry marketing shows how it solves one sector's problems, in that sector's words and with proof from that sector.

Core product marketing owns the product story for everyone: features, launches, pricing. My job starts from the industry instead. I take the same product and show a bank or a hospital how it fits their workflow, their rules and their buyers, with use cases and proof from their peers. A feature becomes a fix for a problem they already name.
You are assigned an industry you have never worked in. How do you learn it in your first 30 days?
How you build real domain knowledge quickly instead of guessing.
You talk to customers and sellers, read what buyers read, and learn their terms, rules and buying process before writing anything.

I book calls with five or six customers and the reps who sell to them, and I ask about their day, not our product. I read the trade publications and analyst reports they read, list the terms they use, and note which rules shape their decisions. By week four I write a one-page industry brief and ask a customer to tell me what I got wrong.
Walk me through turning a general product feature into an industry use case.
Your method for translating a feature into a sector's problem and outcome.
You start from the industry's problem and process, map the feature to one step in it, and prove the outcome with a number or a customer example.

Take automated document extraction. For a bank, I start with the problem: loan files that take days to review by hand. I show where the feature fits in the loan process, what the analyst no longer does, and the result, say review time cut from three days to one at a pilot customer. Then I check the wording with a banker before it goes live.
How does marketing to developers differ from marketing to business buyers?
Whether you can adapt tone, content and proof to very different audiences.
Developers want to try it and see code, docs and honest limits. Business buyers want outcomes, risk and cost. Channels and calls to action differ too.

Developers distrust marketing language, so I lead with what they can do in ten minutes: docs, a quickstart, sample code and a free tier, with limits stated plainly. Business buyers want the outcome, the risk and the cost, in a short brief or a peer story. The call to action changes too: “try it now” for one, “talk to us” for the other.
Banks rarely let vendors use their name. How do you build customer proof for that industry?
How you get credible references in a sector that avoids publicity.
Anonymized stories, private reference calls and peer events, with numbers the customer approves in writing and time built in for their review.

I offer options that do not expose the bank. An anonymized story, like “a US regional bank with 200 branches,” with numbers they approve. Private reference calls with a peer under NDA. Small roundtables where customers speak off the record. I get each approval in writing and give their legal and comms teams time to review, which can take weeks, so I start early.
A sales leader wants our healthcare page to say we are “HIPAA certified.” What do you do?
Whether you know industry claims carry legal weight and handle them correctly.
You know there is no official government HIPAA certification and propose accurate wording, such as signing a business associate agreement, checked with legal.

I would not publish it, because there is no official government HIPAA certification, and a false claim hurts us with buyers and regulators. I would ask security and legal what is true, for example that we sign a business associate agreement and have third-party audits. I write that, and explain to the sales leader that a hospital security team trusts accurate claims more.
How do you decide which industry to go after next?
Your judgement in choosing a vertical with data, not opinion.
You weigh win rates, deal size, existing customers, product fit, market size and the cost of entry, then recommend one with the tradeoffs stated.

I start with our own data: where we already win, with what deal size and sales cycle, and which customers renew. Then market size, how well the product fits without big changes, and the cost of entry, like security reviews buyers expect. If two industries score close, I pick the one where we have reference customers, because peers trust peers.
At a bank, the buying group may include the business owner, IT, security, compliance and procurement. How do you plan content for them?
Whether you can map messages to a buying committee inside one industry.
Each role's concern is named and answered with its own material, plus a summary the internal champion can present without you.

I list what each person needs to say yes. The business owner wants the outcome and the cost. IT wants to know how we connect to their existing systems. Security wants the questionnaire answered and audit reports. Compliance wants to know how we support their rules. Procurement wants terms. I build a short kit for each and give our champion a deck they can present alone.
Two quarters after launching a vertical, pipeline is thin. How do you find out whether the problem is the market, the product or the message?
How you diagnose a struggling industry program before changing it.
You find the funnel step where it breaks, talk to lost prospects, and separate reach, interest and fit before deciding to fix, wait or exit.

I find where it breaks. If few target accounts engage, it is reach or message. If they engage but stall after demos, it is likely product fit or a missing requirement. I call five lost prospects and ask what stopped them. Once the answer was a missing integration with a common banking system, not our copy, so we paused spend until it shipped.
The industry expects a feature our product does not have yet. How do you position us without overpromising?
Your honesty and skill when the product does not fully fit the market.
You never imply a roadmap item exists. You lead with real strengths, offer workarounds or partners, and bring the gap to product with deal data.

I do not write around the gap in a way that implies we have it. I lead with what we do well for that industry, show a workaround or a partner that covers the need today, and give sales a straight answer for when buyers ask. I also bring product the number and value of deals lost to that gap, which is the strongest case for building it.

industry-specialist.heading: Industry specialist and field CTO questions
qs: How is a field CTO different from a sales engineer on the same deal?
Whether you understand where your role sits in the sales team.
The engineer proves the product works in detail. The specialist shapes strategy with senior leaders and ties it to the industry, and the two work together.

The sales engineer owns the demo, the proof of concept and the detailed technical questions. I work higher and earlier. I talk with the customer's CTO or business heads about where their industry is going and where we fit. I hand the detail to the engineer and stay on the few deals where executive trust decides the outcome.
What do you do in the first ten minutes with a CIO to earn a second meeting?
How you build credibility with a senior buyer as a peer.
You talk about their problems and their industry, not the product. You bring a point of view and ask sharp questions.

I don't open with slides. I share one trend I'm seeing across their industry and say how three or four peers are handling it. Then I ask which of those looks like their situation, and I listen. If I learn something they haven't told a vendor before, I've earned the next meeting. If I spend those minutes pitching, I'm just one more vendor.
Which deals should get your time, and which should not?
How you spend a scarce resource across the team's pipeline.
Clear criteria such as size, strategic value, or an executive who wants a peer. You also say no to deals a sales engineer can win alone.

I take deals where an executive conversation can change the outcome. That means large or strategic accounts, a new use case we want to prove in the industry, or a buyer stuck on risk. I turn down deals that only need a demo. I agree on this with sales leaders each quarter, and I track my time against what closed.
How do you get what you hear from customers into the product roadmap?
How you act as the link between the field and the product team.
You bring patterns, not stories: grouped requests with pipeline value and named accounts, raised with product managers on a regular schedule.

Single requests don't move a roadmap. I log what I hear and group it by problem, not by the feature someone asked for. I note which accounts and how much pipeline each problem touches. Each quarter I bring the top three to product managers and offer customer calls with them. When something ships, I go back to the customers who asked for it.
In front of the customer's CTO, their lead architect asks something you cannot answer. What do you do?
Whether you protect trust when you reach the edge of what you know.
You say plainly that you don't know, give a date for the answer and keep that promise. No bluffing.

I say I don't know for sure and won't guess on something they'll build on. I repeat the question to make sure I have it right, write it down and give a date, usually within two days. Then I get the answer from our engineers and send it to the architect with the CTO copied. A bluff in that room would cost far more than one unanswered question.
The account executive told a prospect a feature is coming next quarter. You know it is not on the roadmap. What do you do?
Your integrity when a colleague overpromises.
You raise it with the rep privately first. Then you correct it with the customer before it shapes the deal, and offer an honest alternative.

I talk to the rep that day, in private, and explain what is actually planned. We agree to correct it together so the rep keeps face. Then we tell the customer before they build a plan on it: what exists today, what workaround covers the gap, and what I can't promise. If the deal depends on that feature, it is better to know now than at renewal.
A hospital wants to put patient data on your platform. What has to be in place before you say yes?
Whether you know the rules of the industry you claim as your specialty.
You know that a vendor handling patient data for a hospital is a HIPAA business associate. That means a signed agreement and matching security controls.

Under HIPAA, if we store or process protected health information for the hospital, we are a business associate. We need a signed business associate agreement before any patient data arrives. I check that legal will sign it and which services it covers. I confirm our controls fit the Security Rule: access control, audit logs, encryption. I bring in their privacy officer early.
A competitor's field CTO told your prospect that your platform does not scale. How do you respond?
How you handle a competitive claim without attacking the competitor.
No bad-mouthing. You ask what scale they need, then prove it with evidence, such as a test at their volume or a reference customer.

I don't argue about the other vendor. I ask what scale the customer actually needs: transactions per second, data volume, users at peak. Then I offer proof on their terms: a load test at their numbers, an architecture review, and a call with a reference customer of similar size. Specific evidence usually ends the claim. Arguing keeps it alive.
When have you told a customer your product was not the right fit?
Whether you put the customer's long-term trust ahead of a single deal.
A real example where honesty cost a short-term sale but kept the relationship or brought business later.

A manufacturer wanted our platform for real-time machine control. We are built for analytics, not for split-second control loops. I told them so. I suggested they keep control in their existing system and use us for analytics on top. We lost the larger scope that year. Eighteen months later their COO called me first for a plant-wide data project.
You carry no quota of your own. How should we measure whether you are worth the cost?
How you prove your impact in a role without a direct quota.
Concrete measures: win rate and deal size on deals you joined versus not, influenced pipeline and cycle time. Also honesty about who gets credit.

I'd compare win rate and average deal size on deals I joined with similar deals I didn't, and how fast those deals moved. I'd add pipeline from my talks, papers and executive briefings, plus product changes that came from my field input. I'd be careful with credit. I join the hard deals, so I'd compare like with like and review it with sales leaders twice a year.

inference-engineer.heading: Inference engineer questions
qs: Which latency numbers do you track for a chat model, and why not just the average?
Whether you measure what users actually feel in a streaming product.
Time to first token and time between tokens, read at p50, p95 and p99, plus throughput. Averages hide the slow tail.

I track time to first token, which is how long the user waits before text appears, and time per output token, which sets reading speed. I look at p50, p95 and p99 per route and prompt length. An average can look fine while one request in a hundred stalls for ten seconds, and those are the users who complain.
What is the KV cache, and why does it often limit how many requests you can serve at once?
Your grasp of where GPU memory goes during text generation.
It stores the keys and values of past tokens so they are not recomputed, and it grows with sequence length and the number of requests.

For each layer, the model keeps the key and value vectors of every token already seen, so each new token only computes its own. The cache grows with layers, sequence length and number of requests. With long prompts it can rival the weights in size, so free memory for cache, not raw compute, usually caps concurrency.
Why is the prefill phase usually compute-bound while the decode phase is memory-bandwidth-bound?
Whether you understand the hardware limits behind generation speed.
Prefill reuses each weight across many prompt tokens. Decode reads all the weights for one token per sequence, so memory speed sets the pace.

Prefill runs the whole prompt in one pass, so every weight loaded from memory is used for many tokens: lots of math per byte. Decode makes one token per sequence per step, so the GPU reads all the weights to do little math. Memory bandwidth then sets the speed, which is why batching more sequences into each decode step raises throughput so much.
Explain continuous batching and why it beats static batching for text generation.
Your knowledge of the scheduling idea at the heart of modern serving engines.
Requests join and leave the batch at each generation step, so short answers do not wait for long ones and GPU slots stay full.

With static batching, a batch runs until its longest answer finishes, so slots sit empty and new requests wait. Continuous batching schedules at every decode step: when one sequence ends, a waiting request takes its slot right away. Throughput goes up a lot, and time to first token drops because nobody waits for a whole batch to drain.
You quantize a model from 16-bit to 8-bit weights. What can go wrong, and how do you check it?
How you trade speed and memory against quality without guessing.
Names real risks, such as layers sensitive to outlier values and kernels that give no speedup, and checks with task evals, not perplexity alone.

8-bit weights halve weight memory, but a few layers with outlier values can lose accuracy, and if the kernels do not support the format I get no speedup at all. So I run our task evals and a set of real prompts against the 16-bit baseline, compare outputs side by side, and measure latency at our real batch sizes. If one layer hurts, I keep it in higher precision.
How does speculative decoding speed up generation without changing the output?
Whether you understand a key speed technique and its limits.
A small draft model proposes tokens, the big model checks them in one pass, and a proper acceptance rule keeps the output distribution the same.

A small draft model guesses the next few tokens. The large model checks all of them in one forward pass and keeps the ones it agrees with, using a rejection rule that leaves its output distribution unchanged. The gain depends on how often guesses are accepted: good on code or predictable text, small or even negative when the draft is often wrong.
A 70-billion-parameter model does not fit on one GPU. How do you choose between tensor and pipeline parallelism?
Your judgement in splitting a model across GPUs.
Tensor parallelism inside a node with fast links for lower latency; pipeline parallelism across nodes, where links are slower.

In 16-bit, the weights alone need about 140 GB, before any KV cache. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across GPUs and syncs at every layer, so it needs fast links, usually inside one node, and it lowers per-token latency.
