Pipeline parallelism gives each GPU a block of layers and talks less, but adds idle gaps. I use tensor inside a node, pipeline across nodes.
After a deploy, p99 latency doubled but GPU utilization looks the same. How do you find the cause?
How you debug a performance regression in a live system.
Rolls back if users are hurt, then splits latency into queue, prefill and decode time and compares before and after the change.

If users are hurting, I roll back first. Then I split latency into queue time, time to first token and decode time, and diff the deploy: engine version, batch limits, memory settings. Once a lower memory setting made the engine evict KV cache under load and recompute long prompts. The median was fine, the tail doubled. Traces by prompt length showed it fast.
Traffic spikes fast, but a new GPU replica takes several minutes to start. How do you keep latency under control?
How you plan capacity when hardware is slow to add.
Keeps warm headroom, scales on queue depth or tokens in flight, shortens cold starts, and sheds low-priority load cleanly when full.

I keep spare warm capacity sized to the fastest spike we have seen within one replica start time. I scale on queue depth and tokens in flight, not CPU. I cut start time by caching the image and weights on local disk. When full, I return a clear retry response to low-priority traffic instead of letting every request time out.
A product team wants to cut serving cost in half without hurting quality. What do you try, and in what order?
Your judgement in cutting cost while protecting quality.
Measures cost per token first, tries cheap safe wins before risky ones, and gates each change on evals.

First I measure cost per million tokens and GPU utilization by route. Then cheap, safe wins: tune batch limits, cache the shared system prompt, cap needless output length. Next, quantization and a better-sized GPU type, each checked on our evals. Last, routing easy requests to a smaller model, with an A/B test on quality before full rollout.

influencer-marketing.heading: Influencer and creator marketing questions
qs: How do you check that a creator's audience is real before you offer a deal?
Whether you can spot bought followers and fake engagement.
Looks past follower count: growth history, comment quality, audience data from the creator, and views compared to followers.

I look at the follower growth curve first; a jump of thousands overnight is a warning sign. Then I read the comments: real ones talk about the content, bots say "nice pic". I ask for screenshots of their audience data, country and age, and compare average views to followers. A big account with tiny, flat views gets passed over.
What does a disclosure have to look like to meet FTC rules?
Your knowledge of the FTC Endorsement Guides.
Clear and conspicuous: easy to notice, in plain words, in the post itself, not hidden in hashtags or below the "more" cut.

It has to be hard to miss. Plain words like "ad" or "paid partnership with" the brand, near the start of the caption, not buried in a block of hashtags. In a video it should be said out loud and shown on screen. The platform's paid partnership label helps, but I don't rely on it alone.
We only sent the creator free product, no fee. Do they still need to disclose?
Whether you know what counts as a material connection.
Yes. Free product, discounts, trips and commissions are all connections the audience would want to know about.

Yes. The FTC treats free product as a material connection, just like cash, an affiliate commission or a paid trip. So in the gifting note I say plainly that if they choose to post, they should mark it as a gift from the brand. I also tell them they are free to give an honest opinion; we are not buying a positive review.
Walk me through what goes into a creator brief.
Whether you can guide a creator without killing their voice.
Goal, key message, must-haves and no-gos, disclosure, dates and review steps, then room for the creator's own style.

One page. The goal, the one message we need to land, and two or three facts they must get right. A short list of no-gos, like competitor mentions or health claims. The disclosure we need, posting dates, links or codes, and how many review rounds. Then I leave the format to them, because they know what their audience watches.
How do you work out a fair fee for a creator?
How you price a deal instead of accepting the first number.
Starts from real average views and a cost per thousand views, then prices usage rights, exclusivity and extra deliverables separately.

I take their average views on recent posts, not their best one, and compare the cost per thousand views to what we pay similar creators. Then I price the extras separately: paid usage rights, a category exclusivity window, extra stories. If someone asks $5,000 for posts that average 40,000 views, I can show where that sits and negotiate on deliverables, not only price.
What is the difference between usage rights and whitelisting?
Your grasp of the contract terms that drive cost.
Usage rights let the brand reuse the content on its own channels; whitelisting lets the brand run ads from the creator's account. Both need a scope and a time limit.

Usage rights mean we can repost the creator's video on our own pages or in our ads, for set channels and a set period. Whitelisting means the creator gives us access to run paid ads under their name and handle, so the ad appears to come from them. Both cost extra, and I write the term, say 90 days, and the channels into the contract.
A creator's post went live without the disclosure we asked for. What do you do?
How you fix a compliance problem fast.
Contacts the creator right away to fix it, keeps a record, and closes the gap in the process so it does not happen again.

I message the creator within the hour and ask them to edit the caption, or delete and repost if an edit can't fix it. I screenshot before and after for our records. Then I check why: was the disclosure in the contract and the brief? Brands are expected to monitor their creators, so I add a check of every post on the day it goes live.
A creator delivers a draft that is off-brief but very good. Do you send it back?
Your judgement between brand control and what works with the audience.
Separates real problems (wrong facts, missing disclosure, a no-go) from taste; fixes the first and keeps the creator's voice.

I check it against the must-haves first. If a fact is wrong, the disclosure is missing or it breaks a no-go, it goes back with a specific note. If it's just not how we pictured it, I usually keep it; their audience trusts their style, not ours. I explain that to the client and suggest testing it against a more on-brief version.
The client wants creators to say the product is "clinically proven" to improve skin. How do you handle it?
Whether you know creators cannot make claims the brand cannot back up.
Asks for the evidence first; a creator's claim is treated as the brand's ad claim, and creators speak only from their own experience.

I ask the client for the study behind "clinically proven". If it doesn't support that exact claim, the line comes out of the brief, because what a creator says for us counts as our advertising. I also tell creators to talk only about what they experienced using the product, not results we can't prove. That protects the brand and the creator.
Two days before launch, a creator in your campaign is caught in a public controversy. What do you do?
How you handle a brand-safety crisis under contract and time pressure.
Pauses instead of reacting in public, gets the facts, reads the morals clause, decides with the client, and has a backup creator ready.

I ask the creator to hold their posts and I pause any paid ads; a pause costs little and buys time. Then I get the facts, not just the headlines, and read the morals clause to see our options. I bring the client a recommendation: hold, move the dates, or end the deal and pay what's owed. Meanwhile I line up a backup from our shortlist.

information-security.heading: Information security analyst questions
qs: What is the difference between a threat, a vulnerability and a risk?
Whether you use the basic terms of the trade precisely.
A threat is what could cause harm, a vulnerability is the weakness it could use, and risk combines how likely harm is with how bad it would be.

A threat is something that could do harm, like a ransomware gang. A vulnerability is a weakness it could use, like an unpatched VPN server. Risk is how likely that pairing is to happen, weighed against how bad it would be. I can't remove every threat, so most of my work goes into closing vulnerabilities and lowering the impact.
Should passwords be encrypted or hashed in a database, and why?
Your grasp of how stored credentials are protected.
Hashed, with a unique salt and a slow algorithm built for passwords, because anyone holding the key can reverse encryption.

Hashed. Encryption is two-way: whoever gets the key gets every password. A hash is one-way, so at login we only compare hashes. I'd want a unique random salt per password and a slow algorithm made for passwords, like bcrypt or Argon2, so a stolen table is expensive to crack. A fast hash like plain SHA-256 is not enough on its own.
How would you use the NIST Cybersecurity Framework at a company that has never used one?
Whether you know the main US framework and can apply it, not just name it.
Names the six functions and uses them to measure where the company stands today, set a target and plan how to close the gap.

Version 2.0 has six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover. I'd start with an inventory of systems and data. Then I'd rate where we stand in each area against where leadership wants to be. The gaps become a plan with owners and dates. The framework is voluntary, so I use it as a common language, not a checklist.
An employee calls to say they clicked a link in an email and typed in their password. What do you do in the first hour?
How you contain a common account compromise quickly.
Resets the password and ends active sessions, checks sign-in logs, mailbox rules and MFA changes, then finds who else got the same email.

I thank them for calling fast. Then I reset the password and revoke active sessions and tokens. I check sign-in logs for logins from new places and look for new mail forwarding rules, which attackers often add, and for MFA changes. Then I search other inboxes for the same email, pull it out, and block the sender and the link's domain.
You see 40 failed logins on one account, then a success from a country where the company has no staff. How do you investigate?
How you read logs and tell a real attack from a false alarm.
Checks context first: MFA result, VPN or travel, and what the session did. Acts fast to contain it if the activity can't be explained.

First I check whether MFA was passed and whether that IP belongs to a known VPN or cloud provider. I ask the user's manager if they are traveling. Then I look at what the session did: files opened, mail rules, new devices. If I can't explain it within minutes, I disable the account and revoke sessions. Lost access for a while costs less than a breach.
How do you check that a security policy is actually followed, not just written down?
Whether you can test controls with evidence instead of trusting what people say.
Turns each rule into a test, gathers evidence from systems or samples, and follows up on gaps with owners, dates and a retest.

I turn each rule into a test. If the policy says access is removed on someone's last day, I pull a sample of people who left last quarter and compare exit dates with the dates their accounts were disabled. Where I can, I use system reports rather than interviews. Each gap gets an owner and a fix date, and I retest later.
A department wants a new cloud tool that will store customer data. What do you check before saying yes?
How you assess the risk of a third-party vendor.
Asks what data goes in, reviews independent audit evidence such as a SOC 2 Type II report, and checks login, encryption and contract terms.

I start with what data goes in and who can see it. Then I ask for a SOC 2 Type II report, which covers how controls worked over a period, not one day. I check that the tool supports our single sign-on and MFA, encrypts data, lets us export and delete it, and that the contract says how fast they must tell us about a breach.
A senior executive says multi-factor authentication slows them down and wants an exception. How do you handle it?
Your judgement when policy meets a powerful person.
Takes the complaint seriously, offers an easier secure method, and makes any exception a documented, time-limited risk acceptance.

Executives are prime targets, so I wouldn't just drop it. I'd sit with them and find the friction. Often a security key or passkey is faster than typing codes, and harder to phish. If they still want out, I write up the risk and have the accountable leader formally accept it, with an end date. Most people pick the easier key.
Your team gets thousands of alerts a day and most are false positives. What do you change?
How you keep detection useful when the noise buries the real signals.
Measures which rules are noisy, tunes or retires them, adds context, and reviews each change so tuning does not hide real attacks.

I'd count which rules fire most and how often they lead to something real. The noisiest get tuned: excluding known scanners, adding thresholds, or adding asset and user details so priority is clear. Rules that never pay off get retired or rewritten. Every change is written down and reviewed, because a careless exclusion is a gift to an attacker.
You discover a firewall change you approved left a database open to the internet for a month. What do you do?
How you own a mistake and handle a possible exposure honestly.
Closes the exposure first, reports it at once, checks logs for access, brings in legal if data may be exposed, and fixes the review process.

I close the rule first, then tell my manager within the hour, including that I approved it. Next I pull that month's logs to see who connected and whether data left. If customer data may have been read, legal decides on notice, since state laws set those duties. Afterward I'd add an automatic check that flags database ports open to the internet.

inside-sales.heading: Inside sales representative questions
qs: What changes when you sell by phone and video instead of in person?
Whether you understand what inside sales loses and how you make up for it.
Names the lost cues, like body language, and the habits that replace them: more questions, spoken summaries and next steps confirmed in writing.

I lose most of the body language, so I ask more check-in questions and listen for pauses and tone. Calls are shorter, so I prepare a tighter agenda. I also confirm every next step by email right after the call, because nobody shook my hand on it and it is easy for a buyer to forget.
What do you say in the first 30 seconds of a cold call?
How you earn the right to keep talking.
Name, a short and honest reason for the call tied to the prospect, then a question instead of a pitch read from a script.

I say who I am and admit it is a cold call, because people respect honesty. Then one line on why them: “I saw you opened two new warehouses this year, and teams growing that fast often struggle with scheduling.” Then I ask if that is true for them. If they say no, I ask what is working instead.
What do you put in a voicemail, and how long is it?
Whether your voicemails are short and part of a plan.
Under about 30 seconds, one reason to call back, the number said clearly, and tied to an email sent the same day.

About 20 seconds. My name, my company, one sentence on why I called that relates to their business, and my number said slowly, twice. I say I am sending an email with the same note so they can reply there if that is easier. Then I send it within minutes so the two line up.
How do you write a cold email that gets a reply?
Your writing for a busy reader who did not ask to hear from you.
Short, about the prospect and not the product, one clear ask, and an honest subject line.

I keep it under about 100 words, short enough to read on a phone. The first line is about them: a fact I found, not a compliment. One sentence on a problem we solve for similar companies, one result, then one easy ask, like “Worth a 15-minute call next week?” The subject line matches the content, because tricks lose trust.
A receptionist asks, “What is this regarding?” What do you say?
How you treat a gatekeeper: honestly, with respect, and still moving forward.
The truth in one plain sentence, the gatekeeper treated as someone who can help, and no fake familiarity or tricks.

I tell the truth in one sentence: “I am calling about how your team handles shipping quotes, and I wanted to see if Ms. Lee is the right person or if someone else owns that.” Receptionists often know who decides. If they will not connect me, I ask for the best time to call or an email address, and I thank them by name.
A prospect says, “Just send me some information.” What do you do?
Whether you can tell a brush-off from real interest without being pushy.
Agrees, asks one or two questions to make the material relevant, sets a follow-up time, and accepts a clear no.

I say happy to, then ask: “So I send the right thing, what are you using for this today?” If they answer, there is real interest, so I tailor what I send and ask for 15 minutes on Thursday to go over it. If they give me nothing, it is probably a polite no. I note it in the CRM and try again in a few months.
Halfway through a video demo, the buyer turns the camera off and the answers get short. What do you do?
How you notice and win back attention when you cannot see the buyer.
Stops presenting, asks directly what matters to them, and reshapes or shortens the demo around their main problem.

I stop sharing my screen and ask a plain question: “I may be showing things that do not matter to you. What would be most useful to see in the next ten minutes?” Sometimes they were just pulled into a chat. Sometimes I was showing features they do not need. Either way, I cut to their top issue and end with a clear next step.
You quoted a customer the wrong price on a call, and they have already shared it with their boss. How do you handle it?
Whether you own a mistake fast and protect the customer's trust.
Tells the manager, calls the customer quickly instead of hiding in email, owns the error plainly and puts the right number in writing.

I tell my manager first, so we know whether we can honor the quote or meet partway. Then I call the customer the same day: “I gave you the wrong price, and that is my mistake.” I give the correct number, confirm it in writing, and offer to explain it to their boss myself. A quick fix costs far less trust than a late one.
You connect with plenty of prospects, but few calls turn into booked meetings. How do you find out why?
How you use your own numbers to find and fix a weak step in your calls.
Breaks the call into stages, listens to recordings, changes one thing at a time and compares results over enough calls.

I split the numbers: connects, conversations past the first minute, meetings booked. If people hang up early, my opener is weak. If they talk but do not book, my ask is vague or comes too late. I review ten recorded calls with my manager, change one thing, like asking for a specific time, and compare the next 100 calls with the last 100.

instructional-designer.heading: Instructional designer questions
qs: What makes a learning objective a good one?
Whether you write objectives that can be observed and measured.
An observable action verb, the conditions and a standard of performance, with no vague verbs like know or understand.

I use the parts of a classic objective: what the learner will do, under what conditions, and to what standard. 'Understand the return policy' can't be checked. 'Given a receipt, process a return in the system with no errors' can. I avoid know and understand because I can't watch them happen, and I draft the assessment item right after the objective.
How do ADDIE and SAM differ, and when would you pick each?
Your grasp of the main design models and when each fits.
ADDIE as a phased process suited to stable content; SAM as rapid, iterative prototyping suited to unclear needs.

ADDIE runs in phases: analysis, design, development, implementation, evaluation. It fits stable content and compliance work where sign-offs matter. SAM, the Successive Approximation Model, builds rough prototypes early and revises them in short cycles with learners and stakeholders. I pick SAM when requirements are fuzzy, because people react better to a draft than to a document.
What is cognitive load, and how does it shape the way you build a screen?
Whether you apply how memory works to the way a screen is built.
Cutting extra load: less decoration, chunked steps, no full script on screen with narration, worked examples before practice.

Working memory holds little at once, so I cut what doesn't serve the objective: stock photos, extra text, background music. I break a process into short steps, each beside its graphic. With narration, I don't also put the full script on screen; reading and hearing the same words competes for attention. For hard content I show worked examples before practice.
What do you check to make an e-learning module accessible?
Whether accessibility is built into your work, not added at the end.
A named standard, concrete checks like captions, alt text, keyboard use and contrast, and testing with real tools.

I aim for at least the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1, level AA. That means captions, transcripts for audio, alt text on meaningful images, keyboard-only navigation, a sensible screen reader order, and text contrast of at least 4.5 to 1. I never use color alone to mark right and wrong. Then I test it myself with a keyboard and a screen reader.
What is the difference between SCORM and xAPI, and when does it matter?
Your knowledge of how courses report data to a learning system.
SCORM for packaging and basic tracking inside an LMS; xAPI for richer statements, sent to a record store, even outside the LMS.

SCORM is the older standard for packaging a course so a learning management system (LMS) can launch it and record completion, score and time. xAPI sends simple statements, like 'Ana completed the forklift simulation', to a learning record store, and can track activity outside the LMS, like a mobile app or a job checklist. If the client only needs completions, SCORM is simpler.
Your objective says learners will troubleshoot a jammed printer, but the quiz is ten recall questions about printer parts. What do you change?
Whether you align assessments with the level of the objective.
Spotting the gap between recall and application, and replacing items with scenarios or a simulation of the real task.

The quiz tests a lower level than the objective. Naming parts is recall; troubleshooting is applying a process to a new case. I'd replace it with scenarios: here are the symptoms and the error code, what do you check first? Better still, a simulation where a wrong step has a visible result. Scored that way, a pass means they can actually do the task.
A subject matter expert sends you 200 slides and says all of it must be in the course. What do you do?
How you cut content down to what learners need while keeping the expert on side.
Separating need-to-know from reference material, moving reference to job aids, and showing the expert where everything went.

I thank them, then ask what people get wrong on the job and what those mistakes cost. That gives me the need-to-know. Reference material like specs and edge cases goes into a job aid or a searchable page, not the course. I show the expert a short outline mapped to objectives, so they see their content isn't lost, just placed where learners will use it.
Sales staff are not using the new customer system, and their manager asks for a training course. What do you ask before you agree?
Whether you check that training is the right fix before building it.
A quick analysis: is it a skill gap or a cause like process, tools, incentives or follow-up that training cannot fix.

I'd find out whether it's a skill problem at all. Can they do it if they have to? If yes, training won't fix it. The cause may be that the system adds steps, managers still ask for spreadsheets, or nobody checks. I'd ask to watch two reps work and look at usage data. Training fits only the part that's a real gap in knowledge or skill.
A stakeholder wants a 60-minute course in two weeks. Your honest estimate is six weeks. What do you do?
How you handle scope and deadlines without cutting quality silently.
Offering a smaller version that fits, phasing the rest, and putting the trade-offs in writing so the stakeholder decides.

I'd show what fits in two weeks instead of just saying no. Usually that's the core: a short module on the two or three things people must do on day one, plus a job aid. The rest can follow in a second release. I'd put the trade-off in writing: what's in, what's out, and what risk that leaves, so the stakeholder decides with eyes open.
After launch, 70% of learners miss the same quiz question. How do you find out why?
How you diagnose a problem in an assessment or in the course behind it.
Checking the item first, then which wrong answer was chosen, then whether the content taught it, and asking learners.

First I check the item itself: is the key right, is the wording ambiguous, are two answers defensible? Then I see which wrong option they chose. If most picked the same one, that points to a specific misconception, maybe one the course reinforced. I compare the item to the content to confirm we taught it, and I ask a few learners to talk through their answer.

insurance.heading: Insurance questions
qs: What is the difference between an occurrence policy and a claims-made policy?
Whether you know the two main liability coverage triggers.
Occurrence follows the date of the event; claims-made follows the date the claim is made, with a retroactive date and possible tail coverage.

An occurrence policy responds to injury or damage that happens during the policy period, even if the claim comes years later. A claims-made policy responds to claims first made while it is in force, for events after the retroactive date. If a claims-made policy ends, the client may need tail coverage, which is an extended reporting period.
Explain actual cash value and replacement cost to a homeowner.
Whether you can explain a basic valuation term in plain words.
Replacement cost pays to replace with like kind and quality; actual cash value takes off depreciation, with the method set by the policy and state law.

Replacement cost pays what it takes to repair or replace the item with like kind and quality today. Actual cash value is often figured as replacement cost minus depreciation, though the exact method depends on the policy and state law. On a 12-year-old roof the gap can be large, so I make sure the client knows which one they bought.
What does a combined ratio tell you?
Your grasp of the main measure of underwriting results.
Losses plus expenses as a share of premium; under 100% is an underwriting profit, before investment income.

It adds losses and loss adjustment expenses to underwriting expenses, each as a share of premium. Under 100% means we made money on underwriting before investment income. At 104% we paid out $1.04 for every dollar of premium. I look at the loss part and the expense part separately, because they have different fixes.
Our insured was rear-ended by another driver. How does subrogation work on this claim?
Whether you know how the insurer recovers what it paid from the party at fault.
Pay the insured under their own coverage, then recover from the at-fault party or carrier, protect the evidence, and pursue the deductible too.

We pay our insured under their collision coverage, minus the deductible, so they are not left waiting. Then we pursue the at-fault driver's carrier to recover what we paid. I keep the photos, police report and statements. I tell the insured we will also try to recover their deductible, and if the carriers disagree, it can go to inter-company arbitration.
A building worth $500,000 has an 80% coinsurance clause, $300,000 of coverage, a $1,000 deductible and a $100,000 loss. What do we pay?
Whether you can apply the coinsurance clause correctly.
Required is $400,000; carried is three quarters of that, so the payment is $75,000 minus the deductible: $74,000, with the math explained.

With an 80% clause they should carry $400,000. They carry $300,000, which is three quarters of that. So on a $100,000 loss we pay three quarters, $75,000, minus the $1,000 deductible: $74,000. Before I send it, I confirm the building value is right and explain the math to the insured and the agent in writing.
You start handling a liability claim but are not sure the policy covers it. What do you do?
How you protect coverage positions while still treating the insured fairly.
Keep investigating, send a timely reservation of rights letter citing the wording at issue, and do not let delay waive the insurer's defenses.

I keep investigating and, if we defend, I send a reservation of rights letter. It says we are handling the claim but may later deny coverage, and it quotes the policy wording in question. That protects us from waiving defenses and tells the insured early, so they can involve their own lawyer. Waiting too long can cost the insurer the right to deny.
After binding a policy, you notice you rated the building with the wrong construction class. What do you do?
How you own and fix an underwriting mistake.
Report it promptly, correct it by endorsement under policy and state rules, tell the agent plainly, and change the process that let it through.

I tell my manager the same day; I don't wait for an audit to find it. We correct the class by endorsement and work out the premium change under the policy terms and state rules. I tell the agent plainly what happened. Then I look at why: if I misread the inspection report, I add a check to my routine so it does not happen again.
A claim turns on a word in the policy that can be read two ways. How do you handle it?
Your judgement when policy wording is unclear.
Read the whole policy first; if truly ambiguous, know courts usually read it against the insurer, so get coverage counsel rather than deny on your own reading.

First I read the whole policy: definitions, endorsements, exclusions. Many words that look unclear are defined. If it truly reads two ways, I know courts usually construe that against the insurer who wrote it, so I don't deny on my preferred reading. I take it to coverage counsel and flag the wording so the next edition is clearer.
After a fire, you learn the insured left a prior fire off the application. What now?
How you handle possible misrepresentation without acting rashly.
No reflex denial: check if the question was clear and the fact material, document, meet response deadlines, and involve counsel since rules vary by state.

I don't deny on the spot. I check whether the application asked clearly, and whether underwriting would have declined or priced it differently had they known; materiality is what counts in most states. I document everything, keep the insured updated within required time frames, and bring in counsel before any rescission, because the rules vary by state.
A commercial account's losses jumped last year and the broker wants a flat renewal. How do you price it?
How you weigh loss history, credibility and terms in a pricing decision.
Look past one year, separate one large loss from a trend, weigh credibility and open claims, and use terms like deductibles, not just rate.

I look at five years, not one. One large fire is different from a rise in small claims. I weigh how credible the account's own history is for its size, estimate where open claims will finally settle, and adjust for changes in exposure. Then I might offer flat rate with a higher deductible and a safety plan, instead of only raising the price or walking away.

intellectual-property.heading: Intellectual property and patent specialist questions
qs: What does a provisional patent application do, and what does it not do?
Whether you know the basic filing tools and their limits.
It sets an early US filing date and starts a 12-month clock. It is never examined and never becomes a patent by itself.

It gives us a US filing date and lets us say patent pending. It is not examined, it needs no formal claims, and it expires after 12 months. To keep that date we must file a nonprovisional, and usually foreign applications, within the year. And the date only covers what the provisional actually describes, so a thin one protects little.
A client wants to register QUICK CLEAN for a home cleaning service. What do you tell them?
Your grasp of how strong or weak a trademark is.
Spots a descriptive mark, explains the likely refusal and the options, and steers the client toward a more distinctive name.

The name describes the service, so the examiner will likely refuse it on the Principal Register as merely descriptive. We could try the Supplemental Register, or wait until we can prove customers see it as a brand, but that is slow and weak. I would suggest a coined or unrelated word, or a suggestive one, which is easier to register and to enforce.
What is the difference between a patentability search and a freedom-to-operate search?
Whether you can match the search to the business question.
Patentability asks if we can get a patent. Freedom to operate asks if our product infringes someone else's live claims where we sell.

A patentability search looks at all prior art, any age, any country, including papers and products, to see if our invention is new and not obvious. A freedom-to-operate search looks only at patents still in force where we make or sell, and reads their claims against our product. Owning a patent does not mean we are free to sell; those are separate answers.
An engineer presented the invention at a conference two months ago and nothing has been filed. What now?
Whether you know how public disclosure affects patent rights in the US and abroad.
Knows the US one-year grace period for the inventor's own disclosure, and that most other countries require absolute novelty.

In the US, the inventor's own disclosure gives us one year from the talk to file, so we file fast, ideally within weeks. Abroad it is worse: Europe and many other countries require absolute novelty, so those rights are probably lost. I would get the slides and any recording, check exactly what was shown, and set a rule that talks get cleared before they go out.
Which deadlines keep a US trademark registration and a US utility patent alive after they are granted?
Your command of post-grant deadlines, the core of IP docketing.
Section 8 and 9 filings for marks, maintenance fees at 3.5, 7.5 and 11.5 years for patents, and grace periods only as a fallback.

For a mark, a Section 8 declaration of use is due between the fifth and sixth year after registration, then Sections 8 and 9 together between the ninth and tenth year and every ten years after. For a utility patent, maintenance fees fall due 3.5, 7.5 and 11.5 years after grant. Each has a six-month grace period with a surcharge, but I docket the real due date, never the grace date.
Someone is using our client's product photos on their own shop page. Walk me through a DMCA takedown.
How you handle a common online copyright problem by the book.
Checks ownership and fair use first, knows what the notice must contain, and knows the counter-notice path.

I confirm we own the photos, save dated screenshots and consider fair use. Then I send the host's designated agent a signed notice naming our work, the copies and their links, our contact details, a good-faith statement that the use is not authorized, and a statement that the notice is accurate and, under penalty of perjury, that we may act. After a counter-notice, we must sue fast or the photos go back up.
A client found a competitor copying its software code, but never registered the copyright. What do you do first?
Whether you know when registration matters for enforcement.
Registers now, since a US work needs a registration decision before suit, and explains that late registration limits statutory damages and fees.

Copyright exists without registration, but for a US work we cannot sue until the Copyright Office registers or refuses it. So I file now, with special handling if suit is close; it costs more but is much faster. I also warn the client that since the copying began before registration, statutory damages and attorney fees are likely out, so we will need proof of real losses or the copier's profits.
While drafting, an inventor mentions a competitor's paper that is close to the invention and asks you to leave it out. What do you do?
Your understanding of the duty of candor to the patent office.
Cites it in an information disclosure statement, explains why, and knows that hiding it can make the patent unenforceable.

I say no, kindly but clearly. Everyone substantively involved in the application has a duty to disclose information they know is material, so the paper goes into an information disclosure statement. I explain that hiding it on purpose can make the whole patent unenforceable later, while citing it just means we draft claims that are clearly different. Then I ask what else they have read.
The client wants a cease-and-desist letter sent today to a company using a similar name. What do you check before it goes out?
Judgement before taking an action that can backfire.
Checks own rights, priority, evidence and the risk of the target suing first for a declaratory judgment, and keeps the tone measured.

I check that we own the mark and used it first, how close the names and the goods really are, and that our evidence is saved. I also look at who they are: a firm demand can let them sue us first for a declaratory judgment in a court they choose, and a bullying letter can go viral. If our case is solid, I send a firm, factual letter; if not, a softer one or none.
You find that a response deadline on the docket passed last week and nothing was filed. What do you do?
How you own a mistake when a client's rights are at stake.
Reports it right away, checks extension and revival options and their time limits, and fixes the process that let it happen.

I tell my supervising attorney the same hour, with the dates in hand. Then we check options: many patent deadlines can still be extended for a fee, and an application abandoned by mistake can often be revived by petition, but those have their own time limits. We tell the client honestly and file. Then I find why the docket failed, like a missing reminder, and fix it.

intern.heading: Intern and new grad questions
qs: Someone shows you a new task once, quickly. How do you make sure you can do it alone next time?
How you learn a process after seeing it only once.
Notes in your own words, doing it once while they watch, and a written checklist you test and keep.

I write the steps as they go, in my own words, and note where the files live and who approves what. Then I ask to do the next one while they watch. That evening I turn my notes into a short checklist. The next time, I follow it exactly and fix any step that was wrong.
Your manager gives you a one-line assignment and is in meetings all afternoon. What do you do?
How you handle vague instructions without stalling.
You write down how you understand the task, start on the clear parts, and check your guesses early instead of carrying them to the end.

I write two or three lines on what I think is wanted: the goal, the format, the deadline. I send that as a short message so she can correct me between meetings, and I start on the parts that do not depend on her answer. If a teammate knows the project, I ask them. I would rather show a rough draft at 3 p.m. than a polished wrong one at 5.
How do you decide whether to ask a question or keep trying on your own?
Your judgement about other people's time and your own.
A time limit set in advance, a real search first, and questions grouped together and asked along with what you already tried.

I give myself a set time, often 20 or 30 minutes, to search my notes, the documents and past work. If I am still stuck, I ask, and I say what I tried so the answer is quick. Small questions I save and ask together once a day. Anything that could cause harm, like sending something outside the team, I ask about before I act, not after.
You will miss a deadline by one day. Tell me the message you send your supervisor.
Whether you can write a short, clear message that carries bad news.
An early warning, the fact first, the reason in one line, a new date, and an offer of what can still be delivered on time.

Subject: Market summary, one day late. Hi Dana, the summary will be ready Thursday at noon, not Wednesday. Two data sources disagree and I am checking which one is right. The first two sections are done, and I can send them today if that helps. I would send this as soon as I knew, not on the due date.
Tell me about a group project where one person was not doing their part. What did you do?
How you deal with a teammate problem directly and fairly.
A private, direct talk first, a clear split of tasks with dates, and going to the instructor or lead only if that fails.

In a class project, one teammate missed two meetings and his section was empty. I called him instead of complaining in the group chat. He was working extra shifts. We moved him to the slides, which he could do at night, and set a Sunday check-in. He delivered. If he had not, I would have told the professor the facts, without blame.
A supervisor returns your draft covered in edits. How do you react, and what do you do next?
Whether you take written feedback well and learn from it.
No defensiveness, asking about any edit you do not understand, and spotting the pattern so the same edit is not needed twice.

I read every edit before replying, and I say thanks, because a marked-up draft means someone spent time on me. If I do not understand an edit, I ask why. Then I look for the pattern. Last year most of my edits were long sentences with the main point buried at the end. Now I put the conclusion first and cut each draft hard before I send it.
A big internship deliverable is due the same week as your final exams. How do you handle it?
How you manage school and work without surprising anyone.
Seeing the clash weeks ahead, telling the supervisor early, and offering a plan, such as finishing early or working fewer hours that week.

I put both calendars side by side at the start of the term, so I would see the clash weeks ahead. I would tell my supervisor then, not that week, and offer a plan: finish most of it the week before, work fewer hours during exams, and stay reachable for questions. Then I stick to the plan, so the next request is easy to trust.
On the shared drive you find a spreadsheet with everyone's salaries, which you should not be able to see. What do you do?
Your discretion with confidential information.
Close it, do not copy or share it, and tell your supervisor or IT quietly so the access can be fixed.

I close it and do not open it again, copy it or mention it to the other interns. Then I tell my supervisor privately, or the IT team, that the file seems open to more people than it should be, and where it is, so they can fix the permissions. I would rather report it than hope nobody else finds it.
You notice an error in a report your supervisor already sent to a client. What do you do?
Whether you raise a senior person's mistake in the right way.
Checking you are right, then telling the supervisor privately and quickly, with the evidence and a corrected figure, never going around them.

First I double-check, because I may be missing context. If the error holds, I go to my supervisor alone and soon, not in a team meeting. I would say: I think the total on page 4 should be $18,200, not $21,800, and here is the source. I would have the fix ready. Whether and how to tell the client is their call, not mine.
Your internship ends in two weeks and your project will not be finished. Walk me through how you hand it off.
Whether you leave work that someone else can pick up.
A written handoff with status, files, open issues and contacts, a walk-through with the new owner, and small pieces finished fully.

I agree with my supervisor on who takes over and what I should finish versus leave in good order. Then I write a short handoff document: what is done, what is not, where every file is, open questions and who to ask. I walk the new owner through it in person while I can still answer. A half-done part with clear notes beats a rushed one called done.

internal-communications.heading: Internal communications manager questions
qs: How do you decide which channel a message goes on?
How you match the message to the channel and the audience.
The channel is chosen by urgency, sensitivity and who must act. News that changes someone's job is said in person first.

I ask three things: how urgent is it, how sensitive is it, and does anyone need to act? A policy reminder fits the newsletter. An outage needs chat and email now. Anything that changes someone's job is said live, by their manager or a leader. Only then is it written down, so people can reread it.
How do you know if your internal communications are working?
Whether you measure understanding and action, not only opens.
Open and click rates as a start, plus short surveys, the behavior that changed, and what managers hear back.

Open rates tell me who saw a message, not who understood it. So I pair them with a quick two-question survey, for example: 'Do you know what this change means for your team?' I also track the action we wanted, like enrollment numbers, and ask a few managers what questions came up. If people keep asking the same thing, the message failed.
Walk me through how you plan an all-hands meeting.
Your process for a large live event, from agenda to follow-up.
A clear purpose, a tight agenda, rehearsed speakers, real Q&A, access for remote and shift staff, and a recap afterward.

I start with the one or two things every employee should leave knowing. Then I build a short agenda, brief each speaker and run a tech rehearsal. I collect questions ahead, including anonymous ones, and keep time for live ones. Remote and shift staff get a recording with captions. Within a day I send a recap and answer the questions we missed.
Your CEO drafts a message full of jargon. How do you fix it without offending them?
How you edit a senior leader's words while keeping their voice.
Edits tied to the reader, shown side by side, with the leader's voice and intent kept.

I don't call it bad writing. I say, 'A warehouse lead will read this on a phone; here is how it lands for them.' I rewrite the key paragraph in plain words, keep the phrases that sound like them, and show both versions. Most leaders pick the clear one once they see it. I also ask what they want people to do after reading, and put that near the top.
How do you reach frontline employees who don't have a company email or sit at a desk?
Whether you can reach deskless workers, not only office staff.
Several channels that fit the shift: huddles, supervisors, screens, posters, an app or opt-in texts, timed to when people are on site.

I start with how they actually spend their shift. Short pre-shift huddles led by supervisors work best, so I give supervisors a one-page talking guide. I add break-room screens and posters for reminders, and a mobile app or opt-in texts for urgent news. I check reach by asking a few people on each shift what they heard, not by counting messages sent.
Walk me through how you would announce a reorganization.
Your sense of sequence: who hears what, in what order, and when.
Leaders aligned, managers briefed, affected people told privately first, then the company the same day, with an FAQ and follow-up.

First I get leaders to agree on the why and the core message. Managers are briefed shortly before, with talking points and an FAQ. People whose roles change hear it from their manager in private. The company announcement goes out the same day as those talks, so rumors have no gap. Then I keep a place open for questions and update the FAQ for the next two weeks.
News of a change leaks on the company chat before your planned announcement. What do you do?
How you respond when you lose control of the timing.
Quick agreement with leadership on what can be confirmed, an earlier announcement or holding note, and no guessing in public.

I tell the sponsor right away and ask what we can confirm. Silence lets the rumor become the story. Usually we move the announcement up and send a short holding note: 'You may have seen talk about this. Here is what we can say now; full details come at 3 p.m.' Finding the source can wait. My job is accurate information now.
Leadership wants to say 'there are no plans for layoffs,' but you know cost cuts are being discussed. What do you do?
Your judgement when a message could later prove false.
You push back on promises that may not hold, offer honest wording instead, and protect trust in leadership.

I'd tell them that if layoffs happen in three months, that line will be quoted back and nothing they say after will be trusted. I'd propose something true: 'We are reviewing costs. No decisions have been made, and if anything affects jobs, you will hear it from us first.' Then I'd make sure we can keep that promise. If they insist, I'd raise it with HR and legal.
You send the company newsletter and find it has the wrong deadline for benefits enrollment. How do you handle it?
How you own and correct a mistake that could cost employees.
A fast, plain correction through the same channels, a check with HR on who was affected, and a fix to the review process.

I'd confirm the right date with HR, then send a short correction within the hour through every channel the original used: 'Correction: enrollment closes on the 15th, not the 22nd.' No long apology, just the fact made easy to find. I'd fix the intranet copy and ask HR whether anyone acted on the wrong date. Then I'd add a fact-check step with the owner of each item.
An employee posts a sharp criticism of a new pay policy under the CEO's intranet post, and an executive asks you to delete it. What do you do?
Whether you balance leadership's wishes, open dialogue and the legal limits on removing posts.
No quick deletion: check the posting rules and with HR or legal, since talk about pay and conditions can be protected, and answer the substance.

I wouldn't delete it on the spot. Talk among employees about pay and working conditions can be protected by federal labor law, even without a union, so I'd check with HR or legal first. Unless it breaks a clear rule, like a threat or someone's private data, I'd leave it up and ask the policy owner to reply with facts. A calm public answer builds more trust than a deleted post.

internal-controls.heading: SOX and internal controls specialist questions
qs: What is the difference between SOX Section 302 and Section 404?
Whether you know what the law asks of management and of the external auditor.
302 is the CEO and CFO certification of each quarterly and annual report. 404 is the yearly assessment of internal control, with auditor attestation for larger filers.

Section 302 makes the CEO and CFO certify each 10-Q and 10-K, including that they evaluated disclosure controls. Section 404(a) requires management's annual assessment of internal control over financial reporting as of year-end. 404(b) adds the external auditor's attestation, which applies to accelerated and large accelerated filers.
What is the difference between design effectiveness and operating effectiveness, and how do you test each?
Your grasp of the two basic questions behind every control test.
Design asks if the control, done as written, would address the risk. Operation asks if it was done that way all period. A walkthrough for one, sample testing for the other.

Design is whether the control, performed as written, addresses the risk: right person, right precision, right timing. I test it with a walkthrough: I follow one transaction end to end and look at the real evidence. Operating effectiveness is whether it ran that way across the period, so I pull a sample over the year and inspect or reperform each one.
Give me a segregation-of-duties conflict in purchase-to-pay. What if the team is too small to split it?
Whether you can spot conflicting duties and design around them in a small team.
A clear conflict, such as vendor setup plus payment release, and a compensating control, like an independent review of changes, when duties cannot be split.

If one person can add a vendor and also release payments, they can pay a fake vendor. In a three-person team I may not split it, so I add a compensating control: the controller reviews a system report of every vendor master change each month, ties it to support and signs it. Access logs show who changed what, so the review has real data.
What are IT general controls, and what happens to your automated controls if they fail?
Your understanding of how IT controls support the rest of the control set.
Access, change management and IT operations, plus the link: if ITGCs fail, you cannot rely on automated controls and system reports without extra work.

ITGCs cover who can get into systems, how program and setting changes are approved and tested, and how jobs and backups run. Automated controls rely on them. If change management failed, I cannot assume the invoice matching setting stayed the same all year, so I test it at more points or lean on manual controls.
A reviewer relies on a system report to perform a control. How do you get comfort on that report?
Whether you test the data a control uses, not just the sign-off.
Testing the report's completeness and accuracy: how it is produced, its parameters, whether it can be edited, and tying it back to source data.

That report is information produced by the entity, so I test that it is complete and accurate. I look at how it is run: standard or custom, which parameters were used, and whether anyone can edit it. Then I tie totals to the general ledger and trace a few items both ways, from report to source and from source to report.
Payroll is outsourced. How do you use the provider's SOC 1 report?
Your handling of controls that sit at a service organization.
A Type 2 report, period coverage, exceptions, the user controls you must run yourself, a bridge letter for any gap, and any subservice providers left out.

I want a Type 2 report, because it tests operation over a period, not just design. I check the period against our fiscal year and get a bridge letter for any gap. I read the opinion and the exceptions, then map the complementary user entity controls, the ones we must perform ourselves, to our own tested controls. I also note subservice providers the report leaves out.
You are testing invoice approvals and one of your 25 samples has no approval. What do you do?
How you treat an exception without hiding it or overreacting.
No swapping the sample. Find the cause, see if it is isolated, extend testing only if the method allows, and judge the severity.

I do not replace the sample. First I confirm with the owner that the approval is really missing, not filed elsewhere. Then I find why: a new clerk, a system bypass, a rush. If our method allows, I extend the sample to see if it is isolated. Either way I log the deviation, check whether the invoice itself was valid, and assess the deficiency.
A controller signs a monthly variance review, but there are no notes or thresholds. Does the control pass?
Your judgement on review controls, where a signature alone proves little.
A signature is not evidence of review. You need a set threshold, what was investigated, and how differences were resolved.

Not as it stands. A signature shows someone saw the file, not what they checked. I would ask what threshold triggers a follow-up, which variances crossed it and what was found. If the controller can show the questions and answers, I can document that. Going forward I would agree on a written threshold and a place to record explanations.
How do you decide whether a deficiency is a material weakness?
Whether you can weigh severity the way the standards define it.
A reasonable possibility that a material misstatement is not prevented or detected in time, weighing size, likelihood, other controls and combined deficiencies.

I ask two things: could this failure lead to a misstatement, and how big could it get. It is a material weakness if there is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement would not be prevented or detected on time. I look at the account's size, what else would catch the error, and whether other deficiencies in the area add up. An actual error is not required.
A key control failed in the third quarter. The owner fixed it and wants it closed. What do you need first?
Your grasp of what makes remediation count before the year-end assessment date.
The new control must operate long enough and be tested as effective before year-end. A fix in place is not enough.

The assessment is as of fiscal year-end, so the fix only counts if the improved control has run enough times and we have tested it before then. I would agree on the new design, document it, let it operate, then test a fresh sample from after the fix date. For a quarterly control fixed late in the year, there may not be enough runs to test, and I would say that early.

inventory-specialist.heading: Inventory specialist questions
qs: What is the difference between cycle counting and a full physical inventory?
Whether you know the two main ways to count stock and when each one is used.
A full count checks everything at once, usually with work stopped. Cycle counts cover small parts on a schedule and catch errors sooner.

A full physical inventory counts every item at one time, usually with receiving and shipping stopped, often once a year. Cycle counting means counting a few locations or items every day, so the whole building gets covered over the year. It finds errors sooner, and the business keeps running while we count.
Why would you hand a counter a blank sheet instead of one showing the system quantity?
Whether you understand blind counts and why they matter.
Counters who see the expected number tend to find it. A blind count gives an honest number to compare against the record.

That is a blind count. If the sheet says 48, people tend to count until they reach 48 and stop looking. With no number shown, they count what is really there. The system then compares it, and any location off by more than our tolerance gets a recount by a different person.
How would you decide which items get counted most often?
How you use ABC analysis to spend counting time where it matters most.
Ranks items by value or movement, counts the high-impact A items most often, and adds extra counts where problems show up.

I would sort items by yearly value or by how often they move. The top group, the A items, are few but carry most of the value, so I count them often, maybe monthly. B items get counted less, C items a few times a year. I also add a count when a location had a recent error or a picker reported a short.
A picker reports a bin empty, but the system shows 12 on hand. What do you do?
How you handle phantom stock so orders do not get stuck.
A quick search of likely spots, a count, a fix to the record so the system stops sending pickers there, then a look for the cause.

I go see the bin myself and check the locations around it, the overflow and any staging area. If I find the stock, I put it back and fix the location. If not, I count and adjust so the system stops promising stock that is not there and purchasing knows to reorder. Then I trace the history to see if a receipt went to the wrong bin.
What does it mean when an item shows a negative quantity on hand, and how do you fix it?
Your understanding of how transactions post and what a negative balance says about the process.
Something left the system before it arrived in it, often an unposted receipt or a unit mix-up. You fix the root transaction, not just the number.

You cannot have less than zero on a shelf, so a negative means a transaction is missing or wrong. Most often stock was shipped before its receipt was posted, or cases and single units got mixed up. I find that receipt or error and correct it. Just adjusting up to zero hides the problem, and it comes back.
The system says 50 units in a bin and you count 40. Walk me through what you check before adjusting.
How you research a variance instead of simply overwriting the record.
Recounts, then checks open transactions, nearby and overflow locations, unit of measure and item history before any adjustment.

First I recount, ideally with a second person. Then I look for timing: picks taken but not confirmed, or a putaway not posted. I check nearby bins and overflow for mislocated stock, and whether someone counted cases where the system tracks single units. I read the item history. Only if nothing explains it do I adjust, with a reason code.
How do you set up the cutoff for a full physical inventory?
Whether you can keep counts and paperwork in sync during a wall-to-wall count.
Posts all completed movements, records the last receiving and shipping documents, and keeps late arrivals apart from counted stock.

Before the count I post every receipt and shipment that has physically happened. I note the last receiving document and last bill of lading before the freeze. Goods arriving during the count go to a marked area and are not counted. Orders staged but not shipped count as on hand. Afterward I check against those documents so nothing is counted twice or missed.
Our shrink went up this quarter. Where would you look for the causes?
How you separate the sources of loss: theft, damage, vendor and paperwork errors.
Breaks shrink down by item, area and reason, tests paperwork errors first, and brings in security only when the data points to theft.

I break the losses down by item, location and adjustment reason. A lot of shrink is paperwork: receipts keyed wrong, vendor shortages missed at the dock, returns not posted. I check for damage thrown out without a write-off. If losses cluster on small, high-value items in one area, I bring that data to my manager and security instead of guessing who it is.
You find that an adjustment you posted last week moved 200 units to the wrong item. What do you do?
How you own and fix your own error in the records.
Reports it quickly, reverses it with a clear note, and checks what else the error touched, such as orders or reorders.

I tell my supervisor right away, then post correcting adjustments on both items with a note pointing to the original. I check whether orders were promised against stock that was not real, or whether purchasing skipped a reorder because of it. Then I find out why it happened. If the two items look alike, I ask for a second check on adjustments that large.
Before an audit, a manager asks you to adjust a few items so the system matches the shelves, without researching them. How do you respond?
Your integrity with records and how you push back respectfully.
Will not post unsupported adjustments to hide variances, and offers a fast research plan with proper approval instead.

I would say I understand the time pressure, but adjusting without research hides the real problem, and auditors review adjustments too. I would offer to count and research those items today, starting with the highest values. Whatever still cannot be explained, we post with honest reason codes and the approval our policy requires.

investigations.heading: Investigations specialist questions
qs: What is the fraud triangle, and how do you use it in a case?
Whether you know the basic model of why people commit fraud.
Pressure, opportunity and rationalization, with the point that controls mainly reduce opportunity.

It says fraud usually needs three things: a pressure, like debt or a sales target; an opportunity, like weak controls; and a rationalization, like “I’ll pay it back.” In a case I use it to look for motive and access, but I treat it as a guide for my questions, not as proof. Opportunity is the part a company can fix, so my recommendations focus there.
An anonymous tip says a buyer is “getting kickbacks” and gives nothing else. Do you open an investigation?
How you decide whether there is enough basis, called predication, to start a case.
A quiet preliminary check first, then a decision based on whether facts give reasonable grounds. No confronting anyone on a bare tip.

Not a full one yet. First I check what I can quietly: the buyer’s vendors, price changes, sole-source awards, any vendor added without bids. If I find something that would make a trained person reasonably believe fraud may have occurred, that is predication and I open the case. If nothing turns up, I document what I checked and close it, without tipping off the buyer.
What is chain of custody, and how do you keep it?
Whether your evidence would hold up if the case goes to court or arbitration.
A written record of who held each item, when and why, from collection on, with items sealed, labeled and stored under control.

It is the unbroken record of who had a piece of evidence from the moment I collected it. I label each item with a number, the date and where I found it, seal it, and log every handoff with a signature. Originals stay locked up; we work from copies. If there is a gap in the log, the other side can argue the item was changed.
You are reviewing accounts payable data for a fake vendor. What do you look for?
Your knowledge of the red flags of fictitious vendor schemes.
Concrete tests: matches to employee data, missing vendor details, invoice patterns, amounts just under approval limits, and who set the vendor up.

I match vendor addresses, phone numbers and bank accounts against employee records. I flag vendors with only a P.O. box, no tax ID, or consecutive invoice numbers, a sign we may be their only customer. I look for round amounts and payments just under an approval limit. Then I check who created the vendor and who approves its invoices; one person doing both is a problem.
A manager wants to log in to the suspect’s laptop right now to see what is there. What do you say?
Whether you protect digital evidence before anyone touches it.
Stop the browsing, secure the device, and have a trained examiner make a forensic copy so the original is not altered.

I ask him not to. Logging in and opening files changes dates and other data, and the other side can then say the evidence was altered. I secure the laptop as it is, record who had it, and have a trained examiner make a forensic copy with a write blocker and hash values that prove the copy matches. We review the copy. I also ask IT to preserve email and server logs.
In what order do you interview people in a case, and why?
How you plan interviews so the facts are known before the key conversation.
Neutral witnesses and record keepers first, then people closer to the matter, the subject last, once the facts are known.

I start with people who can explain the process and the records but are not involved, then witnesses closer to the events, then anyone who may have helped. The subject comes last. By then I know the documents and the story, so I can tell when an answer does not fit. Going to the subject first warns them and gives them time to line up a story.
An employee you are interviewing asks you to keep what they say confidential. How do you answer?
Whether you make only the promises you can keep.
No promise of full secrecy: sharing on a need-to-know basis, clarity on who you work for, and a clear word that retaliation is not allowed.

I tell them the truth: I share what they say only with people who need it for the case, but I cannot promise it stays secret, since it may be needed for a decision or a legal process. If lawyers run the case, they explain they represent the company, not the employee. I also say retaliation for helping an investigation is not tolerated, and how to report it.
The subject admits taking the money during your interview. Is the case done?
Whether you back up an admission with independent evidence.
No: get a signed written statement, then match the admission to the records, because confessions are often partial or wrong.

No. I ask them to put the admission in a written statement in their own words, signed, saying it was given voluntarily. Then I check it against the records: the amounts, the dates and the method. People often admit less than they took, or cover for someone else. The report rests on the documents; the admission supports them.
A colleague’s draft report says “Mr. Lee stole $40,000.” What do you change?
How you write findings without deciding guilt yourself.
Replace the conclusion of guilt with facts and their sources. Guilt is for management, lawyers or a court, and the label invites a legal challenge.

I would rewrite it to state what the evidence shows: for example, that 14 payments totaling $40,000 went to an account in Mr. Lee’s name, with the bank records attached. Whether that is theft is a legal conclusion for management, lawyers or a court. The report sticks to facts, cites the source of each one, and leaves out opinions on guilt.
Halfway through a case, the evidence points to the executive your team reports to. What do you do?
Your independence and how you escalate when your own chain of command is conflicted.
Escalate around the conflict as policy sets out, usually to the general counsel or audit committee, secure the evidence, and keep the circle small.

I stop reporting progress through that executive. I follow the escalation path in our policy, usually the general counsel or the audit committee chair, and bring the documents, not a theory. I make sure the evidence is stored where the executive cannot reach it, and I limit who knows. Then the board or outside counsel decides who runs the case from there.

investment.heading: Investment and corporate development questions
qs: Walk me through a discounted cash flow valuation.
Whether you know the core valuation method and its moving parts.
Unlevered free cash flow, a discount rate that matches it, a terminal value, and a sense of which inputs drive the answer.

I project unlevered free cash flow for five to ten years: after-tax operating profit plus depreciation, minus capex and the increase in working capital. I discount it at the WACC and add a terminal value from a perpetuity growth rate or an exit multiple. That gives enterprise value. Then I check how much of it is terminal value, since that is often most of the answer.
How do you get from enterprise value to equity value per share?
Your grasp of the bridge between what the business is worth and what shareholders own.
Subtract debt and debt-like items, add cash, and divide by fully diluted shares, not basic shares.

I start from enterprise value, subtract debt, preferred stock and noncontrolling interest, and add cash. I also look for debt-like items such as unfunded pensions or deferred purchase payments. Then I divide by diluted shares, counting in-the-money options with the treasury stock method.
Two companies in the same industry trade at 8x and 14x EBITDA. Why might that be?
Whether you can read a valuation multiple instead of just applying it.
Growth, margins, capital needs, risk and quality of revenue explain the gap; the cheaper one is not automatically the better buy.

I would look at growth first, then margins and how much capex each needs, since EBITDA ignores capex. Recurring revenue, customer concentration and leverage matter too. If the 14x company grows twice as fast and turns more of its EBITDA into cash, the gap may be fair. Cheap can just mean a worse business.
What drives returns in a leveraged buyout?
Your understanding of how a financial sponsor makes money on a deal.
EBITDA growth, debt paydown and change in the multiple, with a view on which one is safest to count on.

Three things: growing EBITDA, paying down debt with the company's own cash flow, and selling at a higher multiple than we paid. I like deals where the first two carry the return. Multiple expansion depends on the market at exit, so I usually model the exit at the entry multiple or lower and see if the deal still works.
When is an all-stock acquisition accretive to earnings per share?
Whether you can reason about accretion and dilution without opening a model.
Compare the acquirer's P/E with the P/E paid for the target; and know that accretion alone does not mean the deal creates value.

Before synergies and deal costs, it is accretive if the acquirer's P/E is higher than the P/E we pay for the target, premium included. Our shares buy more earnings than they carry. But accretion is not value creation: a deal can lift EPS and still overpay, so I also look at the return on the price we pay.
What do you look for in a quality of earnings report?
Your due diligence judgement on whether reported earnings are real and repeatable.
Testing every add-back, revenue recognition, one-off items and cash conversion, not taking adjusted EBITDA at face value.

I go through every adjustment to EBITDA and ask if it is truly one-off. A real one-time lawsuit cost can be fair; restructuring that happens every year is not. I check revenue recognition, customer churn, and whether EBITDA turns into cash. If adjusted EBITDA is far above reported EBITDA, each add-back needs proof.
In diligence you learn the target's largest customer is 35% of revenue and its contract renews in six months. What do you do?
How you handle a serious risk found in the middle of a deal.
Size the risk, verify it directly, and protect against it through price or deal structure, not just note it in the memo.

First I size it: what happens to EBITDA and the debt plan if that customer leaves or pushes the price down. I ask for the contract, the renewal history, and a customer call with the seller's consent. Then I bring options to the team: a lower price, an earnout tied to renewal, part of the price held back, or walking away if the risk is too big.
Management's plan shows revenue flat for three years, then growing 25% a year. How do you treat it in your model?
Your judgement with optimistic projections from a seller.
Ask what drives the turn, build your own base case, and price the deal on that, with the seller's plan shown as upside.

I ask what changes in year four: a new product, a new market, a price increase, and what evidence exists today. Then I build our own base case from the history and the sales pipeline, and show management's case as an upside. We pay for what we believe, and if the deal only works on the hockey stick, I say so in the memo.
The night before the investment committee, you find an error in your model that lowers the return from 22% to 17%. What do you do?
Your integrity and how you handle your own mistake under a deadline.
Fix it, tell the deal lead at once, and send corrected numbers with a clear note, even if it hurts the deal.

I fix it, check that nothing else depends on the same mistake, and call the deal lead that night instead of waiting. I send updated pages showing what changed and why. A 17% return may or may not clear our hurdle, but the committee must decide on true numbers. Then I add a check to my model so the same error cannot slip through again.

investment-banking.heading: Investment banking analyst questions
qs: What is the difference between enterprise value and equity value?
Whether you know the basic valuation bridge every model and pitch book uses.
Equity value belongs to shareholders; enterprise value covers all capital providers, with the correct items added and subtracted.

Equity value is what the shares are worth: share price times diluted shares outstanding. Enterprise value is the value of the operating business to everyone who funds it. To get there I start from equity value, add debt, preferred stock and noncontrolling interest, and subtract cash. That is why I pair EV with EBITDA and equity value with net income.
Why do bankers compare companies on EV/EBITDA rather than only on P/E?
Whether you match each multiple to the right measure of value.
EBITDA is before interest, so it pairs with EV and removes the effect of capital structure; P/E is distorted by debt levels and taxes.

EBITDA is earned before interest is paid, so it belongs to both lenders and shareholders, and enterprise value matches it. P/E sits below interest and taxes, so two companies with the same business but different debt can show very different P/Es. EV/EBITDA lets me compare how the businesses perform, whatever way they are financed.
Walk me through a DCF.
Your command of the core intrinsic valuation method.
Unlevered free cash flow, a terminal value, discounting at WACC, then the bridge from enterprise value to a value per share.

I project unlevered free cash flow for five to ten years: EBIT less taxes, plus depreciation and amortization, minus capex and the increase in working capital. I add a terminal value using a perpetual growth rate or an exit multiple, discount it all back at WACC to get enterprise value, then subtract net debt and divide by diluted shares.
How do you choose the companies for a set of trading comps?
How you judge which peers are truly comparable.
Filters on business model, size, growth and margins, checked against filings, with outliers flagged rather than hidden in the average.

I start with the same industry and business model, then filter by size, growth, margins and geography. I read the 10-Ks instead of trusting a database label. I would rather show six real peers than fifteen loose ones, and I flag outliers, say a company with a one-time gain, so the median is not skewed.
Why do precedent transaction multiples usually come out higher than trading comps?
Whether you understand what a buyer pays for in an acquisition.
A control premium and expected synergies are in the deal price; market conditions at the time of each deal also matter.

A buyer taking over the whole company pays for control and often for synergies it expects, so the price carries a premium over where the stock traded. Trading comps reflect small stakes changing hands every day. I also check deal dates, because multiples from a hot market several years ago may not fit today.
In an all-stock deal, how can you tell quickly whether it will be accretive or dilutive?
Your grasp of merger math and its limits.
Compare the buyer's P/E with the P/E paid for the target, then say what the shortcut ignores and confirm in the full model.

I compare P/Es. If the buyer's P/E is higher than the P/E it pays for the target, it buys earnings more cheaply than its own stock is valued, so EPS should rise. If it is lower, the deal is dilutive. That ignores synergies, fees and amortization of new intangibles, so I confirm it in the pro forma model.
Walk me through a simple LBO.
Whether you understand how a financial sponsor makes its return.
Purchase price and sources and uses, debt paid down from cash flow, an exit, and IRR, with the drivers of return named.

A sponsor buys the company with mostly debt and some equity.
