I set the price and the sources and uses, project cash flow, use it to pay down debt, then assume an exit after about five years at a chosen multiple. Equity at exit versus equity put in gives the IRR and the money multiple. Returns come from EBITDA growth, debt paydown and any rise in the multiple.
A friend asks you over drinks whether the company you are working on is about to be sold. What do you do?
Whether you handle confidential deal information the way the law and your firm require.
No confirming or denying; knowing it is material nonpublic information, that tipping is illegal, and when to involve compliance.

I do not confirm or deny anything, not even with a joke. What I know is material nonpublic information; passing it on, or trading on it, can break insider trading law for both of us. I change the subject, and if he keeps pressing I tell compliance. I also use deal code names and never discuss work in public places.
Your VP and your MD give you conflicting comments on the same page. How do you handle it?
How you manage competing instructions without wasting time or going around anyone.
Raise the conflict early with the direct supervisor, suggest a solution, and avoid silently picking one version.

I go to the VP first, since that is my direct line, and show both markups side by side. I might suggest a version that meets both points, or ask whether the VP wants to raise it with the MD. Meanwhile I keep both drafts saved so we can switch quickly. What I avoid is guessing and having the page redone at midnight.
It is 1 a.m., the pitch book goes to the client at 8, and you find the comps page uses an old share count. What do you do?
How you handle your own error under deadline pressure.
Fix it at the source, trace every page it flows into, and tell the deal team right away instead of quietly editing.

I pull the share count from the latest 10-Q and fix it in the model, not just on the page. Then I trace everything that links to it: multiples, the football field, the summary. I message my associate with what changed and why, and ask for a second check. I would rather flag it at 1 a.m. than have the client find it at 9.

ios-developer.heading: iOS developer questions
qs: When do you use a struct and when a class in Swift?
Whether you understand value and reference types, the base of Swift.
Structs are copied and classes are shared by reference. Default to structs and use a class when shared identity or inheritance is needed.

A struct is a value type. When I pass it around, each holder gets its own copy, so a change in one place doesn't surprise another. A class is a reference type, so everyone points at the same object. I default to structs for models and use a class when I need shared identity, inheritance, or Objective-C APIs.
Your crash reports show “Unexpectedly found nil while unwrapping an Optional value.” What does that mean and how do you fix it?
How you handle optionals, a common source of Swift crashes.
Finding the force unwrap and handling the nil case on purpose, not hiding it with a silent default value.

Somewhere the code used ! on a value that was nil, either a force unwrap or an implicitly unwrapped optional. I find the line from the symbolicated stack trace, then ask why it can be nil. Usually I replace it with guard let or if let and handle the missing case clearly, like showing an error state. A silent default can hide the real bug.
The app crashes the moment a user taps “Scan receipt” to open the camera, and the console mentions privacy. What is wrong?
Your knowledge of iOS privacy permissions and Info.plist.
The missing usage description key, plus asking for permission at the right moment and handling a denial.

The app is missing the camera usage description in Info.plist, the NSCameraUsageDescription key. iOS terminates an app that accesses the camera without it. I add a clear sentence on why we need the camera, ask for access only when the user taps the button, and show a path to Settings if they said no before.
Where do you store a user's login token on the device, and why?
Whether you protect sensitive data on the device.
In the Keychain, not UserDefaults or a plain file, with an access level that fits when the app needs the token.

In the Keychain. UserDefaults is a plain property list in the app's container and is not meant for secrets. The Keychain encrypts items and lets me choose when they can be read, for example after the first unlock if a background refresh needs the token. On logout I delete the item.
Scrolling a list of photos stutters. How do you find and fix the cause?
How you keep the main thread free and measure performance.
Measuring with Instruments first, then moving heavy work like image decoding and resizing off the main thread and caching the results.

I profile on a real device with Instruments, starting with the Time Profiler, to see what blocks the main thread. Often it is full-size images decoded while scrolling. I resize them to the cell size in a background task, cache the result, and only set the image on the main thread. Then I profile again to confirm the fix.
Memory grows every time a user opens and closes a detail screen. What do you suspect, and how do you prove it?
Your grasp of ARC and retain cycles.
A retain cycle, confirmed with the Memory Graph Debugger or Instruments, and broken with a weak or unowned reference.

I suspect a retain cycle: the view controller holds a closure that captures self strongly, so neither is ever freed. I open and close the screen a few times, then use Xcode's Memory Graph Debugger to see the leftover instances and what holds them. The fix is usually [weak self] in the closure or a weak delegate. A log in deinit confirms it.
Your app is mostly UIKit. Would you build a new settings screen in SwiftUI? How do you decide?
Your judgement in mixing SwiftUI and UIKit in a real app.
Weighing the minimum iOS version, team skills and screen complexity, and knowing the two frameworks can live together.

Probably yes. Forms and lists are where SwiftUI saves the most code. I'd check that our minimum iOS version supports the SwiftUI features I need and that the team can maintain it. I'd host it in a UIHostingController so it fits our UIKit navigation. For a complex custom screen with heavy gestures, I might stay in UIKit.
A user fills in a long form, switches to another app to look up a number, and comes back to an empty form. What happened?
Whether you understand the app lifecycle and that iOS can end a suspended app.
Knowing the system can terminate a suspended app with no warning, and saving the draft when the app leaves the foreground.

In the background the app was suspended, and iOS then terminated it to free memory. The app gets no callback for that, so I can't wait for one. I save the draft when the scene moves to the background, or as the user types, and restore it on the next launch. I test it by backgrounding the app and stopping it from Xcode.
A user leaves a screen while its network request is still loading. What should happen, and how do you make sure it does?
How you use Swift concurrency and cancellation.
Cancelling the work tied to the screen, knowing cancellation is cooperative, and never updating a screen that is gone.

The request should be cancelled so we don't waste data or update a screen that's gone. In SwiftUI I start it in the .task modifier, which cancels the task when the view disappears. In UIKit I keep the Task and cancel it when the screen goes away. Cancellation is cooperative, so long loops check Task.isCancelled, and I don't show an error alert for a cancel.
A release you shipped crashes on launch for some users. What do you do in the first hours?
How you handle a bad release when the App Store has no rollback.
Pausing the rollout, shipping a fix fast with expedited review, and using remote flags, knowing users who already updated can't be rolled back.

I check the crash reports to see who is affected, for example one iOS version. If we used a phased release, I pause it so fewer automatic updates go out. There is no rollback for people who already updated, so I fix the cause, test it, and submit with a request for expedited review. If a remote flag can turn off the broken feature, I do that first.

it-manager.heading: IT manager questions
qs: What does a good laptop lifecycle look like, from purchase to disposal?
Whether you know the full life of an asset, not just the help desk part.
Standard models tracked in an inventory, encrypted from day one, refreshed on a plan, and wiped with proof before disposal.

We buy a few standard models, log each one by serial number and owner, and ship it with disk encryption and device management already on. We plan a refresh every three to four years so costs are predictable. At the end I wipe it, keep the wipe record or the recycler's certificate, and remove it from the inventory and the licences.
Walk me through what happens when an employee leaves the company.
How you close access quickly and keep the company's data.
One checklist, run on time: accounts, sessions, MFA, shared passwords, devices, licences, and data handed to the manager.

HR tells us the date ahead, and on the last day we disable the account in the identity system, which cuts most apps at once. We sign out active sessions, remove MFA devices and change any shared passwords they knew. Mailbox and files go to the manager, the laptop comes back and is wiped, and the licences are freed. A checklist means nothing depends on memory.
What is the 3-2-1 backup rule, and is it enough?
Your grasp of backups as a recovery plan, not a setting.
Three copies, on two kinds of storage, one off site; plus a copy ransomware cannot change and restores that are actually tested.

Three copies of the data, on two different types of storage, with one copy off site. Today I also want one copy that ransomware cannot alter, either offline or immutable. And a backup is only proven when you restore from it, so I schedule test restores and time them against what the business says it can tolerate.
What is the difference between RPO and RTO, and who decides them?
Whether you can turn recovery into business terms.
RPO is how much data you can lose, RTO how long you can be down; business owners choose them and IT shows what each costs.

RPO, recovery point objective, is how much data we can afford to lose, measured in time: nightly backups mean up to a day. RTO, recovery time objective, is how long a system can be down before it really hurts. I don't pick them alone. I ask each department head, show what each target costs, and they choose.
How do you keep software licence costs under control?
Whether you manage licences as spending, not just as tickets.
One inventory, regular usage reviews, seats reclaimed at offboarding, and renewal dates tracked well before notice periods.

I keep one list of every subscription with its owner, seat count and renewal date. Every quarter I compare seats to actual logins and reclaim the unused ones. Renewals go on a calendar months ahead, because many contracts auto-renew if you miss the notice window. Card spending on software gets reviewed so tools bought outside IT come to light.
An employee calls: they typed their password into a fake login page an hour ago. What do you do?
How you respond to a compromised account in the first hour.
Reset and revoke at once, then look for what the attacker did: sign-ins, mailbox rules, MFA changes, mail sent.

I thank them for calling fast, then reset the password, sign out all sessions and check MFA methods for anything new. I review sign-in logs for odd locations and the mailbox for forwarding or delete rules attackers like to add. If mail went out from it, we warn the recipients. Then I block the fake site and warn staff, without naming the person.
Your CEO wants local admin rights on their laptop. How do you handle it?
Your judgement when security meets seniority.
A respectful no to permanent admin rights, a real fix for the need behind the request, and a written exception if leadership insists.

I ask what they are trying to do; usually it is one app they can't install. I fix that today. Then I explain that executives are the top phishing target, and admin rights let malware install itself. If they still insist, I offer a separate admin account used only when needed, and I write the risk down so the decision is theirs, on paper.
A critical security patch comes out on a Friday afternoon for a system everyone uses. What do you do?
How you weigh the risk of an attack against the risk of a bad patch.
Check exposure and active exploitation, test on a small group, roll out with a rollback plan, or apply a workaround if it can wait.

I check whether we are exposed and whether the flaw is being exploited in the wild. If it is and the system faces the internet, I patch this weekend: a test group first, then everyone, with a rollback ready and someone on call. If it can wait, I apply the vendor's workaround now and patch in our normal window. Either way, users hear what to expect.
A change your team pushed took down the network for the whole office. How do you handle it, during and after?
How you own a mistake your team caused.
Service restored first, updates on a steady rhythm, then a blameless review that changes the process rather than blaming a person.

I roll back first and investigate second; getting people working matters more than knowing why. I post updates every 30 minutes, even when nothing has changed. Afterwards we run a blameless review: what we changed, why testing missed it, and what stops it next time. Last time that meant a pilot group and a written rollback step for every network change.
Walk me through how you build next year's IT budget.
Whether you can plan and defend IT spending.
Start from what is already committed, add projects with business cases, separate one-time from recurring costs, and keep a contingency.

I start with what is committed: subscriptions, support contracts, and laptops due for refresh from the inventory. That is the cost to run. Then I list projects, each tied to a business goal with a cost and an owner. I separate one-time from recurring costs, add a small contingency, and walk finance through the trade-offs instead of handing over one total.

it-project-manager.heading: IT project manager questions
qs: What goes into a cutover plan for a system go-live?
Whether you have actually planned and run a go-live weekend.
A step-by-step runbook with owners, checkpoints, a rollback trigger and the communications around it.

A step-by-step runbook: each task with an owner, start time, duration and the check that proves it worked. It covers freezing the old system, data loads, smoke tests, a go/no-go checkpoint, the point after which rollback is no longer practical, and who tells users what and when. We rehearse it at least once in a test environment and time it.
What is the difference between system testing and user acceptance testing, and who signs off UAT?
Your grasp of the test stages on an IT project.
System testing proves it works as built; UAT proves it supports the real business process. The business owner signs UAT, not IT.

System testing is done by the delivery team against the requirements: does each function and integration work. UAT is done by real users running their actual processes, like closing a month or onboarding a hire, with realistic data. The business process owner signs it off, because they accept the risk of using it. If IT signs its own UAT, nobody has really accepted it.
How do you choose between a big-bang go-live, a phased rollout and a parallel run?
How you match the rollout approach to risk, cost and the business.
Trade-offs named for each: big bang is fast but risky, phased limits exposure, parallel is safest but doubles user work.

Big bang switches everyone at once; it is cheapest, but a failure hits everyone. Phased goes by site, region or module, so early waves teach us before the rest. A parallel run keeps both systems live and compares results; it suits things like payroll, but staff enter data twice, so I keep it short. I pick based on how bad a failure would be and how easily we can recover.
Walk me through how you plan a data migration from a legacy system.
Whether you treat data migration as its own workstream, not a single task.
Profiling and cleanup early, mapping signed off by data owners, several trial loads, and reconciliation with agreed counts and totals.

I start by profiling the old data to find duplicates, gaps and odd formats, and give cleanup to the business owners early. Then field mapping, signed off by the data owners. We run two or three trial loads into test, each timed and reconciled: record counts, control totals like open balances, and spot checks by users. The final load uses the same scripts we rehearsed.
What is hypercare, and how do you decide when it ends?
Whether you plan for the weeks after go-live, not just launch day.
A defined period of extra support with exit criteria agreed in advance, then a clean handover to the support team.

Hypercare is the period right after go-live when the project team stays on hand with faster response and daily ticket triage. I agree the exit criteria before go-live: for example, no open critical tickets, ticket volume near normal for two weeks, and the support team trained with runbooks. Then I formally hand over to operations so the project can close.
The tech lead wants to switch off the old system the week after go-live. What do you check first?
Whether you think about everything still depending on the old system.
Data retention and legal holds, hidden integrations and reports, access to history, and contract terms, before anything is shut down.

First, records retention: what data must be kept, for how long, and whether any is under a legal hold. Then dependencies: scheduled jobs, reports or other systems still reading from it, which I confirm from access logs. Then how users will look up history, and the license or hosting contract terms. I would usually make it read-only first and switch it off later.
Your go-live date lands inside the company's year-end change freeze. What do you do?
How you work with IT change control instead of around it.
Raising it early, bringing options with their risks, and following the change approval process; never pushing a change through quietly.

I raise it as soon as I spot it, not in the last week. I take options to the sponsor: go live before the freeze with a tighter plan, move after it, or request an exception through the change advisory board with a clear rollback plan. Freezes exist because finance and operations cannot absorb risk then, so the answer is usually to move the date.
The vendor tells you their integration API will be three weeks late. How do you respond?
How you handle a dependency you do not control.
Impact on the critical path first, then options like resequencing or building against a mock, and a prompt update to the sponsor.

First I check whether the API is on the critical path; if other testing can continue, the real slip may be smaller. I ask the team whether we can build against a mock of the API so our side is ready. I ask the vendor for a firm date in writing and check the contract. Then I give the sponsor the new forecast and options that week, not at the next status meeting.
Two days before go-live, UAT finds that some invoices calculate tax wrong. Do you go live?
Your judgement on a go/no-go decision under deadline pressure.
Sizing the impact first, checking the agreed go/no-go criteria and workarounds, and letting the business owner decide on the facts.

I find out how many invoices are affected and whether a fix can be tested in two days. Wrong tax on customer invoices is a financial and compliance risk, so unless there is a reliable workaround, like holding those invoices for manual review, I recommend no-go. The business owner decides against the criteria we agreed earlier, and I record the decision and why.
Midway through a weekend cutover, reconciliation shows 3% of customer records did not load. What do you do?
How you lead when a cutover goes wrong in real time.
Pausing to diagnose within a time box, using the rollback trigger agreed in the plan, and updating stakeholders on a set schedule.

I pause further steps and get the data lead to find the cause, with a time box. If it is a known, fixable reason, like a date format the load rejected, we fix it, reload and reconcile again. If we cannot explain it before our planned rollback deadline, we roll back as the runbook says. Meanwhile I send updates on a fixed schedule to the sponsor and support leads.

it-support.heading: IT support questions
qs: A laptop shows an IP address starting with 169.254. What does that tell you?
Whether you know basic network addressing on a client device.
The device got no answer from DHCP and gave itself a link-local address, so the fault lies between the laptop and the DHCP server.

It means the laptop asked for an address, got no answer from the DHCP server, and gave itself a link-local one. With that address it cannot reach the gateway. I would check the cable or Wi-Fi connection and renew the lease. Then I would see whether other devices on the same port or network have the same problem.
A user calls and says the internet is down. Walk me through your first five minutes.
How you narrow down a vague complaint step by step.
Scope comes first: one user or many. Then you work up from the physical link to the IP address, the gateway, DNS and the specific site.

First I ask what exactly fails and whether coworkers have the same issue. If many do, it is an outage and I escalate. If it is one person, I check Wi-Fi or cable, then the IP address, then ping the gateway, then try a site by name and by IP. Each step tells me which layer broke, and I note it in the ticket as I go.
A user can reach a server by its IP address but not by its name. Where do you look?
Whether you can tell a name resolution problem from a connection problem.
It points to DNS. Check which DNS servers the device uses, test with nslookup, clear the local cache, and look for a wrong or stale record.

If the IP works, the network path is fine, so it is almost always DNS. I run nslookup on the name to see what answer comes back and from which server. If the device points at the wrong DNS server, say from a home router or VPN setting, I fix that. If the record itself is wrong or old, I flush the cache and tell whoever manages DNS.
What do you write in a ticket before you close it?
Your documentation habits, and whether others can use your notes later.
The cause, what was done, and how the fix was confirmed with the user. Repeat issues get turned into a knowledge base article.

I write what the user reported, the cause I found, the exact steps I took, and how I confirmed the fix, ideally with the user. If it is the third time I have seen the same issue, I write or update a knowledge base article and link it. That way the next tech can fix it in two minutes instead of twenty.
A user asks for local admin rights so they can install software themselves. How do you respond?
Whether you apply least privilege without blocking people's work.
Find out what they need and offer the approved route, such as a one-time install, the software catalog or a temporary approved elevation. Avoid permanent admin rights.

I ask what they want to install and why. Often it is one tool, so I install it for them or add it to our self-service catalog after it is checked. Permanent admin rights make malware and accidental changes much easier, so I do not hand those out. If their role truly needs it, there is an approval process with their manager and security.
Someone calls saying they are a vice president traveling abroad, locked out, and needs a password reset right now. What do you do?
How you hold to identity verification under pressure.
The approved verification applies to everyone, such as a callback to the number on file or a self-service reset with MFA. Urgency plus rank is a red flag.

I stay polite but use the same verification as for anyone. I call back the number on file, not the one they are calling from, or have them use self-service reset with their MFA. Urgency plus a big title is a classic social engineering pattern. If I cannot verify, I do not reset, and I log the call and tell security.
An employee leaves the company today. Walk me through the offboarding on the IT side.
Whether you know the steps that close access cleanly and keep the data.
Disable rather than delete, end active sessions, remove group and shared access, collect devices, and keep the mailbox and files as policy says.

At the agreed time I disable the account and sign out all sessions, so phone apps and webmail stop too. I remove groups, shared mailbox access and admin roles, and change shared passwords they knew. I collect the laptop and badge, pass the mailbox and files to the manager per policy, and free the licenses. I do not delete the account right away.
A user tells you their company laptop was stolen from their car. What do you do?
How you contain the risk from a lost or stolen device.
Confirm the disk is encrypted, lock or wipe it remotely, reset the password and end sessions, and report it as a security incident.

First I check in our device management tool that the disk is encrypted, and I send a remote lock or wipe. I reset the user's password and sign out their sessions, since saved logins may be on it. I ask what data was on it, file the security incident report, and suggest they file a police report. Then I get them a replacement so they can work.
A user clicked a link in an email and typed in their password. They tell you an hour later. What do you do?
Your response to an account that is likely compromised.
Reset the password, end sessions, check for new MFA methods and mailbox rules the attacker added, and hand off to security. Thank the user for reporting.

I thank them for telling me, then reset the password and sign out all sessions. I check whether new MFA methods or devices were added, and look for mailbox rules that forward or delete mail, which attackers often set up. I review the sign-in log for odd locations, send it all to security, and check who else got the same email.
You pushed a settings change to all laptops and it broke the VPN for a hundred people. What now?
How you own a mistake and limit the damage.
Roll back first, tell users and the team plainly, then find the cause and use a small pilot group before wide changes.

I roll the change back first and confirm on a couple of machines that the VPN works again. I send a short note to users and my lead: what broke, that it is fixed, and what to do if it is not. Then I find out why my testing missed it. From then on, changes go to a small pilot group for a day before everyone gets them.

java-developer.heading: Java developer questions
qs: What is the contract between equals and hashCode, and what breaks if you ignore it?
Whether you know the rule that every hash-based collection in Java relies on.
Equal objects must return equal hash codes. Breaking that makes HashMap and HashSet miss keys or hold duplicates.

If two objects are equal by equals, they must return the same hashCode. If I override equals and forget hashCode, a HashSet can hold two equal customers, and a HashMap lookup misses a key that is there. I also keep mutable fields out of both methods, because changing a key after it is in a map makes it unfindable.
Why shouldn't you use double for money, and what traps does BigDecimal have?
Your care with money, the core of most bank and payment code in Java.
Binary floating point cannot hold 0.1 exactly. With BigDecimal: build from strings, set rounding when dividing, and compare with compareTo.

A double stores binary fractions, so 0.1 plus 0.2 is not exactly 0.3, and those errors add up over many transactions. I use BigDecimal, created from a String or valueOf, never new BigDecimal(0.1). I set the scale and RoundingMode when dividing, and I compare with compareTo, because equals treats 2.0 and 2.00 as different.
When do you use a checked exception and when an unchecked one?
Whether you handle errors with a clear rule instead of habit.
Checked for conditions the caller can recover from, unchecked for programming errors. Wrap with the cause kept, and never swallow an exception.

Checked exceptions are for things the caller can act on, like a file that may be missing. Programming errors, like a null argument, are unchecked. In service code I often wrap low-level checked exceptions in a domain exception and keep the original as the cause. What I never do is catch Exception and leave the block empty, because the failure then disappears.
Two threads increment a shared int counter and the total comes out too low. Why, and how do you fix it?
Whether you understand race conditions and the basic Java concurrency tools.
count++ is read, add, write, so it is not atomic. Fix with AtomicInteger, LongAdder or a lock; volatile alone does not help.

count++ is three steps: read, add one, write back. Two threads can read the same value and both write the same result, so one increment is lost. Marking the field volatile does not fix it; it only makes writes visible. I would use AtomicInteger, LongAdder if many threads update it often, or a synchronized block if the counter changes together with other state.
A Spring method marked @Transactional throws an error, but the data is still saved. What could be wrong?
Whether you know how Spring transactions really work behind the annotation.
Names the usual causes: a call from the same class that skips the proxy, a checked exception, or an exception caught inside the method.

First I check how it was called. Spring wraps the bean in a proxy, so a call from another method in the same class skips the transaction. Next, by default Spring rolls back only on unchecked exceptions and errors, so a checked exception commits unless rollbackFor says otherwise. Last, a try-catch inside the method may swallow the error before Spring sees it.
Java has a garbage collector. How can a Java service still leak memory?
Your understanding of how memory is kept alive in the JVM and how to find a leak.
Objects stay reachable by mistake: growing static maps, unbounded caches, ThreadLocals on pooled threads. Found with a heap dump and retained sizes.

The collector frees only objects nothing points to. A static map that only grows, a cache with no size limit, or a ThreadLocal never removed on a pooled thread keeps objects alive. To find it I take a heap dump, for example with jcmd GC.heap_dump, and look in an analyzer for the objects holding the most retained memory and what references them.
A service stops answering requests, but its CPU use is near zero. What do you do?
How you diagnose a hung JVM instead of restarting it blindly.
Takes several thread dumps before restarting and looks for deadlocks, threads blocked on one lock, or workers stuck waiting on a pool or a remote call.

Before restarting I take two or three thread dumps a few seconds apart with jstack or jcmd Thread.print. Low CPU means threads are waiting, not working. I look for a reported deadlock, many threads blocked on the same lock, or every request thread waiting for a database connection or a remote call with no timeout. Then I restart, with the dumps saved.
When would you use virtual threads, and when would they not help?
Whether you know modern Java concurrency and its limits.
Useful for many concurrent tasks that block on I/O. No gain for CPU-heavy work; do not pool them, and still limit access to scarce resources.

Virtual threads, final since Java 21, are cheap, so I can run one per request even with thousands waiting on I/O. They help when threads mostly wait on the network or a database. They do not make CPU-heavy work faster. I create one per task instead of pooling them, and since the database pool is still fixed, I limit concurrent calls with the pool or a semaphore.
Walk me through moving a service from Java 8 to Java 21.
Your experience with real version upgrades and what breaks in them.
Updates build tools and libraries first, handles removed Java EE modules and blocked JDK internals, tests fully, and rolls out gradually.

First I update build plugins and libraries, since old versions often fail on new JDKs. Java 11 removed modules like JAXB, so I add them as dependencies. Since Java 17, most JDK internals are blocked by default, which breaks some old libraries. If we also move to Spring Boot 3, javax packages become jakarta. Then full tests and a canary release with metrics compared.
Response times spike every few minutes and you suspect garbage collection. How do you confirm it and what do you change?
How you tune JVM performance from evidence rather than by guessing at flags.
Proves it with GC logs matched to the spikes, then reduces allocation or fixes heap size before trying a low-pause collector under real load.

I turn on GC logging with -Xlog:gc* and line up pause times with the latency spikes. If they match, I check whether the heap is too small or the code allocates heavily, for example large temporary lists per request. Cutting that allocation often fixes it. If pauses are still too long, I test a low-pause collector such as ZGC under real load before rolling it out.

junior-software-engineer.heading: Junior software engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between a unit test and an integration test?
Whether you know the basic kinds of tests and what each is for.
Unit tests check one small piece alone and run fast. Integration tests check that pieces work together. Both have a place.

A unit test checks one function or class on its own. Outside things like the database are replaced by fakes, so it runs in milliseconds and points right at the failure. An integration test runs real parts together, say my code and a test database, and catches problems in the wiring. I write many unit tests and fewer integration tests.
You pushed a bad commit to a shared branch. How do you undo it in Git?
Whether you can use Git safely when other people share the history.
Uses git revert, which adds a new commit that undoes the change. Avoids rewriting shared history with reset and a force-push.

I would run git revert on that commit. It makes a new commit that undoes the change, so nobody else's history breaks. Git reset moves the branch back and rewrites history. That is fine on my own local branch, but on a shared one it needs a force-push that can wipe out teammates' work. I would also tell the team in chat what happened.
How do you find your way around a large codebase you have never seen?
How you learn unfamiliar code without trying to read all of it.
Starts from one real path through the code, runs it, uses tests and the debugger, and saves questions for a mentor.

I don't try to read it all. I get it running locally, then pick one feature, like login, and follow a request from the entry point to the database with a debugger and breakpoints. Tests show me how pieces are meant to be used, and git blame shows why a line changed. I keep a list of questions and take them to my mentor in one batch.
Walk me through how you fix a bug from a ticket.
Your method for fixing a bug so that it stays fixed.
Reproduce first, find the cause rather than the symptom, add a test that fails before the fix, then check nothing else broke.

First I reproduce it with the exact steps and data from the ticket. Then I narrow down where it goes wrong, with logs or a debugger, until I understand the cause, not just where it shows. I write a test that fails because of the bug, fix the code until it passes, run the full test suite, and note the cause in the pull request.
What makes a pull request easy to review?
Whether you make your work easy for teammates to check.
Small and focused, a clear note on what changed and why, how it was tested, and no unrelated changes mixed in.

It does one thing. If I fixed a bug and also renamed files, those go in two pull requests. The description says what changed, why, and how I tested it, with a screenshot if the screen changed. I read my own diff before asking anyone, to catch debug prints and leftover comments. Then a reviewer can finish it in fifteen minutes instead of putting it off.
You have been stuck on a problem for two hours. When and how do you ask for help?
Your judgement between working things out alone and wasting time.
A time limit set in advance, and a question that shows what was tried, what was expected and what actually happened.

I set a limit before I start, often about an hour without progress, shorter if the task is urgent. At two hours I am past it, so I ask. I write the question so it is quick to answer: what I am trying to do, what I expected, what actually happens, and the three things I already tried. Often writing that out shows me the answer before I send it.
A senior engineer asks for a change in code review that you think is wrong. What do you do?
How you take feedback and disagree with respect.
Asks for the reason first, gives one concrete argument, then accepts the reviewer's or the team's decision without a fight.

First I ask why, because they often know something about the system that I don't. If I still disagree, I reply once with a concrete reason, for example that their version calls the database inside a loop. If we still differ, I suggest a short call. If they still prefer their way, I make the change and move on. One review is not worth a fight.
Your tests pass on your laptop but fail in the CI pipeline. How do you track it down?
How you debug a difference between two environments.
Reads the actual failure log, looks for differences in versions, settings, time zone, test order or timing, and reproduces it locally first.

CI is the server that runs our tests on every push, starting from a clean machine. I read the full failure log first. Then I look for what differs from my laptop: a library version, a missing environment variable, a different time zone, or tests running in another order. I try to reproduce it locally, for example in the same container image, before changing any code.
You estimated a task at two days. It is the end of day three and you are halfway. What do you do?
Whether you raise a slipping deadline early and honestly.
Tells the lead now, with the reason and a new estimate, and offers options like cutting scope or getting help instead of quietly working late.

I should have said something on day two, so I say it now. I tell my lead where I am, what took longer, for example code I didn't know other features shared, and a new honest estimate. Then I offer options: ship the main part first and the rest later, or pair with someone who knows that code. Staying silent only makes the surprise bigger.
You notice you pushed an API key to a public repository an hour ago. What do you do?
How you handle a security mistake, and in what order.
Treats the key as stolen: revokes and replaces it first, tells the team, checks usage logs, and only then cleans the code and history.

I assume it is already compromised, because bots scan public repositories for keys within minutes. First I revoke the key and create a new one, then I tell my lead and our security contact. We check the provider's logs for use we don't recognize. After that I move the key into a secret store and clean the history. Deleting the commit alone does not make it safe.

kernel-engineer.heading: Kernel and operating systems engineer questions
qs: What happens when a user program makes a system call on x86-64 Linux?
Your grasp of the boundary between user space and the kernel.
The register convention, the switch to kernel mode, the handler lookup, careful copying of user data, and the return path with an error code.

The C library puts the call number in rax and the arguments in other registers, then runs the syscall instruction. The CPU switches to kernel mode, and the entry code saves registers and calls the handler from the syscall table. The handler checks its arguments and copies user memory with copy_from_user. The result comes back in rax; a negative value becomes errno in libc.
What is a page fault, and is it always a bug?
Whether you understand virtual memory as the kernel sees it.
Most faults are normal: demand paging, copy-on-write, swap-in. Only an access with no valid mapping or the wrong permissions ends in a signal or an oops.

No, most are normal. The CPU faults when a page is not mapped or the access breaks its permissions. The kernel looks up the memory area. If it is valid, it allocates a page, reads it from a file or swap, or copies it for copy-on-write, then retries the instruction. If no valid area covers the address, the process gets SIGSEGV; in kernel code it can be an oops.
Your interrupt handler needs to update a list that process code also uses. Which lock do you use, and how?
Whether you know what may and may not sleep in the kernel.
A spinlock, not a mutex, because interrupt context cannot sleep; process context disables local interrupts while holding it to avoid a self-deadlock.

A spinlock, because a handler cannot sleep, so a mutex is out. In process context I take it with spin_lock_irqsave. Otherwise the interrupt could fire on the same CPU while the lock is held and spin forever. I keep the critical section short and never call anything that can sleep inside it, such as a GFP_KERNEL allocation.
Your driver's interrupt handler takes too long and hurts latency. How do you restructure it?
How you split urgent work from work that can wait.
Acknowledge the device and save the minimum in the hard handler, then move the rest to a threaded IRQ or a workqueue, chosen by whether it must sleep.

The hard handler should only check that the interrupt is ours, acknowledge the device, and save what is needed. The rest moves out. I usually use request_threaded_irq, so the heavy part runs in a kernel thread that can sleep and be scheduled. If the work is batched or not tied to the interrupt, a workqueue fits. Then I measure latency before and after.
How does a hypervisor run a guest kernel that believes it owns the hardware?
Your understanding of virtualization at the CPU and memory level.
Hardware support such as VT-x or AMD-V, exits on sensitive operations, second-level page tables, and paravirtual devices to cut the number of exits.

With VT-x or AMD-V the guest runs directly on the CPU in a guest mode. Sensitive operations, like some I/O or control register writes, cause a VM exit; the hypervisor handles or emulates them and resumes the guest. Second-level page tables (EPT on Intel, NPT on AMD) map guest memory to host memory in hardware. For devices, virtio queues avoid an exit per register access.
A customer sends you a kernel oops log. Walk me through how you read it.
Whether you can turn a crash report into a source line and a likely cause.
Start with the first oops, read the faulting address, instruction pointer and taint flags, then map function plus offset to source using the exact build.

I read the first oops only; later ones are often fallout. A faulting address near zero suggests a NULL pointer. I note the kernel version and taint flags, since an out-of-tree module changes the picture. I take the function plus offset from the instruction pointer and map it to a source line with faddr2line and the matching vmlinux. Then I read that code against the call trace.
Your driver writes a DMA descriptor, then writes the device's doorbell register, but the device sometimes reads stale data. Why, and how do you fix it?
Your knowledge of memory ordering and DMA between the CPU and a device.
Stores can be reordered or sit in caches. Use the DMA API, a dma_wmb() before handing over ownership, and an ordered writel() for the doorbell.

The CPU or compiler can reorder the stores, and on some platforms the data is still in a cache the device cannot see. I allocate descriptors with dma_alloc_coherent, fill the fields, then call dma_wmb() before setting the ownership bit. For the doorbell I use writel(), which is ordered after earlier memory writes; writel_relaxed() is not.
A fuzzer reports a use-after-free in code you merged last month. What do you do?
How you own and fix a mistake in low-level code.
Reproduce it with memory checking on, fix the real lifetime bug instead of masking it, and mark the fix so it reaches stable kernels.

I reproduce it on a build with KASAN, the kernel's memory error checker, which shows where the object was freed and where it was used later. In my case a timer could still run after the device was removed. I fixed the order: stop the timer, then free. I added a Fixes: tag pointing to my commit, copied the stable list, and added a test that removes the device under load.
Explain RCU and when you would use it instead of a reader-writer lock.
Your depth in kernel concurrency.
Readers take no lock and never wait; writers publish a new copy and free the old one only after a grace period. It suits read-mostly data.

Readers enter rcu_read_lock, follow pointers with rcu_dereference, and must not sleep. A writer makes a new copy, publishes it with rcu_assign_pointer, then waits for a grace period with synchronize_rcu or call_rcu before freeing the old one. So reads are nearly free. I use it for read-mostly data like routing tables; with frequent writes, a plain lock is simpler.

key-account-manager.heading: Key account manager questions
qs: How is a key account manager different from an account executive?
Whether you understand what the role is for.
KAM means long-term ownership of a few large customers and growth over years, not winning a deal and handing the customer on.

An account executive is usually measured on winning new deals and then hands the customer on. As a key account manager I own a few large customers over years. I know their plans, coordinate our service, product and finance people around them, and grow revenue through renewals, new products and new divisions.
What goes into a strategic account plan?
Your grasp of the core working document of the role.
Customer goals, who decides, current spend and share of wallet, gaps, risks, and objectives with owners and dates, reviewed regularly.

Mine fits on a few pages. It covers the customer's goals for the year, a chart of who decides what, what they buy from us and from competitors, gaps where we could help, risks to the account, and three or four objectives with actions, owners and dates. I review it with my manager each quarter and share a short version with the customer.
How do you map the stakeholders in a large account?
Whether you avoid depending on a single contact.
Everyone who touches the decision, rated on influence and attitude, with a plan to build links beyond one person.

I list everyone who touches the decision: the person who signs, the users, technical evaluators, procurement and anyone who prefers a competitor. For each I note influence, how they see us and how often we talk. If all my contact runs through one person, that is a risk, so I set a goal to build real links with at least two more senior people.
How do you find growth in an account that already buys from you and says it is happy?
How you grow an account beyond what it already buys.
A method: map what they buy against divisions and needs, find the gaps, and lead with a business problem rather than a product.

I map each division and site against what we sell and mark where they buy from someone else or nothing at all. Then I ask my contact for an introduction to a division with a problem we have solved elsewhere. At one account only one site used us; a pilot at a second site, backed by results from the first, doubled the account in a year.
How do you run a quarterly business review that the customer actually wants to attend?
Your ability to make a review useful to the customer, not a sales pitch.
Agenda agreed with the customer, results in their terms, honest about problems, a forward look, and clear follow-up actions.

I agree the agenda with my contact two weeks ahead so it covers their priorities. I open with results against the goals we set last time, in their numbers, then issues and what we fixed, then what is coming in their business and ideas for it. Slides stay short and half the time is discussion. I send actions with owners within two days.
How can you tell an account is at risk before the customer tells you?
Whether you watch for early warning signs and act on them.
Concrete signals like falling usage, fewer senior contacts or reorganizations, and early, direct action when they appear.

I watch usage or order volumes, how fast they reply, whether senior people still come to meetings, late payments and new names from procurement. A reorganization or a new executive is a signal too. When two of these move at once I call my sponsor, ask directly what has changed and bring our leadership in early, while there is time to fix it.
Your main contact at your biggest account just left the company. What do you do in the first two weeks?
How you protect a relationship when your champion leaves.
Quick contact with the successor, a clear summary of value delivered, checking other relationships, and staying in touch with the person who left.

I call my contact to thank them and ask who takes over and who else I should know. Then I meet the successor quickly with a short summary of what we deliver and the value so far, and ask what they want to change. I check how strong my other relationships are. I also stay in touch with the person who left; they may buy from us at their new company.
Procurement at a key account demands a 10% price cut at renewal or they will put the contract out to tender. How do you respond?
How you negotiate with professional buyers without giving value away.
No free discount: understand the pressure, involve the business users, and trade any price move for something of value, within a limit set in advance.

I do not cut 10% for nothing. First I find out whether the tender is real or a target, and I remind my business contacts what a switch would cost them in time and risk. If price must move, I trade: a lower unit price for a longer term, more volume or a smaller scope. I know my walk-away point before the meeting, agreed with my manager.
A key account asks for a custom product change or contract term your company does not normally give. How do you decide?
Your judgement in balancing one big customer against your own company's interest.
Weighing cost, precedent and lifetime value with the internal teams, and a fast, honest answer to the customer either way.

I check three things: what it costs us to deliver, whether it sets a precedent other customers will ask for, and what the account is worth over the next few years. I take that to the people who would build it and to finance. If the answer is no, I tell the customer quickly, explain why and offer what we can do instead.
Your company made a delivery mistake that hurt a key account. Walk me through how you handled it with the customer and inside your own company.
How you handle a failure on both sides: owning it with the customer and driving the fix internally.
Fast, honest contact without blaming colleagues, a recovery plan you pushed through internally, and a written cause and fix.

A shipment to a customer's main plant arrived a week late and stopped one of their lines. I called my contact the same day, said what went wrong without blaming the warehouse, and gave a recovery date. Internally I got operations to rush the next orders and held a weekly check until it was stable. I sent the cause and fix in writing within ten days. They renewed.

kubernetes-engineer.heading: Container and Kubernetes engineer questions
qs: When would you use a Deployment, a StatefulSet or a DaemonSet?
Whether you know the basic workload types and pick the right one for the job.
Deployment for interchangeable copies, StatefulSet for stable identity and storage, DaemonSet for one pod per node.

A Deployment runs copies that are all the same, like a web API. A StatefulSet gives each pod a stable name and its own disk, so I use it for things like databases or queues. A DaemonSet puts one pod on every node, or on a chosen set of nodes, which fits log collectors and monitoring agents.
What is the difference between a liveness probe and a readiness probe, and what is a common mistake with them?
Your grasp of how Kubernetes decides to restart a container or send it traffic.
Liveness failure restarts the container; readiness failure only takes the pod out of traffic. Names a real mistake, like a liveness check that depends on the database.

If liveness fails, the kubelet restarts the container. If readiness fails, the pod stays up but is removed from the Service, so it gets no traffic. A classic mistake is a liveness check that calls the database: when the database blips, every pod restarts at once and a small problem becomes an outage.
Why is deploying an image with the tag latest a bad idea?
Whether you know how image tags affect what really runs and whether you can roll back.
You cannot tell which version is running, nodes may run different builds, and rollback is unreliable. Use immutable version tags or image digests.

latest is just a label that moves, so two nodes can pull different builds under the same name, and the manifest does not tell me what is running. Rolling back to latest does nothing useful. I tag each build with a version or the commit ID, or pin the digest, so every deploy is traceable and repeatable.
What are resource requests and limits, and what happens when a container goes over its memory limit versus its CPU limit?
Your understanding of scheduling and of how CPU and memory limits behave differently.
Requests guide scheduling; limits cap use. Over the memory limit the container is OOMKilled; over the CPU limit it is throttled, not killed.

The scheduler places pods based on requests, the amount reserved for them. Limits are the ceiling. If a container goes over its memory limit, it gets killed and shows OOMKilled. If it hits its CPU limit, it is slowed down, or throttled, but keeps running. So memory limits need real headroom.
A pod has been stuck in Pending for ten minutes. What do you check?
How you troubleshoot a scheduling problem in order.
Starts with kubectl describe and the events, then checks resources, taints, node selectors or affinity, and unbound volume claims.

I run kubectl describe pod and read the events, since the scheduler usually says why. Common causes: no node has enough free CPU or memory for the requests, a taint the pod does not tolerate, a node selector or affinity no node matches, or a PersistentVolumeClaim that is not bound. Then I fix the cause, not just add nodes.
A new release goes into CrashLoopBackOff. Walk me through finding the cause.
Your method for debugging a container that keeps crashing.
Reads logs from the previous run, checks exit code and last state, rules out OOM, bad config and a probe killing the app.

First kubectl logs with --previous, because the current container may have no output yet. Then kubectl describe for the exit code and last state: OOMKilled points to memory, exit code 1 usually means the app failed, often a missing env var or secret. I also check whether a liveness probe is killing a slow start. If users are hit, I roll back first.
How does a request from the internet reach a pod in the cluster?
Whether you understand Services, Ingress and how traffic is routed inside the cluster.
A load balancer or Ingress takes the request, a Service picks pods by label, and kube-proxy or the network plugin routes it to a ready pod.

Usually a cloud load balancer sends traffic to an Ingress controller, which routes by host name and path to a Service. The Service finds its pods through label selectors and keeps a list of ready endpoints. kube-proxy, or the network plugin, programs each node so traffic to the Service address lands on one of those pods.
A developer asks you for cluster-admin so they can debug their service. What do you do?
Your judgement on access control and least privilege with RBAC.
Says no to cluster-wide admin but solves the need: a namespaced Role and RoleBinding with only the rights required, ideally time-limited.

I ask what they actually need. Usually it is reading pods, logs and events in their own namespace, maybe exec. I give that with a Role and RoleBinding in that namespace, often starting from the built-in view role. cluster-admin can read every secret and delete anything, so it stays with a very small group.
How do you upgrade a production cluster to a new Kubernetes version without an outage?
How you plan a risky change: version order, API removals and moving workloads safely.
Checks removed APIs first, upgrades control plane before nodes one minor version at a time, and drains nodes gradually with PodDisruptionBudgets in place.

I read the release notes for removed APIs and fix any manifests using them. I try it on a staging cluster. Then I upgrade the control plane first, one minor version at a time, and the nodes after. I cordon and drain nodes a few at a time; drain respects PodDisruptionBudgets, so each service keeps enough pods running.
During every deploy, a few requests fail with 502 errors for a few seconds. What is going on, and how do you fix it?
Whether you understand pod shutdown and why traffic can still reach a pod that is stopping.
Knows endpoint removal and SIGTERM happen at the same time, so pods must keep serving briefly, finish requests, and have readiness probes for new pods.

When a pod is deleted, it gets SIGTERM at about the same time it is removed from the endpoints, and the load balancer learns late. If the app exits at once, requests still arriving fail. I add a short preStop sleep, make the app finish open requests on SIGTERM, set a long enough grace period, and make sure new pods have a readiness probe.

lab-technician.heading: Research associate and lab technician questions
qs: You need 50 mL of 1X buffer from a 10X stock. How do you make it?
Whether you can do basic lab math quickly and correctly.
C1V1 = C2V2 done right: 5 mL of stock brought up to 50 mL, mixed and labeled.

I use C1V1 equals C2V2. 10X times V1 equals 1X times 50 mL, so V1 is 5 mL. I measure 5 mL of stock, bring it up to 50 mL with purified water in a graduated cylinder or volumetric flask, mix it well, and label it with the contents, date and my initials.
What is the difference between a biosafety cabinet and a chemical fume hood?
Whether you know which piece of safety equipment protects what.
A fume hood protects the user from vapors; a Class II cabinet protects user, sample and room from particles, and HEPA filters do not stop vapors.

A fume hood pulls air away from me and out of the building, so it protects me from chemical vapors but does nothing for the sample. A Class II biosafety cabinet uses HEPA-filtered airflow to protect me, the sample and the room from microbes and particles. HEPA filters do not trap vapors, so I do not use volatile chemicals in a cabinet that recirculates air.
How do you know a pipette is still accurate between service visits?
Your habit of checking instruments instead of trusting them.
A gravimetric check with water on a calibrated balance, corrected for temperature, and taking the pipette out of use if it fails.

I do a quick gravimetric check. I pipette purified water onto a calibrated analytical balance several times at the volume I use, note the water temperature, and convert mass to volume with the water density at that temperature. If the average is off or the readings scatter beyond our tolerance, I tag the pipette out of use and send it for service.
The centrifuge starts to shake and get loud as it speeds up. What do you do?
How you react to an equipment hazard in the moment.
Stop the run, wait for the rotor to stop before opening, find the imbalance, and treat a broken tube as a spill.

I press stop and step back, and I do not open the lid until the rotor has fully stopped. Then I check the balance: tubes of equal mass opposite each other, the right adapters, nothing cracked. If a tube with biological material broke, I keep the lid closed for the time our biosafety rules set so aerosols settle, then clean up as a spill.
Your PCR no-template control shows a band. What does that tell you, and what do you do?
Whether you understand what controls are for and act on them.
The run is not trustworthy, so no results go out; fresh reagents, a clean area, a rerun, and a search for the source if it repeats.

It means something is contaminated, usually a reagent, the water or the work area, so I cannot trust any positive in that run. I do not report the samples. I use fresh aliquots of water and master mix, clean the bench and pipettes, and rerun. If it comes back, I test reagents one at a time to find the source and keep pre-PCR and post-PCR work in separate areas.
How do you spot contamination in a cell culture, and what kind can you not see?
Your hands-on knowledge of cell culture and its hidden risks.
Cloudy or yellow medium, fungal threads or yeast under the microscope, plus routine testing for mycoplasma, which you cannot see.

Bacteria often make the medium cloudy and turn it yellow fast as the pH drops. Fungi show as threads or fuzzy clumps, and yeast as small round budding cells under the microscope. Mycoplasma is the one I cannot see: the medium stays clear. So we test on a schedule with a PCR kit, and I discard and decontaminate anything positive instead of trying to rescue it.
Someone knocks over a 1-liter bottle of solvent on the open bench. Walk me through what you do.
How you handle a chemical spill safely and in the right order.
People first, then the SDS, ignition sources off if flammable, and cleanup only if small and trained; otherwise leave and call safety staff.

I warn people nearby and check if anyone was splashed; they go straight to the eyewash or safety shower. I check the SDS and shut off ignition sources if it is flammable. If the spill is small and I am trained for it, I use the spill kit with the right gloves and goggles. If it is large, toxic or I am unsure, I leave, close the door and call environmental health and safety.
The -80 freezer alarm goes off at 6 p.m. and the display reads -55. What do you do?
Your judgement when samples that took months to collect are at risk.
A quick check for a simple cause, samples moved by priority to backup or dry ice, the right people told, and times and temperatures logged.

First I check for a simple cause like a door not fully closed. If it keeps warming, I move samples to the backup freezer, irreplaceable ones first, or onto dry ice if there is no space, with insulated gloves and good ventilation. I tell the lab manager, call for service, and log times and temperatures so we know which samples may be affected.
A new lot of a key antibody arrives. What do you do before using it on real samples?
Whether you know that reagent lots can differ and how to check.
A side-by-side test with the old lot on the same controls, a documented comparison, and lot numbers recorded on every run.

I run it side by side with the old lot on the same control samples, same protocol, same day. If signal and background match within what we accept, I record the lot number and the comparison and switch over. If they differ, I keep the old lot for ongoing work, tell the lead, and we decide whether to titrate the new one again. Every run notes which lot it used.
Your supervisor asks you to leave out one replicate that looks wrong before the data goes into a paper. What do you do?
Your handling of data integrity under pressure from someone senior.
No silent deletion: excluding data needs a documented reason or a set rule, and the raw data always stays.

I would ask what the reason is. If there is a real one, like a failed control or a pipetting error I noted at the bench, we exclude it and document why. If it only looks inconvenient, I would say I am not comfortable dropping it, offer to repeat the experiment, and keep the raw data either way. Leaving out data without cause is falsification.

launch-operations.heading: Launch and test operations questions
qs: What is the difference between a hold, a recycle and a scrub?
Whether you know the basic language of a countdown.
Clear, correct definitions, and an understanding that each choice has different follow-on work for the team.

A hold stops the countdown clock so we can check or fix something, then pick up again. A recycle sends the count back to an earlier point, often to redo steps like propellant conditioning. A scrub ends the attempt for that window. We safe the vehicle, drain if needed and plan a new try.
What is a redline, and what happens when one is crossed?
Your understanding of how limits drive decisions in a count.
A limit set in advance with a response already written: a hold, safing or abort. The candidate calls it exactly as written and does not debate it live.

A redline is a limit on a measurement, like a tank pressure or a temperature, set by engineering. The response is written in advance: a hold, a safing action or an abort. Late in the count the automated sequencer watches most of them because people are too slow. My job is to know my redlines cold and call them on the net exactly as written.
Walk me through what you check before and during liquid oxygen loading.
Whether you understand the main hazards of cryogenic propellant.
Area clear, oxygen-clean hardware, a slow chilldown, and limits watched. Grease and oil kept away from oxygen.

Before loading I confirm the area is cleared, the oxygen-clean lines and seals are verified, and the vent paths are open. We chill the lines and tank slowly so the liquid does not flash to gas and surge. I watch pressure, level and temperatures against limits. Nothing oily goes near, because oil can ignite in rich oxygen.
Why do you do a closeout inspection before closing a compartment, and what do you look for?
How you prevent foreign objects and loose ends from flying.
Tool and part counts, no debris, connectors mated, fasteners torqued and marked, and a second person who verifies.

Once a panel is closed, nobody sees inside again before flight. I count tools and hardware against the kit list and look for debris, tape and caps left on fittings. I check that connectors are mated and locked, fasteners carry torque stripes, and lines are clamped. Then a second person inspects and we photograph the compartment before it is closed.
What precautions do you take when working near ordnance such as pyrotechnic initiators?
Your safety habits with explosive devices.
Treats every device as live. Grounding, safe and arm in safe, shorting plugs, radio controls, minimum people and two-person verification.

I treat every initiator as live. Before handling, I ground myself and the hardware. I check that the safe and arm device is in safe and the shorting plugs stay installed until the procedure says otherwise. We follow the radio and transmitter controls for the area, keep only the people the procedure needs, and make connections in the written order with a second person verifying.
You are working in a compartment during a nitrogen purge and your oxygen monitor alarms. What do you do?
How you react to an oxygen-deficient atmosphere.
Leave at once, warn others, report it, and never go back in unprotected to rescue someone. Re-entry only after the air is tested.

I get out to fresh air right away and tell the people with me to do the same. I call the test conductor or safety so the area is closed and the purge is checked. If someone is down inside, I do not go in without supplied air. I call the rescue team, because many people who die in these spaces were trying to rescue someone. Nobody goes back in until the air is tested and cleared.
An engine shuts down on its own right after ignition, with the vehicle still on the pad. What happens next?
Whether you know how to handle a pad abort.
Nobody approaches. Remote safing per procedure, data watched for fire or rising pressure, and the pad reopened only by the safety lead.

Nobody goes near. The vehicle is still loaded and pressurized, and something made it shut down. We follow the abort safing procedure from the control room: safe the engine, vent or offload as written, and watch the data for fire, leaks or rising pressure. Teams go back only when the safety lead clears the pad. Meanwhile I save the data and my log notes.
A recovered booster or capsule is brought in. How do you approach it?
Your understanding of the hazards in recovered hardware.
Assumes it is hazardous: leftover propellant, charged pressure bottles, unfired ordnance. Safes it step by step and records its condition.

I treat it as unsafe until it is proven safe. There may be leftover propellant, pressure bottles still charged and ordnance that did not fire. We approach from upwind, check for vapors with detectors and look for damage before touching anything. First we vent pressure, safe the ordnance per procedure and cap the open lines. Then we secure it for transport and photograph everything for the engineers.
After a compartment is closed, you notice a wrench is missing from your kit. What do you do?
How you own a mistake that could put a flight at risk.
Stops and reports at once, searches, and accepts reopening the compartment. Hiding it is never an option.

I stop and report it right away, before anyone signs the next step. We search my work area and the vehicle with a light and a mirror, and recount the kit. If the wrench is not found, the compartment gets reopened and inspected, even if that costs a day. A loose wrench in flight can short a harness or jam a valve.
Late in the count, a reading is still within limits but has been drifting, and the window is closing. What do you say?
Your judgement when schedule pressure meets an unexplained trend.
Speaks up with facts on the net and asks for an explanation. Recommends a hold if nobody can explain it, and does not let the window decide.

Within limits is not the same as understood. I would call it out on the net with the value and the trend, and ask engineering whether there is a known reason. If nobody can explain it before the next hold point, I would recommend we hold or scrub. A missed window costs a day. Flying with a problem we cannot explain can cost the vehicle.

legal-counsel.heading: Legal counsel questions
qs: What is the difference between an indemnity and a limitation of liability clause?
Whether you know the two clauses that decide who pays when a deal goes wrong.
An indemnity shifts specific losses, often third-party claims, to one party; a cap limits total damages. You see how carve-outs connect the two.

An indemnity is a promise to cover certain losses, usually claims brought by third parties, such as an IP infringement suit. A limitation of liability caps what one side can recover from the other, often at fees paid in the last 12 months. The key is the carve-outs: I check whether indemnities sit inside or outside the cap, because that decides the real exposure.
A vendor sends its own 20-page form for a software subscription. Walk me through your first read.
How you triage a third-party contract under time pressure.
A clear order: the terms that carry real risk first, a short list of must-haves versus nice-to-haves, and no line-by-line rewrite of boilerplate.

First I ask the business what the deal is worth and what data the vendor will touch. Then I read the cap, the indemnities, data security and breach notice, IP ownership, term, auto-renewal and termination rights, and governing law. I mark three or four must-haves and let minor points go, so the deal closes this week instead of next month.
As in-house counsel, who is your client?
Whether you understand that you represent the company, not the people who call you.
The organization, as ABA Model Rule 1.13 says, and knowing when to give an employee an Upjohn warning.

The company is my client, acting through its authorized people. Most days that makes no difference, but it matters when interests split. If I interview an employee in an investigation, I give an Upjohn warning: I represent the company, not them, the talk is privileged, and the company alone decides whether to waive that privilege.
When is an email to you not privileged, even though you are the company's lawyer?
Your grasp of attorney-client privilege as it applies to in-house lawyers.
Privilege covers confidential requests for legal advice, not business advice; copying a lawyer does not protect an email, and sharing it widely can waive it.

Privilege protects confidential communications made to get legal advice. Many courts look at the primary purpose, and in-house lawyers also give business input, so a pricing discussion with me on copy is not protected. Sharing it with outsiders can waive it too. I tell teams to ask me a legal question directly and keep my answer within the people who need it.
Our purchase order and the supplier's order acknowledgment have conflicting terms. Whose terms govern?
Whether you know the battle of the forms under the Uniform Commercial Code.
For goods, UCC 2-207 rather than the mirror-image rule; conflicting terms often knocked out for UCC defaults; a signed master agreement as the fix.

For goods, UCC 2-207 applies, not the old rule that an acceptance must mirror the offer exactly. Between merchants, an added term joins the deal unless the offer limited acceptance to its terms, the term materially alters the deal, or someone objects. For conflicting terms, many courts knock out both and use UCC defaults. The fix is a signed master agreement that overrides any form.
You learn a salesperson promised a customer, by email, a refund right that is not in the contract. What do you do?
How you handle side promises that can change a signed deal.
Getting the facts, judging whether the email could bind the company, involving finance, and fixing the process rather than blaming.

I get the full email thread and the contract first. Even with a clause requiring signed amendments, a written promise from someone who looked authorized can start a dispute, and it can change how finance books the revenue. I tell finance, decide with the sales lead whether to honor, paper or walk it back, and then tighten who may promise terms.
A former distributor's lawyer sends a letter threatening to sue. What happens in the first 48 hours?
Whether you know when the duty to preserve evidence starts and how to act on it.
A litigation hold once suit is reasonably anticipated, auto-deletion stopped, insurers notified on time, and outside counsel chosen if needed.

A credible threat means litigation is reasonably anticipated, so the duty to preserve starts now. I send a written hold to the people involved and to IT, suspend auto-deletion of their email and chat, and track who has confirmed. I check our insurance policies for notice deadlines, pull the contract, and decide whether to bring in outside litigation counsel.
When would you push for arbitration in a commercial contract, and when would you prefer court?
Your judgement on dispute resolution clauses, not just a default preference.
Weighing privacy, cost, appeal rights and enforcement abroad against the deal at hand, with no one-size answer.

Arbitration fits when we want privacy, an arbitrator who knows the industry, or a foreign counterparty, because awards are easier to enforce abroad under the New York Convention. Court fits when we want a right to appeal, since arbitration awards are very hard to overturn. For small contracts, arbitration fees can exceed what is at stake, so court may be the better choice.
Tell me about a contract issue you missed and what you changed afterward.
Whether you own mistakes and turn them into a better process.
A real miss, told plainly, with the cost, the fix for that deal, and a lasting change such as a checklist or a tracking system.

I once approved a vendor form without catching that it auto-renewed for three years with a 90-day notice window. We missed the window and were locked in at a 12% higher price. I negotiated a partial credit, then set up a contract database that flags notice dates 120 days ahead. No renewal has slipped since.
An employee tells you a senior manager may be inflating sales numbers. How do you handle it?
How you handle a serious internal report when your duty runs to the company.
Taking it seriously, preserving evidence, protecting the reporter from retaliation, reporting up the chain, and independent counsel when leaders are involved.

I thank the employee, take notes, and make clear there will be no retaliation, which federal law also protects at public companies. I preserve the relevant records quietly. Because a senior manager is involved, I report it up to the general counsel and, if needed, the audit committee, and recommend outside counsel run an independent investigation. I do not tip off the manager.

lending.heading: Lending and mortgage questions
qs: What are the five Cs of credit, and which one do you weigh most?
Whether you know the basic framework for judging a borrower.
All five named correctly, with capacity to repay put first, since collateral is a fallback and not a source of payment.

Character, capacity, capital, collateral and conditions. I weigh capacity most: can the borrower's steady cash flow cover the payment? Collateral matters, but it is the way out if things go wrong, not the plan. A loan that only works if we take the house or the equipment is a bad loan.
How do you calculate a borrower's debt-to-income ratio for a mortgage?
Your grasp of the core affordability measure and what goes into it.
Gross monthly income as the base, the full new housing payment plus recurring debts on top, and everyday living costs left out.

I add the new housing payment, meaning principal, interest, property taxes, homeowners insurance, any HOA dues and mortgage insurance, to the monthly debts on the credit report and other obligations like child support. I divide that by gross monthly income. Utilities and groceries are not counted. Housing payment alone over income is the front-end ratio.
What is loan-to-value, and why does it change the terms a borrower gets?
Whether you understand how equity protects the lender.
The correct formula, the lower-of-value-or-price rule on purchases, and the link between thin equity, pricing and mortgage insurance.

It is the loan amount divided by the property value; on a purchase I use the lower of the appraised value and the price. A $320,000 loan on a $400,000 home is 80% LTV. The higher it goes, the less equity protects us if prices fall, so pricing gets worse, and a conventional loan above 80% usually needs mortgage insurance.
A small business shows a debt service coverage ratio of 1.10. What does that tell you?
Whether you can read cash-flow coverage on a business loan.
The ratio explained as cash flow over debt payments, with 1.10 seen as a thin cushion that needs a closer look, not an automatic yes.

It is the cash available for debt, often net operating income, divided by the year's principal and interest payments. At 1.10 the business covers its payments with only 10% to spare. A small drop in sales or a rate rise wipes that out, so I look at trends, the owner's outside income and whether a smaller amount or longer term makes it safer.
When do the Loan Estimate and the Closing Disclosure have to reach the borrower?
Your knowledge of the federal mortgage disclosure timeline.
Loan Estimate within three business days of application; Closing Disclosure received at least three business days before closing.
