Some email apps, like Apple Mail with its privacy setting on, load images automatically, so an email can count as opened when nobody read it. I use opens to compare subject lines loosely, and clicks to judge the email.
Walk me through what you check before a marketing email goes out.
Your attention to detail and basic email rules.
Test send, links, personalization, the right list, plus an unsubscribe link and postal address, as CAN-SPAM requires.

I send a test to myself and a teammate and open it on a phone and a laptop. I click every link, check the discount code, and check that the first-name field has a fallback so nobody gets Hi blank. I confirm the audience list and send time. Last, I make sure the unsubscribe link works and our physical postal address is in the footer, which the law requires.
A local creator will post about our product in exchange for free items. What needs to happen first?
Whether you know the disclosure rules for paid or gifted posts.
The FTC expects a clear, visible disclosure of the connection, even when payment is only free product.

Free product counts as a material connection, so the FTC expects the post to say so clearly. I would put it in writing: the creator adds something like #ad or Gifted by us at the start of the caption or says it in the video, not buried in hashtags. I would also check their posts after they go live and keep a record.
You find a great photo on Google Images for our Friday post. Can we use it?
Your understanding of image rights.
No by default: images are usually copyrighted. Use owned, licensed or properly credited free-license images.

Not unless we know we have the right. Most images online are copyrighted even with no notice on them. I would use our own photos, our paid stock library within its license terms, or ask the owner for written permission. Being findable on Google does not mean free to use, and a takedown or invoice later costs more than a stock photo.
Walk me through planning a customer event for 50 people, six weeks out.
How you organise an event from start to finish.
Budget and goal first, then venue, invitations, RSVPs, vendors and a run of show, with a timeline backwards from the date.

I confirm the goal and budget, then book the venue and catering in week one, since those fill up. Invitations go out about four weeks ahead with an RSVP date. I keep one sheet with vendors, costs and contacts. The week before, I write a run of show: who does what, minute by minute. Afterward, I send a thank-you email and report attendance against the goal.
The designer tells you Thursday's launch banner will be two days late. What do you do?
How you handle a slipping deadline that affects others.
Learn why, look for options, tell the owner early with choices, and update the schedule.

I ask what is holding it up; sometimes it is waiting on copy or feedback I can chase. If it is truly late, I look at options: launch with a simpler version, or move the post and email. Then I tell my manager that day with those choices, not on Thursday morning, and update the calendar and anyone else waiting on it.
Two managers each want their project done first by Friday, and you cannot do both. How do you handle it?
Your judgement when priorities conflict.
Not choosing silently: make the conflict visible and let the person who sets priorities decide.

I would not quietly pick one. I would write down what each task needs and how long it takes, then bring both to my direct manager, or to both managers together, and ask which comes first. While they decide, I would start on any shared piece. Then I tell both people what was agreed and when each will be done.
A promo email went to 8,000 subscribers with the wrong discount code. What do you do in the first hour?
How you handle a public mistake under time pressure.
Stop further sends, tell the manager, fix it at the source if possible, then a short correction, and a check to prevent repeats.

First I pause any scheduled resends and tell my manager right away. Then I check whether we can make the wrong code work at checkout, which fixes it for everyone who already clicked. If not, we send a short correction with the right code and a brief apology. I also tell customer service so they can help callers. Later I add a code test to our pre-send checklist.

marketing-manager.heading: Marketing manager questions
qs: What are CAC and LTV, and how do you use them together?
Whether you know the two numbers that say if growth pays for itself.
Clear definitions, and the point that what you can spend to win a customer depends on what that customer is worth over time.

CAC is customer acquisition cost: total sales and marketing spend divided by new customers won. LTV is lifetime value: the gross profit a customer brings over the whole relationship. If LTV is not comfortably above CAC, each new customer loses money. I also watch how many months it takes to earn back CAC, since cash can run out long before a lifetime ends.
Walk me through what goes into a campaign brief.
How you set up a campaign before anyone starts making anything.
One goal with a number, a defined audience, one main message, channels, budget, dates and the metric that will judge success.

I start with the business goal and a number, like 400 demo requests in eight weeks. Then the audience, the problem we solve for them, and the one message they should remember. Then channels, budget, deadlines, who approves, and the metric we will judge it by. If a brief runs past two pages, it is usually hiding a decision nobody made.
What do you set up before a campaign goes live so you can measure it?
Whether your results can be trusted before the first dollar is spent.
Consistent UTM tags, conversion tracking tested end to end, and a baseline written down to compare against.

I agree a naming scheme for UTM tags, the small labels added to links that tell analytics which source, medium and campaign a visit came from. I fire a test conversion myself and confirm it shows up in analytics and the CRM. And I write down the baseline: leads and sales in the four weeks before, so we can see the real change.
Your email open rate jumped 20 points overnight. What do you check?
Whether you question a number that looks too good.
Knowing that privacy features and security scanners can register opens automatically, and judging email by clicks and conversions instead.

First, I would not celebrate. Some mail apps now preload images for privacy, which logs an open whether or not anyone read the email, and corporate security scanners do the same. I would split opens by mail client, check whether clicks and conversions moved too, and from then on report email results on clicks and revenue.
Our emails started landing in spam. Where do you look?
How you diagnose an email deliverability problem.
Sender authentication, list quality, bounce and complaint rates, and any recent change in volume or content.

First, authentication: the SPF, DKIM and DMARC records that prove to inbox providers the mail really comes from us. Then list hygiene: old addresses, bounces, a bought list someone slipped in. Then spam complaints and any sudden jump in volume. I would pause the least engaged segment and mail only recent clickers and buyers while our reputation recovers.
A creator we pay posted about our product without saying it was paid. What do you do?
Whether you know the FTC rules on paid endorsements.
Get a clear disclosure added fast, since the brand can be held responsible too, then build disclosure rules and monitoring into every deal.

I would ask the creator to edit the post today with a clear disclosure, like #ad or “paid partnership,” placed where people will see it, not buried in a pile of hashtags. FTC guidance says a paid relationship must be disclosed, and brands are expected to instruct and monitor the people they pay. Then I add the rule to our contracts and check posts before payment.
Our ad platforms together claim 650 sales last month, but we only had 400. How do you explain that?
Whether you understand attribution and how each platform counts credit.
Each platform claims any sale it touched, so credit overlaps; the fix is one source of truth, one model, and tests of what is truly incremental.

Each platform claims a sale if its ad was seen or clicked within its own window, so a buyer who saw a social ad and later clicked a search ad is counted twice. I would treat our own order system as the truth, use one attribution model across channels, and run a holdout test, pausing a channel in some regions, to see what it really adds.
Leads are up 40% this quarter but pipeline is flat. Your boss wants to open the report with the 40%. What do you do?
Your honesty in reporting and whether you measure what the business cares about.
Show both numbers, explain the gap, and steer the team toward pipeline and revenue rather than lead volume.

I would put both numbers on the first slide. More leads with flat pipeline usually means lower quality, maybe from an easy content offer or loose targeting. I would bring a breakdown by source showing which leads became sales meetings, and a plan to move spend there. A flattering number gets found out at the next review anyway.
An email with the wrong discount code just went to 200,000 customers. Walk me through the next hour.
How you handle a costly mistake under pressure.
Stop further sends, decide quickly with finance whether to honor it, send one clear correction, and fix the step that let it through.

First I stop any scheduled resends and check whether the code works and what it could cost. With finance and support, I decide fast whether to honor it; a short window often costs less than angry customers. Then one short, honest correction, a script for support, and from now on a second person checks every code before a send.

marketing-operations.heading: Marketing operations manager questions
qs: In lead scoring, what is the difference between fit and engagement, and why keep them apart?
Whether you understand how a scoring model is built.
Fit is who the lead is and engagement is what they do. Kept apart, a busy student does not look like a ready buyer.

Fit scores who the person is: job title, company size, industry, region. Engagement scores what they do: demo requests, pricing page visits, webinars. I keep two scores because a student who downloads everything can pile up points while a VP who asked for a demo once looks cold. Engagement points should also decay over time.
How do you keep UTM tracking clean when many people on the team build their own links?
How you protect the data that every campaign report depends on.
A fixed naming convention, a shared link builder, and regular checks for stray values, since tools treat 'Email' and 'email' as different.

I publish one convention: lowercase only, a fixed list of sources and mediums, campaign names with a date. People build links in a shared builder that only offers those values. Most analytics tools are case sensitive, so 'LinkedIn' and 'linkedin' split into two rows. Once a month I pull the source and medium list and fix anything off it.
What does CAN-SPAM require of a commercial email we send?
Your knowledge of the US law that governs marketing email.
Honest headers and subject lines, a physical postal address, a working opt-out honored within 10 business days, and responsibility even when a vendor sends.

The from line and subject cannot mislead. Each email needs a valid physical postal address and a clear way to opt out that keeps working for at least 30 days after sending. We must honor opt-outs within 10 business days, with no fee and no demand for more than an email address. If an agency sends for us, we are still responsible.
Open rates jumped after Apple Mail Privacy Protection came in. How do you treat opens now?
Whether you know which email metrics still mean something.
Opens are inflated by machine opens, so you rely on clicks and conversions and keep opens out of scoring and test decisions.

Mail Privacy Protection loads images on Apple's servers, so many emails register as opened whether anyone read them or not. I still watch opens as a rough health signal, but I took open points out of lead scoring, judge tests on clicks and conversions, and build re-engagement lists from clicks or site visits instead of opens.
Explain SPF, DKIM and DMARC as you would to a marketing director.
Your grasp of email authentication, the base of deliverability.
SPF lists who may send, DKIM signs the message, DMARC ties them to the from address, sets what happens on failure and sends reports.

SPF is a list in our domain's DNS of servers allowed to send as us. DKIM adds a digital signature proving the message came from our domain and was not changed. DMARC checks that these line up with the visible from address, tells inboxes to deliver, quarantine or reject mail that fails, and sends us reports. Without them, more of our mail lands in spam.
Clicks on the newsletter fell by half overnight and one big mailbox provider seems to send it to spam. What do you do first?
How you diagnose a deliverability problem under time pressure.
Hold big sends, check authentication, complaints and recent changes, then send only to engaged contacts and ramp volume back slowly.

I hold the next big send. I confirm SPF, DKIM and DMARC still pass, since a DNS change can break them, and check the provider's sender dashboard for complaints and reputation. Then I ask what changed: a list import, a new link domain, a bigger send. While it recovers I mail only people who clicked recently and raise volume step by step.
Reps say the MQLs you pass are not ready to buy. How do you find out whether the scoring model is the problem?
Whether you test a scoring model against outcomes instead of opinions.
Follow past leads to their outcomes, compare scores of won deals and rejected leads, and reset the threshold with sales.

I pull two quarters of MQLs and follow each to its outcome: rejected with a reason, opportunity, won. If won deals and rejected leads score about the same, the model is not separating them. Often one action, like a content download, is overweighted. I reweight, test the new model on past data, and agree the threshold with the sales lead before switching.
A workflow you built overwrote the lead source field on 20,000 records. What do you do?
How you own and recover from a data mistake.
Stop the workflow, find the scope, restore from history or backup, tell the people whose reports were affected, and add a safeguard.

I turn the workflow off so it stops spreading. I find exactly which records changed and when, using field history or the last export, and restore the original values. I tell the sales ops and reporting owners which dashboards were wrong for which dates. Then I add a rule that lead source is only set when blank, and I test workflows on a small list first.
The CFO asks which channel drove last quarter's pipeline. How do you answer?
Your judgement about attribution models and their limits.
More than one model, what each one favors, and honesty that attribution shows association, not proof of cause.

I show first touch, last touch and a multi-touch view side by side. First touch favors channels that find people, like paid social; last touch favors ones that close, like branded search. Where they agree I am confident, and where they differ I say so. For a causal answer on a big channel, I would propose a holdout test: pause it in some regions and compare.
Walk me through your first 60 days auditing a marketing tech stack you inherited.
How you take stock of tools, data and processes before changing them.
Inventory tools, owners and costs, map and test data flows, find broken syncs and unused licenses, then rank fixes with stakeholders.

First I list every tool, its owner, cost and renewal date. Then I map how data moves from forms to the email platform, the CRM and reports, and test each sync with a fake lead. I check field definitions, duplicates and old workflows nobody remembers. By day 60 I share a ranked list of what is broken, what is wasted and what to fix first, and agree the order with sales.

materials-engineer.heading: Materials and process engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between yield strength and ultimate tensile strength?
Whether you know the basic numbers on a material certificate.
Yield is where permanent deformation starts, often found by the 0.2% offset method; ultimate is the peak engineering stress. Designs usually work from yield.

Yield strength is the stress where the metal stops springing back and starts to bend for good. Many metals have no sharp yield point, so we use the 0.2% offset method. Ultimate tensile strength is the highest engineering stress on the curve, where necking starts. For most structural parts I design against yield, because a bent part has already failed.
Why do we temper steel after quenching it?
Your grasp of how heat treatment changes the structure of steel.
Quenching forms hard, brittle martensite with high internal stress; tempering trades some hardness for toughness.

Quenching from the austenite range traps carbon and forms martensite. It is very hard but brittle and full of internal stress, so a part can even crack sitting on the shelf. Tempering reheats it below the critical temperature. That relieves stress and lets carbides form, so we give up some hardness and gain a lot of toughness. The tempering temperature sets where we land.
How can you tell a fatigue fracture from an overload fracture by looking at it?
Whether you can read a fracture surface.
Fatigue shows an origin, beach marks and a final overload zone; ductile overload shows shear lips and dimples; brittle shows chevrons and cleavage.

Fatigue usually shows a flat, smooth zone with beach marks that fan out from an origin, often at a notch, thread or machining mark, then a rough final overload zone. Under a scanning electron microscope you may see striations. Ductile overload looks fibrous with shear lips, and dimples at high magnification. Brittle overload is bright and grainy, with chevron marks pointing back to the origin.
You need the lightest beam that meets a stiffness target in bending. How do you compare materials?
Whether you can turn a design requirement into a material choice.
A performance index: for a light, stiffness-limited beam, the square root of modulus over density, then checks on cost, process and environment.

I write the requirement as a performance index. For a beam in bending with stiffness fixed and mass to minimize, the index is the square root of Young's modulus divided by density. I plot candidates on a modulus versus density chart and keep the best ones. Then I screen for cost, how the part will be made, corrosion and supply before I pick.
A designer wants stainless steel screws in an aluminum panel that will see salt spray. What do you tell them?
Whether you spot galvanic corrosion before it happens.
Aluminum is the anode and will corrode; you explain the area ratio and offer isolation, sealing or a different fastener.

Aluminum is more active than stainless, so with salt water as the electrolyte the panel will corrode around the screws. Small screws in a large panel is the better area ratio, but attack still concentrates at the holes. I would isolate the joint with nonconductive washers and sleeves and install the screws wet with sealant. If that cannot be done, we pick another fastener.
How would you set up experiments to find the right settings for a new process?
How you develop a process with data instead of trial and error.
A designed experiment: chosen factors and ranges, randomized runs, a look at interactions, then confirmation runs.

First I agree on the output that matters, say bond strength, and make sure we can measure it reliably. Then I pick the few factors most likely to matter, like temperature, pressure and time, at two levels each. A full or fractional factorial shows main effects and interactions in few runs. I randomize run order, analyze, and confirm the chosen settings with extra runs.
A steel bracket cracked in the field. Walk me through your failure analysis.
Your method for finding a root cause without destroying the evidence.
History first, protect the fracture, nondestructive work before destructive, and a root cause that fits every finding.

I collect the history: load, environment, hours in service. I protect the fracture, so no fitting the halves together and no wire brushing. Then photos, visual and stereo microscope exam, and dye penetrant to find other cracks. Next fractography, a metallographic section, hardness and chemistry against the spec. The root cause I report has to explain every finding.
Zinc-plated high-strength bolts are snapping a day or two after assembly. What do you suspect and what do you check?
Whether you recognize delayed failure from hydrogen embrittlement.
Hydrogen embrittlement from cleaning or plating; check hardness, the fracture surface and whether the bake after plating was done in time.

Breaking under steady load, after a delay, with no extra force points to hydrogen embrittlement. Acid cleaning and electroplating put hydrogen into the steel, and the harder the steel, the more sensitive it is. I check bolt hardness, look for intergranular fracture at the thread root, and ask the plater for bake records, including how soon after plating the bake ran.
One of five tensile specimens comes in well below the others. Can you drop it from the report?
How you handle an outlier in test data honestly.
Only with an assignable cause, such as a break outside the gauge length or a machining flaw, written down; otherwise it stays and you investigate.

Not just because it is low. I look at where it broke and at the fracture. If it broke outside the gauge length or at a machining nick, the test standard lets me treat it as invalid and retest, and I record why. If the specimen was good, the low value is real data. It may mean an inclusion or a weak spot in the lot, and that is what we need to know.
A supplier lot is slightly below the hardness spec and production needs it this week. What do you do?
Your judgement when schedule pressure meets a material that is out of spec.
Verify the measurement, hold the lot, assess the risk, and use the formal nonconformance process; no quiet acceptance.

First I confirm the number: right scale, right test location, a calibrated tester, and a few parts retested. If it is truly low, the lot stays on hold. I look at what hardness protects in this part, like wear or strength, and bring data to the material review board. If we use it, it is a documented deviation, with customer approval when the contract requires it.

mechanic.heading: Automotive and diesel mechanic questions
qs: How does a diesel engine ignite its fuel differently from a gasoline engine?
Whether you know the basic difference between the two kinds of engine you will work on.
Compression ignition versus spark ignition, and what follows from it: higher compression, no spark plugs, cold-start aids.

A gasoline engine mixes fuel and air and lights it with a spark plug. A diesel compresses air alone until it is hot enough, then injects fuel, which ignites from that heat. That is why diesels run much higher compression, have no spark plugs, and use glow plugs or intake heaters to help cold starts.
You are putting a cylinder head back on and the head bolts are torque-to-yield. Can you reuse them?
Whether you know torque-to-yield fasteners and follow the service manual.
Usually no, because the bolt is stretched past its elastic limit. Follows the manual's torque-plus-angle steps and any length check it allows.

Usually no. Torque-to-yield bolts are tightened to a set torque and then turned a set angle, which stretches them past their elastic limit. Once stretched they won't clamp the same way and can break. I follow the service manual: most say replace them, and a few allow reuse only if the bolt length is still within spec.
A car comes in with code P0300. How do you go about it?
Whether you treat a trouble code as a starting point, not as a part to replace.
Knows P0300 means random or multiple misfire, uses freeze frame and live data, and tests the basics before buying parts.

P0300 means random or multiple cylinder misfire, so it names a symptom, not a part. I look at freeze frame data and the misfire counters for each cylinder. Then I check the basics: plugs, coils, vacuum leaks and fuel trims. If trims are high at idle and come back toward normal at higher RPM, I'd suspect a vacuum leak and smoke-test the intake.
Why would you do a voltage drop test when the ohmmeter says a cable is fine?
Your electrical diagnosis method under real load.
Explains that an ohmmeter uses tiny current, while a voltage drop test under load reveals corroded or damaged connections.

An ohmmeter sends only a tiny current, so a cable with just a few good strands can still read fine. A voltage drop test checks the circuit while it carries real load. I put my meter leads at both ends of the wire or connection with the circuit working. If it loses more voltage than it should, I've found the bad cable or connection.
A customer says the A/C blows warm. What do you check first, and what rules apply when you open the system?
Whether you know A/C diagnosis and the federal rules on refrigerant handling.
Confirms the fault and refrigerant type, knows EPA Section 609 certification is required for paid work, recovers refrigerant, never vents it.

First I confirm it: vent temperature, whether the compressor is running, and the refrigerant type on the under-hood label, R-134a or R-1234yf. Servicing it for pay requires EPA Section 609 certification, and refrigerant must be recovered with approved equipment, never vented. I leak-test with dye or an electronic detector before I recharge.
During an oil change you find a worn ball joint. The customer only asked for the oil change. What do you do?
How you handle extra work honestly and with the customer's approval.
Shows the customer the problem, explains the risk plainly, gives an estimate, does nothing without approval, and records a refusal.

I finish the oil change, then show the customer the play in the joint or a photo of it. I explain that it affects steering and that a failed ball joint can let the wheel fold under. I give a written estimate and do no work they haven't approved. If they decline, I note it on the repair order so the record shows I told them.
A truck's battery is dead every morning. Walk me through finding the cause.
Your method for tracking a parasitic battery drain.
Tests the battery and charging first, measures draw after the modules go to sleep, compares with spec, then isolates the circuit.

I charge and test the battery and check the charging system first, so I'm not chasing a weak battery. Then I put an ammeter in series at the negative cable, latch the doors shut, and wait for the modules to sleep. If the draw is above the maker's spec, I measure voltage drop across each fuse to find the circuit without waking anything up.
A customer asks you to delete the DPF and EGR on his pickup because they keep giving trouble. What do you say?
Whether you know emissions law and can still help the customer.
Refuses because tampering breaks the federal Clean Air Act, then offers to diagnose why the filter keeps loading up.

I'd say no. Removing or disabling emissions equipment on a road vehicle violates the federal Clean Air Act, and both the shop and the tech can be fined. Then I'd offer to find why the filter keeps loading: lots of idling and short trips, a leaking injector, an EGR fault or a bad pressure sensor. Fix the cause and the filter usually lasts.
A vehicle you repaired comes back a week later with the same problem. How do you handle it?
How you own a comeback and learn from it.
No arguing, retests from scratch, finds what was missed, fixes it fairly, and changes a habit so it doesn't happen again.

A truck came back a week after I replaced the starter, still not cranking. I didn't argue. I tested again and found the main ground cable corroded at the frame; I had tested the starter but not the ground side. I fixed it with no labor charge, and now I check both power and ground circuits before I condemn a starter.
On a truck with air brakes, one chamber's pushrod stroke is over the limit and it has automatic slack adjusters. Do you just adjust it?
Whether you understand air brake adjustment on heavy vehicles and look for the root cause.
Knows automatic slack adjusters should not need routine manual adjusting; out-of-range stroke means a fault to find and fix.

No. Automatic slack adjusters should keep stroke in range on their own, so adjusting by hand only hides the problem. I look for the cause: a failed adjuster, worn clevis pins or bushings, worn camshaft bushings, or worn brake parts. I fix that, then measure the stroke again against the limit for that chamber size.

mechanical-design.heading: Mechanical design engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between a clearance fit, a transition fit and an interference fit?
Whether you know the basic fits and when each one is used.
Clear definitions tied to real uses: parts that move, parts that locate, parts that must stay put.

A clearance fit always leaves a gap, so the parts slide or turn, like a hinge pin. An interference fit makes the shaft bigger than the hole, so it is pressed or shrunk in and holds by friction, like a bearing on a shaft. A transition fit can land either way within tolerance; I use it to locate parts accurately that still need to come apart.
Why does a drawing need datums, and how do you choose them?
Your grasp of how a part is located, made and inspected.
Datums set where everyone measures from, and they should be the functional surfaces that locate the part in its assembly.

Datums tell the machinist and the inspector where to measure from, so everyone gets the same answer. I choose the surfaces that locate the part in its assembly: the face it sits on as primary, then the bore or edge that positions it. If I pick a surface just because it is easy to dimension from, the part can pass inspection and still not fit.
How do you pick a factor of safety for a part?
Whether you set margins by reasoning rather than by habit.
It depends on uncertainty in loads and material and on the cost of failure; codes rule where they apply, and fatigue is checked separately.

It depends on how well I know the loads and the material, and on what happens if the part fails. A bracket with measured loads and a known alloy can run lower than one facing guessed shock loads. Where a code or customer spec sets a value, that rules. I also check fatigue separately, because a static factor says nothing about a part that cycles millions of times.
What changes in your design when a part moves from machined to injection molded?
Your design-for-manufacturing knowledge for molded plastic parts.
Even walls, draft, radii, ribs thinner than walls, no needless undercuts, and early talks with the molder.

I keep wall thickness even, because thick spots shrink more and cause sink and warp. I add draft to walls along the direction the mold opens so the part releases. Sharp inside corners get radii, ribs are made thinner than the wall they sit on, and I avoid undercuts or plan side actions with the molder. Then I review gate location with the toolmaker before steel is cut.
Walk me through a tolerance stack-up, and tell me when you would use worst case versus RSS.
How you prove an assembly fits before parts are made.
A clear loop through the parts, and knowing that RSS assumes independent, centered variation and accepts a small reject rate.

I draw a loop from one side of the gap I care about, through each part, and list each dimension with its tolerance and direction. Worst case adds all tolerances and guarantees fit, but can force costly tight tolerances. RSS takes the square root of the sum of squares; it assumes independent, centered variation, so I use it for high volume and accept a small reject rate.
How do you keep a bolted joint from loosening under vibration?
Whether you understand preload and how real joints fail.
Preload that prevents joint slip comes first, with a controlled tightening method; locking features are a backup.

Preload does most of the work: if the clamp force keeps the joint from slipping, the nut has nothing to back it off. I specify the tightening method, and for critical joints torque-angle, because friction makes plain torque give a wide spread of preload. Longer grip length helps. Where needed I add thread locker or prevailing-torque nuts rather than split lock washers.
Your FEA shows stress well above yield at a sharp inside corner. What do you do?
Whether you can judge a simulation result instead of trusting it blindly.
Spotting a possible singularity, checking mesh convergence and boundary conditions, then fixing the geometry if the stress is real.

First I check whether it is real. A perfectly sharp inside corner gives a stress that keeps rising as the mesh gets finer, so the peak means nothing. I model the real fillet radius, refine until the result converges, and check that loads and fixtures match reality. If the converged stress is still too high, I enlarge the radius or add material, and treat it as a fatigue risk.
A supplier says one of your tolerances is too tight to hold at a fair price. How do you respond?
How you weigh function against cost when a tolerance is challenged.
Going back to why the tolerance exists, loosening it if function allows, and changing it only through a formal drawing revision.

I go back to why the number is there. If the stack-up shows the fit still works at a looser value, I loosen it and save the money. If it drives function, I explain that to the supplier and ask what they can hold, or change the design so that feature matters less. Either way the change goes through a drawing revision, not a phone call.
A prototype cracked at 20,000 cycles in testing, far below the target. How do you find out why?
How you run a failure investigation on a test part.
Reading the fracture surface, comparing with analysis, checking material and real test loads, then retesting more than one sample.

I keep the broken part and look at the fracture surface. Beach marks spreading from one spot point to fatigue and show where it started. I compare that spot with my FEA, check the material certificate, and measure the real test loads, since rigs often load harder than assumed. Once I know the cause I fix it and retest several samples, not just one.
You find an error in your design after the production mold has been cut. What do you do?
How you own a costly mistake and limit the damage.
Telling the lead fast with options, knowing which mold changes are cheap, and fixing the process that let the error through.

I tell the project lead the same day, with what is wrong, which parts are affected and the options. For a mold, a change that removes steel is usually a cheap rework, while adding steel may mean welding or a new insert, so I check which one my fix needs. Then I update the drawing and find out why our review missed it.

mechanical-engineer.heading: Mechanical engineer questions
qs: Why do injection-molded housings need draft and uniform wall thickness?
Whether you design plastic parts that can actually be molded.
Draft lets the part release from the mold. Even walls cool evenly, which limits sink marks, warp and voids.

Draft is a slight taper on faces parallel to the mold's opening direction, so the part slides off the core without dragging. I usually start around one to two degrees and add more for textured faces. Even walls cool at the same rate. A thick spot shrinks more and leaves a sink mark or warps the part. Where I need stiffness, I add ribs instead of thickening the wall.
What is the difference between a clearance, a transition and an interference fit, and which would you use for a ball bearing on a rotating shaft?
Your grasp of fits between mating parts.
Clear definitions, and knowing that the ring that turns relative to the load usually gets the interference fit, set from the bearing maker's tables.

A clearance fit always leaves a gap. A transition fit may give a small gap or a small press. An interference fit always presses. If the shaft turns and the load direction stays fixed, the inner ring sees a rotating load, so I give it a light interference fit to stop it creeping. The outer ring in the housing can be looser. I take the exact tolerance classes from the bearing maker's catalog.
When do you use a worst-case tolerance stack-up and when do you use RSS?
Your understanding of tolerance analysis methods and their assumptions.
Worst case adds all tolerances; RSS is statistical and assumes independent, centered variation. The choice depends on risk and the number of parts.

Worst case adds every tolerance in the chain, so the assembly works even if every part is at its limit. RSS takes the square root of the sum of the squared tolerances. It gives a smaller predicted spread but assumes parts vary independently and are centered in the process. I use worst case for critical fits or short chains, and RSS for long chains from a stable process.
Why would you put a position tolerance on a hole pattern instead of plus-minus tolerances on the X and Y dimensions?
Whether you use GD&T for function, not just habit.
A round tolerance zone tied to datums, about 57% more area than the matching square zone, and bonus tolerance at MMC where function allows.

Plus-minus on X and Y gives a square zone, but a pin works the same in any direction, so the true limit is round. A round zone that just contains that square has about 57% more area, so more good parts pass. It also ties the holes to datums, so the inspector measures from the same surfaces the assembly uses. With MMC, a larger hole earns extra position tolerance.
Your 3D-printed snap-fit prototype breaks on the third assembly. Does that mean the molded part will fail too?
Whether you know what a prototype can and cannot tell you.
Knowing printed parts are weaker and depend on layer direction, so prints test geometry while strength is checked with the real material or a calculation.

Not necessarily. An FDM print is weakest between layers, and if the hook is printed with layers across the bend it snaps early. The molded part will use a different resin with its own allowable strain. I would check the strain in the hook with the standard beam calculation against the resin's data, reprint with layers along the hook, and confirm on parts in the real material.
A sealed enclosure holds electronics that dissipate 10 W. How do you check whether it will run cool enough before building it?
How you approach a thermal problem from first principles.
A hand estimate with a thermal resistance path and convection from the outer surface, compared to component limits, then simulation and a test with thermocouples.

First a hand estimate: heat flows from the parts to the wall, then leaves the outside by natural convection and radiation. Each step is a thermal resistance, and temperature rise equals power times resistance. I compare the result at the highest ambient in the spec with the hottest part's rating. If margin is thin, I run CFD, then test a prototype with thermocouples.
Your FEA shows a peak stress twice the yield strength at a sharp inside corner. What do you do?
Whether you can judge a simulation result rather than just run it.
Recognizing a possible stress singularity, then checking mesh convergence, boundary conditions and a hand calculation before redesigning.

First I ask whether it is real. A perfectly sharp corner is a singularity: the stress keeps rising as I refine the mesh, so the number means nothing. I check the loads and constraints, run a mesh convergence study, and compare away from the corner with a hand calculation. Then I model the real fillet radius. If the stress is still too high, I add a larger fillet or move material.
A machine shop quotes three times your target cost and says it is because of your tolerances. How do you handle it?
Your judgement on cost versus precision.
Asking which features drive the cost, keeping tight tolerances only where function needs them, and changing the design rather than just loosening numbers.

I ask the shop which features drive the price. Often it is a tight tolerance copied from a default title block. I go through each one and ask what fails if it is looser; if nothing does, I open it up. For a fit that truly matters, I look at other options: a reamed hole only where the pin goes, or a slot so the part can be adjusted at assembly. Then I requote.
Plastic screw bosses on a shipped product start cracking months after assembly. How do you find the cause?
How you work a field failure back to its root cause.
Considering hoop stress from the screw, over-torque, creep, sharp corners and chemical attack, and confirming with the failed parts before changing the design.

I get the failed units and look at the fractures and the lot codes. Then I check the hole size against the screw maker's guide, the assembly torque, and sharp corners at the base of the boss. I also ask what touched it: some threadlockers and cleaners cause stress cracking in plastics like polycarbonate. Once a test reproduces the crack, I fix the cause and retest.
The injection mold is already being cut and testing shows a wall must change. How do you handle the change, and how could you have planned for it?
Whether you understand tooling costs and design changes late in a project.
Knowing that removing steel is cheap and adding steel is not, and leaving uncertain features steel safe so they can be tuned after first shots.

Removing steel from the mold adds plastic to the part and is a cheap cut. Adding steel means welding or a new insert, which costs time and money. So I first see if the fix can be made by thickening the wall rather than thinning it. For the next tool, I would leave uncertain features steel safe: start them on the side that only needs metal removed, then tune after first shots.

mechanical-technician.heading: Mechanical technician questions
qs: On a US drawing, where do you find the right side view and the top view, and why does it matter?
Your reading of standard drawing layout.
Knows US drawings normally use third-angle projection, checks the projection symbol, and knows a misread view can mirror a feature.

Most US drawings use third-angle projection: the top view sits above the front view and the right side view sits to its right. I still check the projection symbol in the title block, because a drawing from an overseas supplier may be first-angle, with the views swapped. Reading it wrong can put a hole on the wrong side of the part.
Before you measure a part with a micrometer, what do you check?
Whether you trust your instruments only after checking them.
Calibration in date, clean faces, a zero check, steady use of the ratchet, and part and tool at the same temperature.

I check the calibration sticker is in date, wipe the anvil and spindle faces, and close it with the ratchet to check zero. For a larger mic I use the setting standard. I let the part and the mic sit at room temperature, hold the frame so my hand does not warm it, and take more than one reading.
How do you mount a rolling bearing onto a shaft with an interference fit?
Your hands-on method for a common part that is easy to damage.
Force only through the ring being fitted, never through the balls, or controlled heating with no open flame; cleanliness and checking it seats.

Small bearings I press with a fitting sleeve that pushes only on the inner ring, because force through the balls dents the races. Larger ones I warm with an induction heater, staying under the maker's temperature limit, never a torch. I keep everything clean, slide it on quickly against the shoulder, hold it until it grips, then check it turns freely.
You are bolting up a flange with twelve bolts. How do you tighten them?
Whether you know how to get even clamping force, not just the final torque value.
Crisscross pattern in stages, a final check pass, and torque applied with the thread condition the spec assumes.

I snug all bolts by hand, then tighten in a star pattern in steps, for example about a third, two thirds, then full torque. I finish with passes around the circle until no nut moves. I use the lubricant the spec calls for, because oil or anti-seize gives more clamping force at the same torque than dry threads. Then I mark each bolt.
Why can stainless steel bolts seize while you are tightening them, and how do you prevent it?
Your knowledge of a common fastener problem and its fix.
Names galling, metal welding to itself under pressure and sliding. Prevention: clean threads, approved anti-seize, slow tightening, matching torque value.

That is galling. Stainless relies on a thin oxide layer; under high pressure and sliding, that layer breaks and the metal welds to itself, so the nut locks up. I keep threads clean, use the anti-seize the spec approves, and run nuts down slowly, not with an impact gun. Since anti-seize changes the torque needed, I use the value for lubricated threads.
Walk me through aligning a motor to a pump with dial indicators.
Whether you can do a precise, step-by-step alignment job.
Lockout, soft foot fixed first, offset and angle measured separately, vertical then horizontal corrections, recheck after tightening.

First I lock out both machines and check for soft foot, a foot that does not sit flat, and shim it. With the rim-and-face method, the rim indicator shows offset and the face indicator shows angle. I turn both shafts together and read at four clock positions. I correct vertical with shims under the motor feet, then horizontal by moving the motor, and recheck after tightening.
During a hydrostatic test, a fitting on a valve body starts to weep. What do you do?
How you handle a test failure without taking risks.
Never tightens under pressure: stops, depressurizes per procedure, records, finds the cause, and repeats the full test after the fix.

I stop raising pressure, keep people clear, and bleed it down per the procedure. I never tighten a fitting while it is under pressure. I record the pressure and where it leaked, then take it apart to see why: a damaged seal, a scratched seat or poor assembly. After the fix I run the whole test again from the start, not just a quick check.
A machined part is 0.002 inch out of tolerance and your lead says to make it fit because the line is waiting. What do you do?
Your judgement when production pressure meets a part that does not conform.
Does not quietly rework or use it; tags and holds the part and writes it up so engineering decides: use as is, rework or scrap.

I would not file it or force it in on my own say. I tag the part, set it aside, and write it up so quality or engineering can decide: use as is, rework or scrap. Often they answer fast, and 0.002 may turn out fine. I tell my lead I am pushing for a quick decision and look for a good spare part so the line keeps moving.
After an assembly is closed and signed off, you realize you may have missed torquing one bolt. What do you do?
Your honesty and how you handle your own mistake.
Speaks up at once, gets the unit held, reopens it per procedure, verifies the fasteners, and changes the habit that let it happen.

I tell my supervisor and quality straight away and get the unit put on hold before it ships. Then we open it per procedure and check that bolt and the ones around it with a torque wrench, and I record it. To stop it happening again, I now mark each fastener with torque paint as I go, so a missed one stands out.

medical-director.heading: Medical director and chief medical officer questions
qs: What is the difference between a severe adverse event and a serious one?
Whether you know a basic safety term that drives reporting rules.
Severity is intensity; seriousness is outcome, with the regulatory criteria named correctly.

Severe describes intensity, like a severe headache, which may not be serious at all. Serious is defined by outcome: death, a life-threatening event, hospitalization or a longer stay, lasting disability, a birth defect, or an important medical event that needs intervention to prevent one of those. Seriousness, not severity, sets reporting duties.
How do you decide whether an adverse event is related to the study drug?
How you reason about causality instead of guessing.
A structured look at timing, dechallenge, rechallenge, pharmacology and other causes, with the bar set at a reasonable possibility.

I look at timing against dosing. I check whether it improved when the drug stopped and came back if it was restarted. I ask whether it fits the drug's mechanism or class, and what else could explain it, like the disease or other medicines. If there is a reasonable possibility the drug caused it, I call it related. I do not need proof, and I write down my reasoning.
A commercial lead asks you to approve a slide that mentions an unapproved use of our product. What do you do?
Whether you hold the line between medical and promotional work.
A clear no to off-label promotion, plus the proper route: balanced answers to unsolicited questions through medical information.

I would not approve it. Promoting a use the FDA has not approved creates real legal risk for the company. I would explain why and offer what we can do: if a doctor asks about that use on their own, our medical information team can send a balanced, scientific answer. Then I would review the rest of the deck for claims the label does not support.
A site reports a death in our trial late on a Friday. Walk me through the next 48 hours.
How you run a serious safety event and whether you know the reporting clock.
Fast medical review, follow-up from the site, a causality and expectedness call, and FDA and investigator reports on time if required.

I review the case that night and ask the site for records, labs and autopsy plans. I judge whether it is related and whether it is expected under the investigator's brochure. If it is a fatal, unexpected suspected reaction, the IND safety report is due to FDA within 7 calendar days, and investigators must be told. I also decide whether dosing should pause.
A site enrolled a patient who did not meet an inclusion criterion, and the patient has had two doses. How do you handle it?
How you balance patient safety, data integrity and follow-up with the site.
Safety first, a case-by-case decision on further dosing, proper documentation and reporting, and a root-cause fix at the site.

First I check whether the missed criterion puts this patient at risk. If it does, dosing stops and we follow them for safety. If not, I decide with the team and the investigator whether to continue. We log it as a major deviation, report it under the IRB's rules, and find out why it happened. Then we retrain the site and tighten eligibility checks.
A doctor asks for our investigational drug for a dying patient who cannot join the trial. How do you decide?
Your judgement on expanded access, applied fairly and consistently.
Applies a written policy: serious disease, no good alternative, benefit that justifies risk, enough supply, and no harm to the trial.

I use our published expanded access policy so every request gets the same test. Is the disease serious or life-threatening, with no comparable option? Does our data suggest a benefit worth the risk? Do we have supply, and would this undercut enrollment? If yes, we support the doctor's request to FDA and the IRB. If no, I call the doctor myself and explain why.
Why shouldn't you, as the sponsor's medical lead, see unblinded data while the trial is running?
Whether you understand how a data monitoring committee protects trial integrity.
Knowing interim results can bias trial decisions; an independent committee reviews them and only passes on recommendations.

If I know which arm is doing better, every later decision I make, from amending the protocol to how I judge an event, can be bent by that. So an independent data monitoring committee looks at unblinded results and tells us only what it recommends: continue, change, or stop. I see blinded safety data and act on their advice.
You see four cases of liver injury across our studies in a year. How do you decide whether it is a real signal?
How you separate a true safety signal from background noise.
Careful case review against Hy's law, comparison with the control arm and background rates, and action in proportion to the evidence.

I pull all four cases with labs, timing and other causes like alcohol, viral hepatitis or other drugs. I check each against Hy's law: liver enzymes over three times the upper normal limit plus bilirubin over twice it, with no better cause. Then I compare the rate with the control arm and the expected rate in this population. Even one true Hy's law case is a serious warning.
The CEO wants to announce strong topline results tomorrow, but the safety tables show an imbalance in deaths you have not explained. What do you do?
Whether you hold your medical judgement under business pressure.
Refuses to sign off on an incomplete picture, explains the risk plainly, proposes a fast path, and escalates if overruled.

I tell the CEO I cannot sign off yet, and why: an unexplained imbalance in deaths is material, and leaving it out could mislead patients and investors. I give a plan to review the cases within days and agree on wording that is complete. If I am overruled, I take it to the board, because my signature means the medical picture is accurate.

mental-health.heading: Mental health and therapy questions
qs: Walk me through the first session with a new client.
How you run an intake assessment and set up the work.
Consent and the limits of confidentiality first, then history, symptoms, a risk screen and the client's own goals.

I start with consent: how sessions work, fees, and the limits of confidentiality, like serious risk of harm and child abuse reporting. Then I ask what brings them in now, symptom history, past treatment, health, substance use, sleep and support. I always screen for suicide risk. I end by agreeing on what they want to be different.
How would you explain CBT to a client who has never had therapy?
Whether you can explain your main method in plain words.
The link between thoughts, feelings and actions, a practical tone, and the fact that the client practices between sessions.

I'd say how we read a situation shapes how we feel and what we do. If you think a friend's silence means she's angry, you feel hurt and avoid her. We'll learn to catch those thoughts, test them against the facts, and try new actions. It's practical, usually time-limited, and includes short practice between sessions.
How do you use measures like the PHQ-9 or GAD-7 in your work?
Whether you use measurement to guide treatment, not just to fill in a form.
Given at intake and regularly after, scores reviewed with the client and used to adjust the plan. A screener alone is not a diagnosis.

I give them at intake and then every few sessions, and I go over the scores with the client. If the PHQ-9 isn't dropping after several weeks, I rethink the plan. They are screeners, not diagnoses. I always read item 9, the question about thoughts of death or self-harm, right away and follow up in that same session.
A client says, “I just want to feel less anxious.” How do you turn that into a treatment goal?
How you write a treatment plan with goals you can measure.
A specific, measurable goal tied to daily life, in the client's words, with a timeframe and a way to track progress.

I ask what she would do if anxiety weren't in the way. Say she'd drive on the highway again. The goal becomes: drive a 15-minute highway route alone, with anxiety under 4 out of 10, within 12 weeks. The steps are learning calming skills and working through a graded exposure list. We also track her GAD-7 score monthly.
What goes into a good progress note?
Your clinical documentation and whether it would hold up to an audit or a records request.
A standard format like SOAP or DAP, linked to the treatment plan, factual, with risk noted and a clear plan for next time.

I use DAP. Data is what the client reported and what I observed, plus any scores. Assessment is my clinical read and progress toward the plan's goals. Plan is homework and next steps. I note any risk screen and what I did about it. I keep it factual, write it the same day, and remember the client may read it.
What do you check at the start of every video session?
Whether you know how to run telehealth safely and legally.
The client's current location and an emergency contact, a private space, a backup plan, and a license valid where the client is.

I confirm where the client is right now: in a crisis I need to send local help, and I must be licensed for the state they are in. I check they're alone and can talk freely, and I have a phone number in case video drops. I use a HIPAA-compliant platform. If they're driving or at work, we reschedule or adjust.
Your client with panic attacks keeps texting you for reassurance between sessions. What do you do?
How you apply CBT when the client's way of coping is part of the problem.
Seeing reassurance as a safety behavior that keeps anxiety going, setting a kind boundary, and building exposure into the plan.

Reassurance calms panic for a minute but teaches her she can't cope alone, so the fear stays. I'd raise it in session without blame, explain that, and agree on clear rules for contact. Then we'd practice sitting with uncertainty and do interoceptive exposure, like spinning in a chair to bring on dizziness, so she learns the sensations are safe.
A former client sends you a friend request on social media. What do you do?
Your judgement on boundaries and dual relationships.
Not accepting, protecting the client's privacy, and explaining the policy kindly, ideally one already set out at intake.

I don't accept, and I don't reply on the platform, since even a reply could show we're connected. My consent form says I don't connect with current or former clients online, so if it comes up I point back to that. If they return to therapy, I'd talk about it openly: it protects their privacy and our work, it's not a rejection.
On a video session, a client says she has been thinking she'd be better off dead. Walk me through what you do.
How you assess suicide risk and act on it.
Asking directly about plan, intent, means and history, building a safety plan, acting on the level of risk, consulting and documenting.

I stay calm and ask directly if she is thinking of killing herself. Asking does not plant the idea. Then plan, intent, access to means, past attempts and reasons to live. If risk is lower, we write a safety plan together and put means out of reach. If she has intent and means, I keep her on the call and get emergency help to her location. Then I consult and document.
Your client has had 10 sessions of CBT for depression and her scores have not moved. What do you do?
How you handle treatment that is not working.
Reviewing it openly with the client, rechecking diagnosis, alliance and barriers, getting consultation, and changing course or referring.

I'd show her the scores and ask what she thinks is getting in the way. Then I recheck: is the diagnosis right, could it be bipolar or a medical issue, is she drinking, is homework happening, does she trust me? I'd take it to consultation. Options include behavioral activation, a referral for a medication evaluation, or a different therapist or level of care.

merchant-support.heading: Merchant and partner support questions
qs: How is supporting a merchant different from supporting a shopper?
Whether you understand that a merchant's problem is a problem for their whole business.
Time is money for them, one issue can hit many orders, and the relationship is long term, so you fix the cause and follow up.

A shopper usually has one order at stake. A restaurant with stuck orders loses sales every minute and has angry customers of its own. So I move faster, look at the whole account instead of one ticket, and follow up, because I will talk to the same owner again next month.
A restaurant owner says this week's payout is smaller than expected. Walk me through how you check it.
How you read a payout statement and explain a gap.
You rebuild it line by line: gross sales, commission, fees, refunds, adjustments and the pay period dates.

I open the statement for that period and rebuild it with the owner: gross sales, minus our commission and processing fees, minus refunds charged back to the store, plus any adjustments. Most gaps are a refund or orders that fall into the next pay period. If the math still does not match, I open a case with the payments team and give a date.
A restaurant's order tablet stops receiving orders in the middle of the dinner rush. What do you do first?
Whether you act fast to stop lost orders during an outage.
Protect open orders first, pause the store if needed, check the simple causes, and see whether other stores are hit too.

First I check whether orders are coming in and failing, so customers are not waiting on food no one is making. I can read them the open orders or pause the store if they want. Then the basics: Wi-Fi, power, app version, logging out and back in. If several stores report the same thing, I flag a possible outage instead of fixing them one by one.
A caller says they own a shop and wants to change the bank account for payouts right now. How do you handle it?
Whether you protect a merchant's money from fraud by verifying identity.
No change without the platform's verification process; a pushy, urgent caller is a warning sign, not a reason to skip steps.

Bank changes are a favorite target for fraud, so I follow our verification process every time: confirm the caller is an authorized owner the way our policy requires, and send the change through the secure flow, not over the phone. If they rush me, I stay polite and still skip nothing. A real owner would rather wait an hour than lose a week of payouts.
A driver writes that their account was deactivated and they need to work tonight. What do you say?
How you handle a partner's income with honesty about what you can and cannot change.
Empathy, the reason as far as policy allows, the appeal path and timeline, and no false promise.

I say I understand this is their income and I will check the account right away. I tell them what I am allowed to share about the reason, explain how the appeal works and what to send, like photos or trip details, and when they should hear back. I do not promise it will be reversed tonight, because I cannot decide that and false hope makes it worse.
A seller asks which tax form they will get from us and whether they owe tax on it. How do you answer?
Whether you stay inside your role on tax and legal questions.
You give the facts the platform owns, which form, when and where to find it, and send tax questions to a tax professional.

I tell them which form our platform sends, when it goes out, and where to download it in their account. I also check that the tax details on file are correct. Whether they owe tax and how much is tax advice, so I say that plainly and suggest a tax professional. A guess from me could cost them real money.
A merchant got a chargeback notice and asks what it means and what they can do.
Your grasp of card disputes and how a merchant can respond.
A chargeback is a buyer disputing a charge with their bank; the merchant can send evidence before a deadline, and you help them build it.

I explain that the buyer asked their card issuer to reverse the payment, so the money is usually taken back while the bank decides. The merchant can often respond with evidence, like delivery proof, tracking, receipts or messages with the buyer, and there is a deadline. I tell them the date, which evidence fits the buyer's stated reason, and how to submit it.
A restaurant asks you for a customer's phone number so they can follow up on a complaint. What do you do?
Whether you protect customer data while still helping the merchant.
You do not share personal data beyond what policy allows, and you offer a channel that meets the merchant's goal.

I would not give out the customer's phone number; it is personal data and our policy limits who sees it. I ask what the restaurant wants to do, maybe apologize or offer a credit, and use the tools we have, like a message through the platform. The owner gets to fix it and the customer's privacy stays safe.
One of our largest merchants says they will leave the platform unless you waive their fees. How do you handle it?
How you keep a valuable partner without making promises you cannot keep.
You listen for the real problem, stay within your authority, and bring in the account manager or the team that owns pricing.

I would not waive fees I am not allowed to waive, and I would not just say no either. I ask what is behind it: falling margins, a fee they did not expect, a competitor's offer. I fix what I can, like a wrong charge, and pass the rest to the account manager with the numbers and the owner's deadline. Then I tell the owner who will call and when.
Within an hour, several merchants in one city report a missing payout. What do you do?
Whether you spot a wider incident and escalate it instead of answering ticket by ticket.
You link the tickets, escalate early with evidence, give merchants one honest message, and update them on time.

Several similar tickets from one city in an hour is a pattern, not bad luck. I tag and link them, check what they share, such as the bank, the pay date or the app version, and escalate to the payments team with examples. Meanwhile every merchant gets the same honest message: we know, we are on it, next update by a set time. Then I keep that promise.

mid-market-account-executive.heading: Mid-market account executive questions
qs: How is selling to a 300-person company different from selling to a 20-person one or a 10,000-person one?
Whether you understand the segment you would be selling into.
More people than small business, less process than enterprise, cycles of weeks to a few months, and many deals run at once.

Compared with a small business, more people are involved: a department head, finance, often IT for security. Compared with enterprise, there is less procurement and legal, so a deal can close in one to three months. That means I carry more deals at once, so I qualify fast and keep each one moving with a clear next step.
How do you prepare a demo for a mid-market prospect?
Whether you show what matters to this buyer instead of the whole product.
A demo built from discovery: it opens on their problem, shows the few workflows they named, and ends with an agreed next step.

I only demo after discovery. I start by repeating the problem they told me, in their words, and check it is still right. Then I show the two or three workflows that solve it, with their kind of data, and skip features they did not ask about. I leave time for questions and end by agreeing who sees it next and when.
What is a mutual action plan, and when do you bring it in?
How you keep a deal on a timeline both sides have agreed to.
A shared list of steps, owners and dates, built back from the buyer's go-live date, introduced once the buyer sees value.

It is a short shared document: the steps both sides need to reach a signed contract and a start date, who owns each one, and by when. I build it backward from the date they want to be live. I bring it up after a good demo, when they agree the problem is worth solving. If they will not commit to any dates, that tells me the deal is not real yet.
Your contact wants to be the only person you talk to. How do you reach the rest of the buying group?
Whether you can multi-thread a deal without going around your contact.
Getting the contact's help to bring others in, framed as helping them succeed, and treating a single-threaded deal as higher risk.

I ask for help, not permission to go around them. I say: deals like this usually need finance and IT to sign off, and it goes faster if I answer their questions early so you are not stuck relaying them. I offer to prep them for that meeting. If they still refuse, I mark the deal as single-threaded and higher risk in my forecast.
You have 35 open opportunities and one week. How do you decide where to spend your time?
How you prioritize a full mid-market pipeline.
Ranking by size, stage and whether there is a real dated next step, and closing out stale deals instead of carrying them.

First I look at which deals have a dated next step with the buyer; those get my prep time. Then I rank by size and how close they are to a decision. Deals with no reply in weeks get a direct note asking if the project is still on; if not, I close them out. A clean pipeline of 20 beats a hopeful one of 35.
How do you decide which deals go in your commit for the quarter, and what happens when one slips?
Whether your manager can trust your forecast.
Commit means the decision, the signer and the paper process are confirmed, not just enthusiasm; slips are reported early with a reason.

A deal goes in commit only when the economic buyer has said yes, we know who signs, and I have walked through their legal and purchasing steps with my contact. An excited champion puts it in best case, not commit. If a commit deal starts to slip, I tell my manager the day I know, with the reason and a new date.
The CFO says they will sign by Friday if you take 25% off. What do you do?
How you handle a discount request as a trade, not a giveaway.
No instant yes: you find what drives the ask, trade any discount for something of value, and stay within your approval rules.

I would not say yes on the call. I would ask what is behind it: budget, a competing quote, or a test. If there is room, I trade rather than give: a longer term, payment upfront, or a reference, and I get any discount approved first. Cutting 25% to close three weeks early often costs more than waiting.
Their legal team sends back heavy redlines and a security questionnaire the week the deal should close. How do you keep it on track?
How you manage the paper process without losing the deal or misleading your forecast.
Bringing in your own legal and security teams at once, finding which points truly matter, and resetting dates openly.

I send the redlines to our legal team and the questionnaire to our security team the same day and ask for a review date. Then I call my contact to learn which changes they truly need and which are standard asks. I update the close date in the CRM and tell my manager. Next time I ask about legal and security steps in the first weeks.
Your champion leaves the company two weeks before the deal should close. What do you do?
How you recover a deal when your inside seller is gone.
Fast contact with the other stakeholders, a recheck of the problem and the buyer, and an honest move of the deal out of commit.

I reach out the same day to the others I have met, ideally the economic buyer, and ask who owns the project now. I set a short call to recap the problem, the value and the plan, and check it is still a priority. I move the deal out of commit until I have a new champion. I also stay in touch with the old one; they may buy again at their new company.

mission-operations.heading: Mission operations and flight controller questions
qs: What is the difference between a real-time command and a stored, time-tagged command, and when do you use each?
Whether you know the basic ways a spacecraft is commanded.
Real-time commands run when they are received during a pass. Stored ones run later by onboard time, so you check timing, order and the onboard clock.

A real-time command executes as soon as the spacecraft receives it, so I use it when I want to watch the result during the pass. A time-tagged command waits in an onboard queue and runs at a set time, often when we have no contact, like imaging over the ocean. For those I check the onboard clock, the order and that nothing in the queue conflicts.
Walk me through how you prepare for a ground station pass.
How you plan a contact so its few minutes are not wasted.
You check the schedule, station and link, review the command plan and procedures, and know the priorities and go/no-go points before the pass starts.

I confirm the pass time and station, and that the antenna and link are set up. I review the command plan against the procedures and the latest health data, and I list what must be downlinked. Before acquisition of signal I know the priorities in order, so if the pass is short or the link drops, the most important commands and data go first.
What do yellow and red limits on a telemetry point mean, and what do you do when one trips?
Your understanding of telemetry limits and how you respond when one is crossed.
Yellow is a caution to watch and report; red calls for action, usually by a written contingency procedure. First you confirm the reading is real.

A yellow limit is a caution: the value is off-nominal but not yet harmful, so I watch the trend and tell the lead. A red limit means a level that can damage the spacecraft or the mission. I first check the reading against related sensors to rule out a bad sensor, then follow the contingency procedure for that point. I do not improvise on a red limit.
You send a command and see no acknowledgment in telemetry. What do you do?
Whether you avoid resending a command blindly.
You find out whether the command arrived before sending it again, by checking counters and telemetry, because a repeat can do harm.

I do not just send it again. I check the uplink status and the onboard command counter, then the telemetry the command should change. It may have run and the report has not come down yet. If it is a toggle, a second send could undo it. If I confirm it was not received, I resend by the procedure and log both attempts.
The spacecraft has gone into safe mode and you see it at the start of a pass. Walk me through your first steps.
How you respond calmly when the spacecraft has protected itself.
Confirm power, attitude and link are stable, stop planned commands, gather the data, and do not rush recovery before the cause is known.

First I confirm it is stable: in its safe attitude, battery charging, link good. I hold the planned command load and tell the flight director. Then I dump the event log and the telemetry around the trigger. Recovery waits until we know the cause, because returning to normal mode on an unknown fault can send it straight back to safe mode, or make things worse.
Why does the battery matter so much in eclipse, and what do you watch?
Your grasp of power as a limit on what you can command.
In Earth's shadow the spacecraft runs on battery alone; you track charge and depth of discharge and plan loads so it recharges in sunlight.

In most low Earth orbits the spacecraft crosses Earth's shadow once per orbit, and then it runs only on the battery. I watch state of charge, voltage and temperature, and how deep each discharge goes, since deep cycles age the battery faster. Before a power-hungry activity, I check it fits the power budget so the battery is full again before the next eclipse.
The reaction wheels are close to their speed limit. What does that mean and what do you do?
Whether you understand momentum management on a wheel-controlled spacecraft.
Wheels absorb small outside torques and speed up over time; a momentum dump with magnetic torquers or thrusters unloads them before they saturate.

Small torques from drag, solar pressure or gravity build up, and the wheels spin faster to hold attitude. At their limit they cannot control it anymore. So we unload momentum: magnetic torquers push against Earth's field, or thrusters fire, while the wheels slow down. I track wheel speeds and schedule dumps so they do not clash with imaging or a pass.
You get a warning that another object may pass very close to your satellite in 36 hours. How do you handle it?
How you handle a collision risk and the decision to maneuver.
Follow updated predictions and collision probability, plan a maneuver early with flight dynamics, screen the new orbit, and decide by the mission's threshold.

I pull the latest conjunction data and look at miss distance, collision probability and how uncertain the orbits are. With flight dynamics I plan a maneuver early while new tracking keeps coming in. We check the new orbit does not create another close approach. If the risk stays above our threshold at the decision time, we execute; if it drops, we stand down and log why.
During a pass, a scientist asks you to send a command that is not in the approved plan. What do you do?
Your judgement when someone pushes for a change outside the approved plan.
No unreviewed commands on a live pass: send it through the flight director and the change process, and offer the soonest safe slot.

I would not send it on the spot, even if it looks harmless. A command outside the plan has not been checked against power, attitude or the other activities. I tell the flight director, write up the request, and see if it can be reviewed and added to the next pass. Usually the scientist gets it within a day, and safely.
Mid-pass, you realize you uplinked a command with a wrong parameter. What do you do?
How you own and contain a mistake on a live spacecraft.
Say it at once, assess the effect with the team, correct it by a reviewed command, then report it and fix the process.

I say it on the voice loop right away; speed matters more than pride. With the flight director we check what the wrong value does and whether waiting for the next pass is too late. Then we correct it with a reviewed command. Afterward I write the anomaly report, and we look at why the check missed it, for example by adding a range check in the command tool.

mlops.heading: ML infrastructure and MLOps questions
qs: What is the difference between batch inference and online serving, and when would you pick each?
Whether you know the two basic ways a model is served and their trade-offs.
Batch scores many records on a schedule; online answers each request live. The choice follows how fresh predictions must be, with cost and simplicity in mind.

Batch inference scores a large set of records on a schedule, like every night, and writes results to a table that apps read later. Online serving answers one request at a time behind an API, so latency matters. I pick batch when predictions can be a few hours old, since it is cheaper and simpler, and online when the answer depends on what the user just did.
What is training-serving skew, and how do you prevent it?
Whether you know a common way models fail quietly in production.
Features computed differently in training and serving. Prevent it with one shared feature definition and by checking served features against training data.

It is when the model gets features computed one way in training and another way in production, so it does worse live than offline. A common cause is two code paths, like a SQL job for training and hand-written serving code. I make both use one shared feature definition, log the features served live, and compare their distributions to the training data.
What do you record so a training run can be reproduced months later?
How you think about versioning data, code and environment together.
Code commit, data snapshot, container image with pinned libraries, config and seeds, plus honesty that some GPU operations are not deterministic.
