I record the code commit, a snapshot or version of the exact data, the container image with pinned library versions, the config and the random seeds, and store them with the model. Even then, some GPU operations are not deterministic, so I either turn on deterministic mode and accept slower runs, or agree that results within a small tolerance count as reproduced.
Explain dynamic batching in a model server and what it trades off.
Your understanding of how serving throughput and latency interact on a GPU.
Requests are held briefly and run together, raising GPU throughput at the cost of a small added wait, tuned with a max batch size and max delay.

The server holds incoming requests for a few milliseconds and runs them through the GPU together. A GPU often takes only a little longer for 16 inputs than for one, so throughput rises a lot. The cost is that each request waits a bit. I set a maximum batch size and a maximum wait, then tune both under load against our latency target.
A training job runs out of GPU memory. What do you try, and in what order?
Whether you know the standard ways to fit a model into limited GPU memory.
Find the cause first, then mixed precision, smaller batch with gradient accumulation, activation checkpointing, and sharding the model only if needed.

First I watch memory over steps to see if it is a leak or just too big. Then I try mixed precision, which stores many values in 16 bits; a smaller batch with gradient accumulation so the effective batch size stays the same; and activation checkpointing, which recomputes some values instead of storing them. If it still does not fit, I shard the model across GPUs.
GPU utilization sits around 30% during training. How do you find the bottleneck?
How you diagnose an expensive, underused GPU.
Profile before guessing. Most often the input pipeline starves the GPU; also check batch size and communication between nodes.

I profile a few hundred steps to see where time goes. Most often the GPU waits on data: slow reads from network storage, image decoding on too few CPU workers, or no prefetching. Fixes are more loader workers, prefetching, a packed file format and caching data on local disk. If data is fine, I check for a batch too small to fill the GPU or slow sync between nodes.
We want to train on cheaper preemptible instances that can be taken away at any time. How do you design for that?
Whether you can make long training jobs survive interruption.
Frequent checkpoints to durable storage with full training state, handling the shutdown notice, and automatic resume from the latest checkpoint.

I save checkpoints to durable storage, not the node's disk, often enough that losing one interval is cheap, say every 20 to 30 minutes. Each holds weights, optimizer state, learning-rate schedule, step count and data loader position. The job catches the shutdown notice and writes a last checkpoint if it can, and the scheduler restarts it from the latest one.
What is the difference between a shadow deployment and a canary release for a new model?
Your grasp of safe rollout patterns for models.
Shadow mirrors traffic with outputs logged but not used; canary serves a small share of real users. Both need clear rollback limits.

In a shadow deployment the new model gets a copy of live traffic, but its answers are only logged, never shown, so users are not at risk. It tests load and lets me compare outputs. A canary sends a small share, say 5%, of real users to the new model. I shadow first, then canary to measure real impact, with automatic rollback if errors or a key metric cross a set limit.
Three teams share 64 GPUs and each says its work is urgent. How do you set up scheduling?
Your judgement on fair, efficient sharing of a GPU cluster.
Guaranteed quotas with preemptible borrowing, priority for production work, gang scheduling for distributed jobs, and usage data shared openly.

Each team gets a guaranteed quota and can borrow idle GPUs, but borrowed jobs can be preempted when the owner needs them back. Production retraining outranks experiments. Distributed jobs are gang-scheduled, so all their GPUs start together or not at all; otherwise half-started jobs hold GPUs and block each other. I publish weekly usage per team so quota talks use data.
A new model version went out, the business metric dropped, but every infrastructure dashboard is green. What do you do?
How you handle a production incident where the system looks healthy but the model is wrong.
Roll back first, then compare versions on the same inputs, look for pipeline causes, and add a check that would have caught it.

I roll back to the previous model first, because rollback is cheap and the loss is real. Then I run both versions on the same inputs. The cause is often outside the weights: a changed preprocessing step, a feature that is null in production, or the wrong model file. Once it was a tokenizer version mismatch. After that I added a fixed test set both versions must pass before any rollout.

mobile-engineer.heading: Mobile engineer questions
qs: Where do you store a user's login token on the phone, and why there?
Whether you know the secure storage each platform provides.
Keychain on iOS, a key in the Android Keystore on Android, never plain preferences or a text file.

On iOS I put it in the Keychain, which the system encrypts and keeps apart from normal app files. On Android I encrypt it with a key held in the Android Keystore, so the key cannot simply be copied out. I never put tokens in UserDefaults or plain SharedPreferences, because those are easy to read on a rooted or jailbroken phone or from an unencrypted backup.
What makes an app freeze or show an "App not responding" message, and how do you prevent it?
Whether you understand the main thread and keep slow work off it.
Slow work blocks the main thread; move it to background threads and come back to the main thread only to update the screen.

The screen is drawn on the main thread, so a network call, a big file read or heavy JSON parsing there freezes everything. On Android, if input gets no response for about five seconds, the user sees an ANR dialog. I run that work with coroutines or Swift async/await off the main thread, then update the UI on the main thread. On Android I turn on StrictMode in debug builds to catch disk access on the main thread.
In Swift, a screen is closed but its memory is never freed. What is a likely cause, and how do you fix it?
Your grasp of memory management on iOS.
A retain cycle, often a closure capturing self strongly; break it with a weak or unowned reference and confirm with the memory tools.

Most often it is a retain cycle: the view controller holds a closure, and the closure captures self strongly, so neither can be released. I capture [weak self] in the closure, or unowned when I am sure self lives longer. To find it I use the Xcode Memory Graph Debugger or the Leaks tool in Instruments, then check that the screen is freed after I close it.
Your crash reports show only memory addresses or names like a.b.c instead of real function names. Why, and how do you fix it?
Whether you know symbolication and deobfuscation for release builds.
Release builds strip or shrink symbols; upload the dSYM files for iOS and the R8 mapping file for Android for every release.

Release builds do not carry readable names. On iOS the names live in dSYM files, so I make sure the build uploads them for every version to the crash tool. On Android, R8 shrinks and renames code, so I upload the mapping file from each release build. I also archive both per version, because a mapping from another build will translate the trace wrongly.
When do you ask the user for permission to send push notifications?
How you balance product goals against platform rules for permissions.
Ask in context, after showing the value, because a refusal is hard to undo on iOS and on recent Android versions.

Not at first launch. I ask when it makes sense, for example after the user orders and wants delivery updates, often with a short screen that explains why first. On iOS the system prompt appears only once; after a no, the user has to change it in Settings. Android 13 and later also needs a runtime permission, and after repeated refusals the system stops showing the prompt.
The backend team wants to rename a field in an API the app uses. What do you tell them?
Whether you know that old app versions stay in use for a long time.
Old versions keep calling the API for months; add the new field, keep the old one until usage drops, and have a minimum version check.

Users do not all update, so versions from many months ago will still call this API. I would ask them to add the new field alongside the old one, ship the app that reads the new one, and watch version adoption. They remove the old field only when the versions using it are a tiny share, or after we force an update through a minimum supported version check.
You need to change the local database schema in the next release. How do you ship it safely?
Whether you protect user data during local storage migrations.
Write migrations that work from every older schema, test real upgrades, and avoid destructive fallbacks that wipe data.

Users can jump from any old version straight to the new one, so I write a migration for each step and test upgrading from every schema we have shipped, using a database file saved from that version. I never rely on a destructive fallback that drops tables, because that silently deletes unsynced data. If the migration is risky, I add logging so a failure shows up in monitoring and does not crash at launch.
The release branch is cut tomorrow and your feature is only half done. What do you do?
How you work with release trains and feature flags.
Do not hold the train or rush; ship the code behind a flag turned off, or leave it for the next release.

I would not ask to delay the release or rush the last part. If the code is merged and stable, I keep it behind a feature flag that is off by default and make sure it is not reachable. Then I finish it and turn it on later, maybe for a small group first. If the half-done work could affect other screens, I keep it out of the branch and ship it in the next train.

motion-designer.heading: Motion designer and animator questions
qs: What is the difference between timing and spacing in animation?
Whether you know the two basic tools that decide how a move feels.
Timing is how many frames a move takes; spacing is how far the object travels between those frames, which creates the ease.

Timing is how long an action lasts, counted in frames. Spacing is how the positions are spread across those frames. Two moves can both last 12 frames, but if the drawings bunch up near the end, the object slows into place. Close spacing reads as slow, wide spacing as fast.
How do you use the graph editor to make a move feel natural?
How you shape motion beyond default keyframe easing.
Reads the speed or value curve, avoids flat linear moves, and adjusts handles so speed builds and settles smoothly without sudden spikes.

I set the key poses first, then open the speed curve. A linear move shows a flat line and looks mechanical, so I pull the handles to get a gentle rise and a long settle. I look for sharp peaks or kinks, because those show up as a jolt on screen. Then I play it back at full speed, not scrubbing.
When would you animate on twos instead of on ones?
Your understanding of frame rate as a style choice, not just a technical setting.
Knows twos means a new pose every second frame, and when that suits the style or saves time versus when smooth ones are needed.

On twos means a new pose every two frames, so 12 poses a second in a 24 fps project. It gives a hand-made, snappy feel and halves the drawing work for character pieces. I switch to ones for very fast actions, smooth camera moves or UI motion, where the stepping would look like stutter.
Walk me through how you build a basic walk cycle.
Whether you know character animation fundamentals, not only moving shapes.
Names the key poses, the rise and fall of the body, and opposite arm swing, and treats the cycle as two steps that loop cleanly.

I start with the contact pose, heel touching down, then the down pose where the body is lowest as weight lands. Next the passing pose as the back leg swings through, then the up pose where the body is highest. Then I mirror it for the other leg. Arms swing opposite to the legs, and I check the last frame flows into the first so the loop does not hitch.
An editor asks for your animated title with a transparent background. What do you send them?
Your knowledge of delivery formats and alpha channels.
Exports in a format that carries an alpha channel and avoids a standard H.264 MP4, which does not; confirms what their software accepts.

A standard H.264 MP4 cannot hold transparency, so I would not send that. I export an image sequence such as PNG with alpha, or a mastering video codec that supports an alpha channel. I ask the editor which one their system handles best, then send a short test clip before the full delivery.
You designed a screen transition for an app. How do you hand it off so it ships the way you made it?
How you turn a motion idea into specs a developer can build.
Gives exact duration, delay and easing values plus a reference video, and keeps UI motion short and purposeful.

I send a reference video and a spec for each element: duration in milliseconds, delay, and the easing written as curve values the developer can paste in. Elements entering usually decelerate into place, elements leaving speed up as they go. I keep it short so it never makes the user wait, then review the build on a real phone.
The director wants motion on every element and the piece now feels busy. What do you do?
Your judgement about hierarchy and where the viewer should look.
Directs attention to one thing at a time, staggers or holds secondary elements, and shows the director an alternative rather than just arguing.

The eye can follow only one main action at a time. I would pick the key message for each beat and let that move first, then let secondary elements settle with small, quiet moves or hold still. I would make a short version side by side with the original so the director can see the difference instead of hearing my opinion.
A client wants 40 versions of an ad in different sizes and languages. How do you set up the project?
How you build files that survive late changes and many outputs.
A master template with shared assets, central controls for text and color, clear naming, and a batch render plan.

I build one master animation with the logo, colors and text driven from a single control layer, so a change happens once. Each size gets its own layout that references the master. Text sits in boxes that adjust to longer languages, and I test the longest one first. Files follow a naming system so I can queue all 40 renders and check them fast.
Your final render will take nine hours and the deadline is tomorrow morning. What do you do?
How you solve a technical problem under time pressure.
Finds what is slow, pre-renders heavy parts, renders to an image sequence that survives crashes, and warns the client early if needed.

I render a few frames to see which section is slow, often blur, motion blur or a heavy 3D layer. I pre-render that part once and swap it in. I output an image sequence, so a crash means restarting from the last frame, not from zero. If it still will not fit, I tell the producer tonight, not at 8 a.m.
You delivered a vertical ad and the client says the call to action is hidden once it runs. What happened and how do you fix it?
How you own a delivery mistake and prevent it next time.
Recognises safe areas and platform interface overlays, fixes and redelivers fast, and adds a check to the process.

The platform puts its own buttons and caption over the edges of vertical video, and my text sat under them. I would own it, move key text and the logo inside the safe area and redeliver the same day. Since then I keep an overlay guide of the platform interface on every vertical project and check exports with it on.

network-engineer.heading: Network engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between a switch and a router?
Whether you know the basic layers a network engineer works with every day.
Switches forward frames by MAC address inside one network; routers forward packets by IP address between networks.

A switch works at layer 2. It learns which MAC address sits on which port and forwards frames inside one local network. A router works at layer 3. It looks at the destination IP address, checks its routing table and sends the packet to another network. A layer 3 switch can do both.
What does a VLAN do, and what is a trunk port?
Your grasp of how one physical switch is split into separate networks.
A VLAN is its own broadcast domain; a trunk carries several VLANs on one link using 802.1Q tags. Traffic between VLANs needs routing.

A VLAN splits a switch into separate broadcast domains, so voice, guests and staff stay apart. An access port belongs to one VLAN. A trunk carries many VLANs between switches by adding an 802.1Q tag with the VLAN number to each frame. To get from one VLAN to another, traffic has to go through a router or a layer 3 switch.
Walk me through what happens when a laptop pings a server on a different subnet.
Whether you understand ARP, the default gateway and how a router forwards a packet.
The host sees the target is off its subnet, ARPs for the gateway, and the router looks up the route, lowers the TTL and builds a new frame.

The laptop compares the server's IP with its own subnet mask and sees it is remote. It sends the packet to its default gateway, using ARP first if it does not know the gateway's MAC address. The router removes the frame, lowers the TTL, finds the route, ARPs for the next hop and sends a new frame. The reply comes back the same way.
What would you monitor on a network, and where does the data come from?
How you see problems before users report them.
Interface use, errors and discards, device health, logs and flow data, plus tests that measure what users feel.

I poll devices with SNMP for interface use, errors, discards, CPU and memory. I send syslog to one place so I can match events across devices. Flow records show who talks to whom when a link fills up. I also run small tests from a few sites, like ping and DNS checks, to see latency and loss the way users see them.
When would you use OSPF and when would you use BGP?
Your knowledge of interior and exterior routing and why each exists.
OSPF inside one organization for fast, automatic convergence; BGP between autonomous systems, such as to ISPs, where policy matters.

OSPF is a link-state protocol for inside one network. Routers share the topology and pick the lowest-cost path, and it converges fast. BGP connects separate autonomous systems, like our network and two internet providers. It is built for policy: I can choose which provider carries traffic in and out, not just the shortest path.
Someone plugs both ends of a cable into the same switch and the floor goes down. What happened, and how do you stop it next time?
Whether you understand switching loops and spanning tree.
A layer 2 loop causes a broadcast storm because frames have no TTL. Spanning tree, BPDU guard and storm control prevent it.

That made a loop. Ethernet frames have no TTL, so broadcasts circle forever and swamp every switch. Spanning tree should block the extra path, so I check it is running on every switch. On user ports I turn on BPDU guard, which shuts a port that hears another switch, and storm control to cap broadcast traffic.
Users say Wi-Fi keeps dropping in one big conference room during meetings. How do you work on it?
How you troubleshoot wireless problems with real data, not guesses.
Survey first: channel overlap, number of clients per access point, signal levels. On 2.4 GHz in the US only channels 1, 6 and 11 avoid overlap.

I go there during a meeting and check how many clients each access point has and what signal they see. Often nearby APs share a channel. On 2.4 GHz I only use 1, 6 and 11, which do not overlap in the US. I push clients to 5 GHz, use narrower channels in dense rooms, and add an AP if one is carrying sixty laptops.
A vendor asks for a firewall rule allowing any traffic from their network to our servers. What do you do?
Your judgement about least privilege and security requests.
You find out what they really need and allow only those sources, hosts and ports, with an owner, a ticket and an end date.

I would not open everything. I ask what the vendor needs to reach and why. Usually it is one or two servers on a few ports. I allow only their source addresses to those hosts and ports, log the rule, tie it to a ticket with an owner and set a review date. Since the firewall is stateful, replies come back without extra rules.
You change a config on a remote router and lose access to it. How do you recover, and how do you avoid it?
How you handle your own mistakes and make changes safely.
Calm recovery through out-of-band access, then habits: timed automatic rollback, saved backups, a tested plan and a change window.

First I tell the team and use out-of-band access, like a console server or a cellular modem, to undo the change. If there is none, I get local hands. Now I always save a backup and set a timed rollback that restores the old config unless I confirm the change worked. I test the plan in the lab and do it in a change window.
After a new site-to-site VPN goes up, small web pages load but large file transfers hang. What do you suspect?
Whether you can find a classic MTU problem that simple ping tests miss.
Tunnel overhead lowers the usable MTU; if ICMP is blocked, path MTU discovery fails. Test with don't-fragment pings and clamp TCP MSS.

I suspect MTU. The tunnel adds headers, so full 1,500-byte packets no longer fit. Normally the router sends an ICMP message saying the packet is too big, but if a firewall blocks it, big packets just vanish. I test with pings of growing size with don't-fragment set, then allow those ICMP messages and clamp TCP MSS on the tunnel.

nlp-engineer.heading: NLP and speech engineer questions
qs: What is word error rate, and how do you compute it?
Your grasp of the core metric for speech recognition.
Substitutions, deletions and insertions divided by the reference word count, found by alignment, and knowing the score can go above 100%.

I align the system output to the human reference transcript using edit distance. Then I count substitutions, deletions and insertions. WER is that sum divided by the number of words in the reference. Because insertions count, a very bad output can score above 100%. I also report it per speaker group, not only as one average.
Why do modern language models use subword tokens instead of whole words?
Whether you understand how text becomes model input.
Explains that subwords avoid unknown words and keep the vocabulary small, and names a real cost, such as uneven token counts across languages.

A whole-word vocabulary either grows huge or maps every new word to “unknown”. Byte-pair encoding starts from characters and keeps merging the most frequent adjacent pairs. Common words stay whole, and rare ones split into known pieces like “un”, “break”, “able”. The catch is that some languages get split into many more tokens, which costs context length and money.
What does self-attention do, and why did it replace recurrent networks for most language tasks?
Your understanding of the transformer, the base of current language and speech models.
Each token mixes in information from all others with learned weights; training runs in parallel; cost grows with the square of length.

Each token builds its representation as a weighted mix of all the other tokens. The weights come from how relevant each token is to it. An RNN passes information step by step. Attention links distant words directly, and training runs in parallel over the sequence. The price is that cost grows with the square of the sequence length, which hurts on long documents.
Your WER jumped after a model update, but listeners say the transcripts read better. What do you check first?
Whether you know how text normalization can distort speech metrics.
Looks at the actual errors and normalizes output and reference the same way before trusting the score: numbers, case, punctuation, contractions.

I would read the errors themselves. Often the new model writes “25” where the reference says “twenty five”, or it adds capitals and punctuation. Each of those counts as an error. I would run one normalizer on both sides, covering numbers, case, punctuation and “don't” versus “do not”, and then recompute. If the gap disappears, the model was fine and the scoring was not.
A team reports a higher BLEU score for their new translation model. What would you want to see before shipping it?
How you judge translation quality beyond one automatic number.
Knows BLEU counts n-gram overlap with reference translations and misses meaning. Asks for human review and targeted checks on names, numbers and negation.

BLEU measures how many word sequences match one or a few reference translations, with a penalty for short output. A correct paraphrase can score low, and a fluent error, like a dropped “not”, can score high. I would want human ratings on a sample, a learned metric alongside, and spot checks on names, numbers, dates and negation.
Your speech model does well on the test set but badly on recorded phone calls. What is likely going on?
Whether you can diagnose a mismatch between training audio and real audio.
Suspects narrowband telephone audio against wideband training data. Measures on real calls, then adapts with matched or simulated phone audio.

First I check the audio. Phone calls are often sampled at 8 kHz and lose most sound above about 3.4 kHz, while many models train on 16 kHz audio. Upsampling does not bring that back. I would measure WER on a labeled sample of real calls. Then I would fine-tune on call audio, or on training audio downsampled to phone quality with added noise and codec effects.
How do you set the detection threshold for a wake word on a smart speaker?
How you balance two kinds of errors in a voice product.
Frames it as false accepts against false rejects, measured on long real-world audio and varied voices, with the product team choosing the point.

I plot false rejects, when a user says the word and nothing happens, against false accepts per hour of background audio like TV and conversation. Then I pick a point with the product team. Waking at random erodes trust and raises privacy worries. Missing the word annoys people. I test across voices, accents and distances, not only clean recordings.
Your text classifier scored 97% offline and 80% in production. You find many near-duplicate texts in the data. What happened?
Whether you can spot data leakage in a language dataset.
Sees duplicates crossing the train-test split. Deduplicates, splits by source so related texts stay together, and re-measures before blaming drift.

Copies or templated variants of the same message were probably in both training and test, so the test rewarded memory, not generalization. I would deduplicate with a similarity check on normalized text. Then I would split by source, for example by customer or by thread, so related texts stay on one side. The honest offline number becomes the baseline.
A support chatbot built on document retrieval gives confident answers that are not in your documents. How do you fix it?
How you debug a retrieval-based chat system step by step.
Separates retrieval failure from generation failure, measures each on real questions, and adds grounding, citations and a way to say “I don't know”.

I split the problem. On a set of real questions, I check whether the right passage was retrieved at all. If not, I fix chunking or the search, maybe adding keyword search. If it was retrieved and the model still invented things, I tell it to answer only from the passages, cite them, and say it doesn't know otherwise. I track the rate on a fixed test set.
The product team wants to keep every voice transcript to improve the model. What do you raise?
Your judgement on privacy when working with speech and text data.
Raises consent, collecting only what is needed, redaction of personal data, retention limits and access control, with legal and privacy staff involved early.

Transcripts hold names, addresses, card numbers and health details. I would ask what users agreed to, and bring in legal and privacy early, since recording consent rules differ by state. Then I would redact sensitive details before storage, keep only the sample we need, set a deletion date and limit access. Redaction models miss things, so I would audit them too.

nurse-practitioner.heading: Nurse practitioner questions
qs: How does practice authority for nurse practitioners differ from state to state?
Whether you know the legal framework you work in.
Names full, reduced and restricted practice, and checks the state board's rules instead of guessing.

States fall into three broad groups. With full practice, I can evaluate, diagnose and prescribe on my own license. Reduced practice requires a collaborative agreement with a physician for at least one area, often prescribing. Restricted practice requires supervision. Before I work in a state I read its board of nursing rules, because details like controlled substance prescribing differ.
On a video visit, what makes you stop and send the patient to be seen in person?
How you judge the limits of telehealth.
Concrete red flags, plus the cases where a needed exam or test cannot be done on camera.

Red flags mean the ER or 911 right away: chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of stroke, a sudden worst-ever headache. Short of an emergency, I convert when I need to touch, listen or test: an ear I must look into, lungs I need to hear, a belly that could be surgical. I tell the patient where to go and how soon, and I document why.
A patient has had sinus congestion for four days and asks for an antibiotic. What do you do?
Your antibiotic stewardship and how you say no without losing the patient.
Knows the signs that point to bacterial sinusitis, offers real symptom relief, and sets a clear point to call back.

At four days most sinus infections are viral, so an antibiotic adds side effects without helping. I look for signs of bacteria: symptoms past ten days without improvement, a severe start with high fever and thick discharge, or getting better then worse. If none fit, I suggest saline rinses, a nasal steroid and pain relief, and say when to call back.
A patient's blood pressure is high at one office visit. How do you confirm hypertension?
Whether you diagnose from good measurements, not from a single reading.
Correct measuring technique, repeat readings, and confirmation outside the office before labeling the patient.

One reading is not a diagnosis. I recheck after five minutes seated, back supported, feet flat, arm at heart level, with the right cuff size. If it stays high and nothing is urgent, I confirm with readings outside the office, home monitoring or an ambulatory monitor, to rule out white coat hypertension. Then we talk about treatment.
Your video patient mentions they are on vacation in another state. Does that change anything?
Whether you know telehealth licensing follows the patient's location.
Knows the license that counts is generally for the state where the patient is, and handles it without leaving them stranded.

Yes. Licensure is generally based on where the patient is during the visit, not where I am. If I am not licensed there, I should not diagnose or prescribe. I confirm location at the start of every visit. If the problem is urgent I direct them to local care or 911; otherwise we reschedule for when they are home or with a clinician licensed in that state.
Before you prescribe a controlled substance, what do you check?
Your safe prescribing habits for drugs that can be misused.
Checks the state prescription monitoring program, registrations, risk factors and interactions, and documents the reason.

I check the state prescription drug monitoring program for other prescribers, early fills, or opioids overlapping with benzodiazepines; many states require this. I review substance use history, other sedating drugs and sleep apnea. I confirm my DEA and any state registration cover that schedule, prescribe the smallest amount that works, and set a follow-up.
A 79-year-old comes in on twelve medications and has had two falls. Walk me through your review.
How you handle polypharmacy and deprescribing in older adults.
A full medication review, a check against the Beers Criteria, focus on fall-risk drugs, and changes made one at a time.

I ask them to bring every bottle, including over-the-counter pills and supplements. I check each drug for a current reason and against the Beers Criteria, looking hard at sedatives, anticholinergics like diphenhydramine, and blood pressure drugs that cause dizziness. I check orthostatic vitals, stop or taper one drug at a time, and follow up within weeks.
A patient on warfarin needs an antibiotic for a urinary tract infection. What are you thinking about?
Whether you catch a serious drug interaction before it happens.
Knows some antibiotics, like trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, can raise the INR, chooses carefully and plans an INR check.

Warfarin interacts with many antibiotics, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is a big one: it can raise the INR fast and cause bleeding. I check kidney function, allergies and any culture, and pick an option with less interaction when I can. Either way I arrange an INR check within a few days, tell whoever manages the warfarin, and teach the patient the bleeding signs.
A patient with two weeks of low back pain asks for an MRI and something strong for the pain. How do you respond?
How you follow the evidence when a patient wants something else.
Screens for red flags, explains why early imaging and opioids rarely help, and offers a plan the patient can accept.

First I screen for red flags: numbness in the groin, bladder or bowel changes, fever, cancer history, worsening weakness. Without them, an early MRI rarely changes care and often shows findings that worry people for no reason. Most back pain improves within weeks, so I suggest heat, staying active, an anti-inflammatory if safe, and physical therapy, and book a recheck.
A lab result you ordered comes back critical at 6 p.m., and the patient does not answer the phone. What do you do?
Whether you own the results you order until the loop is closed.
Acts the same evening, tries every contact route, escalates under clinic policy, and documents each attempt.

A result I ordered is mine until it is handled. I call again, try the alternate number and emergency contact, and send a portal message. If the value is dangerous, like a very high potassium, and I still cannot reach them, I follow our policy, which can mean asking police for a welfare check. I document every attempt with the time and tell the on-call clinician.

nursing.heading: Nursing questions
qs: Walk me through the nursing process.
Whether you know the framework behind every care plan.
All five steps in order, and the point that evaluation feeds back into a new assessment.

It is assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation and evaluation. I gather data, name the nursing problem, like risk for falls, set a goal the patient can reach, carry out the interventions, then check whether the goal was met. If it was not, I reassess and change the plan. It is a loop, not a checklist.
How do you check that a patient really understood what you taught?
How you make patient education stick.
Teach-back: the patient explains or shows it in their own words, and you reteach the gaps instead of asking 'Any questions?'.

I use teach-back. After explaining a new inhaler, I say, 'I want to be sure I explained it well. Can you show me how you will use it at home?' If a step is missing, I teach that part again in simpler words and ask once more. Asking 'Do you understand?' almost always gets a yes, so it tells me nothing.
In a video visit you cannot touch the patient. How do you assess them?
Whether you can assess by telehealth and know its limits.
Using what you can see and hear, home devices and the patient's own hands, with clear triggers for in-person or emergency care.

I watch their breathing, color, alertness and whether they can finish a sentence. I ask them to read their home blood pressure cuff or pulse oximeter on camera, and to press on their shin so I can see any swelling. If I see red flags, like chest pain or struggling to breathe, I have them call 911 and stay on the line until help arrives.
A patient refuses a medication you are due to give. What do you do?
How you balance a patient's right to refuse with their safety.
Respect the refusal, find out why, explain the risk, inform the provider and document. Never hide or force a medication.

First I ask why. Often it is a side effect, a cost worry, or not knowing what the pill is for. I explain what it does and what may happen if they skip it, without pressure. If they still say no, that is their right. I do not give it, I let the provider know, and I chart the refusal, the reason and what I taught. If I doubt they can make decisions, I raise that too.
What can you delegate to a nursing assistant, and what must you keep?
Your grasp of delegation and of the RN's responsibility for it.
Routine tasks on stable patients can go; assessment, care planning and judgment stay with the RN, who stays accountable. Exact rules vary by state.

I can delegate routine tasks with predictable results, like vital signs on a stable patient, bathing or helping someone walk, if that assistant is trained for it. I keep assessment, care planning, teaching and anything needing judgment. I give clear directions, say what to report back right away, and follow up, because I am still accountable for the outcome.
Your patient's blood pressure is dropping and you call the provider. What do you say?
Whether you can report a concern clearly and get action.
A structured report such as SBAR that ends with a specific request, plus a read-back of any new order.

I use SBAR. Situation: Mr. Lee in room 12 has a pressure of 86 over 50, down from 120 over 70 four hours ago. Background: day two after bowel surgery. Assessment: heart rate 112, he is pale and his urine output has dropped; I am worried about bleeding or fluid loss. Recommendation: please come see him; do you want labs and fluids? I read back any order.
A confused patient at high fall risk keeps trying to get up alone. What do you do?
How you prevent falls without jumping to restraints.
Finding the reason, such as toileting, pain or delirium, using rounding, a low bed and alarms, and treating restraints as a last resort with an order.

I look for why. Often they need the bathroom, are in pain or are newly confused, so I take them to the toilet on a schedule and report the confusion. I keep the bed low and locked, the call light in reach, nonslip socks on and the bed alarm set. I may move them closer to the station or ask for a sitter. Restraints need an order and are a last resort.
What early signs make you think of sepsis?
Whether you recognize sepsis before the patient crashes.
Suspected infection plus changes such as fast breathing, high heart rate, new confusion, low blood pressure or low urine output, and acting fast.

Any patient with a known or possible infection who starts breathing faster, has a racing heart, a fever or a low temperature, new confusion, falling blood pressure or less urine. New confusion in an older patient is easy to miss. I do not wait for every sign: I follow our sepsis screening protocol and call the provider or rapid response team right away, because delay costs lives.
After you give an opioid for pain, what do you watch for, and when?
Whether you know how to monitor opioids safely.
Reassessing pain and sedation when the drug peaks, knowing that rising sleepiness usually comes before slowed breathing.

I reassess pain and sedation when the drug should peak, sooner for IV than by mouth, at the times our policy sets. Rising sleepiness usually comes before slowed breathing, so I check how easily they wake and stay awake, plus breathing rate, depth and oxygen. If they drift off mid-sentence, I hold further doses, stay with them and call the provider.
You get an order for a dose that looks far too high. What do you do?
Whether you will question an order instead of just following it.
Hold the dose, verify with references and the pharmacist, clarify with the prescriber, and go up the chain of command if it is not resolved.

I hold it. I check it against a drug reference, the patient's weight and kidney function, and I ask the pharmacist. Then I call the prescriber, say exactly what worries me and ask them to confirm or change it. If it still looks unsafe, I go to my charge nurse and up the chain of command. I am accountable for what I give, not just for following orders.

observability-engineer.heading: Observability engineer questions
qs: What are logs, metrics and traces, and when would you reach for each?
Whether you know the three main signals and what each one is good at.
Metrics for trends and alerts, logs for the detail of single events, traces for following one request across services.

Metrics are numbers over time. They are cheap to store and good for dashboards and alerts. Logs record single events with the detail of what happened. Traces follow one request through every service it touches and show where the time went. I alert on metrics, use traces to find the slow hop, then read the logs to see why.
What are the RED and USE methods, and where does each fit?
Whether you have a system for choosing what to measure.
RED for services that answer requests, USE for resources like CPU, disks and pools; both keep dashboards focused.

RED is rate, errors and duration: how many requests come in, how many fail, how long they take. I use it for every service that answers requests. USE is utilization, saturation and errors, for resources such as CPU, memory, disks and connection pools. A new service gets RED panels on day one, and its main resources get USE panels.
A developer writes plain text log lines like 'checkout failed for user'. What would you ask them to change?
Whether you know what makes logs searchable and useful across services.
Structured fields, a trace or request ID on every line, sensible levels, and no personal data or secrets.

I would ask for structured logs, one JSON object per line, with fields like order ID, error code and duration, so we can filter and count. Every line should carry the trace ID passed in from the caller, so we can join it with other services. And no card numbers, passwords or tokens in any message, ever.
Why is average latency a poor number to alert on, and what do you use instead?
Your grasp of latency distributions and percentiles.
Averages hide the slow tail; use percentiles built from histograms, and know that percentiles cannot simply be averaged.

An average can look fine while one request in a hundred takes eight seconds. I watch p50, p95 and p99, where p99 is the time 99% of requests beat. I record latency as histograms, because bucket counts can be added up across servers and the percentile computed from the total. Averaging each server's p99 gives a number that means nothing.
A developer wants to add customer ID as a label on a request metric. What do you say?
Whether you understand cardinality and what it costs a metrics system.
Each unique label value creates a new time series; unbounded IDs belong in logs or traces, not metric labels.

Each distinct combination of label values is its own time series. With half a million customers, that one label could add half a million series per endpoint, slow every query and raise the bill. I would keep labels bounded, like endpoint, status class and region, and put the customer ID on the trace and in the logs, where we can still search by it.
How would you set an SLO for a checkout service, and what does the error budget do?
Whether you can turn the user experience into a target the team can act on.
A measure taken close to the user, a target below 100% agreed with the business, and a budget that guides release pace.

First the SLI, the measure of good service: the share of checkout requests that succeed within, say, 800 milliseconds, measured at the load balancer. Then a target from past data, maybe 99.9% over 30 days. The 0.1% left over is the error budget, about 43 minutes if it were all downtime. If we burn it early, we slow releases and fix reliability first.
The on-call team gets about 200 pages a week and ignores most of them. What do you do?
How you handle alert fatigue without hiding real problems.
Review each alert's value, page only on user-facing symptoms, turn the rest into tickets or delete them, and track page volume.

I pull a month of pages and mark each one: did someone act, and did users feel it? Pages nobody acted on get deleted or become tickets. Cause alerts like high CPU give way to symptom alerts tied to the SLO, using burn rate, how fast we spend the error budget: a fast burn pages, a slow burn opens a ticket. Then I report pages per week so it does not creep back.
Every dashboard is green, but customers say the app is failing. How can that happen, and how do you close the gap?
Whether you can find blind spots in what is being measured.
Seeing that monitoring may sit behind the point of failure, and adding checks from the user's side: edge, synthetic and client data.

Usually we measure only what reached our servers. If DNS, a certificate, the content delivery network or a mobile release breaks, failed requests never show up in our metrics. Once a bad config cut off one region and our error rate went down. I add synthetic checks from outside, edge and client-side error rates, and an alert when traffic drops below normal.
When would you choose head-based sampling for traces, and when tail-based?
Your knowledge of trace sampling and its trade-offs.
Head sampling is cheap but blind to the outcome; tail sampling keeps errors and slow traces but must hold whole traces before deciding.

Head sampling decides at the start of a request, say keep 5%, and passes that choice downstream. It is simple and cheap, but it drops most errors because it cannot know the outcome yet. Tail sampling waits until the trace is done, so I can keep every error and every slow request. The cost: collectors must hold whole traces in memory, and every span of a trace must reach the same one.
Your monitoring system itself goes down at 3 a.m. How would anyone find out?
Whether you plan for the failure of the observability stack itself.
Monitoring from outside the stack, such as an always-firing heartbeat alert that pages someone when it stops arriving.

If the alerting system is down, it cannot page about itself. I set up a heartbeat: an alert that always fires and goes to an outside service, which pages us if it stops hearing it for a few minutes. I also watch collection failures and ingestion lag, and run the monitoring in a different failure domain from the systems it watches.

office-manager.heading: Office manager questions
qs: How do you decide when to reorder office supplies and how much to order?
Whether you run supplies with a system instead of reacting when something runs out.
A reorder point based on actual use and delivery time, a simple tracking method, and fewer rush orders.

I track how fast we use each core item, like paper, toner and coffee, and how long delivery takes. I set a reorder point that covers that lead time plus a small buffer. I check stock on a fixed day each week and order in one batch. Rush orders get noted so I can adjust the levels.
What does a good visitor check-in process look like?
How you balance a warm welcome with knowing who is in the building.
Greeting, sign-in, host notified, a visitor badge, escort where needed, sign-out, and a log that is kept private.

The visitor is greeted, signs in with name, company and host, and gets a dated badge. I notify the host, who comes to collect them. Visitors are not left to wander. At sign-out the badge comes back. The log is not left open for the next guest to read, and it doubles as our headcount if we ever have to evacuate.
Walk me through how you prepare for a new hire's first day.
Your planning across IT, HR and the space so a new person feels expected.
Work starts days ahead: desk, equipment and accounts arranged with IT, badge and keys ready, and a planned first morning.

About a week out I confirm the start date with HR and the manager. I ask IT for the laptop and accounts, and I set up the desk, chair and badge. On day one I meet them at the door, give a short tour, show the restrooms, kitchen and exits, and hand them to their manager with a lunch plan, so nobody is sitting alone waiting for a password.
An employee's last day is today. What is on your offboarding checklist?
Whether you close access and recover company property without fuss.
Badge and building access shut off on time, keys and equipment returned, IT told in advance, and the person treated with respect.

I agree the timing with HR so access is cut at the right moment, not weeks later. I collect the badge, keys, parking pass, laptop and any company card, and I check them against what was issued. IT turns off accounts and I ask building management to deactivate the fob. I remove the person from desk charts and lists, and I thank them on the way out.
The heat stops working on a cold Monday morning. What do you do?
How you handle a facilities problem: who to call, what to tell staff, and what to do meanwhile.
A ticket with building management or the vendor right away, a clear note to staff with the next update time, and a sensible plan B.

I call building management and put in a written ticket, and I ask for an arrival time. Then I message staff: the heat is out, it has been reported, the next update is at ten. I check with leadership about letting people work from home. I do not bring in space heaters unless building rules allow them, since they can be a fire risk. I log the outage for the landlord.
How would you plan a holiday party for 60 people on a fixed budget?
Your event planning: budget, headcount, logistics and inclusion.
Budget split by line with a reserve, an RSVP count, dietary and accessibility needs, a clear alcohol plan, and a time that works for most staff.

I start from the budget and keep about ten percent in reserve. I send an RSVP with a dietary question and pick a date and time that works for parents and remote staff too. Food gets the biggest share. If there is alcohol, I set limits and offer good non-alcoholic choices. I book the venue early, check access for anyone who needs it, and track every cost in one sheet.
Two teams have booked the big conference room for client meetings at the same time. How do you sort it out?
Your judgement when two fair claims collide, and how you prevent a repeat.
Facts first, a quick fair call or an alternative space, both teams told directly, and a fix to the booking system.

I check the booking system to see who booked first and whether it was a glitch. Then I call both organizers and look for a way out: another room, a nearby meeting space, or shifting one meeting by an hour. If neither can move, the first booking stands and I help the other team find a space. Afterwards I look at why the system allowed it.
You discover the copier lease auto-renewed for three more years at a higher rate. What do you do?
How you handle a contract mistake and how you stop it happening again.
Read the contract, talk to the vendor about options, tell your manager honestly, and set up a contract calendar with notice dates.

First I read the lease for the renewal terms and any exit or downgrade clause. I tell my manager what happened and what it costs. Then I call the vendor: we are a steady customer, and I ask for the old rate, a smaller machine or a shorter term. Afterwards I build a contract list with every renewal and notice date and set reminders well ahead of each one.
How do you get an office ready for an emergency evacuation?
Whether you treat emergency preparedness as a plan people have practiced, not a sign on the wall.
Posted routes and an assembly point, floor wardens with backups, a way to account for everyone including visitors, help planned for those who need it, and drills.

I work from the building's emergency plan and make sure exits and the assembly point are posted and known. Each area gets a floor warden and a backup. At the meeting point we account for staff from the in-office list and visitors from the sign-in log. I ask privately who would need help on stairs and plan that with them. We practice with drills, use the stairs, never the elevators, and fix what was slow.
Walk me through how you would plan moving a 60-person office to a new floor.
Your ability to run a large project with many vendors, a hard date and minimal downtime.
A timeline worked back from the move date, early IT and vendor booking, a seating plan, labeled crates, a weekend move, and a team on hand on day one.

I start from the move date and work back. I book movers and IT early, since network and phones take the longest. I build a seating plan with managers and give each person a numbered label and crates. Most packing happens Thursday, the move over the weekend, and IT tests desks on Sunday. Monday morning I walk the floor with IT to fix problems, and a week later I collect a punch list.

operations-analyst.heading: Operations analyst and associate questions
qs: Walk me through how you map a process you have never seen before.
How you learn a process as it really runs, not as it is written.
Observing and talking to the people who do the work, noting steps, triggers, waits and handoffs, then checking the map with the team.

I start by walking it with the people who do it, not from the written procedure. I note each step, who does it, what triggers it, and how long it waits between steps. I draw it as a simple swimlane, one lane per role, then check it with the team. The handoffs between lanes are usually where the delays and errors are.
What does Little's Law tell you about a work queue?
Whether you can link backlog, throughput and waiting time with a simple rule.
Average work in progress equals throughput times average time in the system, applied to averages in a fairly stable process.

On average, the work in the system equals throughput times the time each item spends there. If we have 200 open cases and close 50 a day, a case waits about four days. So to cut wait time I either close more per day or let fewer cases pile up. It holds for averages in a fairly stable system, not for one bad day.
Our average ticket resolution time is two days, yet customers keep complaining about slow service. What would you look at?
Whether you look past an average to the spread and the segments behind it.
Median and high percentiles, split by type or channel, to find the slice that waits far longer than the average shows.

An average hides the tail. I would look at the median and the 90th percentile, and split by ticket type and channel. Often most tickets close the same day while a slice waits a week, maybe one category that needs a second team. Fixing that slice changes what customers feel more than shaving the average.
A weekly report shows volume dropped 30% overnight. What do you do before telling anyone?
Your habit of checking the data before raising an alarm.
Checking the pipeline, filters, field changes and source outages, then spot-checking raw data, and bringing facts either way.

I treat it as a data problem until proven otherwise. I check whether the job ran fully, whether a filter or field name changed, and whether the source system had an outage. Then I spot-check a few days against the raw system. If the drop is real, I bring the numbers and what I checked, so the conversation starts from facts.
The same error keeps coming back in a process. How do you find the root cause?
How you move from symptoms to a cause you can fix.
Counting errors to see where they cluster, asking why with the people involved, and fixing the process rather than blaming people.

First I count: which error types, which steps, which shifts. A Pareto chart usually shows a few causes making most of the errors. Then I ask why it happens, several times, with the people on that step. Once, wrong addresses traced back to a form field that allowed free text. We changed the field, not the people, and errors fell by more than half.
How do you decide whether a manual task is worth automating?
Your judgement on the cost and benefit of automation.
Frequency, time and error cost weighed against build and upkeep, plus a stable process; sometimes removing the step is better.

I estimate how often the task runs, minutes each time, and the cost of an error, then compare that with build time and upkeep. A 10-minute daily task is about 40 hours a year. I also check the process is stable; automating a step that changes every month just moves the work. And sometimes the better fix is removing the step.
A metric got worse this week and your manager wants an explanation. How do you tell a real change from normal variation?
Whether you can separate a signal from noise before anyone reacts.
Looking at the metric over many periods, using control limits or a clear baseline, and saying plainly when a dip is just noise.

I look at the metric over time, not two points. With 20 or more past periods I can draw a control chart: an average line and limits about three standard deviations out. A point outside the limits, or a long run on one side of the average, says something changed. A single dip inside the limits is usually noise, and I say that before anyone reacts.
A manager wants a new KPI that you think will push people toward the wrong behavior. What do you do?
How you push back on a metric with evidence and respect.
Naming the likely side effect with an example, proposing a balancing measure, and testing it, while respecting the final decision.

I would say what behavior I expect it to drive, with an example. Calls per hour alone rewards short calls, so customers call back and total work goes up. I would suggest pairing it with a balancing measure, such as repeat contacts within seven days, and testing both for a month. If the manager still wants it, I track it and report the side effect honestly.
An automation you built failed silently for a week before anyone noticed. How do you handle it?
How you own a mistake, repair the damage and stop it happening again.
Telling people quickly, fixing the backlog and checking it, then adding monitoring so a failure cannot go unnoticed again.

I tell my manager and the affected team right away, with what failed and since when. Then I fix the backlog: in one case a nightly import had stopped, so I reran the missed days and checked totals against the source. After that I added an alert that emails me when a run fails or loads zero rows. The silent failure was the real bug, not the import.

operations-manager.heading: Operations manager questions
qs: What is the difference between a leading and a lagging indicator in operations?
Whether you manage with numbers that warn you early, not only ones that report the past.
A clear definition with a real example of each, and why you need both.

A lagging indicator tells me what already happened, like on-time delivery last month or cost per order. A leading indicator moves first, like the backlog at noon, open positions or machine downtime this week. I watch the leading ones daily so I can act before the lagging number goes bad, and I use the lagging ones to confirm the result.
How do you find the bottleneck in a process, and why does it matter?
Your grasp of how flow and capacity work.
The slowest step sets the output of the whole process; time saved at other steps does not add output.

I walk the process and look where work piles up and where people downstream sit waiting. Then I check each step's capacity against demand. The slowest step sets the output of the whole process, so an hour saved there is an hour for the whole operation. An hour saved elsewhere often just makes a bigger pile in front of the bottleneck.
The same shipping error keeps coming back every few weeks. Walk me through how you get to the root cause.
How you solve a problem for good instead of patching it.
Facts first, asking why until you reach a cause in the process, a fix that is tried out, and a check that it held.

I pull the recent cases and look for what they share: shift, product, station, person. Then I keep asking why until I reach something in the process, not just “someone was careless.” Say two items have look-alike labels. I change the label or the bin layout, try it on one shift, and track the error rate for a month to make sure it stays down.
Two suppliers quote the same part, and one is 6% cheaper. How do you decide?
Whether you look at total cost, not just the price on the quote.
Total cost of ownership: quality, lead time, reliability, freight, payment terms and the cost of switching.

I compare total cost, not unit price. I look at defect rates, on-time history, lead time, minimum order size, freight, payment terms and what it costs to approve a new supplier. If the cheaper one ships late twice a year and we pay for rush freight and overtime, the 6% is gone. I would also ask for references and start with a trial order.
Cost per unit rose 8% last month. Walk me through how you find out why.
How you break a cost number down before you act on it.
Separating volume from rates, usage and product mix, and checking fixed costs spread over fewer units, before blaming anyone.

First I check volume. If we made fewer units, fixed costs like rent and salaried staff spread over less, and unit cost rises even if nobody spent more. Then I split the rest into rates and usage: did labor hours, overtime, scrap or material prices go up? I also check whether the product mix shifted. Only then do I sit down with the team on a fix.
One key component comes from a single supplier. What do you do about that?
How you weigh supply risk against cost and effort.
Sizing the exposure first, then choosing a fitting response: a second source, safety stock, or contract terms and closer watching.

I first ask how long we could run if they stopped shipping, and how long it would take to approve someone else. If the answer is days against months, that is a real exposure. Options are a second source, extra safety stock, or a contract with notice terms. I pick based on cost and how critical the part is, and I keep an eye on the supplier's health.
Our on-time shipping rate is 98%, but customers say their orders arrive late. How do you explain that?
Whether you question a metric when it does not match what customers experience.
Checking what the number really measures, finding the gap, and adding a measure that matches what the customer sees.

Most likely we measure the wrong thing. On-time shipping may count when the box leaves our dock against our own date, not when it reaches the customer against the date we promised. Carrier delays, split shipments or promise dates changed by staff would all hide there. I would trace a sample of orders end to end, then add a delivered-on-time measure.
One supervisor hits every target, but his team's turnover is twice the site average. What do you do?
How you judge a manager on how results are reached, not only on the results.
Gathering facts first, a direct private talk with clear expectations, and treating turnover as part of performance.

Turnover is a cost, so his numbers are not as good as they look. I would read exit interview notes, talk to a few people on his team, and look at overtime and absences. Then I meet him alone, share what I found, and make retention one of his goals with a date to review it. If what I hear points to mistreatment, I bring in HR right away.
You rolled out a new process, and three months later the teams have slipped back to the old way. How do you handle it?
Whether you know how to make a change stick.
Finding out why people went back before enforcing anything, then written standard steps, an owner and regular checks.

First I ask why. Often the new way is slower in some case we did not plan for, or new hires were trained by someone who never used it. I fix that problem, write the steps as a short standard with photos, and give each area an owner. Then I check it on the floor every week for a while, and less often once it holds.
You are asked to cut operating costs by 10% without hurting service. Where do you start?
Your judgement on cutting costs without damaging the operation.
A map of where the money goes, waste and outside spend before people, and service measures watched during the cuts.

I start with a breakdown of where the money goes, because the biggest lines decide the plan. I look at waste first: overtime caused by poor scheduling, rework, rush freight, unused contracts and supplier prices nobody has rebid in years. Cutting staff is the last lever. I set the service numbers I will not let drop and review them weekly while we cut.

optics.heading: Optics and photonics questions
qs: What is the difference between f-number and numerical aperture?
Whether you know the two basic ways to describe how much light an optical system collects.
F-number as focal length over entrance pupil diameter, NA as index times the sine of the cone half-angle, and the rough link between them.

F-number is focal length divided by entrance pupil diameter, so it is common for camera lenses. Numerical aperture is the refractive index times the sine of the half-angle of the light cone, common for microscopes and fibers. For a lens focusing light from far away, F-number is roughly one over two times NA, so f/2 is about NA 0.25.
Name the main monochromatic aberrations. How would you reduce spherical aberration in a single lens?
Your grasp of the aberrations every lens design starts from.
The five Seidel aberrations named correctly, and real fixes: lens bending, splitting power, higher-index glass, an asphere or a smaller aperture.

Spherical aberration, coma, astigmatism, field curvature and distortion. For a single lens I would first bend it to the best shape, which for a collimated input is close to plano-convex with the curved side facing the incoming beam. If that is not enough, I would split the power over two lenses, use higher-index glass, or make one surface aspheric.
What does an MTF curve tell you, and how would you measure it on a camera module?
Whether you can connect image sharpness to a number you can test.
Contrast transfer versus spatial frequency, read at frequencies tied to the sensor, at center and corners, plus a real method such as slanted-edge.

MTF shows how much of an object's contrast survives the system at each spatial frequency, usually in line pairs per millimeter. I read it at frequencies tied to the pixel pitch, such as half the Nyquist frequency, at the center and the corners. On a camera module I would use a slanted-edge target, a tilted dark-to-light edge that gives MTF from a single image.
An interferometer report gives a peak-to-valley and an RMS wavefront error. Which do you trust more, and what counts as diffraction-limited?
Your reading of interferometer results and the usual pass criteria.
PV is driven by one bad spot or noise; RMS describes the whole aperture. The Maréchal criterion: about 1/14 wave RMS, Strehl ratio near 0.8.

Peak-to-valley is just the two extreme points, so one dust spot or a noisy pixel can inflate it. RMS averages over the whole aperture and predicts image quality better. A common rule is the Maréchal criterion: about one-fourteenth of a wave RMS, a Strehl ratio near 0.8, is called diffraction-limited. I still check the spec, since some customers write PV limits.
Walk me through aligning a laser beam down a rail using two steering mirrors.
Whether you have actually aligned a beam by hand on a bench.
Two irises at beam height; upstream mirror centers the beam on the near iris, downstream mirror on the far iris; repeat until both stay centered, then lock.

I set two irises at the same height, one near and one far along the rail, and work at low power. I adjust the upstream mirror to center the beam on the near iris, then the second mirror to center it on the far iris. Each change disturbs the other, so I repeat until both stay centered. Then I lock the mounts and check again, since tightening can shift the beam.
You need a smaller focused spot from a laser. What can you change?
Your working knowledge of how Gaussian beams focus.
Spot size grows with wavelength, focal length and M squared, and shrinks with a larger input beam; a smaller spot also means a shorter depth of focus.

The focused spot is roughly proportional to wavelength times focal length divided by the input beam size, times the beam quality factor, M squared. So I can expand the beam before the lens, use a shorter focal length, or use a shorter wavelength or a cleaner beam. A smaller spot also gives a shorter depth of focus, and the lens must stay free of aberration at the larger aperture.
The tolerance analysis says one lens needs a centering tolerance the shop says will triple its cost. What do you do?
Your judgement in trading performance against cost and manufacturability.
Confirm the result with compensators and realistic tolerances, look at desensitizing the design or active alignment, and bring options with cost and yield to the team.

First I check the number is real: I rerun the Monte Carlo with focus as a compensator and the shop's standard tolerances to see the yield. If yield is too low, I look at desensitizing the design, for example spreading the power so that surface matters less, or centering that lens actively at assembly. Then I bring each option's yield and cost to the team.
A lens designed and tested in the lab will fly on a satellite. What could move its focus in orbit, and how do you plan for it?
Whether you design for the environment the optics will really work in.
Vacuum removes the air index and shifts focus; temperature changes glass index and housing length. Design for vacuum, athermalize, and verify in thermal vacuum testing.

Two things. In vacuum the index around the lens drops from about 1.0003 to exactly 1, which shifts focus, so I design for vacuum and set focus on the ground with a calculated offset. Temperature changes both the glass index and the housing length, so I pick glass and housing materials whose effects cancel, and I confirm it in a thermal vacuum test before launch.

paralegal.heading: Paralegal and legal operations questions
qs: What tasks must a paralegal leave to the attorney?
Whether you know where your work ends and the practice of law begins.
No legal advice, no setting fees, no taking on clients, nothing signed or argued as a lawyer. Your work is done under attorney supervision.

I don't give legal advice, quote fees, accept a client or appear for one in court. I can draft, research and talk to clients about facts and scheduling, but an attorney reviews my work and signs what goes out. If a client asks me 'should I sign this?', I say I'll get the attorney to answer.
What personal information do you redact before filing a document in federal court?
Your knowledge of the privacy rules for public court filings.
The Rule 5.2 list: last four digits of Social Security, taxpayer ID and account numbers, birth year only, minors' initials. Exhibits are checked too.

Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 5.2, I leave only the last four digits of Social Security, taxpayer ID and financial account numbers, the birth year, and a minor's initials. I check the exhibits too, and I use true redaction so the text is removed from the file, not just covered by a black box.
A signed vendor contract lands on your desk. What do you record in the contract system?
How you turn a signed contract into dates and duties someone will act on.
Parties, dates, renewal and notice terms, termination rights and key obligations, with reminders set well before any notice deadline.

I save the fully signed copy and log the parties, effective date, term, and whether it renews on its own. The notice period matters most: if we must give 60 days' notice to cancel, I set a reminder at 90 days for the business owner. I also note payment terms, termination rights, governing law, and any assignment or change-of-control clause.
How do you count a court deadline that is stated in days?
Whether you count court deadlines the way the rules do.
Find the governing rules, skip the trigger day, count every calendar day, roll a weekend or holiday end date forward, and have the result double-checked.

First I check which rules apply: federal, state, local, and the judge's own orders. Under the federal rules I skip the trigger day, count every day including weekends and holidays, and if the last day is a weekend or legal holiday, it moves to the next day that is not. Then a second person checks it and it goes on the firm calendar with reminders.
Before a case goes into a brief, how do you make sure it is still good law?
Your research habits beyond finding a case that sounds right.
Running a citator, reading the negative treatment, checking whether the court is binding, and reading the full opinion, not just a summary.

I run it through a citator to see if it was reversed, overruled or questioned, and I read the cases that treat it badly rather than trusting the flag. I check that the court is binding in our jurisdiction or note that it is only persuasive. And I read the opinion itself, so the quote and pin cite match what the court actually held.
The company expects to be sued. What is a litigation hold, and what is your part in it?
Whether you know the duty to preserve evidence and how to carry it out.
Preservation starts when litigation is reasonably anticipated. Notices go to custodians, auto-deletion is paused, and acknowledgments are tracked.

Once a lawsuit is reasonably expected, we must keep relevant documents and data. I help list the custodians, send the hold notice the attorney approves, and work with IT to stop automatic deletion of their email and files. I track who has acknowledged it, follow up with those who haven't, send reminders, and log the release when the matter ends.
What goes into a privilege log, and what must stay out of it?
Your grasp of privilege in document review.
Enough for the other side to assess the claim: date, author, recipients, privilege type, general subject. Never the privileged advice itself.

For each withheld document I list the date, author, all recipients, the privilege claimed, like attorney-client or work product, and a short description such as 'email requesting legal advice on lease terms.' The description must not reveal what the advice was. I also flag any outside third party on the email, since that can break the privilege.
The final brief reaches you 30 minutes before the filing deadline, and the court's e-filing system rejects the PDF. What do you do?
How you handle a filing problem against the clock.
Tell the attorney at once, fix the likely cause, document any system failure, and follow the court's rules for technical failures.

I tell the attorney right away and read the error. Often the file is too large or not text-searchable, so I split the exhibits into separate attachments as the local rules allow, or re-save the PDF. If the court's system itself is down, I take timed screenshots and we follow the court's technical-failure rules. Afterward I push for earlier internal deadlines.
You realize a privileged email went out in yesterday's document production. What do you do?
Whether you own a mistake fast and know how it can be fixed.
Telling the attorney immediately, without hiding it. The attorney can then try to claw it back under the protective order or the rules, and speed matters.

I tell the supervising attorney within the hour, with the document's production number and how it slipped through. The attorney decides on a clawback notice, which the protective order or the federal rules allow, and acting fast matters. I don't contact the other side myself. Then I find the gap, like a missed search term, and recheck the rest of the set.
Contract requests reach the legal team by email, chat and hallway talk. How would you fix the intake?
How you design a legal operations process people will actually use.
One front door, a short form with the facts lawyers need, routing by type and risk, templates for routine deals, and simple metrics.

I would set up one intake form that asks the deal type, counterparty, value and deadline, and route by type: an NDA on our template goes to self-service, a high-value deal goes to an attorney. I'd remind people politely that hallway requests go through the form. After a month I'd report volume and turnaround so we can see where the delays are.

partner-manager.heading: Partner manager questions
qs: What is the difference between a reseller, a referral partner and a technology partner?
Whether you know the basic partner types and how each one makes money.
Clear lines on who owns the customer contract, who sells, and how each partner is paid or adds value.

A reseller buys from us or sells our product on its own paper, so it owns the customer contract and earns a margin. A referral partner only introduces the customer; we sell and pay a fee. A technology partner builds an integration with our product; it may sell nothing, but customers who use the integration tend to stay longer.
What is deal registration, and why does it matter?
Your grasp of a core channel tool and the rules behind it.
Explains protection for the partner who found the deal, early pipeline visibility, and why fast, written rules keep partners using it.

The partner logs an opportunity with us early. If we approve it, that partner gets protection, often a better discount, and others should not take the deal for a set period. It rewards the partner who found it and gives me early sight of pipeline. I keep approvals fast and the rules written, or partners stop registering.
How do you measure whether a partner program is working?
Whether you track the numbers that show real partner impact.
Separates sourced from influenced revenue and adds measures like active partners, win rate and time to first deal.

I separate partner-sourced revenue, where the partner brought the deal, from partner-influenced, where they helped close or deliver it. I also watch active partners, win rate and deal size versus direct, time to first deal for new partners, and retention of customers using integrations. A count of signed partners alone tells me little.
A reseller also carries a competitor’s product. How do you get their sellers to sell ours?
How you win mindshare inside a partner’s sales team.
Makes the product easy and worth selling: simple pitch, fast support, fair margin, and help winning the first deals.

Sellers sell what is easy and pays. I make ours easy: a short pitch, a clear customer profile, a demo they can run, and a named contact who answers fast. I check that their margin is competitive. Then I help them win their first deals, because one closed deal together does more than any training session.
A partner signed six months ago and has brought in zero deals. What do you do?
How you handle an inactive partner without wasting time or giving up too early.
