Finds the cause first, agrees on a short plan with named accounts, then lowers the tier if nothing moves.

First I find out why. I talk to the partner owner and two of their sellers: do they know who to target, is the margin worth it, did training happen? Then we agree on a 90-day plan with a few named target accounts and a joint call each month. If nothing moves after that, I move them to a lower tier and spend my time elsewhere.
A partner asks for marketing funds to run an event. How do you decide?
Your judgement in spending partner marketing money.
Ties funds to a written plan with expected results and the partner’s own share, pays against proof, and tracks the pipeline after.

I ask what the event should produce: how many target accounts attend, how many meetings, how much pipeline, and what the partner puts in itself. I tie the funds to that plan and pay against proof, like the attendee list and invoices. Afterward I track which deals came from it, and that decides the next request.
Our direct sales rep and a partner both claim the same customer. How do you handle it?
How you resolve channel conflict fairly and keep both sides working.
Checks the facts, applies the written rules of engagement, escalates fast when rules are silent, and fixes the gap afterward.

I check the facts: who registered the deal, when, and who has really been working the customer. I apply the rules of engagement as written, not who argues louder. If the rules do not cover it, I bring in the sales leader and decide fast; often the best answer is working it together. Then I fix the gap in the rules.
You learn a reseller has been promising customers features our product does not have. What do you do?
How you protect customers and the brand while keeping the partnership workable.
Gets the facts, raises it with partner leadership, corrects it with affected customers, retrains, and escalates under the agreement if repeated.

I get the facts first: which customers, what was said, in writing if possible. Then I call the partner owner, not just the seller, and explain the risk to both of us. We correct it with each affected customer, often with our sales engineer on the call. I retrain their team, and if it happens again I escalate under the partner agreement.
Walk me through the joint business plan you would build with a top partner.
Whether you can plan growth with a partner as a shared commitment.
Shared targets, concrete actions with owners on both sides, and a regular review that changes what is not working.

I start with shared goals for the year: revenue, new customers and certified staff. Then the actions that get there: target accounts we work together, two campaigns, training dates, and who owns each step on both sides. We review it every quarter against the numbers. If only my name is on the actions, it is not a joint plan.

partner-marketing.heading: Partner marketing manager questions
qs: What is the difference between MDF and co-op funds?
Whether you know the two main ways vendors fund partner marketing.
MDF is allocated by the vendor for approved activities. Co-op is earned by the partner from its sales. Both are usually paid against proof of performance.

MDF is money we set aside and give to chosen partners for specific, pre-approved activities, usually based on a plan and how strategic they are. Co-op is earned: a partner builds up a share of what it sells and spends it on marketing within our rules. Both usually need proof of performance, like invoices and results, before we reimburse.
How do you tell partner-sourced pipeline from partner-influenced pipeline?
Your grasp of how partner results are counted and reported.
Sourced means the partner brought the deal; influenced means the partner helped on a deal someone else owned. Rules are agreed upfront and nobody double counts.

Sourced means the partner found the opportunity and brought it to us, usually shown by an approved deal registration. Influenced means our sales team owned it but the partner helped, for example with a reference or a joint demo. I report them separately and agree the rules with sales operations before the quarter starts, so nobody counts the same deal twice.
What goes into a campaign-in-a-box for resellers?
Whether you can build marketing that small partners will actually launch.
Targeting guidance, ready and editable assets, a landing page, a follow-up path for leads, and a check on who actually used it.

I include a short brief on who to target and why, ready emails and social posts with editable fields, a co-brandable landing page, a call script, and a simple way to register leads. I keep it to what a two-person reseller can launch in an afternoon. Then I track who used it and call the partners who downloaded it but never launched.
Walk me through building a joint marketing plan with a new strategic partner.
How you turn a partnership into a shared, measurable plan.
Shared target customers and goals, a few plays with named owners on both sides, agreed budget split and tracking, and a regular review rhythm.

I start with shared goals: which customers we both want and what pipeline number we both sign up to. Then we pick two or three plays, name an owner on each side, agree the budget split and how we track leads. We review monthly against the plan and hold a proper quarterly review with a sponsor from each company in the room.
You run a joint webinar with a partner. Who gets the registrant list, and what do you set up first?
Whether you handle shared lead data properly and plan the follow-up.
Lead sharing is agreed in writing and disclosed on the registration form, both sides honor opt-outs, and follow-up is split so buyers are not hit twice.

Before we promote it, we agree in writing who gets the list and how fast each side follows up. The registration form says plainly that details go to both named companies, with a link to each privacy policy. Both sides honor unsubscribes, and we split follow-up by account or territory so a buyer does not get two calls on the same day.
A partner asks for MDF to host a golf day for customers. What do you ask before you say yes?
Your judgement on whether a funding request will produce business.
Who attends, the cost per guest, the follow-up plan, the pipeline expected, and what proof will be submitted to claim the funds.

I ask who is on the guest list and whether they are real buying prospects or just friends of the account team. Then the cost per guest, which of our products the follow-up will push, and what pipeline they expect within a quarter. If it holds up, I approve it with proof required: attendee list, invoices and the deals registered afterward.
Your product is now listed on a cloud marketplace. How do you drive sales through it?
Your understanding of marketplaces as a sales channel.
Knows why buyers use marketplaces, such as simpler buying and existing cloud spend, and works with both internal sales and the marketplace's partner team.

A listing alone sells little. I tell our sales team why buyers like it: the purchase goes on their existing cloud bill, it can skip a new vendor setup, and for some buyers it counts toward a spend commitment they already have. I make private offers easy to request, add a marketplace buy option to our campaigns, and work with the marketplace's partner team on joint selling.
A reseller runs ads with an old version of your logo and a 'cheapest on the market' claim you cannot back up. What do you do?
How you protect the brand without damaging the partner relationship.
Treats the unsupported claim as the urgent risk, acts the same day, gives the right assets, and adds a check so it does not recur.

The price claim is the bigger problem, because an unsupported claim can be false advertising and it carries our name. I call the partner that day, ask them to pause the ad, and send the current logo pack and approved claims. If the ad used our funds, it is not reimbursed as it stands. Then I add a quick approval step for co-branded ads.
Your direct sales rep and a reseller both claim a deal that came from a joint event. How do you settle it?
How you handle channel conflict fairly and keep partner trust.
Uses the written rules of engagement and deal registration, not opinions, decides quickly, and closes the gap in the rules afterward.

I go to the written rules first. If the partner registered the deal and it was approved before our rep logged the opportunity, the partner keeps it. If the rules do not cover the case, I bring the sales and channel leaders together quickly, we decide once, and I write the gap into the rules. Partners stop bringing deals the moment they think we take them.
Last year's MDF produced a lot of leads but very little pipeline. How do you redesign the program?
How you tie partner funding to results that matter to the business.
Finds where it broke first, then funds fewer partners, pays against pipeline rather than lead counts, and requires a real follow-up plan.

First I find where it broke: poor-fit leads, or good leads nobody called. I pull a sample and check. Then I fund fewer partners, tie the next payment to registered opportunities instead of lead counts, and require a follow-up plan with named sales staff. Partners who turned funds into pipeline get more; the rest get training before more money.

payments-engineer.heading: Payments engineer questions
qs: Why should you never store money amounts as floating-point numbers?
Whether you know the most basic rule of handling money in code.
Floats cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly. Use integer minor units or a decimal type, and keep the currency code with every amount.

Binary floats cannot hold 0.1 exactly, so 0.1 plus 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004, and those errors add up across millions of rows. I store integer minor units, like cents, with a currency code. Not every currency has two decimals: the Japanese yen has none, so I read the exponent per currency.
What is the difference between authorization, capture and settlement on a card payment?
Your grasp of how a card payment actually moves through the system.
Authorization checks the card and places a hold. Capture asks for the money. Settlement is when funds actually move to the merchant's bank. Unused authorizations expire.

Authorization asks the issuing bank to approve the charge and hold the funds, but no money moves. Capture tells the processor to collect that amount. Settlement is when the networks and banks actually move the money, usually in batches. Shops that ship goods often authorize at checkout and capture at shipping, and they have to capture before the hold expires.
Explain double-entry bookkeeping as you would build it into a ledger service.
Whether you can design a ledger that stays correct to the cent.
Every transaction is a set of entries that sum to zero across accounts. Entries are append-only, and balances are derived from the entries.

Every money movement is recorded as at least two entries: a debit to one account and a credit to another, and they must sum to zero. A $50 payment debits the customer receivable and credits merchant payable. I enforce the zero sum in the same database transaction, never edit entries, and compute balances from them. If the books do not sum to zero, I know something broke.
How do you keep card numbers out of your own systems as much as possible?
Your understanding of PCI DSS scope and how to shrink it.
Hosted fields or a processor's page so card data goes straight to the processor, tokens stored instead of numbers, and never storing the CVV after authorization.

I use the processor's hosted fields or payment page, so the card number goes from the browser straight to them and we only get a token back. That keeps most of our servers out of PCI scope. We store the token, the last four digits and the expiry if needed. The security code is never stored after authorization, not even encrypted; PCI DSS forbids it.
A $100 refund has to be split evenly across three sellers. How do you do it?
How you handle rounding so the parts always add up to the whole.
Work in cents, give the leftover cent to one party by a fixed, documented rule, and assert the parts sum to the total.

In cents that is 10,000 split three ways: 3,333 each leaves one cent. I give the remainder to one party by a fixed rule, for example the largest share or the first seller in order, so we get 3,334, 3,333 and 3,333. Then I assert the parts sum to 10,000 before writing anything. Rounding each share on its own is how a cent quietly disappears.
You find a ledger entry posted last week with the wrong amount. How do you fix it?
Whether you correct money records without destroying the audit trail.
Never update or delete a posted entry. Post a reversal and a correct entry, linked to the original, with a reason.

I do not edit the row. I post a reversing entry that cancels the original exactly, then a new entry with the right amount, both referencing the original ID and a ticket explaining why. The history then shows what happened and who fixed it. Before that, I check whether payouts or reports already used the wrong figure, because they may need their own corrections.
Your processor sends webhooks that sometimes arrive twice or out of order. How do you handle them?
How you build reliable event processing for payment status updates.
Verify the signature, dedupe on event ID, process idempotently, and never let an older event move a payment backward.

First I verify the signature so nobody can fake a payment success. I store the event ID and skip ones I have seen. I reply 200 quickly and process on a queue. Payment status is a state machine that only moves forward, so a late pending event cannot overwrite succeeded. If order really matters, I fetch the current object from the processor's API instead of trusting the event body.
A subscription renewal is declined. When do you retry the card, and when don't you?
Your judgement on decline codes, retries and card network rules.
Retry soft declines on a spaced schedule; never retry hard declines like lost or stolen cards. Card networks limit retries and can charge for excess.

I read the decline code. Soft declines, like insufficient funds or issuer unavailable, I retry a few times spread over days, often around when people get paid. Hard declines, like lost card, stolen card or closed account, I never retry; I ask the customer to update the card. Card networks have rules on excessive retries and can fine us, so retry counts are capped in code.
A user tops up their wallet by ACH bank debit. When do you let them spend that money?
Whether you understand that ACH payments can be reversed after they look complete.
ACH debits can be returned days or even weeks later, so funds stay pending or limited by risk, and the ledger models returns explicitly.

Not the moment the debit is sent. ACH debits can come back as returns: insufficient funds usually within a couple of banking days, and a consumer can dispute an unauthorized debit weeks later. So the money sits in a pending account first. New users wait until the return window for common returns passes; trusted users may get a limit. A return posts entries that reverse the top-up.
Your ledger and the processor's settlement report differ by $43.17 for yesterday. Walk me through finding it.
How you run a reconciliation and find the real cause instead of forcing the numbers to match.
Match line by line on transaction IDs, check fees, refunds, disputes and day cutoffs, and never post a plug entry without an explanation.

I match each transaction by its processor ID, not by daily totals, and list what is on only one side. Common causes: fees netted from the payout, a refund or chargeback we booked on a different day, or the processor's cutoff being in another time zone. Once I find the items, I fix the cause. I never post a $43.17 adjustment just to make it balance.

payroll.heading: Payroll questions
qs: What is the difference between a pre-tax and a post-tax deduction?
Whether you know how each kind of deduction changes taxable wages.
Shows that pre-tax does not mean the same thing for every tax, with a correct example of each kind.

A pre-tax deduction comes out before some taxes are figured, so it lowers taxable wages. But not every tax the same way: a traditional 401(k) deferral lowers federal income tax wages but not Social Security and Medicare wages. Cafeteria plan health premiums usually lower both. A Roth 401(k) deferral or a garnishment comes out after taxes.
Walk me through how you get from gross pay to net pay.
Your grasp of the order of a payroll calculation.
A clear sequence: gross earnings, pre-tax deductions, taxes on the right wage bases, then post-tax deductions.

I start with gross: hours times rate, plus overtime, bonuses and other earnings. I take out pre-tax deductions, which gives the taxable wage for each tax. I calculate federal, state and local income tax from the W-4 and state forms, plus Social Security and Medicare. Then come post-tax deductions like Roth deferrals and garnishments. What is left is net pay.
A non-exempt employee earns a production bonus for the quarter. Does that change their overtime pay?
Whether you know what goes into the regular rate for overtime.
Yes: a nondiscretionary bonus belongs in the regular rate, so overtime for the weeks it covers must be recalculated.

Yes. A bonus promised for hitting a target is nondiscretionary, so under the FLSA it goes into the regular rate. I spread it over the workweeks it was earned in, find the extra regular rate for each week, and pay half that extra rate for every overtime hour in those weeks. A truly discretionary bonus, like an unannounced holiday gift, stays out.
An employee comes to you on payday and says the check is short. What do you do?
How you handle a pay error with the person standing in front of you.
Checks the facts quickly, fixes a real error fast with an off-cycle payment, explains it plainly and stops it from happening again.

I pull the pay stub and time records with them, line by line. Last time it was 6 overtime hours a manager approved after the cutoff. I ran an off-cycle payment that arrived two days later, showed the employee the math, and asked the manager to approve time before cutoff. Then I checked whether anyone else on that team had the same gap.
An employee starts working remotely from a different state. What changes in payroll?
Your knowledge of state tax withholding for remote workers.
Moves withholding to the state where the work is done, registers there if needed, and checks reciprocity, local taxes and special state rules.

Income tax generally follows where the work is done, so I get the new address and start date in writing. I register in the new state for withholding and unemployment insurance if needed, collect its withholding form and end the old state from that date. I also check reciprocity agreements, local taxes, and states that tax remote work tied to an office there.
You receive a wage garnishment order for an employee. Walk me through what you do.
How you handle a legal order that has deadlines and limits.
Verifies the order, applies federal and state limits to disposable earnings, respects priority, informs the employee and remits on time.

I confirm the order is valid and for our employee, and note the start date and where to send money. I figure disposable earnings, meaning pay after legally required deductions, and apply the federal limit or a lower state limit. If another order exists, I check priority; child support usually comes first. I give the employee a copy, start on time and keep records.
You find that an employee was overpaid for three months. How do you handle it?
How you fix a mistake that touches an employee's own money.
Talks to the employee first, follows state rules on recovery, agrees a fair schedule, and knows a prior-year error is handled differently for taxes.

I confirm the amount, then talk to the employee before any money moves. State laws differ: some require written consent, and some limit how much I can take per check. I offer a repayment plan in writing. If the overpayment was in a prior year, the tax handling changes and I may need corrected forms. Then I find why it happened and fix the setup.
At year end, the W-2 totals do not match the four quarterly 941s. What do you do?
Your year-end reconciliation and how you trace a difference to its cause.
Compares wage and tax totals by quarter to find the cause, then corrects with the right form, such as a 941-X or a W-2c.

I compare each total: wages, federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare wages and tax, against the 941s quarter by quarter. Once I find the gap, say a manual check entered outside the system in Q3, I fix the source. If a 941 was wrong, I file a 941-X for that quarter; if a W-2 already went out wrong, a W-2c. I reconcile every quarter so January has no surprises.
An American employee moves to work in another country for two years. What do you need to sort out in payroll?
Whether you can run cross-border payroll and avoid double taxation.
Covers host country withholding or shadow payroll, ongoing US withholding, and social security coverage under a totalization agreement.

I check whether the host country requires local payroll or a shadow payroll, which reports and withholds local tax on pay we still run from the US. The employee remains a US taxpayer, so I review US withholding with our tax adviser. If the US has a totalization agreement with that country, a certificate of coverage can keep them in US Social Security only.

pcb-engineer.heading: PCB design engineer questions
qs: Where do you put decoupling capacitors, and why does their placement matter?
Whether you understand the basic power delivery rules that every board depends on.
Close to the power pins with a short path to ground, because loop inductance, not just capacitance, decides how well they work.

I put the small capacitors, often 100 nF, right next to each power pin, with a via to the ground plane beside the pad. The current loop between pin, capacitor and ground has to be tiny, because its inductance limits how fast the cap can supply current. Bulk capacitors can sit a bit further away.
What do you check before you release files to the board fabricator?
Your release habits and how you catch errors before they cost money.
Design rule checks, a netlist compared to the schematic, fab rules met, clear fab notes and stackup, and a final look at every output file.

I run the design rule check with the fab's real limits, and I compare the layout netlist to the schematic. Then I open the Gerbers and drill files in a separate viewer, layer by layer. I check the fab notes: stackup, finish, copper weight, impedance targets. Last, I check the assembly files and the bill of materials match.
What is controlled impedance, and how do you get it on a real board?
Your knowledge of how stackup and geometry set signal behavior.
Impedance set by trace width, dielectric thickness and material, and copper; specified in the fab notes and confirmed with the fab and test coupons.

It means a trace is built to a target impedance, like 50 ohms single-ended or 90 ohms differential for USB 2.0. Width, distance to the reference plane, the dielectric material and copper thickness set it. I calculate a starting width, then put the target in the fab notes so the fab can tune widths for their process and test it on coupons.
How do you lay out a buck regulator so it works cleanly?
Whether you know where switching noise comes from and how layout controls it.
Smallest possible hot loop through the input capacitor and switches, a small switch node, and a quiet feedback trace kept away from it.

I start with the hot loop: the input capacitor and the two switches, or switch and diode, placed tight with a solid ground under them. That loop carries the fast current edges. I keep the switch node copper only as big as the current needs, and I route the feedback trace away from it and from the inductor, back to the output cap.
Walk me through bringing up the first prototype board.
Whether you power up a new board in a careful order that protects parts and finds faults.
Inspect, measure rails for shorts unpowered, power with a current-limited supply, check each rail, then clocks and reset, then program and test.

First I inspect under a microscope for bridges and parts placed backward. Unpowered, I measure each rail's resistance to ground. Then I power it from a bench supply with a low current limit and check every rail's voltage and ripple. Next I check clocks and reset, connect the debugger, load simple test code, and note every finding in a bring-up log.
You power a new board and the supply hits its current limit right away. What do you do?
How you trace a short or a power fault without damaging the board.
Stop, find which rail, check polarized parts and bridges, then use low limited current and a thermal camera to locate the hot spot.

I switch off and measure each rail to ground to find the one that is low. I check polarized parts first: diodes, tantalum capacitors, regulator orientation. If nothing shows, I feed that rail a low voltage with the current limit set low and look for the hot spot with a thermal camera. I compare against a second board to see if it is a build fault or a design fault.
The mechanical team wants the board 20 percent smaller. How do you answer them?
Your judgement on trade-offs between size, cost, risk and schedule.
No flat yes or no: options with their real cost in layers, fab technology, assembly risk and time, so the team can decide.

I would study it before saying yes. Shrinking might mean going from four to six layers, smaller parts, or microvias, and each adds cost and fab risk. I would come back with two or three options, each with a quote, the effect on routing and heat, and the schedule hit. Sometimes moving one connector gets most of the space for free.
Your prototype boards arrive and a connector footprint is mirrored. What do you do?
How you handle your own mistake and stop it from happening again.
Own it, find a workaround so testing continues, log it for the next spin, and fix the library and review process.

I tell the team the same day. For the prototypes I would mount the connector on the back, or use an adapter or wires, so testing can go on. I log it in the errata for the next revision. Then I fix the library part and add a step: print the footprint at full scale and lay the real part on it before release.
The board fails a radiated emissions test with a spike at a few hundred megahertz. How do you find and fix the source?
Whether you can work through an EMC failure in a methodical way.
Match the spike to a clock harmonic, locate it with a near-field probe, check cables as antennas, then slow edges, filter or improve grounding.

First I check if the frequency is a harmonic of a clock on the board. Then I use a near-field probe and a spectrum analyzer to find where it is strongest. Cables are often the antenna, so I check them too. Fixes I try: series resistors to slow edges, spread spectrum on the clock, filtering where cables leave the board, and better ground stitching.

penetration-tester.heading: Penetration tester questions
qs: What do you need in hand before you send the first packet at a target?
Whether you treat written permission and scope as the line between testing and a crime.
Signed authorization from someone who can grant it, a clear scope, rules of engagement, testing windows and an emergency contact.

A signed authorization from someone with the authority to grant it, and a scope listing the IP ranges, domains and apps that are in and out. I also want rules of engagement: hours, whether denial of service or phishing is allowed, and a contact I can call at 2 a.m. If a system is hosted by a cloud provider, I check that provider's testing policy too.
Explain SQL injection and how you would confirm it without damaging data.
Your grasp of a core web flaw and of testing it with care.
User input changing the logic of a query, confirmed with harmless true/false or timing probes, and the fix named: parameterized queries.

It happens when the app builds a database query by pasting user input into it, so the input can change the query's logic. I confirm with harmless probes: a single quote to see an error, then one true and one false condition to see if the page changes. I avoid anything that writes or deletes. The fix is parameterized queries, not filtering characters.
How would you test an app for broken access control between two users?
Whether you test what the app allows, not only what the screens show.
Two accounts with different roles, replaying one user's requests with the other's session, and changing record IDs in URLs and API calls.

I make two accounts, ideally a regular user and an admin. I capture traffic in an intercepting proxy, replay the admin's requests with the user's session, and swap record IDs, like changing invoice 1041 to 1042. If user A can read user B's invoice, the server is not checking ownership. I test the API too, since it is often less guarded than the web pages.
Your scanner flags 40 critical findings on a web server. What do you do before any of them goes in the report?
How you separate real findings from scanner noise.
Manual validation of each one, proof saved, findings with one root cause grouped, and nothing reported as confirmed that you could not confirm.

I verify each one by hand. Scanners often judge by version banners, and a backported patch can make an old version number safe. I try to reproduce the issue, save the request and response as proof, and group findings that share one root cause. Anything I cannot confirm I either drop or label as unverified, with the reason.
How do you write up one finding so that both an executive and a developer can use it?
Your report writing, the part of the job the client keeps.
Plain business impact first, a severity with its reasoning, exact steps to reproduce with evidence, and a specific fix that can be retested.

I open with one or two plain sentences of impact: any logged-in user can read every customer's invoices. Then the severity and why, often with a CVSS score, the common scoring scale. For the developer I give the endpoint, exact steps and the requests that prove it, then a concrete fix, like checking record ownership on the server. I end with how to retest.
You realize mid-test that one of the addresses you scanned for an hour was out of scope. What do you do?
Your honesty and process when you make a mistake on an engagement.
Stop at once, tell the lead and the client promptly, log exactly what was sent and when, and fix the cause so it does not repeat.

I stop all traffic to that address right away. Then I tell my lead and the client contact the same day, with the exact times, tools and traffic sent, because their team may see it in logs or the address may belong to a third party. I note it in the report, then recheck my target list against the scope document so it cannot happen twice.
You found an exploit for a legacy production server, but it has a real chance of crashing the service. What is your call?
Your judgement when proving a flaw could cause real harm.
Not running it alone; gathering safe evidence and agreeing with the client on a watched window, a staging copy, or reporting it as likely exploitable.

I don't fire it on my own judgement. I gather safe evidence first, like the exact version and the public advisory, then call the client contact. They may give me a maintenance window with someone watching, or a staging copy. If they say no, I report it as likely exploitable and explain why, which is still a finding they can act on.
During your test you find a web shell and an admin account nobody on the client's list knows about. What now?
Whether you recognize a live incident and step out of the tester's role.
Pause and call the emergency contact at once, leave the attacker's tools untouched to preserve evidence, document it, and let the client's incident team lead.

That could be a real attacker, so I pause the test and call the emergency contact named in the rules of engagement right away. I don't delete the shell or the account, since that destroys evidence and can tip off the intruder. I write down exactly what I saw, where and when, and hand it to their incident team. Testing resumes only when they say so.
You have a shell as a low-privilege domain user on an internal Windows machine. Walk me through what you do next.
How you move from a foothold toward domain impact with method, not luck.
Enumerating the host and Active Directory, looking for known weaknesses such as Kerberoastable service accounts, and logging every step.

First I look around: my privileges, missing patches, saved credentials and who is logged in. Then I map Active Directory: groups, admins and paths to them. I check service accounts, since any domain user can request a Kerberos service ticket and try to crack its password offline; that is Kerberoasting. I log every command with a timestamp for the report.
You control the instruction pointer in a buffer overflow, but DEP and ASLR are enabled. How do you approach it?
Your depth in exploit development beyond running public code.
DEP stops code running from the stack, so reuse existing code with ROP; ASLR needs an address leak or a module loaded without it.

DEP marks the stack non-executable, so I can't just jump to my shellcode. I'd chain small pieces of existing code, called ROP gadgets, to call a function like VirtualProtect and make my buffer executable. ASLR randomizes where those pieces live, so I need an address leak or a module built without ASLR. I prove it on a matching lab build before the client's system.

people-operations.heading: People operations specialist questions
qs: When does a new hire's Form I-9 have to be completed?
Whether you know the federal deadlines that every new hire depends on.
Section 1 by the end of the first day of work, Section 2 within three business days, and never telling the person which documents to bring.

The employee completes Section 1 no later than the end of their first day of work. We complete Section 2 within three business days of that day, after examining the documents they choose from the lists. I never ask for specific documents, because that can be discrimination. If we use E-Verify, the case is opened only after the I-9 is done.
A new hire starts Monday. What has to be in place before then?
How you organize onboarding so the first day actually works.
A checklist with an owner for each item: paperwork, payroll set-up, accounts, equipment and a manager plan, all confirmed before the start date.

I confirm the signed offer and that the record is in the HR system so payroll picks them up. IT has the laptop and accounts ready, the manager has a first-week plan, and the new hire has an email with start time, place and what to bring for the I-9. On Friday I check each item off myself instead of assuming it was done.
What goes in an employee's personnel file, and what must be kept somewhere else?
Whether you keep employee records with the right separation and access.
Job records in the file; medical information in a separate confidential file, as the ADA requires, with access limited to people who need it.

The file holds the offer, job changes, pay history, reviews and discipline. Medical information, such as doctor's notes or leave certifications, goes in a separate confidential file; the ADA requires that. Many employers also keep I-9s apart so they can be shown in an audit without the rest. Only people who need a record for their job can open it.
A manager wants a new coordinator role to be salaried and exempt from overtime. How do you decide?
Your grasp of exempt and non-exempt classification under federal wage law.
Title and salaried pay do not decide it: the job must meet the salary tests and a duties test, and state rules can be stricter.

Being paid a salary does not make someone exempt. Under the Fair Labor Standards Act the role must be paid on a salary basis at or above the current threshold, and the real duties must fit an exemption, like administrative or executive. I compare the job to the duties test, check our state's rules, and if it is unclear I treat it as non-exempt and ask counsel.
A promotion with a raise is approved the day after the payroll cutoff. What do you do?
How you handle contract changes against payroll deadlines.
Records the correct effective date, makes sure the employee gets the difference, and tells them in writing what will happen and when.

I enter the change in the HR system with the approved effective date, not the date I processed it. I tell payroll so the missed amount goes in the next run as a retro payment, or an off-cycle check if it is large. Then I send the employee a letter with the new title, pay and effective date, and say which paycheck will show the difference.
You find that 15 employees have a different job title in payroll than in the HR system. Walk me through how you fix it.
How you clean HR data without creating new errors.
Picks the source of truth, checks against signed records or managers, fixes it at the source, and closes the gap that caused it.

First I decide which system is the source of truth; usually the HR system feeds payroll. I check the 15 against signed change letters or ask the managers, correct the records with a note of why, and keep a before and after list. Then I look for the cause, like a manual entry step, and add a monthly report that flags mismatches.
An employee resigns with two weeks' notice. Walk me through the leaver process.
Whether you run offboarding completely, from notice to final pay.
Written confirmation, final pay on time under state law, benefits notices, access removed on the last day, equipment back and records closed.

I confirm the resignation and last day in writing and update the HR system. I check our state's final pay deadline and whether unused vacation must be paid out, and tell payroll. Benefits gets the end date so COBRA notices go out. IT removes access at the end of the last day, the manager collects equipment, and I offer an exit interview.
A manager asks you why one of their team is on medical leave. What do you tell them?
Your judgement on confidentiality when a manager asks for medical details.
Shares only what the manager needs to plan the work: that leave is approved, the expected return and any restrictions, never the diagnosis.

I tell them the person is on approved leave, the expected return date, and any work restrictions they will need to plan around. I do not share the diagnosis or the doctor's notes, even if they ask kindly. I explain that the law and our policy limit medical information, and I offer to help plan cover for the work.
You notice you keyed a new hire's pay rate wrong and they were underpaid for two paychecks. What do you do?
How you own and fix a mistake that affects someone's pay.
Fixes it fast with a correction payment, tells the employee directly and honestly, and adds a check so it does not happen again.

I confirm the correct rate from the signed offer, work out the exact shortfall, and ask payroll for an off-cycle payment instead of making them wait. Then I call the employee, say it was my error, and tell them the amount and the date it will arrive. Afterwards I add a second-person check on new pay rates before the first payroll.
An employee asks to move to another state and keep working remotely. What has to happen before you say yes?
Whether you see the payroll, tax and legal steps behind a change of work location.
Manager approval, then registering in the new state for taxes, updating withholding, workers' comp and benefits, and applying that state's labor laws.

Beyond the manager's approval, we must be registered as an employer in that state for tax withholding and unemployment insurance. Payroll updates the work location and state tax forms, and workers' comp must cover that state. I also check its rules on paid sick leave, final pay and pay frequency, and confirm the health plan works there before the move.

performance-marketing.heading: Performance marketing manager questions
qs: What is the difference between ROAS and CPA, and when would you optimize for each?
Whether you know the two core efficiency metrics and when each one fits.
Clear definitions, a rule for choosing based on how much order values vary, and a check against margin rather than revenue alone.

CPA is ad spend divided by conversions. ROAS is revenue from ads divided by ad spend. If every sale is worth about the same, like a fixed-price subscription, I target CPA. If order values range from $20 to $400, I target ROAS so bidding favors bigger baskets. Either way, I check the target against margin, not just revenue.
How do you use match types and negative keywords in a Google Search campaign?
Your hands-on control of search campaigns and wasted spend.
Knows exact, phrase and broad match, ties broad match to smart bidding and good conversion data, and reviews search terms regularly.

Exact match keeps the query close to my keyword's meaning. Phrase match allows words around it. Broad match reaches the widest set of related searches, and I only use it with smart bidding and solid conversion data. Every week I read the search terms report and add negatives, like "free" or "jobs" for a software product, so we stop paying for clicks that never buy.
How can you tell that an ad creative is wearing out?
Whether you can spot creative fatigue in the data and act on it.
Rising frequency, falling click-through rate and rising cost on the same audience, checked against newer ads, followed by a steady flow of new concepts.

I track each ad over weeks. When frequency climbs, click-through rate slides and cost per result rises on the same audience, people have seen it too often. I compare it with newer ads in the same ad set so I don't blame a market-wide dip on one ad. Then I launch new angles, not just a new color, and I keep a few fresh concepts going into testing every week.
A Meta ad set is still in the learning phase and your manager wants changes today. What do you think about first?
Your understanding of how platform algorithms learn and what resets them.
Knows that significant edits restart learning, batches changes, scales budget in steps, and fixes ad sets that can never get enough conversions.

Big edits, like a large budget jump, new targeting or new creative, can restart learning, and results swing while the system relearns. Meta's guidance is about 50 optimization events in a week to exit learning. So I batch the changes into one edit and raise budget in steps. If an ad set can't reach that volume, I merge ad sets or optimize for an earlier event, like add to cart.
How do you work out the most you can afford to pay to get a new customer?
Whether you set targets from the business economics, not from platform benchmarks.
Starts from gross margin and repeat purchases, uses a payback window agreed with finance, and keeps room for other costs.

I start from gross margin per order, not revenue, then how often a customer buys again. Say finance wants payback within six months, and a new customer brings $60 in margin over that time. Then my target CPA sits below $60, with room left for fees and overhead. I agree on the payback window with finance before I set any bid target.
Google, Meta and TikTok together report 1,400 conversions this month, but the store shows 900 orders. How do you explain that?
How you handle attribution overlap and which number you trust.
Explains double credit across platforms and view-through windows, treats the backend as the source of truth, and reports blended figures.

Each platform claims every sale it touched within its own window, including some views without a click. A buyer who saw a Meta ad and then clicked a Google ad gets counted by both. I treat the 900 store orders as the truth and report blended CAC, which is total spend divided by new customers. I still use platform numbers to compare ads within each channel.
Overnight, CPA on your biggest campaign jumped 60%. Walk me through what you check.
Your troubleshooting order under pressure.
Checks tracking and the site before blaming the auction, then recent edits, disapprovals and competition, in a logical order.

First, tracking. If clicks are steady and conversions fell off a cliff, a tag probably broke in a site update. Then I place a test order to make sure checkout works. Next, I check the change history for edits to budgets or bids, and look for disapproved ads. Only then do I look at the auction: competitor overlap and cost per click. Then I tell the team what I found and what I'm fixing.
Should we keep paying for ads on our own brand name?
Your judgement on brand search spend and incrementality.
No blanket answer: weighs competitor bidding and placement, and proposes a test that measures total brand traffic and sales, not just paid clicks.

It depends. If competitors bid on our name, our ad protects the top spot. If nobody else bids, many of those clicks would come through the organic listing anyway. I'd pause brand ads in a few regions for a few weeks and compare total brand clicks and sales with similar regions where ads stayed on. That shows what the spend actually adds.
How would you prove that a channel brings sales that would not have happened anyway?
Whether you can measure incrementality, not just attributed conversions.
Uses a holdout: a geo test or a platform lift study, set up before launch, measuring total sales and turning the result into a cost per extra sale.

I'd run a holdout. Either the platform's lift study, which hides ads from a random control group, or a geo test: pick matched regions, turn the channel off in some, and compare total sales over four to six weeks. I set the success measure before launch. If the regions with ads sell 8% more, I divide the spend by those extra sales to get the true cost of each one.
You find that conversions were double-counted for a month because browser and server events were not deduplicated. What do you do?
How you own a tracking mistake and limit the damage.
Fixes the setup, tells stakeholders with corrected numbers, and knows that automated bidding learned from inflated data and targets need resetting.

First, I fix it. Meta deduplicates when the pixel and the Conversions API send the same event name and event ID, so I make sure both do. Then I tell my manager and finance right away, with corrected figures for the month. Smart bidding learned from inflated data, so I recheck targets and budgets that were set on those numbers, and I annotate the reports.

phd.heading: PhD and doctorate questions
qs: Explain your dissertation research to me as if I were an engineer from another team.
Whether you can explain deep, narrow work clearly to people outside your field.
The problem, why it matters, what you found and where it stops working, in plain words and in about two minutes.

I worked on making image models reliable when the input looks different from the training data, like photos from a new camera. I built a way to flag the inputs the model is likely to get wrong. It caught most bad cases in our tests, but it only works for images, and it adds a small delay every time the model runs.
How do you choose the baselines you compare a new method against?
Whether you compare your own work fairly.
A simple baseline plus the strongest recent methods, all given the same data and the same tuning effort as your own method.

I include the simplest method that could work, like logistic regression or a nearest-neighbor model, and the strongest recent method I can run. I give every baseline the same data and the same tuning budget as mine. If a simple baseline comes close to my method, that is a finding worth reporting, not hiding.
What does an ablation study tell you, and how do you design one?
Your method for showing which parts of your work actually matter.
Removing or replacing one part at a time, keeping everything else fixed, and repeating runs so a real drop can be told apart from noise.

An ablation removes or replaces one part of a method at a time to see how much each part contributes. I change only one thing per run, keep the data and compute budget fixed, and use several random seeds. Sometimes it shows a component I was proud of adds nothing. Then I cut it and the method gets simpler.
How do you make sure someone else can reproduce your results a year from now?
Your habits for reproducible research.
Versioned code, recorded environment, seeds and data versions, settings kept in files, and a test rerun from a clean setup.

I keep code in version control and tag the exact commit behind each figure. I record the environment, package versions, random seeds and the data version or a checksum of the data. Settings live in config files, not in my head. Before I submit, I rerun a key result from a clean setup, which usually exposes one missing step.
Your model scores far better on the test set than anyone expected. What do you check first?
Whether you suspect data leakage before you celebrate.
Looking for leakage: overlap between splits, preprocessing fit on all the data, features that carry the label, or future data used in training.

I assume a bug until I can rule it out. I check for duplicate or near-duplicate items across train and test, for scaling or other preprocessing fit on the full dataset, and for features that carry the answer. With time-series data, I check that training never saw anything from after the test period. Then I confirm on a fresh holdout set.
You tried 20 settings and one gave a significant result at p below 0.05. How do you report it?
Your grasp of multiple comparisons and honest reporting.
Saying that about one in 20 tests would pass by chance alone, correcting for the number of tests, and confirming on new data.

With 20 tests at the 0.05 level, I would expect about one false positive even if no effect is real. So I report all 20, apply a correction such as Bonferroni or control the false discovery rate, and treat the hit as a hypothesis. The real test is a new run on new data, with the analysis fixed in advance.
A reviewer asks for an experiment you think is unnecessary. How do you respond?
How you handle peer review when you disagree.
Finding the concern behind the request, running a small version if it is feasible, and answering politely with evidence.

I first ask what worry sits behind the request. Often it is a doubt about whether the result holds beyond my setting. If a small version of the experiment is feasible, I run it, because data settles a question faster than argument. If not, I explain politely why it would not test my claim and point to results that already address the concern.
A colleague cannot reproduce a result from your published paper. What do you do?
How you handle a possible error in your own published work.
Working openly with them to find the cause and, if the result is wrong, telling coauthors and the journal and correcting the record.

I thank them and ask for their exact setup, then rerun from my archived code and data. If the gap comes from a missing detail, I update the code release and the paper's materials. If I find a real error that changes the result, I tell my coauthors and contact the journal about a correction, or a retraction if the main claim fails.
Your project has shown no progress for six months. How do you decide whether to pivot?
Your judgement about when to persist and when to change course.
Naming what was expected, running the cheapest test that could change your mind, then pivoting on a set deadline while keeping what is useful.

I write down what I expected, what I saw, and the cheapest experiment that could change my mind. If that fails too, I look for the smallest pivot that reuses what I built and agree on a deadline with my manager. I also write up what did not work, because a clear negative result saves the next person months.
How would you turn a research prototype into something a product team can ship?
Whether you can carry research into real use.
Learning the real constraints, testing on real data, handing over clean code with known limits, and watching quality after launch.

First I learn the product limits: speed, cost, and the data it will really see. A model that wins by one point but runs ten times slower may lose. I test on a sample of real traffic, write down where it fails, and work with the engineers on clean, tested code. After launch I watch whether quality drifts as the data changes.

physical-security.heading: Physical security questions
qs: What is tailgating, and how do you stop it at a door you control?
Whether you know the most common way access control fails.
A clear definition and a firm, polite habit: one badge, one person, and a report when it happens.

Tailgating is when someone follows an authorized person through a controlled door without using their own credential. At my post I watch the door until it closes and ask the person behind to badge in themselves. If they have no badge, I send them to the front desk to be verified. Doors that are held or propped open get logged and reported.
Walk me through the first fifteen minutes of your shift.
How you take over a post without missing what happened before you arrived.
Reading the pass-down log and post orders, checking equipment and radio, and asking the outgoing officer about open issues.

I arrive early, read the pass-down log and any new post orders, and ask the officer I am relieving about anything still open, like a broken door or a banned person. Then I do a radio check, test my flashlight, confirm every camera is recording, and sign the log with the time I took the post.
What goes into a good incident report?
Your report writing, the part of the job others rely on after you leave.
Facts in order: who, what, when, where and how, written soon after, with what you saw kept apart from what others told you.

I write it as soon as the scene is safe, while details are fresh. I give times, exact locations, names and descriptions, and what each person did, in order. I write only what I saw or heard, and I mark statements from others as theirs, with quotes where I can. No guesses, no opinions like “he looked guilty.” Then I note who was called and what footage exists.
A senior manager walks up without a badge and says, “You know me, just let me in.” What do you do?
Whether you apply the access rules the same way to everyone.
Polite, firm and by the book: verify identity, issue a temporary badge per policy, log it, and call a supervisor rather than make exceptions.

I greet them by name and say I still have to follow the badge policy. I check their ID against the employee list, issue a temporary badge and log the time and reason. It takes two minutes. Most managers respect it. If someone pushes back, I call my supervisor rather than make an exception on my own.
The fire alarm goes off on your shift. What do you do?
Whether you know your role in the site's emergency plan.
Check the panel for the location, call it in per the plan, move people out by the stairs, meet the fire department, and leave the reset to them.

I read the fire panel to see which zone and device went off, and make sure 911 and my dispatch are called as the plan says. I radio the location, help move people to the stairs and the assembly point, and keep them away from elevators. I meet the fire department at the main entrance with the panel information and keys. I do not reset the alarm; that is the fire department's call.
A person runs out of the store past you with unpaid merchandise. What do you do?
Whether you know the limits of your authority and put safety over property.
Following company policy and state law, which often means observe and report, not chase; getting a good description and calling it in.

I follow the site's policy, and the retail posts I have worked were observe and report. So I do not chase into the parking lot. I note the description, clothing, direction, any vehicle and plate, and the time, and I call it in and contact police if the policy says to. Then I save the footage and write the report. Merchandise is not worth anyone getting hurt.
On camera, you see someone in a restricted area after hours. Walk me through your response.
How you use CCTV and the radio together without putting yourself at risk.
Keeping eyes on the person, calling for backup and police per post orders, guiding responders by radio, and not walking in alone.

I keep the person on camera and follow them from view to view. I radio my supervisor or the patrol officer with the location, a description and whether I can see a weapon or tools, and call police if the post orders say so. I guide responders as the person moves. I note the times and camera numbers so the footage can be saved, then write it up.
Police ask you for video of an incident. How do you hand it over so it holds up as evidence?
Whether you understand chain of custody for video evidence.
Exporting unedited footage in the recorder's original format, noting any camera clock offset, and logging every handoff with signatures.

I export the clips without editing them, in the system's original format with its player, and keep a copy. I check the camera clock against real time and write down any difference. I fill out a chain of custody form: what was exported, by whom, when, and who received it, with a signature. I also lock that time period on the recorder so it is not overwritten.
You answer the phone and the caller says there is a bomb in the building. What do you do?
Whether you stay calm and gather the details responders will need.
Keeping the caller talking, writing exact words and details on a bomb threat checklist, then notifying police and following the site plan.

I stay calm and keep the caller on the line as long as I can. I use the bomb threat checklist by the phone, write the exact words, and ask where the bomb is and when it will go off. I note the voice, accent, background noise and the time. Then I call 911 and my supervisor, and the site's plan decides on search or evacuation. I do not touch any suspicious item.
After you submit a report, you realize you wrote the wrong time for a key event. How do you fix it?
Your honesty and how you correct a record without damaging it.
Owning the error quickly and correcting it openly, with a supplemental report or a dated correction, never by erasing the original.

I tell my supervisor the same day. I do not change or delete the original report. I write a supplemental report that says which time was wrong, what the right time is and how I know, for example the camera timestamp. In a paper log I would draw one line through the error, write the correction and initial it. An honest correction keeps the report credible; a hidden edit ruins it.

physician.heading: Physician questions
qs: Walk me through how you build a differential diagnosis for a new complaint.
Your clinical reasoning when the cause is not yet known.
A structured approach: history first, then causes ranked by likelihood and by danger, so the can't-miss ones are ruled out early.

I start with a careful history, because it gives most of the diagnosis, then a focused exam. I list causes by how likely they are and, separately, by how dangerous. For chest pain I think of heart attack, pulmonary embolism and aortic dissection first, even if reflux is most likely. Then I pick tests that will change what I do.
A patient with three days of low back pain and no warning signs asks for an MRI. What do you do?
Whether you order tests by evidence and can say no kindly.
Checks for red flags, explains that early imaging does not help without them, and gives a clear plan and signs that should bring the patient back.

I ask about red flags: fever, a cancer history, weight loss, leg weakness, numbness in the groin, or bladder and bowel changes. If there are none, I explain that most episodes improve within weeks and an early MRI often shows findings that don't explain the pain. I give a plan for staying active and controlling pain, and tell them exactly what should bring them back sooner.
Your patient speaks little English and her teenage son offers to translate. How do you proceed?
Whether you communicate safely across a language barrier.
Uses a qualified medical interpreter, in person, by phone or by video. Family, and minors above all, are not used for clinical content.

I thank the son but call a qualified interpreter, by phone or video if no one is on site. Family may leave things out or soften bad news, and a teenager should not carry his mother's diagnosis. I speak to the patient, not the interpreter, use short sentences, and ask her to repeat back the plan. I note the interpreter's ID in the chart.
What has to be in place before a patient's consent to a procedure is valid?
Your understanding of informed consent beyond the signed form.
Capacity, enough information (nature, risks, benefits, alternatives including doing nothing) and a free choice. The form only records the talk.

The patient must have capacity to decide, and the choice must be voluntary. I explain what the procedure is, why I recommend it, the common and the serious risks, the expected benefit, and the alternatives, including doing nothing. I check understanding by asking them to explain it back. The signature documents that conversation; it does not replace it.
How do you assess whether a patient has decision-making capacity?
Whether you can judge capacity yourself, one decision at a time.
The four abilities: understand, appreciate, reason and state a choice. Capacity is specific to the decision and can change; disagreeing is not lacking it.

I check four things. Can the patient tell back the facts in their own words? Do they see how those facts apply to them? Can they weigh the options and give reasons? Can they state a clear choice? Capacity is for one decision at one time, so a delirious patient may regain it. And refusing my advice is not, on its own, a sign of incapacity.
A patient with chest pain wants to leave against medical advice. What do you do?
How you balance a patient's right to refuse with keeping them safe.
Assesses capacity, learns the reason, explains the risk plainly, offers the next-best option and documents. The door stays open.

First I sit down and ask why. Often it is a pet at home or a worry about cost, and a social worker can help. If he has capacity, I say plainly that this could be a heart attack. If he still leaves, I offer whatever partial treatment and follow-up I can, give clear return signs, and document the talk. He should never feel he can't come back.
A test you ordered for a disease you thought very unlikely comes back positive. How do you read it?
Whether you interpret results with pretest probability in mind.
Knows that when the chance of disease is low, even a good test gives many false positives; reassesses and confirms before labeling the patient.

The meaning of a positive depends on how likely the disease was before the test. When that chance is very low, many positives are false, even with a good test. I recheck the history and exam and confirm with a more specific test before I treat or put the diagnosis in the chart. It also reminds me to order tests only when I have a clear question.
How do you make sure no test result falls through the cracks after a patient leaves?
How you close the loop on results that come back after discharge.
A named owner for every pending result, the patient told what to expect, a way to reach them, and abnormal results acted on and documented.

At discharge I list pending tests in the summary and name who will follow them, usually me. I tell the patient which results are pending and confirm a working phone number. When an abnormal result comes in, I call the patient, arrange the next step, tell their primary care doctor and note it in the chart. If I can't reach them, I keep trying and record each attempt.
Walk me through how you tell a patient they have a serious diagnosis, such as cancer.
Your skill with the hardest conversations in the work.
A structured approach: private setting, find out what they know, give a warning, say it plainly, respond to emotion, agree on next steps.

I find a private room, sit down and hand my pager to a colleague if I can. I ask what they already know and how much detail they want. I give a short warning, then say it plainly: the biopsy shows cancer. Then I stop and let them react. I name the emotion I see, and before we end we agree on the next step and when we will talk again.
You smell alcohol on a colleague who is about to see patients. What do you do?
Whether you put patient safety first while treating a colleague fairly.
Acts at once to keep the colleague away from patients, privately and with respect, then reports through the proper channel so help can start.

Patients come first, so it can't wait. I speak to the colleague privately, say what I noticed, and ask them not to see patients now. I tell the person in charge, such as the department chief, so care is covered and the right process starts. Most states have a physician health program that offers confidential help. Staying silent protects no one, including the colleague.

platform-engineer.heading: Platform engineer questions
qs: What is a golden path, and why would a platform team build one?
Whether you understand the core idea behind an internal platform.
A supported, easy default way to build and ship, with good practice built in, that teams choose because it saves them work.

A golden path is the standard, supported way to create and run a service: a template, a pipeline, logging and alerts already wired in. Teams can leave it, but they should not want to. It lets a new service reach production in a day, not a month, and security and reliability come built in instead of being added later.
How do you know whether your platform is actually helping the teams that use it?
Whether you treat the platform as a product with users.
Measures adoption and developer outcomes such as lead time and deploy frequency, and talks to users, not just uptime.

I treat the other teams as customers. I track how many services use the platform, how long it takes a new service to reach production, and deploy frequency and change failure rate. Each quarter I also sit with a few teams and watch them ship. If people build workarounds, that tells me more than any dashboard does.
In Kubernetes, what is the difference between resource requests and limits?
Your grasp of how shared clusters schedule and constrain workloads.
Requests drive scheduling; limits cap use. Going over a CPU limit means throttling; going over a memory limit gets the container killed.

A request is what the scheduler reserves when it picks a node, so it decides where the pod fits. A limit is the ceiling. If a container hits its CPU limit it gets throttled and runs slower. If it goes over its memory limit it is killed, which shows up as OOMKilled. So memory limits need to be set from real usage, with some headroom.
Several teams share one cluster. How do you stop one team from hurting the others?
How you design multi-tenancy and isolation on shared infrastructure.
Separate namespaces, access control, resource quotas, default limits and network policies, plus a clear rule for workloads that need their own cluster.

Each team gets its own namespace, and role-based access lets them change only their own. Resource quotas cap what a namespace can use, and default requests and limits catch pods that set none. Pods can talk to each other freely by default, so I add network policies to block traffic between teams. Anything with strict compliance needs gets its own cluster.
Someone changed a setting by hand in the cloud console, and now your infrastructure code wants to undo it. What do you do?
How you handle drift between code and real infrastructure.
Does not blindly apply. Finds out why it changed, then either puts the change into code or reverts it, and closes the gap that allowed it.

I do not just apply the plan, because the change might be an incident fix holding production up. I find who made it and why. If it should stay, I add it to the code so the plan shows no changes. If not, we revert it at a planned time. Then I look at why hand edits were possible, for example by making console access read-only for most people.
A team wants to skip the standard deploy pipeline and use their own tool. How do you respond?
Your judgement in balancing team freedom with a supported standard.
Asks what need the platform is not meeting, sets clear minimum requirements for going off path, and feeds the gap back into the roadmap.

First I ask what is missing, because a team leaving the golden path is feedback. Often it is one feature we can add. If they still need their own tool, that is fine on a few conditions: it meets our security and audit rules, it sends the same logs and metrics, and they own its support. I add their need to our roadmap so the next team does not leave.
You must make a breaking change to a shared module that forty teams use. How do you roll it out?
How you change shared infrastructure without breaking its users.
Versioned releases, old and new supported side by side, a migration guide or tooling, a clear deadline, and tracking who has moved.

I release it as a new major version so nobody gets it by surprise, and keep the old version working for a set period, say one quarter. I write a short migration guide and, where I can, a script that makes the change for them. I track which teams have moved, help the slow ones directly, and only remove the old version once usage is near zero.
Walk me through upgrading your production Kubernetes clusters to a newer version.
Whether you can plan a risky platform upgrade that touches every team.
Checks for removed APIs, upgrades one minor version at a time, test clusters first, control plane before nodes, drains nodes carefully.

I read the release notes and scan every team's manifests for APIs the new version removes, then help teams fix them first. I upgrade one minor version at a time, test clusters before production. The control plane goes first, then node pools, draining nodes a few at a time so disruption budgets are respected. I announce the window and watch error rates after each step.
You pushed a new base build image and now every team's CI builds are failing. What do you do?
How you own and recover from a mistake that blocks many teams.
Rolls back first, tells people fast, finds the cause after, and changes the release process so one push cannot break everyone.

I roll back to the previous image right away, then post in the shared channel that builds are failing because of my change and should recover once teams rerun them. Once things are green I find the cause. Then I fix the process: new images go to a few volunteer teams first, and teams can pin a version instead of always pulling the latest one.
How do you let teams create their own infrastructure without letting them build something unsafe or very expensive?
How you design self-service with guardrails instead of ticket queues.
Templates with safe defaults, policy checked automatically in the pipeline and at deploy time, quotas and budget alerts, and clear error messages.

Teams pick from templates that already have encryption, tagging and sensible sizes. Rules are written as code and checked in the pipeline and again when resources are created, so a public storage bucket or an untagged database is rejected with a message saying how to fix it. Each team gets a budget with alerts. Teams move fast, and nobody waits on a ticket for normal requests.

policy.heading: Policy and government affairs questions
qs: Walk me through how a federal agency rule goes from proposal to final.
Whether you know the notice-and-comment process that most of the regulatory work runs on.
The proposed rule, the public comment period, the agency's duty to answer significant comments, and the final rule with a delayed effective date.

The agency publishes a proposed rule in the Federal Register with a comment period, and anyone can comment in the public docket. The agency must consider significant comments and explain its response in the preamble of the final rule. The final rule is also published and usually takes effect at least 30 days later. Before a proposal, I watch the agency's regulatory agenda.
What makes a comment letter actually change an agency's final rule?
Your understanding of what agencies weigh in written submissions.
Agencies do not count votes; evidence, legal arguments tied to the statute, and workable alternatives do. It also builds the record for any later challenge.

Agencies do not count votes, so a thousand form letters weigh less than one solid comment. What moves them is cost or feasibility data, a legal argument tied to the statute, and a workable alternative with exact proposed text. I write it so a staffer can lift a paragraph into the final rule, and so our points are in the record if a court reviews it.
We track dozens of bills and rules. How do you decide which ones get your time?
How you set priorities across a large policy portfolio.
A simple screen of business impact against the real chance the measure moves, reviewed often, with low-priority items still watched.

I score each item on two things: how much it would cost or help the business, and how likely it is to move this session. A bill with a sponsor on the committee and a hearing scheduled ranks above a messaging bill. High impact and high likelihood get active work, the rest get a watch list. I review the list every two weeks, because a quiet bill can jump onto a must-pass vehicle.
You have a first meeting with a congressional staffer on our issue. How do you prepare, and what do you leave behind?
How you run a meeting with legislative staff.
Research on the member and the district, a short clear ask, local impact, and a one-page leave-behind; then follow-up on what was promised.

I read the member's committee seats, past votes and statements, and find our employees or sites in the district. I go in with one clear ask, explained in under five minutes, and local numbers. I leave a one-page summary with my contact details. Within a day I send a thank-you and anything I promised, and I log the meeting for our disclosure records.
What disclosure and ethics rules do you check before lobbying, federally or in a new state?
Whether you know the compliance rules that govern your own work.
Lobbying Disclosure Act registration and reports, House and Senate gift rules, and each state's own lobbying law, with counsel involved.

Federally, I check whether our activity crosses the Lobbying Disclosure Act thresholds, that we are registered, and that quarterly activity and semiannual contribution reports are right. I check House and Senate gift rules before any meal or event. In a new state I read its lobbying law, since registration triggers and gift limits differ, and some states cover procurement contacts.
Our trade association is about to take a position that hurts us. What do you do?
How you handle a conflict inside a coalition you belong to.
Raise it early through the right channel with a concrete alternative, accept that you may lose, and keep the option to speak separately.

I raise it early in the working group, not after the vote, with data on how it hits us and alternative wording. I look for other members with the same problem. If we still lose, I ask the association to stay silent on that point or I tell leadership we may file our own comments. I keep it professional, because we need that coalition on the next ten issues.
You gave a legislative staffer a figure that turned out to be wrong. What do you do?
How you handle a mistake that touches your credibility with government.
Correct it quickly, in writing, before it is used, with the right number and its source. Credibility outweighs a weaker argument.

I call the staffer the same day and follow up in writing with the corrected figure and where it comes from. I do not wait to see if anyone notices. Then I find how the error happened, usually a stale internal number, and add a second check. Staff trust is the whole job; a weaker number told honestly is better than a strong one that falls apart in a hearing.
How would you build a coalition with groups that disagree with us on other issues?
Your skill at coalition building around a narrow shared interest.
A tightly defined shared goal, clear ground rules on what the coalition speaks to, and credit shared with partners.

I define the one outcome we share, say a fix to a single rule, and keep the coalition's voice to that. I agree ground rules up front: who signs letters, who speaks to press, and what is out of scope. Groups we fight elsewhere often bring credibility we lack, like a consumer group. I share credit and never surprise a partner with a public move.
A bill that hurts us has just passed committee. Leadership wants it stopped. How do you approach the next steps?
Your judgement on strategy once a bill gains momentum.
A realistic read of the odds, more than one path (floor, the other chamber, amendments, the rule that follows), and honest advice to leadership.

First I tell leadership the odds honestly; a bill out of committee is not law, but it has momentum. I would work three paths at once: floor votes and amendments to fix the worst sections, the other chamber's committee, and the agency that would write the rules. Often the best realistic win is a narrower amendment, and I would say so rather than promise a kill.
The CEO asks you to send a company check to a federal candidate who supports our bill. What do you do?
Whether you know the basic campaign finance limits on corporate money.
Corporate treasury money cannot go to federal candidates; personal giving and a company PAC funded voluntarily are the options, and state law differs.

I would stop the check before it goes out. A corporation cannot contribute from its treasury to a federal candidate. The CEO can give personally within the legal limit. If we have a PAC, it can give from voluntary contributions by eligible employees. For state races I would check that state's law, since some allow corporate giving, and I would bring in counsel.

power-electronics.heading: Power electronics engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between a buck and a boost converter?
Whether you know the basic converter topologies well enough to explain them quickly.
Buck steps voltage down, boost steps it up, with the ideal duty-cycle relations and where the inductor sits in each.

A buck steps the voltage down: in continuous conduction the output is about the duty cycle times the input. A boost steps it up: the output is the input divided by one minus the duty cycle. In a buck the inductor is on the output, so output current is smooth. In a boost it is on the input, so input current is smooth and output current is pulsed.
Why would you use a synchronous rectifier instead of a diode in a low-voltage buck converter?
Your grasp of conduction losses and the trade-off that comes with them.
A MOSFET's on-resistance loss beats a diode's fixed drop at low voltage, at the cost of a second driver and careful dead time.

A diode drops around half a volt, so at 10 A that can be close to 5 W when it conducts most of the period. A MOSFET with a few milliohms of on-resistance loses far less. The cost is a second gate driver and dead time: both switches must be off briefly so they never conduct together, and during that gap the body diode carries the current.
