Where do switching losses come from in a hard-switched MOSFET, and how do you reduce them?
Whether you understand the physics behind the loss budget.
Voltage and current overlap during edges, output capacitance energy at turn-on, gate drive loss, all scaling with frequency, plus real ways to cut them.

During each edge the switch briefly has voltage across it and current through it, and that overlap turns into heat. At hard turn-on, the energy stored in the output capacitance is also dumped into the channel. All of it scales with frequency. I cut it with a stronger gate drive, a better device, soft switching like zero-voltage switching, or a lower frequency if the magnetics allow.
Walk me through how you choose the inductor for a buck converter.
Your method for sizing magnetics, not just picking a part number from a catalog.
A ripple target sets the inductance, peak current sets the saturation rating, and copper and core loss set the temperature rise.

I pick a ripple current, often 20 to 40 percent of full load, and solve L = (Vin - Vout) x D / (ripple x fsw) at the highest input voltage, where ripple is worst. Then I check that saturation current is above load current plus half the ripple, with margin when hot. Last, I estimate copper and core loss to confirm it stays within its temperature rating.
On a buck converter layout, which loop do you route first, and why?
Whether you know where parasitic inductance does the most damage on a board.
The hot loop of input capacitor and both switches, kept small with a ground plane right under it to limit ringing, spikes and EMI.

The hot loop: input capacitor, high-side switch, low-side switch and back. Its current jumps on every edge, so any inductance in it causes ringing, voltage spikes on the switches and EMI. I place a small ceramic capacitor right at the switches, keep the loop tight, and return it on a solid ground plane on the next layer so the fields cancel.
How do you measure ringing on a switch node, and what can go wrong with the probe?
Your bench skill and whether your measurements can be trusted.
A short ground connection, enough bandwidth, and differential or isolated probes for floating nodes, never a scope with its ground lifted.

I take off the long ground clip and use a short spring ground at the tip, because a few inches of lead adds inductance that creates ringing that is not really there. The probe and scope need enough bandwidth for the edge. For a floating node like a high-side gate, I use a differential or isolated probe, never a scope with its ground lifted, which can put line voltage on the case.
For a new design, how do you choose between silicon, silicon carbide and gallium nitride switches?
Your judgement in matching device technology to voltage, frequency and cost.
A choice driven by voltage class, switching frequency, thermal needs and cost, with awareness that each needs a different gate drive.

I start from voltage, frequency and cost. For a 48-volt server converter, silicon MOSFETs are cheap and proven, and GaN pays off if I need high frequency and small size. For an 800-volt EV system, SiC is the usual pick: it blocks high voltage with low loss and handles heat well. GaN parts today mostly sit at 650 volts and below. Then I check the gate drive each one needs.
How do you know your control loop is stable, and what margins do you aim for?
Whether you verify stability by measurement rather than trusting a simulation.
A measured loop gain with clear phase and gain margin targets, crossover well below switching frequency, confirmed by a load step test.

I measure the loop gain with a network analyzer, injecting a small signal across a resistor in the feedback path. I look for at least 45 degrees of phase margin and around 10 dB of gain margin, with crossover well below the switching frequency, often a tenth to a fifth of it. Then I run a load step: a clean recovery with little ringing confirms the numbers.
Your prototype keeps killing the low-side MOSFET when the high-side turns on. How do you find the cause?
How you debug a destructive failure methodically instead of swapping parts.
Measure first: gate voltage for false turn-on, drain peak against rating, dead time. Then fix the root cause, not the symptom.

I run at low input voltage with a current-limited supply and watch the low-side gate during the high-side edge. The fast voltage rise can pull that gate up through the Miller capacitance and cause shoot-through. I also check the drain peak against the rating and the dead time. Fixes include a stiffer gate pull-down, a negative off voltage, a slower edge or a snubber.
You add an EMI input filter and the converter starts oscillating. What is going on?
Your understanding of how a filter and a regulated converter interact as one system.
A regulated converter acts as a negative input resistance; the filter's output impedance must stay well below it, usually with damping added.

A regulated converter draws constant power, so when its input voltage rises its current falls: it behaves like a negative resistance. If the filter's output impedance peak comes close to the converter's input impedance, the pair becomes unstable. I compare the two impedances, keep the filter's well below, and add damping, for example a resistor and capacitor across the filter capacitor.

power-plant-operator.heading: Power plant operations questions
qs: What do you cover when you hand over a shift?
Whether you pass on the plant state so nothing is lost between crews.
Unit status, abnormal conditions, equipment out of service and clearances, open work, and a walk of the boards together.

I go through each unit's load and status, any alarms that are in and why, equipment out of service and the clearances hung, and work still open. We look at the boards and logs together, and I don't leave until my relief says they have the shift. If something is unusual, I say it out loud, not just write it in the log.
Walk me through the steam cycle of a fossil plant in plain words.
Your grasp of how the main parts of the plant work together.
A clear loop: pump, boiler, turbine, condenser, back to the pump, plus why the condenser vacuum matters.

Feedwater pumps push water into the boiler, where the heat from the fuel turns it into high-pressure steam. The steam spins the turbine, which turns the generator. Leaving the turbine, the steam goes to the condenser, where cooling water turns it back into water under vacuum. That vacuum lets the turbine get more work out of the steam. The water is then heated and pumped back to the boiler.
Why is drum level watched so closely on a drum boiler, both high and low?
Your understanding of one of the main boiler protections.
Low level can starve and overheat tubes; high level carries water into the steam and toward the turbine. Both are protected by alarms and trips.

Low level means the waterwall tubes can run short of water and overheat, which can rupture them. High level lets water carry over with the steam, which can damage the superheater and send water into the turbine. I watch level, steam flow and feedwater flow together, and I remember that level swells for a moment when pressure drops fast, so I don't overcorrect.
Walk me through hanging a clearance on a pump so a mechanic can open it.
Whether you can isolate equipment so others can work on it safely.
Stop the pump, lock out the motor, close and tag discharge then suction, bleed to zero, verify, and get an independent check.

I stop the pump, rack out or lock the breaker, and try a local start to prove it's dead. I close and tag the discharge, then the suction, plus any seal or cooling lines. I open vents and drains and confirm zero pressure and a safe temperature. A second operator checks every tag against the clearance sheet before I release it to maintenance.
What has to match before you close the generator breaker onto the grid?
Your knowledge of synchronizing, a task where a mistake can damage the generator.
Phase sequence, voltage, frequency and phase angle, with the synchroscope turning slowly in the fast direction and the breaker closed just before 12 o'clock.

Phase rotation has to be right, which is proven at commissioning. Then I match voltage to the bus, and set the generator slightly faster than the grid so it picks up load instead of motoring. I watch the synchroscope turn slowly clockwise and close just before 12 o'clock to allow for breaker closing time, with the sync check relay as a backstop.
Grid frequency drops suddenly after another plant trips. What does your unit do, and what do you do?
Whether you understand how your unit supports the grid.
The governor raises output automatically through droop; the operator watches limits, doesn't fight the response, and follows dispatch.

The governor sees the speed drop and opens the control valves to pick up load in proportion to the drop, before anyone touches a thing. I watch steam pressure, temperatures and the boiler, which has to catch up, and keep us inside limits. I don't pull it back to the old setpoint on my own; I follow the dispatcher as the grid recovers.
Condenser vacuum is slowly getting worse on your unit. How do you work it out?
How you troubleshoot a common problem before it trips the unit.
Checks the usual causes in a sensible order: cooling water, air removal, gland seal, air leaks, and reduces load if it keeps falling.

First I confirm it on a second indication. Then circulating water: pumps, flow, inlet temperature, fouled screens. Next the air removal, the ejectors or vacuum pumps, and gland seal steam pressure. If those look fine, I suspect an air leak and have someone check flanges and valves under vacuum. If it keeps falling, I reduce load before it reaches the trip.
Tell me about an operating mistake you made, or nearly made, and what changed afterward.
Whether you own errors and fix the cause, not just the moment.
An honest story, reported quickly, with a lesson that changed a procedure, a label or a habit.

During a lineup I opened a drain on the wrong heater; the two valves looked alike and sat side by side. A level alarm came in within a minute and I closed it. I reported it to my supervisor that shift. We relabeled both valves, and now I touch the tag and read it aloud before I turn any valve.
Turbine bearing vibration is climbing toward the trip setpoint and dispatch wants you to hold full load for the evening peak. What do you do?
Whether you put the equipment and the people ahead of the schedule.
Follows the alarm procedure, reduces load if needed, tells dispatch early, and never bypasses the protection.

I follow the alarm response: which bearing, the trend, oil temperature and pressure, and any change in steam temperatures. If it keeps rising, I reduce load as the procedure says and call dispatch right away so they can find the megawatts elsewhere. I won't block the trip to make the peak; a damaged turbine is out for months.
The unit trips with no warning. Walk me through your first few minutes.
How you take control after a trip and bring the unit to a safe state.
Verify the trip is complete, protect the turbine and boiler, check auxiliaries and power, then find the cause before any restart.

I confirm the stop valves are closed, the generator breaker is open and speed is falling. I check that station power transferred, the lube oil pumps are running, and later that the turbine reaches turning gear. I verify the fuel is off and the boiler is safe, call dispatch and my supervisor, and read the first-out alarm. No restart until we know why.

power-systems.heading: Power systems engineer questions
qs: Why do power engineers work in per-unit, and how do you pick the bases?
Whether you have the basic tool of system studies in hand.
One base MVA for the whole system, base kV set by transformer ratios in each zone, and the payoff: transformers drop out and errors stand out.

I pick one base MVA for the whole system and a base kV for each voltage zone, following the transformer ratios. Base impedance is kV squared over MVA. A transformer then has the same impedance on both sides, and values land near 1, so a bus at 0.6 per unit or an impedance ten times too large jumps out at once.
In a load flow study, what are the slack, PV and PQ buses?
Your grasp of how a load flow model is set up.
What is fixed and what is solved at each bus type, and that a generator hitting its reactive limit stops holding voltage.

The slack bus holds voltage magnitude and angle fixed and picks up whatever power is left over, including losses. A PV bus is usually a generator: real power and voltage are set, reactive power and angle are solved. A PQ bus is a load: real and reactive power are set, voltage is solved. If a generator hits its reactive limit, the program treats it as PQ.
Customers at the end of a long rural feeder report low voltage at peak load. What do you look at?
How you work a common distribution problem in order, from data to fix.
Confirm with measurements first, then try the cheaper fixes (regulator settings, capacitors, load transfer) before new conductor.

First I confirm it: meter data or a recorder at the end of the line, compared with ANSI C84.1 Range A. Then I run the feeder model at peak. Options in rough cost order: adjust the substation regulator or line drop compensation, add switched capacitors to cut reactive current, add a line regulator midway, move load to another feeder, and last, bigger conductor.
Walk me through an arc flash study for an industrial plant.
Whether you know the steps and the standards behind an arc flash label.
Data, short circuit, coordination for clearing times, IEEE 1584 for incident energy, NFPA 70E for labels, and minimum fault cases checked too.

I build the model from the one-line, utility fault data, cables, transformers and every protective device. I run short circuit, then coordination to get clearing times. Incident energy comes from IEEE 1584. I run both maximum and minimum source cases, since lower current can trip slower and release more energy. The results go on labels and in the safe work program under NFPA 70E.
What drives the design of a substation ground grid?
Whether you know how a grid keeps people safe during a ground fault, following IEEE 80.
Touch and step voltage limits set by clearing time and surface layer, soil resistivity measured on site, and the share of fault current that enters the grid.

The goal is keeping touch and step voltages under IEEE 80 limits during a ground fault. Those limits depend on fault clearing time and the surface layer, like crushed rock. I need measured soil resistivity, usually from a Wenner four-pin test, and the part of the fault current that enters the earth. If the grid fails, I add conductors, tighten spacing, add rods or extend the rock.
A 50 MW solar plant will connect near one of your substations. What changes for protection?
Whether you understand how inverter-based sources behave in a fault.
Inverters give limited fault current set by their controls, so overcurrent, directional or distance elements may not respond as expected; studies must use the real model.

An inverter gives fault current set by its controls, often little more than its rating, unlike a spinning generator. Overcurrent relays may barely see a fault, and directional or distance elements may misread it. I would get the maker's fault model, re-run the studies, and check ride-through rules under IEEE 2800 or 1547.
To save money, a client wants one substation transformer instead of two. How do you respond?
How you weigh cost against reliability and put the risk in front of the client.
No flat refusal: show what a transformer failure means in outage time and cost, offer middle options, and let the client decide in writing.

I would show what one transformer means: if it fails, the site is out until a replacement arrives, and large units can take many months. I would put a cost on that outage next to the cost of the second unit. Then I would offer middle options, like a tie to another feeder or a pad and connections for a mobile substation. It is their call, but I document the decision.
A plant adding many variable frequency drives asks if it will meet IEEE 519. How do you answer?
Your knowledge of harmonic limits and where they apply.
Limits apply at the point of common coupling, current limits depend on the short-circuit to load current ratio, and capacitor banks can cause resonance.

IEEE 519 limits apply at the point of common coupling with the utility, not at each drive. Current limits depend on the ratio of short-circuit current to load current. I would model the drive harmonics, check current and voltage distortion, and look for resonance with capacitor banks. Fixes include line reactors, multipulse drives or active filters.
After energizing a new feeder, you find the relay settings used the wrong current transformer ratio. What do you do?
How you own a mistake that leaves equipment less protected than it should be.
Report it at once, assess and cover the risk, correct and verify the settings, then check the rest of the job and fix the process.

This happened to me: the relay was set for 600:5 but the CT was wired on the 1200:5 tap, so the relay saw half the real current. I told the operations lead that day, confirmed the backup protection covered the feeder, and issued corrected settings. Then I checked every relay in that package and added an in-service load check to our commissioning steps.

pricing.heading: Pricing and economics questions
qs: What is the difference between markup and margin?
Whether you have the basic pricing arithmetic right.
Markup is profit over cost, margin is profit over price, shown with a quick example and why mixing them up costs money.

Markup is profit divided by cost. Margin is profit divided by price. If an item costs $60 and sells for $80, the $20 profit is a 33% markup but only a 25% margin. I always label which one I mean, because a quote built on the wrong one quietly gives away the profit we planned.
An elasticity estimate comes back at -1.5. What does that tell you?
Your grasp of price elasticity and what it means for revenue.
A 1% price rise cuts volume by about 1.5%, so demand is elastic and revenue falls with a price increase, with the note that revenue is not profit.

For small changes, a 1% price increase cuts units sold by about 1.5%. Volume moves more than price, so demand is elastic and raising price would lower revenue. But revenue is not profit. Before I recommend a cut, I check margins, because selling more units at a thin margin can still lose money.
When would you use cost-plus pricing, and when value-based pricing?
Whether you know the main pricing approaches and their limits.
Cost-plus is simple and fits commodity or contract work; value-based ties price to what the customer gains and needs evidence of that value.

Cost-plus adds a set markup to cost. It is quick and easy to defend, so it fits commodity goods or contracts that require it. But it ignores what the customer will pay. Value-based pricing starts from the benefit to the customer, like time or money saved, and prices below that. It earns more but needs real customer research.
We sell at a 40% gross margin and want to cut price 10%. How much more volume do we need to keep the same gross profit?
Whether you can run the break-even math on a price change.
About 33% more units, worked out per unit, plus the point that most people wrongly guess 10%.

Take a $100 item: cost is $60 and gross profit is $40. After a 10% cut the price is $90 and profit per unit drops to $30. To keep the same total profit I need 40 divided by 30, about 1.33 times the volume, so roughly 33% more units. People often guess 10%, which is why so many price cuts lose money.
How do you gather competitor pricing, and where are the limits?
Your competitor research methods and your sense of the legal lines.
Public and customer-facing sources only. Never discuss or exchange prices with competitors, which creates antitrust risk.

I use public price lists and websites, quotes any customer could get, third-party market data, and win-loss notes from our sales team. The hard line: I never talk to a competitor about prices or plans, and I do not use confidential documents a new hire brought from a rival. Sharing price information between competitors can break antitrust law.
What is a price waterfall, and what do you look for in one?
Whether you can trace where list price leaks away before it reaches the bank.
Steps from list price down to pocket price: discounts, rebates, payment terms, freight. Look for leakage that is large, uneven or not tied to volume.

It starts at list price and subtracts each give-away: invoice discounts, volume rebates, early-payment terms, free freight, co-op money. What is left is the pocket price we actually keep. I compare it across customers. Last time I found small accounts getting bigger rebates than large ones, which no one had decided on purpose.
Our main competitor just cut prices 15%. Sales wants us to match by Friday. What do you do?
Your judgement under pressure when a price war could start.
Gathers facts before reacting, checks which customers are at risk, weighs targeted responses against a blanket match.

First I check what was cut: all products or a few, list or net price, and for how long. Then I ask sales which deals are actually at risk. Matching across the board costs margin on customers who were never going to leave. Usually I suggest a targeted answer, like help on specific competitive deals, and review the data again in a few weeks.
You estimated elasticity from two years of sales history and got a positive number: higher prices, more sales. What went wrong?
Whether you spot confounding in observational price data.
Prices moved with demand, such as seasons or promotions, so the estimate is biased; control for those drivers or use test data.

Most likely prices went up when demand was already strong, like peak season, so the model credits price for what demand did. Promotions with ads and displays muddy it too. I would add controls for season, promotion, ads and distribution, and look for clean price changes. If none exist, I would push for a small controlled test instead of trusting history.
Leadership wants a 6% increase across all customers next quarter. How do you model it and roll it out?
How you turn a price decision into a plan with numbers and risks.
Segments by sensitivity and contract terms, models churn scenarios, suggests exceptions, prepares sales and tracks results after launch.

I split customers by size, contract terms and past reaction to increases, then model low, mid and high churn for each group. I check how much notice contracts require. If a few large accounts look risky, I propose a smaller step for them. Sales gets talking points before customers hear. After launch I track churn and extra discounting monthly against the model.

privacy.heading: Privacy questions
qs: What is the difference between a controller and a processor, and what are the CCPA equivalents?
Whether you know the basic roles that decide who carries which duties.
The controller decides why and how data is processed; the processor acts on its instructions. The CCPA terms are business and service provider or contractor.

The controller decides the purpose and the means, so it owns the duties to people, like notices and requests. The processor handles data only on the controller's documented instructions, under a contract. Under the CCPA the matching terms are business and service provider, or contractor. A processor that starts using data for its own purposes becomes a controller for that use.
Why not just rely on consent for everything under GDPR?
Your grasp of the six lawful bases and when each one fits.
Consent must be freely given and can be withdrawn at any time. Contract, legal obligation or legitimate interests often fit better.

GDPR gives six bases: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task and legitimate interests. Consent has to be free, specific and as easy to withdraw as to give. If we would process the data anyway, say for payroll, asking for consent misleads people. I pick the basis that truly fits before processing starts and record why.
Walk me through how you would build a data map for a company that has none.
How you find out what personal data exists and where it goes.
Start from systems and business processes, interview owners, record data, purpose, basis, recipients, transfers and retention, and keep it current.

I start with a list of systems from IT and procurement, then interview each team owner about their processes. For each one I record what data, whose, why, the lawful basis, who receives it, where it is stored, any transfers abroad and how long we keep it. That becomes our record of processing. I tie updates to procurement and project intake so it does not go stale.
When does GDPR require a data protection impact assessment, and what goes into one?
Whether you know the triggers and the content of a DPIA.
Required when processing is likely to be high risk, like large-scale sensitive data or systematic monitoring. It covers purpose, necessity, risks and measures.

It is required before processing that is likely to result in a high risk to people. Examples are profiling with significant effects, large-scale health data and wide monitoring of public areas. It describes the processing, tests necessity and proportionality, weighs risks to people and sets measures to reduce them. If high risk remains, we consult the regulator first.
A customer emails support asking for "all the data you have on me." Walk me through what happens.
How you run a data subject access request from intake to reply.
Log it, verify identity in proportion to the risk, search all systems, remove other people's data, and reply within the legal deadline.

Support logs it the same day and sends it to us. I verify identity in proportion to the risk, often by matching account details. Then I search every system on the data map, not just the CRM, and review the results to remove other people's data. Under GDPR the reply is due within one month, extendable in complex cases; under the CCPA, 45 days.
Our website receives a Global Privacy Control signal from a California visitor. What must we do?
Whether you know the CCPA opt-out rights for selling and sharing data.
Treat it as a valid request to opt out of sale and sharing for that browser, and for the account if known, with no extra steps from the visitor.

Under the CCPA regulations, an opt-out preference signal like GPC counts as a request to opt out of the sale and sharing of personal information. Sharing here means cross-context behavioral advertising. So that browser must not fire ad pixels that sell or share data, and if the visitor is logged in, I apply it to the account too. We cannot make them fill out a form to make it count.
Marketing picked a new email vendor that stores data in the US. What do you check before EU customer data goes there?
How you review a processor and an international data transfer.
A processor contract with the required terms, a security review, and a valid transfer tool such as Data Privacy Framework certification or standard contractual clauses.

First, a data processing agreement with the Article 28 terms: act only on our instructions, security, sub-processor approval, help with requests and deletion at the end. I review their security controls. For the transfer, I check whether they are certified under the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework; if not, we sign standard contractual clauses and do a transfer impact assessment.
The product team wants to use years of customer support chats to train an AI model. How do you approach it?
Your judgement on reusing personal data for a new purpose.
Checks whether the new purpose is compatible, the lawful basis, what notices said, sensitive content and minimization, often through a DPIA.

Those chats were collected to solve tickets, so training a model is a new purpose. I would check whether it is compatible with the original one, what basis applies, and what our privacy notice told people. Chats often hold health or payment details, so I would push for filtering and de-identification first. Likely a DPIA, and a clear way for people to object.
A customer asks us to delete their data, but legal has a litigation hold on their account. What do you do?
How you handle a conflict between a privacy right and another legal duty.
Erasure has exceptions, including legal claims. Keep only what the hold covers, delete the rest, and tell the person what is kept and why.

The right to erasure is not absolute. GDPR allows keeping data needed for legal claims, and the CCPA has similar exceptions. I confirm with legal exactly what the hold covers, delete or restrict everything else, and lock the held data from other use. Then I tell the customer what we deleted, what we kept, the reason, and that we will delete it when the hold ends.
An employee emailed a spreadsheet of 2,000 customers' names and account numbers to the wrong outside address. Walk me through your first 72 hours.
How you contain and assess a breach and decide who must be notified.
Contain first, assess risk and who is affected, notify the regulator within 72 hours where GDPR requires it, check each US state law, and document everything.

First, contain: try to recall the email, ask the recipient to delete it and confirm in writing. Then assess what was exposed and where the people live. Under GDPR, the regulator must hear within 72 hours of us becoming aware unless risk is unlikely. US state laws differ in triggers and timing, so I check each state with counsel. Every step goes into the breach log.

procurement.heading: Procurement questions
qs: What is the difference between an RFI, an RFQ and an RFP?
Whether you know which sourcing tool fits which purchase.
RFI to learn the market, RFQ when the spec is fixed and price decides, RFP when the solution itself is part of the choice.

An RFI, request for information, is for learning who is out there and what they can do. An RFQ, request for quotation, is for a clear spec, like 200 laptops of a set model, where price and delivery decide. An RFP, request for proposal, is for when suppliers propose how to meet the need, like a new IT service, and I score more than price.
What is a three-way match, and why does it matter?
Your grasp of the control that stops paying for goods that were not ordered or received.
PO, receiving record and invoice must agree on item, quantity and price before payment; mismatches are held and resolved.

Before an invoice is paid, it is matched against the purchase order and the receiving report. Item, quantity and price must agree within the set tolerance. If we ordered 500 units at $4, received 480, and were billed for 500 at $4.20, the invoice is held until the supplier corrects it or someone with authority approves the difference.
Two suppliers quote the same machine part, and one is 10% cheaper. How do you decide?
Whether you look at total cost of ownership, not just unit price.
Compares quality, lead time, freight, minimum order, payment terms and the cost of failures, and puts numbers on each.

I build a total cost view. The cheaper one may ship from overseas with a 12-week lead time, a large minimum order and freight on top, so we hold more stock and tie up cash. I also check defect rates and terms. If the lower price disappears once I add freight, holding cost and a 2% scrap rate, I choose the other supplier and show the math.
What is the difference between sole source and single source?
Your precision on a term that changes the risk and the paperwork.
Sole source: only one supplier exists. Single source: others exist but you chose one. The second is a choice you can revisit; the first needs a justification.

Sole source means only one supplier can provide it, for example because it holds the patent. Single source means others could, but we buy from one on purpose, maybe for price or quality. Single source is a choice I can revisit. Sole source needs a written justification and a closer watch on that supplier's risk.
One quote says EXW and another says DDP. What changes for us?
Whether you know how Incoterms shift cost and risk between buyer and seller.
EXW puts nearly all transport, clearance, duties and risk on the buyer; DDP puts them on the seller up to the named destination.

Under EXW, Ex Works, the seller makes the goods available at its premises, and we handle loading, freight, export and import clearance, duties and the risk in transit. Under DDP, Delivered Duty Paid, the seller carries cost and risk to our named place, import duties included. So I compare them only after adding freight, insurance and duties to the EXW price.
Walk me through how you prepare for a negotiation with a key supplier.
How you build leverage before you sit down at the table.
Knows the spend, the market and the supplier's position, sets a target and a walk-away point, and plans trade-offs in advance.

I pull our history with them: volume, price trend, on-time rate, quality issues. I check market prices and get alternative quotes, which tells me my walk-away option if we cannot agree. Then I set a target and a limit, and list what I can give, like a longer contract or a better forecast, for what I want, like price or payment terms.
A supplier announces a 12% price increase, citing raw material costs. What do you do?
How you push back on a price increase with facts rather than a flat refusal.
Asks for evidence, checks the material's share of the price against a market index, counters with a fair figure and lines up alternatives.

I ask for the cost breakdown. If steel is 40% of the part price and steel rose 10%, that supports about 4%, not 12%. I check a published index for that material, counter on that basis, and propose index-linked pricing so the price can come down too. Meanwhile I ask two other suppliers to quote in case we cannot agree.
An engineer has already promised a supplier the order and wants a PO today. How do you handle it?
Your judgement when a colleague skips the buying process.
Respects the urgency but keeps the policy: checks approval limits, gets quotes or a documented justification, and explains why without blocking.

I ask why this supplier and why today. If the amount is under our limit for competitive quotes, I can move fast. If not, I get two quick quotes or a written justification signed by the right approver. I explain that this protects the engineer too. Then I ask to be brought in before anyone talks price with a supplier next time.
You find a software contract auto-renewed for three years at a higher rate because no one gave notice. What do you do?
How you handle a contract mistake and stop it from happening again.
Reads the actual terms, asks the vendor for a fix, reports the miss honestly, and sets up notice-date alerts for every contract.

First I read the contract: the notice window, the renewal term and any cap on price increases. Then I call the vendor; many will agree to a shorter term or the old rate to keep a customer, especially if we can add users. I tell my manager plainly what happened. Then I put every contract's notice date in a tracker with alerts 90 and 30 days ahead.
Your only supplier for a critical component is paying its own vendors late, and lead times are slipping. What do you do?
How you manage supply risk before it turns into a shortage.
Acts early: sizes the exposure, talks to the supplier, builds buffer stock, starts qualifying a second source and informs management and finance.

I size our exposure: weeks of stock on hand and which products stop without the part. I talk openly with the supplier's leadership. I add buffer stock where I can, start qualifying a second source with engineering now, since approval can take months, and check whether we own the tooling so we could move it. My manager and finance hear about it this week.

procurement-operations.heading: Procurement operations specialist questions
qs: What is the difference between a purchase requisition and a purchase order?
Whether you know the basic documents of the buying process.
A requisition is an internal request for approval. A PO is the official order sent to the supplier, which becomes a contract once accepted.

A requisition is an internal request: someone in the company says what they need, how many and roughly what it costs, and it goes for approval. Once it is approved, I turn it into a purchase order. That is the official document sent to the supplier with price, quantity, terms and delivery date. When the supplier accepts it, it is a contract.
Walk me through a three-way match.
Whether you understand the control that protects every payment.
The PO, the receiving record and the invoice are compared on item, quantity and price before payment, and any exceptions are held.

Before an invoice is paid, I compare three documents: the purchase order, the receiving record that shows what actually arrived, and the supplier's invoice. Item, quantity and price must agree within our tolerance. If we ordered 100, received 90 and were billed for 100, the invoice is held until the shortage is resolved or credited.
When would you set up a blanket purchase order instead of single POs?
Your judgement in choosing the right order type.
For repeated buys from one supplier, with a set period, agreed prices and a dollar cap, and with spend tracked against it.

I use one when we buy the same things from one supplier again and again, like janitorial supplies or monthly gas cylinders. One blanket PO with a set period, agreed prices and a total dollar limit replaces dozens of small POs. Each release draws down the balance. I watch that balance so we renew or re-approve before it runs out, not after.
An invoice comes in 8% higher than the PO price. What do you do?
How you handle a price variance without paying blindly or stalling the supplier.
You check the tolerance and the cause, then get either a revised and re-approved PO or a corrected invoice, and you record why.

First I check our tolerance rule. 8% is usually outside it, so the invoice is held. Then I look for the cause: a freight charge, a price increase we never agreed to, or a wrong unit. If the increase is valid, the buyer revises the PO and it is re-approved. If not, I ask the supplier for a corrected invoice. Either way, I note the reason in the system.
A manager bought equipment without a PO and now sends you the invoice to pay. How do you handle it?
Whether you can enforce policy and still keep the supplier paid.
You follow the after-the-fact process, never backdate a PO, explain the rule kindly and escalate repeat cases.

The supplier delivered in good faith, so I do not leave them unpaid. I follow our after-the-fact process: the manager submits a requisition marked as a confirming order, it goes through normal approval, and I never backdate the PO. Then I explain why the rule exists and show how to order next time. If the same person keeps doing it, I report the pattern to my manager.
Someone sends three $4,000 requests to the same supplier on the same day, and anything over $10,000 needs director approval. What do you do?
Whether you spot split purchases made to get around approval limits.
You recognize the split, hold the requests, ask the requester, and route the total through the correct approval level.

Three requests to one supplier on one day that add up to $12,000 looks like a split order. I hold them and ask the requester whether it is really one purchase. Often it is impatience, not bad intent. If it is one need, I combine the three into one requisition and send it to the director. If it keeps happening, I flag it to my manager.
A supplier emails asking you to update their bank account before the next payment. What do you do?
Whether you know how payment-change fraud works and how to stop it.
You never act on the email alone. You verify by calling a known contact at a number already on file, and a second person checks the change.

I treat it as possible fraud until it is proven real, because fake bank change requests are a common scam. I do not reply to the email or call any number in it. I call our contact at the number we already have on file and confirm the request. The change needs their signed form, and a second person reviews it in the vendor file before the next payment goes out.
What do you collect and check before you set up a new supplier in the system?
Your grasp of vendor master data and the controls around it.
Legal name and tax ID from a W-9, address, remit-to and bank details, insurance where needed, and a search for duplicate records.

I get a signed W-9 so the legal name and tax ID are right for 1099 reporting. I also collect the address, the remit-to address and the bank details on our form. For service work on our site, I ask for a certificate of insurance. Before any of that, I search the vendor file for duplicates, since two records for one supplier is how double payments happen.
A supplier confirms only 60 of the 100 units on a PO, and the rest is backordered for six weeks. How do you handle it in the system?
How you manage a partial order so records, receiving and the requester stay aligned.
You update the PO lines and dates, tell the requester, and decide whether to wait or cut the balance and source it elsewhere.

I update the PO with the confirmed date for each part, so receiving expects 60 now and 40 later. I tell the requester right away and ask if six weeks works. If it does not, I reduce the PO to 60 with a change order, close the balance, and buy the 40 from another approved supplier. That way we never wait on, or pay for, units that will not come.
Your approver is out and your manager tells you to just approve your own PO in the system. What do you do?
Whether you protect segregation of duties under pressure.
You decline politely, explain the control, and offer a proper fast path: the delegated approver or the next level up.

I would not approve my own request, even if the system let me. The person who creates a PO should not be the one who approves it. That separation is what catches errors and stops fraud. I would check who is set as the delegate for the absent approver, or route it one level up, and tell my manager how quickly I can get it approved that way.

producer.heading: Producer (games and media) questions
qs: What is the producer's job on a team, and what is it not?
Whether you understand where the producer role starts and stops.
Owns schedule, budget, risks and communication, and clears blockers. Does not make the creative calls that the director or leads own.

I own the plan: the schedule, the budget, the risk list and who needs to know what. I clear blockers so people can do their work. I don't decide how the level plays or how the episode is cut; the director and leads own that. My job is to make sure they can make those calls in time and know what each one costs.
What is a vertical slice, and why would you schedule one early?
Your grasp of a standard game production milestone.
A small part of the game at near-final quality across all disciplines, used to prove the pipeline and estimate the rest.

It is a short piece of the game, say one level or ten minutes of play, built to close to final quality in art, audio, design and code. I want it early because it shows whether the pipeline works and how long one finished minute really takes. That number makes the rest of the schedule far more honest, and it gives the publisher something real to judge.
How do you track whether a project is on budget week to week?
How you watch spending before it becomes a problem.
Compares actual spend and burn rate to plan, ties cost to progress, and flags the gap early with a forecast.

I keep a sheet with planned spend per month by department and update actuals weekly from timesheets and invoices. The key number is burn rate, how fast we spend, against progress: if we have spent 40% of the budget but finished 30% of the deliverables, that gap is the warning. I flag it to the director with a forecast to the end, not just the overage so far.
Marketing wants a popular song in our trailer. What has to happen before we can use it?
Whether you know the basics of music clearance for media.
Two rights: a sync license for the composition, usually from the publisher, and a master use license for the recording, usually from the label.

A recorded song has two sets of rights. The composition is usually controlled by a music publisher, so we need a sync license from them. The recording is usually owned by the label, so we need a master use license too. Each must cover our media, territories and term. If the master costs too much, we can license only the composition and have a cover recorded.
An artist tells you a task you estimated at five days will take ten. What do you do?
How you handle a bad estimate without blaming anyone or ignoring it.
Asks why, checks the impact on dependent work, picks between moving, simplifying or adding help, and updates the plan.

First I ask what changed: unclear specs, a tool problem or a harder task than we thought. Then I check what depends on it. If nothing downstream waits on it, I move it and update the schedule. If it blocks animation, I talk to the lead about a simpler version or moving another artist onto it. I also note the miss so similar tasks get better estimates next time.
Two leads both need the same engineer this sprint. How do you decide?
Your judgement when people compete for the same resource.
Decides by milestone priority and the critical path, gets the leads to agree, and escalates only when they can't.

I look at which task is on the critical path for the next milestone, meaning the chain of work where any delay moves the date. That one usually wins. I bring both leads together with that picture rather than deciding in private. If the priorities really tie, I take it to the director with a recommendation. The lead who waits gets a firm date for when the engineer is free.
An outsourced art vendor sends a batch that is late and below the quality bar. How do you handle it?
How you manage outside partners and protect quality.
Specific written feedback against the agreed spec, a fix plan with dates, and a backup plan if the vendor can't recover.

I review the batch with our art lead and write down exactly what misses the spec, with examples of what passes. Then I call the vendor, go through it, and agree on a fix date per asset. I check the contract for review rounds so we know what is included. Meanwhile I plan for the worst case: which assets our own team could take if the second batch also fails.
Tell me about a time a date slipped. How did you tell the people above you?
How you deliver bad news early and own it.
Told them as soon as the risk was clear, with the cause, the impact and options to choose from, not just an apology.

On a ten-episode podcast series, our host fell ill and we lost two recording weeks. The same day I knew, I emailed the executive producer with what happened, which episodes moved, and two options: push the launch two weeks, or launch on time and release the last two episodes late. They chose to launch on time. Since then I report risks when they appear, not when they land.
Midway through production, the client asks for a new feature but won't change the budget or date. What do you do?
How you handle scope creep and keep agreements intact.
Estimates the cost, shows the tradeoff in writing, and lets the client choose what gives. Never absorbs it silently.

I get the request in writing and estimate the work and its risk with the leads. Then I go back with clear options: add it and drop something of similar size, add it in a later update, or add it with more time or money. I don't absorb it quietly, because the team pays for it in crunch and the client gets a weaker product. Whatever they choose goes into a signed change order.

product-analyst.heading: Product analyst questions
qs: How would you build a funnel for our sign-up flow, and what do you look at first?
Whether you can turn a user flow into steps you can measure.
Clear steps counted as unique users within a time window. The biggest drop is split by device or source before blaming the design.

A funnel counts how many users reach each step in order, for example: landed on the sign-up page, entered an email, verified it, finished the profile. I count unique users, set a window like seven days, and find the biggest drop. Then I split it by device and source, because a drop on only one platform usually means a bug, not a design problem.
What does the DAU/MAU ratio tell you, and when can it mislead?
Your grasp of a common engagement metric and its limits.
It measures habit: the share of monthly users active on a typical day. It fits poorly for rarely needed products and can rise when casual users leave.

It is the share of monthly users who show up on an average day, so it measures habit. At 50%, a typical user comes about 15 days a month. It misleads for products people need only now and then, like a tax app. It can also rise just because casual users left: the ratio looks better while the user base shrinks.
Engineering is about to build a new feature. How do you make sure we can measure it after launch?
Whether you plan event tracking before release instead of after.
A tracking plan built from the team's questions: each event named and defined, with its properties. It is agreed with engineers and tested in a build before release.

I start from the questions the team wants answered, then list each event: its name, exactly when it fires, and its properties, like plan type or screen. I agree on a naming rule with the engineer, such as object_action. Then I check the events in a test build before release. Without that, the first weeks of data are often unusable.
You plot a retention curve for a new app. What are you looking for?
How you read retention beyond a single day-30 number.
Whether the curve flattens, which shows a core of lasting users. Newer cohorts should flatten higher if the product is improving.

I want to know if it flattens. A curve that drops fast and then levels off at, say, 25% means a core group finds lasting value. One that keeps sliding toward zero means people try it and leave. I compare curves by sign-up month to see whether newer groups level off higher, which tells us our changes are working.
What is a guardrail metric? Give an example.
Whether you protect the product from wins that cause hidden harm.
A metric the test is not meant to move but must not hurt. The acceptable limit is agreed before launch.

A guardrail is a metric we do not try to move but must not hurt. If a test sends more notifications, the goal might be sessions, and the guardrails would be unsubscribes, uninstalls and support tickets. Before launch we agree how big a drop in a guardrail would stop the release, so nobody argues about it after seeing a win.
After an app release, the count of one event doubled overnight. What do you do?
How you handle a tracking problem that looks like user behavior.
Suspect the data first. Tie the jump to the release and app version, check whether users and sessions moved too, then warn people and fix it with engineering.

First I suspect tracking, not users. I check whether the jump lines up with the release and app version, and whether users and sessions moved too. If only the event count doubled on the new version, it probably fires twice, for example on screen load and on tap. I warn the team, flag the affected dashboards, and work with engineering to fix it and mark the bad days.
A new design wins big in its first week, but the lift shrinks every day after. What is going on, and what do you do?
Whether you recognize a novelty effect and know how to test for it.
Names the novelty effect, plots the lift by day and compares new with returning users. Waits for the effect to settle before deciding.

It may be a novelty effect: regular users click the new thing because it is new, and the effect fades. I would plot the lift by day and split it by new versus returning users. New users have no old habit, so their result is closer to the lasting effect. If the lift keeps shrinking, I would run the test longer before calling it.
Your test was set to split users 50/50, but with 200,000 users you see 52% versus 48%. What do you do?
Whether you spot a sample ratio mismatch and refuse to trust the results.
Sees that a gap this size is not chance at this sample, calls it a sample ratio mismatch, and finds the cause before reading any results.

With 200,000 users, a 52/48 split is far too uneven to be chance. A chi-square test would give a tiny p-value. That is a sample ratio mismatch, and it means something is broken: a redirect that loses users, a bot filter, or logging that fails in one version. I would not read the results until I find the cause, because the groups may no longer be comparable.
A test showed no overall effect, but the PM found one segment out of twelve with a significant lift and wants to ship for it. What do you say?
How you handle slicing results after the fact.
Explains that many segments make a false positive likely. Treats the segment as a lead to test again, not as a result.

With twelve segments tested at the 0.05 level, the chance that at least one looks significant by luck alone is close to half. So one winning segment is a lead, not a result. I would ask whether we predicted it before the test and correct for the number of comparisons. If it still looks real, I would run a new test aimed at that segment.
A feature was launched to everyone without a test, and the PM asks what it did. How do you estimate the impact?
Whether you can estimate impact without a randomized test, and say how sure you are.
Looks for a natural comparison, such as a staggered rollout, and uses difference-in-differences with its parallel-trends check. States that the evidence is weaker than a test.

I would look for a natural comparison. If the feature rolled out country by country, I compare the change in launched countries with the change in countries not yet launched over the same weeks. That is difference-in-differences. It relies on both groups trending alike before launch, which I check. I also say plainly that this is weaker evidence than a randomized test.

product-designer.heading: Product designer questions
qs: What is the difference between a wireframe, a mockup and a prototype, and when do you use each?
Whether you choose the right level of detail for the question you are trying to answer.
Clear definitions tied to purpose: structure first, visuals next, interaction last, with fidelity matched to what needs testing.

A wireframe shows structure and priority with no styling. I use it to agree on layout fast. A mockup adds real visuals, type and color for visual review. A prototype is clickable, so people can try a flow. I keep fidelity as low as the question allows, because rough work invites honest feedback.
Beyond the main path, which states do you design for a typical screen?
Whether you think past the ideal screen to what users really see.
Names empty, loading, error, partial and success states, plus edge cases like long text or no permission.

I design the empty state for first use, loading, errors with a clear way to recover, partial data, and success. I also test long names, huge numbers and a user without permission. Engineers will hit all of these anyway, so I would rather decide them than leave them to guesswork.
How would you design the interaction for deleting a project?
Your judgement on preventing and recovering from costly user errors.
Matches friction to the damage: undo for recoverable actions, a specific confirmation for permanent ones, never a vague "Are you sure?".

First I ask if it can be undone. If yes, I delete at once and show an undo option, which is less annoying than a dialog. If it is permanent, I use a confirmation that names the project and what will be lost, with a clear "Delete project" button instead of "OK". For big losses I may ask the user to type the name.
A signup form has high drop-off. How would you approach redesigning it?
Your practical knowledge of form design and how you find the real cause.
Looks at where people quit first, then cuts fields, uses visible labels, sensible validation and autofill.

I would check analytics to see which field people abandon on. Then I would remove anything we do not need yet, keep one column, use labels that stay visible instead of placeholder text only, and validate when a user leaves a field rather than on every keystroke. I would support autofill and explain why we ask for sensitive data.
How do you run a usability test without leading the participant?
Whether you can get honest behavior instead of polite answers.
Task-based scenarios without interface words, think-aloud, neutral prompts, no rescuing, and watching behavior over opinions.

I give a goal, like "You want to change your delivery address," never "Click Settings." I ask them to think aloud and reply to questions with "What would you expect?" If they struggle I stay quiet longer than feels comfortable. I trust what they do more than what they say they like.
A team asks you to add a new button style to the design system for one screen. How do you decide?
How you balance consistency of a design system with real product needs.
Asks what problem the variant solves, checks existing components first, and adds only reusable, documented patterns.

I ask what the current buttons fail to do. Often an existing variant or a layout change solves it. If the need is real and likely to come up again, I add it properly, with states, usage rules and code parity. If it is a true one-off, I keep it local so the system does not fill up with exceptions.
In testing, three of five users fail a task, and a stakeholder says they just were not tech-savvy. What do you do?
How you defend findings with evidence without turning it into a fight.
Checks recruiting honestly, then shows clips and the pattern, and frames it as risk to the business.

First I check whether we recruited the right people; if not, that is a fair point. If they match our users, I show short clips of each failure at the same step. Three people stuck in one place is a pattern. I frame it as support tickets and lost signups, and propose a quick fix we can retest.
The product manager wants to ship in two weeks with no time for research. What do you do?
Your judgement on fitting research to real deadlines.
Finds fast, cheap evidence, names the riskiest assumption, and plans to learn after launch with metrics.

I would not block the launch. I would pull existing data and support tickets, then run quick tests with three or four people on a rough prototype, which fits in two or three days. I focus on the riskiest assumption. We agree on metrics to watch after launch and a date to review them.
The business asks for a cancellation flow that makes it hard for users to quit. How do you respond?
Whether you can push back on manipulative design with good arguments.
Refuses dark patterns, explains trust and legal risk, and offers honest retention options instead.

I would explain that hiding the cancel path is a dark pattern. It angers users, drives chargebacks and complaints, and regulators like the FTC have acted against deceptive design. I would offer honest options: ask why they are leaving, offer a pause or cheaper plan once, then let them cancel in a few clear steps.
After your checkout redesign launches, conversion drops 8%. Walk me through what you do.
How you investigate a problem with your own work calmly and with data.
Verifies the data, segments to find where and for whom it dropped, looks at sessions, and rolls back if needed.

First I confirm the drop is real: tracking changes and seasonal effects can fake one. Then I split by step, device and new versus returning users. If mobile users quit at payment, I watch session recordings there. If the loss is costly, I push to roll back or run the old and new versions side by side while we fix it.

product-engineer.heading: Product engineer questions
qs: How do you run a customer interview so you learn what they really need?
Whether you can get real needs out of users instead of opinions about your idea.
Asks about past behavior and real cases, avoids leading questions and pitching, and listens more than talks.

I ask about the last time they hit the problem: what they were doing, what they tried, what it cost them. I do not show my idea first or ask "would you use this?", because people say yes to be polite. I take notes on their exact words and look for the same pain across several people.
A large customer asks for a specific feature. What do you do before writing any code?
How you turn a feature request into the underlying problem.
Digs into the job behind the request, checks if other users share it, and considers simpler solutions before committing.

I ask what they are trying to get done and what they do today without the feature. Often the request is one solution to a wider problem. Then I check usage data and support tickets to see if other customers have the same pain. Only then do I decide whether to build what they asked, something simpler, or nothing.
How do you decide what goes into the first version of a feature?
Your ability to cut scope while keeping the version useful.
Starts from the one problem to solve and the question to answer, ships the smallest version that tests it, and lists what was cut.

I write down the one problem we are solving and what we need to learn. Anything that does not help with those waits. For a recent export feature we shipped CSV only, no scheduling, no custom columns. I wrote the cut items in the ticket so the team knew they were postponed, not forgotten.
When do you build a throwaway prototype instead of production code?
Whether you match the effort to the uncertainty.
Prototypes when the main risk is whether users want it or understand it; clear about throwing the prototype away, not shipping it.

When the big unknown is whether people want it or can use it, I prototype: a clickable mockup or a hacky version behind a flag for five users. It skips tests and edge cases on purpose. I tell everyone up front it gets rewritten, so nobody ships the hack because it happened to work.
How do you choose the metrics for an A/B test?
Whether you can define success before the test starts.
One primary metric tied to the goal, chosen in advance, plus guardrail metrics that must not get worse.

I pick one primary metric that the change should move, like the share of new users who finish setup, and I write it down before launch. Then I add guardrails such as page load time, error rate and cancellations. If I track twenty metrics and pick the winner afterwards, one will look good by chance.
How do you release a new feature to users safely?
Your practice with feature flags and gradual rollouts.
Ships behind a flag, rolls out in steps while watching errors and key metrics, and can turn it off without a deploy.

I put the feature behind a flag and turn it on for the team first, then a small share of users, then more in steps. At each step I check errors, latency and the metric we care about. If something looks wrong I switch the flag off, no redeploy needed. Once it is fully out, I remove the flag so old code does not pile up.
The product manager checks the A/B test every day and wants to stop it the first day it shows a significant result. What do you say?
Whether you understand the risk of peeking at test results.
Explains that repeated checks raise the false positive rate; fix the sample size in advance or use a method built for checking early.

Each time we look and could stop, we get another chance for random noise to look like a win. Checking daily and stopping at the first good day makes false wins much more likely. I would set the sample size before launch from the smallest lift we care about, run for full weeks, or use a sequential test designed for early looks.
Your test was set to split users 50/50, but with 200,000 users it shows 52% and 48%. What do you do?
Whether you spot a sample ratio mismatch and know not to trust the result.
Recognizes the gap is too large to be chance at that size, pauses the analysis, and looks for an assignment or logging bug.

With that many users, a 52/48 split is very unlikely by chance; a chi-square test would confirm it. It usually means a bug: one variant crashes before it logs, a redirect loses users, or bots land in one group. I would not read the results until I find the cause, because the groups are no longer comparable.
Your A/B test raised sign-ups by 6%, but support tickets went up too. Do you ship it?
How you weigh a win on one metric against a cost on another.
Does not ship on the primary metric alone; finds why tickets rose, estimates the net effect, and fixes the cause before deciding.

Not yet. I would read the new tickets to see what confuses people. If the new flow hides a step, the extra sign-ups may churn later or cost more in support than they bring. I would fix the confusing part, rerun the test, and also check whether the new users stay as long as the old ones.
Three months after you shipped a feature, very few people use it. What do you do?
How you handle a feature that did not work and whether you can let it go.
Checks whether users find it or it misses the need, talks to users, and is willing to improve it or remove it.

First I check whether people even see it, using the funnel from the entry point. Then I talk to a few users who tried it once and stopped. If it is a discovery problem I fix the entry point. If it solves the wrong problem, I propose removing it, because every unused feature still costs us in bugs, tests and support.

product-manager.heading: Product manager questions
qs: What makes a good customer interview question, and what makes a bad one?
Whether you can learn from users without leading them to the answer you want.
Asks about real past behavior and its cost, not opinions on future features or yes/no questions that invite polite agreement.

A bad one is “Would you use an export to Excel?” People say yes to be kind. A good one is “Tell me about the last time you needed this data outside our app. What did you do?” I ask about real events, what they tried and what it cost them. Then I stay quiet and let them talk.
What goes into a spec you hand to engineering?
Your ability to write a document a team can actually build from.
The problem, who has it, the goal and metric, scope and non-goals, flows and edge cases, open questions. The what and why, with the how left to engineers.

I start with the problem, who has it and the evidence. Then the goal and the metric we expect to move, what is in scope and what is explicitly out, and the main user flows with edge cases like empty states and errors. I end with open questions. I leave the technical design to engineers and keep the doc updated as we decide things.
Walk me through how you would score a backlog with a framework like RICE.
Whether you know a common prioritization method and where it stops being useful.
Reach times impact times confidence, divided by effort; treated as a way to compare and discuss, not as the final answer.

RICE stands for reach, impact, confidence and effort. I estimate how many users a change touches in a quarter, impact on a small scale, my confidence as a percentage, and effort in person-weeks. The score is reach times impact times confidence, divided by effort. It helps compare similar items, but the inputs are guesses, so I check the top of the list against our strategy.
How do you choose the main metric for a product, and what keeps it honest?
Your grasp of a primary metric and the guardrail metrics that protect it.
A metric tied to the value users get, paired with guardrails that catch gains made at the user's expense.

I pick a number that rises only when users get real value. For a meal-planning app, that might be weekly users who planned at least three meals. Then I add guardrails: unsubscribe rate, support tickets and page load time. If the main metric goes up while a guardrail gets worse, we may be pushing people rather than helping them.
Sales wants a firm date on the roadmap for a feature a big prospect needs. How do you respond?
How you handle roadmap commitments under commercial pressure.
Learns the prospect's real need, commits only to what the team is confident about, and is honest about uncertainty instead of inventing a date.

First I ask sales to set up a call so I hear the prospect's actual problem; often a smaller change or a workaround solves it. If it fits our plan, I give a date only once engineering has scoped it, and I share a range for anything further out. I would rather lose a promise today than break one in six months.
Your A/B test hit statistical significance on day three of a planned two-week run. Do you stop it?
Whether you understand the risk of peeking at test results.
No: checking often and stopping at the first significant result inflates false positives. Run to the planned sample and full weeks unless the test was designed for early stopping.

No. If you check a test every day and stop the first time it looks significant, you raise the chance of a false win a lot. Early results also miss weekly patterns, since weekend users behave differently. I let it run the full two weeks to the planned sample size. If we need early stopping, we design for it up front with a sequential method.
The team will miss the launch date by three weeks. What are your options?
How you trade scope, time and quality when a plan slips.
Raises it early, lays out cutting scope or moving the date, and makes the trade explicit; does not quietly cut testing or quality.

I tell stakeholders as soon as I know, not the week before. Then I lay out options. We can cut scope to the core flow that solves the main problem and ship the rest later, or keep the scope and move the date. Adding people this late rarely helps. What I will not do is skip testing to hit the date, because a broken launch costs more than a late one.
A senior executive asks you to add their idea to this quarter's roadmap, but it does not fit the strategy. What do you do?
How you push back upward without damaging the relationship.
Takes the idea seriously, finds the problem behind it, shows the trade-off in plain terms and lets the decision be made openly.

I ask what problem they want solved, because the goal is often good even if the feature is not. Then I show where it would land against our current priorities and what we would have to drop to fit it in. If they still want it, that is a valid call, but it is made openly, and I tell the team what moved and why.
Weekly active users dropped 8% the week after your release. Walk me through how you investigate.
How you diagnose a metric drop before jumping to a cause.
Rules out tracking errors first, then segments by platform, app version, region and user group, checks outside causes, then ties it to the change.

First I check the data itself: did tracking break, did an event get renamed? Then I segment the drop by platform, app version, region and new versus existing users. If it sits only on the new version, the release is the likely cause. I also check outside factors like a holiday or an outage. Once I find it, I decide with engineering whether to roll back or fix forward.
How would you decide whether to retire a feature that a small group of customers relies on?
Your judgement on removing things, not only adding them.
Weighs the ongoing cost against value to those users, talks to them, and retires with notice, a migration path and a clear date.

I measure what the feature costs us: bugs, support time, how much it slows other work. Then I look at who uses it and talk to some of them. If the cost wins, I announce it with plenty of notice, offer an export or alternative, and give a firm date. In one case, 3% of accounts used an old report, and a simple export covered nearly all of them.

product-marketing.heading: Product marketing manager questions
qs: What is the difference between positioning and messaging?
Whether you know the two building blocks of the job and which one comes first.
Positioning is the strategic choice of who the product is for and why it wins. Messaging is the words built on top of it, so positioning comes first.

Positioning is the decision: which customer, which problem, what we compare against and why we win. It is internal and rarely changes. Messaging is how we say that to a given audience, in headlines, pitches and web pages. If the messaging shifts every quarter, usually the positioning was never agreed.
Where does your job end and the product manager's job begin?
Whether you understand the split of roles you will work in every day.
The PM owns what gets built and why. The PMM owns how it is positioned, launched and sold, and brings market insight back to the PM.

The product manager owns the roadmap: what we build and in what order. I own how the market hears about it: positioning, launch, pricing pages and sales tools. The overlap is customer insight. I bring win/loss findings and competitor moves to roadmap reviews, and the PM tells me early what is coming so I can plan the launch.
Walk me through how you would position a new product from scratch.
Your method for positioning, not just your instinct.
Starts from the best current customers and their real alternatives, then names the unique value, the target segment and the category, and tests it.

I start with the customers who love the product most and ask what they would use if we did not exist. That list is the real competition. Then I note what we do that those options cannot, what value that brings, and which customers care most. Last, I pick the category frame that makes that value obvious and test it on sales calls before writing copy.
What goes into a good competitive battlecard, and how do you keep it current?
Whether you can turn competitor research into something a rep can use in the middle of a call.
Short, honest content: where we win and lose, questions that expose weak spots, objection answers and proof. Plus an owner, a review cycle and input from the field.

One page per competitor: when we win, when we lose, questions that expose their weak spots, answers to their top three objections against us, and a customer story. I admit where they are stronger, or reps stop trusting it. I review each card monthly against win/loss notes, and reps post what they hear in a shared channel so updates come from real deals.
How do you run a win/loss analysis?
How you find the real reasons deals are won and lost.
Interviews with buyers, not only CRM fields, done by someone neutral soon after the decision, with patterns shared with product and sales.

CRM loss reasons mostly say price, so I interview the buyers themselves, won and lost, within a few weeks of the decision. I or a neutral third party ask, not the rep, so people speak openly. I ask how they decided, who else they looked at and what almost changed their mind. Each quarter I share the patterns with product and sales, with quotes.
How do you decide how big a launch should be?
Whether you tier launches by impact instead of treating every release the same way.
A tiering rule based on customer impact, revenue and competitive weight, agreed with product, so the effort and noise match the release.

Three tiers, agreed with product. Tier one is a new product or a new market: full launch, press, sales training. Tier two is a big feature for current customers: email, blog, demo update. Tier three is an improvement: release notes and an in-app note. I score each release on customer impact, revenue and competitive value, so the loudest voice does not set the tier.
Sales says nobody uses the pitch deck you built. What do you do?
How you handle sales materials that are not landing.
Curiosity before defending: check usage, sit in on calls, rebuild with the best reps, and retire what nobody uses.

First I find out why. I check the usage data, sit in on a few calls and ask the top reps what they show instead. Often they built their own slides because ours were too long or led with features. I rebuild it with two of those reps, cut it to the slides that move a deal, and they present it at the next team meeting. Reps trust a peer more than marketing.
An executive wants the launch page to say we are the fastest product on the market. How do you handle it?
Whether you know a claim must be backed up before it goes public.
Knows US ad claims must be truthful and backed by evidence before they run; gets the test data and legal review, or narrows the claim to what can be proven.

I ask what the claim rests on. In the US, an objective claim like “fastest” needs evidence before it runs, and a comparison with rivals must be fair. If we have a recent, repeatable benchmark, I note the test conditions and have legal review it. If not, I write what we can prove, such as “loads reports in under two seconds”, which often persuades better anyway.
Two weeks before launch, engineering says the date will slip a month. Press briefings and a customer webinar are booked. What do you do?
How you handle a launch problem without losing trust.
Gets the facts and a firm new date, decides what moves and what goes ahead, and tells press, customers and sales early and plainly.

First I confirm what is slipping: the whole product or one feature. If the core works, I may keep the date and launch a smaller story. If not, I get a date engineering will commit to, call the journalists myself, move the webinar with a short honest note, and brief sales so nobody promises the old date. Telling people early costs far less than a late surprise.
A main competitor launches a copy of your key feature at a lower price. Sales wants a discount and an attack page. What do you recommend?
Your judgement when a competitor move puts pressure on your positioning.
No panic: measures the real impact in deals, sharpens the differences that remain, and avoids a price war or attack copy not backed by evidence.

I would not react on day one. I get a demo of their version, check where it really matches ours, and track how often it shows up in deals over the next few weeks. Usually a copy covers the headline but not the depth, so I update the battlecard and messaging around what is still unique. A price cut is a leadership decision made with data, not a reflex.

product-operations.heading: Product operations questions
qs: What does product operations own that a product manager does not?
Whether you understand where the role starts and stops.
Clear ownership of the systems around the product: launches, tooling, feedback flow and shared data. Product decisions stay with the PM.

The PM decides what to build and why. I own the machinery that helps PMs do that well: the launch process, the feedback pipeline from support and sales, the tools and templates, and the shared metrics. If a PM spends Friday cleaning a spreadsheet of customer requests, that is a gap I should close.
What is a staged rollout, and when would you push for one?
Your grasp of how to release changes with limited risk.
Release to a small share of users first, check agreed metrics, and widen only if they hold, with a way to switch the feature off.

We release behind a feature flag, which is a switch that turns the feature on for chosen users. We start with about 5% of users, then 25%, then everyone.
