Each screen gets a class that knows its locators and offers actions like logIn or addToCart. The tests call those actions and never touch selectors directly. When a developer renames a button, I update one class instead of forty tests. The tests also read like user steps, which makes failures easier to understand.
Walk me through how you would test an API endpoint that creates an order.
How you cover an API beyond the happy path.
Status codes, response body and stored data, invalid and missing input, authorization, and what a repeated request does.

First the happy path: a valid request returns 201, the body matches the contract, and the order exists in the database. Then bad input: missing fields, wrong types, negative quantity, which should return 400 with a clear message. No token should give 401; a user touching someone else's cart, 403. Last, I send the same request twice to see if it makes a duplicate order.
How do you run an exploratory testing session?
Whether you can test without a script and still be systematic.
A charter with a clear goal, a time box, notes taken as you go, and a short debrief with bugs and open questions.

I write a one-line charter, for example: explore checkout with expired cards to find payment errors. I set a timer for 60 to 90 minutes and note what I tried, what I saw and what seemed odd. At the end I file the bugs, list open questions and suggest which checks are worth turning into automated tests.
A developer closes your bug as "cannot reproduce." What do you do?
How you handle disagreement in triage without making it personal.
Look for what differs between environments, add evidence, and reproduce it together instead of reopening with no new facts.

I first try again myself on a clean build. If it still happens, I look for what differs: browser, test data, user role, feature flags, timing. I add a screen recording, logs and the exact build number to the ticket. Then I ask the developer for ten minutes to watch me reproduce it. Usually we find the missing step together.
The regression suite takes 90 minutes in CI and developers have started skipping it. What do you do?
How you keep automation useful to the team, not just large.
Measure where the time goes, run in parallel, move checks to faster levels, and split a quick gate from the full suite.

I would first measure which tests take longest; often a few slow UI tests eat most of the time. I would run tests in parallel, replace fixed waits with waits for a condition, and move checks that need no browser down to API or unit tests. Then I would split it: a 10-minute smoke set on every pull request and the full suite nightly.
Your tests pass when run alone but fail when the whole suite runs. What is likely going on?
Whether you can spot shared state and order dependence between tests.
Tests depend on each other or on shared data; the fix is that each test creates and owns its own data.

Most likely the tests share state: one test changes a user, a record or a setting that another expects to be untouched, or they run in parallel on the same data. I would run them in a fixed order to find the pair. The fix is that each test creates its own data with unique names and never relies on what an earlier test left behind.
A bug in a feature you tested reached users. What do you do?
How you own a miss and turn it into a better process.
Help contain it first, then find without blame why testing missed it, and add a check so it cannot slip through the same way.

First I help the team confirm the impact and test the fix quickly. Then I look honestly at why I missed it. Once, a date bug only appeared for users in time zones ahead of ours, and all our test machines used one zone. I added a test that runs in a different zone and put time zones on our test checklist.

quality-engineer.heading: Quality engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between Cp and Cpk?
Whether you know the basic measures of process capability.
Cp compares tolerance width to process spread. Cpk also accounts for where the process is centered, so Cpk is never higher than Cp.

Cp is the tolerance width divided by six standard deviations, so it says what the process could do if it were centered. Cpk takes the distance from the mean to the nearer spec limit, divided by three standard deviations. If Cp is 2.0 but Cpk is 0.9, the spread is fine and the process is off center. I would adjust the aim, not buy a new machine.
A process is in statistical control but making parts out of spec. How can that be?
Whether you know that control limits and spec limits are different things.
Control limits come from the process's own data and spec limits come from the drawing. A stable process can still be off target or too wide for the tolerance.

Control limits are calculated from how the process actually behaves, so they show whether it is stable. Spec limits come from the design. A process can be perfectly stable and still run off center, or with too much spread for the tolerance. The chart will not alarm. The fix is a process change, like re-centering or reducing variation, not reacting to single points.
What does a gauge R&R study tell you, and when would you stop trusting the gauge?
Whether you check the measurement system before you trust the data.
Error split into repeatability and reproducibility and compared to the tolerance, using the common guideline: under 10% good, over 30% not acceptable.

It tells me how much of the variation I see comes from measuring rather than from the parts. Repeatability is one person measuring the same part again. Reproducibility is the difference between people. A typical study uses 10 parts, 3 operators and 2 or 3 trials each. Under about 10% of tolerance is good. Over 30%, I fix the gauge or the method before I trust any data from it.
A lot passed AQL sampling. Does that mean it has no defects?
Whether you understand what a sampling plan does and does not promise.
No. AQL is a defect level the plan accepts most of the time, and a passed lot can still contain defects. Critical features need stronger controls.

No. AQL is the acceptance quality limit, the defect level the plan is built to accept most of the time. Sampling gives a probability of catching a bad lot, not a guarantee, so a passed lot can still hold defective parts. For anything critical, like a safety feature, I would not rely on sampling. I would want 100% automated inspection or, better, error-proofing at the source.
In a process FMEA, a failure mode has severity 10 but a low RPN. Do you act on it?
Whether you use FMEA scores with judgement instead of just sorting by the number.
Yes. A top severity needs attention whatever the RPN. A strong answer knows RPN can hide risk and that the AIAG-VDA method uses action priority instead.

Yes. A severity of 10 means a safety or regulatory effect. RPN multiplies severity, occurrence and detection, so low occurrence and detection scores can bury it. The current AIAG-VDA handbook replaced RPN ranking with action priority partly for this reason. I would check the evidence behind the occurrence score and add a prevention control or error-proofing, not just more inspection.
Walk me through a first article inspection on a new machined part.
How thorough you are before a new part or process is released.
Every characteristic on the drawing is numbered and measured, material and process records are checked, and results are recorded against the right drawing revision.

First I confirm the drawing revision and balloon every characteristic, including notes and general tolerances. I measure each one on a part made with production tooling and record actual values, not just pass or fail. I check material certs and special process records, like heat treat or plating. Anything out gets resolved before release, not waved through.
A customer calls: they found cracked housings from your plant on their line. What do you do in the first 24 hours?
How you contain a problem before you start looking for its cause.
The customer is protected first: suspect stock held everywhere, a sort with a defined check, certified parts marked, then the root cause work starts.

First I get photos, part numbers and date codes. Then I put every suspect lot on hold: in our stock, in transit and at the customer. I arrange a sort with a defined check, at their site if needed, and mark certified good parts so they can tell them apart. Once the customer is protected, I start the root cause with the team and send a written update by end of day.
How do you prove you found the real root cause and not just a likely one?
Whether you verify a cause with evidence before closing a corrective action.
You can turn the defect on and off with the suspected cause, you explain why it escaped detection, and you confirm the fix with data over time.

If I can, I reproduce the defect by bringing back the suspected cause, then make it disappear by removing it. On one burr problem, a worn tool made burrs and a fresh one did not. I also ask why our inspection let it escape, because that needs its own fix. Then I watch the data for several weeks before I close the action.
A team proposes "retrain the operator" as the corrective action for a wrong part being assembled. What is your reaction?
Whether you push for corrective actions that actually prevent the problem from coming back.
Retraining alone is weak. You ask why the process allowed the error and look for error-proofing so the mistake cannot happen or is caught at once.

I would ask why the process let a good operator make that mistake. Were two similar parts in look-alike bins? Training fades and people change. A stronger fix is error-proofing: a fixture that only accepts the right part, or a scan that blocks the next step if the wrong one is picked. Training can be part of the fix, but not the whole answer.
Production wants to ship a lot that is slightly over a dimension limit to make the month. What do you do?
How you hold the line on quality under schedule pressure without just saying no.
The lot is held, fit and function are assessed, and it ships only after rework, sorting or a written deviation approved by the customer.

The lot goes on hold, because out of spec is not ours alone to accept. I measure how far off it is, ask design engineering whether it affects fit or function, and look at rework or sorting. If a deviation makes sense, I get written approval from the customer before anything ships. I tell production early so they can plan, and I find out why the process drifted.

quality-inspector.heading: Quality inspector questions
qs: What does a go/no-go gauge tell you, and how do you read it?
Whether you know the most basic fixed gauge in the trade.
The go end must fit and the no-go end must not; it tells you pass or fail, not the actual size.

For a hole, the go pin must enter and the no-go pin must not. If the go will not enter, the hole is too small. If the no-go enters, it is too big. It is fast, but it gives no number, so I cannot see a drift with it. I never force a pin, because force gives a false pass and can damage the gauge.
A feature is toleranced at plus or minus 0.0005 inch. Would you check it with a caliper or a micrometer, and why?
Whether you choose a measuring tool that fits the tolerance.
A micrometer, using the rule of ten: the tool should resolve about one tenth of the total tolerance band.

A micrometer. The total band is 0.001 inch, and by the rule of ten I want a tool that reads to about a tenth of that, so 0.0001 inch. A caliper is fine for rough checks but not for this. I also confirm the micrometer is in calibration and zero it before I start.
Why does it matter if a part comes to you hot from the machine?
Whether you understand that temperature changes size.
Parts grow with heat; dimensions are defined at 68°F (20°C), so you let the part and the gauge soak to room temperature.

Metal grows when it is warm, and the drawing sizes apply at 68°F. A 10 inch aluminum part that is 20 degrees warm can be about 0.0025 inch long, which can pass a bad part. I let it reach room temperature next to the gauge before a final check, or I note the reading as provisional.
What is a first article inspection, and how do you do one?
Your knowledge of how a new part or process gets approved.
Every characteristic on the drawing is checked on the first part and recorded, usually against a ballooned drawing.

It proves a new setup or process can make the part to the drawing. I number every dimension and note on the drawing, then measure each one and record the actual value, not just pass. I also check material certs and specs called out. In aerospace this follows AS9102. If one feature fails, the setup gets corrected before production runs.
What is a datum, and why does it matter how you hold the part when you measure?
Whether you can read a drawing's reference system and set up a part to match it.
Datums are the reference features; the part must be located on them in the order the drawing gives, or the readings mean nothing.

A datum is the feature the drawing measures from, like a flat face or a bore. The order matters: primary first, then secondary, then tertiary. If I sit the part on the wrong face, a perfectly good hole position can read out of tolerance, or a bad one can pass. I set up the fixture or the CMM alignment to the datums exactly as called out.
You find a part out of tolerance in the middle of a run. Walk me through what you do.
How you contain a nonconforming part and get it properly decided.
Stop, tag and segregate it, check the parts around it, write it up, and let the review board decide. You do not decide alone to use it.

First I confirm the reading with a second measurement. Then I tag the part red and move it to the hold area. I tell the operator and the supervisor so the process is checked, and I inspect parts made before it back to the last good one. I write a nonconformance report. Use as is, rework or scrap is decided by the review board, not by me.
A micrometer comes back from calibration marked out of tolerance. What do you do?
Whether you trace the effect of a bad gauge back to the product.
Pull the gauge, find every lot measured since its last good calibration, judge the error against those tolerances, and re-inspect or escalate.

I tag the micrometer out of service. Then I find the last date it passed calibration and list every lot it measured since then. If the error was small next to those tolerances, I document that. If it could have passed bad parts, I quarantine what is still here, re-inspect, and tell quality management so shipped parts can be reviewed with the customer.
A gauge R&R study on a new fixture comes back at 35 percent. What does that mean, and what happens next?
Your understanding of measurement system error.
Over 30 percent is generally unacceptable: the gauge varies too much to trust. Find the cause, fix it, and repeat the study.

It means more than a third of the tolerance is being eaten by the measurement itself, so we cannot tell good parts from bad ones reliably. I would look at whether the spread comes from the gauge, so repeatability, or from people, so reproducibility. Then fix the fixture, the method or the training, and run the study again before using it.
Every part is still in tolerance, but the last several readings on the control chart keep climbing toward the limit. What do you do?
Whether you act on a trend before it makes scrap.
Treat it as a signal: tell the operator or setup person now so the cause, like tool wear, is fixed while parts are still good.

In tolerance does not mean in control. A steady climb usually means tool wear, heat or a loosening setup. I show the chart to the operator and the lead right away, so they can adjust or change the tool now. I keep sampling more often until the readings settle back near the center line, and I note the event on the chart.
A supervisor asks you to pass a lot that is 0.001 inch over on one dimension because the customer needs it today. How do you handle it?
Your integrity under pressure and knowledge of the proper approval path.
You do not sign off a bad part, but you offer the right route: an engineering review and, if needed, a customer deviation, done fast.

I would say I cannot pass it as is, because my stamp says it meets the drawing. Then I help solve the real problem. I get the measurements documented fast, ask engineering to review it, and if they think it will work, the customer can approve a written deviation. That can still ship today, and nobody is hiding anything.

quant.heading: Quantitative researcher questions
qs: Why do you model returns instead of raw prices?
Whether you understand stationarity, the base of most time series work.
Prices drift and their statistics change over time; returns are closer to stationary, and log returns add across periods.

Prices wander: their mean and spread change over time, so a model fit on last year's prices says little about next year's. Returns are much closer to stationary, which most statistical tools assume. I use log returns because they add up across periods. I still check for volatility clustering, since crypto returns are far from constant in variance.
How do you annualize a Sharpe ratio for a crypto strategy, and what is different from stocks?
Your care with a basic metric in a market that never closes.
Scale by the square root of 365 trading days, not 252, and know the rule assumes independent returns.

Crypto trades every day of the year, so I scale a daily Sharpe by the square root of 365, not 252 as in stocks. Mixing the two makes comparisons wrong. The square root rule also assumes daily returns are independent, so I check autocorrelation first; if returns are autocorrelated, the simple scaling can overstate or understate the risk.
What is look-ahead bias? Give me an example from crypto data.
Whether you can spot the most common way a backtest lies.
Using information not available at decision time, with a concrete case such as trading at the same close that built the signal.

Look-ahead bias is using information the strategy could not have had at the time. A common case: a signal built from a daily candle's close, then filled at that same close. The close is only known once the bar ends, so I trade at the next bar's open or later. I also check timestamps, because some data sets stamp a bar with its open time and some with its close time.
Your backtest universe is today's top 50 tokens by market cap. What is wrong with that?
Whether you recognize survivorship bias in a market where many assets die.
The universe only holds winners; rebuild it point in time, keep dead and delisted tokens, and model delistings.

It only includes winners. Many tokens that were in the top 50 three years ago have since collapsed or been delisted, and a strategy holding them would have taken those losses. I rebuild the universe at each date from data available then, keep dead tokens in, and model what happened to a position when an exchange delisted the pair.
What is the funding rate on a perpetual future, and how does it enter your backtest?
Your knowledge of the main crypto derivative and its real cash flows.
Periodic payments between longs and shorts that keep the perp near spot, applied as P&L at each actual funding time.

A perpetual future has no expiry, so exchanges keep its price near spot with periodic payments between longs and shorts. When the perp trades above the index, longs usually pay shorts. In a backtest I apply the historical rate at each funding time to every open position. For a basis or carry strategy, funding is often most of the profit, so leaving it out makes the result meaningless.
For a pairs trade, what is the difference between correlation and cointegration?
Whether you know which property a mean reversion trade actually needs.
Correlation is about returns moving together; cointegration means a spread of prices is stationary, which is what makes it revert.

Correlation is about returns moving together over a window; two coins can be highly correlated and still drift apart for good. Cointegration means some weighted spread of the prices is stationary, so it tends to come back. A pairs trade needs the second. I test it, for example with an Engle-Granger test, on one period and then check the spread still reverts out of sample.
How do you model transaction costs in a backtest for a mid-cap token?
How realistic you are about the costs that kill most strategies.
Fees, spread and market impact sized to order book depth, plus a stress test at higher costs.

I count exchange fees at the taker rate unless the strategy really posts limit orders, then half the spread to cross, then market impact sized against historical order book depth at that hour. A mid-cap token can have thin books at quiet times. I rerun the backtest at two and three times my cost estimate; if the edge disappears, it was never really there.
You tested 200 parameter combinations and the best has a Sharpe of 3. How much do you trust it?
Whether you understand overfitting and multiple testing.
Little, until it is adjusted for the number of trials, stable across nearby parameters and confirmed on untouched data.

Not much yet. With 200 tries, the best one is partly the luckiest one. I would look at its neighbors: if nearby parameters fall to a Sharpe of 0.5, it is a fluke. I would adjust for the number of trials, for example with a deflated Sharpe ratio, and then run the chosen setting once on data I have not touched.
Volume on one exchange looks far higher than its order book suggests. What do you do with that data?
Your judgement on data quality in a market with inflated reported volume.
Suspect wash trading, test volume against depth and price moves, and drop venues that fail from signals and cost models.

Some venues have reported inflated volume through wash trading, where the same party trades with itself. I check whether volume moves with order book depth and price changes, look for odd trade size patterns, and compare with venues I trust. If a venue fails, I drop it from signals and cost models, because fake volume makes liquidity look deeper than it is.
Three months after launch, a strategy is running well below its backtest. Walk me through how you diagnose it.
How you separate bad luck, bad execution and a dead signal.
First test whether the gap is unusual, then break it into execution, costs and signal, and follow stop rules set before launch.

First, is the gap even unusual? I compare live returns with the range of three-month results the backtest itself produces. Then I split the gap: fills versus modeled prices, fees, latency and funding. If execution explains it, I fix the cost model and rerun. If the signal itself decayed, I check for crowding and follow the stop rule we agreed on before launch.

quantum.heading: Quantum computing questions
qs: What is the difference between T1 and T2 for a qubit?
Whether you know the two basic ways a qubit loses its information.
T1 as energy loss to the ground state, T2 as loss of phase, and the fact that T2 can be no longer than twice T1.

T1 is how long a qubit stays in its excited state before it relaxes to the ground state. T2 is how long it keeps a well-defined phase in a superposition. Relaxation also destroys phase, so T2 is at most twice T1. I measure T1 with an inversion recovery, T2* with a Ramsey experiment and T2 with a Hahn echo.
Walk me through preparing a Bell state and checking that you got it.
Your hands-on grasp of entanglement and of how a quantum state is verified.
A Hadamard and a CNOT, then checks in more than one basis, since 00 and 11 counts alone do not prove entanglement.

I start both qubits in 0, apply a Hadamard to the first and a CNOT with the first as control. Ideally that gives 00 plus 11, over root two. Measuring in the standard basis should give about half 00 and half 11, but a classical mix would too. So I also measure in the X and Y bases, or run state tomography, to confirm the phase and estimate fidelity.
If you cannot copy a qubit, how does quantum error correction work at all?
Whether you understand the core idea behind protecting quantum information.
Information spread across many qubits, and errors found by measuring parities with helper qubits, never by measuring the data itself.

The no-cloning theorem forbids copying an unknown state, so we encode it instead: one logical qubit is spread across many physical qubits. Helper qubits measure parity checks, called stabilizers, which reveal which error happened without revealing the stored state. In a surface code, if physical errors are below threshold, a larger code lowers the logical error rate.
Your circuit needs CNOTs between qubits that are not neighbors on the chip. What happens, and how do you limit the cost?
How you think about mapping a circuit onto real hardware.
Knows the compiler inserts SWAPs, each usually three CNOTs, and reduces them through layout, routing and circuit design.

The compiler routes the interaction by inserting SWAP gates, and each SWAP usually costs three CNOTs, which adds depth and error. I choose an initial layout that puts the most connected logical qubits side by side, ideally on the pairs with the best two-qubit fidelity, compare routing settings, and where I can, rewrite the algorithm to fit the chip's connectivity.
Your results lean toward 0 on every qubit. How do you handle readout error?
Whether you can separate measurement error from errors in the circuit itself.
Calibrates readout with known states, corrects with a confusion matrix, and reports both the raw and the corrected numbers.

A lean toward 0 often means qubits relax during readout. I prepare known basis states and measure them to build a confusion matrix, per qubit if crosstalk is small, for the full register if not. I correct the counts with a constrained fit so no probability goes negative, report raw and corrected results side by side, and recalibrate often, because readout drifts.
How would you measure the error rate of a two-qubit gate?
Your knowledge of the standard way gate quality is benchmarked.
Randomized benchmarking, interleaved RB to isolate one gate, and why the method is robust to preparation and measurement error.

I would run randomized benchmarking: random sequences of Clifford gates of growing length, each ending with the inverse so the ideal result is known. Survival probability decays with length, and the decay rate gives an average error per Clifford, separate from preparation and measurement errors. To isolate one gate, I use interleaved RB, inserting it between the random gates.
A colleague says Grover's algorithm will make our database search exponentially faster. How do you respond?
Whether you can correct an overclaim with the right facts.
Grover gives a quadratic speedup on unstructured search, and oracle cost, data loading and error correction overhead can erase it.

Grover gives a quadratic speedup: about the square root of N oracle calls instead of about N for unstructured search. That is real but modest. The oracle must run as a quantum circuit, loading the data can cost as much as the search, and error correction adds heavy overhead per step. For an indexed database, a classical lookup already beats it.
Your variational algorithm stalls and the gradients are near zero from the first step. What is going on and what do you try?
How you diagnose a common failure in near-term quantum algorithms.
Names barren plateaus and shot noise, and tries a shallower or problem-aware circuit, local cost functions and better starting points.

It may be a barren plateau: with deep, random-like circuits or a cost spread over all qubits, gradients shrink exponentially as qubits are added. I check whether gradients are below shot noise. Then I try a shallower, problem-inspired circuit, a local cost function, starting parameters near identity, and growing the circuit one layer at a time.
One qubit's T1 dropped from 90 to 35 microseconds overnight. How do you find the cause?
Your troubleshooting method on real hardware.
Repeats and tracks the measurement, checks neighbors, frequency and fridge logs, and flags the qubit before others rely on it.

I repeat it over a few hours, since a material defect called a two-level system can drift close to the qubit's frequency and pull T1 down. If neighbors dropped too, I check fridge temperature, wiring and shielding. If only this qubit, I scan T1 against frequency and, on a tunable qubit, move it away from the defect. Meanwhile I flag it in the calibration notes.
Your result beats a simple classical baseline and leadership wants to call it quantum advantage. What do you do?
Your scientific honesty when results meet pressure to claim more.
Compares against the best classical methods at the same accuracy, invites scrutiny, and words the claim to match what was shown.

I would not call it advantage yet. Beating a simple baseline is not enough: we need to compare against the best classical methods, such as tensor networks or tuned heuristics, at the same accuracy and with a fair compute budget. I would share data and code with classical experts, state the limits plainly, and propose wording that matches what we actually showed.

real-estate.heading: Corporate real estate manager questions
qs: What is the difference between a gross lease and a triple net lease?
Whether you know the basic lease structures a company signs.
Who pays the operating costs and who carries the risk if they rise, plus comparing total occupancy cost.

In a gross lease the rent covers the building's operating costs, and the landlord carries the risk if they rise. In a triple net lease we pay base rent plus our share of property taxes, insurance and maintenance. The base rent looks lower, so I always compare total occupancy cost per square foot, not just the rent line.
Explain rentable versus usable square feet, and why it matters when you compare buildings.
Your grasp of how office space is measured and priced.
Rentable includes a share of common areas; the load factor changes what you really pay per foot you can use.

Usable is the space we actually occupy. Rentable adds our share of common areas like lobbies, corridors and restrooms. The ratio between them is the load factor. If two buildings both quote 20,000 rentable feet but one has a 12% load and the other 20%, the first gives us more space we can use, so I compare cost per usable foot.
How do you decide whether the company should lease or buy a site?
How you weigh cost, capital and flexibility in a real estate decision.
Starts from how long and how certain the need is, then compares cost over the hold period, capital tied up and control.

I start with how long and how certain the need is. A specialized plant we will run for 20 years leans toward owning; an office in a market where our headcount may change leans toward leasing. Then I compare after-tax cost over the hold period, the capital the company would tie up, and how much control we need over the building.
Walk me through how you would find a site for a new manufacturing plant.
Whether you can run a site selection from requirements to a recommendation.
Clear steps: business requirements, regional screen, shortlist, checks on zoning, utilities, labor and incentives, then a comparison.

I start with the operations team's needs: acreage, power, water, highway or rail access, and the labor pool. I screen regions on cost and workforce, then shortlist sites and check zoning, utility capacity and incentive offers. Before choosing, I visit, get utility lead times in writing, and lay out the top three side by side for leadership.
Besides base rent, what do you negotiate in an office lease?
Your knowledge of the lease terms that carry real value.
Names concrete terms like improvement allowance, free rent, options, expense caps and audit rights, and trades them with purpose.

The tenant improvement allowance, months of free rent, renewal and expansion options, a termination right, caps on controllable operating expenses, and audit rights. On a recent 10-year deal I gave a little on rent to get a larger build-out allowance and a right to leave after year seven, which mattered more given our growth plans.
How does the lease accounting standard ASC 842 affect your work with the finance team?
Whether you understand that the leases you sign show up on the balance sheet.
Leases over 12 months go on the balance sheet as an asset and a liability; finance needs accurate, timely lease data.

Under ASC 842, leases longer than 12 months go on the balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability. So every lease I sign changes reported liabilities. I give finance the lease abstract, the payment schedule and options we are reasonably certain to use, and I tell them early about any amendment so they can remeasure.
What due diligence do you do before the company buys a piece of industrial land?
Whether you know the checks that protect a buyer of land.
Title, survey, zoning, soil and an environmental site assessment, plus utility capacity, all before the contingency period ends.

I order a title search and title insurance, an ALTA survey, a zoning check, a geotechnical study and a Phase I environmental site assessment. The Phase I reviews past uses of the land; if it flags something, a Phase II takes soil or water samples. I also confirm utilities can reach the site at the capacity we need before the contingency period ends.
The landlord's year-end operating expense reconciliation shows our share up 25%. What do you do?
How you control occupancy costs and use your lease rights.
Checks the bill against the lease, asks for backup, looks for common errors and uses the audit right in time.

First I read the bill against the lease: which costs are allowed, whether there is a cap on controllable expenses, and how our share is calculated. I ask the landlord for the backup. Often it is a capital project billed all at once or a wrong square footage. If the answers do not hold up, I use our audit right before the lease deadline.
You find out the notice date for a renewal option passed last week. What do you do?
How you handle a costly mistake and stop it from happening again.
Acts fast with the landlord, builds leverage with alternatives, owns the error and fixes the tracking process.

I would call the landlord right away, before they market the space, and say we want to stay. A landlord who wants a good tenant often agrees to renew, though maybe not at the option rate. Meanwhile I price other buildings for leverage. Then I fix the cause: every critical date goes in our lease system with reminders to two people, months ahead.
Headcount at headquarters has dropped 30% with hybrid work, and the lease has six years left. What do you recommend?
Your judgement on surplus space and long lease commitments.
Confirms the trend is lasting, compares options by net cost over the remaining term, and is realistic about sublease income.

I would first confirm with leadership that the drop is lasting. If so, I compare options: consolidate onto fewer floors and sublease the rest, pay a fee for early termination, or give back space in exchange for an extension. Sublease income rarely covers our rent, so I model the net cost of each over six years and recommend the cheapest that keeps flexibility.

recruiter.heading: Recruiter questions
qs: Walk me through how you run an intake meeting with a hiring manager.
How you turn a vague job request into a clear search.
Outcomes before skills, must-haves separated from wishes, and agreement on pay, interview steps and feedback speed.

I ask what the person must deliver in the first six months, then split the skills into must-haves and nice-to-haves. We agree on the salary range, the interview steps, who decides, and how fast feedback comes back. I end by showing two or three sample profiles to check that we picture the same person.
How would you write a Boolean search for a Java developer with cloud experience who is not a manager?
Whether you can source with search strings, not just job posts.
Correct use of AND, OR, NOT, brackets and quotes, plus testing the results and refining the string.

Something like: (Java OR J2EE) AND (AWS OR Azure OR “Google Cloud”) NOT (manager OR director). Synonyms go in brackets with OR, must-haves are joined with AND, and quotes keep a phrase together. I use NOT carefully, since it drops good people who mention “manager” once. Then I read the first 20 results and adjust.
What goes into a first message to a passive candidate?
How you reach people who are not looking for a job.
Short and personal, a clear reason to care, an easy next step, and polite follow-up rather than spam.

It is short and about them. I mention something specific from their profile and say in one line what the role offers that they may not have now, like a bigger scope or remote work. I give the pay range if I can. I end with a small ask: a 15-minute call this week. I follow up twice, then stop.
Why do you push hiring teams to use structured interviews and scorecards?
Your grasp of what makes interviews fair and predictive.
Same core questions and criteria for everyone, scoring done before the group discussion, and decisions based on evidence.

They predict job performance better than free-form chats and make comparisons fair. Every candidate gets the same core questions, each interviewer scores set skills before the debrief, and we talk evidence, not gut feel. It also leaves a record of why we chose someone, which helps if a decision is ever challenged.
Why does it matter that every candidate in the applicant tracking system gets a disposition?
Whether you keep the applicant tracking system clean and useful.
Accurate funnel reports, closure for candidates, a reusable talent pool and a record of job-related reasons.

A disposition is the recorded reason a candidate left the process, like “not enough experience” or “withdrew.” Without it, funnel reports are wrong, people may never hear back, and we lose a searchable pool for later roles. It also shows we judged people on job-related reasons. I close out every candidate within a few days of the decision.
In a debrief, a hiring manager says he wants someone younger with more energy. What do you do?
How you handle a biased comment from the person you support.
Stopping it at once, naming the legal risk, turning it into job-related criteria, and escalating if it repeats.

I stop it right there, calmly. Federal law bars age discrimination against people 40 and over, and a comment like that is a risk on its own. I ask what he actually needs, maybe a fast pace or comfort with new tools, and we score every candidate on that. If it keeps happening, I bring in HR or legal.
Your top candidate asks for 15% above the top of the salary band. How do you handle it?
Your offer negotiation skills and honesty with both sides.
Learning the reason behind the number, using the whole package, building a case inside, and never promising before approval.

First I ask what is behind the number: a competing offer, market data, or a bonus she would give up. Then I lay out the full package, like bonus, equity and a flexible start date. If she is clearly worth it, I take a case with data to the hiring manager and compensation team. I never promise what is not approved, and I tell her honestly where the ceiling is.
A candidate accepted your offer, then got a counteroffer from her current employer. What do you do?
How you protect an accepted offer without pressure tactics.
A fast, open talk about her real reasons, counteroffers raised before the offer, and respect for her final choice.

I call her the same day and ask what changed and what she wants. Ideally I raised this earlier by asking how she would react if her boss offered more. I remind her why she started looking, since money rarely fixes those reasons. If the gap is really pay, I check whether we can move. If she stays, we part on good terms.
You sent an offer letter with a salary $10,000 higher than approved, and the candidate already signed. What now?
How you own a costly mistake and fix the process.
Fast disclosure, the business deciding with legal input, a direct and honest call to the candidate, and a new check step.

I tell my manager and HR within the hour and own the mistake. Legal and the hiring manager decide whether to honor it; often honoring it costs less than lost trust. If we must correct it, I call the candidate myself, apologize, explain and offer options. Then I add a second person to check every offer before it goes out.
A background check shows an old conviction and the manager wants to withdraw the offer. Walk me through the steps.
Whether you know the legal steps before an offer is pulled over a background check.
The FCRA pre-adverse and adverse action notices, a chance to respond, and an individual look at the offense and the job.

Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, we first send a pre-adverse action notice with a copy of the report and a summary of rights, and give the candidate time to respond, since reports can be wrong. We weigh the offense, its age and its link to the job, as EEOC guidance advises, and follow any local fair chance law. Only then a final adverse action notice.

recruiting-coordinator.heading: Recruiting coordinator questions
qs: What does a well-run interview day look like from the coordinator's side?
Whether you know all the moving parts of an interview loop.
A confirmed panel, a clear agenda for the candidate and interviewers, a backup plan, and feedback deadlines set the same day.

Two days before, I confirm every interviewer and send the candidate an agenda with names, times, the link or address, and who to call. Interviewers get the resume and their focus area. On the day, I check in at the start, keep a backup interviewer on call, and send feedback deadlines that afternoon.
What is the Form I-9, and what are the timing rules for it?
Your grip on the paperwork every new hire in the US must complete.
Section 1 by the first day of work, Section 2 within three business days of the start date, and the employee chooses which acceptable documents to show.

The I-9 verifies a new hire's identity and permission to work in the US. The employee fills in Section 1 no later than their first day of work. The employer completes Section 2 within three business days of the start, after examining the documents. The employee picks which documents from the lists to show. I can't ask for a specific one, like a passport.
How do you schedule a five-person panel across three time zones within one week?
How you solve a scheduling puzzle without endless email.
Starts with the tightest calendar, gets candidate windows in their own time zone, labels time zones clearly, and splits the loop rather than delay it.

I start with the person whose calendar is tightest, usually the hiring manager, and build around them. I ask the candidate for windows in their own time zone and write every invite with the zone spelled out. If no single slot fits all five, I split the loop into two shorter blocks rather than push it a week.
How do you keep candidate records in the applicant tracking system accurate and private?
Your habits with the system that serves as the record of every hiring decision.
Stages updated the same day, rejection reasons in job terms, no side copies of candidate data, limited access, and retention handled by policy.

The applicant tracking system is our official record, so I move each candidate's stage the same day and log rejection reasons in job terms. I don't keep side spreadsheets or forward resumes to personal email. Access stays with the hiring team, and records are kept or removed on the schedule our policy sets.
A candidate asks for an accommodation for the interview, such as extra time or a sign language interpreter. How do you handle it?
Whether you treat accommodation requests as routine, prompt and private.
Arranges it quickly, asks what works for the candidate, tells interviewers only what they need, and brings in HR when unsure.

I thank them and ask what would work best. Then I set it up: book the interpreter, adjust the timing, and tell interviewers only what they need, for example that the session runs longer. I keep the request out of feedback notes and scorecards. If I'm unsure what is reasonable, I bring in HR, but I never leave the candidate waiting for an answer.
An interviewer cancels 30 minutes before a final-round onsite. What do you do?
How you handle a last-minute problem so the candidate doesn't pay for it.
A fast backup from trained interviewers, a plain update to the candidate, a quick makeup session if needed, and a word with the manager later.

I go to my list of trained backups for that interview type and call, not email. If I find one, I brief them and tell the candidate only that the name changed. If not, I shift the order, tell the candidate plainly, and book a short video call within a couple of days. Later I tell the hiring manager so it doesn't become a habit.
The hiring manager hasn't submitted feedback three days after an onsite, and the candidate has another offer. What do you do?
How you push senior people for what you need without hurting the relationship.
A clear ask with the reason and a deadline, an agreed escalation path, and an honest holding message to the candidate.

I message the manager directly with the reason: the candidate has a competing offer that expires Friday, so I need feedback by noon tomorrow. I make it easy, with a link to the scorecard or a five-minute call. If noon passes, I go to the recruiter. Meanwhile I tell the candidate we are deciding this week and ask for their exact deadline.
In debrief notes, an interviewer wrote that a candidate 'probably has young kids, may not handle travel.' What do you do?
Whether you spot a biased, legally risky comment and act on it.
Flags it to the recruiter and HR, keeps the decision on job-related evidence, does not alter the record, and suggests interviewer coaching.

That is a guess about family life, not evidence about the job, and it creates discrimination risk. I wouldn't edit the record myself. I would flag it to the recruiter and HR right away, ask that the decision rest on job-related feedback, and suggest the interviewer get a refresher on what can and can't be asked or assumed.
You send an offer letter and then notice the salary is $8,000 higher than what was approved. What do you do?
How you own a mistake that has money and trust attached.
Tells the recruiter and manager at once, doesn't quietly fix it or contact the candidate alone, and adds a check so it can't recur.

I tell the recruiter and hiring manager within the hour, with the approved figure and what was sent. I don't contact the candidate on my own. Usually the recruiter calls them, apologizes and explains, and sometimes the business chooses to honor the number. Then I add a step: a second person checks every letter against the approval before it goes out.
Walk me through what happens when a background check turns up something that may affect an offer.
Whether you know the steps the law requires before an offer is withdrawn.
No decision alone; HR or legal reviews it; a pre-adverse action notice with the report and rights summary, time to respond, then a final notice.

I don't decide anything myself. I send it to HR or legal, who weigh it against the job and any local fair chance rules. If they lean toward pulling the offer, the candidate first gets a pre-adverse action notice with a copy of the report and a summary of their rights, plus time to respond. Only after that would a final adverse action notice go out.

recruiting-operations.heading: Recruiting operations specialist questions
qs: What is the difference between time to fill and time to hire?
Whether you define recruiting metrics precisely before reporting them.
Time to fill measures the job from opening to acceptance; time to hire measures the candidate. The definition is written down and used the same way every time.

Time to fill usually runs from the day the requisition is approved or opened to the day an offer is accepted. It tells us how long a seat stays empty. Time to hire starts when the hired person entered the pipeline, so it shows how fast our process moves a candidate. I write the start and end dates into the report so nobody compares two different numbers.
Walk me through setting up a new requisition in the ATS, from approval to posting.
Your grasp of the full requisition workflow in an applicant tracking system.
Approval chain, correct template, stages, interview plan and scorecards, then a reviewed posting with the right job code and location.

First the req goes through the approval chain so budget and headcount are signed off. Then I build it from the right template: job code, department, location, pay range, hiring team. I set the stages and attach the interview plan and scorecards. The recruiter and manager review the job ad, and only then do I publish it to the career site and job boards.
How do you make sure candidate source data is accurate?
How you keep the data that drives sourcing spend trustworthy.
Tracking links per channel, a required source field with a short fixed list, clear rules for referrals, and regular audits of blanks and 'Other'.

I use tracked links for each job board and campaign so the ATS records the source automatically. For manual entries the source field is required and picks from a short fixed list, no free text. Referrals must be entered as referrals, not as 'Direct'. Each month I pull every 'Other' or blank and fix the pattern behind them, usually one recruiter or one broken link.
How should voluntary self-identification answers, like gender, race or veteran status, be handled in the ATS?
Whether you protect demographic data and keep it out of hiring decisions.
Answers are voluntary, stored apart from the application, hidden from recruiters and managers, and used only in aggregate compliance reporting.

The questions are clearly voluntary and a candidate can decline to answer. I make sure the answers are kept separate from the application and are not visible to recruiters or hiring managers. Only a few people in HR or compliance have access, and the data is used only in aggregate reports, never to look at one candidate.
You need to schedule a five-person panel across three time zones, and one interviewer cancels the morning of. What do you do?
How you run interview logistics and recover when they break.
Trained backup interviewers, calendar holds, clear time zones in invites, and a fast decision: swap in a backup or move one slot, telling the candidate early.

I keep a list of trained backups for each interview type. If one cancels, I first try to swap in a backup who covers the same focus area, so the candidate's day stays intact. If nobody fits, I move just that one session and tell the candidate right away with new options. Every invite shows the time in the candidate's own zone to avoid a second mistake.
We are posting a remote job open to people anywhere in the US. What do you check before it goes live?
Whether you know that posting rules differ by state and city.
Pay transparency laws in several states and cities, some covering remote roles; a good-faith range agreed with compensation, and legal review when unsure.

Several states and some cities now require a pay range in the job posting, and some of those laws cover remote jobs that could be done from there. So I get a good-faith range from compensation, include it in the ad, and add a benefits summary where a law asks for one. If we truly cannot hire in a state, I say so in the posting. When I am unsure about a rule, I check with legal.
Half the hiring managers never update candidate stages in the ATS, so the pipeline reports are wrong. How do you fix it?
How you get busy people to use the system without nagging forever.
Find why they skip it, make it easier (mobile, email links, recruiter owns moves), show managers what they lose, and report on stale candidates.

I would ask a few managers why they skip it; often it is too many clicks. Then I make it easier: feedback links from email, fewer required fields, and recruiters move stages after debriefs. I add a weekly list of candidates stuck over seven days by team. When managers see their own open roles look slow because of stale data, most start updating.
A former candidate posts a harsh review of our interview process on a public review site. How do you respond?
Your judgement in protecting the employer brand without making things worse.
Check the facts first, reply calmly and briefly without candidate details, offer a private channel, and fix the real problem if one exists.

First I look up what happened: stages, dates, how long they waited for news. Then a short public reply: thank them, say we take it seriously, and invite them to contact us directly. I never share details of their application. If the facts show we went silent for three weeks, I fix that step in the process, because the next review will say the same thing.
A background check comes back with a record, and the hiring manager wants the offer pulled today. What do you tell them?
Whether you know the required adverse action steps under federal law.
Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, a pre-adverse action notice with the report and summary of rights comes first, then time to respond, then the final notice.

I would ask them to wait. Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act we first send a pre-adverse action notice with a copy of the report and the summary of rights, and give the person a reasonable time to dispute or explain. Only after that can a final adverse action notice go out. Some states and cities add their own fair chance steps, so I would bring in HR or legal before deciding.
We are moving to a new ATS in four months. How would you plan the migration, and what usually goes wrong?
How you plan a system change that touches data, integrations and people.
Map and clean data first, decide what to migrate, test integrations, run a pilot, train users, and keep open reqs moving during cutover.

I start by mapping every field, stage and integration in the old system, and decide what we migrate versus archive. I clean duplicates before moving them, not after. Common failures are broken job board feeds, lost interview history and missing records we must keep, so I test those in a sandbox. Then a pilot with one team, training, and a cutover date with no new reqs opened that week.

regional-sales-director.heading: Regional sales director questions
qs: How would you design territories for a region you are taking over?
How you balance opportunity and workload when you divide a region among reps.
Territories built on data, such as account potential, current business and workload, so each rep has a fair shot at quota.

I start with the account list, not the map. I score accounts by potential, using size, industry fit and current spend, then add travel time and existing relationships. I aim for territories with similar opportunity, not similar account counts. Before I finalize, I check them with my managers, who know where the real buying power sits.
What is pipeline coverage, and how do you decide how much your region needs?
Whether you understand pipeline math instead of repeating a rule of thumb.
Coverage tied to your own win rate and sales cycle, not a fixed 3x quoted from habit, plus a check on deal stage and timing.

Coverage is open pipeline divided by the quota still to close in the period. The right ratio comes from our win rate: if we close about one in four qualified deals by value, we need roughly 4x. I also check stages and close dates, because a pipeline full of early deals dated for the last week is weaker than the ratio says.
Walk me through how you run a weekly forecast call with your managers.
How you inspect a forecast instead of just collecting numbers.
Clear forecast categories, inspection of the biggest deals, and calls based on evidence such as dated next steps and buyer actions.

Each manager gives commit, the deals they would bet on, then best case and what changed since last week. We go through the five largest commit deals: who signs, what is next, is it on the buyer's calendar, is procurement involved yet. If a deal has no dated next step from the customer, it moves out of commit. I submit my own number, not the sum of theirs.
How do you split a regional quota among your managers and reps?
Whether you set quotas that are fair, reachable and still add up to the regional number.
Quota tied to territory potential and history, a cushion above the target to cover misses, and reduced quotas while new reps ramp.

I start with the regional number and add some cushion, often a few percent, because not every rep will hit. Then I split it by territory potential and past performance, not evenly. Reps still ramping get a reduced quota for their first quarters. I share the method with managers before the numbers, so the debate is about inputs, not about who complained loudest.
How do you tell if a new rep is ramping on track before their first full quarter ends?
Whether you watch leading indicators instead of waiting for missed revenue.
Early activity and pipeline milestones checked against a ramp plan, with coaching started as soon as one slips.

Revenue comes too late to tell me much. I set milestones with the manager: product certification by week four, a set number of first meetings by week six, and a target amount of qualified pipeline by day ninety. If a rep misses one, the manager joins their calls that week. Most ramp problems show up first as a thin calendar.
One of your managers has a large deal in commit, and you do not believe it. What do you do?
How you challenge a forecast without undermining the manager.
Asking for evidence, joining a customer call if needed, and making your own forecast call while coaching the manager.

I ask the manager the questions I would ask the buyer: who signs, is the budget approved, what happens next and when. If the answers are vague, I ask to join the next customer call. I do not overrule them in front of the team. In my own forecast I carry the deal at the level I believe, and I tell the manager why, so they learn to inspect the same way.
Halfway through the quarter, your region is tracking to about 80% of plan. What do you do?
How you respond to a likely miss: early, honest and with a specific plan.
Finding exactly where the gap is, telling leadership early, and putting effort on deals that can truly close this quarter.

First I find where the gap is: one team, one segment, or deals that slipped. Then I tell my VP the likely number and the plan, not just the bad news. We pull forward deals that are truly ready, managers focus on the top twenty deals, and I join the biggest meetings. I avoid deep discounts that just steal from next quarter.
On the last day of the quarter, a rep asks you to approve a 30% discount to close a large deal. How do you decide?
Your judgement on discounting, margin and the habits a quarter-end deal teaches buyers.
Weighing margin and precedent, and trading discount for value such as a longer term or prepayment, within approval rules.

I ask why the buyer needs it and what we get back. A discount in exchange for a longer term, prepayment or a reference can make sense. A discount just to close today teaches the customer to wait for the last day every year. I check the margin and our approval rules, and if it is above my authority, I take it up with a clear recommendation.
Two of your reps both claim credit for the same account. How do you settle it?
Whether you apply rules of engagement fairly and keep the team working together.
A fast decision based on the written rules and the CRM record, and a fix to the rule if it caused the dispute.

I go to our rules of engagement and the CRM history: who owns the account by territory, who logged the opportunity first, and who did the work. I decide within days, because an open dispute poisons both reps. If the rules were unclear, I may split the credit this time and then fix the rule in writing so it does not happen again.
Your top-producing manager hits the number every quarter, but their team has the highest turnover in the region. What do you do?
Whether you look past revenue to the health of a team and act on what you find.
Treating attrition as a real cost, finding the cause from data and conversations, and coaching the manager with clear expectations.

Hitting the number with constant turnover is expensive: each lost rep means months of hiring and ramp. I look at exit interviews, one-on-one talks with their reps and how long people stay. If the cause is the manager's style, I tell them directly that retention is now part of how I judge them, set a specific goal, and coach them on it.

regulatory-affairs.heading: Regulatory affairs specialist questions
qs: What is the difference between a 510(k), a De Novo and a PMA?
Whether you know the main US routes to market for a medical device.
A 510(k) shows substantial equivalence to a predicate. De Novo is for new low-to-moderate risk devices with no predicate. PMA is for most Class III devices.

A 510(k) shows the device is substantially equivalent to a legally marketed predicate. A De Novo is for a new device of low to moderate risk with no predicate; if granted, it creates a new classification others can use. A PMA is for most Class III devices and must show reasonable assurance of safety and effectiveness, usually with clinical data.
We have a new device and nobody is sure how it is classified. How do you find out?
How you work out the class and the pathway of a product.
Searching FDA databases for similar devices and product codes, reading the classification regulation, and using a 513(g) request when it is still unclear.

I start with the intended use and how the device works. Then I search FDA's product classification database and the 510(k) database for similar devices and their product codes, and read the regulation they fall under. If it is still unclear, I can file a 513(g) request, which asks FDA in writing for its view on the class and requirements.
How do you prepare for a Pre-Submission meeting with FDA?
Whether you can get useful feedback from a regulator before you file.
A focused package with specific questions FDA can answer yes or no, using the meeting for open points, and documenting what was agreed.

I send a short package: device description, intended use, the test plan and a few specific questions, like 'Does FDA agree this bench test protocol is enough?' Vague questions get vague answers. FDA usually sends written feedback before the meeting, so we spend the meeting on what is still open, and I draft the minutes afterward.
An FDA inspection ends with a Form 483. What happens next?
Your grasp of inspection follow-up and what is at stake.
A 483 lists observations, not a final decision. A written answer within 15 business days with root cause, fixes and evidence lowers the risk of a warning letter.

A 483 lists what the investigator observed; it is not a final agency decision. I aim to respond in writing within 15 business days, because FDA can consider that response before deciding on a warning letter. For each item: the root cause, the fix, how we check it works, and dates. Every commitment must be one we will actually meet.
Marketing wants a brochure to say our device also helps with a use it was not cleared for. What do you say?
How you handle claims that go beyond the cleared labeling.
A clear no to promoting an uncleared use, a reason the team can accept, and options: wording within the clearance, or a path to add the new use.

I say we cannot promote a use FDA has not cleared; that can make the device misbranded and lead to a warning letter. Then I offer options: claims that fit our cleared indication, backed by data we have, or a plan to add the new use, which may need a new 510(k) and data. I give the cost and timeline so they can choose.
Engineering changed a material in a cleared device. Do we need a new 510(k)?
Whether you can make and document a change assessment.
Asking whether the change could significantly affect safety or effectiveness, using FDA's change guidance and test data, and documenting the decision either way.

It depends on whether the change could significantly affect safety or effectiveness. For a material that touches the patient, I look at biocompatibility and performance data and work through FDA's guidance on changes to an existing device. If a new 510(k) is needed, we file before we ship. If not, I write a memo to file with the reasoning and evidence.
A complaint says our device failed during a procedure. How do you decide whether it must be reported to FDA?
Your knowledge of the medical device reporting rules.
Applying the MDR criteria: a death or serious injury the device may have caused or contributed to, or a malfunction likely to do so if it recurred, on time.

Under the MDR rule, we report if the information reasonably suggests the device may have caused or contributed to a death or serious injury, or malfunctioned in a way likely to cause one if it happened again. The usual deadline is 30 calendar days from when we become aware. When in doubt, I report, and I document the decision either way.
FDA sent an additional information request on our 510(k), and engineering disagrees with one item. How do you handle it?
How you deal with a reviewer's request under a deadline.
Understanding what the reviewer needs, answering every item fully, disagreeing only with data, and never missing the response deadline.

First I make sure we understand the concern; I may ask for a short call with the reviewer. The file is on hold, and if we miss the response deadline it is treated as withdrawn, so I plan backward from that date. For the item we dispute, I show with test data or a recognized standard why it is covered. Arguing without evidence just costs a review cycle.
After filing, you find a test result in the submission was reported wrong. What do you do?
Your honesty and your process when your own filing has an error.
Confirming the error, telling FDA promptly with a correction, and fixing the cause, never hoping nobody notices.

I confirm the error with the lab and find out how big it is. Then I tell my manager and send FDA a correction promptly, with the right data and a plain explanation, as an amendment if the file is still under review. Then I fix the cause, for example a second check of data tables against the test reports. Trust with a reviewer is hard to rebuild.
The reviewer asks for a clinical study you believe the device does not need. How do you push back?
How you push back on a regulator without hurting the relationship.
Using the least burdensome principle with evidence, such as bench, animal or published data, that answers the reviewer's actual question.

I first ask what question the study is meant to answer. Then I show how other evidence answers it: bench tests to a recognized standard, published data, or the predicate's history. FDA must consider the least burdensome way to get the needed information, so I can cite that, politely. If they still disagree, I ask what would satisfy them and weigh the cost with the team.

reinforcement-learning.heading: Reinforcement learning researcher questions
qs: What is the difference between on-policy and off-policy reinforcement learning?
Whether you know the core split in how RL methods use their data.
On-policy learns from data the current policy just generated; off-policy can learn from data collected by another policy, such as a replay buffer.

On-policy methods, like PPO, update the policy using samples it just produced, so old data goes stale after each update. Off-policy methods, like DQN with a replay buffer, can learn from data gathered by an older or different policy. Off-policy reuses data better; on-policy is usually more stable and simpler to tune.
Why do policy gradient methods subtract a baseline, and what is an advantage?
Your grasp of why variance is the usual problem in policy gradients.
A baseline that does not depend on the action keeps the gradient unbiased but cuts its variance; the advantage is how much better an action did than expected.

Raw returns are noisy, so the gradient jumps around. Subtracting a baseline, often a learned value estimate, does not change the expected gradient as long as it does not depend on the action, but it lowers variance a lot. The advantage is return minus that baseline: positive means the action did better than the policy usually does from that state.
Walk me through how a model is trained with reinforcement learning from human feedback.
Whether you know the standard post-training pipeline end to end.
Supervised fine-tuning, a reward model trained on human preference pairs, then RL against that reward with a penalty for drifting from the starting model.

First we fine-tune the base model on good example answers. Then people compare pairs of responses, and we train a reward model to score the preferred one higher. Last, we optimize the policy with an RL method such as PPO to raise that score, with a KL penalty, a cost for drifting from the fine-tuned model, so it does not wander into odd text.
Why keep a KL penalty against the reference model, and how do you pick its strength?
How you weigh gaining reward against keeping the model sound.
The reward model is only trustworthy near the data it saw; the KL term limits drift. Strength is tuned by watching reward, KL and real quality together.

The reward model was trained on outputs like the reference model's, so far from them its scores mean little. The KL term keeps the policy where the reward is trustworthy and keeps the text fluent. I sweep a few values and plot reward against KL; too weak and the model games the reward, too strong and nothing changes. Held-out and human evals pick the point.
How does DPO differ from PPO-based RLHF, and when would you choose each?
Whether you know the main options for preference training and their costs.
DPO trains directly on preference pairs with a simple loss, no separate reward model or sampling loop; PPO costs more but learns from fresh samples.

DPO turns the preference objective into a classification-style loss on chosen and rejected pairs, using the reference model, so no reward model or online generation is needed. It is cheap and stable. PPO samples new responses during training, so it can go beyond a fixed dataset and use any reward. I often start with DPO and move to online RL when it plateaus.
Explain how GRPO estimates advantages without a value network.
Your knowledge of the methods used in current language-model RL.
It samples a group of answers per prompt and scores each against the group's mean reward, often scaled by the standard deviation, so no critic is needed.

For each prompt the model writes several answers, say eight. Each one's advantage is its reward minus the group mean, usually divided by the group's standard deviation. Answers better than their siblings get pushed up, worse ones down, with no value model to train. The catch: if all eight get the same reward, every advantage is zero and that prompt teaches nothing.
Annotators disagree on about a third of your preference pairs. How do you handle that?
Your judgement about noisy human labels.
Separates real ambiguity from unclear guidelines or weak raters, measures agreement, and fixes the process instead of just throwing data away.

First I check where they disagree. If it is close pairs where both answers are fine, that is real noise, and I may drop ties or give them lower weight. If it clusters on one topic or one rater, the guidelines are unclear or a rater needs retraining. I measure agreement per batch and add gold questions with known answers to catch problems early.
Your reward keeps climbing but people say the answers are getting worse. What is happening and what do you do?
How you recognize and handle reward hacking.
Names it as reward over-optimization, reads samples to find the exploit, rolls back to a good checkpoint and fixes the reward or the penalty.

The policy is exploiting flaws in the reward model, often by getting longer, more flattering or more confident. I read high-reward samples to find the pattern, check length against reward, and go back to the last checkpoint humans preferred. Then I fix the cause: more preference data on that failure, a length control, a stronger KL penalty, or earlier stopping.
How would you train with rewards you can verify, like math answers or code tests, and what can go wrong?
Whether you know the strengths and traps of verifiable rewards.
Checks answers automatically instead of with a learned judge, but guards against weak tests, format tricks and prompts that are too easy or too hard.

I sample several answers per problem and give 1 if the final answer matches or all tests pass, else 0. There is no reward model to fool, but the checker can be fooled: code may special-case visible tests, or a loose parser may accept a bad answer. I use hidden tests, a strict parser, and drop prompts the model always or never solves.
Halfway through a PPO run, KL to the reference spikes and the output turns into repeated tokens. How do you debug it?
How you diagnose an unstable training run.
Stops the run, checks which logged metrics moved first, reads samples, and looks at learning rate, clipping, entropy and data before changing anything.

I stop it and roll back to the last healthy checkpoint. Then I look at what moved first: entropy dropping, clip fraction rising, or gradient norm jumping. I read samples just before the spike and check that batch for bad prompts or a reward bug. Usual fixes are a lower learning rate, fewer epochs per batch or a stronger KL term, one change at a time.

renewals.heading: Renewals manager questions
qs: How far ahead of the end date do you start working a renewal, and what do you do first?
How you plan a renewal so nothing is decided at the last minute.
A start months ahead, set by account size and risk, and the contract read before the first call.

For a typical account I start about 120 days out, earlier for large or shaky ones. First I read the contract: end date, notice period, auto-renew terms and any price clause. Then I check usage and open tickets, and I call the main contact to hear how the year went before price ever comes up.
Which signs tell you an account may not renew?
Whether you spot churn risk early from real signals.
Concrete signals from usage, people and behavior, checked on a regular schedule, not a gut feeling.

Falling logins or seat use, a champion who left, a new executive or a budget freeze, emails that go unanswered, and repeat escalations to support. Questions about exporting data are a loud one. I review my accounts every week, and two signals together put an account on my at-risk list with a plan.
When do you bring up an upsell, and when do you hold back?
Your judgement on selling more without hurting the renewal.
Upsell when the customer gets value and has a clear need; fix problems first and never tie them together.

I raise it when the data shows a need: they are at their seat limit or a team keeps asking for a feature in a higher plan. If they have open problems or low use, I hold back and secure the renewal first. Pushing more product on an unhappy customer turns a safe renewal into a risky one.
We are raising prices 8% this year. How do you tell a customer?
How you deliver a price increase so the customer still renews.
Early notice that respects the contract's terms, a plain reason, the value they got, and options to choose from.

I tell them early, well before the notice date in their contract, and in writing after a call. I say the number plainly, give the reason, and show what they got this year, like hours saved or new features. Then I offer options, for example locking the price with a two-year term. No surprise on an invoice.
A customer asks for 20% off to renew. How do you handle it?
Whether you protect revenue while keeping the customer.
Find the real reason first, and trade instead of giving: any discount gets something back, within approval limits.

I ask what is behind it: budget cut, a competitor quote, or low use. Low use I fix with a right-sized plan, not a discount. If a concession fits, I trade it: a smaller discount for a two-year term or signing a month early. Anything past my limit goes to my manager with the reasons written down.
Your champion at a large account just left, 90 days before renewal. What do you do?
How you rebuild a relationship under time pressure.
Quick contact with the new owner and other users, value shown again from scratch, and the risk flagged in the forecast.

I flag the account as at risk that day. I ask the departing champion, if reachable, who takes over, and I reach out to the new owner and two or three daily users. I book a short review of the results they got this year, since the new person never saw them. I also make sure their admin training is current.
A contract auto-renewed, and the customer says they meant to cancel. What do you do?
Your judgement when the contract is on your side but the customer is upset.
Facts checked first, no hiding behind the clause, finance or legal brought in, and a fair outcome sought.

I check the contract terms and whether our renewal notice went out on time and to the right person. Then I listen to why they want to leave. If we missed a step, I own it and work with finance on a fix. If we did everything right, I still look for a fair middle path, like a shorter term or fewer seats, with my manager's approval.
Walk me through how you forecast your renewals for the quarter.
Whether your forecast rests on evidence your manager can trust.
Categories tied to clear proof, like a verbal yes or paperwork in procurement, updated weekly and honest about risk.

I sort every renewal into commit, likely and at risk. Commit means a verbal yes and paperwork moving through their procurement. Likely means good usage and engagement but no yes yet. At risk means two or more warning signs. I update it weekly, and I would rather call an account at risk and save it than surprise my manager.
Tell me about a renewal you lost. What would you do differently?
Whether you learn from churn instead of blaming the customer.
An honest account of the real cause, your own part in it, and a change you made to your process afterward.

I lost a 40-seat account because I worked only with one manager. Their finance head cut the tool in a budget review I never knew about. Now I map at least three contacts per account, including the budget owner, and I send a short value summary each quarter that the champion can forward upward.

research-analyst.heading: Research analyst questions
qs: What is the difference between market cap and fully diluted valuation, and when does the gap matter?
Whether you know the supply figures that drive a token's valuation.
Market cap uses circulating supply and FDV uses maximum or total supply. A wide gap means future supply that can weigh on price.

Market cap is price times the tokens circulating today. FDV is price times the maximum supply, or total supply if there is no cap. If only 15% of tokens circulate, FDV can be several times market cap. The rest will reach the market through unlocks and emissions, and that future selling is the first thing I check.
What does TVL measure, and why can it mislead?
Whether you can read the most quoted DeFi metric with care.
TVL is the dollar value of assets deposited in a protocol. It moves with token prices and can be inflated by double counting and looped deposits.
