TVL is the dollar value of assets locked in a protocol's contracts. It can rise just because ETH went up, with no new deposits. The same asset can be counted twice, for example a liquid staking token deposited again in a lending market, and borrowers can loop deposits. I look at TVL in native units and at who the largest depositors are.
A dashboard shows a protocol made $40 million in fees last year. Is that its revenue?
Whether you separate what users pay from what the protocol keeps.
Fees are what users pay. Revenue is the share the protocol or token holders keep after paying liquidity providers or lenders.

Usually not. Fees are everything users paid. On a DEX most of that goes to liquidity providers, and on a lending market most interest goes to lenders. Revenue is the slice kept by the treasury or token holders, which can be small. I check the contracts and fee settings, not just the dashboard label, because tools define these terms differently.
A chain reports two million daily active addresses. What does that tell you about users?
How you avoid treating wallet counts as people.
Addresses are not users. One person or bot can run many, so you filter by value, behavior and repeat activity.

Less than it sounds. One person can hold dozens of addresses, and bots or airdrop farmers can create thousands for almost nothing on a cheap chain. I filter out dust-sized transfers, check how many addresses come back over 30 days, and look at fees paid. Two million addresses paying fractions of a cent is a different story from 50,000 paying real money.
How do you check the trading volume a crypto exchange reports?
Whether you know which crypto data is self-reported and how to test it.
Centralized exchange volume is self-reported. You compare it with order book depth, spreads, on-chain flows and peers instead of trusting the headline.

On a centralized exchange trades happen off-chain, so the volume is whatever the exchange reports. I compare it with order book depth near the price, spreads, the deposit and withdrawal flows I can see on-chain, and peers of similar size. Huge volume on a thin order book is a red flag for wash trading. DEX volume I can rebuild from on-chain swaps.
Walk me through how you assess a large token unlock coming next month.
How you size future supply and judge who is likely to sell.
Size against circulating supply and daily volume, who receives the tokens, their cost basis, past behavior and any further vesting.

First the size: the unlock as a share of circulating supply and as days of average trading volume. Then who gets it. Early investors with a low cost basis are more likely to sell than a team still vesting. I read the vesting contract, watch whether recipient wallets move tokens to exchanges, and check price around past unlocks. I write it as a range, not a call.
How do you run an interview with a protocol founder so you get more than the pitch?
Your interview skill with a source who wants good coverage.
Prepare from on-chain data first, ask specific and checkable questions, ask about failures and rivals, and verify claims afterward.

I do the data work first so I can ask specifics: why deposits fell 30% in March, who the five largest wallets are. I ask what went wrong last year and which competitor worries them. I avoid questions that invite a slogan. Any claim, like a partnership or a user count, stays marked unverified until I check it on-chain or with the other party.
You suspect most of a protocol's growth is airdrop farming. How would you show it?
How you test a hunch with on-chain evidence.
Cluster wallets by funding source and behavior, compare activity around reward snapshots, check retention, and state the limits.

I look for clusters: many wallets funded from one source, making the same transactions minutes apart, often in round amounts. Then I compare activity before and after any announced snapshot or points change. If usage drops sharply when rewards end and few wallets return within 30 days, that supports farming. I show the method, the share I flagged, and what I could not rule out.
A protocol offers to pay your firm for a research report on it. How do you handle that?
Your judgement on independence and disclosure.
Payment and holdings disclosed in the report, no client control over conclusions, and compliance involved early.

Paid research can be fine if readers know. I want it in writing that the client sees the draft only to correct facts, not to change conclusions. The report states who paid, plus any tokens I or the firm hold. I bring in compliance early, because rules on paid promotion may apply. If they push to soften findings, we walk away.
After publishing, you find a number in your report was wrong and it changes one conclusion. What do you do?
How you own a mistake that readers may already have acted on.
Tell your lead at once, publish a dated, visible correction stating the impact, and fix the process that let it through.

I tell my lead the same day, with the correct figure and what it changes. We put a dated correction at the top of the report with the old and new number and the effect on the conclusion, and send it to everyone who got it. Then I find the cause. Last time a query counted bridged tokens twice, so I added a check against a second data source.

research-scientist.heading: Research scientist questions
qs: Why should the test set be used only once, at the end of a project?
Whether you keep evaluation honest.
Tuning on test makes the score too optimistic. Choices are made on a validation split, and the test set is run once.

Every choice I make while looking at a split leaks some of that split into the model. If I pick learning rates or checkpoints on test, the score no longer estimates performance on new data. So I tune on validation, freeze the setup, then run test once. If a benchmark has no validation split, I carve one out of the training data.
What makes a baseline fair?
Whether your comparisons would survive a skeptical reviewer.
Same data, a similar tuning budget and compute, a strong recent version, and rerunning it when setups differ instead of copying numbers.

The baseline gets the same data, the same preprocessing and roughly the same tuning effort as my method. I pick the strongest recent version, not an easy one. If my setup differs from the original paper, I rerun the baseline myself rather than copy its reported number. Then any gap comes from the idea, not from extra care.
Your method beats the baseline by half a point on a single run. Is that a result?
How you treat noise from random seeds.
Not yet. Several seeds for both methods, the mean with spread or a confidence interval, and a check that the gap is larger than seed-to-seed noise.

Not yet. On many benchmarks, changing only the random seed moves the score by half a point. I would run five or more seeds for both methods and report the mean and standard deviation. If the gap stays clear of the spread, I believe it. If the ranges overlap heavily, I call it inconclusive and do not claim a win.
Walk me through how you would design ablations for a method with three new parts.
Your ability to show which part of a method does the work.
Remove each part from the full method, and add each to the baseline, with everything else held fixed. Interactions get checked and all seeds reported.

I start from the full method and remove one part at a time, holding data, compute and tuning fixed. Then I add each part alone to the baseline. If removing part A hurts only when B is present, they interact, and I test that pair directly. Each row gets several seeds, so the table shows real effects and not noise.
How do you write a paper so another lab can reproduce your results?
Your scientific writing for reproducibility.
Full hyperparameters, data versions and preprocessing, seeds, compute used, released code where possible, and honest limitations.

I add a table with every hyperparameter, including the ones we never tuned. I name the exact data version, the splits and the preprocessing steps. I state how many seeds we ran and the compute each run took. When I can, I release code and configs. I also write a limitations section, so readers know where the method failed.
Your training loss turns into NaN after 20,000 steps. What do you do?
How you debug a failed training run step by step.
Reload a checkpoint from before the failure, find the batch and layer where it starts, and check usual causes: learning rate, overflow, log of zero.

I reload the last good checkpoint and replay with gradient norms logged per layer. Often the norm spikes a few steps before the NaN. Then I check the usual causes: learning rate too high, a log or division by zero, or overflow in 16-bit math. Fixes might be gradient clipping, a lower learning rate or a numerical guard. I also look at that exact batch.
You suspect test questions from a benchmark are in your pretraining data. What do you do?
Whether you handle data contamination with honesty.
Measure the overlap, report scores on clean and overlapping subsets, and disclose it in the paper instead of hiding it.

I search the pretraining corpus for long word sequences that match each test item, and I flag the hits. Then I report the score on the full set and on the clean subset only. If the clean score drops a lot, the headline number is inflated and I say so. Either way, I describe the check and its limits in the paper.
You have a fixed compute budget for one large training run. How do you choose its settings?
Your judgement in planning expensive experiments.
Small-scale sweeps across sizes, a fitted trend to extrapolate, and checks that key settings transfer. Evals and checkpoints are planned before launch.

I spend a small share of the budget on runs at several smaller sizes. I fit how loss changes with model size and data, then extrapolate to choose the big run's size and token count. I confirm the learning rate trend holds across sizes. Before launch I set regular checkpoints and evals, so a problem shows up early, not at the end.
A reviewer says your gain comes from extra parameters, not from your idea. How do you respond?
How you handle criticism with evidence instead of argument.
Treat it as a fair question: run a baseline with matched parameters, report the result either way, and adjust the claim if needed.

It is a fair point, so I answer with an experiment. I would widen or deepen the baseline until its parameter count matches ours, tune it the same way, and run several seeds. If our gain holds, I add that table to the paper. If it shrinks, I say so in the rebuttal and narrow the claim to what the data support.
After your paper is accepted, you find a bug that inflates the main result. What do you do?
Your integrity when a published result turns out wrong.
Tell coauthors at once, rerun with the fix, contact the venue about a correction, and post a corrected version with a clear note.

I tell my coauthors the same day and fix the bug. We rerun the affected experiments and see what still holds. Then we contact the program chairs about correcting the camera-ready version, post a new preprint with a note saying what changed, and update the code. If others built on our number, I tell them directly. A smaller true result beats a large wrong one.

retail.heading: Retail and store questions
qs: What does FIFO mean when you stock shelves, and why do stores use it?
Whether you know the basic rule of stock rotation.
First in, first out: older stock moves to the front so it sells before newer stock, which cuts waste from expired or dated goods.

It means first in, first out. When I put out new stock, I pull the older items forward and put the new ones behind them, so the oldest product sells first. In a grocery aisle it stops things from expiring on the shelf. In clothing it keeps older styles from sitting in the back until they need a markdown.
What does it mean to face or zone a section, and when do you do it?
Your grasp of everyday floor upkeep and visual merchandising.
Pulling products to the front edge, labels out, in the right spot on the planogram, done all through the shift and not only at close.

Facing means pulling each product to the front of the shelf with the label turned out, so the shelf looks full and neat. Zoning is the bigger pass: putting strays back where they belong and matching the planogram, which is the map of where each item goes. I do quick passes in slow moments and a full zone before close.
Walk me through what you check when you open the store.
Whether you know the routine that has to be done before the first customer walks in.
A set order: entry secured, lights and systems on, tills counted, floor safe and stocked, signs right, doors opened on time.

If the store requires two people to open, I wait for my partner and we lock the door behind us. I turn on lights and systems and count the opening till against the set amount. Then I walk the floor: no spills, exits clear, displays full. I check that sale signs match this week's prices, then unlock right on time.
A shelf tag shows a lower price than what scans at the register. What do you do?
How you handle a price error fairly for the customer and the store.
Checking the tag quickly, following the store's price policy, usually honoring the lower price, and getting the tag fixed.

I have a coworker check the tag so the line keeps moving. If the tag matches the item and is still current, I give the customer the shelf price, with an override or a manager if needed. Then I make sure the wrong tag gets fixed or pulled so the next customer does not run into the same problem.
You spot a spill in an aisle while you are helping a customer. What do you do?
Whether you put safety first without dropping the customer.
Guarding the spill right away, getting a sign up or a cleanup, then going back to the customer. A slip can cause a real injury.

I tell the customer, "Excuse me one second, I need to block this so nobody slips." I stand by the spill or put a wet floor sign over it and call a coworker on the radio. If no one can come, I clean it myself. Then I go back to the customer, thank them for waiting and finish helping them.
A delivery arrives during your shift. How do you check it in?
Your understanding of receiving and why it matters for stock counts.
Counting cartons against the paperwork before signing, noting damage or shortages on the driver's copy, then checking contents against the packing slip.

Before I sign, I count the cartons against the delivery paperwork and look for crushed or wet boxes. Anything short or damaged gets written on the driver's copy, because after I sign it clean a claim is harder. Then I open the cartons, check items and quantities against the packing slip, and tell my manager about any difference.
A customer's card is declined and there is a line behind them. How do you handle it?
How you protect a customer's dignity while keeping the line moving.
Saying it quietly and neutrally, offering to retry or use another payment, and never guessing the reason out loud.

I keep my voice low and say, "It's not going through. Would you like to try again or use another card?" I don't say "declined" loudly or guess why; it could be a chip problem or a bank hold. If they need a minute, I suspend the sale if our system allows it, help the next person, and pick it back up when they're ready.
A customer buying an age-restricted item gets annoyed when you ask for ID. What do you do?
Whether you follow the law and store policy under pressure.
Polite and firm: no valid ID, no sale. In many states the clerk, not just the store, can be fined for selling to a minor.

I stay friendly and say, "Our policy is to check ID for everyone who looks under a certain age. It's nothing personal." If they can't show a valid ID, I can't finish that part of the sale, and I say so calmly. Selling to a minor can mean a fine for me and the store, so I don't bend. If they get loud, I call my manager.
The system says we have six of an item, but the shelf looks empty. What do you do?
Your understanding of how inventory records drift and why that matters.
Searching the likely spots first, then reporting so the record is corrected. A false count can stop automatic reordering.

First I look where it could be: backroom overstock, a second display, the returns cart, the wrong shelf. If I truly find none, I tell my manager or make the count correction our process allows. If the system keeps showing six, it may never reorder, and the shelf stays empty while customers leave without buying.
You think a customer is hiding items in their bag. What do you do?
Whether you know the safe way to deal with suspected theft.
Offering service instead of accusing, never chasing or touching anyone, and telling the manager or loss prevention what you saw.

I don't accuse anyone, because I could be wrong. I walk over and offer help, like "Can I get you a basket or a fitting room?" That often stops it. I quietly tell my manager or loss prevention what I saw and what the person is wearing. I never block, chase or grab someone; most stores forbid it because people get hurt over merchandise.

retail-sales-associate.heading: Retail sales associate questions
qs: What does it mean to face or zone a shelf, and why does it matter?
Whether you know the basic floor tasks of the job.
Pulling products forward with labels out and items behind the right tag, so shoppers find things and real gaps show.

Facing means pulling each product to the front edge of the shelf with the label turned out. Zoning is doing that for a whole section and putting strays back behind their own price tag. It makes the shelf look full, helps people find things fast, and shows me the real gaps I should report for restock.
How do you approach a customer who is just browsing?
How you open a sale without crowding the shopper.
A quick, friendly greeting, an open question tied to what they are looking at, and room to browse.

I greet them within a few seconds of seeing them, then give them a moment. If they stop at something, I ask an open question like, “Is this for you or a gift?” instead of “Can I help you?”, which almost always gets a “no.” If they want space, I tell them my name and where I will be.
What do you do with go-backs, the items customers leave in the wrong place?
Whether you know how stock gets back to the shelf and what needs to move first.
Clearing them often, handling cold or frozen items first by store policy, and putting each item back behind its own tag.

I keep a go-back bin at the register and clear it every hour or when it fills. Anything cold or frozen goes first, and if I don't know how long it sat out, I ask a manager whether it can still be sold. Everything else goes back behind its own price tag, not just on any shelf nearby.
A customer says the shelf tag showed a lower price than what rang up. What do you do?
How you handle a price mistake fairly and fix its cause.
Checking the tag quickly, following store policy on the price, and getting the tag or system fixed so it does not happen again.

I ask where they saw it, or send a coworker to check, so the line keeps moving. If the tag matches that item, I follow our policy, which at most stores means giving the posted price, with a manager override if needed. Then I tell the manager so the tag or the system gets fixed before the next customer.
A customer asks which of two products is better, and you do not know. What do you say?
Your honesty and how you find product facts fast.
Admitting you are not sure, asking about their needs, and checking labels, a coworker or the store system instead of guessing.

I say I want to give them a real answer, not a guess. I ask what they will use it for, then compare the two labels with them or check the product info in our system. If a coworker knows that department, I bring them in. Afterward I read up on both so I can answer it myself next time.
A regular customer brings a coupon that expired yesterday. Do you take it?
Your judgement between store rules and keeping a good customer.
Knowing an expired coupon is not yours to accept alone, and asking a manager instead of giving a flat no.

Not on my own. A manufacturer coupon that has expired usually won't be paid back to the store, so it is not my call. I tell the customer I can't override it myself, but I ask my manager, who can sometimes honor it or give a store discount. Either way, the customer gets a real answer quickly.
Someone buying an age-restricted product has no ID but says they are clearly old enough. What do you do?
Whether you follow ID rules even under pressure.
No valid ID, no sale, said politely, and the store's ID policy applied every time, however old the person looks.

I say I'm sorry, but I need a valid photo ID for this item, no matter how old someone looks. That is our rule, and selling to a minor can bring fines for the store and sometimes for the clerk. I don't argue. I offer to hold the item or ring up the rest of the order, and if they push hard, I call my manager.
A customer hands you a $100 bill that feels wrong. What do you do?
Whether you know how to check a bill and stay safe and polite.
Checking security features like the watermark and security thread, not relying only on a pen, and calling a manager without accusing anyone.

I hold it to the light for the portrait watermark and the security thread, and tilt it to see the color-shifting 100 in the corner. Real bills also have raised print you can feel. If it still seems off, I calmly say a manager needs to approve it and keep it out of my drawer. I don't accuse anyone or put myself at risk; the manager follows our policy.
You think a customer just put something in their bag without paying. What do you do?
Whether you handle a suspected theft safely and within store rules.
No chasing, touching or accusing; attentive service as a deterrent, and a quiet report to a manager or loss prevention.

I don't accuse, block or follow anyone out; that isn't my job and it isn't safe. I go over and offer help, like, “Can I get you a basket for those?” Often that is enough. Then I quietly tell my manager or loss prevention what I saw, what the person looks like and where they are, and let them handle it under our policy.

revenue-accountant.heading: Revenue accountant questions
qs: A customer pays $12,000 up front for a one-year subscription starting January 1. How do you book it?
Whether you can turn a common contract into correct entries.
Cash and a contract liability (deferred revenue) at the start, then about $1,000 of revenue a month as the service is delivered.

When we collect, I debit cash and credit deferred revenue, which is a contract liability, for $12,000. Each month I move $1,000 from deferred revenue to revenue, because the customer gets the service evenly over the year. At March 31, $9,000 is still deferred on the balance sheet.
How do you decide whether implementation services are a separate performance obligation from the software subscription?
Your grasp of the distinct test, the core judgement in step two.
Both parts of the test: the customer can benefit from it alone or with readily available resources, and it is separately identifiable in the contract.

I ask two questions. Can the customer benefit from the setup alone or with resources it could get elsewhere, for example, do other firms offer it? And is it separate in the contract, or does it significantly customize the software into one combined output? If third parties do standard setups, it is usually distinct. If our team heavily modifies the code, I combine them.
When is revenue recognized over time rather than at a point in time?
Whether you know the three criteria for recognizing revenue over time.
Any one of three: the customer consumes the benefit as you perform, the customer controls the asset as it is built, or no alternative use plus an enforceable right to payment.

Over time applies if one of three things is true. The customer receives and uses the benefit as we perform, like a cleaning service. Our work creates or improves an asset the customer controls. Or the item has no alternative use to us and we have an enforceable right to payment for work done to date. If none apply, it is a point in time, when control passes.
Our marketplace sells a third party's products. How do you decide whether to report revenue gross or net?
How you apply the principal versus agent test, which changes reported revenue.
Focus on control of the good before transfer, supported by indicators: fulfillment responsibility, inventory risk and pricing discretion.

The key question is whether we control the product before the customer gets it. I look at who is primarily responsible for delivering what was promised, who carries inventory risk, and who sets the price. If the seller ships, sets prices and handles returns, we are an agent and record only our commission, net. If we do those things, we report the full sale, gross.
A contract gives the customer a rebate if it buys more than 10,000 units this year. How does that affect revenue each quarter?
Whether you estimate variable consideration and apply the constraint.
Estimate the rebate by expected value or most likely amount, include only what is probable not to reverse significantly, and update each period.

The rebate makes the price variable, so I estimate it from the first sale instead of waiting for year end. The outcome is yes or no, so I use the most likely amount. If order trends make 10,000 units likely, I record revenue net of the rebate. I include only what will probably not reverse significantly, and I adjust revenue in the quarter the estimate changes.
Midway through a two-year service contract, the customer adds a new module at a deep discount. How do you account for the change?
How you handle contract modifications, one of the trickiest areas of the standard.
The three outcomes: separate contract if distinct and at standalone price; otherwise prospective if remaining services are distinct; cumulative catch-up if not.

First I check whether the module is distinct and priced at its standalone selling price. It is well below what similar customers pay, so it is not a separate contract. Next, are the remaining services distinct from what we already delivered? Monthly service usually is, so I treat it as a new contract: the unrecognized price plus the new fee, spread over what remains.
How do you account for sales commissions paid on a three-year contract?
Whether you know the rules for costs of obtaining a contract, which revenue teams often own.
Capitalize incremental costs expected to be recovered and amortize them over the benefit period; mention the one-year practical expedient.

A commission is an incremental cost of obtaining the contract: we pay it only because the deal was signed. If we expect to recover it, I capitalize it and amortize it over the period the customer gets the services, which can include expected renewals. If that period is one year or less, we can expense it right away under the practical expedient.
On the last day of the quarter, sales asks you to book a large deal. The customer signs two days later, and an email promises a free extra year of support. What do you do?
Your judgement under pressure and how you protect the integrity of reported revenue.
No revenue until a contract exists under company practice; the side promise is part of the deal and must be accounted for; escalate rather than bend.

If our normal practice is a signed contract, there was no contract at quarter end, so the deal goes in the next quarter. The email matters too: free support is a promise to the customer, so it is a performance obligation that gets part of the price. I would explain this to sales, document it and tell my controller, because side promises are a control issue.

rf-engineer.heading: RF and wireless engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between dBm, dBi and dBc?
Whether you use the basic units of RF work correctly.
dBm is absolute power against 1 mW, dBi is antenna gain against an isotropic radiator, and dBc is a level relative to the carrier.

dBm is power relative to one milliwatt, so 0 dBm is 1 mW and +30 dBm is 1 W. dBi is antenna gain compared with an ideal antenna that radiates equally in all directions; a half-wave dipole is about 2.15 dBi. dBc tells how far below the carrier something sits, like a harmonic at -40 dBc.
An antenna shows a return loss of 10 dB. What does that mean in practice?
Your feel for what matching numbers mean.
About 10% of the power reflects and about 90% is accepted, a VSWR near 1.9. A good match alone does not prove the antenna radiates well.

About 10 percent of the power comes back and roughly 90 percent goes into the antenna, which is a VSWR of about 1.9. For many small devices that is an acceptable target. But a good match only means the power is accepted. A lossy antenna, or even a resistor, can match well, so I also want the radiation efficiency measured.
Why do most RF systems use 50 ohms?
Whether you know the reasoning behind a standard you use every day.
A compromise for air coax: about 77 ohms gives the lowest loss and about 30 ohms the most power handling. Today it is mainly a standard for compatibility.

It is a historical compromise. For air-filled coax, the impedance with the lowest loss is around 77 ohms and the one that handles the most power is around 30 ohms. Fifty sits between them. Cable TV and video picked 75 ohms because low loss mattered more than power. Today 50 ohms is mostly a standard so parts work together.
Walk me through a link budget for a point-to-point link.
Whether you can size a radio link from start to finish.
Transmit power plus antenna gains, minus path and other losses, compared with receiver sensitivity; what is left is the fade margin.

I start with transmit power in dBm, add both antenna gains and subtract cable and connector losses. Then free-space path loss, which grows 20 dB per decade of distance and of frequency, plus extra for rain, trees or anything blocking the clear zone around the line of sight. I compare the received level with the receiver sensitivity at the needed data rate. What is left is my fade margin.
In a receiver, should the filter go before or after the low-noise amplifier?
Whether you understand how noise figure adds up in a receiver chain.
The first stage sets most of the noise figure and loss before the amplifier adds dB for dB, so a filter goes first only when strong signals demand it.

The first stage dominates the noise figure, and any passive loss before the low-noise amplifier adds straight to it: a 1.5 dB filter in front costs about 1.5 dB. So I prefer the amplifier first. If a strong nearby transmitter could overload it, I put a low-loss filter in front and accept that penalty.
Two strong signals at 100 and 101 MHz reach your receiver. Where do the worst distortion products land, and why do they matter?
Your understanding of linearity and intermodulation.
Third-order products at 99 and 102 MHz, too close to filter out. They grow 3 dB per 1 dB of input, which is why the third-order intercept matters.

The third-order products land at 2f1 minus f2 and 2f2 minus f1, so 99 and 102 MHz. They sit right next to the wanted band, so a filter cannot remove them. They rise 3 dB for every 1 dB of input. That is why I check the third-order intercept point of the amplifier and mixer against the strongest signals the receiver will see.
Your network analyzer measurement of a filter is 2 dB off from the simulation. What do you check first?
How you separate a measurement error from a design error.
The setup first: calibration, reference plane, cables, connectors, fixture. Only then the model or the board.

First the setup. I check that the calibration is current, covers the right frequency range, and puts the reference plane at the filter, not at the end of the cable. Then I measure a known load to confirm the cal, watch for cable movement and connector torque, and remove the effect of the fixture traces. If the setup is clean, I compare the board stackup and material values with the model.
The antenna met spec on the test board but is badly detuned in the finished product. What happened, and what do you do?
Whether you know how a real product changes an antenna.
Names likely causes like the plastic housing, nearby metal, battery, ground size or the user's hand, then measures in the real product and re-tunes the match.

The enclosure plastic, the battery, a display, cables and a different ground plane size all shift the resonance, usually downward. I measure the antenna inside the real housing, with a hand or head model if the product is handheld. Then I re-tune the matching network. If the shift is large, I change the antenna length or clearance and push for that change early in the next build.
Your product fails a pre-scan for radiated emissions a week before the certification lab date. What do you do?
How you handle a compliance problem under schedule pressure.
Finds the source with near-field probes, fixes the cause rather than hiding it, rescans, and warns the team early if the date is at risk.

First I find which frequency fails and whether it is a harmonic of the transmitter, a clock or a switching regulator. With near-field probes I locate the source. Then I fix the cause: a harmonic filter, better grounding, a shield can or a slower clock edge. I rescan and tell the project lead early if the lab date is at risk. Going to the lab with a known fail wastes the slot.
The product manager wants to cut the fade margin from 15 dB to 5 dB so you can use a cheaper amplifier. How do you respond?
Your judgement when cost pushes against reliability.
Explains what the margin buys in outages the customer will notice, offers other ways to save, and puts the trade-off in writing.

I translate the margin into what the customer will see. Losing 10 dB means the link drops far more often during rain or signal fading. I show the expected outage time for both cases, then offer other savings: a higher-gain antenna, shorter cable runs or a lower data rate. If we still cut the margin, the decision and the expected outage go in writing.

risk-manager.heading: Risk manager questions
qs: What is the difference between inherent risk and residual risk?
Whether you know the basic language of a risk assessment.
Inherent risk is before controls, residual is after, and residual is what you compare to the risk appetite.

Inherent risk is the exposure before any controls, for example the chance a clerk pays a fake vendor. Residual risk is what is left after controls such as dual approval and calling the vendor back on a known number. We judge whether the residual risk fits our appetite. If it does not, we add controls, transfer the risk or stop the activity.
Explain the three lines of defense and where a risk manager sits.
Your grasp of who owns risk and who oversees it.
The business owns and runs the risk, risk and compliance challenge it, and internal audit gives independent assurance. The risk manager is second line.

The first line is the business: it takes the risk and runs the daily controls. The second line, risk management and compliance, sets the framework and limits and challenges the first line. The third line is internal audit, which tells the board independently whether both work. I sit in the second line, so I advise and challenge, but I do not own business decisions.
How do you estimate the expected loss on a loan or a customer credit line?
Whether you know the building blocks of credit risk.
Probability of default times loss given default times exposure at default, with a worked example and the link to unexpected loss.

Expected loss is probability of default times loss given default times exposure at default. If a borrower has a 2% chance of default in a year, we lose 40% of what is owed after recoveries, and we expect $5 million drawn at default, the expected loss is $40,000. That is priced in or reserved. Capital is there for unexpected loss, the swings around that average.
Explain Value at Risk in plain words, and tell me where it falls short.
Whether you can explain the main market risk number and its limits.
A correct one-line definition plus its blind spots: says nothing about the size of the tail loss and leans on past data.

A one-day 99% VaR of $2 million means that on about 99 days out of 100 we expect to lose less than $2 million, if the model and recent history hold. It says nothing about how bad the other day can be, and it can understate risk just before a crisis. So I pair it with expected shortfall, the average loss in that worst tail, and with stress tests.
The board says it will accept a certain loss in a bad year. How do you turn that into limits a desk can follow?
How you translate risk appetite into working limits.
A cascade from board appetite to business and desk limits, with a buffer, daily measurable metrics, early warnings and named owners.

Say the board accepts losing no more than 5% of annual earnings in a severe year. I turn that into stress loss and VaR limits by business, keeping part unallocated as a buffer. Then desks get limits they can watch daily, such as position size and how much they lose per move in rates. Each limit has an early warning level, an owner and an escalation path.
How would you assess the risk of our main cloud provider going down for a full day?
Your approach to operational risk, not just market and credit risk.
Maps dependent processes, puts a cost on downtime, compares tested recovery time with what the business can tolerate, and closes gaps.

I map which processes depend on it, such as payments and customer logins, and estimate the cost per hour of each being down: lost sales, penalties, overtime. Then I compare how fast we actually recover in tests with how long the business can tolerate. Gaps lead to actions like failover to a second region, manual workarounds or stronger contract terms.
You arrive in the morning and see a trader breached a limit overnight. What do you do?
How you handle a limit breach step by step.
Confirm it is real, size it, escalate per policy the same day, agree a documented fix with a deadline, then look at root cause.

First I confirm it is real and not a data error, then I find the size, the cause and whether it is still open. I escalate to the desk head and my manager that morning, as the policy says, and we agree in writing to cut the position or approve a temporary excess with a deadline. Then I log it and ask whether the limit or the process needs to change.
A 99% one-day VaR model had 9 exceptions in the last 250 trading days. What do you make of it?
Whether you can read a backtest and react to a failing model.
Knows about 2 or 3 are expected, so the model understates risk; checks data first, finds the cause, and adds caution until fixed.

At 99% we expect about 2 or 3 days where the loss beats VaR, so 9 means the model understates risk. I first check the data, for example fees or new trades mixed into the profit and loss. Then I look at where the misses cluster: often the history misses a recent jump in volatility or a product is modeled poorly. Until it is fixed I flag it and add a buffer or tighten limits.
The head of sales wants a deal that would put 30% of our receivables on one customer, against a 15% limit. What do you do?
Your judgement when the business pushes against a limit.
Shows the impact in money, offers ways to make the deal fit, and routes any exception to the right approver with a written view.

I would not just say no. I would show what a default by that customer would do to our cash and earnings, and suggest ways to fit the limit: credit insurance, a letter of credit from their bank, payment upfront or a smaller first order. If he still wants it, the exception goes to whoever the policy names, often the CFO or risk committee, with my view in writing.
Tell me about a time a control you relied on did not work.
How you own a failure and fix the cause, not just the symptom.
A specific failure, quick containment, a fix to the root cause, and a lasting change in how you test controls.

We had a monthly review of access to the payments system, always signed off. When I tested it, the report behind it left out contractor accounts, so three former contractors still had access. We removed them that day and fixed the report. I added a check that the number of accounts reviewed matches the system. Now I test the data behind a control, not just the sign-off.

robot-operator.heading: Robot operator questions
qs: What makes a teleoperated demonstration useful as training data?
Whether you understand what the robot learns from your demonstrations.
Smooth, deliberate, complete motions done the same way each time, with success clear and the cameras seeing what matters.

The model copies what I do, so I move smoothly and with purpose, with no hesitating or wandering. I finish the task fully, keep the gripper and object in camera view, and use one consistent strategy unless the team asks for variety. A fast but jerky demo is worse than a slower, clean one.
Walk me through the checks you do before you start a collection session.
Your setup routine before any data is recorded.
Clear workspace, stop button tested, cameras checked, recording confirmed with a short test episode, and the task sheet reread.

I clear loose items from the cell and make sure nobody is inside the robot's reach. I test the emergency stop, home the arms, and check every camera feed is live, in focus and not bumped. Then I record one short test episode and play it back to confirm all streams saved and line up in time. Last, I reread the task sheet for the day.
Halfway through an episode the object slips out of the gripper. Do you recover or restart?
How you follow the collection protocol when a demonstration goes wrong.
Follows the protocol, knows recovery data can be valuable if labeled, and never saves a messy episode as a clean one.

It depends on what the team asked for. Some projects want recoveries, because a robot that has seen a re-grasp can fix its own slips. If so, I recover calmly and tag the episode as a recovery. If the protocol says clean demos only, I stop, mark the episode failed, reset the scene and start again.
You notice the robot lags behind your hand more than usual. What do you do?
Whether you spot control problems and stop before they spoil data or cause a collision.
Pauses collection, checks the network and computer load, reports it, and does not keep recording with delayed control.

I stop recording and move the arm slowly to a safe position. Lag makes me overshoot, and the data then shows corrections that are not part of the task. I check the network link and whether another program is loading the computer. If I cannot fix it quickly, I report it and flag the episodes recorded just before.
When do you hit the emergency stop, and what happens after you do?
Your judgement on stopping and your routine for restarting safely.
Stops without hesitation when people, the robot or the setup are at risk; then inspects, reports and restarts only once the cause is known.

Anytime someone enters the robot's reach, the arm moves in a way I did not command, or it is about to hit something hard. I do not wait to be sure. After, I make sure everyone is clear, look for damage to the gripper, cables and fixtures, write down what happened and tell the lead. We restart only once we know why it happened.
During an evaluation run, the learned policy drives the arm toward the table edge. How do you handle it?
How you supervise a robot running on its own learned behavior rather than on your hands.
Hand on the stop, a stop rule agreed in advance, early intervention, and the failure logged as useful information.

When the robot runs on its own, I keep my hand on the stop and agree beforehand on when to step in, for example if it leaves the work area. If it heads for the edge, I stop it; I do not gamble on it correcting itself. Then I log the episode with the time and what the arm was doing, because failures like that are what the researchers need to see.
How do you keep your demonstrations consistent over a long shift?
Whether you manage fatigue and drift in your own motions.
Takes regular breaks, watches own success rate and episode times, and flags it when quality drops.

Fatigue shows up in the data before I feel it: longer episodes and more small corrections. I take short breaks on a schedule, stretch my arms and look away from the screen. Every hour I glance at my success rate and average episode time. If they slip, I tell the lead and switch to resets or labeling for a while.
What information do you record with each episode, and why does it matter?
Your understanding of logging and labeling as part of the data itself.
Task, success or failure, operator, setup and anything odd; knows a mislabeled episode can mislead training.

At minimum: the task and its variant, success or failure, my operator ID, the robot and camera setup, and any oddity such as dropped frames or a re-grasp. Researchers filter the data by these tags. If I mark a failed episode as a success, the model learns from a mistake and nobody can find it later.
You find out the wrist camera was loose for the last two hours of recording. What do you do?
How you own a mistake that affects data already collected.
Reports it at once, finds the affected episodes, flags rather than deletes them, fixes the mount and adds a check.

I stop and tell the lead right away, even though it means lost work. I play back episodes to find when the view started to shift, then flag every episode from that point instead of deleting them, so the team can decide. I tighten the mount, recheck the camera, and add a quick camera view check to my hourly routine.
The research team wants more variety in the data. How do you add it without ruining the task?
Whether you can balance variety in the data with a consistent, clear task.
Varies the scene in planned, recorded ways such as positions, objects and lighting, while the goal and success rule stay fixed.

I vary what the robot sees, not what counts as success. I move objects across a grid of positions, swap in similar objects, change the lighting and add clutter, a few changes at a time, and note each one with the episode. The goal stays the same, so the model learns the task and not one table layout.

robotics.heading: Robotics and autonomy questions
qs: What is the difference between open-loop and closed-loop control, and when is open loop good enough?
Whether you understand why robots need feedback.
Open loop trusts the command, closed loop measures and corrects; open loop only fits known, steady loads.

Open loop sends a command and trusts it, like running a motor for two seconds and assuming the arm moved 90 degrees. Closed loop measures the result with a sensor, such as an encoder, and corrects the error. Open loop is fine for a stepper motor with a light, known load. Anything with changing loads or disturbances needs feedback.
Explain what each term of a PID controller does and what can go wrong with it.
Your grasp of the most common controller in the field.
P, I and D explained by effect, with the real failure of each: offset or overshoot, integral windup, noise.

P pushes in proportion to the current error, so it reacts fast but can leave a steady offset or overshoot if set too high. I adds up past error and removes that offset, but it winds up when the motor saturates, so I clamp it. D reacts to how fast the error changes and damps overshoot, but it amplifies sensor noise, so I filter it.
Compare lidar, cameras and radar for an outdoor robot. What is each good and bad at?
Whether you know the strengths and limits of the main sensors.
Honest tradeoffs for each sensor, and the conclusion that they cover each other's gaps.

Lidar gives direct, accurate range and works in the dark, but heavy rain, fog and very dark or shiny surfaces hurt it. A camera gives color and texture, so it reads signs and lanes, but one camera gives no direct depth and struggles in glare or low light. Radar measures speed directly and sees through weather, with low resolution. That is why cars carry all three.
Why would you fuse an IMU with GPS instead of using either one alone, and how would you do it?
Your understanding of sensor fusion and state estimation.
The IMU drifts, GPS is slow and noisy; a Kalman filter combines them weighted by uncertainty.

An IMU is fast and smooth, but integrating it drifts within seconds. GPS does not drift, yet it is slow, noisy and drops out near tall buildings. A Kalman filter predicts the state from the IMU, then corrects it each time a GPS fix arrives, weighting each source by its uncertainty. I tune the noise values from logged data, not by guessing.
When would you plan a path with A* and when with a sampling planner like RRT?
Whether you can pick a motion planner to fit the problem.
A* for low-dimensional grids where shortest paths matter; sampling planners for high-dimensional spaces like arms.

For a warehouse robot on a 2D grid I use A*: with a heuristic that never overestimates the remaining cost, it finds the shortest path on that grid. For a seven-joint arm a grid is far too large, so I use a sampling planner like RRT. It finds a path fast but not the shortest, so I smooth it. RRT* moves toward the best path if given more time.
Your arm misses every grasp by the same 2 centimeters. Where do you look?
How you trace a systematic error through coordinate frames and calibration.
A constant offset means calibration or frames, not noise; you check the camera-to-robot transform, units and tool point.

A constant offset points to calibration, not noise. I check the camera-to-robot transform first: I touch the tool tip to a few known marks and compare with what the camera reports. Then I check frame conventions, like a flipped axis or millimeters read as meters, and the tool center point setting. If the offset changes with arm speed, I look at timestamps instead.
After the team added a heavier gripper, the arm started to oscillate when it stops at a target. How do you fix it?
How you debug a control problem with data instead of guessing gains.
Links the change in load to the tuning, measures the response, and checks the fix across the whole range of loads.

A heavier payload changes the inertia, so gains tuned for the light gripper may no longer fit. I log a step response to see the oscillation frequency and check that the motor is not hitting its limits. Then I retune or add feedforward based on the new mass, and test with both the light and heavy load so the fix works across the range.
A grasping policy succeeds 95% of the time in simulation and 40% on the real robot. What do you do?
How you close the gap between simulation and hardware.
Finds what the simulator models wrong, measures the real values, and makes the policy robust instead of tuning to one setup.

First I check what the simulator gets wrong: friction, motor delay, sensor noise and lighting are the usual gaps. I measure the real values, for example motor delay from a logged step, and put them in the model. Then I randomize those values in training so the policy cannot depend on one exact number, and test on hardware in small steps.
Your delivery robot's main lidar stops sending data while it is moving. What should the robot do?
Your judgement on failure handling and safe degraded behavior.
The failure is detected by design, the robot slows and stops safely, and it does not resume until the sensor is healthy.

I design for it before it happens. A watchdog flags the sensor when data stops for longer than a set timeout. The robot then slows, uses the remaining sensors only for what they can cover, and comes to a safe stop if the gap lasts. It logs the event and does not return to full speed until the sensor is healthy and checked.
Your 500 Hz control loop runs on the same computer as perception and sometimes misses its deadline. How do you fix it?
Whether you understand real-time constraints in a robot's software.
Measures jitter first, isolates the fast loop by priority or hardware, removes blocking work, and fails safe on a miss.

I measure first: loop period and jitter over hours, not seconds. Then I separate the work. The control loop runs at high priority on a real-time kernel or on a microcontroller, and heavy perception runs elsewhere and passes results through a buffer. I keep memory allocation and blocking calls out of the loop, and the controller fails safe if a deadline is missed.

rust-developer.heading: Rust developer questions
qs: What rules does the borrow checker enforce?
Whether you know the core of Rust's memory model.
Many shared references or one mutable one, never both at once, and no reference outliving the value it points to.

At any moment a value can have many shared references or exactly one mutable reference, not both. A reference can never outlive the value it points to. Each value has one owner, and when the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped. That is how Rust stops data races and dangling pointers at compile time, with no garbage collector.
When do you return a Result, and when is it fine to panic?
How you handle errors in code other people depend on.
Result for failures a caller can expect and handle. Panic only for bugs and broken invariants, or in quick tools and tests.

If the failure can happen in normal use, like a missing file or a network error, I return a Result and let the caller decide, often passing it up with the question-mark operator. A panic means a bug: something I believed was always true is false. In a library I avoid unwrap. If I must use it, I use expect with a message that says why it cannot fail.
When would you use a generic type parameter, and when a trait object like Box<dyn Trait>?
Your grasp of static and dynamic dispatch and what each costs.
Generics are compiled per type: fast and inlinable, but more code. Trait objects use a method table: one copy, mixed types together, a small cost per call.

Generics get compiled into a separate copy for each concrete type, so calls can be inlined and are fast, but binary size and compile time grow. A trait object holds a pointer to the data and a table of methods, so one function serves every type and I can keep different types in one Vec. I default to generics on hot paths and use dyn for plugins or mixed collections.
Explain Rc versus Arc, and RefCell versus Mutex.
Whether you know how Rust shares data and why some types cannot cross threads.
Rc and RefCell are for one thread; Arc and Mutex work across threads. Mentions Send and Sync, and that RefCell checks borrows at run time.

Rc counts owners without atomic operations, so it is cheap but cannot go to another thread; Arc uses atomic counts and can be shared across threads. RefCell lets me mutate through a shared reference by checking borrow rules at run time, and it panics if I break them. It is not Sync. Across threads I use Mutex or RwLock instead. The compiler refuses the wrong choice, which catches it early.
A teammate silences every borrow checker error by adding .clone(). What do you do?
Your judgement on when a quick fix is fine and when it hides a design problem.
No blanket rule: cheap clones are fine, but clones of large data on hot paths point to an ownership design worth fixing, explained kindly.

First I look at what is being cloned and where. Cloning a small struct at startup costs nothing and keeps the code simple. Cloning a large Vec inside a loop that runs on every request is a real cost. There I would sit with them and look at ownership: maybe the function should borrow, take ownership, or the data should live in an Arc. I explain the why, not just reject the change.
Can safe Rust leak memory? Give an example.
Whether you know what Rust's safety promise covers and what it does not.
Yes, leaks are not unsafe. Rc or Arc cycles, mem::forget and Box::leak all leak; a Weak reference breaks the cycle.

Yes. Rust promises memory safety, not freedom from leaks. The classic case is two Rc values pointing at each other, like a parent and child in a tree: the counts never reach zero, so nothing is dropped. I fix it by making the back link a Weak reference. Box::leak and mem::forget also leak on purpose, and both are safe functions.
What happens if you call a blocking function, like a large file read from the standard library, inside an async task?
Whether you understand how an async runtime schedules work.
The task holds a worker thread, so other tasks stall. Fix with the runtime's pool for blocking work, an async API, or a dedicated thread.

Async tasks only give up the thread at an .await. A blocking call never yields, so it ties up one of the runtime's worker threads and every task queued behind it waits; with few threads, latency jumps across the service. I move that work to the runtime's pool meant for blocking calls, or use an async version of the API. Long CPU-heavy loops get the same treatment.
Your code holds a standard library MutexGuard across an .await and will not compile when you spawn it. Why, and how do you fix it?
How you reason about Send, futures and locks together.
The std guard is not Send, so the future is not Send. Holding a lock while suspended also risks deadlock. Drop the guard before awaiting.

A future stores everything that stays alive across an .await. The std MutexGuard is not Send, so the whole future is not Send, and a multi-threaded runtime needs Send to spawn it. Even where it compiles, holding a lock while suspended can stall other tasks or deadlock. I copy out what I need and drop the guard in a small scope before the await, and use an async mutex only if I must hold it.
What does unsafe let you do, and how do you review an unsafe block?
Whether you treat unsafe code with the care it needs.
Knows unsafe unlocks a few operations but keeps the borrow checker on. Wants small blocks, written safety reasoning, a safe wrapper and tests.

It unlocks a few extra operations: dereferencing raw pointers, calling unsafe functions like C code, using mutable statics, implementing unsafe traits and reading unions. The borrow checker still runs on everything else. In review I want the block small, a SAFETY comment saying why each rule holds, a safe wrapper around it, and tests run under an undefined-behavior checker.
Your Rust rewrite runs slower than the old C++ version. Walk me through how you find out why.
How you approach performance with measurement instead of guesses.
Confirm a release build first, then profile on real input. Common causes: allocation or cloning in hot loops, unbuffered I/O, the default hasher.

First I check it was built with --release, since debug builds can be many times slower. Then I profile on real input instead of guessing. Usual suspects: allocating or cloning in a hot loop, unbuffered reads and writes on a File, and a HashMap using the default attack-resistant hasher where a faster one fits. I fix one thing, measure again, and keep a benchmark so it does not regress.

sales-coordinator.heading: Sales coordinator and deal desk questions
qs: What is the difference between a quote, a contract and a sales order?
Whether you know the documents of a deal and what each one does.
A quote is an offer, the contract is the signed agreement, and the order is the internal record that triggers delivery and billing.

A quote is our offer: products, prices and how long the price holds. The contract is what both sides sign, and it sets the legal terms. The sales order is our internal record built from the signed deal. It tells fulfillment what to deliver and finance what to bill. If the three don't match, something goes wrong downstream.
How would you explain the difference between ARR and total contract value?
Your grasp of the deal numbers that sales and finance report on.
ARR is the yearly value of recurring subscription revenue. TCV is everything in the contract over its full term, one-time fees included.

ARR is annual recurring revenue: the subscription value of one year, without setup or training fees. TCV is the total the customer commits to over the whole term, one-time fees included. A three-year deal at $40,000 a year plus a $5,000 setup fee is $40,000 ARR and $125,000 TCV.
Walk me through how you check a quote before it goes to the customer.
How careful you are with the document the customer will hold you to.
A set routine: right legal entity, products and quantities, prices against the price book, approvals on record, terms and expiry date.

I open the opportunity next to the quote. I check the customer's legal name and billing address, then each product and quantity against what the rep wrote. Prices must match the price book or have an approved discount on record. Then payment terms, start date and expiry date. Last, I check the total against the rep's number. Five minutes catches most errors.
A customer's purchase order doesn't match the signed quote. What do you do?
Whether you stop an order that would bill the wrong amount.
Holding the booking, finding which document is wrong, and getting the PO or the quote corrected in writing before the order is entered.

I don't book it as is. I compare line by line to find the gap; last time the PO had 50 licenses and the quote had 55. I tell the rep and ask the customer's buyer for a revised PO, or we reissue the quote if ours was wrong. I note it on the opportunity so finance knows why the booking waited a day.
During forecast review, a third of open deals have close dates already in the past. How do you deal with it?
How you keep CRM data honest enough to forecast from.
Getting the reps to fix their own deals rather than guessing for them, and setting up a report so stale dates show up every week.

I pull a list by rep and send it before the next review, asking each one to update the date or close the deal as lost. I don't change dates myself, because I don't know the deal. Then I set up a weekly report of past-due close dates for the sales manager, so it stays a five-minute task instead of a big cleanup.
A rep needs a 25% discount approved today, and the approver for that level is on vacation. What do you do?
Whether you respect the approval rules when a deal is under pressure.
Using the named backup or the next level up, and never putting the discount on a quote before it is approved.

I check the approval matrix for a delegate; most companies name a backup for each level. If there isn't one, I go one level up and send a short deal summary so they can decide fast. What I won't do is put the discount on the quote and get approval later. If it can't be approved today, the rep tells the customer the quote comes tomorrow.
A rep offers 30% off year one and list price in year two. List is $100,000 a year. What is the real discount on the deal?
Your deal math and whether you can show what a discount really costs.
Total paid against total list: $170,000 versus $200,000 is 15% off over the term, and year two is about a 43% price jump for the customer.

Over two years the customer pays $70,000 plus $100,000, so $170,000 against $200,000 at list. That is 15% off the contract. I'd also flag the renewal risk: going from $70,000 to $100,000 is about a 43% jump in year two, and the customer will notice. A flat 15% each year costs us the same and is easier to renew.
A customer sends back the contract asking for net 90 payment terms and uncapped liability. How do you handle it?
Whether you know which changes you can accept and which belong to finance or legal.
Spotting non-standard terms, sending payment terms to finance and liability to legal, and tracking both so the deal does not stall.

Neither is mine to accept. Net 90 means we wait three months for the cash, so finance has to approve it. Uncapped liability means unlimited risk, so legal reviews it. I send each to its owner with the deal size and close date, tell the rep what's pending, and log it in the CRM. Legal often offers a cap tied to fees paid instead.
On the last day of the quarter, a rep asks you to book a deal the customer will only sign tomorrow. What do you say?
Your integrity when there is pressure to make the numbers.
A clear no with the reason, booking only on signature, and real help getting the signature in time.

No. A deal is booked when it is signed, not before. Booking it early would put revenue in the wrong quarter, and auditors compare signature dates with booking dates. I'd help in other ways: have the contract ready for e-signature tonight and help the rep reach the customer's signer. If it lands tomorrow, it counts next quarter.
You find that a quote you prepared had the wrong price and the customer has already signed. What do you do?
How you own a mistake that costs money and touches the customer.
Telling the manager and rep right away with the numbers, letting the company decide to honor or amend, and fixing the step that let it through.

I tell my manager and the rep the same day, with the numbers: what we quoted, what it should have been, and the gap. I don't contact the customer myself; the company decides whether to honor the signed price or ask for an amendment. Then I find how it slipped through, for example a skipped price book check, and add that check to my routine.

sales-development.heading: Sales development representative questions
qs: Where does your job end and the account executive's job begin?
Whether you understand the SDR role and the handoff to the person who closes the deal.
You open and qualify, then hand over a clean meeting with notes. You do not quote prices or try to close.

My job is to start the conversation, check there is a real fit and book a meeting the AE wants to take. Before the meeting I log who the prospect is, the problem they named and who else is involved, so the AE does not ask the same questions twice. Pricing, demos and the deal itself belong to the AE.
Which numbers would you track to know if your outreach is working?
Whether you look past activity counts to the steps that actually lead to meetings.
A funnel from activity to meetings held, with the conversion rate at each step, used to find the weak step.

I track dials, connects, conversations and meetings booked. On email I watch the reply rate, not just opens. The number that matters most is meetings held and accepted by the AE. If I connect a lot but book little, my talk track needs work. If I book but people do not show up, my qualifying or confirming is weak.
Walk me through the first 30 seconds of a cold call.
How you open a call so the prospect keeps listening.
Name and company, an honest reason for the call tied to their role, then a question. No long pitch.

I say who I am and admit it is a cold call, because honesty buys me a few seconds. Then one line on why I called them: teams their size often lose hours on manual reporting. Then a question, like how they handle that today. If they talk, I listen and dig in. If not, I ask for 15 minutes later in the week.
What makes a cold email get a reply?
Your grasp of how a first email is written and why most get ignored.
Short, about the reader, one specific reason for reaching out, and one easy ask.

Keep it short and make it about them, not us. Open with something specific: a new job posting, an expansion, a problem their role usually has. Then one sentence on how we help, with a real result. End with a small ask, like “worth a short call next week?” A plain subject line usually beats a clever one.
A prospect picks up and says, “Just send me an email.” What do you do?
How you handle the most common brush-off without being pushy.
Agree, ask one question so the email is relevant, and set a follow-up in the CRM.

I say sure, and ask what would make the email worth opening: is this something they are working on now, or not on the radar at all? That question often starts a real conversation. If not, I send a short email within the hour that uses what they told me, and I set a follow-up call in the CRM for two days later.
An assistant answers and asks, “What is this regarding?” How do you respond?
Whether you work with a gatekeeper honestly instead of trying to trick your way past.
A short, true reason, respect for the assistant, and a request for their help. Never pretending to know the boss.

I tell the truth in one sentence: I am calling about how their team handles scheduling and want to see if it is a priority. Assistants know who owns what, so I ask who handles that area and when is a good time to reach them. I never claim to be a friend or to be returning a call. That burns the whole account.
How would you build a sequence of touches for a new list of prospects?
Whether you can plan follow-up across channels instead of sending one email and giving up.
Several touches over a few weeks across phone, email and LinkedIn, each adding something new, with a clear end point.

I would plan eight to ten touches over about three weeks, mixing calls, emails and a LinkedIn connection request. Each touch adds something: a short customer story, a question, a useful article, never just “bumping this up.” The last email closes the loop politely. Then I compare reply rates by step and rewrite the weak ones.
A prospect replies, “Stop emailing me.” What do you do, and what does the law require?
Whether you know the basic rules for commercial email and respect an opt-out.
Stop all outreach, mark the contact do-not-contact, and know that CAN-SPAM requires a working opt-out that is honored.

I stop the sequence right away and mark the contact do-not-contact in the CRM, so no teammate emails them either. Under the federal CAN-SPAM Act, commercial email needs an honest subject line, our postal address and a way to opt out, and opt-outs must be honored within 10 business days. I do it the same day and send nothing more.
An account executive tells you a third of your meetings are no-shows. How do you fix it?
How you take feedback and improve the quality of the meetings you book.
Look at which meetings fail, tighten qualifying, confirm the value of the meeting, and remind the prospect before it.

First I check which meetings failed: same lead source, same job title, booked weeks out? Often it is meetings I pushed that the prospect never really wanted. I would ask one more qualifying question, send the invite while still on the call, confirm the day before with a note on what we will cover, and book within a week when I can.
A sequence just went to 300 prospects with “Hi {FirstName}” in the greeting. What do you do?
How you handle a visible mistake quickly and honestly.
Pause the sequence, tell your manager, find the cause, fix the data and test before sending again.

I pause the sequence at once so the next steps do not go out broken, and I tell my manager before anyone asks. The cause is usually contacts with an empty first-name field. I fix or remove those records and send a test to myself. In the next touch I may open with one human line owning the mistake. Some people reply to that.

sales-enablement.heading: Sales enablement manager questions
qs: What is the difference between sales enablement and sales training?
Whether you understand the scope of the role beyond running classes.
Training is one part; enablement also covers content, tools, coaching and onboarding, tied to how reps actually sell.

Training teaches a skill at one point in time. Enablement is everything a rep needs to sell well, all the time: onboarding, playbooks, the content they send buyers, coaching with their managers, and tools that are easy to use. I judge my work by what changes in the deals, not by how many sessions I ran.
How would you build a 90-day onboarding plan for new account executives?
How you structure ramp-up so new reps sell sooner.
Clear stages with milestones, practice before live calls, managers involved, and a measure like time to first closed deal.

Weeks one and two cover the product, buyer personas and our sales process, with a short quiz each week. Weeks three to six are shadowing, role-plays graded against a rubric, and a pitch certification before they run calls alone. After that come live deals with weekly manager coaching. I track time to first meeting booked and time to first closed deal for each group.
What goes into a good sales playbook?
Your grasp of content reps will actually use in a deal.
Built around buyer situations and stages, with questions, talk tracks, objections and proof, short enough to use during a call.

I organize it by buyer and deal stage, not by product feature. For each stage: the goal, the questions to ask, short talk tracks, common objections with answers, and the proof to send, like a customer story. I write it with top reps, keep each section to a page, and give it an owner and a review date so it does not go stale.
How do you decide what to train reps on next?
Whether you base your plans on evidence rather than on requests alone.
Uses data and listening: where deals stall, call reviews, win-loss notes and manager input, then ranks gaps by impact.

I look at where deals stall in the CRM, for example many deals dying between demo and proposal. Then I listen to recorded calls from that stage and ask managers what they see. If reps skip discovery before the demo, that is the topic. I rank gaps by how much revenue they touch and how much training can actually fix them.
A major product launches in three weeks. How do you get the sales team ready?
How you plan and run a launch under a tight deadline.
Agrees the message with product marketing, keeps training short and role-based, checks readiness, and keeps supporting after launch.

First I agree with product marketing on who the product is for, the problem it solves and how it differs from alternatives. Then a short live session, a one-page brief, a demo script and an objection list. Reps record a two-minute pitch that managers review before launch day. After launch I collect the questions buyers ask and update the materials.
How do you measure whether a training program worked?
Whether you measure behavior and results, not only satisfaction.
Goes past survey scores: tests knowledge, checks behavior on real calls, then compares business metrics with a baseline.

I use the four Kirkpatrick levels. Did reps find it useful. Did they learn it, shown by a quiz or a graded role-play. Do they use it, which I check in real calls or CRM fields a month later. And did the numbers move, like conversion at the targeted stage compared with before. The first level is the easiest to get and tells me the least.
Three months after launch, most reps still are not using the new pitch deck. What do you do?
How you handle low adoption without blaming the reps.
Finds out why before pushing harder: checks usage data, asks reps, fixes the deck or access, and gets managers to reinforce it.

I check the usage data, then talk to five reps, including two top performers. Often the deck is too long, hard to find, or does not fit the buyers they meet. I fix what they point to, cut it down, and ask a respected rep to show how she uses it. Then managers ask to see it in deal reviews, so using it becomes routine.
A sales VP asks you for a training because win rates dropped. How do you respond?
Your judgement on whether a problem can actually be solved by training.
Diagnoses first: not every drop is a skills gap. It could be pricing, lead quality, a new competitor or territory changes.

I say yes to looking into it, not yet to the training. I check whether the drop is across all reps or a few, which deal types, and what loss reasons say. If a new competitor is winning on price, a class will not fix it, and I bring that to the VP with the data. If reps lose at the same skill step, training plus coaching is the answer.
Tell me about an enablement program that did not work. What did you change?
Whether you own your mistakes and learn from the data.
A real failure, a clear reason found, and a specific change that was measured afterward.

I ran a full-day negotiation workshop. Reps rated it highly, but a month later call reviews showed almost no change in how they handled discounts. The problem was no follow-up. I rebuilt it as short weekly sessions, each followed by a role-play with their manager. The next quarter, the average discount on that team's closed deals fell from 18% to 13%.
How do you show leadership that enablement drove revenue when so many other things affect it?
How you prove impact honestly when cause and effect are hard to separate.
Uses baselines, comparison groups and leading indicators, and is clear about what the data can and cannot prove.

I avoid claiming all the revenue. I set a baseline before a program starts and, where I can, roll it out to one team first and compare it with a similar team over the same period. I track leading measures like ramp time and stage conversion. When I report, I say what the data shows and what it does not, so leaders trust the numbers I do claim.

sales-engineer.heading: Sales engineer questions
qs: What do you need to learn in technical discovery before you build a demo?
Whether you know what discovery is for in this role.
The business problem, the current setup and where it breaks, who decides and how they will judge success, not just a list of features.

I want the problem in their words, what they use today and where it breaks, which systems we must connect to, who signs off technically and what a win looks like for them. If I only learn which features they asked about, I end up demoing everything and proving nothing.
How do you tailor a standard demo for a specific customer?
How you turn a generic product tour into a story about the buyer.
Lead with their biggest pain, use data and terms that look like theirs, show the few workflows that matter and cut the rest.

I start from the two or three pains I heard in discovery and open with the one that hurts most. I load sample data that looks like theirs, use their job titles and words, and show the outcome first, then how we get there. Features they did not ask about stay out unless they ask. Twenty strong minutes beat sixty tired ones.
A prospect asks a technical question in a demo and you do not know the answer. What do you do?
Your honesty under pressure in front of a buyer.
Say you do not know, write the question down, commit to a time for the answer and follow up in writing. No guessing.

I say I am not certain and I will not guess, because a wrong answer can come back later as a promise. I write the exact question down, ask a short follow-up to understand the context, and give a day for the answer. Then I check with product or engineering and send it in writing, copying the account executive.
Your demo environment crashes in the middle of a live presentation. Walk me through how you handle it.
How you recover from a failure without losing the room.
Stay calm, name it briefly, switch to a prepared backup, keep the conversation useful and follow up with the part they missed.

I say plainly that the environment has dropped and move to my backup: a second instance or a short recording of the same flow, which I keep ready for every call. If neither works, I sketch the workflow on a whiteboard and use the time for their questions. Afterward I book a short session to show the missed part live, and I find out why it failed.
How do you set success criteria for a proof of concept?
Whether you can scope a proof of concept so it ends in a clear decision.
A few measurable tests agreed in writing with the decision maker before work starts, plus dates, owners on both sides and the next step if it passes.
