Before we start I write down three to five tests with the customer, each with a pass mark they agree to, like loading their own data and producing a given report within a set time. We fix the dates, who does what on both sides, and what happens if it passes, such as a purchase decision. The person who signs off reviews the plan, not only the engineer who tests.
When would you push back on a customer's request for a proof of concept?
Your judgement about where scarce technical time is worth spending.
When the deal is not qualified, there are no criteria, or a cheaper step would answer the doubt; you offer that alternative instead of a flat no.

A proof of concept costs weeks of my time and theirs, so I push back when there is no budget, no decision date or no agreed criteria, or when it is really a free trial with no buyer behind it. Often a tailored demo, a reference call or a sandbox answers the doubt. If they still need one, I tie it to a written plan and a decision at the end.
Halfway through a proof of concept, the customer keeps adding new requirements. How do you handle it?
How you control scope creep without damaging the relationship.
Go back to the agreed criteria, separate what changes the decision from what can wait, and reset time or scope openly with the sponsor.

I bring out the written success criteria and ask which new items would change the buying decision. Those I discuss with the sponsor: we add them and move the end date, or swap out a lower priority test. The rest go on a list for after purchase. I keep the account executive informed so a two week trial does not drift into two months.
The account executive promised a prospect a feature the product does not have. What do you do?
Whether you protect the customer's trust and your working relationship at the same time.
Raise it privately with the account executive first, then correct it with the customer plainly, sharing a workaround and only confirmed roadmap facts.

I talk to the account executive privately first, so we correct it together and not in front of the customer. Then we tell the prospect plainly what the product does today, show the closest workaround, and mention a roadmap date only if product management has confirmed it. Losing a deal now is cheaper than a customer who finds out after signing.
How do you handle a security questionnaire or a request for proposal with hundreds of technical questions?
Your process for accurate, consistent written answers at volume.
Reuse approved answers, route certification and legal items to their owners, never claim more than is true, and track the deadline.

I start from our library of approved answers and update anything that has changed. Questions about certifications, data handling or contract terms go to the security or legal owner, because a wrong yes can turn into a contract promise. I mark partial items as partial with a short explanation, and I keep a tracker so nothing misses the deadline.
Tell me about a deal where you won the technical evaluation but still lost. What did you learn?
Whether you understand that the technical win is only one part of the sale.
An honest story with a clear reason outside the technology, such as budget, champion or timing, and a real change in how you work since.

We passed every test in a proof of concept for a mid-size logistics company, then lost on price to a tool their finance team already used. I had worked only with the engineers and never met the person who controlled the budget. Now I ask in discovery who approves the spend, and I make sure that person sees the business case, not just the IT team.

sales-manager.heading: Sales manager questions
qs: What do you look for when hiring a salesperson, and how do you test for it in the interview?
How you hire reps on evidence rather than on charm.
A mock call or role play, specific proof of past results, and a test of coachability: give feedback and see if they adjust.

I ask for numbers: quota, attainment, deal size, and how they found their deals. Then we do a short mock discovery call. Halfway through I give one piece of feedback and run it again. If they use it, I can coach them. A smooth talker who ignores the feedback is a risk.
Walk me through how you coach a rep after listening to one of their recorded calls.
Your coaching method, as opposed to just giving opinions.
The rep reviews the call first, the manager picks one or two behaviours, and they practise the change before the next call.

I ask the rep to listen first and tell me what went well and what they would change. Then I pick one thing, say, they pitched before asking about the buyer's problem. We role-play that part twice, and I listen to their next call to see if it stuck. One fix at a time works better than ten notes.
How do you run a weekly deal review with your team?
Whether you inspect deals or just collect status updates.
The same questions on every deal: buyer, pain, decision process, next step with a date. Deals without those facts get flagged.

Each rep brings their top deals. For each one I ask: who signs, what problem we solve for them, how they decide, and what the next step is with a date on the calendar. If the answer is "they will get back to me", the deal goes back to an earlier stage. It takes 45 minutes and it stops surprises.
How much pipeline do you need going into a quarter, and how do you work out that number?
Whether you understand pipeline coverage beyond a rule of thumb.
Coverage is derived from the team's own win rate and slippage, not a fixed 3x copied from a blog.

I start from our history. If we win about a quarter of qualified pipeline by value, I need about four times the quota in pipeline, plus a bit for deals that slip. I check it by stage too: early-stage pipeline converts less, so a big number made of first meetings is not the same as real coverage.
How do you build a revenue forecast you are willing to stand behind?
Your forecasting method and its discipline.
A bottom-up call by deal with clear category rules, checked against history and a top-down view, adjusted for each rep's track record.

I put each deal in commit, best case or pipeline using written rules: commit means the buyer confirmed the timeline and the signer. I add it up, then compare with what our weighted pipeline and past quarters suggest. I also know which reps are optimistic and which sandbag. If the numbers disagree, I dig in before I submit.
You have six reps and one region to split. How do you draw the territories?
How you plan territories so they are fair and workable.
Balance by revenue potential and workload, not just account count or map size, while keeping existing customer relationships where possible.

I score accounts by potential: company size, industry fit, and what we already sell them. Then I build six groups of about equal potential and check travel time and current relationships. I do not move a rep off an account they are about to close. I share the logic with the team so nobody thinks the split was personal.
How do you set a quota for a new rep who starts in the middle of the year?
Whether you plan for ramp time instead of setting new people up to fail.
A ramped quota based on how long new reps really take to reach full productivity, prorated for the months left.

I look at how long our past hires took to close at full pace, say five or six months. The new rep gets a low target the first months that rises step by step, and the annual number is prorated. I also give activity goals early, like meetings booked, because results lag. My own team forecast counts them as ramping, not full.
Your best rep asks for a 30% discount to close a deal before quarter end. How do you decide?
Your judgement on discounting and its long-term cost.
Find out why the buyer needs it, trade the discount for something of value, and think of the precedent for this customer and the team.

First I ask what the buyer actually said. Often the issue is budget timing, not price. If we discount, I want something back: a longer contract, payment up front, or a reference. I keep it within what I can approve and explain it. If every quarter ends with big discounts, buyers learn to wait, and that hurts every future deal.
A deal in a rep's commit has slipped for the third quarter in a row. What do you do?
How you handle a stuck deal and protect the forecast.
Take it out of commit, requalify it with the rep, and test whether the buyer is real, possibly by joining a call.

I take it out of commit now; it has not earned its place. Then I sit with the rep and go through what changed each time. If nobody can name the signer or a reason to buy this quarter, it goes back to an early stage. I may join a call with the buyer myself. Sometimes the right move is to stop spending time on it.
Two of your reps claim the same account and the commission on a new deal. How do you settle it?
How you handle conflict between reps fairly and fast.
Decide quickly from the written rules of engagement and CRM records, explain the decision, and fix the rule if it was unclear.

I check the territory rules and the account history: who owned it, who sourced the opportunity, what was logged and when. I decide within a day and tell both reps the reason face to face. If the rule was vague, I may split this one and rewrite the rule for everyone. A slow decision costs more trust than either answer.

sales-operations.heading: Sales and revenue operations questions
qs: What forecast categories do you use, and what does each one mean?
Whether you know the basic language of a sales forecast and why it must be defined.
Clear categories like commit, best case and pipeline, each with written entry rules that every rep applies the same way.

I use pipeline, best case, commit and closed. Commit means the rep would bet on it this period: a confirmed buyer, agreed terms and a signing date. Best case is likely but has a gap, like legal not started. Pipeline is everything else open. The labels only work if everyone uses the same definitions, so I write them down with clear exit criteria.
What is pipeline coverage, and how do you decide how much is enough?
Whether you can calculate coverage and tie the target ratio to real win rates.
Open pipeline divided by the remaining target, with the needed ratio derived from the team's own win rate, not a borrowed rule of thumb.

Coverage is open pipeline closing in the period divided by what is left of the target. The ratio we need comes from our own history: if we win about one in three qualified dollars, we need roughly three times the gap. I also look at it by stage, because coverage made of early-stage deals dated for next week is not real coverage.
Explain how accelerators and decelerators work in a commission plan.
Your grasp of commission mechanics and the behavior they drive.
Accurate definitions plus the reason behind them: reward overperformance, pay less for weak results, and avoid caps that make reps hold deals.

An accelerator raises the rate once a rep passes quota, say from 10% to 15% on bookings above 100%. A decelerator pays a lower rate below a threshold, so a rep at 40% earns less per dollar than one at 90%. I avoid hard caps where I can, because a cap tells top reps to push deals into the next period.
How would you design territories for a team of twelve reps?
How you balance opportunity and workload when splitting a market.
Territories balanced on potential and workload, built from account data, tested against history, with input from sales leaders before launch.

I start with account data: industry, company size and current spend, to score the potential of each account. Then I group accounts so each rep has similar potential and a workload one person can cover, not just the same number of names. I test the split against last year's bookings and review it with the managers before we announce it.
Reps keep leaving old close dates and wrong stages in the CRM. How do you fix it?
How you improve data quality without just nagging people.
A mix of system rules, clear stage definitions, manager follow-up and making the cost of bad data visible to reps.

First I make the stage rules clear: what must be true to enter each stage. Then I add checks, like flagging any deal with a close date in the past. I send managers a weekly list of stale deals to review in one-on-ones. Last, I show reps that the forecast and their territory reviews use this data, so clean data helps them.
A rep says their commission statement is wrong and they are upset. What do you do?
How you handle a pay dispute fairly and keep trust in the plan.
Listen, check the deal against the written plan and crediting rules, explain the result in writing, and fix real errors fast.

I thank them for flagging it and ask which deals they think are off. I check each one against the signed plan and our crediting rules: booking date, split, product type. If we made a mistake, I correct it on the next payroll and tell them when. If the statement is right, I walk them through the math in writing so they can see it.
How do you set quotas for next year?
Your method for quotas that are both ambitious and reachable.
Top-down company target checked against a bottom-up capacity model with ramp time, attrition and territory potential.

I start with the company bookings target, then build a capacity model from the bottom: number of reps, their ramp time if new, expected turnover and the potential in each territory. If the two numbers do not meet, I show leaders the gap before quotas go out. A plan where most reps miss quota usually means the quotas were wrong.
We missed last quarter's forecast by 20%. How would you find out why?
How you diagnose forecast error instead of blaming one cause.
Trace what was in commit at each point, where deals slipped or were lost, and whether the miss was judgement, data, or process.

I would take snapshots of the forecast from each week and compare them with what closed. For each commit deal that missed, I check: did it slip, shrink or get lost, and why? Then I look for patterns by rep, segment and stage. Often it is a few big deals called too early, which tells us to tighten what counts as commit.
Your top rep wants to keep a large account that moves to another territory in a realignment. How do you handle it?
Your judgement when fairness, the plan and a key person's pay collide.
Hold to the design rule, but offer a fair transition such as a short split credit, decided with leadership and applied the same way to everyone.

I would not make a one-off exception, because others would ask too. But I understand the loss. I would propose a rule for all reps: if a deal is already far along, the original rep keeps credit or shares it for that deal only. I take that to the sales leader, agree it, and then explain it to the rep before the change is announced.
The new commission plan is causing heavy discounting at quarter end. What would you change?
Whether you can trace a behavior back to the plan design and fix it without new side effects.
Confirm with data, then tie pay to what the company values, like discount level or margin, and check the fix will not create a new problem.

I would first confirm it: compare discount rates by week and by rep before and after the plan. If pay is based only on bookings, discounting is the easy path. I might pay a lower rate on deals above a set discount level and require approval for deep discounts. I would model past deals under the new rules before changing anything.

sales-representative.heading: Sales representative questions
qs: What is the difference between a feature and a benefit? Give me an example from something you sold.
Whether you sell outcomes rather than reading out a spec sheet.
A clear split: the feature is what the product has, the benefit is what it changes for this buyer, tied to a real example.

A feature is what the product has; a benefit is what it does for the buyer. When I sold scheduling software, automatic text reminders were the feature. The benefit for a dental office was fewer no-shows, so fewer empty chairs and more billed hours. I lead with the benefit and use the feature as the proof.
How do you ask for the close? Tell me the words you actually use.
Whether you ask for the business directly instead of waiting for the buyer to offer.
A plain, direct ask after confirming value, then silence, and a clear next step whatever the answer.

First I check we agree: 'You said the main goal is cutting setup time, and the trial showed that. Is there anything we haven't covered?' If not, I ask: 'Shall we get the order in so you start on the first of the month?' Then I stop talking. If they hesitate, I ask what is holding them back.
On a cold call, the receptionist asks what this is about. How do you get through to the decision maker?
How you treat gatekeepers and reach the right person without tricks.
Respect and honesty: a short, clear reason, asking for help, and using the gatekeeper as a source of information.

I tell the truth in one sentence: 'I work with clinics on billing errors and wanted to see if Dr. Lee is the right person for that.' I ask for help, not permission, and get the right name and the best time to call. I never pretend to be returning a call. Gatekeepers remember, and they often have a say in the decision.
A prospect says, 'Just send me some information.' What do you do?
Whether you can tell a brush-off from real interest and keep the conversation going.
Agree, then ask a question that narrows what to send, and book the follow-up before hanging up.

I say yes, then ask: 'So I send something useful and not a stack of brochures, what matters most to you right now, cost or speed?' The answer tells me if there is interest. If there is, I send one page on that point and set a 15-minute call for later that week. If they won't answer anything, it was a polite no, and I note it and move on.
A buyer tells you, 'We're happy with our current supplier.' How do you respond?
How you handle the status quo, the most common objection in sales.
No knocking the competitor; curiosity about what could be better, and a low-risk way in such as a second source or a small trial.

I take it at face value: 'Good, that's hard to find. What do you like most about them?' Then: 'If you could change one thing, what would it be?' There is usually something, like lead times. I don't attack the competitor. I offer to be the backup on one product line, so they can compare us at low risk.
A prospect asks if your product does something it doesn't. What do you say?
Your honesty when the truth may cost you the deal.
A straight no, then how much the need matters, a workaround if a real one exists, and no roadmap promises you can't keep.

I say no, plainly. Then I ask how they would use it and how often, because sometimes it is a must-have and sometimes a nice-to-have. If there is a real workaround, I show it. I don't hint that it is coming soon unless the product team has committed to it. Overselling wins a deal and loses the account at renewal.
The demo went great, then the prospect stopped answering. What do you do?
How you follow up on a stalled deal without pestering or giving up.
A few spaced touches that add value, a different channel or contact, and a polite closing message that often gets a reply.

I look back at what we agreed as the next step; often there wasn't a firm one, which is on me. Then I send something useful, like a short case study tied to their goal, and try a call. After two or three tries over two weeks I send a short note: 'Should I close your file for now?' That gets a reply more often than anything.
Your contact loves the product but can't sign. How do you get the deal through?
Whether you understand that deals are bought by a group, not by one fan.
Mapping who decides and who can block, helping the champion sell inside, and reaching the budget holder with them, not around them.

I ask my contact: 'Who else has to say yes, and what will each of them worry about?' Finance cares about cost, IT about security. I give my champion a one-page business case in their own numbers and offer to join the meeting with the budget holder. I don't go over their head; that loses me the person who wants us.
You can discount up to 10%. The buyer wants 15% to sign today. What do you do?
How you negotiate within your authority and trade concessions instead of giving them away.
No promise beyond your authority; ask for something in return, like volume, a longer term or prepayment, and take that trade to your manager.

I don't say yes to 15%, and I don't jump straight to 10 either. I ask what the extra 5% is about. Then I trade: 'If you sign for two years, or prepay the year, I can take that to my manager.' Every discount gets something back. If my manager says no, I offer what I can and explain why, honestly.
You promised a delivery date, then learn operations can't meet it. What do you do?
How you own a mistake with a customer and fix it with your own team.
Tell the customer early, with the new date and options, work with operations rather than blame them, and change how you promise dates.

I call the customer the same day, before they find out on their own. I say I gave a date without checking, give the real date, and offer what I can: a partial shipment or faster freight if operations agrees. I don't blame the warehouse. Afterward I confirm stock and lead times with operations before I quote any date.

salesforce.heading: Salesforce specialist questions
qs: What is the difference between a profile, a role and a permission set?
Whether you know how Salesforce decides what a user can do and what they can see.
Profiles and permission sets grant what a user can do. Roles shape which records a user sees through the role hierarchy.

A profile is the base every user has: which objects, fields and apps they can use. A permission set adds rights on top for some users, without making a new profile. A role sits in the role hierarchy and controls record visibility: a manager can see records owned by people below them. I keep profiles lean and grant extra access with permission sets.
When would you use a master-detail relationship instead of a lookup?
Your grasp of the data model and what each relationship type changes.
Master-detail ties the child to the parent: the parent is required, deletes cascade, sharing is inherited and roll-up summaries work. A lookup is looser.

I use master-detail when the child cannot exist alone, like invoice lines on an invoice. The child then takes its sharing from the parent, is deleted with it, and I can build roll-up summary fields such as a total on the parent. If the child should survive without a parent or needs its own owner, I use a lookup.
Walk me through a validation rule that stops reps from marking an opportunity Closed Lost without a loss reason.
Whether you can write formula logic and know the rule blocks the save when it is true.
A formula that returns true for the bad case, a clear error message on the right field, and a test before release.

Say Loss Reason is a text field. The formula is AND(ISPICKVAL(StageName, "Closed Lost"), ISBLANK(Loss_Reason__c)). When it is true, the save is blocked. I show the error on the Loss Reason field with a message that says what to fill in, then test it in a sandbox as a rep before it goes live.
A team hands you a spreadsheet of 200,000 contacts to load. Which tool do you use and how do you prepare?
Whether you can load data cleanly without creating duplicates or orphan records.
Picks Data Loader for a large load, cleans and deduplicates first, links records to parents by ID, and tests a small batch.

At that size I use Data Loader; the Import Wizard suits smaller loads of standard objects. First I clean the file: trim spaces, fix formats and check it against existing contacts so I do not create duplicates. I link each contact to its account by ID or an external ID, load 50 rows as a test, check them, then run the rest and keep the success and error files.
A sales rep says she cannot see an account her colleague can see. How do you find out why?
How you troubleshoot record access step by step.
Checks object permissions first, then org-wide defaults, ownership, role hierarchy and sharing rules, using the record's sharing tools.

First I check that her profile or permission sets give read access to accounts. If they do, the issue is record sharing. I look at the org-wide default for accounts, the record owner, and where both reps sit in the role hierarchy. The Sharing Hierarchy button on the record shows who has access and why. If a sharing rule should cover her and does not, I fix the rule, not just this one record.
How do you choose between a validation rule, a flow and Apex code for a new requirement?
Whether you pick the simplest tool that does the job well.
Clicks before code: validation rules to block bad data, Flow for most automation, Apex only for logic or volume that Flow handles badly.

If the need is to stop bad data, a validation rule is enough. If records must be created or updated, I build a record-triggered flow; Salesforce is ending support for workflow rules and Process Builder in favor of Flow. I use Apex when the logic is complex or must run over large volumes efficiently, and Apex needs test classes before it can be deployed.
Walk me through how you move a change from a sandbox to production.
Whether you build outside production and deploy with a plan.
Build and test in a sandbox, deploy with change sets or the CLI, validate first, meet Apex test coverage, and tell users.

I build in a developer sandbox, then test as real users in a sandbox with realistic data. I package the components in a change set or deploy with the Salesforce CLI. I run a validation-only deploy first, which also runs the Apex tests; production needs at least 75% code coverage. I deploy at a quiet hour and tell users what changed.
The sales VP asks you to make fifteen new fields required on the opportunity. How do you respond?
Your judgement in balancing a request against user adoption and data quality.
Asks what each field is for, requires fields only when they matter, often by stage, and keeps the page short so reps keep using it.

I ask what decision each field feeds. Often only a few matter, and only at certain stages. I would require those with validation rules by stage, not on every save, and show the rest only when they matter using conditional visibility on the record page. Fifteen required fields at creation means reps type junk to get past them, and the VP's reports get worse.
A flow that loops over related records works in testing but fails with a limit error when 500 records are loaded at once. What is likely wrong?
Whether you understand governor limits and bulk-safe design.
Names queries or updates inside a loop hitting per-transaction limits, and fixes it with one query before the loop and one update after.

Most likely there is a Get Records or Update Records element inside the loop. Salesforce caps how many queries and updates one transaction can run, and a bulk load puts many records into one transaction. I query once before the loop, change values in a collection inside it, and save with one Update Records at the end. Then I test with a few hundred records in a sandbox.
You ran a mass update that wrote the wrong values into a field on 3,000 accounts. What do you do?
How you handle your own mistake on live data.
Stops, tells people quickly, restores from a backup taken before the update, and checks what automation the update set off.

I stop any further loads and tell my manager and the account owners right away. Before every mass update I export the records with their IDs, so I restore the old values from that file with Data Loader. Then I check what the update triggered, like flows or emails to customers, and clean that up too. Afterwards I add a peer check before large updates.

sap.heading: SAP consultant questions
qs: What is the difference between configuration and custom development in SAP?
Whether you know when the standard system is enough and when code is needed.
Configuration sets standard behavior through customizing. Code comes last and is kept out of standard objects so upgrades stay safe.

Configuration means setting up standard SAP through customizing in SPRO, like company codes or tolerance limits. Development means ABAP code, such as an enhancement or a custom report. I try configuration first, then a process change, and only then code. When I do write code, I use released extension points so an upgrade does not break it.
Walk me through the procure-to-pay process in SAP.
Your grasp of the core purchasing flow and where finance enters it.
The steps in order, the role of the GR/IR clearing account, and the three-way match between order, receipt and invoice.

A purchase requisition becomes a purchase order. When goods arrive, the warehouse posts a goods receipt in MIGO, which credits the GR/IR clearing account. Accounts payable posts the vendor invoice in MIRO, which debits GR/IR and credits the vendor. SAP checks that order, receipt and invoice match. Then the payment run in F110 pays the vendor.
How does a change move from development to production in an SAP landscape?
Whether you work within the transport system and change control.
Change built in development, recorded on a transport request, tested in QA, imported to production in order after sign-off.

I make the change in the development client and save it to a transport request. Customizing and code changes go in separate requests. Once released, it is imported into QA, where key users test it. After sign-off, Basis imports it to production in the agreed order. Production is locked against direct changes, so the transport is the only path and the record of what changed.
What changed for finance when companies moved from ECC to S/4HANA?
Your knowledge of the current SAP finance model.
The Universal Journal, cost elements as GL accounts, and business partners replacing separate customer and vendor masters.

The biggest change is the Universal Journal, table ACDOCA, which holds finance and controlling line items in one place, so FI and CO agree by design. Cost elements are now GL accounts. Customers and vendors are kept as business partners. Many old totals tables became views, so reports read line items directly and some reconciliation steps went away.
A user says they cannot post because the posting period is not open. What do you check?
How you troubleshoot a common month-end error.
Knowing finance and materials periods are separate, checking which one blocks, and not opening periods without finance approval.

First I read the exact message, because finance and materials periods are separate. Finance periods are kept by period variant in OB52; the materials period moves forward in MMPV. Then I check the posting date, since the user often picked the wrong month. If a period truly needs opening, the controller approves it, because it affects the close.
An invoice was posted but is blocked for payment. How do you find out why and get it released?
Whether you know invoice verification and fix the cause, not the symptom.
Reading the block reason, linking it to tolerances or a missing receipt, and releasing it properly instead of loosening tolerances.

I display the invoice in MIR4 to see the block reason. Often price or quantity differs from the order or receipt beyond the tolerance set in configuration. If the goods receipt has since been posted, MRBR can release it automatically. Otherwise the buyer confirms the price and AP releases it in MRBR. I would not widen tolerances just to clear one invoice.
The finance lead asks you to make a quick configuration change directly in production. What do you do?
Your judgement under pressure from the business.
A polite no with the reason, and a fast, controlled alternative such as an emergency change with approval.

I say no and explain why: a change made only in production is not in development or QA, so nobody tested it and the next transport can overwrite it. If it is urgent, I use the emergency change process: build it in development, test it fast in QA, and import it with approval. I give a realistic time, often the same day.
How do you run a fit-to-standard workshop?
How you steer the business toward standard processes in a new implementation.
Demo of the standard process on real data, each step rated fit or gap, and gaps questioned before anyone writes code.

Before the session I set up the standard process in a sandbox with their sample data. I demo it end to end and let key users try it. For each step we mark it as fits, fits with configuration, or gap. For each gap I ask what business result it protects, because often a report or a small process change solves it. I log every decision with an owner.
How do you plan the migration of master data and open items into a new S/4HANA system?
Your method for moving data safely and proving it arrived correctly.
Agreed scope, cleansing at the source, several mock loads, and finance reconciling totals before go-live.

First we agree what moves: usually master data, open items and balances, not years of closed documents. We clean data in the old system. Then we run at least two mock loads into a test system, and finance reconciles each one: record counts, totals by account, open payables and receivables. Cutover follows a timed plan with sign-off after each step.
You imported a transport to production and goods receipts started failing. What do you do?
How you handle your own mistake in a live system.
Telling people fast, knowing transports cannot simply be undone, a tested correcting transport, and checking the damaged postings.

I tell the support lead and the warehouse right away so users stop and report. A transport cannot simply be rolled back, so I use the transport log and version history to find what changed. I build a correcting transport in development, test it quickly in QA and import it. Then I check which receipts failed or posted wrongly and why our test missed it.

scrum-master.heading: Scrum master and delivery manager questions
qs: What is the difference between the Definition of Done and acceptance criteria?
Whether you know the basic quality rules a Scrum team works by.
Done is one shared quality standard for every item. Acceptance criteria are specific to one story. A story needs both.

The Definition of Done applies to every backlog item, for example: code reviewed, tested, merged and documented. Acceptance criteria belong to one story and say what that feature must do, like 'a user can reset a password by email.' A story is finished only when it meets its own criteria and the Definition of Done.
Walk me through how you get a team ready for sprint planning.
How you prepare the meeting that shapes the whole sprint.
Refined top items, known capacity and a proposed Sprint Goal, so planning is about choices, not first reads.

In the week before, I make sure we have held refinement so the top items are small, clear and estimated. I collect capacity: holidays, on-call duty, training days. I ask the Product Owner to bring a proposed Sprint Goal. In planning, the developers decide how much they can take. I keep time and make sure we leave with a goal and a plan for the first days.
Your daily scrum has turned into each person reporting status to you. How do you fix it?
Whether you know who the daily scrum is for.
It belongs to the developers and is about progress toward the Sprint Goal. The scrum master steps back so they talk to each other.

First I stop being the center. I stand to the side, and some days I skip it on purpose. I ask the team to walk the board from the right, finishing work first, and to talk about the Sprint Goal, not their own tasks. Long problems go to a short follow-up after the 15 minutes, with only the people who are needed.
How do you run a retrospective that leads to real change, not just complaints?
How you turn reflection into actions the team actually takes.
Checks last time's actions, uses facts from the sprint, and ends with one or two small actions that each have an owner.

I open by reviewing the actions from last time: did we do them, and did they help? I bring a few facts, like carry-over or bugs found late, so we do not argue from memory. We pick one or two improvements small enough to finish in a sprint, each with an owner, and often add them to the Sprint Backlog. I change the format so it does not go stale.
Stories keep rolling over from sprint to sprint. How do you find out why?
How you diagnose a delivery problem instead of guessing.
Looks at the data: story size, work in progress, unplanned work, waits on others. Then tests one fix at a time.

I look at the last few sprints. Often stories are too big, so I check how many we split in refinement. I check how much was started at once: ten items in progress for five people means little gets finished. I measure unplanned work and waits on other teams. Then the team picks one change, like a work-in-progress limit, and we watch whether carry-over drops.
Mid-sprint, a director asks a developer directly to drop everything for an urgent request. What do you do?
Whether you protect the sprint while still respecting real business needs.
Routes the request to the Product Owner, who decides. Any change in scope is agreed openly, not slipped in quietly.

I thank the director and bring the request to the Product Owner the same day, since they own the backlog. If it truly cannot wait, the Product Owner and developers agree what comes out to make room, and we say so openly. If it makes the Sprint Goal pointless, only the Product Owner can cancel the sprint. What I avoid is a developer quietly doing both.
A blocker sits with another team that keeps putting it off. How do you get it removed?
How you remove blockers that sit outside your own team.
Talks to the other team first, makes the cost visible, escalates with facts if needed, and plans around the wait.

I go to their scrum master or lead and ask what is in their way; often they lack details or have their own deadline. I show the cost: three stories and a release date depend on it. If it still stalls, I bring both product owners together to set priority. Meanwhile we work on what does not depend on it, and we flag such dependencies earlier in refinement.
Your manager wants to compare velocity between teams to see who works harder. How do you respond?
Whether you understand what velocity can and cannot measure.
Explains that story points are relative to each team, so comparing them means little and invites inflation. Offers better measures.

I explain that each team sizes points against its own past work, so one team's 40 is not another team's 20. If points become a score, they inflate and stop helping anyone plan. I offer what the manager really wants to know: cycle time, how often we release, defects found after release and whether we meet Sprint Goals. Velocity stays a planning tool inside the team.
On the last day of the sprint, a story is almost done but its testing is not finished. The Product Owner wants it in the release. What happens?
Whether you hold the Definition of Done under pressure.
An item that is not Done cannot be released; it returns to the Product Backlog. You explain the risk and look for the cause.

In Scrum, an item that does not meet the Definition of Done is not released or shown as done; it goes back to the Product Backlog. I explain to the Product Owner that untested code is a risk our users would carry. Next sprint it is usually first in line. In the retro we ask why testing came last, and often the fix is to test as we build.
Your Product Owner is rarely available, and the team keeps guessing what to build. What do you do?
How you handle a gap in a role you do not own.
Raises it with the Product Owner, sets fixed time for questions and refinement, escalates if needed, and does not take over the role.

I talk to the Product Owner first and find out why; often they cover too many teams. We agree on fixed slots: refinement twice a week and a daily time for questions. I help them write clearer items and a Product Goal. If nothing changes, I raise it with whoever assigned the role. I do not start setting priorities myself, because that only hides the problem.

search-engineer.heading: Search and recommendations engineer questions
qs: What is an inverted index, and why does search need one?
Whether you know the basic data structure behind text search.
A map from each term to the documents that contain it, so a query reads short lists instead of scanning every document.

It works like the index at the back of a book. For every term, it stores a postings list: the documents that contain it, often with counts and positions. A query for two words reads two lists and intersects them, instead of scanning millions of documents. The positions let me answer phrase queries too.
How does BM25 decide that one document matches a query better than another?
Your understanding of the classic lexical scoring function.
Term frequency with diminishing returns, rare terms weigh more, and length normalization so long documents do not win by size.

It adds up a score for each query term. A term counts more the more often it appears in the document, but with diminishing returns, so the tenth mention adds little. Terms that are rare across the collection weigh more than common ones. It also adjusts for document length, so a long page does not win just because it mentions everything.
Users search for “sneakers” and get no results, but you sell hundreds of running shoes. How do you fix it?
How you handle the gap between the words users type and the words in the catalog.
Starts from the query logs, uses synonyms, stemming or meaning-based retrieval, and checks the fix does not hurt precision.

First I pull the zero-result queries from the logs to see how big the gap is. For a known gap, a synonym rule linking sneakers, trainers and running shoes is quick. For the long tail, I would add vector retrieval that matches by meaning. Then I check precision, because broad synonyms can flood results with wrong items.
How do you measure whether a new ranking is better before it reaches users?
Your knowledge of offline ranking metrics.
Names a position-aware metric like NDCG or MRR on labeled queries, and knows an offline gain still needs an online test.

I build a test set of real queries with relevance labels, from human raters or from past clicks and purchases. Then I compute NDCG, which rewards putting the most relevant items near the top, and MRR when there is one right answer. I compare both rankings on the same set, read the queries that got worse, and only then run an A/B test.
Your click data says the first result is the best one almost every time. Why might that be wrong?
Whether you understand position bias in click data.
Users click the top slot partly because it is on top; you correct for that before training a model on clicks.

People click what they see first, so top slots get clicks even when lower results are better. Trained on raw clicks, a model learns to copy the old ranking. I would estimate the bias with small randomized position swaps, then weight clicks by how likely each position was to be seen. Interleaving tests also compare rankings more fairly.
A new product was added today and no one has clicked on it yet. How does your recommender handle it?
How you handle the cold start problem.
Uses content features like title, category and price, plus a little controlled exploration so new items can earn data.

A model trained only on clicks cannot place an item with no history. So I use content: title, category, brand, price and text or image embeddings, to find similar items that do have history. I also keep a small share of slots for showing new items, so they collect clicks. Once there is enough data, behavior signals take over.
Why do most search and recommendation systems retrieve candidates first and rank them in a second step?
Your grasp of the two-stage architecture and its speed and recall trade-offs.
Cheap retrieval narrows millions of items to hundreds; a heavier model reranks only those, inside the latency budget.

Scoring millions of items with a heavy model on every request is too slow. So a cheap stage, like BM25 or a nearest neighbor search on embeddings, pulls a few hundred candidates fast. A richer model then ranks only those. The catch: if retrieval misses a good item, the ranker never sees it, so I measure the recall of each stage separately.
Your new model beat the old one on every offline metric, but the A/B test shows no change. What do you do?
How you reason when offline and online results disagree.
Checks the experiment and the data pipeline first, then looks for gaps between offline labels and what users value, without forcing a launch.

First I check the experiment: is traffic split correctly, is the new model really serving, is the test big enough to detect the lift we expected. Then I look for a mismatch, like labels built from old clicks that reward copying the old ranking, or features that arrive late in production. I would not ship on offline numbers alone.
Your “you may also like” list shows the same bestsellers to everyone. Is that a problem, and what would you do?
Your judgement about popularity bias and feedback loops.
Sees the feedback loop, weighs short-term clicks against discovery, and proposes measured fixes like diversity rules.

It can be. Bestsellers get shown, so they get clicked, so the model shows them more, and the rest of the catalog never gets a chance. I would measure catalog coverage and how personal the lists are. Then I would try a popularity penalty or a diversity rule, like at most two items per category, and check engagement over weeks, not days.
The business team wants to push high-margin items higher in search. How do you handle it?
How you balance revenue goals against relevance and user trust.
Neither refuses nor blindly complies: boosts only among relevant results, tests long-term effects, and labels paid placements.

I would not add a flat boost, because irrelevant items on top cost us searches and trust. I would boost only among items that already pass a relevance threshold, and test it on revenue per search and repeat visits, not margin alone. If a supplier pays for the spot, it is an ad, and it has to be clearly labeled as sponsored.

security-analyst.heading: Security analyst and incident response questions
qs: What is the difference between an event, an alert and an incident?
Whether you use the basic terms of the work precisely.
Events are anything logged, alerts are events a rule flagged, incidents are confirmed or likely harm that needs a response.

An event is anything a system records, like a logon. An alert is an event or pattern that a rule flagged as worth a look. An incident is when we confirm, or strongly suspect, that something is actually threatening our systems or data. Most alerts I close never become incidents, and that is normal.
Which Windows event IDs do you check first when looking at logon activity?
Your hands-on knowledge of the Windows Security log.
4624 and 4625 for success and failure, the logon type, and related IDs such as 4672 and 4688, with a clear idea of what each one tells you.

4624 is a successful logon and 4625 a failed one. I always read the logon type: 10 means Remote Desktop, 3 means a network logon such as a file share. 4672 shows special privileges were assigned at logon, so an admin session. If process creation auditing is on, 4688 tells me what ran after the logon.
How would you tell password spraying apart from a brute-force attack in the logs?
Whether you can turn an attack pattern into something a detection rule can find.
Brute force is many tries on one account. Spraying is a few common passwords across many accounts, so the rule must count distinct users per source.

Brute force hammers one account, so I look for many failures on a single user. Spraying tries one or two common passwords across hundreds of accounts to stay under the lockout limit. For that I count distinct usernames with failed logons from one source IP in a time window, and I check whether any of those accounts then had a success.
An alert shows PowerShell running with an encoded command on a finance laptop. How do you triage it?
How you work through a common alert step by step.
Decode the command, check the parent process, the user and the network activity, then decide on isolation based on what it actually does.

First I decode it: the -EncodedCommand value is Base64 of UTF-16 text. Then I check the parent process. Word or Outlook launching PowerShell is a bad sign; a management tool may be normal. I look at what it connected to and what files it wrote. If it downloads code from an unknown site, I isolate the laptop through the endpoint agent and open an incident.
One of your detection rules fires 300 times a day and almost all are false positives. What do you do?
How you tune detections without creating blind spots.
Find why it is noisy and narrow it with specific, documented exceptions. Never just turn it off or let analysts get used to ignoring it.

I group the hits to see what drives the noise; often one backup job or admin script causes most of it. I add a narrow exception for that exact host, account and command line, write down why, and set a date to review it. Then I test the rule against a known bad sample to make sure it still fires. Disabling it would just hide the next real attack.
A user reports they clicked a phishing link and typed in their password. What do you do in the first hour?
Whether you know the full set of steps after stolen credentials, not just a password reset.
Reset the password and revoke sessions, check sign-ins and MFA changes, look for mailbox rules, and find and remove the email from other inboxes.

I reset the password and revoke active sessions, since a reset alone may not end a session the attacker already has. I check sign-in logs for logons from new places and whether a new MFA device was added. I look for inbox forwarding or delete rules, a common trick. Then I search all mailboxes for the same email, remove it, and block the sender and link.
How would you look for malware beaconing in proxy or DNS logs?
Your ability to hunt for threats that no rule has caught yet.
Regular connection timing, rare destinations and steady request sizes, then checking against what is normal before calling it malicious.

Malware often calls home at steady intervals, say every 60 seconds with a little random variation. I group connections by host and destination and look for very regular gaps, similar byte counts and domains few other machines visit. Software updaters do this too, so I check the domain's age and the process making the calls before I raise it.
Why shouldn't you just power off a machine you think is compromised?
Whether you protect evidence while containing a threat.
Memory holds evidence that is lost at shutdown. Isolate from the network instead, capture the most volatile data first, and hash what you collect.

Memory holds running processes, network connections and sometimes code that never touches the disk, and a shutdown wipes it. I cut the machine off the network, usually through the endpoint agent, then capture memory before the disk image. I hash each file I collect and log who handled it, so we can show later it was not changed.
Tell me about an alert you closed as a false positive that turned out to be real. What did you change?
How you own a mistake and fix the process behind it.
Honest about the miss, quick to reopen and escalate, and a concrete fix such as a better rule, a checklist step or a second review.

I closed a login alert from a new country because the user often traveled. Two days later the same account sent internal phishing. I reopened it, escalated, and we contained it that afternoon. I had assumed instead of checked. Now I confirm travel with the user or manager, and we added device details to that alert so the next analyst sees more.
The IT manager wants to wipe and rebuild an infected server right now to get the business running. What do you say?
Your judgement when speed and investigation pull in different directions.
A fast path that preserves evidence first and finds how the attacker got in, so the rebuilt server is not breached again the same way.

I would say I want it back up too, but if we rebuild before we know how they got in, they can use the same door again tonight. I ask for an hour or two to capture memory and a disk image and check for other infected hosts. Meanwhile we keep it isolated, restore from a backup we have checked is clean, and close the entry point.

security-architect.heading: Security architect questions
qs: What does zero trust mean to you, beyond the buzzword?
Whether you understand the model itself and not just the label.
No trust is granted from network location alone. Every request is checked on identity, device and context, and access is kept narrow.

It means being inside the network earns you nothing by itself. Each request is checked on who the user is, the state of the device and what is being asked for. Access is granted per app, not to a whole subnet. It is a direction you move toward over years, through identity, device health and segmentation, not one product you buy.
In the cloud shared responsibility model, what stays with us?
Whether you know where the provider's job ends and the company's begins.
The provider secures the underlying infrastructure. The customer owns identities, configuration and data, and the split shifts between IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.

The provider runs the data centers, the hardware and the base platform. We own who gets access, how services are configured, and our data. On plain virtual machines we also patch the operating system; with SaaS we mostly own users and settings. Most cloud breaches I have studied were customer-side mistakes, like a storage bucket left public.
Walk me through how you threat model a new service.
Your method for finding design risks before anything is built.
Draw data flows and trust boundaries, list threats with a framework like STRIDE, rank them, and turn them into design changes.

I sit with the team and draw the data flow: users, services, data stores, and where data crosses a trust boundary. At each boundary I go through STRIDE: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege. We rank what we find by likelihood and impact, and each real threat becomes a ticket or a design change.
Which MFA methods would you allow for admin accounts, and why?
Whether you know which second factors actually stop phishing.
Phishing-resistant methods such as FIDO2 security keys or passkeys, because SMS codes and simple push prompts can be phished or approved by mistake.

For admins I want phishing-resistant MFA: FIDO2 security keys or passkeys. They are tied to the real site's domain, so a fake login page gets nothing usable. SMS codes can be stolen through SIM swaps, and push prompts invite fatigue attacks where a tired user taps approve. Those are not acceptable for privileged accounts.
How would you segment a flat network where everything can talk to everything?
How you plan a big structural change without breaking the business.
Map real traffic first, build zones by function and sensitivity, default-deny between them, and roll out in monitored stages.

First I learn what really talks to what from flow logs, since diagrams are often wrong. Then I group systems into zones, such as user devices, servers, payments and management, with the tightest rules around the most sensitive. I run new rules in log-only mode, fix what would break, then switch to default deny. Ransomware on one laptop then cannot reach the database servers.
How should we encrypt sensitive data at rest, and where should the keys live?
Your grasp of key management, which matters more than the cipher itself.
Keys held in a key management service or HSM, apart from the data, using envelope encryption, rotation and tightly controlled, logged key use.

I would use envelope encryption: each data set is encrypted with a data key, and that data key is encrypted by a master key held in a key management service or hardware security module. The master key never leaves it. Key use is limited by role and logged, so a stolen copy of the files alone is useless.
A developer pushed a cloud access key to a public repository an hour ago. What do you do?
Whether you act in the right order when a secret leaks.
Revoke and rotate the key first, since deleting the commit is not enough. Then check logs for any use of the key and fix the cause.

First I have the key disabled and replaced, right now. Bots scan public repos within minutes, and deleting the commit does not remove it from history. Then I check the audit logs for any use of that key. Last, I fix the cause: secret scanning in the pipeline and short-lived credentials that expire on their own.
A critical legacy system cannot be patched or replaced this year. How do you protect it?
How you reduce risk when the ideal fix is not available.
Compensating controls: isolate it, allow only needed connections, add monitoring, and document the risk with an owner and a review date.

I put it in its own segment and allow only the few connections it really needs, with admin access through a jump host. I remove internet access, add logging and alerts around it, and harden what can still be changed. Then a business owner signs the documented risk with a review date, so the exception does not quietly become permanent.
The business wants to launch next week, and your review found a serious design gap. What do you do?
How you weigh security risk against business needs without simply blocking.
Explain the risk in business terms, offer options with mitigations, and have an accountable owner accept any remaining risk in writing.

I explain the gap plainly: what an attacker could do and what it would cost us. Then I offer options, for example launch with the feature behind login and a rate limit, and fix the root issue within thirty days. If they go ahead, a named business owner accepts the risk in writing with a fix date. My job is to make the risk clear, not to own every decision.
How should our services authenticate to each other instead of using shared passwords?
Your design for machine identity, a common weak point in modern systems.
Each workload gets its own identity with short-lived, automatically issued credentials, such as mutual TLS or platform tokens, and no long-lived secrets in code.

Each service gets its own identity and short-lived credentials issued automatically. That can be mutual TLS, where both sides present certificates that rotate often, or tokens the cloud platform issues to the workload. Each call is checked against a policy of which service may call which. No passwords sit in config files, and a stolen credential expires quickly.

security-compliance.heading: Security compliance (GRC) questions
qs: What is the difference between a SOC 2 Type I and a Type II report?
Whether you know the basic shape of the audit you would be running.
Type I tests control design on one date. Type II tests design and operation over a period, so it needs evidence across months.

A Type I says the controls were designed properly on a single date. A Type II says they were designed properly and actually worked over a period, often six to twelve months. Most customers want the Type II, so a company often gets a Type I first and then runs its first observation period.
SOC 2 has five Trust Services Criteria. How do you decide which ones go in scope?
How you scope an audit to what customers actually need.
Security is always in. The others are added when customer commitments or the product call for them, not for show.

Security is required; its controls are called the common criteria. Then I look at what we promise customers. If contracts include uptime commitments, Availability makes sense. If we hold their confidential data, Confidentiality. Processing Integrity and Privacy fit fewer companies. Every extra criterion adds controls and evidence, so I add one only when a customer need backs it.
What is the difference between a policy, a standard and a procedure?
Your skill at writing documents people can follow and auditors can test.
Policy says what and why, the standard sets the measurable rule, the procedure gives the steps. Keeping them apart keeps policies short and stable.

A policy states the rule and who owns it, for example: access follows least privilege. A standard makes it measurable: access is reviewed every quarter. A procedure is the steps: export the user list, send it to managers, record the changes. I keep policies short so they rarely need new approval, and put details that change into standards and procedures.
Walk me through how you run a risk assessment.
Whether your risk assessment drives decisions or just fills a spreadsheet.
Assets and threats, likelihood and impact, a treatment and an owner for each risk, and a review on a set schedule.

I start with the assets that matter: customer data, production systems, key vendors. With system owners I list threats and rate likelihood and impact to get inherent risk. Then I map existing controls, rate residual risk, and pick a treatment: reduce, transfer, avoid or accept. Every risk gets an owner, and accepted risks get a leadership sign-off. I rerun it at least yearly.
The auditor asks for evidence of your quarterly user access reviews. What do you hand over?
Your sense of what makes evidence complete and believable to an auditor.
A system-generated user list, proof of who reviewed it and when, and tickets showing the requested removals were actually made.

For each quarter: the user list pulled straight from the system, with the date and source visible, so it is complete. The reviewer's dated sign-off. And the tickets for every change they asked for, showing the access was really removed. A spreadsheet someone typed by hand, with no trail back to the system, usually gets questioned.
A prospect asks for our SOC 2 report, but the period ended five months ago. What do you send?
Whether you know how SOC 2 reports are shared and kept current.
The report under NDA, since a SOC 2 is meant for specified users, plus a bridge letter covering the gap since the period ended.

A SOC 2 is meant for specified users, so I share it under an NDA. Because the period ended months ago, I add a bridge letter: a statement from our management that there have been no material changes to the controls since then, and when the next report is due. If they only want a public summary and we have a SOC 3, that can go out freely.
Sales wants to tell a big prospect we are 'SOC 2 certified' while our first audit is still underway. How do you handle it?
How you protect the company from claims it cannot back up.
No overclaiming: SOC 2 is an auditor's attestation report, not a certification. Then an accurate line sales can still use to close.

I would stop that wording. SOC 2 is not a certification, it is an auditor's report, and we do not have one yet. A false claim could cost the deal or breach a contract. I would give sales an accurate line: our Type II observation period is underway with an independent CPA firm, and we expect the report in the fall. I would also offer a call with me.
Mid-audit, you find two quarterly access reviews were never done. An engineer offers to do them now and date them back. What do you do?
Your integrity when the audit result is on the line.
Refuse backdating, tell the auditor, fix the control and write a management response. An honest exception beats a falsified record.

I would say no right away. Backdated evidence is falsified evidence, and if the auditor finds it, the whole report is in doubt. I would tell the auditor about the gap, run a review now with today's date, remove any access that should not be there, and fix the cause, such as a missing owner or reminder. The exception goes in the report with our management response.
We run on a large public cloud provider. How does that show up in our SOC 2?
Whether you understand subservice organizations and shared responsibility.
The provider is a subservice organization, usually carved out. You review its own SOC 2 and cover your side of the shared controls yourself.

The provider is a subservice organization. Most reports use the carve-out method: its controls are left out, and our report lists the ones we rely on it for, such as data center physical security. Each year I review the provider's own SOC 2 and its exceptions, and make sure our side, like access and configuration, is covered by our own controls.
Leadership now wants ISO 27001 on top of SOC 2. How do you avoid doing everything twice?
How you build one control program that serves several frameworks.
One control set mapped to both, plus the ISO-only pieces: a defined ISMS scope, the Statement of Applicability, internal audit and management review.

I keep one set of controls and map each to both the SOC 2 criteria and ISO 27001's Annex A, so one piece of evidence serves both audits. Then I add what ISO needs that SOC 2 does not: a written scope for the management system, a Statement of Applicability explaining which controls apply and why, an internal audit, and a management review.

security-engineer.heading: Security engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between cross-site scripting and cross-site request forgery?
Whether you know two classic web flaws well enough to tell them apart.
XSS runs attacker script in the victim's page; CSRF makes the browser send a request the user did not mean. Each has its own fix.

In cross-site scripting, attacker input ends up running as script in another user's browser, so it can read the page and act as that user. The fix is output encoding for each context plus a content security policy. In CSRF, another site makes the user's browser send a request with their cookies. The fix is anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies.
A developer asks how to store user passwords. What do you tell them?
Whether you know current password storage practice.
A slow, salted hash built for passwords, such as Argon2id or bcrypt. Never plain text, reversible encryption, or a fast hash alone.

Never store the password itself or encrypt it so it can be decrypted. Use a password hashing function made to be slow, such as Argon2id or bcrypt, with a unique salt per user, which the library handles. A fast hash like SHA-256 alone is wrong because attackers can try billions of guesses a second. Tune the cost so login stays quick but cracking stays expensive.
How do you stop SQL injection, and why is escaping input not enough?
Your grasp of the root cause of injection and the reliable fix.
Parameterized queries keep data apart from code. Escaping is easy to get wrong, and raw queries inside ORM code still need checking.

Injection happens when user input is glued into the query text, so the database reads it as code. Parameterized queries send the query and the values separately, so input can never change the structure. Escaping depends on getting every case right for every database. In review I also search for raw SQL and string building inside ORM code, where it sneaks back in.
You are reviewing code that uses JSON Web Tokens for sessions. What do you check?
Whether you can spot common token mistakes in a code review.
The signature is always verified with a fixed algorithm, nothing secret sits in the payload, lifetimes are short, and tokens can be revoked.

First, that the server verifies the signature and pins the expected algorithm, so a token with alg set to none or a swapped algorithm is rejected. Second, nothing sensitive in the payload, since it is only encoded, not encrypted. Third, expiry is checked and short, with a way to revoke, because a stolen token works until it expires. And the signing key is strong and not in the repo.
A tester changes the invoice number in an API call and sees another customer's invoice. How do you fix it?
Whether you fix broken access control at the root, not by hiding IDs.
A server-side check, on every request, that the caller may see that object. Random IDs alone do not fix it. Then look for the same pattern elsewhere.

This is an insecure direct object reference. The fix is on the server: before returning the invoice, check that it belongs to the caller's account, every time. Random IDs make guessing harder but are not a fix. Then I search other endpoints for the same pattern, move the check into a shared layer, and add a test that uses a second user's ID and expects a denial.
A cloud access key with admin rights was pushed to a public code repository an hour ago. What do you do?
How you act in the first minutes of a credential leak.
Revoke the key first, then check logs for use, then clean up and stop it recurring. Deleting the commit is not enough; bots scan public repos within minutes.

I disable the key right away and issue a new one to whatever needs it. Bots find public keys within minutes, so I assume it was used. I check the cloud audit logs for activity by that key since the push: new users, new keys, new machines. Then the history gets cleaned, secret scanning goes into the commit checks, and we ask why an admin key was in code at all.
Our app fetches an image from any URL the user enters. What worries you, and how do you lock it down?
Whether you see server-side request forgery and its cloud risk.
The server can be pointed at internal systems, such as the cloud metadata service that hands out credentials. Use allowlists and network blocks, not just URL checks.

That is server-side request forgery. Someone can make our server call internal addresses, including the cloud metadata service at 169.254.169.254, which can return temporary credentials. I would allowlist domains if possible, resolve the name and block private and link-local ranges, not follow redirects blindly, and require session tokens on the metadata service.
The team wants to release tomorrow, and you found a medium-severity flaw that takes a week to fix. What do you do?
How you balance risk against delivery without being the blocker by default.
Judge real exploitability, look for a quick mitigation, and if the business accepts the risk, get it in writing from an owner with a fix date.

First I check how reachable it is: is it behind login, is the data sensitive. Often a quick control, like a feature flag, a web application firewall rule or a rate limit, cuts most of the risk. If they ship, the product owner signs a written risk acceptance with a fix date, and I track it. I block only if it exposes sensitive data or is easy to exploit from the internet.
Tell me about a security change you made that broke something. What did you learn?
Whether you own mistakes and roll out controls carefully.
An honest story: quick rollback, clear communication, and a changed process such as staged rollout or report-only mode first.

I tightened our content security policy, the browser rule for which scripts may load, and pushed it to everyone at once. The payment page used a script from a domain I had missed, and checkout failed for about 20 minutes. I rolled back, told the team, and fixed the list. Now I run new policies in report-only mode for a week and read the reports before enforcing.

semiconductor-fab.heading: Semiconductor fab engineer questions
qs: Walk me through the main steps of photolithography on a wafer.
Whether you know the core patterning flow and where it can be reworked.
The steps in the right order: prime, coat, soft bake, expose, post-exposure bake, develop, measure. Also that resist can be stripped and reworked before etch.

First the wafer is cleaned and primed so the resist sticks, often with HMDS. Then resist is spin-coated and soft baked to drive off solvent. The scanner exposes the pattern through the mask, then comes a post-exposure bake and develop. We measure critical dimension and overlay. If they fail, we strip the resist and rework before etch makes the pattern permanent.
What is the difference between control limits and spec limits?
Whether you understand the basis of statistical process control.
Spec limits say what the product needs. Control limits describe the stable process. A point can be in spec and still out of control.

Spec limits come from the design or the customer: what the product needs to work. Control limits come from the process itself, usually the mean plus or minus three sigma of stable data. A point can be inside spec and still out of control, which tells me something changed. I act on that signal before it turns into scrap.
When would you choose a wet etch over a dry plasma etch?
Your grasp of etch basics and their trade-offs.
Wet etch is isotropic, selective and cheap. Dry etch can be anisotropic for vertical walls on small features. The choice follows the feature.

Wet etch uses liquid chemicals. It is cheap and very selective, but it etches in all directions, so it undercuts the mask and is poor for small features. Plasma etch, like reactive ion etch, drives ions toward the wafer, so it can cut nearly vertical walls. I use dry for fine patterns and wet for cleans or film strips where undercut does not matter.
What does Cpk tell you, and what do you do if Cp is high but Cpk is low?
Whether you can read process capability and act on it.
Cpk accounts for centering; Cp does not. High Cp with low Cpk means a tight process that is off center, so you recenter it.

Cpk compares the spec window with the process spread and accounts for centering. It is the distance from the mean to the nearer spec limit divided by three sigma. A Cpk of 1.33 means that limit is four sigma away. If Cp is high but Cpk is low, the process is tight but off center, so I recenter the target rather than try to cut variation.
A tool just came back from preventive maintenance. How do you decide it is ready for production?
How you qualify a tool before it touches product.
Data, not a verbal OK: particles, rate and uniformity on test wafers compared to the pre-maintenance baseline, then a logged release.

I never release on a verbal OK alone. If a plasma chamber was opened, I run seasoning wafers first. Then particle monitor wafers, then rate and uniformity on test wafers, compared to the baseline from before the maintenance. If everything sits inside the control charts, I release it and watch the first production lot closely. All of it goes in the tool log.
An etch rate point lands above the upper control limit but still inside spec. What do you do?
How you respond to an out-of-control signal.
Hold the tool, confirm the measurement is real, look for what changed, check the lots run since the last good point, follow the written action plan.

I put the tool on hold so no more lots go through. Then I check the data is real: remeasure and check the metrology tool. If it holds up, I look for what changed: recent maintenance, a new gas bottle, chamber hours, recipe edits. I review lots run since the last good point and follow the out-of-control action plan, writing up what I found.
Yield drops and the failing dies form a ring near the wafer edge. How do you find the cause?
How you use wafer maps and lot history to trace a yield loss.
A pattern means a systematic cause, not random defects. Commonality analysis across tools and chambers, then confirmation with data or a split.

A ring says systematic, not random particles. I run a commonality analysis: which tools, chambers and recipes did the bad lots share that the good lots did not. Edge rings often point to a step with uneven results from center to edge, like etch, deposition or edge bead removal. I check that step's uniformity data and confirm with a split lot before changing anything.
You find that a lot was run with the wrong recipe on your tool. What do you do?
How you handle a misprocessing mistake, including your own.
Hold and report at once, find out how far it went, rework only where possible, send the rest to disposition, then fix the cause.

I hold the lot and tell my supervisor and the lot owner right away, not after I have a fix. Then I find which step went wrong and how far the lot got. If it was a litho step, the resist can usually be stripped and reworked. If it went through etch or implant, it goes to disposition. Then I fix what allowed it, like a recipe selection with no check.
A lot is slightly out of spec and production is pushing you to release it. How do you handle it?
Your judgement under schedule pressure.
It goes to formal disposition with the facts, not a quiet release. The decision is documented by the people who own it.

It is not my call alone, and it should not be. I put the facts in front of the review board or whoever owns disposition: how far out it is, what it may do to yield or reliability, and any past data on similar lots. They may approve a waiver or scrap it. What I will not do is release it quietly because the line is waiting.
You want to change an etch recipe to improve uniformity. How do you get from idea to production?
How you run a process change with data and proper control.
A designed experiment, a split lot through to yield, then the formal change process with sign-offs. No undocumented recipe edits.

I start with data showing the problem and a theory for it. Then a designed experiment on test wafers, changing pressure, power and gas flow together so I can see how they interact. The best setting goes on a split lot, half old recipe and half new, through electrical test and yield. Only then do I file the change through the formal change process, with sign-offs.

senior-accountant.heading: Senior and staff accountant questions
qs: A December utility bill arrives in January. What entries do you book, and when?
Whether you know accrual entries and cutoff in practice, not just in theory.
Accrue the estimate in December, reverse it in January, and let the real invoice settle the difference.

In December I debit utilities expense and credit accrued liabilities for my best estimate, based on recent bills or usage. I set the entry to reverse on January 1. When the invoice arrives, AP books it to expense as usual, and the reversal cancels the accrual, so only the small true-up lands in January.
A vendor bills $12,000 in January for a one-year software subscription. How do you record it?
Your handling of prepaid expenses and their monthly amortization.
Book it to a prepaid asset, expense it evenly over the service period, and keep a schedule that ties to the balance sheet.

I debit prepaid expenses and credit accounts payable for $12,000. Each month I debit software expense and credit prepaid for $1,000. I keep a prepaid schedule by vendor, with start and end dates, and at close I check that its total matches the general ledger balance.
How do you decide whether a purchase is capitalized or expensed?
Whether you apply a capitalization policy with judgement.
Future benefit beyond a year, above the policy threshold, including costs to get it ready for use; repairs are expensed, improvements capitalized.

I capitalize it if it benefits more than one year and is above our capitalization threshold. Cost includes shipping and installation, not just the invoice. Routine repairs that keep an asset working are expensed; upgrades that extend its life or add capacity are capitalized. Depreciation starts when the asset is placed in service.
How do you record the allowance for credit losses and a write-off?
Your grasp of receivable reserves and their journal entries.
Expense hits when the allowance is set or adjusted; a write-off against the allowance has no new expense.
