I check our status page and internal monitoring to see if others are affected. Then I look up their recent requests: which endpoint, what status codes, what error messages. If only they fail, it is often an expired key, a wrong base URL or a network block on their side. I ask for one failing request with its timestamp and full response so I can match it in our logs.
Webhooks stopped reaching a customer's server yesterday. How do you troubleshoot it?
Your ability to follow one request across two systems.
Read the delivery attempts on your side first; the response code or timeout usually shows whether the fault is yours or theirs.

I open our delivery log for their endpoint. Timeouts mean their server is slow or unreachable; 4xx or 5xx codes mean their app rejected the call. Common causes are an expired SSL certificate, a firewall blocking our IP addresses, a changed URL, or a failed signature check after they rotated a secret. If we sent nothing at all, the problem is ours and I escalate.
A customer pastes a log into the ticket that contains their API key. What do you do?
Whether you treat customer secrets as a security issue, not a detail.
Redact the secret from the ticket, tell the customer to revoke and replace the key, and follow the company's data handling rules.

I redact the key from the ticket right away, or ask an admin to if I cannot. Then I tell the customer politely that the key was exposed and they should revoke it and create a new one. HAR files are similar, since they can hold cookies and tokens: I ask customers to remove those first, and I never forward a raw file to a chat channel.
A customer's script retried a payment request after a timeout, and now they have duplicate charges. What do you explain?
Whether you understand why retries can create duplicates and how APIs prevent it.
A timeout does not mean the request failed. Explain idempotency keys where the API supports them, and check the first request's real outcome.

A timeout only means they did not get the answer in time; the first request may have gone through, so the retry made a second charge. First I help them find and reverse the duplicates. Then I show them how to send an idempotency key, a unique ID per payment, so a retry with the same key returns the first result instead of charging again.
Five customers report the same error within one hour this morning. What do you do?
Whether you spot a possible incident early and raise it the right way.
Treat the pattern as a likely incident: alert the incident channel with evidence, link the tickets, and give customers one consistent update.

Five matching reports in an hour is a pattern, not five problems. I check monitoring and recent deploys, then raise it in the incident channel with ticket links, times, the error text and what the accounts share. I link the tickets to one parent so updates go out together, and I tell customers we are investigating, without guessing at a cause or a fix time.
A large customer asks you to fix their data with a quick change in the production database. How do you handle it?
Your judgement about access, risk and process when a customer pushes for speed.
No one-off writes to production. Confirm the problem read-only, get the fix reviewed and run through the change process with a backup, and keep the customer informed.

I would not run a write on production on my own, even with access. I would first use a read-only query to confirm exactly which records are wrong and why. Then I write up the fix, have an engineer review it, and run it through our change process with a backup. I give the customer an honest timeline; a fast wrong update can damage far more records.

support-manager.heading: Customer support manager questions
qs: What is shrinkage, and why does it matter when you build a schedule?
Whether you understand the basic math behind support staffing.
Paid time when agents cannot take contacts, such as breaks, training and time off, and the step of scheduling above the forecast need to cover it.

Shrinkage is the share of paid hours when an agent cannot take contacts: breaks, meetings, coaching, training, sick days and vacation. If the forecast says I need 20 agents live at 10 a.m. and shrinkage runs 30%, I schedule about 29, because 20 divided by 0.7 is 28.6. If I ignore it, the queue grows every time someone is in training.
What is the difference between first response time and resolution time, and how can a team make one look good while customers suffer?
Whether you know the core support metrics and how they get gamed.
Clear definitions, an example of gaming such as quick empty replies, and pairing metrics so one cannot be faked alone.

First response time is how long until the customer gets a first human reply. Resolution time is until the problem is actually solved. A team can hit first response with fast "we're looking into it" notes while tickets sit for days. So I track both, plus reopen rate, and I never count auto-replies as a first response.
What do you look for when hiring a support agent, and how do you test it?
How you hire for the traits that are hard to teach.
Clear writing, patience and problem solving tested with a realistic exercise, not just interview talk. Product knowledge can be trained.

I hire for clear writing, calm under pressure and curiosity; I can teach the product. Candidates answer a short written exercise: an annoyed customer with a problem they cannot fully fix. I look at whether they answer the real question, set honest expectations and stay warm without over-apologizing. Then a short phone role-play.
How do you run a QA calibration session?
Whether you keep quality scores fair and consistent across reviewers.
Several reviewers score the same tickets on their own, compare, discuss the gaps and tighten the scorecard until they agree.

I pick five recent tickets, including one tricky one. Each reviewer scores them alone on our scorecard, then we compare. Where scores differ by more than a few points, we discuss why and rewrite the vague criterion, like "empathy," into something observable. I repeat it monthly, because agents stop trusting QA the moment scores depend on who reviewed them.
A product outage triples ticket volume in an hour. Walk me through your first 30 minutes.
How you manage a sudden spike without losing control of the queue.
Confirm with engineering, tell customers proactively, give agents one approved message, tag tickets for bulk follow-up and update on a fixed rhythm.

I confirm the issue with engineering and get a named contact. I post a known-issue note on the status page and add it to the auto-reply so people stop opening duplicates. Agents get one approved macro, and every related ticket gets a tag so we can update them all at once later. I pull people off low-priority queues and share updates every 30 minutes.
Your customer satisfaction score drops sharply, and most negative comments are about a price increase. What do you do?
Your judgement in separating service problems from product or policy problems.
Reading the comments, splitting scores by cause, protecting agents from blame and taking the real driver to the people who own it.

First I read the comments and tag them by cause. If 70% are about price, my agents are not the problem, and I say so before anyone starts coaching them. I report the price feedback to the pricing owner with numbers and quotes. For my team, I make sure they have a clear, honest script on the change and know what they can offer.
An agent promised a customer in writing a refund that our policy does not allow. How do you handle it?
How you deal with an agent's mistake while protecting customer trust.
Usually honoring the written promise, coaching the agent privately and finding the root cause, such as an unclear policy article.

In most cases I honor it. The customer relied on our written word, and one refund costs less than broken trust. If the amount is large, I check with finance first. Then I talk with the agent privately to learn why: an outdated article, a confusing macro or pressure from the customer. If the policy was unclear, I fix it for the whole team.
You pushed to lower average handle time, and now the reopen rate is climbing. What went wrong, and how do you fix it?
Whether you can spot when a target is hurting the work it is meant to improve.
Owning that the target caused rushed closures, dropping or rebalancing it and pairing speed with quality measures.

I made speed the goal, so agents closed tickets before the problem was solved. That is on me. I would stop ranking people on handle time alone, look at reopened tickets to find where corners were cut and pair handle time with reopen rate and QA scores. Then I would cut time by fixing slow tools and adding better macros, not by rushing people.
The same bug drives hundreds of tickets a month, but the product team keeps putting it off. How do you get it fixed?
How you turn support data into action from other teams.
Numbers on volume and agent hours, real examples, a named owner and regular follow-up instead of complaints.

I bring cost, not anecdotes. For example: the password reset bug caused 900 tickets last month at about five minutes each, so 75 agent hours, plus three angry quotes from customers. I ask for one owner and a decision: fix it, or accept the cost. Each month I report the count again, so the trade-off stays visible.
Leadership wants to cut two agents and keep the same response time targets. How do you respond?
Your ability to show staffing trade-offs clearly instead of just agreeing or refusing.
Showing the impact with the staffing model, offering real options with costs and asking leadership to choose the trade-off.

I would show the math from our staffing model: volume, handle time, shrinkage, and what two fewer agents does to response times by hour. Then I would give options: keep the staff, relax targets on low-priority channels, or invest in deflection like better help articles, with a realistic timeline. I would ask them to pick the trade-off, not promise the same result for less.

system-administrator.heading: System administrator and IT operations questions
qs: What is the 3-2-1 backup rule?
Whether you know the basic rule for keeping backups safe.
Three copies, two kinds of storage, one copy offsite, and ideally one copy that cannot be changed or reached from the network.

Keep three copies of the data: the original and two backups. Put them on at least two different kinds of storage, and keep one copy offsite. Today I also want one copy that is offline or immutable, meaning it cannot be changed or deleted for a set time, so ransomware cannot reach it.
Our file server uses RAID. Why do we still need backups?
Whether you know the difference between redundancy and a backup.
RAID survives a failed disk, but it copies deletions, corruption and encryption at once. Only a separate backup lets you go back in time.

RAID keeps the server running when a disk dies. But if someone deletes a folder, a bad update corrupts files or ransomware encrypts them, RAID writes that change to every disk right away. A backup is a separate copy from an earlier point in time, so I can restore what was there yesterday.
A user cannot open a folder on a Windows file share that a colleague opens fine. How do you find the cause?
How you troubleshoot permissions step by step.
Compare group membership, check both share and NTFS permissions, and remember new group membership needs a fresh logon.

First I compare the two users' group memberships, since access should come from groups. Then I check both the share permissions and the NTFS permissions; the user gets the more restrictive of the two. If we just added her to the right group, she has to log off and on, because her logon token still holds the old groups.
A Linux server says the disk is full, but du shows far less in use. What do you check?
Your hands-on knowledge of how Linux uses disk space.
Deleted files still held open by a process, running out of inodes, and files hidden under a mount point.

The usual cause is a large log that was deleted while a process still has it open, so the space is not freed. I run lsof +L1 to find it, then restart that service or empty the file. I also run df -i, because running out of inodes looks like a full disk, and I check for files hidden under a mount point.
An employee leaves the company today. Walk me through what you do.
How complete and careful you are with offboarding.
Disable rather than delete, cut every way in including sessions and keys, rotate shared secrets, and keep the data the business needs.

I time it with HR so access ends when the person leaves. I disable the account rather than delete it, revoke active sessions and MFA devices, and remove SSH keys and VPN access. I rotate any shared passwords they knew, hand the mailbox and files to the manager, collect the laptop and log every step.
A senior manager asks for full admin rights on his laptop because installing software takes too long. What do you do?
Your judgement on least privilege when the person asking has authority.
Solve the real problem, faster installs, without giving standing admin rights; explain the risk plainly.

I ask what software he needs and how often. Admin rights mean any malware he opens runs with full control, so I would rather fix the delay: add the tools to our self-service catalog or approve them within a day. If he truly needs admin now and then, a separate admin account or time-limited elevation is safer.
How do you roll out operating system patches to 200 servers without breaking anything?
How you balance speed and safety in patch management.
Test group first, then waves in maintenance windows, with a way back and checks after each wave. Actively exploited flaws go faster.

I group servers by role and risk. Patches go first to a test group for a few days, then to less critical servers, then to the rest in maintenance windows. I make sure there is a snapshot or backup to roll back, check services after each reboot, and stop the rollout if something fails. Patches for actively exploited flaws get a faster track.
You are writing a script that deletes old files every night. How do you make it safe?
Whether you write scripts that cannot do damage when something unexpected happens.
Dry-run mode, guards against empty variables, strict error handling, logging, and testing on a copy first.

I add a dry-run mode that only lists what it would delete. In bash I use set -euo pipefail and write paths as "${DIR:?}" so an empty variable stops the script instead of pointing at the wrong place. It logs every file it removes, and I test it on a copy of the folder before it runs on the real one.
You find out the backup job for a key server has failed silently for two weeks. What do you do?
How you handle a gap you are responsible for.
Get a good backup now, find the cause, tell the manager honestly, and fix the monitoring so silence is noticed.

First I run a backup by hand and confirm it completes, then test a restore of a few files. I tell my manager the exposure: two weeks with no recent copy. Then I find why it failed and why nobody knew. I change the alert so it fires when a successful backup is missing, not only when the job reports an error.
A user calls: files on the shared drive have strange extensions and there is a ransom note. What are your first steps?
Whether you contain damage fast and follow a plan under pressure.
Isolate the infected machine and stop the spread first, keep evidence, escalate at once, restore only from clean backups.

I have the user's machine disconnected from the network but not wiped, so evidence stays. I disable the user's account, cut the share off if encryption is still spreading, and alert security and my manager per our incident plan. Then we find the scope and restore from backups we know were made before the infection.

systems-engineer.heading: Systems engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between SAML and OpenID Connect, and when would you use each?
Whether you know the two main single sign-on standards and where each one fits.
Both let one identity provider sign users in to many apps. SAML is older and XML-based; OIDC sits on OAuth 2.0 and suits modern web and mobile apps.

Both let an app trust our identity provider instead of keeping its own passwords. SAML passes signed XML messages through the browser, and many older business apps support only SAML. OpenID Connect adds identity on top of OAuth 2.0 and uses JSON tokens, so it fits mobile and single-page apps better. For a new app I prefer OIDC. I use SAML when that is all the vendor offers.
Walk me through what should happen to an account when someone joins, changes team and leaves.
Your grasp of the joiner, mover and leaver process at the heart of identity work.
The HR record and roles drive access. A move removes the old rights. An exit removes access fast and completely, including sessions and shared items.

The HR record should drive it. On joining, the account gets its access from role-based groups, and the laptop is ready on day one. On a move, the new role's groups are added and the old ones are removed, so rights do not pile up. On leaving, the account is disabled at the agreed time and sessions are revoked. Mail and files go to the manager, and licenses are reclaimed.
A user says they cannot sign in to anything since this morning. How do you work through it?
How you troubleshoot sign-in problems in a sensible order, from the common causes to the rare ones.
Starts with the sign-in logs and the account state, then checks MFA, the device and the network, such as a clock out of sync breaking Kerberos.

First I read the sign-in logs. They usually name the reason, such as a locked account, an expired password or a failed MFA prompt. If the account looks fine, I check whether it is one device or all of them. On a domain laptop I check the clock, because Kerberos, the protocol behind domain logins, rejects requests when time drifts too far. I also check DNS, because the laptop must find a domain controller.
You have a script that must run on 3,000 laptops. What do you do before it reaches all of them?
Whether you roll out changes to a fleet of devices safely.
Tests on a few machines first. The script is safe to run twice and logs its result. Rollout goes in stages with a stop rule set in advance.

I make it idempotent, meaning that running it twice does no harm. It checks the current state first, logs what it did and returns a clear exit code. I test it on my own machines, then on a pilot group of about 30 laptops from different models and teams. Then I roll out in rings and watch success rates in the management console. I stop if failures pass a limit I set in advance.
An employee wants work email on a personal phone but will not let IT manage the whole phone. What do you offer?
How you balance protecting company data with an employee's privacy on their own device.
App-level protection instead of full enrollment: work data stays in managed apps, and a selective wipe leaves personal data alone.

I offer app protection instead of enrolling the whole phone. Work mail and files live only in approved apps that need a PIN. Those apps block copying into personal apps, and IT can wipe them without touching photos or texts. I explain clearly what we can and cannot see on the phone. Most people agree once they hear we cannot read their personal messages.
How would you make sure only company-managed, up-to-date devices can reach company email and files?
Whether you can join device management and identity into one access control.
Compliance rules in device management feed a conditional access policy in the identity provider, with a report-only phase first and a plan for exceptions.

I define compliance in device management: disk encryption on, screen lock set, OS up to date. The device reports its status to the identity provider. A conditional access policy then requires a compliant device for mail and files. I run the policy in report-only mode for two weeks to see who would be blocked and fix those devices. Then I enforce it, with an emergency admin account kept outside the rule.
How do you manage service accounts and other non-human identities?
Your judgement on accounts that no person signs in to but that often hold the most access.
Each account has an owner and a purpose and only the rights it needs. No interactive sign-in. Secrets are rotated or replaced by managed identities. Regular review.

Every service account gets a named owner, a purpose and an entry in an inventory. It gets only the rights the job needs and is blocked from interactive sign-in. Where the platform allows, I use managed identities, so there is no password at all. Otherwise the secret sits in a vault and rotates. Each quarter I review last-use dates and remove accounts nobody claims.
A sales manager reports a company laptop stolen from a car. What do you do in the first hour?
How you contain a lost device quickly and in the right order.
Resets credentials and revokes sessions, locks or wipes the device, confirms encryption from records, and brings in security to judge the data exposure.

I reset the user's password and revoke their sessions, so the logins saved on the laptop stop working. I send a remote lock and, after checking with security, a wipe. I pull the device record to confirm disk encryption was on, because that decides how serious the exposure is. Then I hand the details to security and legal, who decide on any reporting. I also get the manager a loaner laptop.
A senior executive asks you to turn off MFA for their account because it slows them down. What do you do?
Whether you hold a security line with a senior person while still solving their problem.
No quiet exception. You remove the friction with a smoother method, explain the risk plainly, and send any real exception in writing to whoever owns the risk.

I would not just switch it off, because executives are prime targets for phishing. I ask what slows them down. Often it is repeated prompts, so I set up a phishing-resistant method such as a passkey and make sure their devices are compliant, which cuts the prompts. If they still want an exception, I write up the risk and send it to the security lead to decide.
Your cleanup script for inactive accounts disabled 40 people who were still working. What do you do?
How you own a mistake, restore service and stop it from happening again.
Restores access first and tells people honestly. Then finds the root cause in the script's logic and adds safeguards such as a dry run and a cap on changes.

I stop the scheduled job, re-enable the 40 accounts using the script's own log and check that each person can sign in. I tell my lead and the help desk before tickets pile up. Then I find the cause. For example, the script may read the last logon from one domain controller when each controller keeps its own copy. Before it runs again, it gets a dry-run report, a cap on changes per run and a peer review.

systems-software.heading: Systems software engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
Whether you know the basic units an operating system schedules and protects.
Separate address space versus shared memory, what each thread owns, and why sharing makes switches cheaper but needs locks.

A process has its own virtual address space, open file table and other resources. Threads in one process share that memory and those files, but each has its own stack and registers. Switching between threads of one process skips the address-space change, so it is usually cheaper. Shared memory is also the risk: threads need locks or atomics to stay out of each other's way.
What happens when a program touches a page of memory that is not in RAM?
Your grasp of virtual memory and page faults.
The trap to the kernel, the valid-or-invalid check, loading the page and retrying, and the cost gap between minor and major faults.

The memory management unit finds no valid mapping and traps into the kernel. The kernel checks that the address is in a valid region. If it is, it gets a free frame, fills it from the file or swap if needed, updates the page table and reruns the instruction. If not, the process gets a segmentation fault. A fault that must read from disk is a major fault and is far slower.
When would you use a spinlock instead of a mutex?
Whether you match the lock type to how long it is held and where the code runs.
Spinlocks for very short holds or code that cannot sleep; mutexes when the section may block or run long.

A spinlock busy-waits, so it only pays off when the lock is held very briefly and the holder is running on another core. In kernel code it is also the choice where you cannot sleep, like an interrupt handler. If the critical section can block or run long, I use a mutex, which puts the waiter to sleep instead of burning CPU.
What conditions cause a deadlock, and how do you prevent one in practice?
Your knowledge of deadlock and the habits that keep it out of real code.
Names the four conditions and breaks one on purpose, usually circular wait through a fixed lock order.

Four conditions must all hold: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. In practice I break the circle. Every lock gets a place in a fixed order, and code always takes them in that order. Where I cannot, I use a try-lock and back off. I also keep lock-order checking turned on in debug builds so a violation shows up in tests.
What is a data race, and why do passing tests not prove you have none?
How well you understand memory ordering in concurrent code.
The exact definition, that it is undefined behavior in C and C++, and that compilers and CPUs reorder memory access.

Two threads access the same memory at the same time, at least one writes, and nothing orders them: no lock, no atomic. In C and C++ that is undefined behavior. The compiler may keep a value in a register or reorder stores, and some CPUs, like ARM, reorder more than x86. So a green test run proves little; I run a race detector and fix the ordering.
Each thread updates only its own counter, yet the program gets slower as you add threads. What do you suspect?
Whether you can spot a hardware-level performance problem from its symptoms.
Names false sharing, explains cache-line bouncing, fixes it with padding or local counts, and measures again.

False sharing. If the counters sit on the same cache line, usually 64 bytes, every write by one core invalidates the other core's copy, and the line bounces between them. I check the struct layout, then align each counter to its own line, or let each thread count locally and add the totals at the end. Then I measure again to confirm the fix.
A write returned success, then the machine lost power and the data was gone. What went wrong?
Your understanding of durability and what the kernel does with your writes.
Knows write() only reaches the page cache, uses fsync or fdatasync, syncs the directory after renames, and takes fsync errors seriously.

write() only copied the data into the kernel's page cache; it reaches the disk later. For durability you call fsync or fdatasync before reporting success, and after creating or renaming a file you also fsync the directory so the entry survives. I treat an fsync error as serious, because retrying it can report success while the data is already lost.
What is priority inversion, and how is it fixed?
Whether you understand how scheduling and locking interact.
Describes the low, medium and high priority chain clearly and names priority inheritance or a priority ceiling as the fix.

A low-priority thread holds a lock that a high-priority thread needs. A medium-priority thread then preempts the low one, so the high one waits on work it has nothing to do with. The usual fix is priority inheritance: while the low thread holds the lock, it runs at the waiter's priority. A priority ceiling on the lock is another option.
Walk me through how you would find out why p99 latency doubled after a release.
How you profile a performance regression with method instead of guessing.
Compares builds under equal load, looks at tail histograms, checks both CPU time and waiting time, and narrows down the commit.

First I compare old and new builds under the same load, with latency histograms, not averages. A CPU profile shows where busy time goes, but tail latency is often time spent waiting, so I also look at off-CPU time: lock contention, disk I/O, page faults and scheduler delays. Then I bisect the release's commits until one change explains the shift.
A use-after-free crashes the service about once a week, and a teammate wants to add a null check and ship. What do you do?
Your judgement on memory-safety bugs and fixing causes instead of symptoms.
Explains why a null check does not help, reproduces with sanitizer builds and stress tests, and fixes object ownership.

A null check will not help: the dangling pointer still holds the old address, not null, and the real bug is who owns the object. I build with an address sanitizer and run a stress test to catch the bad access and the free that came before it. Then I fix the lifetime, with clear ownership or reference counting, and keep the test that reproduced it.

tax.heading: Tax questions
qs: What is the difference between a permanent and a temporary book-tax difference?
Whether you know the building block of every tax provision.
Temporary differences reverse over time and create deferred tax. Permanent ones never reverse and move the effective rate.

A temporary difference is about timing: the item hits book and taxable income in different years, like faster tax depreciation on equipment, so it creates a deferred tax asset or liability. A permanent difference never reverses, like fines paid to a government or the nondeductible half of business meals, so it changes the effective tax rate instead.
How does a VAT differ from US sales tax?
Your grasp of indirect tax across countries.
VAT is charged at each stage with credit for tax paid on inputs. US sales tax is charged once, on the final sale, under state and local rules.

US sales tax is collected once, on the sale to the final consumer. A buyer who resells gives an exemption certificate. Rates and rules are set by states and local governments. VAT is charged at every step of the chain, and each business recovers the VAT it paid on purchases, so in effect it taxes only the value added. The US has no federal VAT.
What is the arm's length principle, and how do you show a price meets it?
Whether you understand the basis of transfer pricing.
Related parties must price as independent parties would, supported by a fitting method, comparables and documentation prepared on time.

Related companies must set intercompany prices as independent parties would in the same situation. I pick the method that fits the facts, for example comparable uncontrolled price if there are good outside deals, or the comparable profits method for a routine distributor. Then I benchmark against comparable companies and write it up in contemporaneous documentation.
When does a deferred tax asset need a valuation allowance?
Your judgement on one of the most debated areas of the provision.
When it is more likely than not that some of the asset will not be realized, weighing positive and negative evidence, with objective evidence counting more.

Under ASC 740, I record one if it is more likely than not that some or all of the asset will not be realized. Recent cumulative losses are strong negative evidence. On the positive side I look at deferred tax liabilities that will reverse, carrybacks where the law allows them, and tax planning strategies. Forecasts of future profit count less after a history of losses.
What is a return-to-provision adjustment, and what do you do when it is large?
Whether you can tie the filed return back to the books.
The true-up between the provision estimate and the actual return, booked when filed. A large one is explained and the process is fixed.

When we file, I compare each line of the return with what the provision assumed and book the difference, current and deferred. A large one means the estimate missed something, say a bigger research credit or depreciation computed differently. I explain the cause, check whether it is a change in estimate or an error, and fix the process so next year's provision catches it.
Explain how an uncertain tax position is recognized and measured.
Your knowledge of the two-step test for uncertain tax positions.
Recognize only if more likely than not to be sustained on technical merits, then measure the largest benefit more than 50% likely on settlement.

Step one: the position must be more likely than not to be sustained on its technical merits, assuming the tax authority examines it with full knowledge. If it passes, step two measures the benefit as the largest amount that is more than 50% likely to be realized on settlement. The rest is an unrecognized tax benefit, and I track interest and penalties on it too.
We start selling online to customers in states where we have no staff or offices. What do you check?
How you spot nexus before it turns into back taxes.
Economic nexus for sales tax since Wayfair, the limits of Public Law 86-272 for income tax, and registering before thresholds are crossed.

For sales tax, since the Wayfair decision most states use economic nexus, so I track our sales into each state against its threshold and register before we cross it. For income tax, Public Law 86-272 protects only the solicitation of orders for tangible goods, so it will not cover services or software. It also does not cover gross receipts taxes, so I check those too.
Your quarterly effective tax rate jumped five points from last quarter. How do you find out why?
How you investigate a provision result before it goes to the controller.
Separate discrete items from the estimated annual rate, then check forecast changes, profit mix by country and permanent items.

First I split out discrete items, like a settled audit or stock compensation shortfalls, from the estimated annual rate, since discrete items hit only the quarter they occur in. Then I compare the new annual forecast with the old one: profit moving to higher-tax countries, lower credits, or bigger nondeductible items. I reconcile the change before anyone sees the number.
After filing, you find an error in last year's return that underpaid tax. What do you do?
Your honesty and process when you find a mistake in your team's work.
Tell the manager, size it, amend the return, and assess interest, penalties and the provision. No quiet fix buried in next year's return.

I tell my manager the same day with a first estimate of the amount. Then I confirm the numbers, prepare an amended return, for a US corporation the Form 1120-X, and work out interest and any penalty exposure. We decide together how it hits the financial statements and whether disclosure is needed. Last, I find out why the review missed it and add a check.
A distributor that should earn a routine margin under our transfer pricing policy will end the year at a loss. What do you do?
Whether you can handle a transfer pricing fix and its effects on other taxes.
A year-end adjustment backed by the policy and booked before close, with customs, VAT and withholding effects checked first.

I confirm the loss is not caused by one-off items the policy treats separately, then compute an adjustment that brings the margin back into the benchmark range. Before booking it, I check with the customs and indirect tax teams, since changing product prices after import can affect duty and VAT, and confirm no withholding applies. It is invoiced and documented before close.

tech-lead.heading: Tech lead and team lead questions
qs: As a tech lead, how much of your week do you spend writing code, and on what kind of work?
Whether you know how coding fits with leading a team.
A realistic share of the week, and keeping off the critical path so the team never waits on the lead.

Around a third to half, depending on the phase. I avoid owning tasks on the critical path, because meetings and reviews interrupt me and the team would end up waiting on me. I take prototypes, tooling, small fixes and spikes that unblock others. Staying in the code keeps my reviews and estimates honest.
How do you break a large feature into work for a team of four?
How you plan work so people can move in parallel.
A thin end-to-end slice first, agreed contracts between pieces, small tasks, and the riskiest unknown tackled early.

I build a thin end-to-end slice first: one request through the API, the database and the screen, even if it is rough. Then we agree on the contracts between the pieces, like the API shape, so people can work in parallel. Each task should ship in a few days and be reviewable on its own. The riskiest unknown goes to someone in week one.
What goes into a design doc, and when do you skip writing one?
Your sense of when a decision needs writing down and reviewing.
Problem, goals, non-goals, rejected alternatives, rollout and rollback. A doc for hard-to-reverse choices, none for small, easy-to-undo changes.

The problem and why now, goals and non-goals, the proposed design, the alternatives I rejected and why, the risks, and how we roll it out and roll it back. I skip it for small changes that are easy to undo. A decision that is hard to reverse, like a data model or a public API, always gets a doc and a review, even a short one.
A junior engineer has been stuck on the same task for three days and has not said anything. What do you do?
How you unblock people without making them feel watched.
A private, curious check-in, hands-on help, a clear rule for asking sooner, and a look at whether the team makes asking feel risky.

I would go to them privately and ask them to show me where they are, not ask whether it is done. Usually one piece of context is missing. I pair for an hour to unblock it, then agree on a rule: stuck more than half a day, post what you tried in the team channel. I also ask myself whether I made asking feel risky, because silence often means that.
Product asks for a delivery date on something nobody on the team has built before. What do you give them?
How you estimate under real uncertainty and talk about it.
A short spike to reduce the risk, then a range with what drives it, a smaller first version, and updates as the team learns.

Not a single date. I ask for a week to spike the riskiest part, then give a range and what drives it, like six to ten weeks depending on whether the vendor API supports batching. I offer a smaller first version with a firmer date. And I update the range as we learn, instead of surprising them at the end.
Only one person on your team understands the billing service. What do you do about it?
Whether you see and reduce single points of failure in people.
Treats it as a risk and a burden on that person, spreads knowledge by doing real work, and sets a measurable goal.

That is a risk for the product and a heavy load on that one person. I have them pair with two others on the next billing changes, with the others typing. We write a short runbook as we go: how deploys work, where alerts come from, what usually breaks. Then someone else takes billing on-call with the expert as backup. Within a quarter I want two more people who can ship a change alone.
Two senior engineers have argued about an approach for a week. How do you settle it?
How you make a technical call and keep both people on board.
Finds the real criteria, makes each side argue the other's case, decides if tied, records why, and keeps respect on both sides.

First I check they are arguing about the same thing; often one is optimizing for speed and the other for flexibility. We agree on the criteria together and each writes the best case for the other option. If it is still close and easy to reverse, I decide, write down why, and set a date to revisit. I tell both it was a close call, not a loss.
One engineer's pull requests keep coming back with the same problems. How do you handle it?
How you turn repeated review comments into feedback that changes behaviour.
Names the pattern privately with examples, finds the cause, agrees on a concrete fix, follows up, and escalates early if nothing changes.

I stop fixing it comment by comment. In a one-on-one I name the pattern with two or three examples, like missing error handling, and ask what is going on. Sometimes they do not know the standard; sometimes they are rushing. We agree on something concrete, like a checklist or pairing on the next task, and I check back in two weeks. If nothing changes, I involve my manager early.
Halfway through the quarter you realize the team will miss a date it committed to. Walk me through what you do.
Your honesty and judgement when a plan is failing.
Tells people early with facts, brings real options instead of hoping, decides with stakeholders, and learns why the estimate was off.

I tell my manager and the product owner as soon as I am confident, not on the due date. I bring what is done, what is left and why the estimate was off. Then options: cut scope to the must-haves, move the date, or add people, which rarely helps this late. We choose together, I tell the team the new plan, and later we look at why we missed.
Tell me about a technical decision you made as a lead that turned out to be wrong.
Whether you own your mistakes and correct course without blaming others.
A real mistake, owned publicly, reversed at a sensible cost, and a lasting change in how decisions are made.

I split a service into three so we could deploy them separately. With four engineers it tripled our deploy and on-call work, and most changes touched all three. After two months I said in our retro that it was my call and it was not working. We merged two back in one sprint. Now I write down what would prove a decision wrong, and check it.

technical-account-manager.heading: Technical account manager questions
qs: How is a technical account manager different from a support engineer and a customer success manager?
Whether you understand where the role sits after the sale.
Clear lines: support fixes tickets, the CSM owns adoption and renewal, the TAM owns the technical relationship and long-term health of the setup.

Support works the ticket in front of them and closes it. The customer success manager owns adoption and the renewal talk. I am the one who knows the customer's environment over time. I spot patterns across tickets, plan upgrades with them, and push fixes through engineering so the same problem does not come back.
What do you need to learn about a new account in your first 30 days?
How you build a picture of a customer's setup before you advise on it.
Architecture, versions, integrations, key contacts, ticket history and business goals, written down where the team can find them.

I want a diagram of how they run our product: versions, where it is hosted, what it connects to, and who owns each piece. I read six months of tickets for patterns, meet their admin and their sponsor, and ask what a bad day costs them. I write it into an account plan so anyone covering me starts from the same page.
What goes into a quarterly technical review, and what should the customer leave with?
Your ability to run a review that leads to decisions, not just slides.
Health data, incidents and their causes, upgrade and risk items, and a short list of agreed actions with owners and dates.

I cover ticket trends, incidents and what caused them, usage, versions nearing end of support, and roadmap items that matter to them. Then I propose three or four actions. The meeting worked if they leave with owners and dates, not just a deck they will never open again.
Walk me through planning a major version upgrade for a customer.
How you reduce risk when a customer's production system changes.
Breaking changes found in the release notes, testing outside production, a rollback plan, an agreed change window and checks afterward.

I start with the release notes and list breaking changes that touch their integrations. We test in their staging environment with real workflows. I write the steps, the timing and a rollback plan. We pick a low-traffic window, support is on standby, and afterward we run an agreed checklist before calling it done.
A customer's production system is down and the ticket has sat for two hours without engineering. What do you do?
How you manage an escalation when the normal process stalls.
Right severity, the defined escalation path to a named owner, a fixed update rhythm for the customer, and staying on it until service is back.

First I confirm the impact and that the ticket has the right severity. Then I use our escalation path to get a named engineer and an incident lead, not a queue. I tell the customer who is on it and that I will update them every 30 minutes, even with no news. I stay on the bridge call until service is restored.
The customer asks you to promise a date for a bug fix engineering has not committed to. What do you say?
Whether you protect trust by not promising what you do not control.
No invented dates. You share what is known, offer a workaround if there is one, and commit to when the next real update will come.

I tell them I will not give a date I cannot stand behind. I share what I know: the bug is confirmed, it is prioritized, and here is the workaround we tested. I commit to a date for my next update, and I take the business impact back to engineering so the priority reflects it.
In a review you see the customer runs everything on one server with no backup. They have had no problems. How do you raise it?
How you give architecture advice the customer did not ask for.
The risk named in business terms, options with rough effort, the advice in writing, and their decision respected but kept on the risk list.

I say it plainly: one hardware failure would take them down, and with no backup they could lose data. I put it in their terms, like hours of downtime. I offer two options, a backup schedule now and a second server later, with rough effort for each. If they wait, I note the risk in the account plan and raise it at each review.
After an outage, the customer wants a root cause analysis. What makes a good one?
Your understanding of what a post-incident report must contain.
A timeline, the impact, the real cause and not just the trigger, how service was restored, and preventive actions with owners, without blame or spin.

It has a clear timeline, the impact on the customer, the real root cause and not just what set it off, how we restored service, and actions to stop a repeat, each with an owner and a date. I check it with engineering for accuracy, then walk the customer through it so they can ask questions instead of just getting a file.
Three of your accounts opened tickets about the same odd behavior this month. What do you do?
Whether you look for patterns across accounts instead of treating each ticket alone.
Find what the setups share, raise one linked problem with engineering with the evidence, and warn other exposed accounts before they hit it.

I compare versions and configurations to find what the three have in common. I link the tickets and open one problem record with engineering, with the evidence, because three customers carry more weight than one. Then I check which other accounts share that setup and warn them before they run into it.
The customer's own configuration change caused the outage, but their manager blames our product. How do you handle it?
How you handle blame with facts while keeping the relationship intact.
Facts from the logs shared privately and without blame, a focus on preventing a repeat, and honesty if the product made the mistake easy.

I get the facts first: logs showing the change and when it happened. I share them with the manager privately, not in front of the admin's peers. I keep it about the system, not the person, and suggest a guard like a change review step. If our product made the mistake easy to make, I say so and log it as feedback.

technical-product-manager.heading: Technical product manager questions
qs: Why would you track p99 latency rather than the average for an API?
Whether you read performance numbers the way engineers do.
Averages hide the slow tail. p99 shows what the slowest 1% of requests feel, which often hits the heaviest users.

An average of 80 ms can hide a tail where one request in a hundred takes two seconds. p99 means 99% of requests are faster than that number. A page or job that makes many calls is likely to hit the slow tail, so customers feel p99 more than the mean. I watch p50 and p99 together, broken down by endpoint.
Explain idempotency to a sales lead, and why a payments API needs it.
Whether you can turn an engineering idea into plain business terms.
A repeated request has the same effect as one. With an idempotency key, a client can retry after a timeout without charging twice.

Idempotent means doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Networks drop replies, so a client that times out does not know if the charge went through. If it sends a unique key with the request, we recognize the retry and return the first result instead of charging the card again. That protects customers from double charges.
Which API changes count as breaking, and which are usually safe?
Your knowledge of how changes hit the people who integrate with you.
Removing or renaming fields, changing types or making inputs required break clients. Adding optional inputs or new fields is usually safe.

Removing an endpoint or field, renaming it, changing its type or format, or making an optional parameter required will break someone. Adding a new optional parameter, a new endpoint or a new response field is usually safe, if clients ignore unknown fields. Even a new enum value can break a client with strict parsing, so I flag those in the changelog too.
How do you test an API design with developers before it ships?
How you get real user feedback when your users are engineers.
Spec and docs first, a few design partners building against it, and watching where they get stuck before the contract is frozen.

I share the spec and draft docs with three to five design partners and ask them to build a small real task against a beta or mock server. I watch where they read twice, what they guess wrong and how long the first working call takes. Fixing names and error messages then is cheap; after general release, every change is a migration for someone.
Walk me through retiring an old API version that customers still call.
Whether you can run a deprecation without breaking trust.
Usage data, a clear timeline and migration guide, direct outreach to top callers, warnings in responses, and a sunset date you keep.

First I pull usage by customer to see who still calls v1. Then I publish a notice with a sunset date months out, a migration guide and code samples. We add a deprecation header to v1 responses and email owners of active keys. I call the top accounts myself. Near the end we may run short planned brownouts so stragglers notice, then turn it off on the date.
A large customer keeps hitting your rate limits and wants them raised today. What do you do?
How you balance one customer's request against platform stability.
First learn why they hit limits. Fix their pattern, or grant a scoped temporary raise if capacity allows, then decide on a lasting policy.

I ask engineering to look at their traffic first. Often it is a retry loop without backoff, or polling that a webhook could replace. If the load is real and we have headroom, I agree a temporary higher limit on their key with an end date. Then I bring the pattern back to the team: maybe our tiers are wrong, or we need a bulk endpoint.
Product teams are building their own tools instead of using your internal platform. How do you respond?
Whether you treat an internal platform as a product that must earn its users.
Treating the bypass as user feedback: finding the gap and cutting the cost of adoption before reaching for a mandate.

I take it as a signal, not disobedience. I sit with two or three of those teams and ask what they needed that we lacked: a missing feature, slow onboarding, a support queue that took a week. Then I fix the biggest gap and track time to onboard. A mandate can come later, but forced users of a bad platform just find quieter workarounds.
Engineering wants a quarter for a database migration with no visible features. How do you make the case to leadership?
How you justify platform work in terms leadership can act on.
Tying the work to cost, risk and speed with numbers, and cutting it into phases that deliver value along the way.

I translate it into outcomes. For example: the current database caps us below next year's expected peak, incidents from it cost us 20 engineer days last quarter, and two planned features need the new schema. I ask for a phased plan so the first slice lands in six weeks, and I name what we will not ship meanwhile so the trade is clear.
You shipped a fix and a customer's integration broke because it relied on the old, undocumented behavior. What now?
How you handle a breaking change you did not see coming.
Restore service first, communicate plainly, then decide openly whether to keep the old behavior, and add tests so it is caught next time.

First I get them working: roll back, or add a flag that restores the old behavior for their account, and tell them what happened and when. Then I check logs for others with the same pattern. With enough users, someone depends on any behavior you expose. So we add a test for it and decide openly: support it, or deprecate it with notice.

technical-program-manager.heading: Technical program manager questions
qs: What is the critical path, and why does it matter on a program?
Whether you know the basic scheduling idea behind every date you commit to.
The longest chain of dependent work sets the earliest finish. A slip on it moves the date; a slip elsewhere may not.

It is the longest chain of tasks that depend on each other, from start to finish. Its length is the shortest time the program can take. A task on that path has no slack, so a two-day slip there is a two-day slip at launch. I watch those tasks closely and look for parts I can run in parallel.
How does your job differ from the product manager's and the engineering manager's on the same program?
Whether you understand where the TPM role starts and stops.
Product owns what and why. Engineering managers own people and technical choices. The TPM owns how the pieces come together across teams, and when.

The product manager decides what we build and why it matters to users. The engineering manager owns the team, its hiring and its technical choices. I own the execution across teams: the plan, the dependencies between them, the risks and the dates. If the product manager changes scope, I show what it does to the schedule.
Walk me through how you build a dependency map for a program that touches eight teams.
How you find and record the links between teams before they cause trouble.
Sessions with each team, every dependency with a provider, a consumer, a need-by date and named owners, and a map reviewed often.

I start from the end state and work backward: what has to exist on launch day. Then I meet each team and ask what they need from others and what others need from them. Every dependency gets a provider, a consumer, a need-by date and a named owner on each side. Both teams confirm it in writing. I review the map weekly, because it changes.
A team tells you their API will be ready “in a sprint or two.” How do you turn that into something you can plan on?
How you turn a vague estimate into a date you can schedule against.
Asking what drives the range, setting an interim milestone, and planning on the later date with a set point to confirm it.

I ask what makes it one sprint versus two. Usually it is an unknown, like a design review or a schema decision. I get a date for that unknown to be settled and an interim milestone, such as a stub endpoint other teams can build against. I plan on the later date and tell the consuming teams when I will confirm it.
What do you look at before a go or no-go decision on a release?
Your release readiness criteria and whether you set them before the meeting.
Criteria agreed in advance: open bugs by severity, test and load results, a tested rollback, monitoring and on-call ready, support briefed.

I agree the criteria with engineering and product weeks before, so the meeting checks facts, not opinions. I look at open bugs by severity, test results, load test numbers, whether rollback has actually been tested, dashboards and alerts, on-call staffing, and whether support is briefed. If a criterion fails, we openly decide to waive it or to slip.
How would you plan the rollout of a risky change to a service millions of people use?
Whether you reduce release risk with staged exposure and a way back.
A feature flag or canary, a small share of traffic first, stop thresholds agreed in advance, a tested rollback, and timing away from peak hours.

I would ship the code turned off behind a feature flag, then enable it for internal users, then for 1% of traffic as a canary. We agree in advance which metrics stop the rollout, like error rate or latency above set limits. Rollback is one switch, and we test it first. We widen in steps, during working hours, with the owning team watching.
Your status report says green, but you hear engineers saying privately that the date is impossible. What do you do?
Whether your status reporting reflects reality and how you surface hidden schedule risk.
Going straight to the engineers, testing their concern against the plan, and changing the status quickly with a cause and a path back to green.

I sit down with those engineers and ask what they see that the plan does not. Often it is work nobody estimated, like a data migration or a security review. If it holds up, I change the status to yellow or red that week, with the cause and the options. A status that turns red the week before launch means I was reporting hope, not progress.
After a major outage, how do you run the follow-up?
How you turn an incident into fixes that actually get done.
A blameless review with a timeline and contributing causes, a short list of owned and dated action items, and tracking them to closure.

Within a few days I hold a blameless review. We build the timeline from logs and chat, then ask why the system allowed the failure, not who caused it. We agree a short list of action items, each with an owner and a due date, and separate urgent fixes from longer work. I track them in the teams' own backlogs and report open items until they close.
Three teams need the same platform team, and the platform team can only take on one of them this quarter. What do you do?
How you settle a dependency conflict between teams with competing priorities.
Making the trade-off visible with impact and dates, looking for workarounds, and escalating to the priority owner with a recommendation.

First I check that each ask is real and sized; sometimes one can be met with an existing feature or a workaround. Then I lay out each request with its business impact and what slips if it waits. If the teams cannot agree, I take that one page to the leader who sets priorities across them, with my recommendation. Then I give the waiting teams their new dates.
Two weeks before launch, you learn that a team you depend on never put your work on their roadmap. How do you handle it?
How you recover from a missed dependency and what you change afterward.
Quick facts, options with their costs, a decision by the right people, honest updates, then closing the process gap that let it happen.

I meet that team the same day to learn what is needed and what it would take. Then I bring options: they pull it in and something of theirs slips, we launch without that feature behind a flag, or we move the date. Leaders decide with the costs in front of them. Afterward I add a written confirmation step to my dependency map, so a hallway yes never counts again.

technical-recruiter.heading: Technical recruiter questions
qs: What is the difference between a frontend, a backend, and a DevOps or platform engineer?
Whether you know the roles well enough to search and screen for them.
Clear, correct lines between the roles, and what each changes in how you search and screen.

Frontend engineers build what the user sees in the browser or app, mostly in JavaScript or TypeScript. Backend engineers build the servers, APIs and databases behind it. Platform or DevOps engineers own deployment, cloud infrastructure and uptime. So for a platform role I look for automation and on-call experience, not UI work.
Looking at a résumé, how do you tell a senior engineer from a mid-level one?
How you read engineering experience beyond titles and years.
Scope and ownership: design decisions, systems owned end to end, mentoring. Not title or years alone, since titles mean different things at different companies.

Titles vary too much, so I read the bullets. A senior person describes owning a system, choosing between designs, handling scale or reliability problems and mentoring others. A mid-level résumé lists features built on a team. Then I confirm it on the call by asking what they decided themselves.
Walk me through the Boolean search you would build for a backend engineer who writes Go.
Your hands-on sourcing skill with search strings.
Correct use of AND, OR, NOT, quotes and parentheses, with synonyms covered and noise removed.

I would start with (Go OR Golang) AND (backend OR "back end" OR "server side") AND (engineer OR developer). Go alone pulls junk, so Golang matters. I add NOT (recruiter OR sales) to drop noise, then narrow by location. If results are thin, I widen the titles before loosening the skill.
What goes into a first message to an engineer who is not looking for a job?
Whether you can write outreach that engineers actually answer.
Short, specific to the person, says what is technically interesting about the role, and makes replying easy.

Three or four lines. Something specific I saw in their work, the real technical problem the team is solving, the level and pay range if I can share it, and an easy ask like a 15-minute call. No buzzwords. Engineers ignore mass messages, so if I cannot say why it fits them, I do not send it.
What do you ask a hiring manager in the intake meeting for a new engineering role?
How you turn a vague request into a search you can run.
Must-haves versus nice-to-haves, level, the team's real problems, the interview plan, and sample profiles to calibrate.

What will this person build in the first six months, and what level is it really. Which two or three skills are must-haves and which can be learned. Who is on the panel and what each interview tests. Then I ask them to react to three sample profiles, so we agree on what good looks like before I source.
A résumé says the candidate led a migration to microservices. What do you ask on the screen?
Whether you can probe technical claims without being an engineer.
Questions on their personal role, the why, the tradeoffs and what went wrong; vague or team-only answers are a flag.

I ask why they moved off the monolith, what their own part was versus the team's, how they split the services, and what broke along the way. Someone who did it talks about data ownership, deployment pain and things they would redo. If every answer is "we" with no detail, I note it for the technical interviewer.
When and how do you ask a candidate about work authorization and visa sponsorship?
Whether you handle sponsorship early and lawfully.
Ask early, ask only whether they are authorized and whether they will need sponsorship, never national origin; involve immigration counsel.

On the first call, because it decides whether we can move forward. I ask two questions: are you authorized to work in the US, and will you now or in the future need sponsorship. I do not ask about citizenship or where they are from. If sponsorship is needed, I check our policy and loop in immigration counsel before promising anything.
Your top candidate has a competing offer above your pay band and asks you to match it. What do you do?
How you negotiate offers within real limits.
Learns the full competing package and what the candidate values most, works with the manager on level and non-salary terms, stays honest.

I ask what the other offer includes and what matters most to them, cash, equity, title or the work. Then I go to the manager and comp team with facts: is the level right, can we use a sign-on bonus or more equity. I tell the candidate exactly what is possible and by when. I never bluff about a number I cannot get.
A candidate accepted your offer, then calls to say their current employer made a counteroffer. How do you handle it?
Your judgement in a late-stage risk most recruiters face.
Calm, asks what drove the search in the first place, does not pressure, and has prepared for this risk before the offer.

I thank them for telling me and ask what made them start looking. Usually it was the work, growth or the manager, and money does not fix that. I remind them of what they said they wanted, answer any doubts, and ask for a decision date. I raise counteroffers in the first screen, so this call is rarely a surprise.
The panel says a candidate you screened was far below the level you presented. How do you handle it?
How you own a screening miss and fix your process.
Takes responsibility, finds where the screen failed, recalibrates with the manager, and tells the candidate kindly and promptly.

I own it with the manager first. Then I compare my notes with the panel's feedback to see what I missed, often depth on system design. I add a probing question to my screen and ask an engineer to review my next few submittals. I close the loop with the candidate within a day or two, politely, so the miss does not cost them a bad experience.

technical-writer.heading: Technical writer questions
qs: What are the main topic types in structured writing, and why keep them separate?
Whether you know how technical content is organized.
Concept, task and reference, each answering a different reader question, kept apart so they are easy to find and reuse.

Concept explains what something is and why it matters. Task gives numbered steps to get one thing done. Reference holds the facts people look up, like parameters or settings. I keep them apart so a reader in the middle of a task is not slowed by background, and so one reference table can be reused in several guides.
How do you write a good numbered step?
Your craft at the level of a single instruction.
One action per step, an imperative verb, the condition before the action, and the expected result where it helps.

One action per step, starting with the verb: Click Save. If there is a condition, it comes first: If the file is open, close it. Where the reader needs reassurance, I add the result: The status changes to Active. I keep explanations out of the step itself, or put them in a short line underneath.
In safety messages, what is the difference between DANGER, WARNING, CAUTION and NOTICE?
Whether you know the US signal words for hazards in product documentation.
Matches ANSI Z535.6: severity and likelihood of injury decide the word, and NOTICE covers property damage, not injury.

Under ANSI Z535.6, DANGER means a hazard that will cause death or serious injury if not avoided. WARNING means it could cause death or serious injury. CAUTION means it could cause minor or moderate injury. NOTICE is for equipment or data damage with no injury risk. I place the message before the step it applies to, not after.
What does a complete reference entry for a REST API endpoint include?
Your knowledge of API documentation.
Method and path, authentication, every parameter with type and required flag, request and response examples, and error codes.

The method and path, a one-line purpose, and how to authenticate. Then every parameter with its type, whether it is required, its default and allowed values. A full request example and a real response, then the error codes the call can return and what each means. If there are rate limits or pagination, I say so on the same page.
What does docs-as-code mean, and how have you worked that way?
Whether you can work inside an engineering team's tools and process.
Docs kept as plain text in version control, reviewed like code, published by an automated build, ideally shipped with the feature.

It means treating docs like software: plain-text files with simple markup, stored in version control next to the code, changed through pull requests that engineers review, and published by an automated build. On my last team the docs change went into the same pull request as the feature, so the two shipped together and nothing was forgotten.
How do you check that a procedure actually works before it is published?
How you verify accuracy instead of trusting the draft.
Running every step yourself in a clean setup, copying commands from the draft, and noting the version tested.

I run it myself, step by step, in a test account or a clean environment, not on a machine that already has everything set up. I copy every command and code sample from the draft instead of typing my own. Where I cannot run it, I ask an engineer to run it with me, and I note which version I tested.
The style guide has no rule for a term that engineers spell three different ways. What do you do?
How you make and record a style decision.
Choosing a form based on the interface and the base style guide, recording it with a reason, and fixing old uses in one pass.

I check which form the product interface and the code use, since readers will see that, and what our base style guide suggests. I pick one, add it to our word list with the reason, and tell the team. Then I search the docs and fix the old forms in one pass, so consistency does not depend on anyone's memory.
A feature ships Friday and engineering says the docs can wait. How do you respond?
Your judgement when a deadline squeezes documentation.
Defining the minimum users need on day one, getting a short technical review, and naming the risk plainly.

I ask what users need on day one: usually setup steps, any change in behavior and known limits. I write that minimum now and ask for 20 minutes of an engineer's time to check it. Fuller guides follow, with a date. I also name the risk: support tickets in launch week cost more than a short review.
After a release, users report that a code sample in your guide fails. Walk me through what you do.
How you handle an error in published docs.
Reproduce, fix or flag the page fast, find the root cause, and change the process so it does not recur.

First I reproduce it against the current version to see whether the sample or the product changed. I fix the page or add a clear note right away, so no one else hits it. Then I find the cause, say a renamed parameter missed in review, and propose a fix such as testing samples in the build or a docs check on every API change.
How do you know your documentation is working?
Whether you measure docs by reader outcomes, not page count.
Signals tied to reader goals, such as support tickets, failed searches and time to first success, checked against real users.

I look at signals tied to what readers are trying to do: support tickets on topics we documented, site searches that return nothing, page feedback, and for an API how long a new developer takes to make a first successful call. I pair numbers with a few user sessions, because high traffic on a page can just mean people keep coming back lost.

technician.heading: Technician questions
qs: What is lockout/tagout, and when do you use it?
Whether you know the basic rule that keeps you from being hurt by live or stored energy.
You isolate every energy source, put your own lock and tag on it, and prove zero energy before any work starts.

It means shutting a machine off, isolating every energy source, putting my own lock and tag on each disconnect, and then proving it is dead before I work. I use it any time I service a machine or clear a jam where I could be hurt if it started up. That covers electrical, gas, air pressure, springs and stored energy in capacitors.
How do you prove a circuit is dead before you touch it?
Your habit of testing your tester instead of trusting a switch or a breaker label.
The live-dead-live check: confirm the meter on a known live source, test the circuit, then confirm the meter again.

First I lock out the breaker or disconnect. Then I check my meter on a known live source, test the circuit phase to phase and phase to ground, and check the meter on the live source again. If the meter failed in between, the dead reading means nothing. Breaker labels are wrong often enough that I never trust them alone.
On a wiring schematic, what does a normally open contact mean?
Whether you can read the drawings you will use to find faults.
Schematics show devices at rest with no power; a normally open contact is open until its coil or switch is actuated.

Drawings show every device in its resting state, with no power and nothing pressed. A normally open contact is open in that state and closes when its relay coil is energized or the switch is pushed. So if a motor starter does not pull in, I look at which contacts in that line of the drawing should be closed and measure across them to find the open one.
Walk me through how you find the fault on a machine that has stopped.
How you find faults in a logical order instead of swapping parts.
Ask the operator, check the simple things first, then narrow it down with the schematic and a meter before replacing anything.

I ask the operator what happened just before it stopped and whether there was an error code. Then I check power, fuses, breakers, door switches and resets. If those are fine, I take the schematic and measure along the circuit, splitting it in halves until I find where the voltage stops. I only order a part once I have measured that it is the cause.
A walk-in cooler is running warm in the middle of service. What do you check?
Your practical refrigeration knowledge and your sense of what matters to the kitchen.
Tell the manager at once so food can be protected, then check the simple causes before the sealed system.

First I tell the manager so they can check product temperatures and move food if needed. Then I check the easy things: the thermostat setting, the door closing and its gasket, the evaporator fans running and the coil not iced over. Outside, I see if the condenser coil is clogged and the compressor and condenser fan run. Refrigerant work comes only after those are ruled out.
How would you set up a preventive maintenance schedule for a store's equipment?
How you plan maintenance so equipment fails less often.
Start from the manufacturer's manuals and the most critical equipment, adjust by repair history, and record every task.

I list every piece of equipment and rank it by what it costs the store when it fails; refrigeration and ovens come first. I take the intervals from the manufacturer's manuals, like cleaning condenser coils or checking belts, and write a short checklist for each. Every task gets logged, and if a unit keeps failing between checks, I shorten its interval.
A unit is low on refrigerant. Can you just top it up?
Whether you know the federal rules on refrigerant and why a top-up is not a repair.
Only an EPA Section 608 certified technician may open the system; venting is illegal, and the leak should be found and fixed.

Only if I hold the right EPA Section 608 certification, because federal rules require it to service the sealed system. And refrigerant does not get used up; if it is low, there is a leak. I find it with an electronic detector or soap bubbles, repair it, then charge the system properly. A top-up alone just leaks out again, and venting refrigerant on purpose is illegal.
A manager asks you to bypass a safety interlock so a machine can run until the part arrives. What do you do?
Your judgement when pressure to keep running meets a safety rule.
A clear no, the machine tagged out of service, and a practical workaround offered so the store can keep going.

I say no, politely and plainly: that interlock is there so nobody loses a hand, and a bypass tends to get forgotten. I tag the machine out of service, tell the manager when the part will arrive and see if I can rush it. Then I help find a workaround, like moving the work to another machine or doing it by hand for a day.
Tell me about a repair that did not hold. What did you learn?
Whether you own your mistakes and look for the root cause.
An honest story: what failed, how you found the real cause, and what you now do differently.

I replaced a blown fuse on a conveyor and it ran fine. Two days later the fuse blew again. This time I traced the wiring and found a cable rubbing on the frame, worn through and shorting now and then. I fixed the cable and added a protective sleeve. Now when a fuse blows, I always find out why before I call the job done.
You have a fault that comes and goes and never shows up while you are there. How do you track it down?
How you handle the hardest kind of fault, the intermittent one.
Gathering patterns from staff and logs, checking connections and heat, and monitoring until the fault shows itself.

I ask staff to note the time and what was running each time it happens, and I check any error log. Then I look for patterns: only when hot, only at opening, only when another big load starts. I check connections for looseness and burn marks, wiggle wires while watching readings, and if needed leave a recording meter on the circuit until it catches the event.

technology-consultant.heading: Technology consultant questions
qs: What goes into total cost of ownership when a client compares two systems?
Whether you look past the license price.
Licenses plus setup, integration, migration, training, support, internal staff time and exit costs, compared over several years.

I count the subscription or license, setup and configuration, integrations, data migration, training and ongoing support. Then the hidden parts: internal staff time, modules priced later, renewal increases and the cost to leave. I compare both options over three to five years, not just year one.
Walk me through how you run discovery with a new client.
How you learn the business before proposing a solution.
Starts from the business goal, talks to the people doing the work, maps current process and systems, and confirms understanding before recommending.

I start with the business goal and who owns it. Then I interview the people who do the work, not only managers, and watch the process live if I can. I map the current process, list pain points with rough costs, and list systems and data. I end with a short readback so the client confirms I understood before I propose anything.
What is a fit-gap analysis, and what do you do with the gaps?
Your method for matching requirements to a product.
Mapping each requirement to standard, configurable or missing, then choosing per gap: change the process, configure, integrate, customize or accept.

I list each requirement and mark whether the product meets it as standard, with configuration, or not at all. For each gap I first ask if the process can change, since custom code costs money at every upgrade. If not, I look at configuration, an add-on or an integration, and customize only when the gap is core to the business.
How do you build a vendor scorecard for a software selection?
