Clear roles at the booth, trained staff, a fast way to capture candidates, and follow-up within days.

I confirm the roles we are hiring for and brief the engineers or managers who will staff the booth. We use a QR code so students apply on the spot instead of handing us paper. Each evening we tag strong candidates, and I send interview invites within a week, while they still remember us.
A student at your booth asks whether you sponsor work visas. What do you say?
Whether you handle sponsorship questions accurately and without discriminating.
A straight answer on company policy, the same sponsorship question for everyone, and no questions about nationality or national origin.

I tell them our policy for that role plainly, so they do not waste their time. In the process we ask every candidate the same thing: will you now or in the future need sponsorship to work here. I do not ask where they are from or about their citizenship; national origin is not something we screen on.
A hiring manager wants to interview only students with a GPA of 3.7 or higher from five schools. What do you do?
How you push back on narrow screens with data and keep the manager on side.
Asks what the manager is really looking for, shows how the filter shrinks the pool, and proposes job-related screens instead.

I ask what the cutoff is meant to predict. Usually it is coding skill or follow-through. I show how few candidates the filter leaves and that our best interns last year included people outside it. Then I suggest a short skills exercise for everyone, and we compare results after one cycle.
How do you set deadlines for offers to students?
Your judgement on giving students fair time while protecting your hiring plan.
Reasonable time to decide, respect for school policies, no pressure tactics, and extensions handled case by case.

I give enough time for a student to finish their fall interviews, and I check each school's career center policy first. I avoid exploding offers; a forced yes often turns into a renege later. If someone asks for more time, I ask what they are waiting on and extend when it is reasonable.
A student accepted your internship offer in October and calls in February to say they took another job. What do you do?
How you handle a renege calmly and recover the hire.
Stays professional, learns the reason, moves to backup candidates fast, and follows the school's reporting policy if it has one.

I thank them for telling me directly and ask what made the difference, because that tells me if our offer has a gap. I do not threaten or guilt them. That afternoon I go back to our strong runners-up. If the school asks employers to report reneges, I do that factually.
What numbers do you track to know if an internship program is working?
Whether you measure the program by results, not by activity.
Return offer rate, offer acceptance, first-year retention and performance, by source school, plus intern feedback and cost per hire.

I track how many interns get return offers and how many accept them, then how those hires perform and stay after a year. I break it down by school to guide next year's list. I also run an end-of-summer survey; last year it showed managers who skipped weekly check-ins had lower acceptance.
Halfway through the summer, a manager tells you an intern is not performing. What do you do?
How you handle a struggling intern fairly before the return offer decision.
Gets specifics, makes sure the intern hears clear feedback and gets support, documents it, and keeps the final decision fair.

I ask the manager for specific examples and whether the intern has heard them. Often the goals were never made clear. We hold a midpoint talk with two or three concrete targets and weekly check-ins. I write it down so the return offer decision at the end is based on the same facts everyone saw.

ux-designer.heading: UX designer questions
qs: How would you explain the difference between UX and UI design?
Whether you understand where your work starts and ends.
UX covers the whole experience: needs, flows and structure. UI is the visual and interactive layer. They overlap but are not the same.

UX is whether the product makes sense for the person: what steps they take, in what order, and whether they reach their goal. UI is how each screen looks and behaves: type, color, buttons, spacing. A beautiful screen can still sit in a confusing flow. On many teams I do both, but I start with the flow before I touch the visuals.
When do you use a low-fidelity prototype instead of a high-fidelity one?
How you match the tool to the question you need answered.
Low fidelity early, to test structure and flow cheaply. High fidelity when details, interactions or visual cues matter, or for final checks.

Early on, I use paper sketches or gray wireframes. They are fast, and people comment on the flow instead of the colors. Once the structure holds up, I move to a clickable high-fidelity prototype to test labels, button states and anything where the look changes behavior. I do not polish what I may throw away next week.
Besides the main path, what states do you design for a screen?
Whether you think past the happy path.
Empty, loading, error, partial and too-much-content states, plus permission cases, each with a clear next step for the user.

For a list screen I design the empty state for a new user, with a clear first action. Then loading, an error with a way to retry, a partial state when some data fails, and the case with very long names or hundreds of items. I also check what a user without permission sees. Engineers will build these states anyway; if I skip them, they get invented on the spot.
How do you write a task for a usability test without leading the participant?
Your skill at running research that gives honest results.
A realistic goal in the user's own words, no interface labels or hints, and neutral follow-up questions.

I give a goal, not instructions. Instead of “Click Transfer Funds,” I say “You owe your roommate $40 for groceries. Pay them back.” I avoid the words on the buttons, since that turns the test into word matching. During the session I stay quiet, and if they ask what to do, I say “What would you do if I were not here?”
What is the difference between card sorting and tree testing, and when do you use each?
Your knowledge of the methods for organizing navigation and content.
Card sorting shows how users group content and helps build a structure; tree testing checks whether people can find items in a proposed structure.

In card sorting, people group topics into piles that make sense to them, and in an open sort they name the groups. It tells me how users think about the content. Tree testing comes after: I give a text-only menu, no visual design, and ask people to find specific items. Card sorting helps me build the navigation; tree testing tells me whether it works.
How many people do you test with in a usability study, and why?
Whether you understand the tradeoffs of small qualitative tests.
Small rounds of about five per user group find the major problems, and several rounds beat one big one. Measuring numbers needs a much larger sample.

For a qualitative test, I usually run about five people per distinct user group. By then the same big problems keep showing up. I would rather fix them and run another round of five than test fifteen at once. If I need numbers, like a success rate to compare two designs, that is a different study and needs a much larger sample.
In interviews, users say they love a feature, but analytics show few people use it. What do you believe?
How you combine what users say with what they actually do.
Behavior outweighs stated opinion, but you dig into why: the feature is hard to find, needed rarely, or praised out of politeness.

I trust behavior more than opinion, but I do not stop there. The gap is a question. Maybe people cannot find the feature, maybe they need it twice a year, or maybe they were being polite to me. I would check where it sits in the flow, look at who does use it, and watch a few sessions. Then I decide whether to move it, explain it, or cut it.
You have one week and no research budget before a design goes to development. How do you get evidence?
How you do useful research under real limits of time and money.
Cheap, fast methods aimed at the riskiest assumption: support tickets, analytics, quick tests with real users, and a clear note of what stays untested.

I pick the one assumption that would hurt most if wrong. On day one I go through support tickets and analytics for that flow. Then I run quick tests with three to five people who fit the user profile, recruited through support or sales, using a clickable prototype over video. I share a one-page summary and list what we still have not tested, so the risk is known.
Your redesign ships and sign-ups drop 10% in the first week. What do you do?
How you own and work through a design that made things worse.
Check the data is real, find where in the funnel the drop happens, watch sessions, decide on a rollback with the team, and share what you learn.

First I check it is real: a tracking change, a bug or a seasonal dip can look like a design problem. Then I find the step where people drop off and watch session recordings or run quick tests on it. If the cause is clear and serious, I propose rolling back or fixing that step while we learn. I tell the team early; hiding a bad result costs more than the drop.
A product manager asks you to hide the cancel button to cut churn. How do you respond?
Your judgement when business goals push toward a dark pattern.
You refuse the trick, name the risks to trust and the legal exposure, and offer honest ways to keep customers.

I would say that hiding cancel does not cut churn; it delays it and turns leaving customers into angry ones who complain and dispute charges. Regulators also act against subscriptions that are hard to cancel. Then I offer real options: ask why people leave, offer a pause or a cheaper plan, and fix the top reasons from the exit survey. Cancel stays easy to find.

ux-researcher.heading: UX and market researcher questions
qs: When would you run interviews instead of a survey?
Whether you match the research method to the question being asked.
Interviews to learn why and to discover unknowns; surveys to measure how many, once you know what to ask.

I run interviews when we do not yet know the problem. I need stories, reasons and the words people use. I use a survey when we know the options and need to know how common each one is. Often I do both in that order: eight interviews to find the themes, then a survey to size them.
How many participants do you need for a usability test?
Your grasp of sample size in qualitative testing.
It depends on the goal: about five per distinct user group to find problems, tested in rounds; many more to measure task success rates.

For finding problems, I plan about five people per distinct user group, then fix what we saw and test again. The most common problems show up early and repeat. If the goal is a number, like a task completion rate to compare with the last release, five is far too few. That needs a larger quantitative study.
How do you keep from asking leading questions in an interview?
Whether you can get honest answers rather than the ones the team hoped for.
Open, neutral questions about past behavior instead of guesses about the future, shown with a concrete rewrite.

I ask about what people did, not what they would do. Instead of “Would you use a feature that saves your receipts?” I ask “Tell me about the last time you needed a receipt. What happened?” I work from a discussion guide, avoid words that hint at an answer, and let a pause sit instead of filling it.
What is wrong with the survey question “How satisfied are you with the speed and design of our app”?
Your eye for survey questions that produce data you cannot use.
Spotting that it asks two things at once and splitting it, with a balanced scale for each part.

It is double-barreled: it asks about two things at once. Someone who finds the app fast but ugly has no honest answer, and we cannot tell which part the score reflects. I would split it into two questions, each with the same balanced five-point scale from very dissatisfied to very satisfied, plus a “not sure” option.
During a test, a participant stops and asks you, “Am I doing this right?” What do you say?
How you moderate a session without steering the participant.
You stay neutral, hand the question back, and remind them that the design is being tested, not them.

I say something like, “There is no right way here. What would you do if I were not in the room?” If they seem anxious, I remind them we are testing the design, not them, and that getting stuck shows us what to fix. I only step in if they would otherwise give up, and I note exactly where that happened.
Walk me through how you turn twelve interview transcripts into findings.
How you do synthesis, the step between raw notes and a clear conclusion.
A visible method from notes to clusters to insights, with support counted and tied back to the research question.

I put each observation on its own note with the participant ID, then group notes by what they share, not by my interview questions. I name each cluster as a statement, count how many participants support it, and keep the quotes that show it best. Then I tie each theme to the decision the team has to make, so it becomes a finding with a recommendation.
Your usability test found fifteen problems. How do you present them so the team fixes the right ones first?
How you rate and present findings so they lead to action.
A severity rating based on impact and how many people hit it, the worst few first, each with evidence and a suggested fix.

I rate each problem by how badly it blocks the task and how many participants ran into it. Anything that stopped people from finishing goes to the top. I open with the three most severe, each with a short clip, the count, such as four of five participants, and a suggested fix. The rest go in a table the team can work through later.
A product manager asks you to run a study to “validate” a feature they have already decided to build. What do you do?
How you handle pressure to confirm a decision instead of testing it.
No refusal, but a reframe: agree in advance what result would change the plan, and design a study that could show it.

I ask what we would do if the study showed people do not need it. If the answer is “build it anyway,” I suggest we test how to build it well instead, with usability tests of the flow. If the decision can still change, I agree on success criteria up front, in writing, so the result counts whichever way it goes.
In interviews people said they love a feature, but analytics show almost no one uses it. How do you explain the gap?
How you handle conflict between what people say and what they do.
Trusting behavior data on usage, then finding the cause: hard to find, an unrepresentative sample, or polite answers.

What people say they like and what they do often differ, so on the question of use I trust the analytics. Then I look for why. Maybe people cannot find the feature, maybe my participants were heavy users unlike most customers, or maybe they were being polite. I would check who I recruited, then watch a few people try to find it in a quick test.
A senior leader asks for the raw session videos, with participant names, to show at a company-wide meeting. How do you respond?
Your handling of consent and participant privacy.
Using recordings only as participants agreed, and offering a safe alternative such as anonymized clips or asking for new consent.

I check the consent form first. If it said only the research and product team would see the videos, a company-wide meeting goes beyond that, and names should not travel with clips in any case. I offer a short highlight reel with names removed, or I ask participants for consent to the wider use. People speak openly to us because we keep that promise.

value-engineer.heading: Value engineer and business value consultant questions
qs: Walk me through how you build a business case, from discovery to the number the CFO sees.
How you structure the work and whose numbers go into the model.
Starts from the customer's problems and data, ties each value driver to a metric, includes all costs, and is reviewed with the customer before finance sees it.

I start with discovery: what hurts, what it costs today and who owns that budget. I pick three or four value drivers and tie each to a metric the customer already tracks. I build the baseline from their data, add our full cost including implementation and their staff time, then walk the champion through it line by line before it goes to finance.
The customer will not share their baseline numbers. How do you build the model?
How you work with incomplete data without making numbers up.
Uses benchmarks or ranges as clearly labeled placeholders and asks the customer to confirm or correct each one.

I start with ranges from published benchmarks or similar customers, clearly marked as estimates. Then I ask narrow questions they can answer, like whether it is closer to 10 or 30 hours a week. People who will not share a spreadsheet will often react to a number. Every assumption gets a source column, so finance can see which ones are theirs and which are mine.
Why should a business case not show full benefits from month one?
Whether you model the realistic timing of costs and benefits.
Costs come early while benefits ramp up with rollout and adoption. Ignoring this inflates ROI and shortens payback on paper only.

Costs land early: licenses, implementation, training and the customer's own staff time. Benefits arrive as people adopt the product, often over several months. I model a ramp, for example a quarter of the benefit in the first quarter rising to full by month nine. It lowers year-one ROI, but the payback date is one the customer can actually hit.
How do you show a CFO how solid your numbers are?
Your use of sensitivity analysis and conservative cases.
Shows which assumptions drive the result, gives a conservative and an expected case, and shows the deal still works on the cautious one.

I run a sensitivity check: move each key assumption up and down and see which ones swing the result most. Usually two or three drivers do most of the work. I show a conservative case and an expected case, and I aim for a deal that still pays back on the conservative one. Then the CFO debates two numbers, not twenty.
A CFO says, “These are your numbers, not ours.” How do you respond?
How you earn trust from a skeptical finance buyer.
Does not defend the model. Invites the CFO to change inputs, uses their own figures and cost of capital, and makes the case theirs.

I agree that it should be their numbers. I open the model, show every input with its source, and ask which ones they would change. I swap in their cost of capital and their labor rates on the spot. Once a CFO has edited the assumptions, it becomes their case, and they tend to defend it in their own approval meeting.
The champion asks you to raise the numbers so the case clears their approval bar. What do you do?
Your judgement when pressure to close meets an honest model.
Refuses to inflate, looks for missed value or a scope that truly clears the bar, and protects the champion's credibility.

I explain that an inflated case hurts them most: they own it in front of finance and again at renewal. Then I look for real value we missed, check whether a phased rollout pays back sooner, or adjust scope and price with my sales lead. If it still does not clear, I would rather know now than sell a case that fails in a year.
At renewal, the value review shows the customer got half the savings you projected. What do you do?
How you handle a shortfall honestly when the account is at stake.
Finds the cause first, shows the gap openly before the customer raises it, and brings a plan with owners and dates.

First I find out why: low adoption, a missed integration, or an assumption that was wrong. I show the customer the gap myself. Then I bring a plan, for example retraining two teams and turning on a feature they skipped, with a target and a date. If my original assumption was too high, I say so and fix it for future cases.
After a deal closes, you find your model counted the same saving twice. What do you do?
Your honesty and how you repair a mistake in your own work.
Sizes the error, tells the account team and the customer promptly with corrected figures, and adds a check so it does not recur.

I recalculate first so I know the real size of the gap. Then I tell my manager and the account lead, and we tell the champion with corrected figures before their finance team finds it. The deal may still pay back; if not, we discuss it openly. Afterward I add a check to my template: each saving must map to one budget line and be claimed once.

video-editor.heading: Video editor and producer questions
qs: What is the difference between a J-cut and an L-cut, and when would you use each?
Whether you know the basic editing grammar that makes dialogue feel smooth.
Correct definitions (audio leads in a J-cut and trails in an L-cut) plus a real reason to use each.

In a J-cut the audio of the next shot starts before its picture, so you hear someone before you see them. In an L-cut the audio of a shot carries on over the next picture. I use J-cuts to pull the viewer into a new scene and L-cuts to show a listener's reaction while the speaker keeps talking.
You're shooting at 24 frames per second. What shutter speed do you set, and why?
Your camera basics and how they shape the look of motion.
The 180-degree shutter rule: about double the frame rate, so 1/48 or 1/50. Also when and why you would break it.

I'd set 1/50, or 1/48 if the camera offers it. That's the 180-degree rule: the shutter is open for half of each frame, which gives the motion blur people read as natural. Under some lights in the US, 1/50 can flicker, so I use 1/60 there. If it's too bright I add ND filters instead of raising the shutter speed, unless I want a crisp, choppy look on purpose.
Walk me through how you offload camera cards on a shoot.
Whether you protect footage that can't be shot again.
Verified copies on at least two drives before any card is formatted, with a clear naming and logging system.

I copy each card to two separate drives with software that does checksum verification, so I know every file matches the original. I name folders by date, camera and card number, and log it. A card only gets formatted in the camera once both copies are verified. Back at the office a third copy goes offsite or to the cloud.
When do you edit with proxies, and what can go wrong with them?
How you manage heavy footage without slowing the edit or hurting the final file.
Lightweight copies for smooth editing, then a relink to the full-quality originals before color and export.

With 4K or raw footage I make lower-resolution proxy files so playback stays smooth on any machine. The risk is exporting from the proxies by mistake, which gives a soft master. Before color and the final export I switch back to the original media and check a few shots at full size. I also keep the same file names so relinking doesn't break.
What's the difference between color correction and color grading?
Your grasp of the finishing order and the tools you use to judge color.
Correction comes first and makes shots accurate and consistent. Grading adds the look on top. You judge with scopes, not just your eyes.

Correction comes first: I set exposure and white balance and match shots so a scene doesn't jump between cameras. If the footage is log, I convert it to standard color first. Grading is the creative look on top, like warmer skin or cooler shadows. I check with the waveform and vectorscope, because my eyes adjust to a bad monitor and the scopes don't.
A client wants a 9:16 vertical version of a 16:9 interview piece. How do you approach it?
Whether you can adapt one edit for social platforms without losing the story.
Reframing shot by shot, keeping text and faces clear of on-screen buttons, and burning in captions for silent viewing.

I don't just crop the center. I reframe each shot so the face or action stays in frame, and I shorten the cut because vertical viewers scroll fast. I keep titles and captions out of the areas where the app puts its buttons and text. I burn in captions, since many people watch with the sound off. Next time I'd shoot wider so there's room to reframe.
The client wants a hit pop song under their brand video. What do you tell them?
Your knowledge of music rights and how you protect the client.
That it needs a sync license for the song and a master use license for the recording, and realistic options if that doesn't fit.

I explain that buying the song or crediting the artist isn't permission. For a video we'd need a sync license from the publisher for the song and a master use license from the label for the recording. For a hit that can take weeks and cost a lot, if they agree at all. I'd ask the budget, and if it doesn't fit, pitch two or three tracks from a licensed music library with a similar feel.
In a documentary interview, you could cut two answers together so the subject seems to say something stronger. Would you?
Your ethics when editing real people's words.
Cuts can tighten an answer but must not change its meaning. Check each edit against the full transcript and raise doubts with the director.

Not if it changes what they meant. I tighten answers all the time, removing ums and repeats, and I cover the cut with B-roll so it isn't jarring. But joining two answers to make a claim they never made is putting words in their mouth. I check each edit against the full transcript, and if I'm unsure, I show the director the original take.
You get to the edit and the lav mic on the main interview has loud rustle and dropouts. What do you do?
How you solve a technical problem in the material you're given.
Check backup audio first, then repair tools, then cut choices. Tell the producer early if a re-record is needed.

First I check what else was recorded: the camera's mic or a boom track. Often the backup is clean enough for the bad sections, and I sync it and match its tone with EQ. For rustle I try repair tools on short spots. Where nothing works, I pick other answers or cover with B-roll. If a key line is lost, I tell the producer the same day so they can plan a re-record.
A video went live and the client spots a misspelled name in a lower third. How do you handle it?
How you own a mistake and fix it without making it worse.
A fast fix and replacement, honest ownership, and a new checking step so it doesn't happen again.

I'd tell the client it's my error and I'm fixing it now. I correct the title, re-export, and watch the new file through before sending. Then I'd check how to swap it: some platforms let you replace the video, others need a new upload that starts at zero views, so the client decides. After that, every name and title gets checked against a written list from the client.

video-motion.heading: Video and motion questions
qs: What shutter speed would you set when shooting at 24 frames per second, and why?
Whether you know how shutter speed shapes the way motion looks on camera.
The 180-degree rule: about 1/50 second at 24 fps for natural motion blur, plus when and why you would break it on purpose.

Around 1/50 of a second, about double the frame rate. That is the 180-degree shutter rule, and it gives the motion blur viewers read as natural. A much faster shutter makes movement look choppy, which can suit an action scene. In bright sun I add ND filters, which cut light like sunglasses, rather than raise the shutter speed.
What is the difference between a J-cut and an L-cut, and when do you use them?
Your command of basic editing technique.
Correct definitions, with the audio leading or trailing the picture, and why it makes edits feel smoother.

In a J-cut the audio of the next shot starts before its picture, so you hear someone before you see them. In an L-cut the audio of the current shot keeps going after the picture changes, like an interview answer running over cutaway footage. Both hide the cut and make the edit flow like a conversation instead of a slideshow.
A client says your logo animation looks stiff. What is the first thing you check?
Whether you understand easing and timing in motion design.
Easing first: linear keyframes look mechanical, so you shape the speed curves. Timing next, since a move that runs a few frames long also reads as stiff.

The easing. Real objects speed up and slow down, so linear keyframes look robotic. I open the graph editor, which shows speed over time, and shape the curves so the logo eases out of its start and settles into its end, maybe with a small overshoot. Then I check timing; a move a few frames too long often feels stiff too.
Why would you build an animatic before animating a two-minute explainer video?
How you use storyboarding to control time, cost and client approval.
The animatic tests timing and structure cheaply, and client sign-off on it keeps later notes about polish, not about rebuilding scenes.

An animatic is the storyboard frames cut to a scratch voiceover and music with rough timing. It shows whether the script fits two minutes and where a scene drags, before I spend days animating. Changing a sketch takes minutes; changing a finished scene takes a day. I get client sign-off on it, so later notes are about polish, not structure.
On an interview shoot, what do you do for sound besides clipping a mic on the speaker?
Whether you protect audio on set, where most fixes are cheaper than in the edit.
Constant headphone monitoring, a backup audio source, controlling background noise, and recording room tone for the editor.

I monitor on headphones the whole time, not just at the start. I run a second source, a boom mic or a backup recorder, in case the clip-on lav mic rustles on clothing. I turn off fridges and air conditioning where I can, and before we wrap I record 30 seconds of room tone so the editor can fill gaps without the background going dead.
The client wants one video for a 16:9 website player and for 9:16 vertical social feeds. How do you plan it?
How you plan for several aspect ratios from the start instead of fixing it in the edit.
Planning both formats at the storyboard stage: centered framing, room to reframe, text in safe zones, and graphics rebuilt per format.

I plan for both at the storyboard stage, not in the edit. I keep key action near the center so a vertical crop still works, and shoot at a higher resolution than delivery to leave room to reframe. Text stays inside the safe zone so app buttons and captions do not cover it. Titles and graphics I rebuild for each format instead of cropping them.
A training video needs captions. Do you burn them in or deliver a caption file?
Your grasp of open and closed captions and of accessibility.
It depends on the platform: a sidecar file for closed captions in players, burned-in open captions for muted social feeds, and always a proofread.

It depends where it plays. A sidecar file, a small SRT or VTT text file with timestamps, gives closed captions viewers can turn on or off in the player or learning platform. On social feeds, where many people watch muted, I often burn in open captions in the brand style. Either way I proofread against the audio, because auto-captions get names and terms wrong.
The client says the music drowns out the narrator. How do you fix the mix?
Your sound mixing method and whether you mix for how people will actually listen.
Dialogue set first, music ducked and EQ'd under it, checks on small speakers, and loudness measured against the delivery spec.

Dialogue comes first. I set the voice level, then bring the music under it and duck it, meaning lower it further while the narrator talks, with a small EQ cut where the voice sits. I check on laptop speakers and a phone, not just good headphones. Then I measure the mix in LUFS, the standard unit of perceived loudness, against the target in the delivery spec.
The marketing manager wants a hit pop song under the new product ad. What do you say?
Whether you understand music licensing and protect the client from legal and platform problems.
A commercial use needs a sync license for the song and a master use license for the recording; you explain the risk and offer licensed options.

I explain that an ad needs two licenses: a sync license from the publisher for the song itself and a master use license from the label for the recording. For a hit that is often slow and expensive, and an unlicensed track can get the ad muted or taken down. I offer stock music licensed for ads, or a composer, and keep the license paperwork with the project.
Two days before launch, after the cut was approved, a VP sends notes that contradict the approved version. How do you handle it?
How you manage late, conflicting feedback without losing the deadline or the client.
Sorting notes by impact, estimating time, sending the decision back to the client, starting quick fixes, and agreeing what gives on big changes.

I do not just pick a side. I list the new notes, mark which change the approved structure and which are small fixes, and estimate the time for each. I send that to my main contact and ask them to settle it with the VP. Small fixes I start right away. If the big changes go ahead, we agree on what gives: the deadline, the scope or the budget.

vip-relationship.heading: VIP and institutional relationship manager questions
qs: How do the needs of a fund differ from those of a very active individual trader?
Whether you know who you are actually serving on an institutional account.
A fund means many people and roles: traders, operations, compliance, auditors. A good answer names them and what each needs.

An active trader wants fast answers, good fee terms and someone who picks up when the market moves. A fund also needs the entity onboarded, several authorized users, API access, reports its auditors accept and clear answers on custody. So with a fund I work with traders, operations and compliance staff, not just one person.
Explain maker and taker fees and how volume tiers work.
Your grasp of the fee model your biggest clients care about most.
Maker adds liquidity, taker removes it. Tiers usually follow volume over a rolling period. Clients are never pushed to trade just to reach a tier.

A maker order rests on the book and adds liquidity. A taker order fills right away against a resting order and removes it. Most exchanges charge takers more. Tiers usually depend on volume over a rolling period, often 30 days. If a client is close to the next tier I show the numbers, but I never push extra trading just to reach it.
When would you send a client's order to the OTC desk instead of the order book?
Whether you understand market impact on large orders.
When the size is large next to the book's depth. The answer weighs the quoted spread against the slippage and information leak on the book.

When the order is large compared with the depth of the book. Selling a big block on the book would walk the price down and show the market what the client is doing. The OTC desk quotes one price for the whole size and settles it in one trade. I check the depth first and explain the trade-off: a quoted spread against the slippage.
A new fund says the API keeps rejecting their orders during busy periods. What do you do?
How you handle a technical problem for a client without dropping it on them.
Gets error codes and times, suspects rate limits, brings in API support, and follows through until it works.

First I get the exact error codes and timestamps. Rejections in busy periods are often rate limits: too many requests per second on one key. I check their limits, see whether their code retries too fast, and bring in our API support. If their volume justifies it, I ask whether a higher limit is possible. Then I follow up until fills are clean.
Walk me through onboarding a new hedge fund as a client.
Your knowledge of entity onboarding and how you keep it smooth for the client.
Covers entity documents, beneficial owners and controllers, authorized users, compliance review and account setup, with one clear checklist.

I collect the formation documents, the fund structure, the beneficial owners and the people who control it, and who may trade and withdraw. Compliance screens them and reviews the source of funds. Meanwhile I set up sub-accounts, API keys and withdrawal address whitelists. The client gets one checklist and one timeline, so nobody asks twice for the same paper.
You told a fund their withdrawal would settle the same day, and it did not. What now?
How you own a mistake you made with an important client.
Tells the client first, with confirmed facts, escalates any harm, and changes the habit that caused the error.

I call before they find out. I say what I told them, what actually happened and when the funds will arrive, based on what operations confirms, not a guess. If it caused a missed trade or a margin problem, I escalate it. Then I fix my side: I stop quoting times I have not checked against current processing.
A top client asks you whether a certain token is about to be listed. How do you answer?
Whether you protect confidential information even under pressure from a big client.
A clear no, no hints, a friendly tone, and a word to compliance if the client keeps pushing.

I say I cannot share that, and nobody on our side can, because listing decisions are confidential until they are announced. Tipping one client would be unfair to everyone else and could be treated as trading on inside information. I keep it friendly, point them to our public announcements, and tell compliance if they keep pushing.
A large client asks you to split a big withdrawal into smaller ones so it does not get flagged. What do you do?
Whether you recognize structuring and refuse to help with it.
Says no, gives no tips on thresholds, informs compliance per policy, and never tells the client whether a report was filed.

I say no, plainly. Splitting amounts to stay under reporting thresholds is called structuring, and it is a federal crime even if the money is clean. I do not coach anyone on thresholds. I tell compliance about the request as our policy requires, and I never tell the client whether a report was filed, because that is confidential.
Our platform went down during a sharp market move and a fund lost money. They want compensation. How do you handle it?
How you balance client loyalty with the firm's rules on losses.
Gathers facts, makes no promises on the call, routes the case to whoever decides, gives a timeline, and explains the outcome in writing.

I listen, then get the facts: their order IDs, times and what they expected to happen. I do not promise money on the call. I pass the case with our logs to the team that decides and tell the client when they will hear back. If our system failed, I push for a fair answer under our terms. Either way I explain the decision in writing.
A fund's due diligence team asks how they can be sure their assets are safe with us. What do you tell them?
Whether you can explain proof of reserves and custody honestly, limits included.
Explains what proof of reserves shows and does not show, and adds segregation, custody controls and independent reports instead of overselling.

Proof of reserves shows that wallets we control held certain assets at one moment, and a Merkle tree lets each client check their balance was counted. It is not a full audit and does not prove there are no hidden debts. So I also show how client assets are kept apart from company assets, our custody controls, and any independent reports we can share under NDA.

vp-engineering.heading: Director and VP of engineering questions
qs: How is leading engineering managers different from leading engineers?
Whether you understand how the job changes at the director and VP level.
You work through managers: you set goals, coach, and build systems, and you resist fixing team problems yourself.

With engineers I saw the work directly. With managers I see it through them, so my job is clear goals, coaching, and building the system: hiring, career ladders, planning. I judge success by how their teams run when I am not in the room. I resist jumping in to fix things, because that takes the learning away from the manager.
How many direct reports should an engineering manager have, and how do you decide?
Your sense of span of control and what drives it.
A working range with reasons, adjusted for seniority, team stability, on-call load and how new the manager is.

I aim for roughly six to eight engineers per manager. Fewer, and the manager tends to micromanage or code full time. More, and one-on-ones and coaching get thin. A team of seniors on stable work can be larger. A team with many new hires or heavy on-call should be smaller, and a first-time manager starts small.
How do you run skip-level meetings without undermining your managers?
How you get honest signal from the org while keeping managers in charge.
Managers know in advance, you share themes rather than names, and problems go back to the manager, except serious conduct issues.

I tell the manager before I start, and I share themes, not who said what. I ask about blockers, what people would change, and their growth. Problems I hear go back to the manager to solve. The exception is something serious like harassment: that goes to HR right away, and I say upfront I cannot keep that kind of thing confidential.
How do you keep architecture decisions consistent across teams without making every decision yourself?
How you scale technical decision-making as the org grows.
A light written process for cross-team changes, recorded decisions, senior engineers reviewing, and team autonomy inside their own area.

Changes that affect other teams start as a short design doc, and decisions are kept as architecture decision records, short notes on what we chose and why. A small group of senior engineers reviews cross-team proposals. Inside their own services, teams decide freely. I step in only to break a deadlock or when cost or risk is high.
How do you decide how much engineering time goes to technical debt versus new features?
How you turn a technical concern into a business decision.
Debt named by its cost to the business, the biggest items funded with clear outcomes, plus a standing slice for small cleanup.

I ask teams to name the debt that hurts most in terms the business feels: incidents, slow releases, onboarding time. The top items go on the roadmap with a measurable outcome, like cutting build time from 40 minutes to 10. A standing slice of each team's time covers small cleanup, so it does not need a fight every quarter.
A team wants to rewrite a core system from scratch. How do you respond?
Your judgement on one of the riskiest bets in engineering.
You probe the real problem, know rewrites run long and freeze features, and prefer an incremental migration with value along the way.

I ask what problem the rewrite solves and how we would measure it. Full rewrites usually run long while the old system still needs fixes. I push for an incremental path: route traffic through a new layer, move one piece at a time, and retire old parts as we go. If a rewrite is truly needed, I want milestones that ship value early.
The CEO asks you for a firm date on a large project six months out. What do you say?
How you handle commitments under uncertainty with senior leaders.
A range with stated confidence and risks, a firm near-term milestone, and scope as the lever if the date cannot move.

I would not give one date six months out; that is a guess dressed up as a promise. I give a range, say most likely end of Q3, Q4 at worst, and name the big unknowns. I commit firmly to a first milestone in six weeks and narrow the range as we learn. If the date is fixed by the business, we talk about what scope to cut.
Walk me through how you run promotion calibration across several managers.
Whether you can keep career decisions fair and consistent across teams.
Written cases against a career ladder, comparison across teams, active checks for bias, and specific feedback to those not promoted.

Each manager writes a case against our career ladder with concrete examples of impact. In the room we compare cases at the same level, so one manager's senior means the same as another's. I watch for bias: the loudest advocate, flashy projects, people who were on leave. Every decision gets a written reason, and anyone not promoted gets clear next steps.
A major outage hit a team you oversee, and another VP wants someone held accountable. How do you handle it?
How you protect a learning culture while still owning the failure.
You take public ownership, run a blameless review focused on the system, and track fixes to done. Blameless does not mean ignoring repeated negligence.

I own it publicly as the leader of that org. The engineer who pushed the change is not the root cause; the system that let it through is. We run a blameless postmortem: timeline, contributing factors, and actions with owners and dates. I share it with the other VP and report until the fixes ship. Blame would only teach people to hide the next mistake.
You need to reorganize your teams. How do you design the new structure and roll it out?
How you connect org design to the system you build, and how you manage change.
Structure follows product and architecture, is tested against real work, gives clear ownership, and people hear it one-on-one first.

I start from the product and architecture, because teams tend to build systems that mirror how they communicate; that is Conway's law. I draft it with my managers, test it against upcoming projects, and make sure each team owns something end to end. Affected people hear it from their manager one-on-one before any announcement, with the reasons and a date.

vp-sales.heading: Sales leader and VP of sales questions
qs: What is the difference between your pipeline and your forecast?
Whether you separate what might close from what you will stand behind.
Pipeline is the full set of open deals. The forecast is a judgement call, with clear categories and rules for what counts as commit.

The pipeline is every open opportunity with a value and a stage. The forecast is my call on what will actually close this period. I split it into commit, which I would stake my credibility on, and best case. A deal reaches commit only when we know the buyer, the decision date and the steps to signature, not just because it sits in a late stage.
How do you inspect a deal in a pipeline review?
Your method for testing whether a deal is real.
A repeatable set of questions about pain, the economic buyer, the decision process and dated next steps, used to coach as well as to forecast.

I ask the same questions every time. What problem does the buyer have, and what does it cost them? Who signs, and have we met that person? How will they decide, and against whom? What happens if they do nothing? What is the next step, with a date the buyer agreed to? If the rep cannot answer, the deal is not lost, but it is not commit.
Walk me through how you set quotas for a team of reps.
How you turn a company target into fair, reachable quotas.
A top-down target checked against bottom-up capacity, a cushion for misses, ramped quotas for new hires, and quotas most reps can reach.

I start from the company number and assign a bit more than that across reps, because some will miss. Then I check bottom-up: territory potential, each rep's history and ramp. New hires get a reduced quota for their first months. I want most of the team able to reach quota with good work. If only two of ten could, the plan is wrong, not the reps.
How would you design a comp plan for account executives?
Whether you know how pay drives sales behavior.
Few simple measures tied to company goals, accelerators that reward over-performance, clear written rules, and the cost modelled with finance.

I keep it to one or two measures a rep can recite from memory, paid on what the company values most, like new annual revenue. Accelerators above 100% keep top reps selling, and I avoid caps. Rules on clawbacks for early cancellation are written in the plan each rep signs. Finance models the total cost before we launch, so there are no surprises.
Marketing says sales ignores its leads, and sales says the leads are bad. How do you fix it?
How you align sales and marketing around one number.
Shared lead definitions, a follow-up commitment from sales, closed-loop reporting and one common revenue goal.

First we agree in writing on what a qualified lead is, with sales in the room. Then a service level: sales follows up on every qualified lead within a set time, say one business day, and records an outcome. Marketing gets the results back, so we see which sources turn into revenue. We share one pipeline target, so both teams win or lose together.
Next year's new bookings target is $12 million. How many reps do you need?
Your capacity planning: ramp, attrition and hiring time.
Math from ramped productivity, adjusted for ramp time, attrition and hiring lead time, plus a check on managers and pipeline.

If a fully ramped rep closes about $1 million a year, I need 12 ramped equivalents, but that is not 12 people. A rep hired in January with a six-month ramp delivers well under a full year. I also plan for a couple of departures and about three months to hire. So I would hire early, plan for 15 or 16 heads, and check that managers and pipeline can support them.
Your top rep is at 180% of quota but skips CRM updates and goes around the deal desk. How do you handle it?
How you hold a high performer to the same standards as everyone else.
Credit for results, a clear explanation of the cost, the same rules for everyone and follow-through if it continues.

I talk to her privately and start with what I value: her results. Then I explain the cost. Without her CRM data my forecast is wrong, and when she skips the deal desk, others learn that rules are optional. I set a clear expectation and a date. If it continues, it goes into her review like any other issue. Exceptions for stars cost me the rest of the team.
At quarter end a rep brings a big deal with an extra discount, free months and a promise of a feature not yet built. What do you do?
Whether you protect the company while still trying to win the deal.
Wanting the deal but refusing side agreements, involving finance on revenue impact, and trading discount only for real value.

I want the deal, but every term goes in the contract that legal and finance review. No side emails or side letters. A promised feature that is not built can change when we may recognize the revenue, so finance decides that, not me. On discount, I trade: more off only for a longer term, a larger order or a firm signing date. If it cannot close clean, it moves to next quarter.
Win rates dropped from 28% to 19% over two quarters. How do you find the cause?
How you diagnose a revenue problem before acting on it.
Rules out data changes first, then breaks losses down to find where and why, and talks to lost buyers before choosing a fix.

First I check the data: did we loosen what counts as a qualified opportunity, so more weak deals entered? Then I cut the drop by segment, lead source, rep, deal size and competitor, and see at which stage deals now die. I read the loss notes and call some lost buyers myself. A new competitor, a price change or one team slipping each needs a different fix.

warehouse-associate.heading: Warehouse associate questions
qs: What is the difference between FIFO and FEFO, and when do you use each?
Whether you know how stock rotation works.
FIFO ships the oldest received stock first. FEFO ships the earliest expiry date first, and it is the rule for food, medicine and anything dated.

FIFO means first in, first out: the stock that arrived first leaves first. FEFO means first expired, first out: I pick the lot with the closest expiry date, even if it arrived later. For dated goods like food or supplements, FEFO is the rule, because a newer delivery can carry an earlier date.
A truck arrives with an inbound order. What do you check before the driver leaves?
How you protect the company at the receiving dock.
Count against the bill of lading, look for damage, and write any shortage or damage on the paperwork before signing.

I count the pallets or cartons against the bill of lading and the purchase order. I look at every side for crushed corners, wet spots or torn wrap. If something is short or damaged, I write it on the bill of lading before I sign and take photos. A clean signature tells the carrier everything arrived fine.
How do you build a pallet so it arrives in one piece?
Your hands-on knowledge of loading goods for shipment.
Heavy on the bottom, no overhang, a flat top, and stretch wrap that locks the load to the pallet itself.

Heaviest and strongest cartons go on the bottom, lighter ones on top. I keep boxes inside the pallet edges, because overhang gets crushed and tips. I stack in columns for strength or interlock layers for stability, keep the top flat, and start the wrap low so it ties the load to the pallet. Then I label two sides.
Where would you put away a fast-moving item, and where would you put a heavy one?
Whether you understand slotting and safe storage.
Fast movers in easy reach near packing; heavy items on low or floor locations, never overhead.

Fast movers go in the golden zone, roughly waist to shoulder height and close to the pack stations, so pickers walk and bend less. Heavy items go on low shelves or floor locations, so nobody lifts them from overhead. Slow movers can go high or in far aisles. Then I scan the location so the system knows where it is.
Before you drive a forklift or electric pallet jack at the start of a shift, what do you check?
Whether you treat equipment checks as part of the job.
Only drive what you are trained and authorized on. Do a walk-around and function check every shift, and take a faulty truck out of service.

I only drive equipment I'm trained and authorized on. Before use I walk around it: tires, forks for cracks or bends, chains, leaks, and the battery or propane connection. Then I test the horn, brakes, steering, lights and lift controls. If anything fails, I tag it out, tell my lead and don't use it.
Your scanner sends you to a location for 6 units and the bin is empty. What do you do?
How you handle a short pick without guessing.
Check nearby and overflow locations, report the short in the system, and never substitute or skip it silently.

First I look in the bins next to it, above and below, since misplaced stock is common, and check the overflow location if there is one. If it's not there, I mark the short pick in the scanner so it triggers a count and the order can be rerouted. I don't grab a similar item. If it's a rush order, I tell my lead.
You open a carton two days after receiving and the product inside is broken, but the box looked fine. What now?
Whether you know how to handle concealed damage.
Stop, keep all the packaging, take photos and report it the same day, because carriers set short deadlines for concealed-damage claims.

That's concealed damage, so speed matters. I stop unpacking, set the carton aside with all its packaging and labels, and photograph the outer box, the inside and the broken items. I tell receiving or my supervisor the same day with the PO and tracking numbers. Carriers set short claim deadlines, and throwing the box away usually kills the claim.
You find a carton on a shelf leaking a liquid you don't recognize. Walk me through what you do.
How you respond to a possible hazardous spill.
Keep people away, don't touch or clean it unprotected, report it, and follow the safety data sheet and spill procedure.

I don't touch it or smell it. I keep people back, block the area with cones if I have them, and tell my supervisor right away. From the label we look up the safety data sheet, which says what the product is and how to clean it up. Only trained people with the right gloves and spill kit handle it. Then the stock is adjusted.
A coworker bumps a rack upright with a forklift and it is visibly bent. The rack is full. What happens next?
Your judgement when damaged storage could collapse.
Report it at once, keep people out from under it, stop using the bay, and let a qualified person decide on unloading and repair.

I tell the supervisor immediately and keep people out of that aisle. I don't add or pull anything from that bay, because a bent upright can fold under load. The area gets taped off. Someone qualified decides how to unload it safely, and the bay stays out of use until the rack is repaired or replaced.
You're behind on your pick rate and a coworker shows you how to skip a scan to go faster. What do you do?
Whether you protect accuracy when speed is pushed.
No skipped scans. You explain the cost down the line and take the rate problem to your lead instead.

I don't do it. A skipped scan means the system count is wrong, the next picker gets sent to an empty bin, and a customer may get the wrong item. If I'm behind, I tell my lead what is slowing me down, like bad slotting or a slow scanner, and ask how to fix it. Hitting the number with errors just moves the work to returns.

web-developer.heading: Web developer questions
qs: What does semantic HTML mean, and why does it matter on a real site?
Whether you know HTML as more than boxes to style.
Elements chosen for their meaning, with real gains named: keyboard and screen reader support, clearer structure for search engines, less code.

It means picking the element that says what the content is: a nav for navigation, a button for an action, headings in order. A real button can be reached with Tab and works with Enter and Space for free; a div with a click handler needs all that rebuilt by hand. Search engines and screen readers also read the structure, not the styling.
A CSS rule you wrote is not being applied. How do you find out why?
How well you understand the cascade and specificity.
Uses dev tools to find the crossed-out rule, and explains specificity and source order instead of reaching for !important.

I inspect the element in the browser's dev tools. If my rule is crossed out, a stronger one wins: an ID beats classes, classes beat element selectors, and with equal weight the later rule wins. If my rule is not listed at all, the selector does not match or the file did not load. I fix the selector rather than add !important.
When do you use Flexbox and when do you use CSS Grid?
Your judgement in choosing a layout tool.
Flexbox for items along one direction, Grid for rows and columns together, and the point that both often work on the same page.

Flexbox is for one direction: a row of menu links, or a button with an icon and a label where the content decides the sizes. Grid is for two directions: a page frame or a card gallery where rows and columns must line up. I often use Grid for the overall layout and Flexbox inside each card.
How do you serve images that look sharp on a phone and on a large monitor without wasting data?
Whether you know responsive images, often the biggest part of page weight.
srcset and sizes so the browser picks the file, modern formats, set dimensions, and lazy loading only for images below the fold.

I export each image in several widths and list them in srcset, with sizes telling the browser how wide the slot is at each screen width. The browser then picks the smallest file that still looks sharp. I use the picture element when the crop must change on mobile, and lazy loading for images below the fold, never for the main hero image.
The text on a page jumps down while it loads and people tap the wrong link. What causes this and how do you fix it?
How you handle layout shift, one of the measures of page experience.
Names the usual causes (images without size, late banners or ads, font swaps) and reserves space before the content arrives.

That is layout shift. Usually an image or embed has no width and height, so the browser gives it no space until it loads, or a banner is injected at the top. I add width and height or an aspect ratio so the space is held, give ad and cookie notice slots a fixed box, and pick a fallback font close in size to the web font.
You deployed a CSS fix, but the client still sees the old design. What is going on, and how do you stop it from happening again?
Whether you understand browser and CDN caching.
Points to the browser or CDN cache, and fixes it for good with hashed file names and the right Cache-Control headers.

The old file is cached in their browser or at the CDN. Short term, I purge the CDN and confirm with a hard reload. For good, the build puts a content hash in each file name, like main.3f9a1c.css, so new code means a new URL. Those files can be cached for a long time, and the HTML that points to them gets a short cache or none.
A client wants to edit the homepage in the CMS without calling you. How do you set that up so they cannot break the layout?
How you build a content management system for the people who will use it.
Structured fields and reusable blocks instead of one free HTML box, limited roles, a preview step and a short guide.

I model the page as blocks with fields: headline, image with alt text, button label and link. The layout lives in the template, so editors change content, not structure. Rich text allows only bold, links and lists. I add length hints, a preview before publishing, an editor role without access to settings, and a one-page guide with screenshots.
You update a plugin on a client's CMS site and the checkout page goes blank. What do you do?
How you handle a broken live site and prevent the next one.
Restores service first by rolling back, then finds the cause on a staging copy, and changes the update process.

First I get the site working: roll the plugin back to its last version or restore the backup taken before the update. Then I read the error log on a staging copy; often it is a conflict with another plugin or the server's PHP version. From then on updates go to staging first, with a fresh backup and a quick test of checkout and forms before going live.
We are moving the site to a new CMS and the URLs will change. How do you keep the search traffic?
Whether you can plan a migration without losing visitors or rankings.
A full map of old to new URLs with 301 redirects to matching pages, no redirect chains, updated sitemap and links, and checks after launch.

Before launch I crawl the old site and list the pages that get traffic or outside links. Each old URL gets a 301 permanent redirect to its closest new page, not everything to the homepage. I update internal links and the XML sitemap and keep titles and content close. After launch I watch the 404 errors and search reports for weeks and fix the gaps.
Marketing wants to add a chat widget, a heatmap tool and two more tracking scripts this week. How do you respond?
Your judgement in weighing business requests against speed and privacy.
Not a flat no: measures the cost, loads scripts late, checks consent rules, and removes old tags no one uses.

I would not just say no. I test the page with and without each script and show the cost in load time. Scripts load asynchronously or after the page is usable, the chat loads when someone clicks the chat button, and tracking waits for consent where our privacy rules require it. I also ask which existing tags nobody reads anymore; usually a couple can go.

welder.heading: Welder questions
qs: When do you choose stick, MIG or TIG welding?
Whether you know the main processes and where each one fits.
Matches the process to the conditions: stick for outdoors and dirty steel, MIG for fast shop work, TIG for control on thin or special metals.

Stick is my choice outside or on rusty structural steel, because the flux shields the weld and the wind does not blow that protection away. MIG is fast for long production welds in the shop, where the shielding gas stays put. TIG is slower but gives the most control, so I use it on thin sheet, stainless, aluminum and pipe root passes.
On a welding symbol, what does it mean when the weld symbol sits below the reference line?
Whether you can read a welding symbol on a drawing correctly.
Below the line is the arrow side, above is the other side, and the candidate knows where size, length and process notes go.

Below the line means arrow side: I weld on the side of the joint the arrow points to. Above the line means the other side, and symbols on both sides mean weld both. Then I read the rest: the size to the left of the symbol, the length and spacing to the right, and the tail for the process or spec.
What is a 6G pipe test, and why is it considered hard?
Your understanding of welder qualification positions.
The pipe is fixed at a 45 degree angle and cannot be turned, so one joint covers every position; passing usually qualifies you for all positions.

In 6G the pipe is fixed with its axis tilted at 45 degrees and I am not allowed to rotate it. Going around one joint, I weld overhead, vertical and flat, and I keep changing my body and rod angle as I go. That is why passing it usually qualifies a welder for all positions within the limits the code sets.
What changes when you switch from welding steel to welding aluminum?
Whether you know how aluminum behaves differently under the arc.
Mentions the oxide layer and how to clean it, AC for TIG, fast heat loss, and that aluminum gives no color warning before it melts.

Aluminum has a tough oxide skin that melts far hotter than the metal under it, so I clean with a stainless brush used only for aluminum and TIG weld on AC, which breaks up the oxide. It pulls heat away fast, so I start hot and back off as it warms. It also does not glow before it melts, so I watch the puddle, not the color.
Your MIG welds suddenly show porosity. Where do you look?
How you troubleshoot a common weld defect step by step.
A logical order: gas supply and drafts, gun and nozzle, clean base metal, then technique, instead of just turning up the machine.

I check the gas first: is the cylinder empty, is the flow set right, is a door open or a fan blowing across the bench. Then the gun: spatter in the nozzle, or a loose or cracked fitting letting air in. Then the metal: oil, paint, rust or moisture on the joint. Last, my technique: too long a wire stickout or too steep a gun angle.
Why do low-hydrogen rods like 7018 go in a rod oven, and what do you do with ones that were left out?
Whether you understand moisture, hydrogen and cracking in stick welding.
Moisture in the coating adds hydrogen to the weld, which can cause delayed cracks; exposed rods are reconditioned as the procedure allows or scrapped.

The coating soaks up moisture from the air, and that water puts hydrogen into the weld, which can cause cracks hours later. So I keep them in the oven and take out only what I will use soon. If rods sat out longer than the procedure allows, I set them aside to be re-baked as the procedure says or thrown out. I never weld code work with them.
You need to weld a bracket in a room with cardboard boxes and a wooden pallet nearby. What do you do before you strike an arc?
How you prevent fires during hot work.
Permit if required, combustibles moved or covered, openings checked for sparks, and a fire watch that stays after the welding ends.

I get the hot work permit if the site uses one. I move what can burn well away and cover what cannot move with fire-resistant blankets. I check for gaps in floors and walls where sparks can fall through. A fire watch with an extinguisher stands by during the work and stays afterward, because smoldering fires often start after the welder leaves.
You are welding a long fillet along thin plate and it keeps pulling out of line. How do you control the distortion?
Your practical methods for controlling heat and warping.
Several methods: clamping or fixtures, no oversized welds, short or backstep sequences, balanced welding, and presetting parts.

I tack it well and clamp it to a fixture or a stiff bar. I keep the weld no bigger than the drawing asks, since extra metal means extra pull. I break the weld into short sections, skip around or backstep, and balance welds on both sides so they pull against each other. If it still moves, I preset the parts slightly the other way.
The foreman tells you to skip the preheat the procedure calls for because the job is late. What do you do?
Whether you hold to the welding procedure under schedule pressure.
Refuses politely, explains why preheat matters, offers a faster way to do it right, and sends any change to whoever owns the procedure.

I would not skip it. Preheat slows the cooling so thick or high-carbon steel does not get hard and crack, and that crack can show up after inspection. I would explain that, check the temperature quickly with a temperature crayon, and offer to heat the next joint while I finish this one. Any change to the procedure goes through the welding engineer or inspector in writing.
Your root pass fails X-ray for lack of fusion. What likely caused it, and how do you repair it?
How you handle a rejected weld, from cause to repair.
Knows what lack of fusion is and its usual causes, and repairs by grinding out, rewelding to the repair procedure and re-testing.

Lack of fusion means the weld metal lay against the side wall or root without melting into it. Usual causes are amperage too low, travel too fast, a bad angle or a root gap too tight. I would have the spot marked, grind it out until the defect is gone, check the groove, reweld per the repair procedure and get it X-rayed again. Then I fix my settings so it does not repeat.

workday.heading: Workday specialist questions
qs: What is a supervisory organization in Workday, and why does it matter so much?
Whether you understand the structure most of Workday is built on.
It groups workers under a manager, and it drives approvals, role-based security and reporting.

A supervisory organization is the reporting structure: a manager and the workers and positions under them. Roles like manager or HR partner are assigned on it, so it decides who approves a hire or a pay change and who can see whose data. If the sup orgs are messy, routing and security break with them.
What is the difference between a constrained and an unconstrained security group?
Your grasp of how Workday decides who sees which records.
Constrained limits access to the orgs or people the user is tied to. Unconstrained gives access to every record the domain covers.

A constrained group gives access only within a context. For example, an HR partner sees workers in the supervisory orgs she supports. An unconstrained group sees all the data the domain covers, across the company. I default to constrained and keep unconstrained for small central teams like the HRIS group.
You changed a domain security policy in the sandbox and nothing happened. What did you forget?
Whether you have actually made security changes, not just read about them.
Security policy changes stay pending until someone runs Activate Pending Security Policy Changes, with a comment.

Probably the activation. Edits to domain or business process security policies sit as pending until I run Activate Pending Security Policy Changes and add a comment. I always write what changed and the ticket number in that comment, because it shows in the audit trail and makes it easier to go back to an earlier version.
A manager says she cannot see the compensation of a new team member. How do you troubleshoot it?
How you work through a security problem step by step.
Check whether the worker is in her org yet, which domain secures the data, and whether her role grants that domain.

First I confirm the worker is actually in her supervisory org. If the hire or move is still in process, that alone explains it. Then I run View Security for Securable Item to find the domain, and check her security groups to see whether the manager role grants it. Often the role assignment simply has not happened yet.
A hire was entered with the wrong start date and payroll has not run yet. Do you correct it or rescind it?
Whether you know the difference between correcting and rescinding a business process.
Correct changes data on a completed event; rescind undoes the whole event. Pick the lighter fix and check what depends on it.

If only the date is wrong, I correct the hire event. It keeps everything else and leaves an audit trail. Rescind removes the hire entirely, and later events on that worker may need to be undone first. Either way, I check benefits and payroll dates afterward and tell payroll what changed.
Walk me through loading 500 job changes with an EIB.
Your hands-on method for mass data loads.
Template from the right web service, clean data, a test load in the sandbox, error review, then production with a check after.

I create an inbound EIB for the Change Job web service, generate the spreadsheet template and fill it from the source data. I load it in the sandbox first, read every error in the background process, then fix and reload until it is clean. In production I start with a small batch and spot-check workers with a report.
A custom report times out when run for the whole company. What do you look at?
Whether you can build reports that work at scale.
The data source, where the filters sit, heavy calculated fields and long chains of related objects.

I start with the data source. An indexed one, or one with prompts that narrow the population, is far faster than all workers filtered afterward. Then I look at calculated fields evaluated on every row and long chains of related business objects. Often I move a filter to the data source level or split the report in two.
Workday is about to deliver its next major release. How do you prepare?
How you manage the twice-yearly release without surprises.
Read the release notes, test key processes and integrations in the preview tenant, decide on opt-in features, and tell users.

I read the release notes and sort changes into automatic and opt-in. In the preview tenant I run our regression list: hires, terminations, comp changes, key reports and every integration that touches payroll or benefits. I raise issues early, decide which new features to turn on, and send users a short note on what will look different.
An HR director asks you to give a recruiter unconstrained access to all worker data today, to speed up a project. What do you do?
Your judgement on access requests and data privacy.
Find the real need, offer the least access that covers it, and get approval through the normal process, on record.

I would ask what the recruiter actually needs to see. Usually it is a few fields for certain orgs, which a constrained group or a shared report covers. If broader access is truly needed, it goes through our access request with approval and an end date, and I flag it for the next access review. Pay and personal data are not opened up on a phone call.
The nightly benefits integration to a carrier failed and enrollments are due. Walk me through what you do.
How you handle a production failure that affects employees and a vendor.
Read the error, find out whether anything was sent, fix the cause, rerun safely, and keep the vendor and HR informed.

I open the integration event and read the messages and any error file. I check whether a partial file reached the carrier, because a blind rerun could duplicate records. Then I fix the cause, often one worker's bad data or an expired credential, rerun for the affected window, confirm with the carrier that it loaded, and tell benefits what happened.

workplace.heading: Office and workplace questions
qs: What do you check on a daily or weekly walk-through of the office?
Whether you know the routine that catches problems before they reach people.
A set route covering exits, safety gear, kitchens, restrooms, meeting rooms and supplies, with issues logged and followed up.

Every morning I walk the floor: exit routes clear, exit signs lit, fire extinguishers in place, no cables across walkways. I check the kitchen, restrooms and meeting rooms, and note low supplies. Anything for the landlord or a vendor goes into a ticket that day, so I can show when it was reported and when it was fixed.
A visitor arrives without an appointment and asks to go straight up to see an employee. What do you do?
How you balance a friendly front desk with security.
Polite but firm: sign-in, a call to the host, and a wait in reception. No access without the host confirming.

I greet them, ask who they are visiting and sign them in. I call the employee and let them decide; the visitor waits in reception until the host comes down. I do not say whether the person is in or where they sit. If the host is unknown or the visitor insists, I keep them in the lobby and bring in my manager or building security.
What goes into an emergency plan for an office, and how do you make sure it works?
Your grasp of evacuation and of accounting for everyone on site.
Alerts, routes, an assembly point, floor wardens, a headcount that includes visitors, help for those who need it, and drills with a debrief.

It covers how people are alerted, exit routes from every area, an assembly point away from the building, and floor wardens who sweep their area. Headcount uses the day's attendance and the visitor log, so guests are counted too. I plan for people who need help to evacuate. We drill, time it and fix what went wrong, like a door blocked by boxes.
Half the team says the office is too cold and the other half says it is too warm. How do you handle it?
Your judgement on a complaint with no single right answer.
Rule out a fault first, use real readings, adjust within building rules, and offer practical fixes instead of thermostat fights.

First I check it is not a fault: I log temperatures at a few desks over a week and ask the building engineer to check the zones and vents. If the system works, the difference is often seating, like desks under a supply vent. I move a few seats, ask about adjusting the airflow, and set one agreed temperature range so it is not changed all day.
Water is dripping through a ceiling tile above a row of desks. Walk me through the next hour.
How you handle a facilities emergency in the right order.
People and electrics safe first, then contain, report to the building, document, and follow through on drying and repairs.

I move people away from the drip and any wet power strips; if water is near electrics, I ask building engineering to cut that circuit. I put down buckets and cover equipment. I call the property manager, since the source is often above our space. I take timed photos for the insurance claim, then follow up on drying and mold checks before new tiles go in.
How do you manage a cleaning or maintenance vendor who keeps missing things?
How you manage a supplier against what the contract says.
The scope of work as the reference, documented misses, a direct talk, a fix plan, and contract remedies or new quotes if nothing changes.

I go back to the scope of work, which says what gets done and how often. I log misses with dates and photos for two weeks, then meet the account manager with the list, not complaints in general. We agree on fixes and a check date. If the misses keep coming, I use the contract terms, such as credits, and start getting quotes from other vendors.
A contractor shows up to rewire a meeting room, and you have no certificate of insurance on file. What do you do?
Whether you protect the company before outside workers start on site.
No work until proof of coverage arrives, the building's contractor rules are followed, and the gap in the process gets fixed.

They do not start yet. I ask their office to email the certificate showing general liability and workers' comp coverage, listing us and the landlord as the lease requires. Most buildings also need the contractor approved by building management first. Then I fix why it slipped: every job request now needs the certificate before I confirm a date.
An employee trips over a cable and hurts her wrist. What do you do, and what changes afterward?
How you handle an injury and prevent the next one.
Care first, a written report the same day, HR involved for workers' comp and injury records, and the hazard removed.

First she gets first aid or medical care, and I call 911 if it looks serious. I write down what happened, when and where, with photos and witness names, the same day. HR handles workers' comp and checks if it must be recorded on the OSHA injury log. Then I fix the cause: the cable goes in a floor cover, and I check other rooms for the same problem.
You are moving 60 people to a new floor over one weekend. Walk me through your plan.
Whether you can plan and run an office move from start to finish.
A timeline worked back from the move date, a seating plan, IT and building coordination, labeled crates, a move-day checklist and Monday support.

I work back from the date. Eight weeks out: seating plan agreed with managers, movers quoted, elevator and loading dock booked with the building. IT plans network, phones and printers. Each person gets labeled crates keyed to their new desk number. On Saturday I check off every crate. Monday I walk the floor early with IT so problems are fixed before people log in.
